analysis.label: Player fails to capture an opponent's completely undefended bishop on g4 or g5 with their queen in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 95% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), and 95% of best moves are captures, while only 3% of played moves are captures — confirming the player consistently misses a free capture. All 12 top boards reveal the identical geometric pattern: the opponent's bishop has ventured to g4 or g5 completely undefended in the opening, and the player's queen has a direct, unobstructed capture (Qxg4 or Qxg5) that wins a full piece for nothing. Instead, the player makes quiet developing or pawn moves (f3, Be2, Nc3, d5, etc.). The 41% own-hang rate (median 3.0) reflects cases where the ignored bishop on g4/g5 subsequently wins the player's own queen via discovered or diagonal attacks.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a completely free piece. The bishop on g4/g5 is undefended and the queen can take it immediately with no tactical complications. By playing quiet moves instead, the player throws away a full piece of advantage (~3 pawns), and in many cases the ignored bishop then threatens or wins the player's own queen (explaining the cp_loss averaging 616).

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting Queen (or Rook) capture with check that leaves the capturing piece en prise after the king moves, missing a far stronger alternative.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player plays a flashy capture-with-check (92% of moves are captures; all 12 top examples end in '+') that hangs their own major piece (91% leave own piece hanging, median value 9 = Queen; piece class distribution is 75 major pieces out of 80). The best move also frequently delivers check (59%) but with a different piece (knight, bishop, or rook), winning material worth a median of 91 centipawns via SEE — often leading to mate or winning the opponent's queen. The average cp_loss is 1838, reflecting positions where mate-in-few was missed in favor of a superficially attractive but self-destructive queen grab.
analysis.why_bad: After the greedy capture-check (e.g., Qxh6+, Qxe8+, Qxf4+), the opponent's king simply sidesteps, and the capturing Queen (or Rook) is left unprotected on the capture square where it can be recaptured for free. The player wins a pawn or minor piece but loses their Queen. Meanwhile, the correct move (often a discovered check or check with a minor piece/rook) would have led to checkmate or won decisive material by exploiting the exposed enemy king with a forcing sequence.

analysis.label: Player grabs material with a tempting capture instead of playing a winning check (often checkmate) that would have won decisively more.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a sharp pattern: the player's move is a capture 94% of the time, but the best move is a check 78% of the time that wins massive material (81% win material, median value 91 = queen-equivalent). The greedy capture leaves the player's own major piece hanging 85% of the time (median value 8, with 63 of 76 hung pieces being majors—rooks or queens). The player is seduced by an immediate material grab while overlooking a forcing check that either delivers checkmate outright (positions 3, 7, 10, 12) or wins a queen via a discovered/follow-up attack. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating a very specific tactical geometry where a flashy capture coexists with a lethal check.
analysis.why_bad: The captures fail because they ignore a forcing check that either mates immediately or wins far more material. After the greedy capture, the opponent gets a tempo (since no check was given) to exploit the player's now-hanging major piece, often recapturing it or launching their own counterattack. The average cp_loss of ~4900 reflects that many of these are missed checkmates or missed queen wins.

analysis.label: The player promotes a pawn to a queen that is immediately capturable, when a non-promotion move (positional or tactical) was far superior.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., a queen), while the best move wins material only 53% of the time (median 3.0) and is a capture 56% of the time. The 'major' piece class dominates the hung-piece distribution (17 out of 23 cases). Across the top 12 boards, 8 of 12 moves played are pawn promotions (a8=Q+, b8=Q+, b8=Q, b1=Q, a1=Q, f8=Q+, c8=Q+, c8=Q) that create a new queen which is immediately captured. The best moves were instead quiet king maneuvers (Kd5, Kc5, Kxf4), bishop captures (Bxe2, Bxd4, Bxh5, Bc6, Bxf3), or knight tactics (Nxc4, Nxd5+) that maintained or increased the advantage without giving away material.
analysis.why_bad: The promoted queen lands on a square controlled by an enemy piece (bishop, knight, or rook), so it is immediately captured for free or with a large material gain. The player fixates on the 'obvious' promotion rather than recognizing the new queen has no safe square, whereas a preparatory or alternative move preserves or converts the winning advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a materialistic capture (usually taking a pawn) instead of advancing or supporting their own passed pawn, leaving an own pawn hanging in the process.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 75% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being overwhelmingly a pawn (33 pawns out of 36 hung pieces). Meanwhile, 48% of the played moves are themselves captures, indicating the player is greedily taking enemy material. The best move wins material in 56% of cases (median 1.0), but crucially best moves are rarely captures themselves (only 6%), suggesting the correct approach is usually a quiet move—typically advancing or supporting one's own passed pawn. The positions are predominantly endgames (10/12) where passed pawn advancement is decisive.
analysis.why_bad: In these endgame positions, the player's own passed pawn (or key structural pawn) is the winning trump. By capturing an enemy pawn instead of advancing/supporting their own passer (e.g., c3, f2, b5, a4), the player removes their piece from a defensive/supportive role, leaving their critical pawn undefended and capturable. The enemy pawn taken is usually less valuable strategically than the passed pawn that gets hung, often costing hundreds of centipawns or the entire game advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple winning capture of an undefended or under-defended enemy piece, playing a quiet non-capturing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly confirms a 'missed winning capture' pattern: 88% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. roughly a rook or queen), and 96% of the time the best move is a capture. Yet the player's move was a capture only 9% of the time, meaning they almost always played a quiet, unrelated move. The 38% own-hang rate is secondary noise rather than the primary mistake. Across the top boards, we see best moves like Nxd8, Nxc2, Bxf8, Bxh4, Kxf3, Kxc5, bxc2, and Bxe6+ — all straightforward captures of high-value enemy pieces that are undefended or inadequately protected. The average centipawn loss of 1281 reflects how catastrophic it is to overlook a free major/minor piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player completely overlooks a high-value enemy piece (typically a rook or queen, median SEE value 5.0) that can be captured immediately for free or near-free. Instead of taking the hanging piece, the player makes an irrelevant quiet move (king move, pawn push, piece relocation), throwing away a decisive material advantage and often converting a winning position into an equal or lost one.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player gives a rook check that leaves the rook en prise after the king steps away.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 54% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece being a major piece (rook) in 69 out of 93 hanging cases (74%). Meanwhile, only 12% of best moves are checks, showing the played check was usually unnecessary. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top boards), where the player gives an impulsive rook check instead of making a constructive move like capturing material (best move wins material 52%, median 1.0 pawn) or improving piece placement. The average cp_loss of 1099 reflects how catastrophic these moves are — often converting a won or drawn position into a lost one.
analysis.why_bad: The rook check looks active but after the opponent's king simply steps to a safe square, the rook is left undefended on an exposed square with no escape. The player prioritized giving check ('patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check') over productive moves like capturing hanging material, promoting pawns, or repositioning the rook to a safe active square. The rook is often lost outright or trapped.

analysis.label: A greedy capture (pawn or piece take) that leaves the player's own queen undefended and en prise to an opponent's piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a tempting capture (93% of moves are captures) but in doing so exposes their own queen to attack — 100% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging with a median value of 6.0 (queen). The captures typically remove a defender of the queen, move a piece that was shielding the queen, or open a line (file/diagonal) directly to the queen. Meanwhile, the best move (often a quiet prophylactic like g4, f3, Bf2, or a queen retreat) would have maintained material balance or even won material (63% of best moves win material, median 2.0). The feature activates almost exclusively in openings or early middlegames where queens are centrally placed and vulnerable to discovered attacks along diagonals.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they prioritize a small material gain (a pawn or minor exchange) while catastrophically overlooking that the capture opens a line or removes a defender, allowing the opponent to win the player's queen outright. The net material loss (typically losing a queen for a pawn or minor piece) vastly outweighs what was captured, resulting in the observed average cp_loss of ~240.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture the opponent's en-prise queen (median value 6.0), often with a minor piece or rook, and typically leaves their own piece hanging instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 86% of the top-500 activating positions the best move wins material (median value 6.0, corresponding to a queen), and 99% of best moves are captures. Examining the top 12 boards confirms that in nearly every case (11/12), the opponent's queen sits on a square directly capturable by a bishop, knight, or rook (Bxd8, Nxd8, Bxd3, Nxd4, Nxb6, Bxd7, Nxd1, Nxd2, Bxd8 etc.). Instead of taking the queen, the player makes a quiet move (62% non-captures) — usually repositioning their own queen — and 73% of the time this move additionally leaves one of their own pieces hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minors at 68 instances). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating a rare but catastrophic oversight.
analysis.why_bad: The player overlooks that their piece (typically a minor piece or rook) directly attacks the opponent's queen, which is undefended or insufficiently protected. By playing a different move — often a queen relocation — they forfeit winning the opponent's most valuable piece (≈9 points net) and simultaneously expose one of their own minor pieces to capture, compounding the loss from roughly +5 to a swing of 400-800 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player misses a g-pawn (or f-pawn) advance that traps an enemy bishop stranded on the h-file or g5.
analysis.description: In 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), yet that best move is a capture only 8% of the time and never a check (0%). The winning idea is almost always a pawn advance (g4 trapping a Black bishop on h5, g5 trapping a White bishop on h4, or f6 trapping a bishop on g5). Instead, the player's move is a quiet developing move only 13% of the time a capture. In 43% of cases (median hung value 3.0), the alternative move also leaves the player's own piece en prise, compounding the error. The feature fires on Italian Game and related openings where one side has aggressively posted a bishop on the rim (h5/h4/g5) and the opponent fails to punish it with the simple pawn thrust.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Qe2, Bg5, Be3, Bg4, Bb5+, etc.) are routine developing or centralizing moves that completely ignore a concrete pawn advance trapping the opponent's exposed bishop. Because the bishop has no safe retreat square once the pawn advances, missing the move throws away a clean piece. In several cases the quiet alternative also hangs the player's own queen or minor piece, turning a winning position into a losing one.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move (usually a king move) instead of resolving critical pawn tension with an essential pawn capture in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 87% of cases, yet these captures win 0 material (SEE=0 in all top-12 positions), indicating pawn-takes-pawn exchanges. Meanwhile, the player's move left their own piece hanging 56% of the time (median value 1.0), with pawns dominating the hung-piece distribution (64 pawns vs 8 minors vs 3 majors). Only 12% of played moves were captures. The pattern is strikingly consistent: in endgame pawn-tension positions, the player declines the critical pxp capture and plays a quiet king move or pawn advance instead, leaving their own pawn en prise to the opponent's recapture on the next turn.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn or minor-piece endgames, pawn tension must often be resolved at the precise moment. By playing a king move instead of the critical pawn capture, the player allows the opponent to capture first, gaining a structural or material advantage (often a passed pawn, tempo, or outright pawn loss). The opponent captures the hanging pawn under more favorable circumstances, frequently leading to catastrophic positional deterioration (average cp_loss of 1086).

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop move to b4 or b5 (or capture on those squares) that wins material, instead playing a passive developing or pawn move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 56% of the top 500 positions (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while the player's move was only a capture 11% of the time—indicating a consistently missed winning opportunity. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is specifically a bishop move to or capturing on b4/b5 (Bb5, Bxb5, Bb4, Bxb4, or Bc4) that either pins a knight to an uncastled king, captures a hanging b-pawn, or exploits a tactical weakness on the b-file. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (7/12) with both kings in the center, the classic scenario for Bb5/Bb4 pins. The 35% own-hang rate (median 2.0, mostly pawns/minors) reflects that instead of playing the winning bishop move, the player sometimes plays a pawn push (like b4 or e4) that leaves their own material loose.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity—a bishop move to b4 or b5 that wins material (typically via a pin against an uncastled king or by capturing an undefended b-pawn). Instead, the player makes a slow positional or developmental move (b4, Bb3, Bd3, c3, Rb1, f5, etc.) that squanders a significant material advantage and often creates its own weaknesses.

analysis.label: Player ignores a straightforward material-winning capture (usually of a minor piece or better) and instead plays a quiet positional move that frequently also leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this pattern: 84% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 80% of best moves are simple captures. However, only 23% of the actually-played moves are captures—the player overwhelmingly chooses quiet, non-tactical moves instead. Compounding the error, 68% of the played moves also leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed across minors (138), majors (119), and pawns (85). The boards confirm this: in nearly every case, a simple recapture or take of an inadequately defended enemy piece (bxc6, Rxe7, bxc4, Rxf4, Bxe3, Qxf6, Bxe5, Bxb2) is available, but the player instead makes an 'active' quiet move (Nd3, Ne6, Bc4, Nb5, Bd2, etc.) that both forfeits the winning capture and often creates a new tactical vulnerability.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity—a free or winning capture of an enemy piece—in favor of a positional continuation that the position does not require. By declining the capture, the player forfeits material worth roughly a minor piece; worse, the 'active' quiet move often places or leaves their own piece on an undefended square, compounding the mistake into a double material swing. The average centipawn loss of 1018 reflects this catastrophic combination of missed gain plus new vulnerability.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own piece (typically a major piece) undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 91% of the time the player's move left their own piece en prise, with a median hung value of 5.0 (rook-equivalent). The piece class distribution skews heavily toward major pieces (82 major vs. 26 minor and 36 pawns out of hung instances). Only 30% of the played moves were captures, meaning most were quiet repositioning moves that inadvertently abandoned defense of a key piece. The best move won material in 58% of cases (median 3.0), suggesting many positions also had tactical opportunities the player ignored while simultaneously blundering their own material. The enormous average cp_loss of 1825 reflects the catastrophic nature of leaving queens and rooks hanging.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player either moves a piece that was defending a more valuable piece (e.g., a bishop leaving a queen or rook unguarded), moves to a square where the piece itself is immediately capturable, or makes a greedy/irrelevant move while their own major piece is already under attack. The result is an immediate material loss—often a queen (value 9) or rook (value 5)—that typically decides the game.

analysis.label: The player moves a rook away from its critical duty of preventing an advanced passed pawn from promoting, leaving the rook lost after the pawn queens.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 62% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0 = rook), with major pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (112 of 170). In nearly every top-activating position, the opponent has a passed pawn one square from promotion that is being restrained or blockaded by the player's rook. The player makes a tempting capture elsewhere (33% capture rate) or an unrelated move, abandoning the anti-promotion duty. The best move (a capture only 46% of the time, often a quiet king move or the rook addressing the pawn) maintains the blockade. The 54% 'best wins material' stat reflects positions where the best move also captures something while maintaining promotion defense.
analysis.why_bad: By abandoning the blockade or restraint of a pawn one square from promotion, the player allows an immediate queen creation. The new queen then captures the now-undefended rook (explaining the consistent 'own hung: 5 (R)' across positions), resulting in catastrophic material loss — often checkmate — as shown by the average cp_loss of 5472 and numerous '#' evaluations in the top boards.

analysis.label: Player avoids a necessary queen exchange (or major-piece trade), leaving own pieces vulnerable to the opponent's active queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 99% of best moves are captures (almost all queen-takes-queen exchanges with median SEE value 0, meaning equal trades), yet only 12% of played moves were captures—the player systematically declines the exchange. As a consequence, 61% of the time the player's quiet move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors: 96, pawns: 70, minors: 31), because the opponent's queen remains active on the board and can exploit undefended material. The best move wins material only 13% of the time (confirming these are equal trades, not free captures). The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, targeting the specific scenario where a queen trade is the critical defensive or simplifying resource.
analysis.why_bad: By refusing the queen trade, the player keeps the opponent's powerful queen active in positions where it dominates (open files, exposed kings, piece pressure). The opponent's queen then exploits the situation—either delivering forced mate (several positions show cp_loss of 9000+, i.e., mate-in-N) or winning hanging material that was previously protected only by the threat of the queen exchange itself. The queen trade would have defused the attack or simplified into a survivable endgame.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player missed a critical pawn push that wins material, instead playing a passive king or piece move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 69% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), yet the player's move was a capture only 10% of the time. Crucially, the best move is a capture only 9% of the time and a check only 4%, meaning the material is won via a pawn advance rather than a direct take. Examining all 12 top-activating positions confirms that every single best move is a pawn push (b4, b5, f6, f4, h4, g4, h3, h4, a5, a5, f5, b4) — typically a pawn break attacking an enemy pawn or piece that cannot adequately be defended. The played moves are overwhelmingly passive king relocations (Kb7, Ka5, Kb3, Kg2, Kg5) or aimless piece moves (Nd6, Ra7, Ne6, Re7), or the wrong pawn advance (e6, a4). The secondary 29% own-hang rate (mostly pawns: 111/146) reflects that the passive moves occasionally also leave a pawn undefended. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (10/12 positions).
analysis.why_bad: These passive king or piece moves fail because they ignore a concrete pawn advance (break or push) that immediately wins material — typically attacking an enemy pawn or piece that lacks adequate defense in the simplified endgame position. By playing aimlessly, the player loses the window for the tactical pawn thrust and often allows the opponent to consolidate or advance their own counterplay.

analysis.label: Player makes a developing or active-looking move while leaving their own piece (usually queen) en prise to an existing or newly-created threat in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 76% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with major pieces (queens/rooks) accounting for 8 of 13 classified cases. Only 12% of positions involve the best move winning material, confirming this is a 'hung own piece' pattern rather than a missed capture. The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase (11/12 top boards) with both kings in the center. The typical scenario is that an enemy piece (often a knight on b4/b5) is directly attacking the player's queen, and instead of retreating or addressing the threat, the player makes a tempting developing move (Nf6, Nc3), an aggressive check (Qb4+, Qa4+), or moves the queen to an attacked square (Qc2, Qc5). The best moves in these positions are almost always quiet retreats or defensive consolidations (Qd8, Qd1, Qb3, Bf5).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical threat to the player's own piece—most commonly the queen. The player prioritizes development, activity, or checks over piece safety, losing significant material (average cp_loss 363). A knight fork, a direct attack, or simple capture is available to the opponent on the next move, winning the undefended piece outright.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a passive or wrong-direction king move instead of a concrete winning action (pawn advance, capture, or correctly-directed king move).
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a passive or misdirected king move when a concrete, urgent action was required. The SEE aggregate shows that 58% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, reflecting pawn promotion sequences), 28% of best moves are checks (often pawn advances with check like g5+ or cxd5+), and 22% are captures. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet king moves (11/12 top activations are king moves), while the best moves include pawn advances toward promotion, king captures of hanging pawns, and correctly-directed king moves toward critical squares. Only 18% of played moves were captures and just 26% hung own material (median 1.0, i.e., a pawn), confirming the mistake is not about hanging pieces but about choosing an aimless king move over the decisive concrete action.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves fail because endgames are decided by tempi and pawn races. Moving the king in the wrong direction or making a passive king move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent's passed pawns to advance, failing to capture vulnerable enemy pawns (Kxd4, Kxe5), missing pawn breaks that create unstoppable promotion threats (g5+, cxd5+, g3, h5), or walking away from the critical squares where the king is needed to support or stop passed pawns.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player captures material (often with check) but leaves the capturing piece itself undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player hung their own piece: 86% of moves left an own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (28 major vs 6 minor). The player's move was itself a capture 67% of the time, while the best move was a capture only 12% and a check 0% of the time. This means the best moves were overwhelmingly quiet (typically king repositioning moves like Ke4, Kg3, Kd5, Ka7), not tactical captures. The player chose greedy captures—usually rook takes with check (Rxc6+, Rxc5+, Rxb5+, Rxb7+, Rxf6+)—that win a pawn or minor piece but leave the rook stranded on an undefended square where it is immediately recaptured.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece (usually a rook) lands on a square where it has no protection and can be immediately won back by the opponent, often netting the opponent a full exchange or more. The check gives a false sense of initiative—after the king moves, the rook is simply lost. The quiet king moves recommended as best preserve the piece and maintain a positional advantage worth more than the captured material.

analysis.label: Player ignores a mutual bishop-vs-bishop tension (Bxe7 or Bxe2 needed), leaving their own bishop hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 72% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a bishop), with the hung-piece distribution overwhelmingly minor pieces (104 minor vs 16 pawns vs 5 major). The best move is a capture in 99% of cases, always either Bxe7 or Bxe2 — a bishop exchange that 'wins 0' (equal trade). This indicates a recurring situation where two bishops are in mutual tension (e.g., Bg5/Bh4 eyeing Be7, or Bg4/Bh5 eyeing Be2), and the correct move is to resolve the tension by capturing first. Instead, the player plays another move (only 24% play a capture at all), leaving their own bishop en prise to be taken for free by the opponent's bishop on the next move.
analysis.why_bad: When two bishops are in mutual attack (e.g., Bg5 vs Be7 or Bh5 vs Be2), failing to exchange first allows the opponent to capture your bishop freely on their turn. The player's move (a pawn capture, knight move, castling, etc.) ignores this critical tension, effectively donating a minor piece (~3 pawns of material) because the opponent simply takes the now-undefended bishop.

analysis.label: Player grabs material with a capture while missing a winning check (often checkmate) that was available.
analysis.description: In 94% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 94% it wins decisive material (median value 97, i.e., queen-equivalent or mate). Yet the player instead plays a capture 96% of the time—seduced by an available enemy piece—completely overlooking the forcing check. Only 26% of the best moves are themselves captures, meaning the winning check is typically a quiet or non-capturing move that the player's pattern-matching fails to detect. The average centipawn loss is 7507, reflecting that many of these missed checks are outright checkmates (Positions 1, 3, 9 show mate-in-1 missed). The 76% own-hang rate (median value 3) is a secondary consequence: by capturing instead of delivering the decisive blow, the player often leaves their own piece undefended in the resulting position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a tangible but low-value capture over a forcing check that either delivers immediate checkmate or wins overwhelming material through a forced sequence. The capture is irrelevant when a mating attack exists—the opponent gets to move next and often escapes or counter-attacks fatally. The player's greed blinds them to the most basic tactical principle: checks first.

analysis.label: In the opening, a knight (or minor piece) jumps aggressively to an advanced or rim square where it is left undefended and can be captured.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 83% of the time (median value 3.0 = minor piece), the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging, with the hung piece being a minor in 302/413 cases (~73%). Only 8% of positions involve a missed material win, confirming this is a 'hung own piece' pattern, not a missed capture. The best moves are never checks (0%) and rarely captures (5%), indicating quiet developmental moves (castling, bishop development, central pawn pushes) were the correct alternative. The feature fires on opening positions (11/12 boards) where players impulsively lunge a knight to squares like h4, h5, g4, g5, e5, or d6—squares that look aggressive but are completely unprotected, allowing the opponent to simply win the piece.
analysis.why_bad: These knight moves (Nh4, Nh5, Ng4, Ng5, Ne5, Nd6, etc.) jump to advanced or rim squares without any support from pawns or other pieces. The knight lands on a square where it can be immediately captured by an enemy pawn, bishop, or other piece with no recourse. The player prioritizes an 'attacking look' (often chasing a bishop on f5 or aiming at a weak point) over the basic requirement that a piece must be defended or that the square must be safe. Standard development (castling, Be2, d4) was always preferable.

analysis.label: Player makes an attacking queen move that leaves their own piece undefended elsewhere on the board.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 67% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns: 128, minors: 121, majors: 85), while 57% of the time the best move won material (median 3.0). The played move was almost never a capture (9%). In 11 of the top 12 activating positions, the move is a queen relocation to an aggressive-looking square (Qh3, Qh5, Qh6, Qg5, Qg7, Qe5, Qe4, etc.), typically aimed at the opponent's king. Meanwhile, the best moves are concrete tactical shots—captures (37%), checks (23%), or defensive consolidations—that the player overlooked in favor of the flashy queen maneuver.
analysis.why_bad: These queen moves prioritize a vague attacking idea (often a kingside queen sortie) while the queen either abandons a defensive role or the player ignores that another piece is left without protection. The opponent can simply capture the hanging piece, gaining material and neutralizing the 'attack,' which typically has no forced continuation. The best moves instead cash in concretely—winning material through captures, delivering checks that win pieces, or addressing the position's real tactical demands.

analysis.label: Player ignores a critical rook capture of an enemy pawn (often a dangerous passed pawn), instead making a passive move that frequently leaves their own rook hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 71% of the time, and across all top 12 positions the best move is specifically a rook capturing a pawn (Rxa2, Rxc2, Rxf7, Rxb7, Rxg7, Rxa7, Rxb2, Rxh2, Bxa3). Despite the best move being available, the player makes a quiet or irrelevant move instead, and 49% of the time their played move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 17 major pieces in the distribution). The best move 'wins 0' by SEE because the target is typically just a pawn, but positionally these captures are critical—often stopping an advanced passed pawn from promoting or securing a decisive material/positional advantage. The 33% 'best wins material' cases (median 5.0) likely reflect positions where the rook capture also wins additional material indirectly.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the available rook capture of a critical pawn (especially passed pawns near promotion), the player allows the opponent's pawn to promote or maintain a decisive advantage. Worse, the played move frequently leaves the player's own rook undefended and en prise—the very rook that should have been actively capturing. This results in catastrophic material loss and/or immediate checkmate, as reflected in the average cp_loss of ~3999.

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece (often with check) hanging their own major piece, when a forced checkmate or decisive mating attack was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced checkmate (or overwhelming winning continuation) but instead plays a flashy capture that leaves their own major piece en prise. The SEE aggregate shows: 93% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91, indicating mate-winning positions), the played move is a capture 89% of the time, yet that capture hangs the player's own piece 96% of the time (median value 5, i.e., a rook; piece class distribution heavily skewed toward majors: 42 major vs 8 minor). The best move is a check 66% of the time but a capture only 11%—meaning the correct continuation was typically a quiet or non-capturing check that initiates the mating net, not a material grab. The average cp_loss of 7772 confirms these are catastrophic blunders turning forced mates into merely advantageous positions.
analysis.why_bad: The captures look aggressive (often giving check themselves) but the target piece is defended—so the attacker's queen or rook is immediately recaptured. Meanwhile, the actual best move (usually a precise check with a different piece, or a quiet mating move) would have delivered checkmate in 1-8 moves. The player is seduced by the immediate material grab or check when patient calculation reveals a forced kill.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing move instead of the critical central pawn capture needed to resolve pawn tension.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a remarkably consistent pattern: the best move is a capture in 100% of cases, yet these captures win zero material (only 3% show material gain, median value won just 1.0 — indicating pawn-takes-pawn exchanges). The player's move was itself a capture only 6% of the time, and 38% of the time the played move left an own piece hanging (median value 1.0, split between minor pieces and pawns) — likely because failing to resolve the tension allows the opponent to advance with tempo against now-misplaced pieces. Across all 12 top positions, the best move is a central pawn capture (dxe4, dxe5, cxd4, exd5, fxe4) resolving closed-center tension, while the player instead develops a piece (Bd7, Bb7, Bg4, Be2, Bd6, Bf4) or plays another quiet move (O-O, c5, c3, f6, f4).
analysis.why_bad: By failing to capture the opponent's central pawn at the critical moment, the player allows the opponent to push their center pawn (typically e4-e5 or d4-d5) with devastating tempo, gaining space, kicking developed pieces (especially knights on f6/c6), opening lines against the king (often still uncastled), and seizing a crushing spatial and dynamic advantage. The developing moves are not bad in isolation but catastrophically mistimed — the position demanded immediate resolution of the central tension before any further development.

analysis.label: Player misses a non-capturing tactical move that wins a minor piece (median value 3.0) through threats like forks or traps.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 3.0 (a minor piece). Crucially, only 7% of these best moves are captures and 0% are checks, meaning the winning move is almost always a quiet tactical shot — a fork, trap, or piece-winning threat rather than a direct take. The player's actual move was itself a capture only 14% of the time, and 42% of the time it also left their own piece hanging (median value 2.0). The concrete boards confirm this: Rd4 forks two bishops (positions 5, 7), Nd5 traps a bishop with no retreat (position 9), Nf3 saves and activates a knight to win material (position 1), and Qc2/Rd1/Re4 create unavoidable tactical threats. Players instead choose aimless quiet moves or inferior captures.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity where a quiet developing or repositioning move creates an irresistible threat (fork, trap, or attack on a piece with no escape squares). By playing passive moves like king moves (Kf3, Kh2, O-O), pawn pushes (a6, h6), or misdirected rook moves (Rc8, Rc2, Rgg7), the player squanders the chance to win a full minor piece and often leaves their position worse or even hangs their own material.

analysis.label: The player makes an active or capturing move that leaves their own major piece (usually a queen or rook) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 97% of activating positions show the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e. rook/queen level). The hung piece class distribution (84 major, 48 minor, 8 pawn) confirms that rooks and queens are the most commonly left en prise. While 68% of positions also have a best move that wins material, the dominant and near-universal signal is the self-inflicted hanging. The player's move is a capture 45% of the time, suggesting players often grab material or play aggressively while failing to notice their own piece is left undefended. The average cp_loss of 1805 reflects the catastrophic cost of hanging a major piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player focuses on their own tactical idea (capturing a piece, making an active move, or playing a check) while overlooking that the move removes a defender or relocates a piece such that one of their own major pieces (queen or rook) is left completely unprotected and can be simply captured by the opponent on the next move.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move that leaves their own queen en prise, when the best move was typically a queen capture that would save it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 82% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to queen-level material), with major pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (34 out of 59 classified). The best move is a capture 85% of the time, and in 10 of the top 12 boards the best move is specifically a queen capture (Qxb5, Qxe3, Qxe4, Qxd4, Qxg5, Qxc3, Qxd5, Qxg6, Qxf3, etc.). In those same boards, the piece left hanging after the played move is overwhelmingly the queen (value 9) in 9 of 12 cases. The player's move was itself a capture only 22% of the time, meaning most moves are quiet diversions that ignore the queen's vulnerability.
analysis.why_bad: The player's queen is under attack or undefended, and the correct response is to use the queen offensively—capturing an enemy piece to simultaneously save itself and win material. Instead, the player makes an unrelated move (a king retreat, a rook move, a bishop development) that completely ignores the queen's precarious situation, allowing the opponent to simply capture it for free on the next move, resulting in catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss of 4120).

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy pawn (typically e5) attacking their knight and plays an unrelated move, leaving the knight hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of activating positions involve the player's move leaving their OWN piece hanging (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece). The piece class distribution is overwhelmingly minor pieces (47 minor vs 1 major out of 48 counted). Across the top 12 boards, the recurring geometry is a knight (almost always on f6, sometimes c6) under direct attack from an advanced enemy pawn (e5 or d5). Instead of addressing this concrete threat—by capturing the pawn (dxe5), retreating the knight (Ne8, Nd5, Nfd7), or otherwise resolving the tension—the player plays an unrelated developing or pawn move (d5, a6, h6, e6, etc.), effectively gifting the minor piece. The best move wins material 41% of the time (median 1 pawn) and is itself a capture 41% of the time, reflecting that the principled response is often simply taking the attacking pawn.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore an immediate, concrete threat to a knight from an enemy pawn. After the played move, the opponent simply captures the knight with the pawn (e.g., exf6 or dxc6), winning a minor piece for free. The player treats the position as though no tactical threat exists, prioritizing a strategic or developmental idea while losing material worth ~3 pawns.

analysis.label: Player plays a non-forcing move that leaves their own piece en prise, missing a simple forcing capture (often with check) that would have resolved the tactical tension.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 77% of the time, the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value: 3.0, with major pieces accounting for 34/66 hung pieces and minor pieces 24/66). Meanwhile, the best move was a capture 77% of the time (often also a check at 41%), typically a straightforward exchange or recapture that resolves tactical tension on open files or against undefended enemy pieces. The player consistently ignores these forcing opportunities — such as back-rank captures (Rxc8+, Rxd8, Rxa1+), queen trades (Qxg5, Qxe3), or natural recaptures — and instead plays quiet or irrelevant moves (Nd2, Na3, Ra2, Kb1) or misguided aggressive captures (Bxh7, Bxh2+, Bxf7+) that leave their own rook, bishop, or queen undefended. The average cp_loss of 1218 reflects the catastrophic nature of hanging major material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical necessity — a forcing capture or exchange that the position demands — and instead play a move that leaves the player's own piece undefended. The opponent can simply take the hanging piece on the next move, winning significant material (rooks, bishops, or queens) for free.

analysis.label: Player ignores an attacked rook on an open file that should be exchanged, leaving it hanging for free capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 53% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with major pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (81 of 141 cases). Critically, the best move is a capture 98% of the time yet wins material only 14% of the time (with SEE = 0 in most top positions), indicating the correct move is an even rook exchange. The player instead plays quiet moves (king walks, pawn pushes) while their rook remains en prise on an open file contested by the opponent's doubled rooks, resulting in the rook being captured for nothing.
analysis.why_bad: The player's rook is attacked (typically by opponent's doubled rooks on an open file) and the only way to save it is to exchange it (Rxc3, Rxd2, Rxe4, etc. — equal trades). By playing an unrelated quiet move, the player leaves their rook undefended and loses a full exchange (5 points of material) for free, turning winning or equal positions into losing ones (average cp_loss ~368).

analysis.label: The player makes an apparently purposeful rook move (or repositioning) that leaves their own piece undefended and hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 70% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across major pieces 137, pawns 125, and minor pieces 88), while 63% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0). Only 5% of played moves were captures, indicating the typical move is a quiet rook redeployment. In 9 of the top 12 activating positions, the played move is a rook move (Reb8, Rg1, Rxc7, Rg8, Rh1, Rfb1, Ra1, Rae8, Rh7), confirming the overwhelming pattern of rook repositioning that neglects existing tactical vulnerabilities. The best moves are captures (37%) or checks (14%), indicating concrete tactical opportunities that the passive rook maneuvers completely ignore.
analysis.why_bad: These rook moves look superficially purposeful (occupying open files, doubling rooks, activating to the 7th rank), but they ignore urgent tactical realities. The rook either abandons a defensive duty (leaving another piece unprotected), moves into a square where it is itself captured, or simply wastes a tempo while the opponent wins material. The player prioritizes abstract piece activity over concrete tactical calculation, missing that a piece is en prise immediately after the move.

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the player moves their king in the wrong direction, away from the critical zone needed to win or hold the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the player's king move heads toward an irrelevant or counterproductive square. The SEE aggregate shows that 32% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece (overwhelmingly pawns — 30 out of 34 cases) hanging, with a median value of 1.0, indicating the king abandons pawn-defense duties. Only 15% of best moves win material and only 6% are captures, confirming this is not about missing a tactical shot but rather a positional/strategic king-placement error. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, exclusively in endgames, with an average cp_loss of 213 — often converting winning positions into draws or drawn positions into losses.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king's placement is the decisive factor. These moves send the king toward the board edge or wrong flank — away from passed pawns that need support, away from enemy pawns that need blockading, or away from pawns that need the king's protection. By marching the wrong direction, the king loses critical tempi in the race to reach the key squares, often leaving its own pawns defenseless or failing to stop the opponent's pawn promotion.

analysis.label: Player misses a powerful forcing move (check or capture) that wins decisive material or forces checkmate, instead playing a passive or inferior alternative.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 61% of positions the best move wins material with a median value of 8.0 (queen-level or mate-equivalent), while 40% of best moves are checks and 59% are captures. The player's actual move was a capture only 39% of the time (often a lesser capture like taking a pawn instead of delivering mate), and left their own piece hanging 46% of the time (median value just 1.0, mostly pawns — a secondary side-effect). The enormous average cp_loss of 3377 confirms these are game-deciding oversights, frequently involving missed checkmates (Positions 3, 6, 8) or missed queen captures (Position 10). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically those where a crushing tactical blow exists but is overlooked in favor of a non-forcing queen repositioning move or a materially inferior capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available forcing sequence (a check or capture) that either delivers checkmate or wins decisive material. The player instead makes a 'normal-looking' move — often repositioning the queen to a central square (Qd6, Qc8, Qe5, Qb8, Qd7) or capturing a less valuable piece (Qxh8 grabbing a rook instead of g4# mating, Nxb5 taking a pawn instead of Rg1# mating) — completely missing the most powerful continuation available.

analysis.label: The king retreats from an enemy bishop sacrifice instead of simply capturing it with Kx, forfeiting a free piece worth ~3 pawns.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a bishop), and 96% of best moves are captures. Only 14% of played moves were captures, meaning players consistently declined available material. Across all 12 top-activating positions, an enemy bishop sits en prise on a square adjacent to the player's king (f7, h7, f2, or h2) — typically the result of a speculative bishop sacrifice — and the correct response is a simple king capture (Kxf7, Kxh7, Kxf2, Kxh2). Instead, the king retreats (Kf8, Kh8, Kf1, Kh1, Ke2), fleeing the sacrifice rather than accepting it. The 54% own-hang rate (median 2.0) reflects that retreating often leaves other pieces undefended as a secondary consequence.
analysis.why_bad: By retreating the king rather than capturing the sacrificed bishop, the player donates a full piece (~3 pawns of material) to the opponent for free. The sacrifice was unsound or speculative — the opponent's attack would not have succeeded after the king simply takes — so declining it converts a defensible or even advantageous position into a losing one. The retreat also often worsens king safety (cramping the king into a corner) without gaining any compensating activity.

analysis.label: The player plays a flashy rook capture/move with check that leaves the rook itself undefended and hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 86% of the top 500 positions show the player's move leaving their own piece en prise (median value 4.0, corresponding to a rook), with the piece class overwhelmingly being major pieces (78 of 114 classified instances). All top 12 activating moves are rook checks (Rxg7+, Rxb7+, Rxg2+, Rfxf7+, R7c6+, R8g7+, etc.) — typically captures that deliver check but leave the rook unprotected on the destination square. While 61% of these positions had material available to win via the best move (median 2.0), and 56% of played moves were captures, the players chose the tempting-but-unsound forcing check instead of a superior quiet or alternative tactical continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The rook delivers check (often capturing a pawn or minor piece), but after the king escapes the check, the rook is left undefended on an exposed square where it can be freely captured. The check gains one tempo but costs an entire rook, resulting in catastrophic material loss — average cp_loss of 2585 confirms many of these lead directly to lost games or forced mate against the player.

analysis.label: Player misses a knight capture winning an insufficiently defended central pawn (Nxe4, Nxd4, or Nxd5), opting for a quiet positional move instead.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where a knight can profitably capture a central pawn (e4, d4, or d5) that is insufficiently defended, but the player instead makes a quiet developing or prophylactic move. The SEE aggregate shows that 61% of positions have a best move winning material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), 62% of best moves are captures, yet only 15% of played moves are captures — the player overwhelmingly plays quiet moves. All 12 top-activating boards show the identical pattern: the best move is Nxe4, Nxd4, or Nxd5 winning exactly one pawn, while the played move is a quiet positional move (castling, bishop development, rook lift, queen move). The 47% own-hang rate (median 2.0, mostly minor pieces) in the broader dataset likely reflects that some of these quiet moves additionally leave the player's knight or bishop tactically exposed to the opponent's now-intact center.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity to win a central pawn with a knight capture. In nearly every case, the central pawn (e4/d4/d5) is insufficiently defended — typically only protected by one piece while attacked by the knight plus a supporting piece (often a fianchettoed bishop). By playing a slow move, the player allows the opponent to reinforce the center or create counterplay, squandering a material advantage of roughly one pawn that would also destabilize the opponent's pawn structure.

analysis.label: Player ignores the opportunity to win the opponent's overextended queen via a queen move, playing a different piece instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 9.0 (a queen). The best move is a queen move in every single top-12 case (Qe7, Qg6, Qe2, Qd7, Qd2, Qb3, Qf3, Qc3, Qf6), yet it is a capture only 16% of the time and a check only 1% — meaning the winning queen move typically challenges, traps, or forces the trade of the opponent's overextended queen rather than directly capturing it. The player's actual moves were captures only 15% of the time and left their own piece hanging 61% of the time (median value 1.0, mostly pawns). The opponent's queen is typically deep in the player's territory (g2, f2, b2, g7, f7, e6) where it appears dominant but is actually vulnerable to being challenged by the player's own queen.
analysis.why_bad: The player's moves fail because they ignore the opponent's dangerously infiltrated but tactically vulnerable queen. Instead of using their own queen to challenge, trap, or force a favorable trade of the overextended enemy queen (winning ~9 points of material), the player makes routine developing moves (Be2, Nge2, Be7, Nd7), pawn grabs (Qxb2, fxe5), or irrelevant moves (h3, Kd6) that leave the opponent's lethal queen in place, typically resulting in devastating attacks or immediate losses.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple pawn capture of an enemy piece that has infiltrated to an aggressive square, leaving their own rook or piece hanging to the invader.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 78% of positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0), and 80% of best moves are captures—specifically pawn captures (hxg6, hxg3, axb4, hxg4) taking enemy pieces that have landed on aggressive squares. Meanwhile, 61% of positions see the player's own piece left hanging after their move (median value 3.0, class distribution: minor 33, pawn 31, major 28). The concrete pattern across the top boards is remarkably consistent: an enemy knight (or occasionally bishop) infiltrates to g6/g3/b4/g4, directly attacking a higher-value piece (usually a rook on h8 or h1), and a simple pawn capture would eliminate the threat while winning the piece. The player ignores this elementary capture and plays a different move, compounding the error by leaving their own piece en prise to the invader. Only 17% of played moves were captures, confirming the player chose quiet moves instead of the obvious pawn take.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to capture the invading piece with a pawn, the player simultaneously misses winning a minor piece (free capture) and leaves their own more valuable piece (often a rook, seen in 8 of 12 top positions) hanging to that very invader. The two errors compound into massive material swings averaging 362 centipawns lost.

analysis.label: Player makes a normal-looking developing move in the opening while ignoring an immediate knight fork threat (typically Nc7+), leaving a pawn unguarded and allowing devastating material gain.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 78% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with pawns accounting for 118 of 152 hung pieces), while only 12% of moves played are captures. The feature fires almost exclusively in opening positions where an aggressive knight (typically on b5) threatens a fork on c7 (hitting the king on e8 and rook on a8). The player's move ignores this urgent threat, leaving the c7 pawn unguarded and allowing the fork to execute. The 34% 'best wins material' cases (median 2.0) reflect positions where the correct defense also happened to win material. The cp_loss averages 362, consistent with losing an exchange via the fork.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize development, pawn pushes (c5, e6, a6, c6), fianchettoing (Bg7), or castling over addressing an immediate tactical emergency. The knight on b5 threatens Nc7+, which forks the king and rook. By not playing moves like Na6 (blocking c7), d6 (blocking the knight's path), or Qa5+ (counterattacking), the player allows the fork to land, typically losing the exchange (rook for knight) or more. Moves like ...c6 are especially catastrophic as they remove the c7 pawn, directly opening the square for the knight.

analysis.label: The player missed a check (usually a knight fork or pawn advance) that wins decisive material, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: In 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 95% it wins material (median value: 100, i.e., decisive). The player's move was a capture only 10% of the time—overwhelmingly they played quiet king moves or pawn pushes instead. The positions are predominantly endgames (67%) with exposed kings on both sides, creating fertile ground for tactical forks and forcing pawn checks. While 36% of played moves also left the player's own piece hanging (median value: 3), this is a secondary consequence of the wasted tempo rather than the primary mistake. The core error is failing to exploit the exposed enemy king with a check that simultaneously wins material—often via knight forks (Nf4+, Nc1+, Ne4+, Ne2+, Nxd3+, Nxe6+) or pawn advances with check (g3+, a3+, fxe5+, exf6+, dxc5+).
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves waste a crucial tempo in positions where a forcing check would immediately win material or the game. By not delivering the check, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, escape the fork square, or even seize the initiative—turning winning positions into drawn or lost ones (average cp_loss: 418).

analysis.label: White fails to capture the opponent's queen with an advanced pawn (typically exf6), missing a massive material gain.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of positions have a best move winning material with a median value of 8.0 (queen minus pawn), and 90% of best moves are captures. The pattern is overwhelmingly consistent: White has an advanced e5-pawn (or c-pawn in one case) that directly attacks Black's queen on f6 (or b6), yet White plays quiet or irrelevant moves instead. The player's move left their own piece hanging 63% of the time (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), but this is incidental—the primary catastrophe is failing to win the opponent's queen for a pawn. The feature fires on 0.0% of all positions, indicating this is a rare but devastating blind spot.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most basic tactical opportunity on the board: a pawn directly attacking the opponent's queen. By playing quiet moves like Re2, h3, Qf1, or Re1, White passes up winning a queen (worth ~9 points) for free with a simple pawn capture, typically losing 800-1000+ centipawns of evaluation. The opponent's queen is literally en prise to a pawn, but the player appears blind to pawn captures of major pieces, perhaps because pawns capturing queens feels counterintuitive or the queen seems 'too big' to be taken by a pawn.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move ignoring a clearly winning capture, often simultaneously leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 90% of the top-500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-level), and 94% of best moves are captures. Yet the player's move was a capture only 8% of the time — they consistently play quiet moves (pawn pushes like h3/g3, king moves, or rook repositionings) instead of taking free or underdefended enemy pieces. Compounding the error, 65% of played moves also leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0), with the distribution skewed toward major pieces (25 major, 8 minor, 13 pawn). The average centipawn loss of 1856 reflects this catastrophic double mistake: ignoring a winning capture while simultaneously blundering material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available material-winning capture (typically Rx or Bx taking an undefended or underdefended piece worth a rook or more). In many cases the quiet move also relocates a piece to an unprotected square (e.g., Rb7+ instead of Rxa7+, Rd3 instead of Rxd4, Rh1 instead of Rxc2), compounding the blunder by both missing material gain and hanging their own piece.

analysis.label: The player ignores a necessary bishop capture (Bx...), instead playing a different move that leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 97% of top-activating positions, the best move is a capture — and in every single top-12 example, that best move is specifically a bishop capture (Bxg2, Bxg7, Bxe3, Bxd2, Bxe2, Bxd1, Bxf8). Despite this available bishop trade/capture, the player chooses a different move, and 63% of the time this leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece). The hung-piece distribution (123 minor, 57 pawn, 29 major) confirms that most often it is the neglected bishop itself that becomes en prise. The best move typically 'wins 0' by SEE (an equal trade), meaning the bishop capture is a necessary exchange to avoid losing material, not a free win — yet ignoring it costs a full piece.
analysis.why_bad: The player's bishop has a critical capture available (often a necessary trade to relieve pressure or avoid losing the bishop), but the player instead develops, advances a pawn, or makes a different capture. This leaves their own piece (frequently that same bishop or a knight) undefended and capturable by the opponent on the next move, resulting in a net material loss of roughly a minor piece.

analysis.label: Player misses a crushing queen check (Qh4+ or Qh5+) exploiting an open f-pawn diagonal against the uncastled enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91, i.e., a queen), and 97% of the time the best move is a check — yet only 7% of best moves are captures, confirming the winning mechanism is a check that forces concessions rather than a direct capture. The player's actual move was a quiet developing move or irrelevant capture (only 32% captures played), with only 14% leaving own pieces hanging. Across all top-activating positions, the f-pawn is missing from the opponent's kingside, leaving the e1-h4 or e8-h5 diagonal fatally exposed. The player consistently chooses standard development (Nc6, Nf6, Nf3, d6) instead of the immediately winning Qh4+ or Qh5+.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Nc6, Nf6, Nf3, d6, etc.) are normal developing moves but completely squander a one-move tactical knockout. By failing to play Qh4+/Qh5+, the player allows the opponent to castle, block the diagonal, or otherwise neutralize the weakness, converting a winning position (often -400+ cp) into an equal or losing one. The queen check exploits the absent f-pawn with devastating immediacy — there is typically no defense that doesn't lose the queen or worse.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own bishop undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 95% of the top 500 positions show the player's move leaving their own piece en prise (median value 3.0), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly minor pieces (363 out of 380 hung pieces). All 12 top-activating boards confirm the hung piece is specifically a bishop (marked 'B', value 3). Only 39% of positions have a best move that wins material, and 37% of played moves are captures, indicating the core mistake is not missing a winning capture but rather carelessly exposing one's own bishop. The moves include bishop relocations to unprotected squares (Ba3, Ba6, Bf3, Bxc5, Bxg4) as well as non-bishop moves that inadvertently abandon the defense of a bishop elsewhere (Qc7, Nd3, Rc8, Ne7, d4).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the player's bishop completely undefended, allowing the opponent to simply capture it for free (gaining ~3 pawns of material). Whether the bishop was moved to an unsafe square or another piece moved away from defending it, the result is the same: the opponent wins a minor piece with no compensation.

analysis.label: Premature bishop sacrifice on f7 (or f2) with check in the opening that simply loses the bishop without compensation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a speculative Bxf7+ (or Bxf2+) bishop sacrifice in the opening. The SEE aggregate confirms this is a 'hung own piece' pattern: 99% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = bishop), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being minor pieces (435/497). The move is itself a capture in 91% of cases (bishop takes the f-pawn), but the best move wins material only 51% of the time, meaning the quiet developing alternatives (Nc3, O-O, d3, c3, h3, Nbd2) were typically superior. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, corresponding to this very specific opening motif where the Bc4 (or Bc5) bishop targets f7/f2 with an unsound sacrifice.
analysis.why_bad: After Bxf7+ Kxf7, the bishop is simply captured and the attacker lacks sufficient follow-up (no coordinated pieces to sustain the attack, king escapes easily). The check gains one tempo but the opponent's king is safe enough — typically the attacker hasn't completed development (knights on b1, bishops on c1 still undeveloped) so there's no mating attack or material recovery. The result is being down a full minor piece (~300cp) for nothing but a displaced king that quickly finds safety.

analysis.label: Player makes a routine developing move in the opening while a strong capture (often winning material or gaining a decisive positional advantage) goes unplayed.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 93% of best moves are captures, yet only 3% of the played moves were captures—an extreme mismatch. In 37% of the top 500 positions the best move wins outright material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while the remaining captures are critical exchanges that yield large positional advantages (average cp_loss of 1104). The player's own move left a piece hanging only 3% of the time, confirming this is a 'missed winning capture' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. All 12 top-activating positions are in the opening phase, and the played moves are stereotypical quiet development (Nf3, Bg2, Bb3, g3, d3, Be7, Bd7, f3) while enemy pieces sit exposed on central squares (e5, e6, e4, g4, d5, f6).
analysis.why_bad: The player defaults to 'autopilot' opening development—moving pieces to natural squares—without checking whether an opponent's piece is unprotected or tactically vulnerable. This causes them to miss free or highly favorable captures on exposed central/kingside squares, throwing away advantages of 200–9970 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player moves a piece (predominantly a knight) to a square where it is left undefended and can be captured for free.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player's own move leaves a piece hanging: 97% of the top 500 positions result in the moved piece being en prise (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece). The piece class distribution confirms this with 175 minor pieces (knights/bishops), 60 major pieces, and 19 pawns. While 59% of the played moves are themselves captures—suggesting the player is lured by taking an enemy pawn or piece—the capturing piece ends up undefended. Only 18% of best moves win material, and just 8% of best moves are captures, confirming the optimal play was typically a quiet consolidating move rather than a tactical exchange. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, targeting specifically these blunders where an aggressive-looking piece maneuver backfires.
analysis.why_bad: The player's piece (usually a knight) moves to a square—often capturing an enemy piece there—but the destination square is unprotected by friendly pieces. The opponent can simply recapture or take the hanging piece, winning material. The player is attracted by the apparent gain (capturing a pawn on e4, e5, e3, etc.) or an aggressive-looking placement, but overlooks that their piece has no support on its new square.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive king move instead of capturing a high-value hanging enemy piece that would save or dramatically improve the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player plays a quiet move (almost always a king move) instead of capturing a valuable undefended enemy piece. The SEE aggregate shows that 57% of best moves win material with a median value of 9.0 (queen-level), while the player's move is a capture 0% of the time. The best move is a capture in 43% of cases. Secondarily, 43% of the played moves also leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), compounding the error. All top-activating positions are endgames with enormous centipawn losses (avg 5444), often converting drawn or survivable positions into immediate forced mate.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet king moves fail because they ignore a free capture that would either equalize (e.g., Kxf8 drawing with K+B vs K, Nxh5 capturing a queen, Bxg5 capturing a queen) or avoid immediate mate. By choosing a passive king move, the player walks into mating nets or allows the opponent's overwhelming material to deliver checkmate quickly, when the capture was the only resource keeping the game alive.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning knight fork with check that would have won major material (typically a queen).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 94% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 97, consistent with winning a queen), and in 100% of cases the best move is a check. Examining all 12 top boards confirms the best move is always a knight delivering check while simultaneously attacking an undefended high-value piece (usually the queen): Ne2+, Nd6+, Ne4+, Nf3+, Ne7+, Nf6+. Only 22% of best moves are captures — the rest are non-capturing knight checks that fork. The player's actual move was a capture only 30% of the time, and 48% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3, typically a minor piece), suggesting the player often made an inferior exchange or positional move instead of the crushing tactic. The feature fires on just 0.4% of positions, consistent with the relatively rare but devastating geometry of an available knight fork with check.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a knight fork that simultaneously checks the king and attacks an undefended queen (or other major piece). Instead of collecting decisive material with a forcing check, the player makes quiet moves (d3, O-O, Ne2, f4, h4, Nc5), positional captures (Bxf3, Nxf3), or greedy but inferior captures (Qxa7+, Nxf8), all of which allow the opponent to keep their queen and remain in the game.

analysis.label: Player overlooked a winning bishop capture (usually taking an undefended or under-defended enemy minor piece) and played a non-capturing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 71% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 79% of the best moves are captures, while only 12% of the actually-played moves are captures. This indicates the player consistently missed a tactically available capture. Examining the top 12 boards reveals the best move is almost always a bishop capture (Bxc6, Bxd4, Bxf6, Bxg8, Bxg4, Bxa6, Bxc3) winning a minor piece that is inadequately defended. The own-hang rate of 27% (median pawn) is a secondary noise factor; the dominant pattern at 71% is the missed winning capture. The feature fires in just 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific geometry where an available bishop capture cleanly nets material.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (quiet repositioning like Ng3, Nf1, Bb5, Qb3, O-O, or greedy but inferior captures like Qxb2) fail because they ignore an immediately available bishop capture that wins a full minor piece. By not taking the hanging or under-defended enemy piece, the player throws away a decisive material advantage, often converting a winning position into an equal or losing one (average cp_loss: 264).

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing queen check (Qa4+ or Qh5+) that wins an undefended minor piece in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 91, corresponding to a minor piece), and crucially 92% of best moves are checks while only 6% are direct captures. This means the winning mechanism is a queen check that forces a response, after which the queen captures an unprotected piece. The player's move was a quiet developing move (only 20% were captures), and only 31% left own material hanging (median value 2, i.e. a pawn—incidental). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, highlighting the specificity of this opening tactical motif where Black has left a minor piece undefended while the king remains exposed on the e-file.
analysis.why_bad: Moves like Be3, O-O, h3, d3, d4, and Nf3 are routine developing moves that completely ignore the tactical opportunity. They allow Black to consolidate by castling or defending the loose piece, squandering a position where a simple queen check (exploiting the uncastled king on the a4-e8 or h5-e8 diagonal) would have netted a free bishop or knight. The player appears to follow opening principles blindly rather than checking for forcing moves first.

analysis.label: The player missed a decisive Queen capture with check (Qx__+), instead playing a move that usually left their own Queen en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a strikingly consistent pattern: in 92% of the top 500 activating positions the best move is a check, and in 98% it is a capture — specifically a Queen capturing a piece with check (Qx__+). Despite this powerful forcing move being available, the player chose something else, and in 64% of cases that move left their own piece (median value 9.0 = Queen) hanging. The hung-piece class distribution (33 major, 5 pawn, 3 minor) confirms the Queen is overwhelmingly what gets lost. Every top-12 position shows the same geometry: an enemy piece near the opponent's king is capturable by the Queen with check (Qxf1+, Qxf7+, Qxd2+, Qxc6+, etc.), which tactically exploits the fact that the king must move, preventing recapture on the captured square. Instead, the player made a different move — sometimes a different capture, sometimes a quiet move — ignoring the forcing continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The Queen capture-check is a tempo-winning tactic: by giving check while capturing, the opponent cannot recapture because they must address the check first. The player's alternative moves fail because the Queen (or another major piece) was already tactically vulnerable — the capture-check was the ONLY way to both save the Queen and win material. By playing something else, the player leaves their Queen hanging to the very piece or line that the capture-check would have neutralized, resulting in catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss of 2161).

analysis.label: The player fails to capture a dominant enemy centralized piece with a knight (Nxd5/Nxe5/Nxd4/Nxe4) when it is tactically critical, instead making a quiet developing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture in 100% of cases, yet wins only 0 material by SEE (equal exchange) in nearly all instances (only 4% register as winning material). The player's move was a quiet non-capture in 97% of cases. In 28% of positions, the quiet move additionally left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns, minors, and majors). All 12 top-activating positions share identical geometry: the best move is a knight capturing an enemy piece on a central square (d5, e5, d4, or e4), which appears as a simple equal trade by SEE but is actually essential — failing to execute it leads to average centipawn losses exceeding 1000. The feature fires in the opening/early middlegame (83%) when centralized enemy knights or pawns become tactically critical to eliminate immediately.
analysis.why_bad: The centralized enemy piece (usually a knight on d5/e5/d4) is a tactical and positional monster. Although capturing it looks like 'just an exchange' (SEE=0), not taking it allows the opponent to exploit outposts, create threats, or win material through the unchallenged piece's influence. In many cases (28%), the quiet move even directly hangs one's own piece because the centralized enemy piece attacks it. The player prioritizes development or quiet plans over the urgent need to neutralize the dominant centralized piece.

analysis.label: Player fails to execute a readily available capture that would win significant material, instead playing a quiet or inferior move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture in 68% of activating positions, and in 50% of cases the best move wins material outright (median value 4.0, i.e., roughly a rook). Yet only 18% of played moves are captures, confirming the player consistently fails to take hanging or winnable enemy pieces. While 58% of played moves also leave something of the player's own hanging (median 1.0, mostly pawns), this is a secondary consequence of making a passive move rather than the primary error. The top boards illustrate this vividly: positions 1-3 all require Rxd6 to capture an undefended bishop, positions 5/7/11 need rook captures on available targets, position 10 shows taking the wrong fork target (bishop instead of rook), and positions 6/12 show the wrong pawn capture direction.
