The average cp_loss of 974 reflects how costly these missed captures are.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are terrible because a free or clearly winning capture is available (often a rook taking an undefended piece), and the player either plays a quiet move, moves the attacking piece to the wrong square without capturing, or captures the wrong (less valuable) target. This squanders material gains worth a minor piece to a full rook, turning winning positions into equal or losing ones.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting material capture (usually with a rook) instead of a stronger non-capture move that wins material indirectly through checks, forks, or positional threats.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 84% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0), yet crucially only 6% of those best moves are themselves captures—most win material through checks (22%), forks, or quiet positional threats. Meanwhile the player's actual move is a capture 64% of the time, and in 51% of cases this greedy capture leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, predominantly major pieces—24 out of 37 cases are rooks). The pattern is unmistakable: the player sees a tempting pawn or piece to snatch and takes it directly, but the superior move was typically a king retreat, a piece reposition, or a check that either wins more material indirectly or avoids leaving the capturing piece undefended. All 12 top positions are endgames where this greedy-grab error is catastrophic (avg cp_loss 1133).
analysis.why_bad: The greedy capture either (a) places the capturing piece (usually a rook worth 5) on an undefended square where it can be won back with interest, or (b) forfeits a stronger tactical sequence—often a check or fork—that wins material cleanly without leaving anything hanging. The player trades a small material gain (e.g., capturing a pawn) for a much larger positional or material loss.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy knight that can be captured for free, typically by a simple pawn take.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 87% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), and 74% of the time the best move is a capture, yet the player's move was a capture only 16% of the time. Across the top boards, the consistent pattern is an enemy knight sitting undefended on an aggressive square (f4, d5, e4, a4, d4, f7, e5, c6) that can be trivially captured—most often by a pawn push (exf4, exd5, dxe4, exd4, dxe5) or a simple piece take (Qxa4, Kxf7, Nxc6). Instead of collecting the free piece, the player makes a quiet developing or positional move, throwing away roughly a full piece of advantage. The secondary stat that 47% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0) reflects the compounding error: not only did they miss free material, but their alternative move often worsened their position further.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring a cleanly hanging enemy knight, the player forfeits a full minor piece (≈3 pawns) of material. The knight is typically undefended and capturable with a simple pawn or piece take requiring no calculation. The quiet moves played instead (castling, developing a bishop, pushing a flank pawn) address no tactical need and allow the opponent to rescue the knight on the next move, permanently squandering the opportunity.

analysis.label: The player makes an irrelevant or weakening move instead of urgently contesting a critical open file with a rook.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 43% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, spread across pawns/minors/majors), while only 12% of played moves were captures and best moves win material just 29% of the time. This indicates the core error is not missing a tactical shot but rather making a positionally negligent move that allows the opponent's file dominance to create threats. Across the top 12 boards, 10 of 12 best moves involve deploying a rook to an open file (Rac8, Red1, Rfe8, Rbe8, Rhe1, Rge8, Rae1 repeatedly), while the played moves are pawn pushes (b4, b5, h4), rook moves to the wrong file (Rh8, Ra8, Rhd1), or unrelated piece moves (Bb4, Qc6, Nh4). The positions consistently feature an opponent already occupying or threatening to dominate an open e-file or c-file, making immediate rook contest urgent.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the open file, the player cedes full control to the opponent's rooks, which then penetrate along the file to attack undefended pieces or invade the 7th/8th rank. The weakening pawn pushes (b5 exposing knights, b4 creating holes) or passive piece retreats compound the problem by creating new targets for the opponent's newly-dominant rooks, explaining the 43% rate of leaving one's own piece hanging as a downstream consequence.

analysis.label: The player ignores an undefended enemy piece (typically a rook) that can be captured immediately with a simple one-move capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 93% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), and 98% of the time the best move is a direct capture. Yet the player's move is a capture only 14% of the time — meaning in the vast majority of cases, the player plays a quiet, non-tactical move while an enemy piece sits completely undefended. The 43% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary effect of the player making an aimless move that sometimes leaves a pawn loose, but the dominant pattern is failing to take a free enemy rook or queen. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating these are unusual situations where a major piece is genuinely en prise yet goes uncaptured.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (king walks, bishop retreats, pawn pushes) fail because they completely ignore a free capture worth 5-9 points of material. The enemy piece — usually a rook — is completely undefended and directly capturable by a king step, bishop take, pawn take, or similar trivial capture. By playing a quiet positional move instead, the player throws away a decisive material advantage, often turning a winning position into an equal or losing one.

analysis.label: Player misses a tactical bishop sacrifice on f7 (or f2) with check, instead playing a quiet developing or prophylactic move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a highly distinctive pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of cases and a capture in 99%, yet it only registers as 'winning material' in 2% of positions (because the static exchange on the f7/f2 square itself is bishop-for-pawn, showing net 0 in SEE). The player's move was a capture only 8% of the time, and left their own piece hanging just 22% of the time (median value 2.0). This means the core mistake is not about hanging pieces or missing simple captures — it's about missing a deep tactical sacrifice (Bxf7+ or Bxf2+) whose value comes from follow-up moves (typically winning the opponent's pinning bishop on g4 or launching a decisive attack) rather than from material gain on the target square alone. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, reflecting the specific geometry required: a bishop on c4/c5 targeting f7/f2, an enemy king still in the center, and typically an opponent bishop on g4 creating a 'punishable' pin.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves (h3, O-O, Be3, Bb3, Bg5, h6) waste the critical window to exploit the opponent's uncastled king and the alignment of Bc4 against f7. After Bxf7+ Kxf7, the king is exposed and the pin on the knight (by Bg4) is broken, allowing Nxe5+ or similar forks that win the g4 bishop back with extra material and a devastating attack. By playing a slow move, the opponent gets time to castle or neutralize the tactical alignment, squandering 200-500 centipawns of advantage.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player makes a pawn capture (or advance) that leaves one of their own pawns undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 95% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being overwhelmingly a pawn (73 pawns out of 79 instances). The player's move is itself a capture in 76% of cases, yet the best move is rarely a capture (only 5%) or check (1%), indicating the correct approach is typically a quiet king move or non-capturing pawn advance. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, predominantly king-and-pawn endgames, where the structural consequence of a pawn capture is more consequential due to the absence of piece defenders.
analysis.why_bad: When a pawn captures diagonally, it abandons its previous file and the squares/pawns it was defending. In these endgame positions, the capturing pawn was providing critical structural support to a neighboring pawn. By making the tempting capture, the player removes that defensive link, leaving their own pawn unprotected and capturable by the opponent's king or pawns. The better moves (typically king maneuvers like Kh6, Kd6, Kxg7, or quiet pawn pushes like h5, g5, h3) maintain the pawn structure's integrity while pursuing more important strategic goals.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes an aggressive or advancing move (typically a pawn push or check) that leaves their own rook undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 77% of activating positions involve the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with major pieces comprising 41 of 60 identified hung pieces. Simultaneously, 72% of positions have a best move that wins material (median 4.0), and 49% of best moves are captures — often the rook itself could have captured an enemy piece instead. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (9/12 top boards), where players push passed pawns toward promotion (a7, h2, c7, c4, g5+) or play other seemingly purposeful moves while completely neglecting that their rook is left unprotected. The 12% capture rate for played moves confirms players are choosing quiet advancing moves over the material-winning options available.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a secondary goal (pawn promotion, giving check, advancing their king) while overlooking that their rook — often their most valuable remaining piece — is left undefended and immediately capturable. The opponent simply takes the free rook, transforming a winning or equal position into a lost one (average cp_loss: 1643). The rook was typically the key piece maintaining the advantage, and losing it collapses the position entirely.

analysis.label: The player misses a winning knight relocation that would win significant material, instead making a passive or counterproductive move that often leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: In 97% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 6.0 (queen-level), and in every single top-12 position the best move is a knight move (Nf1, Nc3, Nh6, Nf4, Nd6, Nc6, Ne2, Ng6, Nd4, Nc5, Nd4, Na4). The best move is a capture only 12% and a check only 2% of the time, indicating these are quiet knight repositioning moves—likely forks or attacks on undefended major pieces. Instead of playing the winning knight tactic, the player makes a passive move (often a king retreat: Kf1, Kf8, Kc2, Kd8, or a wrong-piece move) that 70% of the time leaves their own piece en prise (median value 3.0, predominantly minors at 103 instances). The played move is a capture only 19% of the time, confirming players are choosing quiet, often defensive moves while ignoring the decisive knight resource.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a knight that can jump to a tactically dominant square—forking the enemy king and queen, attacking undefended major pieces, or winning material through a discovered/double attack. By playing a passive king move or repositioning the wrong piece, the player both misses winning ~6 points of material and simultaneously exposes their own minor or major pieces to capture, converting a winning or defensible position into a losing one.

analysis.label: The player missed a forcing check (usually Qg6+) that wins decisive material or delivers checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 80% of best moves are checks and 84% win material with a median value of 91 (a full Queen). Only 32% of best moves are captures, meaning the winning blow is overwhelmingly a non-capturing check that creates an unstoppable threat. Players instead chose quiet moves or greedy captures (27% capture rate), completely overlooking the devastating checking resource. The dominant concrete pattern across the top boards is Qg6+ winning a Queen's worth of material, though Bg5+, Qxh5#, and similar checks also appear. The 27% own-hang rate is incidental noise; the consistent story across 500 positions is a missed winning check.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most forcing move available—a check that either wins the opponent's Queen outright through a fork/discovery, creates an unstoppable mating net, or delivers immediate checkmate. By playing quiet developing moves (Kf1, Rd3, Qh3, f4) or greedy captures (Qxh6, cxb4, Nxc7+), the player surrenders the initiative and allows the opponent to escape the tactical crisis unscathed.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy pawn attacking their own bishop, developing another piece and leaving the bishop en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung-piece class overwhelmingly being minor pieces (22 out of 25 identified cases). Meanwhile, the best move wins material 82% of the time (median value 1.0 = a pawn) and is a capture 78% of the time. The concrete pattern visible across all top boards is consistent: in the opening, the player has a bishop on an active diagonal (Bf4 attacked by ...e5, or Bc4 attacked by ...d5), and the opponent's pawn directly attacks it. The correct response is to capture that pawn (Bxe5, Nxe5, exd5, Bxd5, etc.), winning a pawn. Instead, the player ignores the threat and plays a quiet developing move (Nf3, Nc3, e3, Bd3, Qh5, b3), leaving their bishop hanging for free.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical threat to the player's own bishop. The enemy pawn attacks the bishop directly, and by not resolving this tension (capturing, retreating, or blocking), the player simply donates a minor piece (worth ~3 pawns) for nothing. A simple pawn capture would both save the bishop and win material, but the player prioritizes development over the concrete tactical requirement.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but losing check with a major piece that leaves their own piece hanging after the king escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 74% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, with 46/70 being major pieces), while only 17% of played moves are captures. Critically, ALL top-12 moves are checks (Qb1+, Rb1+, Ra1+, Rd1+, etc.), yet only 5% of the BEST moves are checks — confirming the player chose a flashy but unsound check over the objectively winning move. The best move wins material 70% of the time (median 4.0) and is a capture 48% of the time, meaning the correct play was usually to take material or make a quiet winning move instead of giving check. The hung piece class distribution (major: 46, minor: 10, pawn: 14) shows it is overwhelmingly the checking queen or rook itself that ends up en prise once the opponent's king sidesteps.
analysis.why_bad: These checks are 'patzer checks' — they look forcing because they attack the king, but after the king simply moves to a safe square, the checking piece (usually a queen or rook) is left en prise with no follow-up threats. The player wastes their turn on a non-productive check, losing the initiative and often a full major piece, instead of playing the objectively superior move (typically a material-winning capture or a quiet move consolidating a decisive advantage).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move in a sharp opening instead of exploiting a tactical opportunity (queen capture or queen check) that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 75% of the time (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), the best move wins material, and 54% of best moves are captures while 26% are checks. Yet the player's move is a capture only 5% of the time—they almost always play a quiet piece development instead. All 12 top-activating positions are in the opening phase with both kings in the center. The tactical opportunities involve either capturing an undefended enemy knight (Qxg5/Qxg4 patterns) or delivering a queen check along an open diagonal (Qa4+/Qa5+) that exploits the centralized king to win material. The 35% own-hang rate (median 2.0) is a secondary consequence—sometimes the quiet developing move also leaves the player's own piece tactically loose—but the primary error is failing to seize winning material.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet developing moves (Be6, Na6, Be3, Bd7, Na3, Rc1, Nh6, Ke2, f6) ignore an immediate tactical win—typically a hanging enemy knight on g4/g5 capturable by the queen, or a queen check on the a4-e8/a5-e1 diagonal that forks or wins material against the uncastled king. By prioritizing routine development over a concrete tactical shot, the player forfeits 3+ pawns worth of material on average and converts a winning or equal position into a losing or neutral one.

analysis.label: Player plays an aggressive-looking move (usually a check or capture with a minor piece) that leaves the moved piece hanging and unrecoverable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of activating positions result in the player's own piece being left hanging (median value 3.0), with the piece class distribution heavily favoring minor pieces (100 minor vs 38 major vs 5 pawn). 64% of the played moves are captures, and the majority deliver check (Bxf7+, Bxf2+, Rg7+, Bxd7+, Rd1+, Qh2+). Despite looking tactically aggressive, these moves leave the attacking piece en prise once the opponent deals with the check or recaptures. The best move wins material only 46% of the time, confirming this is primarily about hanging one's own piece rather than missing an opponent's hanging piece. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a specific tactical pattern of pseudo-sacrifices.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player delivers a check or capture expecting a forcing continuation (e.g., a follow-up tactic after the king moves), but the piece that delivered the check/capture simply ends up on a square where it is immediately captured with no compensation. The check buys one tempo but the piece has no escape square and no follow-up tactic justifies the material loss. The average cp_loss of 254 confirms these are full-piece blunders disguised as sacrifices.

analysis.label: Player ignores a freely capturable enemy Queen or Rook (typically on an open file) and plays a different move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 6.0, corresponding to a rook or queen capture), and 100% of the best moves are captures. Despite this obvious winning opportunity, the player's move was a capture only 39% of the time — meaning 61% of the time they played a quiet move entirely ignoring the hanging piece. Additionally, 74% of the time the player's own move left one of their pieces hanging (median value 2.0), compounding the error. The positions consistently feature open files (especially the d-file) where enemy major pieces sit exposed and capturable, yet the player becomes distracted by checks, developing moves, or less valuable captures.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a simple, high-value capture that would win decisive material (often a Queen worth 9 or Rook worth 5). Instead, the player pursues secondary ideas — flashy checks (Nc3+, Kf2+), positional moves (Be6, Rf1, Rc8), or inferior captures (exd5, gxf3) — while leaving their own pieces exposed. The result is typically a swing of hundreds or thousands of centipawns, often converting a winning or equal position into a lost one.

analysis.label: In the opening, the player makes a premature aggressive move (knight sortie, sacrifice, or ignoring a threat) that leaves their own minor piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 77% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly being minors (74 out of 92 instances). The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening (11/12 top boards). The best moves are never checks (2%) and rarely captures (9%), indicating the correct play was quiet development (Nc3, Nf3, Be7, Bd3, etc.). The played moves are flashy-looking attacks — knight checks (Nc7+), knight captures on f7/f2 (Nxf7, Nxf2), aggressive centralization (Ne5, Ne4, Nd5), or ignoring an existing threat to one's own bishop (a5, Ne5 with bishop on b5). In all cases the aggression is premature, and the minor piece is simply lost.
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they prioritize a superficially aggressive action (a check, a pawn grab, or a flashy knight jump) over basic piece safety. The knight sortie lands on a square where it is trapped or easily captured (Nc7+ gets stranded, Nxf7 has no escape), or the move ignores that another piece (often a bishop on b4 or b5) is already attacked by a pawn. The opponent simply captures the hanging minor piece, gaining material worth approximately 3 pawns while the 'attack' yields nothing concrete in return.

analysis.label: A natural-looking bishop development move in the opening that carelessly leaves the player's own material undefended or places the piece on a capturable square.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a seemingly standard bishop development move (or similar piece activation) that leaves their own material hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 73% of played moves left the player's own piece en prise (median value 1.0, split between pawns and minors), while 53% of positions had a best move that would have won material. Only 13% of played moves were captures, and the best move was almost never a check (0%) or capture (7%), meaning the correct alternative was usually a simple developing or prophylactic move. The feature activates almost exclusively in the opening (10/12 positions), where players choose active-looking bishop placements (Bg4, Bc5, Bb7, Bg5, Bb4, Bc4) without noticing that these moves either expose a previously defended pawn (e.g., b7 left unguarded after the c8-bishop moves) or place the bishop itself on a square where it can be immediately captured.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes general opening principles (develop pieces to active squares) over concrete calculation. The bishop moves look thematic—pinning a knight (Bg4/Bg5), fianchettoing (Bb7), or targeting a diagonal (Bc5/Bc4)—but each one either abandons a defensive duty (leaving a pawn like b7 unguarded against an opponent's queen on f3) or places the piece directly where it can be won by an existing attack. The opponent typically has a queen or piece already trained on the vulnerable square.

analysis.label: Player misses a forced checkmate or decisive winning continuation by playing a passive, irrelevant, or inferior move instead.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced mate or crushing winning attack available but fails to convert. The SEE aggregate shows that 71% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0 pawn), while the average cp_loss is an enormous 5567 centipawns—reflecting that 7 of the top 12 positions have literal forced checkmate (#+3, #+4, #-6, #-14) squandered into merely large advantages. In 42% of cases the played move also leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns:94, minors:58, majors:56), indicating the chosen moves are not only failing to win but are carelessly weakening the position. The best move is a check only 11% of the time and a capture just 23%, meaning the winning continuations are typically quiet but lethal moves (pawn advances like f6, queen redeployments like Qf6/Qg5) that initiate unstoppable mating nets rather than obvious forcing moves.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they squander a forced checkmate or decisive attack. Instead of delivering the killing blow—often a quiet but lethal move like f6 cutting off the king's escape, or Qg5/Qf6 creating an unstoppable mating net—the player makes irrelevant quiet moves (a6, h4, Kh2), captures secondary material (Nxh8, Kxh7, Rxc3), or repositions pieces to passive squares (Bd8, Qb2, Bf6). This converts positions with forced mate into merely large but non-decisive advantages.

analysis.label: The player avoids a clearly beneficial queen exchange, instead making a weaker move that often leaves their own pieces hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 100% of top-500 positions, yet wins material only 3% of the time (median value 1.0), meaning the best move is nearly always an equal queen trade. All 12 top-activating boards confirm the best move is a Qx__ exchange (Qxd5, Qxe6, Qxd3, Qxf6, Qxf5, Qxf3, Qxd6, Qxe4, Qxd4). Instead of taking the trade, the player makes a different move—often a quiet developing move, a check, or capturing a lesser piece—that leaves their own material hanging 59% of the time (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns: 125, majors: 116, minors: 54). The player's actual move was only a capture 17% of the time, showing they systematically avoid the simplifying exchange.
analysis.why_bad: By refusing the queen trade, the player leaves mutual queen tension unresolved in positions where their own king safety or piece coordination is inferior. The opponent's queen then exploits the player's vulnerabilities—hanging pieces, exposed kings, or underdeveloped positions—leading to an average centipawn loss of ~296. Trading queens would have neutralized the opponent's attacking potential and equalized or maintained the position.

analysis.label: Player fails to immediately promote an advanced passed pawn, typically playing a slow king move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 71% of positions with a median value of 5.0 (a full queen, consistent with pawn promotion). The player's move is rarely a capture (14%) and is almost always a quiet king move. Own-piece hanging is low at 29% (only pawns, median 1.0), ruling out a 'hung own piece' pattern. Across the top boards, positions 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7 all feature advanced passed pawns on the 7th rank where the best move is immediate promotion (g8=Q+, c8=Q, d7 advancing to promote), but the player instead temporizes with a king move (Kh7, Kxd2, Kc6, Kd7, or advances a different pawn with d6). The phase distribution (5/7 endgame) confirms these are late-game conversion situations with connected or advanced passers.
analysis.why_bad: Delaying promotion gives the opponent time to set up defensive resources (queen checks, rook captures of the promoting pawn, or even checkmate threats against the exposed king). In position 2, the delay costs an immediate mate (cp_loss 10001), and in position 3 it turns a winning position into a losing one (cp_loss 911). Even in positions 4-5-7 where the delay is near-harmless, the principle is the same: promoting immediately is cleanest and eliminates counterplay.

analysis.label: The player makes an active-looking move that leaves their own piece undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates this feature detects positions where the player's move leaves their own piece hanging: 76% of the top 500 positions show the played move left an own piece en prise (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece). The piece class distribution (major: 27, minor: 22, pawn: 18) shows bishops and knights are most commonly hung. While 65% of positions also had a best move that wins material (median 3.0), the dominant and most consistent signal is the self-inflicted tactical error of leaving one's own piece undefended. The played moves are often superficially active—checks (Bf8+, Nf3+), captures (Bxg6, fxe6), or piece development (Bg5, Bd6, Re1)—but each fatally neglects the safety of an existing piece, typically a bishop left on an unprotected square.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an active idea (giving check, making a capture, repositioning) without verifying that their existing pieces remain defended. The opponent can simply capture the hanging piece on the next move, gaining material. In many cases the player simultaneously misses a winning capture or recapture of their own, compounding the blunder into massive evaluation swings (avg cp_loss: 284).

analysis.label: Player ignores a necessary bishop capture (equal exchange) and plays a quiet move, often leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 95% of activating positions the best move is a capture, yet these captures win only 0 material (SEE=0) in the vast majority of cases—meaning they are equal exchanges rather than material wins (only 11% actually win material). Crucially, 60% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/minors/majors roughly evenly: 112/101/85). Examining the top 12 boards reveals the best move is almost universally a bishop capture (Bxf3, Bxd5, Bxd6, Bxb6, Bxc5, Bxd4) representing a forced or necessary exchange. The player instead plays a quiet non-capturing move, failing to execute this obligatory trade.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the necessary bishop exchange, the player leaves their own pieces (often the bishop itself or a piece it was defending/shielding) tactically vulnerable. The opponent can then exploit the unresolved tension to win material—frequently capturing the very piece that should have traded. The quiet move fails to address the immediate tactical obligation, converting an equal exchange into a material loss.

analysis.label: Player misses capturing an undefended enemy queen, instead playing a quiet king move that often leaves their own queen en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 85% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (queen), and 85% of best moves are captures. Simultaneously, 83% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging with a median value of 9 (queen). This dual signature arises because positions feature mutual queen-takes-queen geometry: the enemy queen is undefended and capturable, but the player fails to take it. By not capturing the enemy queen, the player's own queen remains en prise. The own-hang piece distribution (major: 36, pawn: 17, minor: 9) confirms queens dominate. Only 16% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead of the winning capture.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (almost exclusively king moves like Kc8, Kb7, Kh7, Kf5, Kf7, Kc2, Kh2, Kh6) ignore that the enemy queen is completely undefended and capturable. By failing to take the free enemy queen, the player not only forfeits decisive material gain but typically leaves their own queen hanging, resulting in catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss: 5055). The player seems fixated on king safety/activity while blind to the elementary tactic of capturing an undefended queen.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing move instead of an available winning capture, simultaneously leaving their own piece undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player ignores an urgent tactical capture to play a passive or developing quiet move. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 84% of the time (winning material 47% of the time with a median gain of 6.0 — often a full piece or more), yet the player's move was a capture only 20% of the time. Critically, in 70% of positions the player's quiet move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with minor pieces comprising 48/91 of hung pieces, pawns 33/91, and majors 10/91). The pattern often involves tactical tension (e.g., a pawn that can capture a knight on c3, or a piece that can take an undefended enemy piece) where the player must resolve the tension NOW with a capture, but instead plays a repositioning move (a6, Bc5, f6, Nc3, Be7, etc.) that both forfeits the winning capture and leaves their own material en prise.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore immediate tactical obligations. The position has tension requiring resolution via capture — either a pawn can take a piece (dxc3, exf6, exd6, cxb6), or a piece can capture an undefended enemy piece (Nxg8, Nxe4, Bxe2). By playing a quiet move instead, the player not only misses free material but often leaves the very piece that should have captured (or another piece) undefended, turning a winning position into a lost one (average cp_loss of 508).

analysis.label: The player ignores an undefended enemy piece that is trivially capturable, instead playing a quiet developing or autopilot move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates missed captures: 83% of best moves win material (median value 3.0 pawns), and 92% of best moves are simple captures, yet the player's move is a capture only 6% of the time. The player consistently plays quiet 'autopilot' moves—castling, pawn pushes, piece development—while an enemy piece sits undefended in plain sight. As a secondary consequence, 63% of the quiet moves played also leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0), compounding the blunder. The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase (10/12 top positions), where one side makes an aggressive incursion (e.g., a queen or bishop deep in enemy territory) and the opponent simply ignores it.
analysis.why_bad: By playing routine developing moves instead of capturing the free enemy piece, the player forfeits material (typically a full minor piece or more) and often simultaneously leaves their own pieces undefended, leading to catastrophic evaluation swings averaging over 1300 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player develops a piece instead of making a free central pawn capture, often leaving the developed piece en prise to the unresolved pawn tension.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where a simple central pawn capture (dxe4, dxe5, exd5, dxc4) wins material, but the player instead develops a piece—typically a bishop to f4, f5, g5, or c4. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 73% of cases (median 1 pawn) and is a capture 89% of the time, while the player's move left their own piece hanging in 78% of cases (median value 1.0, distribution: 50 pawns, 24 minors, 2 majors). Only 4% of played moves were captures. The dual signature—both missing a free capture AND hanging one's own piece—arises because the unresolved central tension leaves the newly developed piece (or an existing pawn) tactically exposed. For instance, playing Bf4 while ...e5 attacks it, or playing Bf5 while the d-pawn could have safely captured on e4.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore free material (a central pawn capture worth at least one pawn) while simultaneously placing or leaving a piece on a square where it is en prise due to the very pawn tension that should have been resolved. The player loses tempo and material by prioritizing development over a simple winning capture, often resulting in a 400-600 centipawn swing.

analysis.label: Player missed a devastating knight fork with check that wins material by simultaneously attacking the king and an undefended piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a knight fork delivering check (99% of best moves are checks, 88% win material with a median value of 3.0). The best move is a capture in 64% of cases — typically the knight captures a pawn on c2, c7, or f7 with check, simultaneously forking the king and a rook or other major piece. Only 20% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet developing moves instead of the tactical shot. The 48% own-hang rate on the played move reflects that these suboptimal alternatives often leave pieces loose, compounding the error. The feature fires heavily in the opening (9/12 top positions) where uncastled kings on e1/e8 create classic Nxc2+/Nxc7+/Nxf7+ fork geometries against corner rooks.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Be6, Qe7, e6, f4, c4, Bd3, Nf6, etc.) are typically slow developing or positional moves that completely miss a forcing tactical sequence. By not playing the knight fork with check, the player surrenders a winning advantage (avg ~300cp loss) — the opponent's exposed king and undefended rook created an immediate winning combination that cannot be exploited later once the opponent castles or consolidates.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture/exchange a dominant enemy piece on a central square (d4/d5/e4/e5), instead making an inferior move that often hangs their own minor piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 97% of positions the best move is a capture (with SEE = 0, i.e., an even exchange), yet only 15% of played moves were captures. The best move consistently involves taking an enemy piece sitting on a powerful central square (Nxd5, Nxd4, Nxe4, Nxe5, Bxd4, Bxe5). Meanwhile, 49% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution heavily weighted toward minor pieces (52 minor, 26 pawn, 15 major). Only 7% of best moves actually win material outright—indicating the correct capture is an equal exchange that simply eliminates a dominant enemy outpost. The feature fires in early opening positions (10/12) where one side has established a powerful centralized knight or bishop that the opponent neglects to neutralize.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the enemy's dominant centralized piece (typically a knight on d4/d5), the player allows it to remain as a tactical anchor generating threats (forks, discovered attacks, pressure on weak squares). The alternative moves chosen—aggressive knight leaps (Ng5, Ng4, Nh5), pawn pushes (b4, g4), or passive retreats (Nd1)—often leave the player's own pieces tactically loose, and the unchallenged central piece then exploits these weaknesses to win material.

analysis.label: Player makes a routine developing move instead of a tactical shot (often a queen check on the e-file or a bishop diagonal) that wins an undefended rook.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 95% of positions have a best move winning material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), while the played move is overwhelmingly quiet (only 21% captures). Only 10% of best moves are checks and 27% are captures, indicating a mix of direct captures and indirect tactics (forks, discovered attacks) that win rooks. The own-hang rate of 34% is secondary noise. Across the top boards, the recurring geometry involves an undefended rook sitting on a1 or a8, attackable via a long diagonal (Be4 hitting Ra8) or via an e-file queen check (Qe5+/Qe4+) that forks the enemy king in the center with the corner rook. The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening (10/12 boards) where kings remain centralized and rooks haven't been connected, making them vulnerable to long-range tactical strikes.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet developing moves (castling, piece development, pawn pushes) ignore a concrete tactical opportunity to win a full rook. The player prioritizes routine development or king safety over a forcing sequence—typically a queen check on the open e-file forking king and rook, or a bishop sliding to a long diagonal targeting an unprotected rook on a1/a8. The missed tactic is often a one-move shot with an immediate material gain of ~5 points.

analysis.label: The queen greedily captures a piece but lands on a square where it is en prise and lost.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 100% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging after the move (median value 9.0, all 500 cases classified as 'major' = queen), while 92% of the played moves are captures. In 79% of cases, a better move existed that would win material (median value 3.0), often via a check (30%) or different capture (40%). The pattern is unmistakable: the player's queen takes a pawn or minor piece but lands on an undefended square where it can be recaptured or trapped, sacrificing the queen for far less material. All 12 top-activating boards show Qx__ moves (Qxd4, Qxf6, Qxb4, Qxd5, Qxe4, Qxc4, Qxc5, Qxd6, Qxg4) where the queen is immediately lost after the capture, with an average centipawn loss of 1097.
analysis.why_bad: The queen captures a piece (typically a pawn or minor piece worth 1-3 points) but moves to a square where it is undefended and can be immediately recaptured by an enemy piece, effectively losing the queen (9 points) for trivial material. The player was lured by the available capture and failed to notice the queen would be hanging, when instead a superior move—often a check, a different capture, or a quiet retreat—would have maintained or increased the advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes an active-looking move that inadvertently leaves one of their own pieces undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 89% of the top 500 activating positions show the player's move leaving their own piece en prise (median value 3.0). The hung pieces are distributed across minor pieces (191), major pieces (188), and pawns (65), indicating no single piece type but a general failure to maintain defensive coverage. While 51% of positions also feature best moves that win material, this reflects the opponent exploiting the newly hanging piece. The player's move was a capture only 35% of the time, meaning most blunders are quiet moves that abandon a defensive duty. The feature fires on 2.7% of all positions with an average centipawn loss of 252.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an active plan (developing, attacking, capturing) while removing a piece from a defensive assignment, leaving another piece unguarded. For example: Rf5 leaves the rook capturable (position 6), Qf3 abandons defense of a rook (position 7), Bxe6 removes a bishop that was shielding the queen (position 8), Nf6 leaves a knight en prise (position 2). The opponent simply captures the undefended piece for free or with favorable exchange.

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player makes a passive/aimless rook move instead of the critical concrete action (usually king activation, a capture, or a pawn push).
analysis.description: This feature fires on rook endgame positions where the player makes a quiet, positionally aimless rook move when a concrete decisive action was available. The SEE aggregate shows best_wins_material at 45% (median value 1.0), indicating that nearly half the time a piece or pawn was winnable. The played move was a capture only 13% of the time, and own-hang rate is a modest 19%. Across the top 12 boards, 9 of 12 played moves are rook moves to passive squares, while the best move was overwhelmingly a king move (7/12), a pawn push, or a rook capture. The feature fires on only 0.2% of positions, targeting specifically critical endgame moments where routine rook maneuvering squanders a concrete opportunity—whether capturing an undefended piece (Position 3: Rxg6), avoiding a catastrophic rook exchange via king retreat (Position 7: Ke6), or activating the king decisively (Positions 2, 4, 6, 10, 11).
analysis.why_bad: These passive rook moves fail because in rook endgames, king activity and concrete actions (captures, pawn pushes, avoiding forced exchanges) are paramount. By shuffling the rook aimlessly, the player misses winning material outright (e.g., capturing an undefended rook on g6), allows devastating rook exchanges that convert to lost pawn endgames (e.g., Rc7 walking into Rxc7), or neglects king centralization that decides the game. The average cp_loss of 366 reflects how these single passive moves convert winning/drawn positions into losses.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive or routine move, missing a quiet (non-capture, non-check) tactical move that wins significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet only 8% of best moves are captures and only 4% are checks—meaning ~88% of the winning moves are quiet tactical blows (threats, piece penetrations, forks, traps). The player's actual move is also overwhelmingly quiet (only 16% captures) and usually doesn't even hang their own material (only 36% leave something en prise, median just a pawn). The player simply fails to recognize the available quiet tactical shot—rook penetrations to the 7th rank (Rd7, Ra1), knight forks/jumps (Ng6, Nb4), pawn thrusts that trap pieces (c5), or bishop attacks (Bg5)—and instead plays a developmental, retreating, or repositioning move that squanders the tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are bad because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity where a quiet move (not an obvious capture or check) wins material by creating an unavoidable threat—such as attacking an undefended piece, penetrating with a rook, setting up a fork, or trapping a high-value piece. The played moves are passive or routine (retreats like Ng8, developments like Bd2/Bd3, repositioning like Re8) that allow the opponent to consolidate and eliminate the tactical vulnerability.

analysis.label: The player has a pawn on the 7th (or 2nd) rank ready to promote but plays a temporizing move instead of queening immediately.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 62% of activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 5.0—consistent with promoting a pawn to a queen (net gain ≈ queen minus pawn). Only 12% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks, confirming the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet promotion. The played moves are almost entirely quiet king moves or secondary pawn pushes (only 12% captures). The 38% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, exclusively pawns) reflects that delaying promotion sometimes leaves the promotable pawn or a supporting pawn en prise to the opponent. Across the top 8 boards, 6 out of 8 positions feature a pawn one square from queening (c7→c8=Q, f2→f1=Q, f7→f8=Q, b2→b1=Q) where the player instead played a king move or pushed a different pawn.
analysis.why_bad: Delaying promotion allows the opponent time to bring defensive pieces (usually a rook) into contact with the promoting square, to capture the pawn, or to generate counterplay. In the worst case (Position 6, cp_loss 1067), promoting immediately wins trivially while the temporizing move allows the opponent's bishop to permanently block the dark-square promotion, turning a winning position into a draw.

analysis.label: A knight makes a tempting capture but leaves itself or a more valuable piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player's move left their own piece hanging (92%, median value 3.0), and the move was itself a capture 71% of the time. The hung piece class is predominantly minor pieces (51 minor vs 22 major vs 6 pawns), consistent with the knight that just captured landing on an undefended square, or occasionally the knight's departure removing protection from a queen or rook. The best move wins material only 45% of the time (median 3.0), often by addressing an immediate threat (like h3 kicking a pinning bishop) or making a superior exchange (like Qxd8+ trading queens before the tactic is lost). The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening (8/12 top boards) with both kings in the center, where rapid tactical punishment is available.
analysis.why_bad: The knight capture looks attractive because it grabs material, but it either lands on a square where it has no defenders and is immediately recaptured for free, or by moving the knight, it abandons a critical defensive duty (e.g., blocking a pin on the queen from a bishop on g4, or leaving the back rank vulnerable to a queen trade that then wins the displaced knight). The net result is typically a loss of a full piece (~3 pawns) or more.

analysis.label: Player greedily captures with a rook while an enemy pawn one square from promotion is ignored, leaving the rook hanging to the newly-promoted queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 99% of fired moves are captures, and 97% leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5 = rook), with 82 out of 88 hung pieces being major pieces (rooks). Across all 12 top-activating positions, the player plays a rook capture (Rxg1, Rxb1, Rxe1, Rxc1, Rxb8, Rxf8, Rxe8, Rxa8, Rxd1) while the opponent has a critically advanced passed pawn one square from promotion (d2, c2, f2, g7, b7, etc.). The best move (62% win material, median 1.0) typically addresses the promotion threat via king moves, blockades, or prophylaxis rather than grabbing material. The average cp_loss of 4849 reflects that these greedy captures almost always result in immediate mate or decisive material loss once the pawn promotes.
analysis.why_bad: By capturing with the rook, the player removes it from defensive duties (blocking or controlling the promotion square). The enemy pawn then promotes to a queen, which immediately captures the now-undefended rook on its new square. The player trades a rook capture (typically winning a minor piece or pawn worth 1-3) but loses the entire rook (worth 5) to the new queen, resulting in catastrophic net material loss or immediate checkmate.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but pointless queen check, missing a stronger move that wins material or delivers checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 66% of activating positions the best move wins material (median 3.0 pawns), yet only 20% of best moves are themselves checks—meaning the player's habitual queen check is almost always the wrong idea. The played move is overwhelmingly a queen check (11/12 top boards show queen moves, mostly with '+'), while the superior alternative is typically a quiet or non-check move. In 46% of cases the premature check even leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns/majors/minors), often because the queen lands on an exposed square after the king simply steps away. Only 29% of played moves are captures, confirming these are mostly non-productive intermezzo-style checks rather than forcing sequences.
analysis.why_bad: A pointless queen check allows the opponent's king to move to a safe square (often improving its position), wastes tempo, and frequently leaves the queen or another piece vulnerable. Meanwhile, the player misses concrete winning moves—capturing hanging pieces, executing decisive tactical blows, or even delivering checkmate (positions 11 and 12 miss mate). The check gives the illusion of initiative but actually surrenders it.

analysis.label: Player's knight prematurely captures the e-pawn in the opening, leaving it hanging to immediate recapture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being minor pieces (205/218). The player's move is a capture 78% of the time, and all 12 top-activating positions occur in the opening phase. The pattern is a knight (or rarely bishop) greedily grabbing the undefended e-pawn (e4 or e5) before proper preparation, landing on a square where it is immediately recapturable or tactically exploitable. The best moves (Bb5, Bc4, d3, d5, Nc6, etc.) are all quiet developing moves that maintain the center rather than prematurely snapping off a pawn.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures the e-pawn before the position supports it. In classic openings (Four Knights, Vienna, Scotch, etc.), Nxe5 or Nxe4 looks like a free pawn but the knight lands en prise — the opponent immediately recaptures (e.g., ...Nxe4 after Nxe5 Nxe5) or plays a discovered/fork idea that wins the knight outright. The player loses a 3-point piece to gain only a 1-point pawn, resulting in a net loss of ~2 points, exactly matching the typical cp_loss of ~284.

analysis.label: Player makes an opening move that leaves their own queen en prise to an enemy minor piece or pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 95% of activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 9 (queen) and the piece class distribution dominated by major pieces (117/126). All 12 top-activating positions are in the opening phase. The pattern manifests in two ways: (1) moving the queen to an exposed square (Qg5, Qh5, Qh4, Qf6, Qc5, Qxh7) where it can be immediately captured by a developed minor piece or pawn, or (2) ignoring an existing attack on the queen (e3, e6, Nf6 when the queen is already attacked by Nc3). Only 26% of best moves win material and only 16% are captures, confirming the main issue is not a missed tactic but rather the player blundering their own queen.
analysis.why_bad: These moves either place the queen on an undefended square within striking range of enemy pieces (especially knights and bishops that can attack it with tempo), or completely ignore an existing attack on the queen. In the opening, with so many minor pieces able to develop with tempo against an exposed queen, these moves result in immediate queen loss (~9 points of material), turning a roughly equal position into a decisive disadvantage.

analysis.label: The player gives a pointless check (usually with a rook) that leaves the checking piece undefended and capturable after the king escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 88% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with major pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (112 major vs 62 minor vs 42 pawn). Crucially, 0% of best moves are checks, yet 11 of the top 12 activating moves ARE checks — confirming the pattern of impulsive, purposeless checks. Only 34% of played moves are captures, meaning many are quiet checks that simply place the piece in danger. The best move wins material only 37% of the time, indicating the correct continuation is usually a calm repositioning move (e.g., Rc3, Rh5, Be7, Rd7, Re8, Rf1, Rg1), not a tactical shot.
analysis.why_bad: The check forces the king to a safe square (or is blocked), after which the checking piece — typically a rook placed on the back rank or an exposed file — has no defender and is simply captured. The player gains one tempo of check but loses an entire piece. The average cp_loss of 2336 reflects that these are game-ending blunders where a rook or queen is donated for nothing.

analysis.label: Player gives an aggressive check (usually a Queen check) that leaves their own piece—often the Queen itself—hanging and undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 83% of the top 500 activating positions see the player's move leave their own piece en prise (median value 3.0, with roughly equal distribution across minor: 24, major: 23, pawn: 22 piece classes). Only 20% of played moves are captures and only 1% of best moves are checks, yet the top 12 boards overwhelmingly show the player choosing a Queen check (Qh5+, Qh7+, Qh8+, Qb4+) when the best move is a quiet retreat or consolidation (Qf2, Qh3, Rad1, Qxd5). The checking Queen ends up trapped or capturable (own hung after: 9 in most top cases), often leading to forced mate against the player. The average cp_loss of 5211 confirms these are catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The checks look aggressive and force the opponent's king to move, but they accomplish nothing constructive. After the king sidesteps, the checking piece (usually the Queen) is left en prise with no escape square, or the check allows the opponent to consolidate a winning attack. The player was seduced by the forcing nature of a check instead of playing the only viable defensive or positional move.

analysis.label: Playing a pointless Qa5+ or Qa4+ check against the opponent's uncastled king, which accomplishes nothing while often leaving own pieces hanging.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player impulsively delivers a queen check (Qa5+ or Qa4+) targeting an uncastled king on e1, but the check is easily blocked or evaded and achieves no lasting benefit. The SEE aggregate shows that in 58% of the top 500 activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0 pawns), meaning the player missed a concrete winning opportunity. Simultaneously, in 56% of cases the played queen check leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the distribution across minor pieces (92), pawns (65), and major pieces (59) — indicating the queen's departure from its prior square removes critical defensive coverage. The played move was a capture only 10% of the time, confirming the checks are non-forcing quiet moves. The best move was a check in only 7% of cases, showing that the correct continuation was almost never another check but rather a developing, capturing, or consolidating move.
analysis.why_bad: These queen checks look aggressive but are easily parried (the king steps aside, a piece interposes, or the queen is chased with tempo). Meanwhile, by moving the queen to the a-file, the player abandons defense of their own pieces — particularly knights and bishops that were previously protected by the queen's scope — leaving them en prise. The check wastes a critical tempo in the opening, allowing the opponent to develop with threats while the queen must retreat, often resulting in a lost piece or a completely collapsed position.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move (usually a king move) while an undefended enemy piece sits freely capturable on the board.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly identifies this as a 'missed winning capture' pattern: 70% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), and the best move is a capture in 76% of cases, yet the player's actual move was a capture only 7% of the time. Own-piece hanging is low at 21% (median value just 1.0 — a pawn). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the player overlooks a completely undefended enemy piece (rooks, queens, pawns) that can be taken for free — often by a bishop along an open diagonal — and instead plays a passive quiet move, most commonly a king retreat (Ke7, Kf8, Kh3, Kg7 appear repeatedly). All positions occur in the endgame where piece counts are low and the hanging piece should be easy to spot.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave a massive material gain on the table. In every case, the opponent has left a piece completely undefended and the player can simply capture it for free (e.g., Bxc6 winning a rook, Nxd4 winning a queen, Qxe3 winning a queen). Instead, the player makes a purposeless or slow positional move — typically a king walk — transforming a trivially won position into something drawn or even lost. The quiet move gains nothing meaningful while the free capture would have ended the game immediately.

analysis.label: Player missed a winning check (often checkmate) exploiting an open diagonal to the opponent's exposed king in the opening.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a devastating check—usually along a wide-open diagonal aimed at the enemy king stuck in the center. The SEE aggregate shows 92% of best moves win material (median value 91, representing queen-level gains or checkmate), 85% of best moves are checks, and only 26% are captures, confirming that the winning blow is typically a non-capturing check that either mates or wins heavy material. The player's own move is almost never a capture (6%) and rarely hangs material (10%, median 1.0), indicating they play quiet developing moves instead of the killer blow. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, highlighting how rare yet critical these opportunities are.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Ne7, Nf3, Be7, b6, g4, etc.) are slow, quiet developing or pawn moves that completely ignore the opponent's fatally exposed king. In each case, the king sits in the center with a wide-open diagonal (typically d8-h4 or d1-h5) unguarded by any pawn or piece. The correct move—usually Qh4+, Qh5+, Bg6#, or Bg3+—delivers immediate checkmate or wins decisive material through a forcing check. By playing routine development instead, the player squanders a winning tactical shot that may never recur.

analysis.label: Player delays or ignores an immediately available pawn promotion (usually to queen), choosing instead a check, king move, or rook maneuver.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 73% of best moves win material with a median value of 5.0 (consistent with the net gain of promoting a pawn to a queen), and 66% of best moves are captures or promotions. Only 18% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet alternatives. The feature fires in endgame positions (100% of top 12) where a pawn sits on the 7th rank ready to promote. In 10 of the top 12 boards, the best move is an explicit pawn promotion (a8=Q, c8=Q, h8=Q, e1=Q+). Instead of promoting, players gave rook checks (Rb5+, Rb6+, Rg2+), made king moves (Kh1, Kf5, Kd7, Kc6, Ke3), or played other pawn/rook moves (d6, Ra6, Rxg7+). The 45% own-hang rate (median value 3.0) is a secondary consequence—by not promoting, the player sometimes leaves pawns or pieces tactically vulnerable on the next move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they forgo an immediately decisive pawn promotion that would create a new queen and typically win by overwhelming material advantage. Giving checks or making king moves merely prolongs the game (or worse, throws away the win entirely), since the opponent can use the extra tempo to reposition their rook to block or capture the would-be promoted pawn. In several cases (Positions 3, 7, 10, 11), the delay converts a forced mate or trivial win into a drawn or losing position.

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece with a rook or queen, but the capturing piece lands on a square where it is left hanging and can be won back with interest.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a highly consistent pattern: 96% of the time the player's move is a capture, and 98% of the time that move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 5, i.e., a rook). The hung piece is a major piece (rook or queen) in 77 of 92 cases. Meanwhile, 77% of the time the best move wins material (median 91 centipawns won), and 45% of best moves are checks — indicating the player missed a stronger tactical continuation (often a check-then-capture sequence) in favor of a greedy but self-destructive capture. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific catastrophic error pattern with an average cp_loss of 1115.
analysis.why_bad: The player is lured by an available capture (usually taking a pawn or minor piece) but fails to notice that the destination square is attacked or that the opponent gains a tempo (often via check or counter-threat) to win the now-undefended major piece. The net result is a massive material loss — typically trading a rook or queen for a pawn or minor piece — when a safer move (frequently a check) would have maintained or increased the advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores a critical capture (usually an even exchange or recapture) and plays a quiet move that leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 92% of cases, yet only 18% of those actually win material on SEE (median 3.0 when they do), meaning ~74% are equal exchanges or recaptures that are tactically forced. The player's move is a capture only 7% of the time—they overwhelmingly play quiet moves instead. Crucially, 59% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed across majors (31), pawns (31), and minors (17). The enormous average cp_loss of 3203 confirms these aren't optional captures—they're tactically essential. The pattern across the top boards is consistent: the best move takes an opponent's piece (often SEE=0, indicating equal trade), but the player plays a king move, pawn push, or other quiet move, thereby leaving their queen, rook, or other piece undefended.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to make the required capture—whether a recapture after an opponent's take or a necessary exchange of attacked pieces—the player leaves their own material unprotected. The opponent then simply takes the hanging piece on the next move. In many cases (positions 4, 5, 7, 9) this leads to immediate mate or decisive material loss because the ignored capture was the only way to maintain piece coordination and material balance.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move (usually a king move in an endgame) instead of simply capturing an undefended enemy rook or major piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 88% of the top 500 activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 91% of the time the best move is a capture—yet only 15% of the moves actually played were captures. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top boards) where an enemy rook (or occasionally queen) is sitting en prise to a pawn capture (hxg3, gxf3, axb4, fxe6) or a king capture (Kxd6, Kxc5, Kxc3, Kxa2). The 64% own-hang rate (median value 3.0) reflects that the quiet moves played often also leave the player's own pieces undefended, compounding the error, but the primary and consistent mistake is ignoring the freely capturable enemy major piece.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (overwhelmingly king retreats or repositioning moves) fail because they pass up a free capture of a major piece—typically a rook worth 5 points of material—that is completely undefended. By not taking the hanging piece, the player forfeits a massive material gain (or loss reduction) that would drastically change the evaluation, often converting a lost position into a drawable one or throwing away a winning one.

analysis.label: In won king-and-pawn endgames, the player advances a pawn instead of using precise king infiltration to win material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 75% of the time the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), yet the played move is almost never a capture (2%) and rarely hangs own material (8%). The best move is also rarely a check (6%) or capture (2%), indicating the winning material is achieved indirectly—through king maneuvering to win pawns. Across all 12 top-activating positions (100% endgame, avg cp_loss 436), the player pushes a pawn (h5, g4, g5, b4, b5, f4+) or moves the king in the wrong direction (Kf4, Kf5, Kg4) when the best move is a king infiltration (Kh3, Kh6, Kb2, Kb3, Kc7, Kd3) that wins an enemy pawn through superior positioning.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, premature pawn advances squander critical tempi and often allow the opponent's king to reach a drawing position. The correct technique requires the king to lead the pawns—infiltrating to win enemy pawns or achieve zugzwang—before committing to pawn pushes. Pushing pawns first frequently allows the opponent to achieve opposition or a fortress, converting a won position into a draw.

analysis.label: Player repositions their queen with a quiet move instead of executing an available tactical capture, often simultaneously leaving their own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of best moves are captures (median value won 5.0) while only 15% of played moves are captures, indicating the player consistently misses concrete tactical strikes. Simultaneously, 60% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minors: 137, pawns: 99, majors: 64), suggesting the queen was often defending something before being moved away. The pattern across the top 12 boards is stark: 10 of 12 played moves are queen moves (Qc7, Qf2, Qb6, Qe2, Qb7, Qb4, Qd1, Qb6, Qb2), while the best moves are almost exclusively tactical captures (Bxf3, dxe4, Nxe6, exf3, Nxc6, Bxf6, dxc4) — many exploiting pins on knights at f3/f6 or capturing loose material.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet queen moves fail because they ignore concrete tactical opportunities (captures winning material, pin exploitation) that are immediately available. By moving the queen to a different square for vague positional reasons, the player both forfeits material gain and frequently removes the queen's defensive coverage from their own pieces, compounding the error into a double-blunder that loses significant evaluation (average 230cp loss).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move (often a king move) in an endgame while an undefended enemy piece worth major material sits available for simple capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'missed capture' pattern: 84% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, i.e. rook/queen-level), and 81% of best moves are captures, yet only 12% of the actually-played moves were captures. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top boards), where pieces are spread across the board and undefended enemy pieces go unnoticed. The 50% own-hung rate (median 3.0) is a secondary effect—when a player makes a purposeless quiet move instead of the correct capture, they sometimes also leave their own material exposed. The own-hang class distribution (major: 114, pawn: 100, minor: 34) reflects typical endgame piece arrays. The feature fires on only 0.5% of positions, indicating these are severe oversights rather than common tactical misses.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (mostly king retreats, pawn pushes, or aimless queen moves) waste a tempo doing nothing productive while leaving a completely free capture on the board. In the endgame, losing a full piece (or more—median 5 points) of material is almost always immediately decisive. The average centipawn loss of 2755 confirms these moves frequently convert winning positions into draws or losses.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free capture worth ~5 points and instead plays a quiet move (often a king move) that additionally leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 79% of activating positions, the best move wins material via capture (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and the best move is a capture in 95% of cases. However, the player's move was a capture only 18% of the time—they overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead. Additionally, 64% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung pieces distributed across pawns (48), major pieces (37), and minor pieces (22). This compound error—missing a straightforward winning capture while simultaneously creating a new vulnerability—is the signature pattern. The top boards confirm this: best moves like Bxd7, Rxe3, Bxe6, Rxc8 are simple captures of undefended enemy pieces, but players instead chose king moves (Kc4, Kb3, Kb5, Kg6, Kg3) or aimless pawn pushes that ignored the tactic entirely.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (predominantly king retreats or pawn pushes) fail because they ignore an immediately available capture that wins a full rook or equivalent. By playing a passive move instead of taking free material, the player not only forgoes a decisive material advantage but often moves their king to a square that leaves another piece undefended, compounding the error by both missing a win and creating a new weakness.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture (usually with a minor piece) that leaves the capturing piece undefended and en prise on its destination square.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes an alluring capture that leaves their own piece hanging. The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of played moves are captures, and 100% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece). The hung-piece distribution confirms 75% are minors (bishops/knights), 20% majors, and 5% pawns. Meanwhile, 58% of the time the best move wins material (median 2.0) through a superior tactical path — often a quiet repositioning move, a fork, or a check — that avoids leaving anything en prise. The best move is only a capture 23% of the time, showing that the correct approach usually involves a non-capturing tactical idea rather than a direct material grab.
analysis.why_bad: These captures are bad because the piece lands on an undefended square where it can be recaptured, leading to a net material loss or squandering of a decisive advantage. The player is drawn to the immediate material gain (taking a pawn or piece) but overlooks that the opponent can simply recapture the now-hanging piece. The better move typically wins material cleanly through geometry (forks, discovered attacks, intermediate moves) or maintains a crushing positional advantage without gifting the opponent a free recapture.

analysis.label: Player misses a devastating knight capture on f7 (or f2) exploiting the opponent's uncastled king.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player has a powerful Nxf7 (or Nxf2 for Black) knight strike available but plays a quiet move instead. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 92% of cases, yet the player's move was a capture only 16% of the time—overwhelmingly quiet, passive alternatives were chosen. The best move 'wins 0' by static exchange (the knight is recaptured), explaining the modest 31% 'wins material' rate (median 1.0), but the true value lies in king exposure, forks, and devastating attacks against the uncastled king. In 38% of cases the played move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, mostly minors at 73 instances), compounding the error. All 12 top-activating positions feature an uncastled enemy king on e8 (or e1) with a knight poised to strike f7 (or f2), the classic weak square defended only by the king.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves played (a3, Qb6, Bh2, O-O, Ndf3, etc.) squander a critical tactical window: Nxf7/Nxf2 exposes the uncastled king to devastating follow-ups (forks, discovered attacks, mating nets) that yield far more than the nominal piece exchange. By playing passively, the player allows the opponent to castle or regroup, permanently closing the tactical window and converting a winning attack into an equal or losing position.

analysis.label: Player ignores capturing an opponent's bishop aggressively posted against their fianchetto, allowing a dangerous attacking setup to persist.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 94% of cases, yet wins material only 16% of the time (median 3.0 when it does), indicating the critical best move is overwhelmingly an equal-value trade (bishop for bishop, SEE=0). The player's actual move left their own piece hanging 39% of the time (median value 2.0). Across the top 12 boards, 9 of 12 show the best move as Bxh6 or Bxh3—trading off an opponent's bishop that is aggressively placed against the player's fianchettoed structure (typically White's Bh6 vs Black's Bg7, or Black's Bh3 vs White's Bg2). Instead of making this critical defensive trade, the player plays an unrelated move (a5, b5, a6, Qb6, etc.) or a greedy capture elsewhere (Bxa2, Nxf2), allowing the opponent's bishop to persist in a dominating attacking posture.
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's bishop on h6 (or h3/g5) is a key attacking piece aimed at the fianchetto king shelter. Failing to trade it off allows the opponent to maintain crushing pressure on the weakened dark (or light) squares around the castled king. The ignored trade costs an average of 307cp because the persisting bishop enables mating attacks, piece coordination, and pawn breaks (like hxg6) that crack open the king position.

analysis.label: Player missed a knight capture (Nxe5/Nxe4/Nxd5/etc.) that wins material through tactics, playing a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best move is a capture 85% of the time, yet individual position SEE values for the knight captures are 0 (appearing to break even). This indicates the knight captures win through deeper tactics (forks, discovered attacks) beyond what static exchange detects. Only 25% of best moves directly win material by SEE (median 3.0 = minor piece), meaning 75% profit through follow-up tactics. The played moves were captures only 8% of the time — players chose passive developing moves (O-O, Bd7, Nge2, a6, Qd2) instead of the critical tactical blow. The 32% own-hang rate (median 2.0) suggests the quiet moves also sometimes left pieces loose, compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores a knight capture into the center (typically Nxe5, Nxe4, or Nxd5) that appears to break even on simple piece counting but actually wins material through tactical motifs like forks, pins, or discovered attacks after recapture. By playing routine developing/quiet moves, the player loses the window for this concrete tactic, often suffering 200-400 centipawn losses.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive rook penetration or capture that wins significant material, instead playing a distracted or passive alternative move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 82% of the time the best move wins material (median value 4.0, i.e., a whole piece or rook), yet the player's move was a capture only 17% of the time — indicating the player consistently failed to execute the winning blow. In 47% of cases the played move also left an own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 80/111 cases), compounding the error. Across the top 12 boards, 11 of 12 best moves are rook moves (Re2, Rb2, Rd7, Rc2, Rxg3, Rxf3, Rxf5, Rf6, Rg8, Rg6-intended-Re2) that penetrate to the 2nd/7th rank along open files or capture undefended pieces. The positions consistently feature open files with rooks already aligned, making the invasion immediately available. The best move is a check only 6% of the time and a capture 30%, meaning the winning rook move is often a quiet infiltration rather than an obvious tactical shot.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore the rook's decisive potential on an open file or rank. Instead, players get distracted by pawn grabs (Qxb3, fxg6), pointless checks (Qd5+), passive repositioning (Rc1, Rc5, Rg6), or slow plans (g5, e5, d5, h3, Kf1). These moves squander a position where an immediate rook invasion wins a piece or more, often by penetrating to the 7th/2nd rank to attack the opponent's queen, undefended pieces, or create unstoppable threats.
