analysis.label: Player captures on d4/d5 with a knight (or abandons its protection), leaving it hanging undefended in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 97% of positions leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 215/226 cases (95% knights). The moves are captures 34% of the time (mostly Nxd5 or Nxd4), the phase is overwhelmingly opening (11/12 top boards), and the feature fires on only 0.1% of all positions. The specific geometry is consistent: a knight lands on or remains on a central square (d4 or d5) without adequate protection. In several cases (Positions 2, 4), the king retreats from f7 to e8, abandoning its defense of a knight on d5. In most others (Positions 3, 5-8, 10-11), the knight itself captures a pawn on d4/d5 and becomes immediately undefended. These arise predominantly in Italian Game / Two Knights Defense structures.
analysis.why_bad: The knight that captures on d4/d5 (or that was protected by the king on f7) is left completely undefended. The opponent can simply win it via recapture, fork, or piece coordination (e.g., Qf3 attacking both the hanging Nd5 and f7). The player gains a pawn but loses a full minor piece, a net loss of ~2 points, explaining the average cp_loss of 381.

analysis.label: Player fails to advance a critical passed pawn toward promotion, instead making an irrelevant king or piece move in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material 43% of the time (median value 5.0, reflecting promotion-level gains) while the played move is rarely a capture (17%). The 40% own-hang rate (mostly pawns, 133 of 201 instances) likely reflects the unadvanced passed pawn subsequently being lost. Across all 12 top-activating boards (11/12 endgame), the best move is invariably a passed pawn advance toward the 7th/8th rank (a2, h2, f2, bxa7, d7, c7, c2, a7, e7, c7+, e2, exf7), yet the player instead makes a king move or piece move that squanders the decisive promotion race. The best move being a check only 7% and a capture only 9% confirms these are predominantly quiet pawn pushes, not tactical strikes.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn promotion races, every tempo is critical. By playing a king shuffle or piece repositioning instead of the decisive pawn advance, the player loses the race to promotion, allowing the opponent to either capture the passed pawn, promote their own pawn first, or establish a defensive blockade. The resulting position swings from winning to losing (average cp_loss 1450) because the promotion threat was the sole source of the position's advantage.

analysis.label: Player captures with a rook on a contested open file, but this move leaves their own major piece (rook or queen) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a tempting rook capture on an open file (94% of played moves are captures, all 12 top examples are Rx__ moves), but the capture leaves one of the player's own major pieces hanging (99% of cases leave own piece en prise, median hung value 5.0, with 248/252 classified hung pieces being major pieces—rooks or queens). The best move was typically a non-capture defensive or prophylactic move (only 35% of best moves are captures, 21% are checks), often a king retreat (Kg2, Kb8, Kg8, Kb1) or a queen reposition (Qe7, Qf7, Qc6, Qg7). While the best move does win material 71% of the time (median 3.0), the player forgoes this opportunity by choosing the impulsive rook exchange that backfires catastrophically.
analysis.why_bad: The rook that captures was serving a critical defensive role—shielding the king, protecting a queen, or guarding another major piece. By playing the rook capture (often a rook exchange on a shared open file), the player removes their own defensive piece, immediately exposing a rook or queen to capture by the opponent. The net result is a massive material loss (avg ~1110cp), turning equal or winning positions into losing ones, and in one case allowing immediate checkmate.

analysis.label: Player missed a check (usually a queen or piece check) that wins the opponent's queen or delivers checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the best move is a check in 96% of cases, and 96% of best moves win material with a median value of 91 (queen-equivalent). Only 23% of best moves are captures, meaning most are non-capturing checks that set up winning the enemy queen on the next move or deliver mate. The player's actual move was a capture only 20% of the time and was typically a quiet move (castling, king moves, pawn pushes). In 50% of cases the played move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2). The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, targeting a very specific tactical blindness to forcing check sequences.
analysis.why_bad: By playing a quiet or non-forcing move instead of the available check, the player forfeits a decisive tactical blow—typically winning the opponent's queen (value ~91) or delivering checkmate (value ~97). The checks exploit the enemy king's exposed position to create a fork, skewer, or mating net. The played moves not only miss this winning tactic but often worsen the position by leaving the player's own pieces undefended, turning a winning position into a losing one (avg cp_loss: 199).

analysis.label: In queen endgames, the player captures an enemy piece with their Queen (with check), allowing a queen trade that destroys their drawing or winning chances.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a Queen capture with check (90% of played moves are captures) that leaves their own Queen hanging for recapture (88% own piece hung, median value 9 = Queen, class 'major'). The best move wins material 80% of the time (median value 91) and is a check 61% of the time but only a capture 16% of the time — meaning the correct approach is typically a non-capturing Queen check that keeps the Queen active rather than trading it off. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames where the greedy Qx__+ trade leads to a catastrophically worse pawn ending (avg cp_loss: 303), while maintaining the Queen would preserve perpetual check resources or positional superiority.
analysis.why_bad: In queen endgames with exposed kings, the Queen's ability to deliver perpetual check or dominate the position is far more valuable than the material gained from a trade. By playing Qx__+ and allowing recapture, the player enters a lost pawn endgame or eliminates their only source of counterplay (perpetual check), often converting drawn positions into decisive losses or slight advantages into overwhelming ones.

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop capture winning an undefended pawn (or piece) on b7, b2, or g2 along the long diagonal.
analysis.description: In 95% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 1 pawn), and 76% of the time the best move is a capture. Across all 12 top boards, the best move is a bishop capturing on b7, b2, or g2—almost always taking an undefended pawn on the long diagonal in fianchetto or quasi-fianchetto structures. The played move was a quiet non-capture 87% of the time, and 39% of the time it additionally left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2, predominantly minor pieces). Many positions feature fianchettoed bishops (g2, b7, b2, g7) where the opposing b-pawn or g-pawn has become undefended, yet the player ignores this free material in favor of developing moves (Bd7, Qe2, f5, Bb2) or inferior captures (exd4, Nxc4, Bxd5).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore free material—a bishop can simply capture an undefended pawn on the long diagonal (b2, b7, or g2), often gaining a clean pawn or more. Instead the player makes a developing or positional move, forfeiting concrete material advantage, and sometimes even hangs their own piece in the process, compounding the error.

analysis.label: Player gives check (often capturing an advanced pawn) with a rook or queen that is left en prise after the king moves.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 69% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with the hung piece class heavily skewed toward major pieces (7 major vs 3 minor). Meanwhile, 44% of moves are captures, and examining the top boards reveals nearly all moves are checks (Qxa7+, Rxa7+, Rxg7+, Rxd7+, Rg7+, Qxh6+, Rxb7+, Rc1+). The best moves are almost never checks (0%) or captures (6%), confirming the player is attracted to a flashy check/capture instead of the correct quiet move. The pattern occurs overwhelmingly in endgames (10/12) where the opponent has an advanced passed pawn near promotion; the player captures the pawn with check using a major piece but leaves that piece undefended and capturable once the king sidesteps.
analysis.why_bad: The check appears tempting because it simultaneously captures a dangerous passed pawn and delivers check, feeling like a 'free' win. But after the king moves (or recaptures), the checking piece sits unprotected on the capture square with no escape. The correct approach is typically a quiet positional move (advancing own pawns, centralizing the king) that wins without material sacrifice, exploiting the already-winning position without trading a major piece for a pawn.

analysis.label: Player miscoordinates king and pawn in a won king-and-pawn endgame, either pushing the pawn prematurely without king support or moving the king to the wrong square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate confirms this is NOT primarily about material captures or hanging pieces: best move wins material only 6% of the time, player's move is a capture 0% of the time, and own piece left hanging only 11% (median value: pawn). Best move is neither a check (0%) nor a capture (0%). Instead, all 12 top-activating positions are minimalist endgames (100% endgame phase) featuring king+pawn vs king or near-equivalent setups. The feature fires on positions where the winning side has a technically won pawn endgame but fails the coordination between king positioning and pawn advancement—either pushing the pawn when the king must lead (Position 1: g2 instead of Kg4; Position 5: f7 instead of Kf5) or placing the king on the wrong square relative to the pawn's path (Position 12: Kh5 instead of Kg5; Position 3: Kc4 instead of Ka5).
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, the key principle is that the king must get in front of the passed pawn to escort it to promotion. Pushing the pawn too early without king support allows the opponent's king to reach a blockading or opposition square, often resulting in a draw (stalemate or forced capture). Moving the king to the wrong side of the pawn similarly cedes the critical opposition or allows the defending king to reach the promotion square. These moves convert winning positions into draws.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture the opponent's fianchettoed bishop (Bxg7 or Bxg2), a strategically devastating exchange, and instead plays a move that often hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is capturing the opponent's fianchettoed bishop on g7 or g2 (best move is a capture 97% of the time), but the player plays something else. The SEE of the best capture is 0 (bishop-for-bishop, materially even), so 'best_wins_material' registers only 6%. However, the exchange is strategically crushing because it strips the king's fianchetto shield. Instead of taking it, 60% of the time the player's actual move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minors at 46/70 cases). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting the specific geometry of an available Bxg7/Bxg2 that the player ignores.
analysis.why_bad: The fianchettoed bishop is the cornerstone of the castled king's defense. Capturing it (even for an equal exchange in material) devastates the king's pawn cover and opens the long diagonal for attack. By playing a different move, the player not only misses this positional/attacking coup but frequently places their own piece (often the very bishop that should have captured, or a knight) on an undefended square, compounding the error with an immediate tactical loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move that leaves their own major piece (queen or rook) en prise to an opponent's capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move leaves their own piece hanging at an alarming 96% rate (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook-equivalent or higher). The piece class distribution is heavily skewed toward major pieces (58 major, 18 minor, 6 pawn out of the top activations). Only 26% of the played moves are captures — the vast majority are quiet moves (king retreats, knight hops, bishop developments, queen relocations) that catastrophically ignore a tactical threat. Meanwhile, 82% of the time the best move would have won material (median 5.0), often by capturing the threat or delivering a check first (20% checks, 38% captures). The average cp_loss of ~4369 reflects that these blunders are frequently game-ending.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediate tactical threat to their own queen or rook. Instead of addressing the threat (by capturing the attacker, interposing, or moving the threatened piece to safety), they play an unrelated quiet move, allowing the opponent to freely capture a major piece — often resulting in immediate checkmate or decisive material loss.

analysis.label: Player moves a knight that is pinned to their queen by a bishop, hanging the queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 6.0, i.e. the queen), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (139 of 152 instances). In virtually every top-activating position, a bishop on g4 pins a knight on f3 to the queen on d1 along the diagonal. The player ignores this pin and moves the knight (typically Nxe5 or Ne5), removing the blocking piece and exposing the queen to capture. The best moves (h3 challenging the bishop, Bxe5 recapturing without moving the pinned piece, exd5, castling, etc.) all avoid moving the pinned knight. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, capturing this specific and severe blunder pattern, with an average cp_loss of 509.
analysis.why_bad: The knight on f3 is the only piece blocking the enemy bishop's diagonal attack on the queen. By moving the knight (even to capture a pawn on e5), the player removes the shielding piece and leaves the queen en prise to the pinning bishop on g4, losing the queen for at most a minor piece or pawn.

analysis.label: A knight captures on f7 (or f2) in the opening without support, leaving itself hanging with no tactical follow-up.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player plays an unsupported knight capture on f7 or f2 in the opening. The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung-piece class being overwhelmingly minor pieces (427/465). The move played was itself a capture 77% of the time. The best move wins material only 49% of the time (often simply retreating or developing was better), confirming that the key mistake is not missing an opponent's hanging piece but rather hanging one's own knight. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, indicating a specific recurring opening pattern: a knight on g5 (or g4 for Black) lunges to f7/f2 capturing a pawn but is immediately recapturable with no compensation.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures a pawn (worth ~1) but is left completely undefended on f7/f2, where it can be trivially recaptured by the king or another piece, netting the opponent a full minor piece (~3 points). The hoped-for king displacement or tactical complications don't materialize because the attacker lacks supporting pieces (typically still on the back rank in the opening), so the sacrifice has no follow-through.

analysis.label: Player moves king instead of capturing a hanging enemy rook in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 92% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5, i.e., a rook), and 99% of the time the best move is a capture—yet only 18% of moves actually played were captures. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (10/12 top positions) where an enemy rook is en prise to a minor piece, pawn, or knight, but the player instead makes a king move (11 of 12 top activations are king moves: Ke2, Ka7, Kg6, Kf5, Kd3, Kg3, Kh2, Kf6, Ke2, Kf4). The 37% own-hang rate is a secondary consequence in some positions, not the primary pattern. The consistent theme is an undefended enemy rook sitting within one-move capture range of an existing piece, completely overlooked in favor of a 'natural' endgame king walk.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves lose roughly 5 pawns' worth of material (median cp_loss ~850) because the player forgoes a free rook capture. The king move adds marginal king activity or avoids phantom threats, while the simple capture of the undefended rook would be immediately decisive. The player appears fixated on king centralization—a common endgame heuristic—but catastrophically ignores the concrete tactical opportunity right in front of them.

analysis.label: Player ignores a winning capture/tactic and instead plays a quiet move that simultaneously leaves their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a compound blunder: both missing a clear winning capture (78% of positions have a best move that wins material, median value 5.0 pawns, with 62% being simple captures and 23% being checks) AND playing a move that hangs their own piece (82% of played moves leave an own piece undefended, median value 3.0, distributed roughly equally among minor pieces 142, pawns 135, and major pieces 132 out of 500). Only 21% of played moves are captures, meaning the player overwhelmingly chooses quiet, 'positional' moves in positions demanding immediate tactical action. The feature fires broadly (25.6% of positions) and catches catastrophic blunders (avg cp_loss ~3356).
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail on two fronts simultaneously: they pass up free or near-free material (hanging enemy rooks, undefended queens reachable via checks, capturable pieces) and they relocate the player's own pieces to squares where they become undefended or tactically exploitable. Moves like Rd2 leaving a rook hanging, Bc5 placing a bishop en prise, or Rc7 dropping a rook all represent the player completely misreading the tactical demands of the position — often playing 'improving' moves while the position screams for an immediate capture or forcing sequence.

analysis.label: Player ignores a necessary bishop capture (Bx_) that would neutralize a dangerously-placed enemy piece, instead playing a quiet move that allows threats to materialize.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 97% of best moves are captures and all are bishop captures (Bx_) with SEE = 0 (equal exchanges), yet only 17% of played moves were captures — meaning the player systematically avoids a necessary trade. Despite the exchange being materially neutral, failing to make it is catastrophic: 57% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns/37%, majors/28%, minors/28%). The enemy piece being ignored is almost always an aggressively-posted knight (on squares like f4, f5, g4, e5, f6) that creates immediate tactical threats against the player's queen or other pieces. The average cp_loss of 1142 confirms these are severe blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The aggressively-placed enemy piece (usually a knight) is generating concrete tactical threats — attacking queens, creating mating nets, or pressuring key squares. By playing a quiet move instead of the equal-value bishop exchange, the player leaves their own pieces exposed to these threats. The enemy piece's continued presence means its attacks execute on the next move, often winning a queen or creating checkmate. The exchange was 'free' (SEE = 0) but strategically essential.

analysis.label: Player makes a move that leaves their own piece (typically queen) en prise, missing a safer check or capture that would win material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move hangs their own piece 100% of the time (median value 9.0, i.e., queen-level), while the best move would have won material 100% of the time (median value 2.0). The best move is a check in 67% of cases and a capture in 33%, indicating safer tactical continuations were available. The played move was itself a capture only 33% of the time, meaning most hung pieces result from quiet or promotional moves. The own-hang piece distribution (major: 2, minor: 1 in top 3) combined with the median value of 9 across 500 positions indicates queens are overwhelmingly the piece left hanging. The feature fires on essentially 0% of all positions, marking this as a rare but devastating pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player makes an aggressive-looking move (often a check, capture, or promotion) that places their piece on an unsafe square where it can be captured. In Position 1, Qxb7+ wins a pawn with check but leaves the queen capturable, while Qc5+ safely wins. In Position 2, b8=Q+ promotes with check but the new queen is immediately lost, whereas an underpromotion or king move preserves the advantage. In Position 3, Ng5 develops the knight to an unprotected square when exd7+ wins a pawn safely with check. The player sees the flashy move but misses that their piece has no escape after the opponent responds.

analysis.label: Player missed a tactical bishop capture (typically Bxe6) that exploits a structurally weak pawn, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 91% of activating positions, yet the player's move was a capture only 17% of the time — indicating the player consistently overlooked a concrete capturing opportunity. The best move wins outright material in only 35% of cases (median value 1.0), and the SEE on the best capture is typically 0, meaning these are positionally motivated bishop captures (sacrifices or exchanges) where the real advantage comes from structural damage or tactical follow-ups (forks, open lines toward the king) rather than immediate material gain. The player's quiet alternative left their own piece hanging 35% of the time (median value 2.0, predominantly minor pieces). Across all 12 top boards, the best move is a bishop capture targeting a vulnerable pawn (e6 in 8/12 cases, also d5, f3, f6, e3) in Sicilian/Italian/Philidor pawn structures.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves (b3, e5, b4, Nce4, Nf3, Bb3, O-O, Nb3, Nh5, Qh5, etc.) waste the critical tactical moment when the bishop can strike a key pawn. The Bxe6 (or similar) capture typically opens the f-file, demolishes the pawn shield, creates discovered attack or fork possibilities, or exposes the enemy king. By playing a non-forcing move, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, shore up the weakness, or castle to safety — permanently losing the tactical window.

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player misses an active rook move (penetration, attack, or redeployment) that would win a vulnerable pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0 = one pawn), yet only 5% of best moves are direct captures — meaning the winning move is typically a rook redeployment that creates an unavoidable threat against a loose pawn rather than an immediate take. The played move was a capture only 20% of the time, indicating players chose passive or aimless moves instead. The feature fires mostly in endgames (7/12 top positions), predominantly rook endgames where the best moves are rook penetrations (Rc7, Re7, Ra8, Rb5, Rd1, etc.) targeting undefended pawns. In 32% of cases the played move also hangs the player's own piece (median value 2.0, often major pieces), compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: Instead of activating the rook to attack a vulnerable pawn (via penetration to the 7th rank, attacking from behind, or targeting an isolated/undefended pawn), the player makes a passive king move, aimless pawn push, or misguided rook move to a less effective square — failing to exploit the opponent's pawn weakness and often forfeiting a full pawn or more of advantage.

analysis.label: The player gives a tempting check (or aggressive move) that leaves their own piece en prise once the king escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move left their OWN piece hanging 60% of the time (median value 3.0, distribution across major/minor/pawn pieces). Critically, 10 of the top 12 activating moves are checks (+), yet the best move is a check only 10% of the time — revealing the player is drawn to a forcing check that accomplishes nothing after the king sidesteps. The best move wins material only 46% of the time (median 1.0), meaning in most cases the correct plan was a quiet consolidating move rather than a flashy check. The played move was a capture only 27% of the time, confirming many checks are non-capturing moves like b4+ or e7+ that simply expose the player's pieces.
analysis.why_bad: After the check, the opponent's king simply moves to safety, and the checking piece (or a piece left undefended by the checking move) is captured. The check feels forcing but gains no tempo on anything meaningful — the king escapes to a safe square while the attacker's piece remains en prise with no follow-up. The player squanders a winning or equal position by prioritizing the psychological comfort of 'giving check' over calculating what happens next.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an undefended enemy queen (or high-value piece), instead playing a quiet or checking move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'missed capture' pattern: the best move wins material in 80% of cases with a median value of 9.0 (queen), the best move is a capture in 100% of cases, yet the player's move is a capture in 0% of cases. Only 20% of played moves hang the player's own piece, confirming this is overwhelmingly about MISSING an available winning capture rather than blundering one's own material. The feature fires almost exclusively in queen endgames (9/10 positions) where the opponent's queen is undefended and directly capturable (Qxf2, Qxe2, Qxe1, Qxf1, axb4, etc.), but the player instead plays a quiet queen move, a king move, or a tempting check.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they pass up a trivially available capture of an undefended enemy queen (or major piece). The played moves—often checks (Qe6+, Qc3+, Nd6+) or repositioning moves (Qg2, Qg3, Kh2)—look active but squander decisive material advantage. A check is not inherently good if a free queen capture is available; after the missed capture, the position equalizes or even reverses entirely (average cp_loss: 3335).

analysis.label: Player makes a routine rook-to-open-file (usually d-file) move instead of executing a concrete tactical blow that wins significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 72% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 4.0 — roughly a rook), while only 17% of the played moves were captures. The best moves are captures 52% of the time and checks 18% of the time, yet the player consistently opts for quiet positional moves. Additionally, 53% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns, minors, and majors). The feature fires overwhelmingly in positions with open d-files where the player deploys a rook to an open file (Rd8, Rad1, Rad8, Rac1, Rf8 — 8 of the top 12 boards) as a generic 'good move' rather than calculating the concrete tactical opportunity available, which often involves checks winning the queen (Qc3+, Qe3+, Qg3+), captures on the d-file itself (Rxd8, Rxd1), central pawn thrusts (e5), or decisive pins (Bb5).
analysis.why_bad: These routine rook deployments fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity that would win material immediately. By playing a 'positional autopilot' move — placing a rook on an apparently logical open file — the player squanders a winning advantage (median cp_loss ~255). Worse, in 53% of cases the routine move actually leaves one of the player's own pieces undefended, compounding the error by turning a winning position into an equal or losing one.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player fails to capture a nearby enemy pawn with their king, instead making a quiet move elsewhere.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 90% of best moves win material (median value 1.0 = one pawn) and 92% of best moves are captures, yet only 10% of played moves were captures. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames where the king is adjacent to a capturable enemy pawn—typically a dangerous passed pawn (often near promotion)—and the correct move is a simple Kx capture. Instead, the player makes a quiet move (pawn push, piece relocation, or king move in the wrong direction). The 39% own-hang rate (mostly pawns) reflects that the alternative quiet moves sometimes inadvertently leave the player's own pawns undefended, but the primary and consistent mistake is ignoring the king capture of the enemy pawn.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the capturable pawn is almost always a dangerous passed pawn (often one or two squares from promotion). By not capturing it immediately with the king—which is already adjacent—the player allows the opponent to either promote, use the pawn as a decoy, or gain a decisive tempo advantage. In positions 5, 9, and 10 the ignored pawn is one square from queening, making the omission catastrophic.

analysis.label: Player moves their king to the wrong square in an endgame, missing a move that would win significant material (median value ~5 pawns).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 97% of best moves win material with a median value of 5.0, while the played move was itself a capture only 4% of the time and best move is a capture only 6%—meaning the material is won positionally rather than by immediate tactical strike. Own piece left hanging occurs 32% of the time but only at median value 1.0 (mostly pawns), a secondary effect. Across the top 12 boards, 11 of 12 played moves are king moves and 9 of 12 are endgame positions, with a catastrophic average cp_loss of 3092. The pattern is consistent: in endgames where the player has material available to win (often an enemy piece to approach/capture, or a pawn to promote), the king walks to the wrong square—sometimes into a mating net, sometimes away from the winning action—while the correct move (a different king square, a pawn advance, or occasionally a king capture) would secure decisive material.
analysis.why_bad: The wrong king move fails because in endgames, king placement is the decisive factor—one wasted tempo or wrong direction can transform a winning position into a loss. By routing the king away from capturable material, walking into mating patterns, or abandoning defense of key squares, the player squanders positions where precise king centralization or approach would win a piece or force promotion. Many of these blunders turn won endgames into immediate forced mates.

analysis.label: Player misses a classic Greek Gift bishop sacrifice (Bxh7+/Bxh2+/Bxf7+) with check that wins material or leads to a decisive attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 91% of positions the best move wins material, and crucially 93% of best moves are checks while 64% are captures — pointing overwhelmingly to a missed bishop sacrifice with check. The median value won is just 1 (a pawn), consistent with the initial Bxh7+/Bxh2+ capturing only the h-pawn, but the enormous average cp_loss of 2647 shows the sacrifice unleashes a devastating attack (often mate). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is a bishop capturing on h7, h2, or f7 with check — the textbook 'Greek Gift' sacrifice. The player instead plays quiet moves (25% captures), and in 49% of cases even leaves their own piece hanging (median value 2.0, mostly minors), compounding the error by both missing the tactic and worsening their position.
analysis.why_bad: The played quiet moves (Ne7, b3, O-O-O, Rf1, etc.) completely ignore the decisive tactical opportunity of a bishop sacrifice with check on h7/h2/f7, which would crack open the opponent's castled king position and typically lead to mate or heavy material gain. By not playing the sacrifice, the player loses a winning or near-winning advantage, and often the quiet alternative even weakens their own position.

analysis.label: Developing a bishop to a seemingly natural square (Be3/Be6/Be2/Bd3) in the opening while ignoring critical tactical opportunities or creating vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a quiet bishop development move (always to a square on the e-file or d-file like e3, e6, e2, d3) that looks natural but is tactically misguided. The SEE aggregate shows that 44% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 42% of the time the played bishop move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed as 113 pawns, 91 minors, 4 majors). Only 7% of played moves are captures, confirming these are passive development moves. The best move is a capture 28% of the time, indicating available tactical opportunities being ignored. The feature fires on 0.4% of all positions, exclusively in the opening phase.
analysis.why_bad: These bishop moves fail because they prioritize 'development' over concrete tactical demands. For Black, Be6 often places the bishop on a square directly attacked by a White d5 pawn advance or exposed to a Bc4+Ng5 battery targeting f7/e6. For White, Be3 often blocks the e-pawn, misses forcing moves like Qh5+ or Qxg4 that win material, or leaves pawns undefended. In all cases, the player makes a routine-looking move while ignoring that the position demands a specific tactical response—either capturing hanging pieces or avoiding creating new weaknesses.

analysis.label: Player misses a forced checkmate beginning with a queen capture-check onto a defended pawn (appearing as a sacrifice) that leads to mate in 2.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals the signature unmistakably: 92% of best moves are checks, 68% are captures, and every top-activating position shows Qxb6+, Qxg6+, or Qxg3+ winning SEE=0 (i.e., the queen captures a defended pawn, looking like a sacrifice). The 46% 'wins material' at median 91cp reflects only the static exchange, not the forced mate. The enormous average cp_loss of 8273 confirms these are missed mates-in-2. The 51% own-piece-hanging stat (median value 3, distributed across minor/pawn/major) is a secondary consequence—players make aimless moves (f3, g3, Nh4, c4, Bxf8, etc.) that sometimes leave pieces loose, rather than delivering the lethal queen check.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a forced checkmate in 2 that begins with the queen capturing a defended pawn with check. The queen 'sacrifice' is only apparent—after the king moves to its forced square, a follow-up piece delivers mate. By playing quiet moves or irrelevant captures instead, the player converts a trivially won position (forced mate) into one that is merely advantageous or even losing.

analysis.label: A premature bishop sacrifice on f7 (or f2) with check that leaves the bishop hanging without adequate tactical compensation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates a 'hung own piece' pattern: 93% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the piece class distribution showing 38 minors out of 41 cases. The played move is a capture 82% of the time. The top 12 boards confirm the specific geometry: virtually all are Bxf7+ (or Bxf2+) played from a bishop on c4 (or c5) in opening Italian Game / similar positions. The best move is a check only 2% of the time and a capture only 20%, showing that quiet developing or preparatory moves (h3, Be3, c3, cxd4) were typically superior. The 61% 'best wins material' rate (median 1.0) often reflects simple captures or trades available as alternatives.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures on f7/f2 with check, but after the king recaptures (Kxf7/Kxf2), the attacker lacks sufficient follow-up pieces to create a mating attack or win back material. Unlike a sound Fried Liver or Greek Gift sacrifice, the position doesn't have the necessary supporting pieces (e.g., a knight ready to jump to g5/d5, a queen able to exploit the exposed king). The result is simply losing a bishop for a pawn — a net loss of approximately 2 pawns worth of material, explaining the average ~305 centipawn loss.

analysis.label: Player missed that h3/h6 would challenge and win an opponent's pinning bishop that has no safe retreat.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 99% of the time the best move wins material (median value 2-3, i.e., a minor piece), yet only 2% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks — meaning the winning move is a quiet pawn advance. Examining the top 12 boards confirms the pattern overwhelmingly: the opponent has placed a bishop on g4 (pinning Nf3 to the queen) or g5 (pressuring Nf6), and the best move is h3 or h6, a pawn kick that traps or wins the bishop because it lacks safe retreat squares. The player's move was a capture only 20% of the time, and 40% of the time it left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, primarily minor pieces at 83 instances), consistent with the pinned knight remaining exploitable when the pin goes unchallenged.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the pawn kick (h3/h6), the player leaves the opponent's aggressively-placed pinning bishop unchallenged. The bishop on g4/g5 has often overextended with limited retreat squares (h5/h4 leads to further trapping via g4/g5). Playing other moves instead allows the pin to persist, often leading to the pinned knight being captured or the pin creating devastating tactical consequences. Some players even launch premature attacks (Bxf7+, Nxe5) trying to exploit f7 rather than simply winning the trapped bishop.

analysis.label: Player overlooked a tactical check (often a fork) that would have won major material, instead playing a lesser capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly shows this feature fires when the best move wins significant material (71% of the time, median value 5.0 — approximately a queen). Critically, 44% of best moves are checks, indicating these are positions with devastating tactical checks available — typically forks or discovered attacks that win the queen. The player's actual move is a capture 44% of the time (grabbing lesser material while missing the bigger shot) and hangs their own piece 43% of the time (median value 2.0). The concrete boards confirm this: Position 1 (c2+ wins 97), Position 4 (f2+ wins 99), Position 10 (Nf3+ wins 97), and Position 8 (exf6+ wins 8) all show checks that win a queen or equivalent. Players consistently chose routine captures or quiet developing moves instead of the crushing tactical blow.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing check (fork, discovered attack, or intermezzo) that wins far more material than whatever the played move accomplishes. The player often captures a minor piece or plays a quiet positional move while a simple check would fork the king and queen, or trigger a winning tactical sequence. The played move sometimes compounds the error by also leaving the player's own piece hanging.

analysis.label: Player plays a passive repositioning move instead of the critical capture or forcing move demanded by the position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player missed capturing or taking tactical action: the best move is a capture 70% of the time (with 40% winning material, median value 3.0 pawns), yet the player's move was a capture only 7% of the time. Best moves were checks 17% of the time. The player's own-piece hanging rate is only 20% (median 1.0, mostly pawns), confirming the primary error is not hanging pieces but rather failing to take immediate tactical action. Across all top positions, the player consistently chose quiet, non-forcing moves (Ke7, Rf1, Rg1, Ra1, Nh6, Nb5, etc.) when the position demanded an immediate capture of a vulnerable enemy piece/pawn (often an advanced passed pawn or intruder on d6) or a critical saving check in endgames.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore the most pressing tactical demand: capturing a strong enemy piece/pawn (especially advanced passed pawns on d6 in openings) or finding the only saving check in endgames. By playing a passive development or repositioning move, the player allows the opponent to consolidate a dominant piece, promote a passed pawn, or deliver a mating attack. The position required immediate forcing action, not quiet improvement.

analysis.label: Player fails to play the critical central pawn advance (d5 or d4) that supports a centralized knight while winning material from an exposed enemy bishop.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 85% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 57% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0). The best move is a capture only 20% of the time and a check only 15%, indicating the winning resource is typically a quiet pawn advance. Across the top boards, the overwhelmingly consistent pattern is: the player has an aggressively centralized knight (usually on e4 for Black or e5 for White) facing an enemy bishop on c4, and the correct move is d5 (or d4) which simultaneously supports the knight, attacks the enemy bishop, and wins a full minor piece. Instead, the player makes passive or tangential moves (Nf6, Ng5, Bd6, Qb6, b3) that abandon central control. In 57% of cases, the played move actually leaves the formerly-strong centralized knight (or another piece) en prise because without the pawn support, the knight becomes tactically vulnerable on its advanced square.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they abandon the centralized knight without pawn support. The knight on e4/e5 was a powerful piece but tactically depends on the d-pawn advance to remain secure and generate threats. By playing irrelevant moves, the player both misses winning the enemy bishop (worth ~3 pawns) via the fork/attack on c4 and often leaves their own knight hanging on its exposed central square, resulting in huge material and positional losses.

analysis.label: Player makes a capture (predominantly with a bishop) that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise on its new square.
analysis.description: This feature identifies moves where the player hangs their own piece, firing when the played move leaves an own piece en prise (92% of activating positions, median value 3.0 = minor piece). The most common hung piece class is minor (94 instances), consistent with the overwhelmingly bishop-centric pattern in the top boards. 44% of the played moves are captures, and the recurring motif is a bishop capturing a pawn or piece (Bxd4, Bxe4, Bxc6, Bxd6) only to land on a square where it is undefended and immediately recapturable, resulting in a net material loss. The best move often wins material elsewhere (54%, median 3.0)—frequently Nxc4 winning White's hanging bishop—showing the player chose a greedy but self-destructive capture instead of the correct tactical shot.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop (or other piece) captures a target but lands on a square where it has no defender, allowing the opponent to recapture it for free or with material gain. This trades a minor piece for a pawn (or nothing), when the correct move would win material or maintain the advantage by exploiting a different tactical vulnerability in the opponent's position.

analysis.label: The player made a quiet move instead of capturing the opponent's hanging or inadequately defended queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 93% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material via capture (93% captures) with a median value of 9 (queen). The player's move was itself a capture only 10% of the time, meaning the overwhelming pattern is playing a passive or unrelated quiet move while the opponent's queen sits en prise. The boards confirm this: in positions 3, 6, 10, and 12, the opponent's queen is explicitly described as undefended or directly capturable by a pawn or minor piece (hxg6, fxg3, Nxd7, Nxe7). Additionally, 64% of the time the player's chosen move also left one of their own pieces hanging (median value 3), compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores the highest-value tactical opportunity on the board — capturing the opponent's queen for free or near-free — and instead plays a developing or repositioning move that has no tactical urgency. In many cases the alternative move even worsens the position further by leaving the player's own material undefended, turning a potential material windfall into a deepening deficit.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy major piece (queen or rook) that can be captured immediately, playing a quiet or irrelevant move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 75% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. rook-to-queen level), and 94% of best moves are direct captures, yet the player's actual move was only a capture 16% of the time. This means the player overwhelmingly plays quiet developing or repositioning moves while a high-value enemy piece sits undefended and capturable. The 47% own-hang rate (median 3.0) is a secondary consequence — the suboptimal move sometimes also leaves the player's own piece loose — but the defining error is failing to take the free enemy material. Across the top boards, the missed targets are queens (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12) and rooks (positions 3, 5, 11), almost always completely undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate, simple capture of an unprotected high-value enemy piece. Instead of collecting a free queen or rook (often worth 5-9 pawns of material), the player makes a 'normal' move — developing a piece, retreating, or capturing a lower-value target — throwing away a decisive material advantage. The tactical pattern is usually trivially simple (one-move capture on an open line or by a piece already attacking the target), making these pure oversight/blindness errors.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free/hanging central pawn capture in favor of a quiet developing move, often leaving their own piece en prise to that same pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 90% of cases (median: 1 pawn) and is a capture 96% of the time, while the player's actual move was a capture only 12% of the time. In 68% of activating positions the player's quiet move left their own piece hanging (median value: 2, predominantly minor pieces at 86 instances). The pattern is almost entirely in the opening (10/12 top boards) where an enemy pawn has advanced into the center (d4, e4, d5) creating tension, and the correct response is a simple recapture (exd4, Nxe4, cxd5, dxe4, exd5). Instead, the player makes a developmental or prophylactic move (h3, Bb2, Nf3, Be2, a6, etc.), leaving their own knight attacked by the uncaptured pawn.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to recapture the central pawn, the player both misses winning free material and leaves their own piece (typically a knight on c3, f3, or similar) attacked by that very pawn with no adequate defense, resulting in material loss averaging ~4 pawns worth of evaluation swing.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet or suboptimal move instead of a forcing tactical blow (capture or check) that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 40% of positions the best move wins material (median value: 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the best move being a capture 64% of the time and a check 24% of the time. Yet the player's move was only a capture 25% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly chose quiet, passive moves over the winning tactical continuation. In 26% of cases the played move also hung the player's own piece (median value 3.0), compounding the error. The top boards show king retreats (Kb5, Kc7), quiet pawn moves (e6, a5), passive piece placements (Ng2, Qe1, Rd3, Qb2), and wrong captures (Bxd6, Qxa6, Bxd5) when strong tactical shots like forks (Ne2+), checks (Qf5+), or material-winning captures (Bg4, b6, e7, Bxf8) were available.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity—typically a forcing capture or check—that would immediately win material. Instead of calculating the available tactic, the player makes a passive or misdirected move, missing the chance to gain a decisive material advantage (often a piece or more), and sometimes even leaving their own pieces hanging in the process.

analysis.label: Player makes a slow, natural-looking quiet move while missing a concrete winning opportunity (usually a simple capture).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 61% of positions the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), and 47% of best moves are captures, yet the player's move was a capture only 10% of the time. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet repositioning moves—typically rook relocations (Ra6, Rc7, Rd8, Re3, Rf2, Rb1) or king walks—that look positional or 'active' but ignore concrete tactical opportunities. The feature fires in mostly endgame positions (9/12 of top boards) with an enormous average cp_loss of 1859, indicating these aimless moves often convert winning positions into draws or losses. The 29% own-hang rate (median value 3.0) further shows that some of these quiet moves inadvertently expose pieces to tactics the player didn't foresee.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is operating on positional autopilot—making 'normal-looking' rook improvements or king moves—instead of calculating concrete variations. They miss hanging enemy pawns/pieces (Rxg2, Qxf7, gxh6, Rxa3, Rxb2), urgent pawn captures (bxc3), promotion threats (b7), and critical defensive necessities (g3 preventing back-rank mate, Ke7 addressing king vulnerability). The quiet moves accomplish nothing urgent while the opponent's tactical opportunities grow or material is simply left on the table.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player reflexively advances a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (2nd/7th) when a superior move—often a king activation or check—is available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player pushes a passed pawn to the pre-promotion square (2nd rank for Black, 7th rank for White) prematurely. The SEE aggregate shows that 57% of the time the best move wins material (median value 9.0, i.e., queen-level wins, often via eventual promotion through a better path), and 31% of the time the best move is a check. The played move is almost never a capture (8%), confirming it's a quiet pawn push. In 50% of cases the move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with pawns dominating at 142/234 of the hung pieces), meaning the advanced pawn itself becomes capturable after the premature push. All 12 top-activating boards are endgames, and every played move (g2, f2, h2, e2, d2, b2, d7, f7) is a pawn advance to the penultimate rank.
analysis.why_bad: Pushing the pawn to the 7th/2nd rank without proper preparation often leaves it unsupported and capturable (explaining the 50% own-hang rate on pawns). The correct move—typically a king activation (Kc6, Kd5, Kf5, Ke3), a winning check (Bg4+, Re7+), or a supporting pawn move—either secures the promotion path or wins material outright. The reflexive push telegraphs the player's intent without addressing defensive threats, allowing the opponent to blockade, capture, or counterattack.

analysis.label: The player missed a knight or pawn fork that delivers check while simultaneously attacking a higher-value piece, winning decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 95% of best moves win material (median value ~97 centipawns, roughly a minor piece or exchange), and 67% of the best moves are checks — while only 18% are captures. This signature indicates the winning tactic is a discovered attack via check rather than a direct capture. The top boards confirm this: positions 1-5 all feature f5+ (a pawn fork checking the king on e4 and attacking the rook on g4), while positions 6-12 all feature knight forks with check (Nf2+, Ne2+, Nc5+, Nc7+, Nd5+, Nd3+) that attack the king plus a rook or other major piece. The player's moves were overwhelmingly quiet (78% non-captures), showing passive play that overlooked the explosive tactical shot. Only 29% of played moves hung the player's own piece, confirming this is a missed-winning-tactic pattern rather than a hung-piece pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (b6, Rbd8, a6, Ra8, Nb5, h4, etc.) are slow positional or prophylactic moves that completely miss the immediate tactical fork. By not playing the check-fork, the player forfeits winning a full piece (knight or rook) essentially for free, squandering enormous advantages — in several cases missing forced checkmate sequences (positions 4, 5, 8 show #-11 to #-15 evaluations).

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece instead of delivering an available check or checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a materialistic capture (85% of played moves are captures) while missing a far superior checking move (93% of best moves are checks, with median SEE value of 100 indicating checkmate). The best move wins material 95% of the time, but is itself only a capture 19% of the time—meaning the optimal move is almost always a non-capturing check that delivers immediate or near-immediate mate. The player's greed-driven capture sometimes even leaves their own piece hanging (57%, median value 3.0 = minor/major piece), compounding the error. The average centipawn loss of 5459 reflects that most missed opportunities are outright checkmates (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10 are all mate-in-one).
analysis.why_bad: The player is seduced by the immediate material gain of capturing an enemy piece and fails to scan for forcing checks. In nearly every case, a simple check (often a back-rank mate, smothered mate, or king-hunt check) ends the game immediately. By capturing instead, the player throws away a won game—often converting a forced mate into merely a large advantage or even allowing counterplay.

analysis.label: Player fails to initiate a perpetual check sequence with their queen against an exposed enemy king, losing a drawable position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a strikingly coherent pattern: 99% of the time the best move is a check, yet only 9% are captures, indicating non-capturing queen checks are the missed resource. 97% of best moves 'win material' (median value 91, representing the enormous eval swing from saving a draw), consistent with perpetual check salvaging hopelessly lost or equal positions. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 23% captures), showing players retreating or making positional moves instead of forcing a draw. The 46% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, 69 pawns) is a secondary consequence—once the perpetual is missed, the position collapses and pieces become en prise. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting these critical moments where a perpetual check is the only saving resource.
analysis.why_bad: By playing quiet moves (Qa1, Qb4, Qd7, Kf7, etc.) instead of initiating perpetual check against the exposed enemy king, the player abandons their only drawing resource. The opponent's material advantage or mating threats then become decisive, converting drawn positions into immediate losses—often mate in a few moves (average cp_loss: 4973). The queen's unique ability to deliver continuous checks from multiple angles is squandered.

analysis.label: In critical endgame positions, the player misses a game-deciding check or urgent tactical move (often to stop a promotion), instead playing a less important capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 70% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0 pawns—roughly a rook), and 36% of the time the best move is a check, yet only 12% involve a direct capture, indicating the winning blow comes through forks, skewers, or promotion-related tactics rather than simple recaptures. The player's actual move was a capture only 33% of the time (often grabbing an insignificant pawn), and only 24% of played moves hung the player's own piece. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames with exposed kings and average cp_loss of 1966, signaling that these are game-losing oversights. The consistent pattern is a player distracted by a peripheral capture (Rxg2, Kxh4, Nxa5, Rxe5, Rxh6) or aimless quiet move (Ke4, Kg4, d5) while missing an immediately decisive check (Ne5+, Bd5+, Bb7+, Rf7+, Be1+) or a critical move to stop/exploit a promotion threat (Ra1, Rb1, Rf8, Rd1).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a secondary concern (winning a pawn, improving king position) while ignoring the most urgent tactical priority in the position—typically a forcing check that wins major material or the game outright, or a defensive move to prevent an opponent's passed pawn from promoting. In sharp endgames with exposed kings and advanced passed pawns, one tempo determines the outcome, and these moves waste that critical tempo.

analysis.label: Player moves a piece (typically the queen) to a square where it is immediately capturable by the opponent in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 100% of the top 500 activating positions involve the player's move leaving their own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 6.0 (queen-value). The piece class distribution (2 major, 1 minor) confirms this is predominantly about queens being placed en prise. Only 33% of moves are captures, meaning most of the time the player simply drops a piece onto an unsafe square rather than grabbing something and landing in danger. The best move wins material only 33% of the time (median 3.0), confirming the primary issue is not a missed opportunity but a self-inflicted blunder. All three top positions occur in the opening phase with both kings uncastled.
analysis.why_bad: These moves place a valuable piece (usually the queen) on a square directly attacked by an opponent's piece—for example, Qxh5 landing on a square covered by Black's rook on the open h-file, Ba6 placing the bishop where it has no escape or defense, and Qd2 putting the queen in the line of fire of Black's intruding bishop on c3. The player fails to check whether the destination square is adequately defended, resulting in immediate material loss of a major piece.

analysis.label: Player ignores a straightforward winning capture in the endgame, instead playing an 'active' quiet move like a check, pawn push, or king maneuver.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 93% of cases (with 50% winning material outright, median value 2.0), yet the player's move was a capture only 14% of the time. This means in the vast majority of activating positions, a simple winning or simplifying capture was available but completely ignored. The played moves occasionally left the player's own piece hanging (36%, median value 1.0), compounding the error. All 12 top positions are endgames where the correct move is an obvious take—Nxa4, Nxa6, Rxa8, bxc3, Bxg7, Kxh4, Bxg5, Nxd6 (appearing twice), gxf3, bxa5—but the player chose checks (Nd3+, Na8+, b5+), pawn advances (h6, a5, a4), king walks (Kf4, Kf3, Kb4), or piece repositioning (Nb5, Nd3) instead.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they forgo immediate, decisive material gain. In endgames, material is paramount—a free pawn or piece capture often converts trivially. Playing a check or pawn push instead wastes the opportunity: the hanging enemy piece may escape, or the opponent gets counterplay. In several cases (positions 8, 11), the player missed capturing an entire rook with a knight, turning a won game into a draw. The players appear seduced by 'active' moves (checks, passed pawn advances) while overlooking that the simplest path to victory is just taking free material.

analysis.label: Player makes an ambitious piece move instead of a necessary pawn capture, leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly shows the 'hung own piece' pattern: 66% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/minors/majors), while 78% of best moves are captures (mostly simple pawn captures like hxg4, fxe5, dxe4, cxd5, exd4). The player ignores these straightforward pawn captures—often recaptures or tension-resolving takes—and instead plays ambitious developing or attacking moves (Ne5, Bg4, Bc4, Nd5, Qh5, Bxf7+) that leave material undefended. Only 24% of played moves are captures themselves, confirming the player systematically avoids the available capture in favor of flashy alternatives.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring a required pawn capture (recapture, tension resolution, or material-winning take), the player leaves a piece undefended or creates a tactical vulnerability. The opponent then wins the hanging piece on the next move, typically netting a minor piece (3 points median). The ambitious alternative move provides no compensation for the material lost.

analysis.label: The player missed a queen check that would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a queen check (99% of the time) that wins significant material (97% of positions, median value 100 — often corresponding to checkmate or queen-winning sequences), but the player instead made a quiet move, king move, or unrelated capture. Only 10% of the best moves are captures, confirming these are non-capturing queen checks (forks, mating attacks, or checks winning material indirectly). The player's move was itself a capture only 27% of the time, and 42% of the time the played move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, mostly pawns). The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, typically in endgames with exposed kings where a queen check exploits the geometry decisively.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore an immediately available queen check that either delivers checkmate or forces the opponent's king into a position where material is lost. Players instead make positional moves, grab lesser material, or move their king, completely overlooking the tactical geometry of the queen check. The result is enormous centipawn losses (avg 3558), often converting a winning or mating position into a drawn or losing one.

analysis.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended edge square (h3, h6, a6, a3) in the opening where it immediately hangs.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward minors (46 out of 56). The best move almost never wins material (10%) or delivers check (0%), indicating the correct play was simply quiet development. In all 12 top-activating positions (100% opening phase), the player moves a bishop to a rim square—h6, h3, a6, or a3—where it lands completely undefended. In many cases, the opponent already has a fianchettoed bishop (e.g., Bg7) or another piece ready to capture the exposed bishop immediately.
analysis.why_bad: These bishop moves place the piece on an unprotected edge square where it can be captured for free. The bishop has no pawn cover or piece support on these rim squares, and the opponent typically has a piece (often a fianchettoed bishop or knight) that can take it immediately. Instead of developing purposefully toward the center or castling, the player makes a premature bishop sortie that simply loses a piece.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive or routine move (often a king retreat or wrong-piece capture) while a decisive tactical opportunity exists, frequently also leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on catastrophic blunders where the player ignores critical tactical demands. The SEE aggregate shows 74% of best moves win material (median 3.0 pawns), indicating a consistently available tactical opportunity. Simultaneously, 57% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed across pawns (109), major pieces (107), and minor pieces (68). Only 26% of played moves are captures, confirming the passive nature of the errors. The best moves are overwhelmingly active piece deployments (captures 33%, often rook or queen moves), while the played moves are king walks (Kg7, Kh6, Kg6), quiet rook shuffles (Rhc1, Re8, Rh8), or captures with the wrong piece (Bxd2 instead of Rxd2, Nxh5 instead of Rxh5, Bxd6 instead of Rxd6). The average cp_loss of 2401 reflects that many positions go directly to forced mate.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores the tactical urgency of the position, choosing a 'natural-looking' passive continuation while a concrete winning or defensive tactical resource was available. The passive move simultaneously forfeits the chance to win enemy material and often leaves the player's own pieces undefended on their new squares, compounding the error into a catastrophic two-way blunder that frequently allows forced mate.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but inferior check that leaves their own piece en prise, missing a stronger move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check (100% of the top 12 moves are checks) that leaves their own piece hanging (75% of activating positions, median value 3.0 — spread across minors: 70, pawns: 64, majors: 63). Meanwhile, the best move wins material 69% of the time (median value 3.0), often being a quiet move, a capture, or even a superior check (best move is a check 33% of the time). The average cp_loss of 1737 is catastrophic, with several cases missing checkmate entirely (e.g., Nxa7+ instead of Qxc7#, Bxh2+ instead of Qxd4+ leading to forced mate). The feature captures the classic 'patzer check' — reflexively giving check without calculating whether the opponent's forced reply leaves the checking piece (or another piece) undefended.
analysis.why_bad: The checks are purposeless — after the king sidesteps, the checking piece (or another piece left unguarded) is simply captured. The player gains one tempo of check but loses a piece or more in return, while missing moves that would have won material, delivered checkmate, or maintained a winning position. The check creates the illusion of activity but actually worsens the position dramatically.

analysis.label: Player missed a winning capture that simultaneously gives check, allowing free material gain in an endgame with exposed kings.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 92% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and critically, 66% of best moves are checks while 72% are captures — meaning the dominant pattern is a capture+check combination. Only 25% of played moves were captures, indicating players chose quiet moves or inferior captures instead. The 21% own-hang rate is a secondary consequence in some cases (e.g., leaving a queen en prise while making a pointless move), not the primary pattern. All 12 top positions are endgames with both kings exposed, where an undefended enemy piece sits on a square from which it can be captured with check. In 11 of 12 positions, the best move is explicitly a capture with check (Qxc1+, Bxa3+, Qxh7+, Qxd7+, Qxc8+, Qxh1+, Rxh3+, Qxf1+, Qxg6+, Rxg5+, Qxf2+).
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a forcing capture-with-check that wins material essentially for free. Since the opponent must respond to check, they cannot recapture or compensate. By playing quiet king moves, pawn pushes, or non-check captures, the player squanders a tempo-free material gain, often turning winning positions into draws or losses (average cp_loss: 3482).

analysis.label: Player makes a passive quiet move in an endgame instead of an available critical capture or decisive action.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 53% of best moves are captures (with 27% winning outright material, median value 3.0), yet the player's actual move was a capture only 7% of the time. Own-piece hanging is just 7% (trivial pawns), confirming this is about MISSING the opponent's vulnerable pieces, not hanging one's own. The feature fires in endgame positions (10/12 top boards) where a concrete, often forcing move—typically a capture of an undefended or poorly-defended piece/pawn—is available, but the player instead makes a quiet, passive, or directionally wrong king/piece move. The average cp_loss of 2632 reflects that these quiet moves are often game-losing, as they squander a decisive tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, tempo and concrete calculation are paramount. By playing quiet repositioning moves (Kd8 instead of Kxf6, Be5 instead of Bxd2, Kg2 instead of f8=Q, etc.), the player ignores immediately available captures or decisive actions that either win material, stop promotions, or resolve the position. The opponent then consolidates or promotes, turning a winning/equal position into a loss.

analysis.label: Playing a pointless queen check in a queen endgame instead of making a constructive move (capturing material, advancing pawns, or improving the king).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player gives a queen check that accomplishes nothing constructive and often leaves the queen hanging. The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is NEVER a check (0%) while the played move is always a queen check. In 65% of positions the best move wins material (median value 1.0, with 51% being captures — typically grabbing an undefended pawn). Crucially, 63% of the time the played queen check leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, with 'major': 38 being the dominant class), meaning the queen itself becomes en prise after the opponent's king simply sidesteps. The feature fires in queen endgames (10/12 top boards) where both kings are exposed, tempting the player into fruitless checking sequences.
analysis.why_bad: These queen checks fail because the opponent's king has safe escape squares, and after moving away, the queen often lands on an undefended or tactically vulnerable square. Meanwhile, the player misses concrete improvements — capturing hanging pawns (Qxa2, Qxd3, Qxg4, Qxa7), advancing passed pawns (h5, b5, c2), or improving king position (Kb7). The checks give the opponent's king a tempo to improve while the player's queen ends up worse-placed or outright hanging.

analysis.label: In rook endgames with exposed kings, the player missed a rook check that wins decisive material or the game.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, yet it is a capture in only 4% of cases — meaning the check itself forces a winning sequence rather than immediately capturing. The best move wins material 99% of the time (median SEE value: 100), while the player's actual move was a quiet non-check move 80% of the time. The positions are overwhelmingly rook endgames (all 12 top boards feature rook checks like Rh4+, Re7+, Rg4+, Rf8+, Rc2+, Rc7+) where both kings are exposed. The missed check typically deflects the opposing king, enabling promotion threats, rook captures, or forced mating nets. The 34% own-hang rate (median value 3, heavily major pieces and pawns) reflects that the quiet alternative sometimes also leaves the player's rook or pawn tactically vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: By playing a quiet move instead of the available rook check, the player forfeits a forced winning sequence. The check exploits the exposed enemy king to win material (an enemy rook or decisive promotion advantage), but without the check, the opponent consolidates or promotes first — explaining the enormous average cp_loss of ~4079 and frequent mate-in-N evaluations.

analysis.label: Player ignores a capturable enemy piece and instead makes a quiet move that simultaneously hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a devastating dual-error pattern: in 80% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0, with 81% of best moves being captures), yet the player's move is a capture only 12% of the time. Simultaneously, 68% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across major pieces [56], minor pieces [50], and pawns [19]). This combination—missing a free enemy capture while also exposing one's own piece—produces catastrophic evaluation swings (avg cp_loss 2149). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating these are rare but extreme tactical blindness events.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet/positional moves (pawn pushes like d6, c6, c5, a3; piece placements like Be2, Bf8, Qg4, Qf6) are catastrophic because they ignore an immediately available tactical win (a hanging enemy piece worth ~3+ pawns) while simultaneously creating a new vulnerability by leaving the player's own piece—often the queen—completely undefended. The player appears to be 'sleepwalking' positionally, blind to both the offensive opportunity and the defensive liability their move creates.

analysis.label: An aggressive knight jump to an advanced square in the opening that leaves own material (typically the knight itself or a piece it was guarding) hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 69% of positions have the player's own piece left hanging after the move (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution heavily skewed toward minors (16 minor vs 6 pawn vs 2 major). Only 14% of best moves win material and only 11% are captures, confirming the mistake is not about missing enemy hanging pieces but about self-inflicted losses. The feature fires almost exclusively on opening knight moves (11/12 boards) where the knight lunges to an aggressive square (f4, e5, g5, d5, d4, e4, h5, b4) while the best moves are simple developing or consolidating moves (O-O, Nf3, Nc3, e6, Bc4). The knight either lands on a square where it is immediately capturable, or its departure abandons defense of another piece (e.g., Ne5 leaving a bishop on b5 en prise to ...c6).
analysis.why_bad: These premature knight lunges violate opening principles by prioritizing an aggressive-looking move over development and king safety. The advanced knight lands on a square controlled by enemy pawns or pieces and can be captured for free, or its departure from its original square removes a key defender of another piece, resulting in a net material loss averaging ~317cp.

analysis.label: Player's knight captures a well-defended enemy piece on a central outpost square, leaving the knight hanging and losing material after recapture.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where a player impulsively captures a well-supported enemy piece (typically a knight on e5, d5, d4, or e4) with their own knight, leaving it en prise. The SEE aggregate shows 99% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = knight), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 297/331 cases. The played move is a capture 90% of the time, while the best move is rarely a capture (28%) or check (4%) — indicating the correct approach was a quiet positional move (castling, retreating, developing). The feature fires on 0.2% of positions with an average cp_loss of ~301, consistent with net loss of a minor piece after the pawn recapture creates additional threats against the player's remaining pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures into a square defended by pawns (and often other pieces), so after the recapture (typically pxN), the player's knight is simply lost. The resulting pawn advance often simultaneously attacks another piece (e.g., a bishop on d6 or knight on f6), compounding the loss. The correct approach — seen in the best moves like O-O, Ne7, Bb7, Bb5, Na4 — was to develop, castle, or reposition pieces rather than prematurely resolve the central tension by capturing into a defended outpost.

analysis.label: The player makes a superficially active or greedy move that catastrophically ignores the position's critical tactical demands, hanging material or missing winning combinations.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions (0.1% of all) where the player commits a catastrophic blunder (avg cp_loss 1754) by making a move that ignores urgent tactical necessities. The SEE aggregate shows 60% of positions had a best move winning material (median 3.0 pawns), while 50% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minors 37%, majors 30%, pawns 24%). The played moves were captures 33% of the time—often greedy grabs—while best moves were checks only 16% and captures 27%, indicating the critical responses were often quiet defensive or positional moves. The coexistence of both high missed-win and high hung-own rates shows these are positions where tactical chaos reigns but the player 'sleepwalks' through with a routine or materialistic move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a superficially attractive action (repositioning a rook, grabbing a pawn, making a flashy check) over the position's actual tactical priority—whether that's escaping a back-rank threat (Kf1/Kf7 needed), capturing a hanging major piece (Nxd8), or delivering forced mate (Rd8). The played moves treat the position as calm when it's in full tactical crisis, resulting in hanging pieces, allowing mate, or squandering decisive advantages.

analysis.label: Player captures material (often with check) but leaves their own major piece (rook or queen) en prise, typically to the opponent's king recapturing.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of positions have the player's own piece left hanging after their move (median value 5.0), with the overwhelming majority being major pieces (42 out of 46 classified). The player's move was itself a capture 79% of the time, and examining the top boards reveals these are almost always endgame positions where a queen or rook captures a piece/pawn (frequently delivering check), only to be recaptured by the opponent's king. The best move is a capture only 2% of the time and a check only 19%, indicating the correct play was typically a quiet repositioning move rather than the flashy tactical capture chosen.
