analysis.why_bad: In these endgame positions, the player's major piece (queen or rook) is their key strategic asset—needed for perpetual checks, blockading passed pawns, or maintaining active defense. By capturing material on a square where the opponent's king can simply recapture, the player trades their irreplaceable piece for trivial material gain, allowing enemy passed pawns to promote unopposed or converting a drawable position into a lost one.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own queen en prise, typically by opening a diagonal, misplacing the queen, or ignoring an existing threat to it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 100% of the top 500 activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0), with 499/500 being a major piece—specifically the queen based on the board examples. Only 13% of played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet moves that inadvertently expose the queen. While 52% of best moves win material (median 3.0), this is secondary—the primary signal is the universal queen-hanging pattern. The feature fires on just 0.5% of positions, highlighting the specificity: these are moves where the queen is left completely undefended or a line is opened that creates an immediate tactical threat against it.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they either (1) push a pawn (especially ...e6) that opens a diagonal directly to the queen for an enemy bishop (e.g., Bg5/Bh4 hitting Qd8), (2) place the queen on a square controlled by an enemy piece (e.g., Qh3 where it's trapped or attacked, Qc7 into Bf4's line), or (3) ignore an existing attack on the queen to make an unrelated developing move (e.g., O-O while the queen on c3 is attacked by Bg7, or Bd7 while the queen hangs). In all cases, the opponent can simply capture or win the queen on the next move.

analysis.label: Player misses a decisive Queen capture (often a sacrifice on a defended square) and plays a passive quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture in 92% of positions (almost always a Queen capture based on the top examples: Qxg3+, Qxd7, Qxe3, Qxc3, Qxd2, Qxa5, Qxc7, Qxf4, Qxd4, etc.), yet these captures show SEE value of 0—meaning the target square is defended and the capture appears to be a sacrifice or even exchange. Despite SEE neutrality, these Queen captures are tactically decisive (avg cp_loss of 1821 for missing them), often involving mating attacks or winning back more material through follow-up tactics. The player's move was a capture only 15% of the time, confirming they chose quiet moves instead. Additionally, 42% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, spread across major pieces, pawns, and minors), compounding the error. Best move is a check 18% of the time, supporting the pattern of missed Queen captures with king-attack follow-ups.
analysis.why_bad: The player fails to recognize that their Queen can capture on a seemingly defended square with devastating tactical consequences (checkmate threats, winning sequences, or decisive positional domination). Instead they play passive quiet moves that not only miss the winning opportunity but often leave their own pieces en prise, turning a winning position into an equal or lost one.

analysis.label: Player ignores a winning rook move to an open file that captures or traps material worth ~5 points (a rook).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 80% of the time with a median value of 5 (rook-value), while the player's move is rarely a capture (only 21%). In 49% of cases the played move also hangs the player's own piece (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/95, majors/91, minors/59). Examining the top 12 boards, the best move is almost universally a rook move to an open file (Rad8, Rd1, Rbe8, Re8, Rfd8, Rac8, Rc8, Rb8, Rd8) that decisively wins material—typically an undefended or trapped enemy rook on that same file. Position features consistently show open d-files, e-files, or b-files with enemy pieces vulnerable on them. The player instead plays quiet developing moves, pawn pushes, or knight/queen maneuvers that completely miss the tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical win available via rook activation on an open file. The opponent's pieces (usually a rook or major piece) are undefended or trapped on that file, and the winning rook move exploits this immediately. By playing an irrelevant move, the player both forfeits winning material (~5 points) and often simultaneously leaves their own pieces undefended, compounding the error.

analysis.label: The player chose a quiet move instead of a tactically winning knight capture that appears materially even in static exchange but yields a large advantage through follow-up tactics.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a capture 82% of the time, yet the SEE value of the best move is consistently 0 (i.e., the capture appears to be an even trade statically). Only 23% register as 'winning material' by pure SEE, and the player's actual move was a capture just 11% of the time—confirming the player chose quiet moves over the tactical knight capture. The played moves left own pieces hanging 31% of the time (median value 1.0, mostly pawns: 94 pawn, 52 minor, 9 major), a secondary consequence of the passive alternative. All 12 top-activating boards show the identical pattern: the best move is a Nx__ capture (Nxd5, Nxd4, Nxb5, Nxe4, Nxb4, Nxe5, Nxc5) with SEE=0, but the resulting position after recapture enables devastating follow-up tactics (forks, discovered attacks, or structural collapses) that produce 180-380 centipawn advantages.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Bg5, Rc1, Na4, Qe7, Rfe8, Nf6, Nb4, Rf1, Ne2, Nb5, Ng3) fail because they forfeit a concrete tactical opportunity where a knight capture—though apparently an even trade by static exchange—triggers a chain of tactics (forks, pin exploitation, discovered attacks, or positional destruction of the opponent's structure) that the opponent cannot adequately parry. The player likely dismissed the knight capture as 'just a trade' without calculating the consequences of the recapture.

analysis.label: Player delivers a check with a major piece that is left en prise after the king moves away.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, overwhelmingly major pieces: 273 out of ~300 hung pieces). Every single top-12 move is a check (+), yet only 24% of the best moves are checks, meaning the player is choosing a check over a superior quiet or non-checking alternative. The best move wins material 68% of the time (median 3.0), indicating the player had strong continuations available but was drawn to the flashy check instead. The average cp_loss of 2535 confirms these are catastrophic blunders—often throwing away a won or even mating position.
analysis.why_bad: These checks fail because after the opponent's king simply sidesteps, the checking piece (Queen or Rook) lands on a square where it has no support and is captured for free. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check without calculating one move further—after the king escapes, there is no follow-up threat, and the major piece is lost. In many cases (positions 3, 7, 11, 12) the player had a forced mate or decisive advantage but threw it away by choosing an unsound check over the correct continuation.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive forcing move (often a major-piece check or infiltration) that wins significant material through threats rather than direct capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 94% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-equivalent), yet only 7% of best moves are captures and 30% are checks. The player's move was a capture only 16% of the time, and own-piece hanging (32%, median just a pawn) is a secondary side effect rather than the core mistake. The pattern is overwhelmingly: a crushing forcing continuation exists — typically a rook or queen infiltration/check (Rc1, Qd2, Rb5+, Rg2+, Rd2+, Qc3+, Rb6+, Qc7) that creates unstoppable threats (promotion support, mating attack, or winning pinned/trapped pieces) — but the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push, king move, or misplaced rook move) that squanders the decisive advantage. The average cp_loss of 1012 reflects how catastrophic these missed tactical blows are.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves fail because they surrender the initiative in positions where a single forcing move would have created an unstoppable threat (queening a pawn, exploiting an exposed king, or winning trapped/pinned material). By playing passively, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, escape the tactical vulnerability, or generate counterplay, converting a winning position into an equal or lost one.

analysis.label: Player gives a pointless queen check that leaves their own major piece (usually the queen itself) hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies the pattern: 89% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 6.0), with 'major' pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (100 major vs 15 minor vs 9 pawn). Meanwhile, 71% of the best moves win material (median 3.0) and only 6% of best moves are checks—indicating the player chose a flashy but tactically empty check over a materially superior alternative. All 12 top-activating boards show queen checks (Qf4+, Qf3+, Qh4+, Qd5+, etc.) or discovered checks (Kg1+), and after the opponent calmly steps out of check, a major piece—most often the queen itself—is left en prise. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, consistent with a specific catastrophic blunder pattern averaging ~1830cp loss.
analysis.why_bad: These checks accomplish nothing: the opponent simply moves their king (or interposes), and then captures the now-undefended major piece. The check gives a tempo but gains nothing in return—no mating net, no perpetual, no fork—while the player forfeits a queen or rook. The best move was typically a capture or quiet move that won material or maintained a winning position without exposing pieces.

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player makes a passive/aimless rook relocation instead of an active move that wins material (capturing undefended pawns, giving critical checks, or attacking passed pawns).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 62% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), yet the player's move is a capture only 10% of the time—indicating the player consistently misses available material-winning opportunities. The best move is a check 26% of the time and a capture 23% of the time, confirming that active, tactical moves are available but ignored. Only 17% of played moves hang own material, so the primary mistake is not self-inflicted hanging but rather failing to exploit the opponent's weaknesses. All 12 top-activating positions are rook endgames where the player moves the rook to a passive square (Ra6, Rg6+, Ra8, Rc3, Ra7, Rh1, etc.) instead of an active square that captures pawns (Rxa5, Rxh5, Rxe4+), attacks passed pawns from behind (Ra5, Rd5), or delivers critical forcing checks (Rf8+, g5+).
analysis.why_bad: These passive rook moves fail because in rook endgames, piece activity is paramount. Moving the rook to an aimless square allows the opponent's passed pawns to advance unchecked, leaves capturable material untouched, or squanders tempo that could be used for forcing checks. The best moves exploit concrete tactical features—undefended pawns, exposed kings, or the geometry of passed pawn restraint—while the played moves simply relocate the rook without addressing the critical demands of the position.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing or repositioning move instead of the critical pawn capture that resolves central/structural tension favorably.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture 89% of the time, yet the player's move was a capture only 14% of the time — indicating a systematic failure to take a crucial pawn exchange. The best captures have SEE = 0 (pawn-takes-pawn exchanges), meaning they are materially equal trades, but positionally decisive. By declining these exchanges, the player's move left their own piece (usually a pawn) hanging 43% of the time (median value 1.0; class distribution: 9 pawns, 2 majors, 1 minor). The feature fires in both French Defense openings (where dxc5 resolves center tension with tempo against a queen on b6) and pawn endgames (where captures like exd5, fxg5, bxa4 create or prevent passed pawns). In all cases, the player instead makes a quiet piece/king move, failing to recognize that the specific pawn capture is the only way to maintain the advantage.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the critical pawn exchange, the player allows the opponent to either maintain structural pressure (e.g., Black's c5 pawn continues attacking d4 while Qb6 pressures b2), or seize the initiative by capturing first on their terms. In opening positions, Be3/Bd2/Nb3 directly hang the d4 pawn to the knight on f5 or cxd4, while in endgames, the king moves waste tempo allowing the opponent to favorably resolve the pawn structure themselves, often creating unstoppable passed pawns.

analysis.label: Player makes a routine knight move or capture while missing a much stronger check (often Bxf7+ or checkmate) exploiting the enemy king stuck in the center.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), and crucially 67% of best moves are checks — yet the player's move was only a capture 48% of the time and typically a routine knight action. All 12 top-activating positions are in the opening phase with kings in the center. The best moves are devastating checks (Bxf7+, Nf6#, Qxf2#, Qh4+, Qe8+) that exploit uncastled kings, but the player instead opts for 'natural' knight captures (Nxe4, Nxf7, Nxe5, Nxd5) or developing moves (Nc3, Nf3, Ng4) that look reasonable but squander massive tactical opportunities. The average cp_loss of 1934 reflects how catastrophic these misses are — multiple positions involve missed checkmate-in-one.
analysis.why_bad: These knight moves fail because they pursue ordinary material gains or development while ignoring far more powerful checks and checkmates. In sharp opening positions with both kings uncastled, a check on f7 (via bishop sacrifice) or a discovered/double check often wins immediately or nets decisive material. The knight captures look productive but allow the opponent's king to escape the critical danger, converting a winning attack into an equal or lost position.

analysis.label: Player missed a rook move that would win the opponent's rook in a rook endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 90% of activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 5 (a rook). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is always a rook maneuver (Ra4, Re2, Re7, Rd4, Rh7, Rc5, Rc3, Rb2, Rf6, Rxc1, Re4). Only 19% of best moves are direct captures, meaning most rook wins come from attacking/trapping the enemy rook rather than immediately taking it. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 12% are captures) — typically passive king moves or pawn pushes. 46% of played moves also leave the player's own pawn hanging (median 1.0), but the primary error is failing to exploit the opponent's vulnerable rook. Positions are predominantly rook endgames (9/12) with exposed kings and open files.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves are passive (king retreats, pawn advances, misplaced rook moves) that squander a decisive tactical opportunity. The best move repositions the rook to a square that attacks, traps, or forks the enemy rook, winning a full exchange worth of material. By missing this, the player converts a winning position into an equal or even lost one (average cp_loss: 237).

analysis.label: In pawn endgames, the player advances a pawn to a square where it is left undefended and capturable by the opponent's king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 80% of moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly showing pawns (97 pawns vs 11 major and 6 minor pieces). All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, mostly pure king-and-pawn endings. The played moves are almost exclusively pawn advances (c4, f5, g4, b3, a5, b5, h4, c4, a4) that push the pawn to an undefended square reachable by the enemy king. Only 12% of best moves are captures and 4% are checks, confirming the best alternative is typically a positional king move rather than a tactical strike. The best moves frequently involve king repositioning (Ke7, Ka6, Ke6, Kc7, Kg6, Kh7, Kg8) rather than the reflexive pawn push.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, advancing a pawn to an undefended square allows the opponent's king to capture it for free. The correct approach is usually to improve king position first or choose a pawn advance that maintains pawn protection. These premature pushes gift the opponent a free pawn, which in endgames is often decisive material.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but inferior knight check, missing a much stronger move and often leaving the knight itself hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player plays a knight check (100% of top-12 moves are Nx_+ or N__+) that is objectively a serious mistake. The SEE aggregate shows that in 68% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0), meaning the player missed a far superior continuation—often a crushing capture, a better check, or a positionally decisive move. Meanwhile, 57% of the played knight checks leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung-piece distribution heavily skewed toward minor pieces (116 minor vs 65 pawns vs 30 major), strongly suggesting the knight itself is the piece left en prise after delivering its check. The best move is a check only 32% of the time, meaning the player is drawn to the flashy knight check when a quiet but devastating alternative exists. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions with an average cp_loss of 1004, confirming these are severe blunders driven by the irresistible lure of giving check with a knight.
analysis.why_bad: The knight check achieves nothing concrete—after the forced king move, the knight is often stranded on a bad square where it can be captured for free, or the tempo gained by check is meaningless compared to what was available. Meanwhile, the player misses winning a full piece or more (median 5.0 pawns), delivering checkmate, or executing a far more effective tactical blow. The check is a classic 'patzer sees a check' trap where the immediate forcing nature of the move blinds the player to superior alternatives.

analysis.label: Player makes a slow, quiet pawn advance ignoring a concrete tactical opportunity (capture, development, or check) that demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the played move is virtually never a capture (1%) — every activating position involves a quiet pawn push. In 28% of cases the best move wins material outright (median value: 3.0, a full piece), and in 31% of cases the pawn push itself leaves the player's own pawn hanging (median value: 1.0; distribution: 120 pawns, 24 minor pieces, 9 majors). The best moves are a mix of winning captures (17%), checks (6%), and strong piece moves. The feature fires at 4.1% of positions, predominantly in the opening (7/12 top boards) when development and concrete play are critical. The played moves (b4, d4, b3, g4, e5, f6, f3, c3, f4, e5, a3, b3) are all single-step pawn advances — often flank pawns — that ignore pressing tactical demands.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn moves waste a tempo on a passive or weakening advance while the position demands immediate tactical action: capturing an undefended enemy piece (e.g., cxd5 winning a knight, dxe4 winning a piece, exf6 winning material), or making a strong developing/centralizing move. The pawn push frequently creates new weaknesses (hanging the pushed pawn or opening lines toward the player's own king), compounding the missed opportunity with positional damage.

analysis.label: Player avoids an obligatory equal exchange, leaving their own piece hanging or positionally stranded.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a distinctive pattern: the best move is a capture in 99% of cases, yet that capture only 'wins material' 5% of the time (median value won: 2.0, i.e., these are equal exchanges with SEE=0). Meanwhile, the player's actual move left their OWN piece hanging in 50% of positions (median value: 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution heavily skewed toward minors (153 minor, 53 pawn, 12 major). The player's move was itself a capture only 13% of the time, confirming they overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead of the forced trade. The feature fires on opening positions (10/12 boards) where a piece—typically a bishop on b4 pinning Nc3, or a bishop attacked by a pawn advance—must immediately complete an exchange or become stranded and tactically vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: When a piece is under direct attack and the only way to 'save' its invested tempo is to complete the intended exchange (e.g., Bxc3, Bxf3, Bxe6, Nxc6), declining that trade by retreating or playing elsewhere wastes the piece's activity. The unexchanged piece then hangs (it's still on the attacked square or retreats to a passive square where tactical motifs exploit it), resulting in material loss or a catastrophic positional collapse—averaging 320cp loss across these positions.

analysis.label: Player captures an advanced passed pawn (usually 7th rank) with a major piece, leaving that piece en prise and losing it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 71% of played moves are captures and 71% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 9.0, exclusively major pieces — queens and rooks). Only 7% of best moves are captures, while 29% are checks, indicating the correct approach involves indirect tactics rather than greedy pawn-grabbing. The positions consistently feature an enemy passed pawn on the 7th rank one square from promotion. The player panics and captures the pawn directly with their queen (value 9) or rook (value 5), but the piece lands on a square where it is immediately lost — typically recaptured by the enemy king or trapped with no retreat. The best moves demonstrate that the promotion threat should be handled indirectly via checks exploiting the exposed enemy king, attacking the pawn from behind, or advancing one's own pawns.
analysis.why_bad: Directly capturing the 7th-rank pawn places the major piece on a square surrounded by enemy forces (usually the enemy king), leaving it immediately en prise. The player trades a queen or rook for a single pawn, converting winning positions into losses or draws. The correct technique is to restrain or attack the pawn indirectly while exploiting the enemy king's exposed position.

analysis.label: Player missed a knight fork with check that would win the queen or equivalent major material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'missed winning move' pattern: 92% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 97, i.e., a queen), the best move is a check 71% of the time, yet only 14% of best moves are captures—indicating the winning tactic is a non-capturing check that forks king and queen. The played move was a capture only 20% of the time, confirming the player made a quiet or misguided move instead. Across all 12 top-activating positions, the best move is a knight (or occasionally pawn) check that simultaneously attacks the enemy queen (Ne2+, Nf4+, Nf2+, Ng4+, Nf5+, Nd2+, Nxb5+). The player frequently moves the same knight to a wrong square (Nc5, Ne6, Nc6, Nb4, Nc8+, Ng7+), sometimes even delivering a check—but not the geometrically correct fork square. The feature fires on only 0.2% of positions, targeting this specific and devastating tactical oversight in mostly endgame scenarios (9/12 endgames) with exposed kings and queens on vulnerable diagonals.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they squander a decisive tactical opportunity. The knight has exactly one square from which it simultaneously checks the king and attacks the queen (a royal fork), winning the queen for free. By moving the knight elsewhere—or giving a check on the wrong square—the player loses the geometric alignment needed for the fork, allowing the opponent's queen to escape and maintain a massive material advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores a forced capture (often with check) that was the only justification for their major piece's aggressive position, leaving it hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 66% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., Queen or Rook), with the own-hang piece class dominated by major pieces (100 major vs 32 minor). The best move is a capture in 98% of cases and a check in 54%, yet the player's actual move was a capture only 23% of the time. The best move's SEE value shows 0 material won (because it's a trade or the piece captured equals the capturer), meaning the Queen or Rook was in a tactically committed position where it HAD to execute a forcing capture—often a Qx check—to justify being there. By playing a quiet move instead, the player abandons their major piece to be taken for free.
analysis.why_bad: The player's Queen (or Rook) was on an aggressive but precarious square, safe only because it had a forcing capture available (often with check). Playing any other move allows the opponent to simply capture the exposed major piece on the next turn, resulting in catastrophic material loss (~600+ centipawns on average).

analysis.label: In endgames, the player moves the king to an adjacent square (or makes a quiet move) instead of capturing an available enemy pawn or piece with the king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 48% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), yet the player's move was a capture only 5% of the time — a massive gap indicating consistently missed captures. The best move is a capture 28% of the time. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and in at least 8 of 12, the best move is specifically the king capturing an enemy pawn (Kxc5, Kxb4, Kxh5, Kxf4, Kxf3, Kxd6, Kd3 winning e3, Kc5 winning b5). The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet king moves to nearby squares that fail to collect the available material. The 22% own-hang rate (mostly pawns) appears secondary, sometimes resulting from the wasted tempo allowing the opponent to counter-attack.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in king-and-pawn endgames, every tempo is critical. By moving the king to an adjacent square instead of directly capturing the available pawn or piece, the player wastes a tempo, loses material worth roughly a pawn, and often allows the opponent to advance passed pawns, escape with their king, or convert their own advantages. The king is the primary attacking piece in endgames, and failing to use it to collect material immediately when possible leads to lost pawn races and decisive positional deterioration.

analysis.label: The player captures an available piece or pawn instead of addressing a critical passed pawn or urgent threat, typically losing the game in endgames.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a tempting material capture while ignoring a far more critical positional priority—almost always an advanced passed pawn threatening promotion. The SEE aggregate confirms: 85% of played moves are captures, yet only 12% of best moves are captures, revealing a systematic pattern of 'greedy' material grabs over urgent non-capture solutions. The best move wins material 76% of the time (median value 3.0), but typically through indirect means—stopping an enemy pawn from promoting (saving ~9 points), advancing one's own passed pawn, or delivering a check leading to decisive advantage. The feature fires in endgame positions (10/12 boards) with an enormous average cp_loss of 2840, showing these greedy captures routinely convert winning or equal positions into losses or even forced checkmates.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they prioritize an immediate but small material gain (often a pawn or minor piece) while allowing an unstoppable passed pawn to promote or permitting a lethal tactical shot. In typical cases, the captured piece is a 'poisoned' lure—the opponent's advanced passed pawn reaches the 7th/8th rank during the time spent capturing, converting to a queen and winning immediately. The correct move (usually a king retreat toward the passed pawn, a blocking piece placement, or advancing one's own passer) addresses the existential threat and preserves the material-equivalent advantage long-term.

analysis.label: Player gives a wasteful queen check instead of capturing winning material (usually the enemy queen).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 64% of the best moves win material with a median value of 9.0 (queen-level), and 58% of best moves are captures, yet only 11% of the played moves are captures. All 12 top-activating moves are queen checks (Qe6+, Qc8+, Qd7+, etc.), while the correct moves are overwhelmingly queen captures of undefended enemy pieces (Qxd3, Qxg5, Qxh3, Qxc6, Qxe4+, etc.). The best move is itself a check only 32% of the time, confirming the player is choosing checks over captures. The average centipawn loss is an enormous 2660, often converting forced mates or winning positions into draws, because the player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check rather than simply collecting the hanging material.
analysis.why_bad: These queen checks are tactically pointless — they force the opponent's king to move but accomplish nothing strategic. Meanwhile, the opponent's queen or major piece is hanging and can be won immediately. After the check, the opponent stabilizes, the hanging piece is no longer available, and the winning advantage evaporates. The player prioritizes the psychological appeal of 'giving check' over the objectively superior material-winning move.

analysis.label: Player missed a queen capture on f7 or f2 that delivers check or checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 93% of positions have the best move winning material (median value 1.0, i.e., the f-pawn), with an extraordinary 99% of best moves being checks and 82% being captures. The player's actual move was a capture only 26% of the time and left their own piece hanging 33% of the time (median 3.0). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the missed best move is specifically Qxf7 or Qxf2 delivering check or checkmate—the classic exploitation of the weak f-pawn adjacent to an uncastled or exposed king. The enormous average cp_loss (5096) reflects that most of these are missed forced checkmates.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediately available Qxf7 or Qxf2 that delivers check or outright checkmate, instead making developing moves, castling, or irrelevant captures. This squanders a forced win (often mate-in-one or mate-in-two) and allows the opponent to survive or even gain the advantage.

analysis.label: Quiet pawn advances or king moves in endgames that leave the player's own pawn undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly points to a 'hung own piece' pattern: 59% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging, with a median value of 1.0 (a pawn). The piece class distribution confirms this is overwhelmingly about pawns (55 pawns vs 9 minors vs 2 majors). The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (9/12 top boards), where the played moves are quiet pawn pushes (b5, g4, h5, d5, f4, g5, c4) or king retreats (Ke3, Kf2) rather than captures (only 12% of played moves are captures). The best moves are often more forcing—7% are checks and 12% are captures—suggesting the player chose a passive structural move while missing that it leaves a pawn tactically unprotected.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, every pawn is critical. These quiet pawn advances or king moves look structurally natural but tactically fail because they either push a pawn to an undefended square where it can be captured, or move the king away from a pawn it was protecting. The opponent can then simply win the hanging pawn, converting a drawn or slightly worse endgame into a lost one. The average cp_loss of 416 reflects how devastating losing even one pawn is in simplified positions.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy pawn directly attacking their knight, leaving it hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of the top 500 activating positions involve the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 2), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 499/500 cases (virtually always a knight). Only 9% of the played moves are captures, and the best moves are typically quiet retreats or repositions (only 25% captures, 3% checks). The pattern is overwhelmingly consistent: an enemy pawn (usually an advanced central pawn like e5 or d4) directly attacks the player's knight, and instead of saving the knight, the player makes an unrelated developing or quiet move, leaving the knight en prise to the pawn.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore an immediate tactical threat—an enemy pawn attacking the player's knight. Since pawns are worth less than knights, the opponent can simply capture the knight with the pawn next move, winning approximately 2 points of material. The player prioritizes development or positional ideas (like ...e6, ...d6, h3, d4, c4) over the urgent necessity of relocating the attacked knight to safety. In opening positions with advanced pawns (e5 vs Nf6, d4 vs Nc3, e4 vs Nf3, g4 vs Nf3), the knight must move before anything else.

analysis.label: The player missed a queen capture of the opponent's undefended central d-pawn in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 96% of positions (median value: 1 pawn), with the best move being a capture in 100% of cases and never a check (0%). The player's move was itself a capture only 32% of the time, meaning they usually played a quiet move instead. Only 20% left their own piece hanging, confirming this is overwhelmingly a 'missed winning capture' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' mistake. Across all 12 top-activating boards—exclusively opening positions—the best move is always a queen capturing an undefended d-pawn (Qxd4, Qxd5, or Qxd3), typically in Scandinavian or early-queen openings where the opponent's central d-pawn lacks adequate defense.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (quiet queen retreats like Qd8/Qa5/Qc4, developing moves like Bf5/Be3/e6, or flashy checks like Qe6+/Qa4+) all fail because they ignore a free pawn sitting on the d-file. The queen is already active and can immediately collect the undefended d-pawn, gaining a clean pawn with a good position. Instead, the player prioritizes development, retreats under pressure, or seeks premature tactics, squandering a concrete material advantage averaging ~295 centipawns.

analysis.label: The player makes a catastrophic blunder that leaves their own piece hanging while simultaneously allowing forced checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move is a catastrophic defensive failure. The SEE aggregate shows 61% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/25, majors/21, minors/19), and the average cp_loss is an extreme 6282, with most positions transitioning from 'bad but playable' to 'forced mate.' The best move wins material 66% of the time (median 3.0), indicating there was often a tactical resource available. Only 21% of played moves were captures, meaning the player typically made a quiet/passive move that ignored critical threats. The best move is a check 24% and a capture 39% of the time, suggesting defensive counter-tactics existed. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, targeting specifically these multi-dimensional catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore the opponent's mating threats while simultaneously leaving the player's own material undefended. The player makes a 'hope' move, a meaningless check, or a passive piece placement that neither defends against mate nor preserves material. In almost every case, a better defensive resource existed (capturing an attacker, interposing, or finding a stalemate trick) that would have at least prolonged the game significantly.

analysis.label: The player makes a capture (usually with a bishop) that leaves the capturing piece undefended on its new square, allowing the opponent to win it back with interest.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a premature capture—81% of the time the played move is a capture—that leaves their own minor piece hanging (99% of positions, median hung value 3.0, overwhelmingly bishops at 172/176 minor pieces). The captures are almost exclusively bishop takes (Bxd5, Bxf6, Bxe5, Bxf3, Bxc3) in opening positions (9/12 top boards). The player grabs material but ignores that their capturing piece lands on an undefended square or that the capture exposes another piece. Only 24% of best moves are captures, and the best moves (Bb6, Bb3, Nh4, Bg6, Ne8) are typically quiet retreats or repositioning moves that maintain piece safety, showing the player should prioritize piece coordination over material greed.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing bishop lands on a square where it is undefended (or the capture removes defense from another piece), allowing the opponent to recapture at a profit. In many cases an enemy pawn was already attacking a knight (e.g., e5 attacking Nf6), so making the bishop trade elsewhere loses the second piece as well. The player sees an available capture and executes it without noticing that the resulting position leaves their minor piece en prise for free or that a more pressing defensive need existed.

analysis.label: Player ignores a fianchettoed bishop's ability to capture a completely undefended rook sitting on a corner square along the open long diagonal.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 96% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0 = a rook), and 95% of the time that best move is a capture. The player's actual move is a quiet non-capture (only 15% are captures), meaning they simply overlook the free rook. In all 12 top-activating boards, the pattern is identical: a bishop (usually fianchettoed on g2, b2, g7, or b7) has a completely clear long diagonal aimed at a corner square (a8, h8, a1, or h1) where the opponent's rook sits undefended. The best move is always Bxa8, Bxh8, Bxa1, or Bxh1 — winning a full rook for nothing. The 34% own-hang rate is incidental to some played moves creating secondary weaknesses, but the dominant and consistent error (96%) is the missed winning capture.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (O-O, e3, h6, Na5, g3, Ne4, Rg1, f3, Nc6, Bg7, Be2) are all quiet developing or prophylactic moves that completely ignore the open long diagonal. They forfeit a free rook (worth ~5 pawns) by failing to recognize that the fianchettoed bishop's diagonal is completely unobstructed all the way to the enemy's undefended corner rook.

analysis.label: Player gives an unproductive check that leaves their own piece hanging, when the best move (never a check) would maintain or gain material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a strikingly consistent pattern: 81% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 4.0, with 223 major pieces, 93 minor pieces, and 91 pawns hung), while the best move is NEVER a check (0%) but frequently wins material (69%, median 3.0). Every single top-12 activating move is a check (Qh8+, Re1+, Nd3+, Qe7+, Qf7+, Qf1+, Qb5+, Kg1+, Qb1+, Qh5+, Qb1+, Ng3+), yet the engine's recommended moves are quiet or capturing moves that address the actual needs of the position. The player's move captures only 19% of the time, confirming these are quiet checks rather than capturing ones. The average cp_loss of 2641 shows these are catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The checks are tactically empty — they force the opponent's king to a square it's often happy to go to (or simply sidestep), after which the checking piece or another piece left undefended is captured. The player prioritizes giving check (a psychologically tempting but non-constructive forcing move) over addressing the real demands of the position: capturing hanging enemy material, eliminating critical threats, or defending vulnerable pieces. The check gains one tempo but loses a whole piece.

analysis.label: Player misses a classic Greek Gift bishop sacrifice (Bxh7+ or Bxh2+) and plays a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a textbook Greek Gift sacrifice is available but the player opts for a passive developing move. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check 92% of the time and a capture 98% of the time, perfectly matching Bxh7+/Bxh2+ as the missed opportunity. The 'wins material' stat is only 14% because SEE evaluates the sacrifice statically (bishop for pawn, with king recapturing) as approximately neutral, while the true advantage comes from the ensuing mating attack—not raw material gain. The played moves were captures only 11% of the time, confirming quiet moves dominate. The 29% 'own piece hanging' (median value 2.0) is a secondary effect of the suboptimal quiet moves occasionally leaving pieces loose. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, reflecting the rarity of this specific tactical constellation.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Be2, Be3, Nf1, O-O, Nbd2, etc.) squander a decisive tactical opportunity. The Greek Gift sacrifice Bxh7+/Bxh2+ strips the opponent's king of pawn cover, and the follow-up Ng5+/Ng4+ with Qh5 creates an irresistible mating attack. By playing passively, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, shore up the h-pawn, or reroute defensive pieces, converting a winning position (avg +400 cp) into a merely favorable one (avg +130 cp), losing roughly 270 centipawns on average.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (usually with a rook) that leaves their own major piece en prise on the resulting square or elsewhere.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a greedy move—81% of the time a capture—that leaves their own major piece hanging (99% of positions, median value 5.0 = rook). The hung-piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (257 out of 272), primarily rooks. Meanwhile, the best move wins material 70% of the time (median 5.0) and is often a check (28%) or a superior tactical continuation. The player is lured by an attractive-looking capture (Rxd1, Rxc7, Rxb4, Kxb7, etc.) but fails to notice that after their move, their rook (or occasionally queen) is left unprotected and immediately capturable by the opponent. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, indicating a specific and costly tactical blindspot.
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes grabbing material or making a 'natural' recapture without checking whether their own major piece is left undefended after the move. The rook lands on (or remains on) a square where it can be immediately captured, often by a back-rank piece, a discovered attack, or simply an uncontested recapture. The best move typically either wins even more material, delivers check first, or avoids the hanging piece entirely.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an undefended enemy piece (usually a rook or queen) that is directly en prise, playing a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 78% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), and 79% of the time the best move is a simple capture. Yet the player's move was a capture only 9% of the time, confirming they consistently failed to take freely available material. The 38% own-hang rate (median 1.0, i.e., pawns) is secondary noise rather than the primary pattern. Across the top 12 boards, the missed captures involve undefended rooks (positions 1-3, 6-7, 9, 11), queens (positions 8, 12), and bishops (position 5), typically in endgame positions (11/12 boards) where the piece sits completely unprotected and adjacent to or on a clear line from the capturing piece—often the player's own king.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a free capture of a high-value enemy piece (usually a rook or queen worth 5-9 points) and instead plays a passive or repositioning quiet move. After the quiet move, the opponent moves the hanging piece to safety, and the player has squandered a decisive material advantage—often converting a winning position into a losing one (average cp_loss: 860).

analysis.label: Player makes a routine pawn advance or exchange that leaves their own pawn undefended, while missing a stronger tactical continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a pawn move (all 12 top activations are pawn moves — captures like exd5/dxe5/cxd5 or advances like f5/e5/d5) that leaves their own material hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 89% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being a pawn in 328/445 cases (74%). Meanwhile, the best move wins material 58% of the time (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and only 30% of best moves are captures — indicating the missed opportunities are often tactical moves like knight forks, queen captures of undefended pieces, or exchange sacrifices. The player's move is itself a capture 50% of the time, suggesting 'autopilot' recaptures in pawn exchanges that overlook the resulting structural weakness.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn captures/advances are bad because they prioritize an obvious or routine pawn exchange while simultaneously leaving a pawn undefended (often the pawn that was protecting a key square or the pawn left behind after the exchange opens the file). The player focuses on the local pawn tension rather than seeing the broader tactical picture where a piece move (Nh5, Nf6, Qxc5, Rxc6, etc.) would win significant material or exploit a more important weakness.

analysis.label: Player makes a move that leaves their own pawn (often a key defensive pawn like f2/f7/c7) en prise, frequently allowing immediate checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of positions have the player's move leaving their OWN piece hanging (median value: 1.0), with the piece distribution overwhelmingly being pawns (446 out of 486 cases). The best move wins material in 54% of cases (median 3.0), indicating many positions also had winning captures available that were ignored. Only 28% of played moves were captures, and the feature fires on 0.7% of all positions. The average cp_loss of 5061 (with many mate-in-1 blunders) reveals these are not ordinary pawn losses—the hung pawn is typically a critical defensive pawn (f2, f7, or c7) whose capture delivers checkmate or wins decisive material. Positions 3, 5, and 11 specifically show f2/f7 under attack from bishop-queen batteries, while Position 12 shows c7 targeted with a mating pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediate tactical threat to a structurally critical pawn—often one shielding the king. By developing a piece, making a capture elsewhere, or pushing a different pawn, the player leaves the key defensive pawn unprotected. The opponent then captures it, frequently delivering checkmate (as seen in positions 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 12) because the pawn was the last barrier between an attacking piece and the king.

analysis.label: The player makes an active-looking or greedy move that leaves their own queen or rook en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player's move left their own piece hanging in 98% of cases, with a median hung value of 5.0 (rook/queen). The hung piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (170 major vs 29 minor vs 8 pawn). While the best move also wins material 72% of the time (median 3.0), the defining signature is the self-inflicted blunder. The played move was a capture 46% of the time, suggesting greedy captures that overlook the opponent's reply winning back a major piece. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions with an average centipawn loss of 1310, indicating catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player either moves their queen/rook to an undefended square where it can be captured, makes a greedy capture with or near a major piece that allows a recapture or fork winning it back, or moves a defending piece away leaving their own major piece unprotected. The player focuses on an immediate tactical idea (a check, a capture, an aggressive reposition) while overlooking that their queen or rook is left completely en prise to the opponent's next move.

analysis.label: Playing a pointless queen check that leaves the queen en prise on the checking square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 69% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0), with 'major' pieces overwhelmingly dominant in the hung-piece distribution (97 of 161 classified instances). Every single top-12 activating move is a queen check (Qa8+, Qd5+, Qf4+, etc.), yet the best move is a check only 35% of the time, proving these checks are unnecessary. The best move wins material 71% of the time (median 5.0), meaning strong alternatives existed. Only 15% of played moves were captures, confirming these are pure check moves rather than productive exchanges. The average cp_loss of 1807 reflects the catastrophic cost of losing a queen for nothing. Positions are mostly endgames and queen-heavy scenarios where perpetual check might seem tempting but fails tactically.
analysis.why_bad: The queen moves to give check on a square where, after the opponent simply steps away or blocks, the queen has no retreat and is left undefended — it can be captured for free. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of check without calculating the opponent's reply, blundering their most valuable piece in a position where a quiet or alternative move would maintain equality or advantage.

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop capture on c3 or c6 delivering check, which initiates a winning tactical sequence.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the strongest move is a bishop capturing a knight on c3 (or c6) with check — an extremely specific tactical motif. The SEE aggregate confirms: 98% of best moves are checks and 96% are captures, with a median material gain of 1.0 (pawn equivalent from the initial exchange, though follow-ups often win much more). Only 26% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet developing moves instead. In 49% of cases (median value 3.0, with 39 minors among the hung pieces), the alternative move played actually left the player's own piece vulnerable — often the very bishop that should have executed the tactic. The feature fires in just 0.1% of positions, reflecting the specificity of this opening/early-middlegame geometry where a bishop on the a5-e1 or a4-e8 diagonal can capture a knight on c3/c6 with discovered or direct check.
analysis.why_bad: By playing quiet moves (Nh6, c6, Bd7, Ba5, Nf6, etc.) instead of the forcing Bxc3+ or Bxc6+, players miss a check that wins material through the subsequent tactical sequence (often shattering the pawn structure, winning the exchange, or picking up additional pieces). The check forces the opponent to deal with king safety first, giving the attacker tempo to collect material. Missing this tactic often leaves the position equal or worse, squandering advantages of 150-440 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player makes an active-looking but misguided move instead of the critical rook deployment to an open file, often leaving their own piece hanging or missing material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 51% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/99, minors/92, majors/65), while 61% of best moves win material (median 3.0). Crucially, best moves are almost never checks (1%) or captures (13%) — they are quiet rook placements. In 9 of 12 top-activating positions, the best move is a rook move to a contested open file (Rd1, Re1, Rc7, Re8, Rc1, etc.). Instead, the player makes a different 'active' move — a knight maneuver (Nf4, Nb5, Nc4), a king walk (Kg2, Kh7), or a wrong capture (Bxe5, Rxc3, Rxa4) — that ignores the tactical necessity on the open file. The position features consistently show open d/e/c-files with rooks requiring activation.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical obligation on an open file. The rook move was needed either to (a) save an own piece that is attacked along the file (positions 3, 5, 7 where rooks/bishops are left en prise), (b) contest the file to prevent the opponent from dominating it (positions 2, 6, 11), or (c) win material by infiltrating or capturing along the open file (positions 4, 9, 10). The played moves address secondary concerns while the primary open-file dynamic punishes them immediately.

analysis.label: Player advances a pawn to deliver check when a quiet positional move (typically king centralization) was far superior, often leaving the advanced pawn hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 44% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with pawns dominating the hung-piece distribution (96 pawns vs 43 minors vs 11 majors). Meanwhile, best moves are checks only 3% of the time and captures only 11%, indicating the correct moves are overwhelmingly quiet. All 12 top-activating positions show a pawn push delivering check (c5+, e4+, h3+, g4+, a3+, f5+, etc.) in endgame positions where the opponent's king is exposed. The best moves are nearly always quiet king maneuvers (Kc5, Ke5, Kd6, Kh2, Ke3, Kg2, Kf7) or positional piece moves (Rd3, b3). The feature fires on 0.2% of all positions, isolating this specific temptation pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The pawn check looks forcing but accomplishes nothing strategically—the opponent's king simply sidesteps, and the advanced pawn is now overextended, often left en prise (44% hung rate). Meanwhile, the player squanders the opportunity for critical king centralization or piece activation that would have maintained or increased their advantage. In endgames especially, tempi are precious, and a check that doesn't improve the position is a wasted move that can turn winning positions into draws or draws into losses (avg cp_loss: 155).

analysis.label: Player advances a passed pawn (often to the 2nd/7th rank) while hanging their own piece, missing a superior tactical continuation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 77% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns:61, majors:32, minors:29), while 69% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0). The played moves are overwhelmingly passed pawn advances to the penultimate rank (b2, e2, c7, d7, e7) or captures creating such pawns (cxb2), appearing in 41% as captures. The player is fixated on advancing a dangerous passed pawn toward promotion but neglects piece safety and misses stronger tactical shots. Only 14% of best moves are checks and 28% are captures, showing the superior alternatives are often quiet but tactically sound moves that protect material while maintaining the advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player tunnel-visions on the promotion threat while ignoring that advancing the pawn removes support from other pieces or opens lines against their own material. The passed pawn one square from queening looks devastating but the opponent can often ignore it (or deal with it later) while winning the now-undefended piece. Meanwhile, the correct move usually consolidates by winning material or addressing tactical threats first, after which the passed pawn remains a long-term advantage.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet move (usually a king move) instead of capturing an undefended high-value enemy piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a missed-winning-capture pattern: 67% of best moves win material (median value 9.0, i.e., queen-level), 89% of best moves are captures, yet 0% of played moves are captures and 0% hang the player's own piece. All 9 top-activating positions are endgames where an enemy piece (often a queen or rook) is en prise and capturable by the player's own piece, but the player instead makes a quiet move—almost always a king retreat or sidestep. The feature fires on only 0.0% of all positions, indicating it targets a very specific failure mode in simplified endgame positions where the capture is the only critical move.
analysis.why_bad: By playing a quiet king move instead of capturing the hanging enemy piece, the player throws away a drawn or near-equal position—often turning it into an immediate forced mate or a hopelessly lost endgame. In many cases the capture was the ONLY move to save the game (e.g., capturing a queen to reach insufficient material, or taking a rook to reach a theoretical draw), and ignoring it results in catastrophic cp_loss (average 4671cp).

analysis.label: The player makes an active-looking or greedy move that leaves one of their own pieces hanging and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 82% of the top 500 activating positions show the player's move left their OWN piece en prise (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece). The piece class distribution is broad (major: 201, minor: 139, pawn: 72), indicating no single piece type but a general blindness to own-piece vulnerability. While 73% of positions also had a best move winning material (median 3.0), the dominant and consistent signal is the self-inflicted hanging. The played move was a capture 40% of the time, suggesting players often make greedy captures that overlook the tactical consequences for their remaining pieces. The feature fires on just 1.1% of all positions, indicating these are significant blunders rather than routine positional errors.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore that a piece (often a queen, rook, or knight) is left undefended or insufficiently protected after the move. Whether the player captures a less valuable piece (e.g., bxa4 while the queen hangs), makes a flashy check (Nxc4+ leaving the knight en prise), repositions a piece to an unsafe square (Rd3 where it's trapped/capturable), or simply overlooks an existing threat to their own piece (Nd3 ignoring the queen being attacked), the result is the same: the opponent can capture the hanging piece for free or with a significant material advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a premature developing move or pawn advance in the opening that leaves their own piece (pawn or minor piece) undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively shows this feature fires when the player's own move leaves a piece hanging: 88% of the top 500 positions have the player's move leaving their own piece en prise (median value 1.0), with the hung pieces split between pawns (13) and minor pieces (10). Only 12% of the played moves were captures themselves, and best moves are rarely checks (0%) or captures (8%), meaning the correct alternative was typically a quiet developing move. The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase (11/12 top boards), identifying positions where players make careless pawn pushes into opponent-controlled squares (e.g., ...d5 into Nc3+c4) or develop pieces to undefended squares where they are immediately lost (e.g., Nd4, Ba6, Ne5 into pawn-controlled territory).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they either push a pawn into a square jointly controlled by the opponent's pieces (e.g., ...d5 into cxd5/Nxd5), move a piece to an unprotected square attacked by an opponent's pawn or minor piece (e.g., Ne5 into a d4-pawn's control), or ignore an existing threat to one's own piece by playing an irrelevant move (e.g., ...d6 instead of retreating an attacked knight). In each case the opponent wins material by simply capturing the undefended piece.

analysis.label: Player missed a Queen check that wins the game via mate or decisive material, playing a quiet or inferior move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that 96% of best moves are checks and 98% win material (median value 91, indicating forced mate or queen-level gains), while only 25% of played moves were captures and most were quiet moves. Across all 12 top boards, the best move is consistently a Queen delivering check (Qd4+, Qa1+, Qe5+, Qf3+, Qf1+, Qe4+, Qe8#, Qxf5+, Qxe3+, Qxe4+), typically leading to immediate checkmate or winning massive material. The enemy king is usually on the back rank (h8, h1) or otherwise exposed. Players instead chose non-forcing moves: pawn pushes (b6, b7, b5), rook moves (Rf2, Re2), non-checking queen moves (Qd3, Qf6, Qa6, Qe1, Qe2), or captures on wrong squares (Qxa7, Qxe5). The 38% own-hang rate (median value 3) is secondary—some played moves also blundered material, compounding the missed win.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing Queen check that delivers immediate checkmate or wins decisive material through irresistible threats. By playing quiet or non-forcing moves, the player allows the opponent to escape the mating net, cover the vulnerable king, or otherwise neutralize the attack, squandering a won position.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player makes a quiet king or piece retreat instead of executing a critical capture or check that wins or saves material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move wins material 50% of the time (median value 9, i.e., queen-level captures available), while the played move is NEVER a capture (0%). Additionally, 31% of the time the played move leaves the player's own minor piece hanging (median value 3). Best moves are captures 50% of the time and checks 25% of the time. The feature fires exclusively in endgames where the player opts for a quiet, often aimless king move or piece repositioning (Ne6+, Ba1, Ke5, Kc5, Kb4, Ke7, Kf5, Kh3, Kf2, Bd1, h4) when the position demands an immediate tactical strike—either capturing an undefended enemy piece (often a queen) or giving a tempo-gaining check that saves one's own hanging piece.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they waste a critical tempo in sharp endgame positions where an immediate capture or check resolves the tactical tension favorably. By playing passively, the player either misses winning a hanging enemy queen/piece outright (positions 1, 3, 6, 11), blunders their own minor piece into a capture (positions 2, 4, 9, 10), or allows the opponent's passed pawns to promote unchallenged (positions 7, 8). The endgame's razor-thin margins mean one wasted tempo converts a draw or win into a decisive loss.

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player makes a tempting rook capture that leaves the rook (or another major piece) en prise, when a quiet king move or repositioning was correct.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 53% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging with a median value of 5.0 (a rook), and the hung-piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (58 major vs. 20 pawn vs. 4 minor). Meanwhile, 48% of played moves were captures—indicating the player grabbed material with their rook but left it undefended or trappable afterward. The best move wins material only 33% of the time (median 1.0), and is a check only 3% / a capture only 10%, confirming that the correct continuation was almost always a quiet positional move (typically a king centralization like Kd3, Ke6, Ka4) rather than a greedy rook capture. The feature fires exclusively in endgames on 0.1% of positions.
analysis.why_bad: The rook lunges to capture a pawn or piece but lands on a square where it is immediately capturable, trappable, or cut off from the rest of the position. By prioritizing short-term material gain, the player loses their rook (worth 5 points) or creates a decisive positional collapse. The correct move—usually a king move—would have maintained coordination, kept the rook safe, and addressed the critical strategic demands of the endgame (blockading passed pawns, centralizing, or escorting one's own passers).

analysis.label: The player makes a bishop or knight move (often a tempting capture) while ignoring that their own queen is attacked or left en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player leaves their own queen hanging by playing an unrelated minor-piece move. The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 100% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0), with the hung piece class being exclusively 'major' across all 500 samples. Examining the boards confirms these are all queens (values 6-9). The best moves are queen relocations in every single case (Qh4, Qd2, Qb2, Qe2, Qc4, Qxd6, Qg5, Qe2, Qg7, Qd1, Qa5, Qh5). Meanwhile 50% of the played moves are captures—often enticing knight or bishop takes (Nxe6, Nxf2, Bxf6, Bxc3, Bxe7)—that ignore the existential threat to the queen. The best move also wins material 63% of the time (median 3.0 pawns), typically because the queen's safe square also attacks something.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a tempting tactical idea (a capture, an attack, or piece development) while their queen is under direct attack from an enemy piece along a diagonal or file. After the played move, the opponent simply captures the undefended queen, gaining massive material. The correct move in every case was to move the queen to a safe (often also aggressive) square first.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet/passive move (usually a king move in the endgame) that leaves their own pawn undefended while missing a stronger tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player's move leaves their own piece hanging 65% of the time (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 8/11 with 3 minors), while the best move would have won material in 47% of cases (median value 3.0, i.e., a full minor piece). The best move is a capture 41% of the time but the player's move is only a capture 12% of the time, confirming the player chose passivity over action. The pattern overwhelmingly occurs in endgame positions (7/12 top boards) where the player makes an aimless king move (Ke3, Kf8, Kc2, Ka7, Kh3, Kf3) or quiet piece retreat (Bb2, Bg6) that walks away from pawn defense, while a much stronger active move—often a capture winning a piece—was available.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail doubly: they abandon defense of the player's own pawn (or minor piece), immediately losing material, while simultaneously missing a far stronger tactical move that wins enemy material. The king or piece moves to an irrelevant or passive square instead of the active square required by the position's tactical demands, turning winning or equal positions into lost ones (average cp_loss: 2014).

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting queen capture (grabbing material) that leaves their own pieces hanging or abandons critical defensive duties, missing a stronger tactical continuation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 79% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns: 77, majors: 74, minors: 43), while 72% of the time the best move would have won material (median 5.0). The played move was itself a capture 46% of the time. Nearly all top-activating moves are queen captures (Qxc4, Qxc3, Qxh6, Qxe3, Qxd4, Qxd6, Qxe4, etc.) where the queen greedily snatches a piece but the resulting position collapses — either the queen abandons defensive duties allowing checkmate, or other pieces are left undefended. The best moves (21% checks, 27% captures) represent stronger tactical blows the player missed in favor of the superficially attractive queen capture.
analysis.why_bad: These queen captures are superficially appealing because they win immediate material, but they ignore the larger tactical picture: the queen leaves its defensive post (allowing mate or major-piece wins), moves to a square where it can be trapped or where the vacated position exposes hanging pieces, or simply misses a far stronger move like a checking sequence or a mating attack. The average cp_loss of ~4951 reflects that many of these lead to immediate checkmate or catastrophic material collapse.

analysis.label: Player misses a forcing check against an exposed enemy king that wins decisive material or forces mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of best moves are checks and 96% win material (median value 100, i.e., queen-equivalent or forced mate). The player's move is typically quiet (only 22% are captures), often a rook move to the 7th rank or a piece development that ignores the exposed enemy king. The 50% own-hang rate (median value 1.0 = pawn) is incidental—the defining pattern is the missed check. The feature fires on positions where the opponent's king is exposed (on squares like c2, g3, h4, f3, e3, a3, d4) and a forcing check with a rook, knight, or queen delivers a decisive blow, yet the player opts for a natural-looking but non-forcing alternative.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they surrender the initiative in positions where a single forcing check exploits the opponent's exposed king to either deliver checkmate or win massive material (often the queen). By playing a quiet move, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, escape the danger zone, or generate counterplay, turning winning or drawn positions into losses. The average cp_loss of 1848 confirms these are game-deciding blunders.

analysis.label: Player captures a central pawn with a minor piece that is left unprotected and hanging on the capture square.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player (predominantly using a knight) captures a central pawn on d4/d5/e4/e5/e6 but leaves the capturing piece en prise. The SEE aggregate shows 94% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), with the overwhelming majority being minor pieces (409/500). The played move was a capture 75% of the time, confirming the pattern of greedy material grab. While the player wins a pawn (~1), they lose a minor piece (~3), explaining the median best-move material advantage of 2.0 (47% of best moves win material). The best moves are rarely captures themselves (only 15%) and only 9% are checks, indicating the correct play was typically quiet development or prophylaxis rather than snatching material.
analysis.why_bad: The knight or bishop captures a tempting central pawn but lands on a square where it has no support. The opponent simply recaptures the minor piece, netting roughly two pawns of material advantage. The player trades a 3-point piece for a 1-point pawn—a classic case of greed overriding piece safety. Better alternatives (development moves, checks, or retreats) would maintain the minor piece's safety while preserving positional advantages.

analysis.label: Player misses an available checkmate or forced mating check, playing a quiet non-forcing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: 99% of the time the best move is a check, and 99% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 100 (representing king capture / checkmate). Only 25% of best moves are captures, meaning 75% are pure checks that force mate. Meanwhile, the player's actual move is a capture only 9% of the time and leaves their own piece hanging only 15% of the time — indicating the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet, aimless moves. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions. Across the top 12 boards, we see direct mates (Ra1#, Rf1#, Rd4#) and short forced mating sequences beginning with checks (Re1+, Ra1+, Nc4+, Bf4+, Nf6+, Ne7+, Rg3+), all missed in favor of moves like h2, Kf3, g5, c6, h5, b4, e5 — completely non-forcing moves that squander the win.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available checkmate or forced mating sequence starting with a check. Instead of delivering the killing blow, the player makes an irrelevant pawn push or piece move that allows the opponent to survive, often converting a forced mate into merely a large advantage or even allowing counterplay.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning check (almost always a queen check) that delivers immediate checkmate or forces a short mating sequence.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, and in 98% of cases the best move wins material with a median value of 95 (essentially game-decisive). Only 23% of best moves are captures, meaning the checks are overwhelmingly non-capturing queen checks exploiting exposed kings. The played moves were a mix of quiet moves and captures (33% captures) that completely ignored the forcing check. In 61% of cases the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), but this is incidental — the catastrophic error is missing the decisive check. The average cp_loss of 10049 confirms these are predominantly missed forced checkmates.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore an available check that either delivers immediate checkmate or initiates a forced mating sequence. By playing quiet developing moves, material-grabbing captures, or positional improvements, the player squanders a won position — often allowing the opponent to either escape or launch their own counterattack that flips the evaluation from winning to losing or even getting mated themselves.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet or irrelevant move that leaves their own major piece (usually Queen) en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 72% of positions have the player's move leaving their OWN piece hanging (median value 4.0), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (66 major vs 33 minor vs 21 pawn). Only 33% of played moves were captures, meaning most blunders are quiet repositioning moves. The best move wins material 66% of the time (median 3.0), typically because the correct line either defends the hanging piece or wins enemy material first. In the top 12 boards, 8 out of 12 positions show the Queen being hung (SEE value 9), with the player making moves like Bg7, Qf8, Qa7, Qh4, or Nb8 — moves that look like normal development or repositioning but catastrophically ignore that their Queen is now undefended or moved to a capturable square. The average centipawn loss of 1714 confirms these are game-losing blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player makes a 'positional' or routine-looking move while ignoring an immediate tactical reality: their major piece (usually the Queen) is either moved to an undefended square, or a defender of their Queen is moved away, allowing the opponent to simply capture the exposed piece. The player prioritizes an irrelevant plan over the board's tactical demands.

analysis.label: Player misses a queen check that wins significant material or decisively exploits the opponent's king position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the best move wins material in 95% of positions (median value 91, indicating queen-winning or game-deciding gains), and 89% of the time the best move is a check. Only 45% are captures, meaning many checks win material indirectly through forks or forced sequences. The player's actual move was a capture only 11% of the time and was almost always a quiet, non-tactical move. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, isolating specifically those rare cases where a devastating queen check was available but entirely overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves are universally quiet (Bg2, g3, Qd8, Rh6, h4, Rb8, c6, etc.) and completely ignore the opponent's king vulnerability. By missing the queen check, the player forfeits winning material worth roughly a queen (median SEE value 91) or a decisive attack. In many cases the position swings from a large advantage to equality or even a losing position (avg cp_loss 288), because the opponent gets time to consolidate their king safety and neutralize the tactical threats.

analysis.label: The player missed a bishop move that wins the opponent's queen (or equivalent major material worth ~6 points net).
analysis.description: In 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median SEE value of 6 — consistent with winning a queen (value 9) while the bishop is recaptured (net 9-3=6). Strikingly, every single top-12 best move is a bishop deployment (Be4, Bg5, Bf3, Bg4, Bb5, Bc6) that attacks or forks the opponent's queen. The best move is a capture only 7% of the time and a check only 5%, meaning the winning resource is typically a quiet bishop move to a powerful square that creates an unavoidable queen-winning threat (fork, pin, or undefendable attack). Instead, players chose routine developing moves, captures on other squares, or castling (22% captures, 78% quiet moves), completely overlooking the bishop's tactical potential.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a concrete tactical shot — a bishop move that attacks the enemy queen from a square where even if the bishop is recaptured, the queen is lost. Players instead play natural-looking but strategically irrelevant moves (Re1, O-O, Qd2, c3, Nc6) or misguided captures (Nxe5, Bxf6, Bxd6), missing the one-move bishop resource that wins approximately a queen for a bishop (net +6).

analysis.label: A knight (or minor piece) is aggressively placed on a central square like e4 or d5 where it is left en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player's own move left a piece hanging in 96% of the top 500 activating positions, with a median value of 1 (one pawn's worth of net material lost). The hung piece class is predominantly a minor piece (336 out of 410 non-pawn cases). Only 6% of the played moves were captures, confirming these are quiet piece-placement moves rather than failed exchanges. The best move wins material in 40% of cases (median 2.0), suggesting the player also frequently misses tactical opportunities while making this positional blunder. Across the top 12 boards, 8 of 12 played moves are literally 'Ne4', with Nd5 and Ne5 also appearing—all knight jumps to central squares that appear aggressive but leave the knight undefended and capturable.
