analysis.why_bad: The knight lands on an attractive-looking central outpost (most commonly e4, also d5/e5) but lacks pawn or piece support, making it immediately capturable. The player is seduced by the visual appeal of a centralized knight and overlooks that no friendly pawn or piece adequately defends the square. Simple developing moves like castling (O-O) or consolidating captures (Bxd3, Nxd2) would have maintained material equality or even an advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores that their own undefended major piece (usually a rook) is en prise, failing to resolve the tension by capturing the opponent's piece first.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 79% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (19/27 instances). The best move is a capture 82% of the time and a check 47% of the time, indicating the correct resolution is to 'fire first' — capturing the opponent's piece (often with check) to exchange off the exposed piece favorably. Instead, the player makes a different move (44% are captures elsewhere — greedy diversions), leaving their undefended rook to be won. The pattern consistently shows an aggressively placed but unprotected rook (e.g., Ra8 deep in enemy territory, or a rook in mutual contact with an opponent's piece) that is only tactically justified if the player trades immediately.
analysis.why_bad: The player's rook sits on an exposed square justified only by the ability to capture/exchange immediately. By playing a quiet move or greedy capture elsewhere, the player allows the opponent to simply take the undefended rook for free, losing approximately 5 points of material (a whole rook or equivalent). The 'tension' that kept the position viable is broken in the opponent's favor.

analysis.label: Player fails to exchange queens on the open d-file (Qxd1/Qxd8), leaving their own queen hanging to the opponent's queen.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where both queens face each other on the open d-file and the correct move is to trade queens (best move is a capture 99% of the time, almost always Qxd1 or Qxd8 winning 0 material — an equal exchange). Instead, the player makes another move (36% captures elsewhere, others quiet), and 57% of the time their own piece is left hanging (median value 6.0, with 'major' pieces dominating at 59 out of 94 instances — primarily the queen itself left en prise on the d-file). The best move wins material only 10% of the time because the queen trade is equal, but failing to trade is catastrophic since the opponent's queen remains active on the open file targeting the player's undefended queen.
analysis.why_bad: When queens face each other on an open d-file with no intervening pieces, the trade is essentially forced — ignoring it allows the opponent to capture your queen for free on the next move. Players get distracted by other tactical ideas (capturing pieces, developing, attacking) without recognizing that their queen is immediately capturable on d1/d8 by the opposing queen. The average cp_loss of 1148 reflects that leaving a queen hanging is typically game-ending.

analysis.label: Player captures or ignores a passed pawn threat, leaving their own rook/bishop en prise to the enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 84% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (21 major, 8 minor). 51% of moves played are captures, and the best move wins material only 32% of the time (meaning the position was already winning without needing to capture). The pattern involves endgame positions with dangerous enemy passed pawns near promotion, where the player's rook or bishop is restraining the pawn. The player either captures the pawn directly (Rxd7+, Rxa7+, Rxg7, Rxh7, Bxg6+, Bxf5+) with the enemy king immediately recapturing, or plays a different move while their piece is attacked by the enemy king (Kb1, a3, Bg7), in both cases losing the piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player trades a rook (worth 5) or bishop (worth 3) for a mere pawn. The enemy king sits adjacent to the passed pawn and simply recaptures after the piece takes. The player had winning positions by maintaining their material advantage and restraining the pawn from a distance (e.g., blockading, using the rook from behind, or keeping the bishop on a safe diagonal controlling the promotion square), rather than panicking and sacrificing material to eliminate the immediate threat.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive quiet move (usually a queen retreat/reposition) instead of executing an available tactical capture that exploits a pin or structural weakness.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 77% of the time, yet the played move is a capture 0% of the time — a stark contrast indicating the player consistently chooses quiet moves over available forcing captures. The best move wins material outright in 23% of cases (median 3.0 pawns), but even when the immediate exchange is nominally equal (like Bxf3 in positions 1-8), it unlocks a follow-up that wins a critical pawn or shatters the opponent's structure. The own-hang rate of 20% is modest and secondary; the dominant pattern is the missed tactical capture. In 8 of the top 12 positions, the exact scenario is a Scandinavian-type opening where Black has Bg4 pinning Nf3 to White's queen, and instead of playing Bxf3 (exploiting the pin to subsequently win d4), Black retreats or repositions the queen passively.
analysis.why_bad: The passive queen moves (Qd8, Qd7, Qa5, Qe6+) abandon the tactical tension without extracting any concrete advantage. By failing to play Bxf3, Black releases the pin voluntarily, allowing White to consolidate the d4 pawn and complete development freely. The quiet moves lose tempo, surrender Black's only source of dynamic compensation (the pin + central pressure), and allow White to seize a lasting structural and developmental advantage — resulting in 250-375 centipawn losses.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet king move instead of capturing an undefended enemy queen (or major piece worth ~9 points) that is freely available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 87% of the time (median value 9.0, i.e., a queen) and is a capture 97% of the time. The played move was itself a capture only 15% of the time—instead, 11 of the top 12 activating moves are quiet king moves. In 68% of positions the played move also left the player's OWN queen hanging (median value 9.0), meaning the king move not only missed capturing the opponent's undefended queen but often exposed the player's own queen to recapture. The own-hang distribution (41 major, 20 pawn, 2 minor) confirms queens are the primary pieces left en prise. All positions are endgames with exposed kings and mutual queen tension, where capturing first is critical.
analysis.why_bad: In these queen endgames with mutual piece exposure, tempo is everything. The opponent's queen (or major piece) is undefended and can be taken immediately, often with check. By playing a purposeless king move, the player forfeits a free queen capture, frequently leaves their own queen undefended on the next move, and converts a winning or equal position into an immediate loss (average cp_loss: 7194). The king move addresses no threat and ignores the most basic tactical principle: capture the hanging piece first.

analysis.label: The player needed to move their king to a specific safe square but either chose the wrong escape direction or neglected to move the king at all, leaving own material hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 52% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 1.0, distribution: 39 pawns, 16 major, 8 minor), while 34% of best moves win material (median 1.0). Critically, in 10 of the top 12 positions the best move is a king move to a precise safe square (Ka8, Kh1, Ke3, Kd8, Kh8, Kg8, Kh1, Kh3, Ke2, Kg7), but the player either moved the king to the wrong square (Kb8 instead of Ka8, Ke1 instead of Ke3, Kf8 instead of Kd8, Kg1 instead of Kh3, Kc2 instead of Ke2) or ignored the king's need to flee and played a piece move instead (Qd8, Ne4, Bg4, Rd8, Bf4). The enormous average cp_loss of 1939 reflects that the wrong king destination often walks into mating nets or leaves pieces undefended along the abandoned lines.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the king lands on (or stays on) a square where it either blocks its own pieces' defensive duties, walks into tactical motifs (forks, discovered attacks, checkmates), or abandons defense of pieces that become hanging. The correct king square typically sidesteps all attacking lines while maintaining coordination, whereas the chosen square falls victim to the opponent's active pieces on open files and diagonals.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available winning pawn capture in the center (typically resolving tension) and instead plays a quiet developing or flank move, often leaving their own pawn en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 75% of the time, winning material in 65% of positions (median value: 1 pawn). The player's move is almost never a capture itself (3%), and 48% of the time the quiet move played leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with 44 of 48 hung pieces being pawns). All 12 top-activating positions are openings with unresolved central pawn tension — pawns directly attacking each other on central files (d4 vs e5, e4 vs d5, c4 vs d5, etc.) — where a simple pawn or piece capture would win material or at minimum resolve the tension favorably. Instead, the player plays quiet moves like Nf3, Be2, f4, b3, or c5, ignoring the hanging center pawn.
analysis.why_bad: In positions with direct central pawn tension, the available capture is often winning a free pawn (the opponent's pawn is undefended or insufficiently defended). By declining this capture and playing a quiet move, the player not only forfeits material but frequently leaves their own pawn in the center vulnerable to recapture or counter-attack, resulting in a net swing of ~1-2 pawns and a large positional disadvantage (average cp_loss: 281).

analysis.label: Player makes a slow, non-forcing 'developing' move while missing a critical tactical opportunity to win material or while inadvertently leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 62% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), yet the player's move is a capture only 18% of the time — overwhelmingly they play quiet, repositioning moves instead. Additionally, 34% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed evenly across pawns, minors, and majors). Best moves are checks 16% of the time and captures 30% of the time — forcing moves the player ignores. The average cp_loss of 974 confirms these are catastrophic blunders. The boards show the player choosing 'natural-looking' moves like Rae1, Ra2, Re1, Be6, b4, Bd7 — standard developing/centralizing moves — while the position screams for immediate tactical action (including a missed mate-in-one with Ba3#, a missed queen-winning d6 advance worth 8 pawns, and missed captures worth 4-6 pawns).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player treats a tactically critical position as if it were a quiet positional one. By playing routine developing or repositioning moves, they either miss capturing or winning an enemy piece that is currently available (62% of cases) or leave their own pieces undefended on squares now attacked by the opponent (34% of cases). The position demands concrete, forcing play — captures, checks, or threats — but the player chooses a slow move that ignores the immediate tactical reality, resulting in catastrophic material or positional loss.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet piece repositioning move (usually Queen or Bishop) instead of a decisive check or capture that wins major material or forces mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 84% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0 — a rook's worth), yet the player's move was a capture only 12% of the time, confirming the player consistently missed the winning tactical shot. The best move is a check 47% of the time and a capture 48% of the time, meaning the missed moves are overwhelmingly forcing. Only 34% of played moves left own material hanging, making this primarily about missed wins rather than self-hanging. The average cp_loss is a staggering 4846 centipawns, with many positions involving missed forced mates. The played moves are almost exclusively quiet Queen or Bishop moves to 'active-looking' squares (Qg2, Qg6, Qh2, Bg6, Bg3, etc.) that do not force anything concrete.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet repositioning moves fail because they surrender a decisive tactical opportunity — typically a check or capture that either delivers forced mate or wins a full piece/rook. By playing a non-forcing move, the player allows the opponent to escape the tactical crisis, converting a completely won position into one that is merely better or even equal. The moves look superficially aggressive (centralizing a queen, activating a bishop) but ignore the concrete forcing sequence that ends the game immediately.

analysis.label: The player misses a queen check that would win significant material, instead playing a quiet or inferior move.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a queen check (100% of the time across 500 positions) that wins material (99%, median value ~91 centipawns in SEE). The player instead plays a non-checking move — only 27% are captures — and in 60% of cases the played move even leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3, distribution: 123 major pieces, 123 pawns, 55 minor pieces). The best move is only a capture 19% of the time, indicating the queen check typically wins material indirectly (via fork, discovered attack, or follow-up threat after the king moves) rather than by directly taking a piece. The enemy king is characteristically exposed (seen across virtually all top-activating positions), creating the queen-check opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: By missing the winning queen check, the player forfeits decisive material gain (often winning a full queen or rook via fork/follow-up). Worse, in 60% of cases the alternative move leaves their own major piece (often the queen itself) en prise, compounding the error — the queen that should be delivering a devastating check instead ends up on a vulnerable square where it can be captured.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of immediately capturing a dominant enemy centralized knight (or piece) that demands resolution.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a capture (99% of cases) — almost always taking an opponent's powerfully centralized knight on d4/e4/d5/e5 — but the player instead makes a quiet developing or repositioning move. The best move wins outright material 36% of the time (median value 1.0 = minor piece). By failing to challenge the dominant enemy piece, the player's position deteriorates: 48% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging afterward (median value 1.0; split evenly between minor pieces and pawns at 104 each, with 31 major pieces). The feature fires on only 0.5% of all positions, reflecting situations with unusually strong centralized enemy pieces in mostly closed-center openings.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the dominant centralized enemy knight, the player allows it to remain on its powerful outpost where it exerts enormous pressure on the position. The unchallenged knight generates tactical threats that often win material back or more — explaining why 48% of the quiet moves played leave the player's own pieces vulnerable. The immediate exchange would neutralize the opponent's strongest piece and simplify to a stable or advantageous position, but the quiet move gives the opponent time to exploit their centralized piece's dominance.

analysis.label: Player fails to initiate a critical rook exchange on an open file that would simplify into a decisively winning position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 94% of the top 500 activating positions the best move is a capture, yet only 18% win material outright (the captures are mostly equal exchanges with SEE = 0). The player's move is a quiet non-capture 84% of the time. In all 12 top boards, the best move is a rook exchange (Rxe8, Rxb1, Rxd7+, Rxg8, Rxg6, Rxg1) on an open file where both sides have rooks. The position features consistently show doubled rooks facing enemy rooks on the same open file. The 39% own-hang rate (median value 3.0) reflects a secondary consequence: by refusing the exchange, the player often makes a passive or misguided move that also leaves material loose. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting the specific geometry of rooks facing each other on open files where the exchange unlocks a winning simplification.
analysis.why_bad: The rook exchange, though materially neutral, is strategically decisive—it typically removes a key defender, enables passed pawn promotion, or simplifies into a won endgame. By playing quiet moves (rook repositions, pawn pushes, king moves) instead of capturing, the player allows the opponent to maintain defensive resources, often costing 150-450 centipawns of advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes an active-looking move (capture or check elsewhere) while missing a simple winning capture, simultaneously leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a double error: they miss a straightforward winning capture (95% of positions have best move winning material, median value 3.0 pawns, with 80% of best moves being captures) AND they leave their own piece en prise (73% of played moves hang an own piece, median value 3.0). The played moves are often captures on the wrong square (36% are captures) or flashy checks/active moves. The own-hung piece distribution (minor: 21, major: 15, pawn: 7) shows bishops and knights are most commonly left undefended. The best moves are frequently simple recaptures with the king (Kxe2, Kxg8, Kxg2, Kxg7) or straightforward pawn captures (fxe6, gxf3), while the played moves chase tactical ideas on different parts of the board.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an active-looking operation (a distant capture, a check, or an aggressive push) over a simple free capture, while their 'active' move removes a defender or leaves a piece unprotected. The result is a net material swing of roughly two pieces: they forfeit the material they could have won AND lose the piece they left hanging, often resulting in catastrophic evaluation drops (avg cp_loss: 895).

analysis.label: Player misses a back-rank checkmate or winning back-rank capture with check, playing an inferior move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 98% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. a rook), with 87% of best moves being checks and 79% being captures — the hallmark signature of back-rank tactics where the winning move captures a piece on the opponent's back rank delivering check or immediate checkmate. The player's move was itself a capture only 38% of the time, meaning they were often distracted by quiet moves or inferior captures elsewhere on the board. Only 33% of played moves hung the player's own piece, confirming this is overwhelmingly a 'missed winning tactic' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, reflecting how rare yet catastrophic these oversights are (average cp_loss: 7789).
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a lethal back-rank vulnerability. In nearly every case, the opponent's king is entombed behind its own pawns on the first/eighth rank, and a simple capture (Qxe1#, Qxe8#, Rxd1#, Qxa1#, Qxd8#, etc.) delivers immediate checkmate or wins decisive material with check. Instead, the player grabs a less important piece, makes a positional move, or delivers an inferior check — completely missing the instantly winning back-rank blow.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (usually a rook recapture) instead of a much stronger intermediate check—typically a knight fork—that wins far more material.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player grabs material with a natural-looking capture but misses a devastating checking move. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check 86% of the time (yet only a capture 19%), winning material in 95% of positions with a median value of 97 (approximately a queen). The player's move is itself a capture 74% of the time, and critically leaves their own piece hanging 76% of the time (median hung value: 5, i.e., a rook; piece distribution skewed toward majors at 26/44). The typical geometry involves a rook recapture on an open file that looks natural but misses a knight or bishop check that forks the king and a high-value piece, or initiates a forced mating attack.
analysis.why_bad: The played captures are 'greedy'—they win material on the current square but ignore a stronger intermediate check (usually a knight fork) that would win far more (often a queen or force mate). After the capture, the player's piece typically sits en prise on the destination square because the opponent can recapture, netting back most or all of the material, while the missed check would have exploited the exposed enemy king to win decisively.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy piece (typically a bishop) attacking their queen along a diagonal, missing both the free capture and the threat to their own queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 82% of positions the best move wins enemy material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 88% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 6.0, i.e., a queen). The own-hang piece distribution confirms major pieces dominate (13/15). The best move is a capture in 88% of cases. This dual signature reveals a consistent pattern: an undefended enemy bishop sits on a diagonal directly attacking the player's queen, creating a position where capturing the bishop both wins material AND removes the threat. Instead, the player plays an unrelated quiet move (88% non-captures), leaving their queen en prise on the diagonal. Positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 all feature Qxg4 as best (capturing an undefended Bg4 attacking Qd1); positions 4, 5, 11 feature bishop-queen diagonals in the reverse direction.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a critical diagonal attack on the player's queen by an undefended enemy bishop. By playing a quiet developing move instead of simply capturing the free attacker (or deflecting the threat), the player simultaneously misses winning a piece worth ~3 pawns and leaves their queen (worth ~9 pawns) hanging on the same diagonal, resulting in catastrophic material loss.

analysis.label: In endgames with advanced passed pawns, the player makes a king move instead of the critical pawn advance or promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player moves their king when the best move is typically a pawn push toward promotion. The SEE aggregate shows only 25% of best moves win material (median 91cp, consistent with promotion value), while the played move is almost never a capture (12%) and rarely hangs material (12%). The low hung-own and low best-captures percentages indicate the mistake is not about material exchange but about tempo: the player wastes time with a king move when a passed pawn should be advanced immediately. The average cp_loss of 1712 reflects catastrophic cases where missing a promotion or critical pawn push throws away a winning position entirely (e.g., Position 8: Kb8 instead of c8=Q+ loses mate-in-10; Position 1: Kf7 instead of g7 loses mate-in-5).
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames with advanced passed pawns, tempo is everything. A king move wastes a critical turn that should be used to push the pawn to promotion or force the opponent's king into zugzwang. The extra king move often allows the opponent's king to reach a drawing square, block the pawn, or escape a mating net—converting a won position into a draw or even throwing away a forced mate.

analysis.label: A minor piece captures on f7 or f2 in the opening without support, leaving it hanging for recapture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of positions feature the player's own piece left hanging (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), with the piece class distribution showing 76 out of 80 hung pieces are minor pieces (bishops/knights). The player's move was itself a capture in 88% of cases. Crucially, the best move is a check only 0% of the time and a capture only 8% of the time, meaning the correct continuation was quiet development, not a premature tactical strike. All 12 top-activating positions occur in the opening, where a bishop or knight captures on f7 (or f2 from Black's side), often with check, but the piece is completely unsupported and will simply be recaptured.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop or knight captures the f7/f2 pawn—often with superficially attractive check—but without sufficient attacking infrastructure (supporting pieces, open lines, or real follow-up threats). After the king recaptures or sidesteps, the minor piece is simply lost for a pawn, resulting in a net material loss of approximately 2 points. The positions universally lacked the tactical preconditions (developed pieces, exposed enemy king, concrete mating threats) that would justify a genuine sacrifice on f7/f2.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (often a flashy Queen check or capture) that leaves their own Queen en prise, throwing away a winning position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 97% of activating positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 6.0, corresponding to a Queen). The piece class distribution confirms this with 384 major pieces (predominantly Queens). While 79% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0) — often via check (25%) or capture (47%) — the player instead chose a move that blundered their Queen. Only 32% of played moves were captures, meaning most were quiet moves or non-winning checks. The feature fires on just 0.4% of positions, highlighting how catastrophic and specific this error type is.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player, often in a clearly winning position (many with forced mates available), plays an impulsive Queen move — frequently a check or capture that looks aggressive — but places the Queen on a square where it is immediately capturable by the opponent. The average cp_loss of 5486 centipawns reflects positions going from forced checkmates to merely slight advantages, as the Queen (worth ~9 points) is simply lost. The player prioritizes giving check or taking material over board safety, ignoring that the Queen lands on a defended square.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet/passive move in a critical endgame position, missing a forcing move (often a check) that would win, mate, or draw.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 66% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91), and 44% of best moves are checks, while the player's move was a capture only 10% of the time and left own pieces hanging just 17% (with only pawns at risk). This indicates the player consistently misses critical forcing moves. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames (avg cp_loss: 4166) featuring exposed kings on both sides. The player chooses passive king moves or quiet retreats (Ke3, Kc3, Kh2, Re8, Rh1, Ra7, a5) when precise checks (Qf3+, Qd4+, Qb4+, Rd2+, Rxg6+) or active rook centralizations would either deliver forced mate, establish perpetual check to draw, or win decisive material. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically those critical endgame moments where passivity is catastrophic.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because in endgames with exposed kings, tempo and forcing moves are everything. A passive move allows the opponent to escape a mating net, advance passed pawns to promotion, or deliver checkmate themselves. The best moves (checks, active captures) either immediately win by creating unavoidable threats, draw via perpetual check when behind, or prevent the opponent's own mating threats. Playing quietly wastes the critical initiative.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own rook or queen undefended and capturable, typically while missing a winning capture of an enemy piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move leaves their own major piece hanging at an overwhelming 98% rate (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook). The hung piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (98 major vs. 21 minor vs. 5 pawn). Simultaneously, in 76% of these positions, the best move would have won enemy material (median value 5.0), with 69% of best moves being captures and 23% being checks. The played move was only a capture 42% of the time, meaning the majority were quiet moves that ignored both the available winning capture AND left their own rook or queen en prise. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions with an average centipawn loss of 5191, indicating catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores the tactical reality of the position—they play a quiet or irrelevant move (king move, pawn push, piece repositioning, or wrong capture) that leaves their own rook or queen undefended on an open file or exposed square, allowing the opponent to simply capture it. Meanwhile, a straightforward winning capture (Rxe1, Qxf8, Rxh8, Rxe8, Qxh5+, Rxb1#, etc.) was available that would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate.

analysis.label: The player missed a critical pawn advance that would have won material through a tactical breakthrough or decisive threat.
analysis.description: In 83% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 2.0 pawns), yet only 28% of those best moves are captures and 0% are checks — meaning the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet pawn push. Examining all 12 top boards confirms this: the best moves are g6, e3, d5, f5, e6, d6, d4, gxf3, e3, e3, d3, e7 — nearly all pawn advances that create forks, open lines against exposed kings, or reach the 7th rank. Instead of these breakthroughs, players chose piece moves (78% non-captures) that often also left their own material hanging (45% of positions, median value 1.0, distributed across pawns/129, minors/51, majors/43). The feature fires on only 0.4% of positions, indicating it identifies specifically those tactically rich moments where a pawn push is the non-obvious winning resource.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a pawn advance that exploits concrete tactical features — exposed kings, pinned/overloaded pieces, or promotion threats. By playing routine piece moves or inferior captures instead, the player squanders a breakthrough opportunity (median 2 pawns of material) and frequently leaves their own pieces undefended in the process, compounding the error.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move (often f3 or a developing move) instead of simply capturing an undefended enemy minor piece, usually a bishop that has ventured out without support in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player missed winning free material: 62% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 62% of best moves are captures, while the player's actual move was a capture only 6% of the time. Own-piece hanging rate is only 20% (median 1.0, mostly pawns), confirming this is NOT a 'hung own piece' pattern but a 'missed capturing enemy piece' pattern. The top boards reveal a highly specific geometry: an enemy bishop is undefended (commonly on g4 after ...Bg4, or on b4 attacked by a c3-pawn), and the player plays a quiet positional or developing move (f3 to 'chase' the bishop, Ne2, d3, b4, etc.) instead of the trivially winning capture (Qxg4, cxb4, fxg5, Rxa5). This occurs overwhelmingly in the opening (10/12 top positions) when both kings are still in the center.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes positional ideas (development, pawn structure, piece placement) over a free material capture. Playing f3 to 'chase' or 'block' a bishop that could simply be taken by the queen (Qxg4) or a pawn (cxb4, fxg5) loses a full piece's worth of value (~3 pawns). The opponent's bishop is genuinely undefended, making the capture completely safe and objectively winning.

analysis.label: Player makes a plausible-looking move (predominantly a queen move) that catastrophically ignores the position's critical tactical or safety requirement, causing a massive evaluation collapse.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions (1.4% of all positions) where the player commits a devastating blunder, typically involving the queen. The SEE aggregate shows that 41% of the time the best move would win material (median value 3.0), while 36% of played moves hang the player's own piece (median 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 158/178). The average cp_loss of 706 far exceeds either material amount, indicating the move triggers a positional/tactical cascade. In 7-9 of the top 12 positions, the played move is a queen move to a wrong square (Qe3, Qxc3, Qc1, Qb2, Qxd5, Qd7, Qd4) or the best move required using the queen differently (Qxe8 over Kxe8). The best moves frequently require king moves (Kh2, Kd2, Ke2, Kf6) or precise piece coordination that the player's queen move overlooks.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the queen goes to a plausible-looking square that either exposes pawns to capture, misses winning available material, or ignores that the position demands immediate king safety (king move) or a specific tactical response. The queen move addresses a secondary concern while the position's critical requirement—often king safety or winning hanging material—goes unmet, allowing the opponent to exploit the position catastrophically.

analysis.label: Player plays a weakening move (often an f-pawn push) instead of the correct knight development or repositioning that would win or save material.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, 66% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = minor piece), while 54% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with minor pieces dominating at 162/270 of hung pieces). Strikingly, all 12 top-activating positions share the same best move type: a knight move (Nd7, Nc3, Nc6, Nbd2, Nd2, Ne2, Nge7, Nd5). The played moves are instead weakening alternatives—most commonly f-pawn pushes (f6, f3, f4) or passive piece moves—that fail to address the position's demands. Many positions feature an opponent's powerfully centralized knight (on e4 or e5) that the correct knight move would challenge, while the pawn push weakens the king position and/or leaves existing pieces undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they use a pawn to address a tactical/positional problem that requires a piece solution. The f-pawn push (f3/f6) weakens the king's pawn shield and diagonal cover, often leaves existing pieces (particularly knights) undefended, and squanders the opportunity to develop or reposition a knight to a square where it wins material, challenges the opponent's strong centralized knight, or defends critical squares. The knight move simultaneously solves multiple problems—developing, defending, and winning material—while the pawn push creates new weaknesses.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an overloaded/pinned knight on f3 or f6 (via Bxf3 or Bxf6), missing that this wins a loose bishop elsewhere.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best move is a capture 97% of the time (almost always Bxf3 or Bxf6 with SEE=0, an even exchange), yet best_wins_material is only 7% — meaning the exchange itself is equal but unlocks winning a second piece tactically. The player's move left their own piece hanging 45% of the time (median value 3.0, heavily minor pieces at 77/122), often because their alternative move failed to address the underlying tactical vulnerability. The pattern across all 500 positions involves a bishop (on g4/h5 for Black, or g5 for White) pinning or pressuring a knight on f3/f6, while the opponent has a loose bishop (typically on g5 or g4) that the knight alone defends. The best move captures the overloaded knight, after which the now-undefended bishop falls (e.g., Bxf3 then Qxg5).
analysis.why_bad: Moves like f3/f6 try to chase away the pinning bishop rather than exploit the pin; other moves (Be7, Nf6, Qb6, Bh5, Qxg5) either ignore the tactic entirely or grab the loose piece in the wrong order (e.g., Qxg5 takes the bishop first but leaves the queen exposed since the knight still guards key squares). All these moves squander a position where capturing the overloaded knight forces winning the undefended bishop, typically netting a full piece worth of compensation through the two-step tactical sequence.

analysis.label: Player plays a non-forcing move that leaves their own major piece (rook or queen) en prise, missing a winning tactical shot.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player's move hangs their own major piece (98% of positions leave an own piece hanging, median value 5.0, with 35/41 being major pieces—rooks or queens) while simultaneously missing a decisive tactical opportunity (81% of positions had a best move winning material, median value 9.0). The best move is a check 55% of the time and a capture 43% of the time, indicating that the position demanded an urgent forcing continuation. Instead of striking first with a check or winning capture, the player plays a quiet or irrelevant move (only 38% played captures), leaving their own undefended major piece to be taken. The average cp_loss of 6020 reflects the catastrophic nature of these blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the position contains mutual tactical tension—often pieces attacking each other on a shared file or adjacent squares—where the correct resolution is to strike first with tempo (check, capture, or mate). By playing a slow, non-forcing move, the player cedes the initiative and leaves their major piece undefended, allowing the opponent to simply capture it. The player essentially ignores the urgency of the position, treating a razor-sharp tactical moment as quiet play.

analysis.label: The player missed a knight (or minor piece) check that forks the king and a major piece, winning decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 97% of best moves are checks and 91% win material (median value: 100, typically a queen or rook), yet only 21% of best moves are captures — indicating the check itself is not a capture but a fork that wins material on the next move. Only 15% of played moves were captures, showing players chose passive moves instead. Examining the top 12 boards, 10 of 12 best moves are knight checks (Nxe6+, Nd7+, Nf2+, Ng6+, Ne7+, Ne2+, Nb2+, Nf6+) that fork the king and a high-value piece. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet king retreats (Kb7, Kf4, Kf5, Kc6, Kg6) or knight moves to non-forking squares (Nc4, Ne3, Nd6, Nc5). The 63% own-hang rate (median value 1, mostly pawns) is a secondary consequence of playing aimless moves in tactically critical positions.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a devastating knight fork check that would win a queen or rook for free. Instead of exploiting the geometric alignment of the enemy king and a high-value piece, the player makes a passive retreat or repositioning move, throwing away a won game or missing the chance to dramatically improve a lost position.

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece in an endgame but leaves their own capturing piece hanging, when the correct strategy was to preserve that piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 93% of the time the player's move is a capture, and 89% of those moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces: 16 minor, 7 major, 1 pawn). Crucially, the best move is a capture only 0% of the time, indicating the correct approach was never to trade. The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions where the player greedily takes an enemy piece but places their capturing piece (usually a bishop or knight) on a square where it is immediately recaptured. The 56% 'best wins material' stat reflects that the piece being preserved would itself later win material or maintain a defensive stance worth ~3 points of evaluation.
analysis.why_bad: In these endgames, the player's piece (typically a lone bishop or knight) serves a critical strategic role—blockading passed pawns, maintaining fortress potential, or preserving drawing chances. By capturing and allowing recapture, the player trades down into a hopeless position. The opponent benefits from the simplification because they hold a structural or material advantage that becomes decisive once the defender's key piece disappears from the board.

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move in a hopelessly lost position instead of finding an available tactical resource (check, capture, or material-winning shot).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the side to move is already in a desperately losing position and plays a passive quiet move, ignoring a best move that is forcing or material-winning. The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material 47% of the time (median value 6.0, i.e., queen-level), best moves are checks 26% of the time and captures 38% of the time, yet the played move was a capture only 13% — overwhelmingly quiet. The 58% own-hang rate (median 1.0, mostly pawns at 206/271) is a secondary consequence: by playing an aimless move, the player neglects defending pawns. The average cp_loss of 5301 reflects positions transitioning from 'very bad' to immediate forced mate. All 12 top-activating moves are quiet (king walks like Kg1/Kh6/Kb4/Kg3, passive rook moves like Rf1/Rf2/Rg1/Rg8, or irrelevant piece moves like h3/Nd3/Bc6), played in positions where engine evaluations were already -800 to -1200 or worse.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player effectively 'gives up' by playing an aimless quiet move when a forcing continuation (check, capture, or tactical resource recovering material) exists. In desperate positions, the only chance is to find counterplay through forcing moves. Instead, these passive moves allow the opponent to execute their winning plan unimpeded, typically converting a large advantage into immediate forced checkmate.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player pushes a pawn forward (often toward promotion) when they should instead activate their king or reposition a piece, frequently leaving the pushed pawn undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 67% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the overwhelmingly affected piece class being pawns (35 out of 44 hung-piece instances). The positions are almost exclusively endgames (11/12), and the played moves are nearly all quiet pawn advances (e2, h2, e6, h6, h4, g6, d6, g7, g5, d2). The best moves are typically king moves (Kd3, Kf3, Kd6, Kg6, Kf8) or piece repositioning (Bf5, Bc7, Be7+, Nd4). Only 39% of best moves win material (median 3.0), indicating the mistake is often purely positional/strategic rather than a tactical miss. The average cp_loss of 982 shows these premature pushes are catastrophic, often converting winning positions into draws or losses.
analysis.why_bad: Pushing a pawn prematurely in an endgame fails because: (1) the advanced pawn becomes undefended and capturable since the king or pieces haven't been repositioned to support it; (2) the player neglects the critical endgame principle of king activation before pawn advancement; (3) the pawn push often creates a target that the opponent can exploit, or misses a narrow window where only king/piece coordination preserves the advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a move in the endgame that leaves one of their own pawns undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the overwhelming majority being pawns (445/500 = 89%). Only 24% of the played moves were captures themselves, meaning most of the time the player made a quiet move (king move, piece relocation, or pawn push) that inadvertently abandoned the defense of one of their own pawns. The best move wins material only 42% of the time (median 3.0 when it does), and is a check only 12% or a capture only 9%, indicating the correct alternatives are typically quiet prophylactic or defensive moves that maintain pawn protection. The feature fires in only 0.6% of positions, concentrated heavily in endgames (10/12 top boards).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in endgames, every pawn matters enormously. By moving the king, rook, or knight away from a defensive duty, the player drops a pawn to the opponent's active piece (usually a rook on an open file or rank). Losing a single pawn in a rook endgame typically converts a winning or equal position into a drawn or lost one, as reflected by the average 282 centipawn loss across the top activations.

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player captures a defended pawn or piece with their rook (often with check), leaving the rook hanging to immediate recapture.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player's rook captures a defended pawn or minor piece in an endgame, leaving the rook itself en prise. The SEE aggregate shows 96% of played moves are captures and 98% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being major pieces (279/313). All 12 top-activating positions are rook endgames where the player's rook grabs a defended pawn (often with check — 10 of 12 moves include '+'), but the rook is then recapturable, effectively trading a rook for a pawn. The best move wins material 65% of the time (median 3.0), typically by maintaining the rook's activity rather than sacrificing it for a pawn. The feature fires on only 0.2% of positions, targeting this specific temptation pattern.
analysis.why_bad: In rook endgames, rook activity is paramount. By capturing a defended pawn with the rook (even with check), the player allows recapture and effectively trades a rook (value 5) for a pawn (value 1). This transforms a playable rook endgame into a lost king-and-pawn endgame, as the opponent retains their rook while the player does not. The check creates an illusion of forcing play, but after the king sidesteps, the rook is simply lost. Keeping the rook alive with a quiet move preserves critical defensive or offensive resources.

analysis.label: Player makes a natural-looking developing or capturing move in the opening that leaves one of their own pieces undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 84% of positions show the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung pieces distributed roughly equally between pawns (197) and minor pieces (186), with some majors (38). Only 25% of the moves are captures, and the phase is overwhelmingly the opening. The best move wins material in 50% of cases (median 2.0), often because the correct move would defend the threatened piece while simultaneously gaining something. The best move is rarely a check (1%) or capture (5%), indicating the correct response is typically a quiet defensive/consolidating move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a routine development, a tempting capture, or a positional idea while ignoring an existing or newly-created tactical threat to one of their own pieces. In the opening, where pieces are still being coordinated and many remain undefended, moving one piece can leave another fatally exposed. The player's attention is drawn to their own plan (developing a bishop, capturing a pawn, pushing a pawn) rather than recognizing that an opponent's piece is already attacking something that will become unprotected.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of capturing an undefended enemy pawn (usually with the king in endgame positions).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material via a capture (100% capture rate, 0% check), with a median value of 1.0 (one pawn). The player's move is never a capture (0%), meaning they consistently ignore a free take. Only 20% of positions involve hanging their own piece afterward, confirming the primary mistake is failing to capture rather than self-hanging. The pattern predominantly occurs in endgames where the king can simply walk onto an unprotected pawn (Kxh7, Kxb6, Kxc3) or a piece can take a vulnerable pawn (Rxg2), but the player instead makes a passive or misdirected quiet move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediately available free capture—typically a king recapturing or taking an undefended passed pawn. By playing a quiet move instead, the player forfeits material (usually a pawn) that was trivially available, often transforming a winning position into a drawn or significantly worse one. In endgames especially, a single pawn can be decisive, making these oversights catastrophic.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive knight advance (or ignores an attacked knight) in the opening, leaving a minor piece hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a flashy, aggressive knight move (or another attacking move) instead of the required retreat or defensive consolidation. The SEE aggregate shows 40% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution heavily skewed toward minors (25 minor vs 10 pawn vs 1 major). Meanwhile, 52% of best moves win material (median 2.0), often because the best alternative either captures an enemy piece or saves the threatened knight to a productive square. Only 18% of played moves are captures themselves, confirming the mistake is usually a quiet aggressive advance rather than a recapture gone wrong. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, all concentrated in the opening phase (10/12 top boards).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize aggression over piece safety. Typically a knight sits on an advanced but attacked square (e5, e4, d4) and instead of retreating it (Nf3, Nce7, Nf6, Nfd2), the player either jumps it to an even more exposed square where it hangs, makes a different aggressive move (Bb5+, f4, Bf4) that ignores the threat, or plays a premature sacrifice (Nxf7, Nxd4) without sufficient compensation. The opponent simply captures the undefended piece, winning material immediately.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet move instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece that is directly available (often adjacent to the king).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a missed-winning-material pattern: 92% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-level), and 79% of best moves are captures, yet only 8% of the actually-played moves were captures. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames where a major or minor piece sits undefended and adjacent to the player's king or attackable by a pawn. In 7 of the 12 top boards, the best move is a direct king capture (Kxe5, Kxd4, Kxd6, Kxe4, Kxc3, Kxc2, Kxf6), while others involve simple pawn captures of hanging queens/knights. The 38% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary effect—by not capturing the free piece, the player's quiet move sometimes inadvertently exposes their own pawn—but the dominant mistake is ignoring the free capture entirely.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (king retreats, pawn pushes, bishop repositions) are catastrophic because they leave massive free material on the board uncaptured. In already-difficult endgame positions, failing to grab a free rook, queen, or knight means the position immediately collapses—often transitioning from a survivable deficit into forced checkmate (average cp_loss of 6253). The captures are trivially available with no tactical complications, making these pure oversights.

analysis.label: Player missed a quiet bishop move that wins the opponent's queen (or equivalent major material) via pin, skewer, or decisive diagonal attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 93% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 6.0, consistent with netting a queen), yet the best move is only a capture 15% of the time and a check 11% of the time—meaning the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet bishop deployment. In 11 of the top 12 boards, the best move is a Bishop move (Bg5, Bf4, Bd4, Be6, Bc5, Bf5, Bh4, Bb5, etc.) that exploits a diagonal to pin, skewer, or trap the opponent's queen. The player's move was a capture only 29% of the time—often a tempting but inferior capture—and 45% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0, spread across pawns/minors/majors). The feature fires on just 0.5% of positions, reflecting the specific geometry needed for a decisive bishop diagonal tactic.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore the most powerful tactical resource on the board—a bishop placement along an open diagonal that attacks or pins the enemy queen against the king or a critical square. Players are seduced by captures (Nxf3, Bxa6, Qxa1, fxg6), checks (Qd3+), or 'improving' moves (Re8, Rf1, O-O-O), missing that a single quiet bishop move wins decisive material immediately by exploiting the geometric alignment of enemy pieces on a vulnerable diagonal.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting queen/pawn capture but leaves their own undefended minor piece en prise, when the correct move was to capture with that vulnerable minor piece first.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a clear pattern: 91% of the played moves are captures, yet 86% of those captures leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece, with distribution showing 17 minors vs 2 pawns). Meanwhile, the best move is a capture in 100% of cases and typically wins 0 material by SEE (meaning it's an equal trade using the threatened piece). The player consistently grabs material with the queen (Qxe2, Qxe7, Qxd3, Qxd6) or a pawn (fxe6, gxf3) while ignoring that their knight or bishop is hanging. The correct move was to capture with that vulnerable minor piece first (Nxc6, Bxe7, Nxc3, Nxe6, Nxe3, Nxd2, Bxf6), simultaneously removing it from danger and completing a productive exchange before taking the other capture.
analysis.why_bad: By making the greedy queen/pawn capture first, the player leaves a minor piece (worth ~3 pawns) undefended. The opponent simply takes it next move, netting material. The correct move order captures with the threatened piece first, solving the defensive problem while the other capture remains available afterward (or becomes unnecessary).

analysis.label: In critical king-and-pawn endgames, the player pushes a pawn (or moves the king incorrectly) when the correct technique requires the opposite — typically a king maneuver instead of a premature pawn advance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king-and-pawn endgame positions where the player chooses the fundamentally wrong plan, almost always a premature or misguided pawn advance when a precise king move was essential (or rarely, the reverse). The SEE aggregate shows that best moves win material only 22% of the time (mostly via eventual promotion threats, median value 5.0 = queen), the played move is almost never a capture (7%), and own-piece hanging is low (14%, median 1.0 — just pawns). The feature fires on 0.0% of all positions, confirming it targets a very specific endgame scenario. All 12 top boards are pawn endgames (11/12 explicitly labeled endgame), and the average cp_loss is an enormous 1179cp — typically converting wins to draws or draws to losses. The quiet pawn pushes (d6, f4, e5, h4, g5, g4, a4) are played instead of critical king moves (Kd7, Kd5, Kg6, Kb3, Ke5, Ke3) or the correct pawn advance on the opposite wing.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king activity and precise move order are paramount. Premature pawn advances fix the pawn structure, give up tempo, or allow the opponent's king to achieve opposition or infiltrate. The correct technique typically requires activating the king first (to gain opposition, outflank, or escort a pawn) before committing pawns. The played moves throw away the win by either creating a drawn pawn race, allowing the opponent to blockade, or losing critical tempi.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture with check (usually a bishop) that leaves their own piece hanging after the opponent responds to the check.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player plays a capture giving check—most commonly a bishop capture (Bx_+)—that leaves their own piece en prise once the opponent deals with the check. The SEE aggregate shows 83% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 72% of played moves were captures. Crucially, the best move is NEVER a check (0%), yet nearly all played moves give check, revealing the player was seduced by the forcing nature of the check. The own-hang distribution (minor: 15, major: 12, pawn: 3) shows both bishops left on attacked squares and queens left undefended elsewhere. The best move wins material 61% of the time (median 2.0), indicating the player had strong alternatives that consolidated their advantage without exposing pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The check is a tactical illusion: the player captures material and gives check, which feels forcing and aggressive, but after the opponent simply moves their king or interposes, the attacking piece (often the bishop that just moved) or another piece (often the queen) is left undefended on a vulnerable square. The net result is losing more material than was gained by the capture, typically costing a full minor piece or queen.

analysis.label: The player moves a piece to an active-looking square but abandons the defense of their own pawn, leaving it en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that 83% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn). The piece-class distribution confirms the pattern: 264 pawns, 121 minors, and 32 majors—predominantly pawns. Only 11% of moves played were captures and only 14% of best moves win material, ruling out a 'missed winning capture' pattern. The best moves are rarely checks (0%) or captures (9%), instead being quiet consolidating or prophylactic moves that maintain pawn defense. The player consistently relocates a piece (often the queen: Qh5, Qf5, Qf3) or another piece (Ng6, Bb4, d5) to a seemingly active square, neglecting that it was the sole defender of a pawn.
analysis.why_bad: By prioritizing piece activity or an aggressive-looking placement over defensive obligations, the player's move allows the opponent to capture a free pawn (or occasionally a minor piece). The positional gains from the 'active' square are far outweighed by the material loss—typically costing 100-300 centipawns as the opponent simply takes the undefended pawn.

analysis.label: A developing or repositioning move inadvertently leaves one's own pawn (usually g2/g7 on the long diagonal) undefended against an enemy fianchettoed bishop.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of positions have the player's own piece left hanging after the move (median value: 1.0, i.e., a pawn), with the hung piece class heavily skewed toward pawns (283/500) and minor pieces (192/500). Only 10% of played moves were captures, and the best move rarely wins material (23%) or gives check (1%). The top activating boards reveal a recurring geometry: the player develops a piece (especially the f1-bishop to d3/c4, or another piece) that was the sole defender of the g2 or g7 pawn, while an enemy fianchettoed bishop (typically on b7) is already aiming down the long diagonal at that pawn. The best moves (usually Nf3 or Nf6) either add defense to the vulnerable pawn or avoid removing its defender. A minority of cases involve a knight jumping to an undefended square (Nh5, Nh4), hanging the knight itself.
analysis.why_bad: These moves remove the only defender of a critical pawn (usually g2/g7) from the long diagonal, or place a piece on an unprotected square. The opponent's fianchettoed bishop already targets that pawn, so the moment the defender moves, the pawn is lost for free. The player prioritizes piece activity or development without recognizing the defensive duty their piece was performing.

analysis.label: Player aggressively moves a bishop to h3 or h6 (or a queen to a kingside attacking square) but leaves the piece undefended and hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 65% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), with the piece-class distribution dominated by minors (112 instances). Only 13% of the played moves were captures, confirming these are quiet aggressive lunges rather than exchanges. The best move wins material 62% of the time (median 3.0), indicating the player is also frequently missing a tactical opportunity. The top 12 activating positions overwhelmingly feature bishop moves to h3 (Black) or h6 (White)—8 of 12 moves are Bh3/Bh6—with the remainder being aggressive queen relocations to kingside squares (Qh5, Qh4, Qg4). In nearly every case the bishop arrives on the h-file square undefended, creating an immediate tactical target worth a full piece.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop on h3/h6 looks aggressive (often pairing with a queen already on g4/g5/g6 to threaten the enemy king), but it lands on an unprotected square far from allied piece support. The opponent can simply capture or threaten the bishop with tempo, winning material. Meanwhile, the player passes up stronger alternatives—captures, central exchanges, or defensive necessities—that would have maintained or increased their advantage.

analysis.label: Player missed a queen check along the weakened f-pawn diagonal (h4/h5/g3) that wins the opponent's queen or decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 91, corresponding to a queen), and 100% of the time the best move is a check — yet only 13% are captures. The played move was a quiet non-capture 78% of the time. The median value of 91 indicates the check consistently wins the opponent's queen. Only 35% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value just 2.0, a pawn), confirming the primary mistake is the missed winning tactic, not self-inflicted hanging. All 12 top boards show the same geometry: both kings remain in the center (e1/e8), the f-pawn has advanced or been captured opening the e1-h4 or e8-h5 diagonal, and the correct move is Qh4+, Qh5+, or Qg3+ exploiting that gaping weakness to win material. The feature fires on only 0.4% of positions, reflecting the specificity of this f-pawn-diagonal queen-check pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (typically quiet developing moves like Nf6, Ne7, Nc3, Nf3, Bb5, d6) ignore the immediate tactical opportunity. By not playing the queen check on the exposed diagonal, the player forfeits a forced win of the opponent's queen (or checkmate), allowing the opponent to consolidate, castle, or otherwise neutralize the diagonal weakness. The average cp_loss of 1073 reflects that these missed checks often convert from winning/mating positions to merely equal ones.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting or aggressive move while leaving their own bishop en prise, losing a minor piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates that the player's move hangs their own piece: 73% of played moves leave an own piece hanging (median value 3.0, matching a bishop), with the piece class distribution showing 15 minor pieces and 1 pawn. Meanwhile, 68% of best moves win material (median 1.0, typically a pawn), and 73% of best moves are captures. The pattern consistently involves opening positions where the player's bishop is under attack (commonly by a b4 pawn against a c5 bishop in Evans Gambit structures) or where the player lunges a bishop to an undefended square via a flashy capture/check (Bxf2+, Bxf7+, Bxe7) instead of addressing the concrete threat or capturing the free pawn.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player either ignores a direct attack on their own bishop (e.g., b4 attacking Bc5 in the Evans Gambit, where simply taking with Bxb4 wins a pawn) or aggressively places their bishop on an undefended square via a speculative sacrifice/check (Bxf2+, Bxf7+). In both cases, the opponent simply captures the hanging bishop, netting a full minor piece (≈3 points) that far outweighs any tactical compensation from the check or initiative the player imagined.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple pawn capture (hxg4, hxg5, or gxh3) winning an enemy bishop that has ventured to the g4/g5/h3 square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 90% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 2.0, consistent with winning a bishop for a pawn), and 94% of the time the best move is a capture. Only 18% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead. The 35% own-hang rate is secondary noise; the dominant signal is a missed winning capture. Across all top-12 boards, the best move is specifically a pawn capturing an enemy bishop on the g-file or h-file (hxg4, hxg5, or gxh3). The enemy bishop has typically ventured aggressively to g4/g5 to pin a knight or pressure the kingside, but is inadequately defended—a simple pawn push captures it outright. Players instead play natural-looking developing or positional moves (Bd2, Bf4, Rc1, a5, d4, Kf2, etc.), completely overlooking the free material.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical opportunity: the enemy bishop sitting on g4/g5/h3 is attacked by a pawn and either undefended or insufficiently defended. By playing a positional move instead, the player forfeits a clean material gain of roughly a minor piece (worth ~3 pawns), often turning a winning position into an equal or losing one (average cp_loss of 265).

analysis.label: Player ignores a forced rook exchange on an open file, leaving their own rook hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 75% of positions left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the hung piece class heavily skewed toward major pieces (74 major, 19 minor, 10 pawn). The best move is a capture 90% of the time and a check 25% of the time, with nearly every best move being a rook capture on a contested open file (Rxe2+, Rxe4, Rxe1+, Rxd1, Rxe8+, Rxf7, Rxd6, etc.). Only 14% of positions have the best move winning net material — the critical exchange is usually even (SEE=0) but necessary to avoid leaving one's own rook en prise. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, capturing a specific geometry: rooks face off on an open file (almost always the e-file), the player neglects the forced exchange/capture, and their undefended rook is left hanging.
analysis.why_bad: When rooks contest an open file and the opponent has superior file control (extra attackers or the ability to capture with check), the rook exchange is effectively forced. Playing a quiet pawn move (a6, f6, d5, f5, c5, etc.) or irrelevant capture instead leaves the player's own rook unprotected on the open file, allowing the opponent to win it outright on the next move — typically a ~5-point material loss.

analysis.label: Playing a quiet rook or queen repositioning move that ignores concrete tactical demands, either missing winning opportunities or leaving pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players make passive major piece (rook or queen) moves that look purposeful—placing on open files, centralizing, or shifting to seemingly active squares—but miss the actual tactical requirements of the position. The SEE aggregate shows 43% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the played move was a capture only 3% of the time. Additionally, 49% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece distribution being heavily pawn-weighted (144 pawns, 59 majors, 43 minors), indicating these quiet repositioning moves often abandon defense of a pawn or minor piece. The feature fires on 3% of all positions, always on quiet major-piece moves (Qd3, Rb1, Re1, Rae1, Rh6, etc.) that address superficial positional goals while ignoring concrete tactics like checks winning material (13% best move is check) or captures (25% best move is capture).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize vague positional concepts (rook on open file, queen centralization) over concrete tactical necessities. In many cases, the position demands an immediate tactical strike (a check forking material, a pawn advance trapping a piece, a capture resolving tension) or requires maintaining a defensive duty. By moving the major piece to a 'nice-looking' square, the player either misses a winning combination or removes a key defender, leaving pawns or minor pieces en prise.

analysis.label: Player misses Qa4+ or Qa5+ that delivers check while simultaneously attacking an undefended bishop on b4/b5, winning a full piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions the best move wins material (median value 91), and crucially 99% of the time that best move is a check while only 9% are captures — confirming the winning mechanism is an indirect fork, not a direct take. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 15% captures) and leave no own pieces hanging in most cases (31% hung-own with median value just 1.0, i.e. pawns). The concrete pattern across all 12 boards is identical: one side has placed a bishop aggressively on b4 (or White's bishop on b5) without support, both kings remain uncastled in the center, and the opponent can play Qa4+ (or Qa5+) exploiting the a4-e8/a5-e1 diagonal to check the king and simultaneously attack the loose bishop, winning a full minor piece. Instead, players choose routine developing moves like Nf3, O-O, Bg2, or e5.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Nf3, O-O, Bg2, e5, Bg4, Bc4, a6, etc.) are standard developing moves that ignore the concrete tactical opportunity. By failing to play the queen check, the player allows the opponent to consolidate — typically by castling or retreating the bishop — permanently eliminating the fork geometry and squandering a full piece advantage (~300 cp).

analysis.label: In endgames, the player advances a pawn straight forward instead of capturing diagonally with that same pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 61% of best moves are captures yet only 4% of played moves are captures, revealing a systematic failure to take with a pawn when available. The best move wins material only 24% of the time (median 4.0 — those rare cases like Kxf8), because most of these pawn captures are equal exchanges (SEE=0). The pattern is strikingly geometric: in 9 of the top 12 positions, the exact same pawn that should capture diagonally (gxf6, axb5, hxg4, axb4, hxg5, fxg5, gxf4, cxd4+, hxg3) is instead pushed straight ahead (g6, a5, h4, a4, h5, f5, g4, c4, h3). The own-hang rate is only 10% (all pawns, median value 1.0), confirming the mistake is not about hanging pieces but about choosing the wrong pawn advance direction.
analysis.why_bad: Advancing the pawn instead of capturing typically worsens the pawn structure, misses critical simplification or liquidation, loses tempo in the race to queen, or allows the opponent's pawn chain to remain intact. In these endgames, the diagonal capture often opens lines for the king, eliminates a defender, or creates a passed pawn, while the straight advance merely creates a fixed, weak pawn or throws away a crucial exchange opportunity.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a simple, direct capture of an undefended enemy piece (typically queen or rook) in favor of a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 92% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-equivalent or higher), and 95% of the time the best move is a straightforward capture. Yet only 9% of played moves were captures — the player almost always chose a quiet move instead. In 45% of cases (median value 5.0), the played move also left the player's OWN piece hanging, which makes sense because many of these positions involve mutual vulnerability: both sides have undefended pieces, and the player who captures first wins decisively. The own-hang distribution (major: 24, pawn: 21, minor: 3) confirms that queens and rooks are the most common pieces left exposed. The feature fires overwhelmingly in endgames (11/12 top boards) where the tactical simplicity should make the capture obvious.
analysis.why_bad: The played quiet moves (Kh2, Na3, Nb5, Kh7, b4, etc.) ignore a freely capturable enemy piece — often a queen or rook sitting undefended. In mutual-vulnerability positions, failing to capture first means the opponent can then take YOUR piece on the next move, turning a winning position into a losing one. The enormous average cp_loss of 2346 reflects that these are typically game-deciding oversights of trivial one-move captures.

analysis.label: Player ignores a straightforward material-winning capture in favor of a slow quiet move, often also leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly shows the pattern: in 83% of activating positions the best move is a capture, and in 78% it wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece worth of material). Yet the player's move was a capture only 7% of the time — meaning they almost always played a quiet move instead. Compounding the error, in 55% of cases the quiet move also left the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0, distributed across major pieces, minor pieces, and pawns). The feature fires predominantly in endgames where simple captures of undefended or loosely-defended pieces/pawns are available (Kxf8, Rxc3, bxa5, cxb4, fxg3, Rxa6, etc.), but the player pursues a slow plan — a pawn push, king walk, or rook repositioning — completely overlooking the free material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they forfeit immediately available material (typically worth ~3 pawns) by ignoring an undefended enemy piece or pawn. Worse, the quiet alternative often leaves the player's own piece undefended, meaning they not only miss winning material but also risk losing material themselves. In endgames especially, a full piece or exchange of material is usually decisive, making these oversights game-changing blunders.

analysis.label: Knight (or bishop) grabs a seemingly free central pawn (d4/d5/e5) when a quieter move was superior.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player impulsively captures a central pawn with a minor piece (76% of moves are captures, almost all Nxd4/Nxd5/Nxe5/Bxe4) instead of playing a stronger quiet move. The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material 71% of the time (median value 1.0) yet is a capture only 10% of the time—meaning the correct approach was typically a non-capturing move (like Bd7, h6, Qd5, Rfd8) that exploits existing tactical pressure rather than grabbing the pawn directly. In 39% of cases the greedy capture actually leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces at 51 instances), confirming the pawn is 'poisoned.' The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific class of premature central captures.
analysis.why_bad: The knight capture releases central tension prematurely and often walks into a tactical refutation. The central pawn appears free but is protected tactically (discovered attacks, pins, or the knight landing on an undefended square). A quiet developing or consolidating move would have maintained the tension while safely collecting material or exploiting the opponent's vulnerabilities—the greedy capture forfeits this advantage, frequently leaving the capturing knight (or another piece) en prise.

analysis.label: Player ignores or unblocks an enemy bishop's attack on their f1/f8 rook along the a6-f1 or a3-f8 diagonal, leaving the rook en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 99% of positions feature the player leaving their own piece hanging (median value 2, i.e., the exchange), with the overwhelming majority (386/395 = 98%) being major pieces—specifically rooks. The best move wins material in 42% of cases (median 3.0), often because addressing the rook threat also gains tempo. Only 8% of played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet moves that neglect the diagonal threat. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the geometry is remarkably consistent: an enemy bishop sits on the a6-f1 diagonal (Ba6 attacking White's Rf1) or the a3-f8 diagonal (Ba3/Bb4 attacking Black's Rf8). The player either ignores the existing attack or—critically—advances a blocking pawn (d3→d4 or d6→d5), unmasking the diagonal and exposing the rook.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the rook on f1 or f8 completely undefended against an enemy bishop bearing down the long diagonal. In some cases the player's pawn advance actively removes the only piece blocking the bishop's line of attack. The bishop captures the rook winning the exchange (~2 pawns net), as seen in the consistent 'own hung after: 2 (R)' across all positions. The correct moves (Re1, Re8, Rf2, Rf3, or maintaining the blocking pawn) address the threat directly.

analysis.label: Player missed a winning rook (or piece) check that would have won decisive material, instead playing an inferior pawn move or suboptimal check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 82% of best moves are checks and 88% win material (median value 100cp), yet only 11% of best moves are captures—indicating the winning checks create forks or deflections rather than direct captures. The played moves were captures only 15% of the time, and 50% left the player's own piece hanging (mostly pawns: 51 pawn, 13 major, 8 minor, median value 1.0).
