The top positions reveal the best move is almost universally a rook check (Rh7+, Rc3+, Rf4+, Re1+, Rg3+, Rb3+, Rg5+, Rd3+, Ra2+) in endgame positions with exposed kings. Instead of the decisive piece check, the player chose pawn pushes (d3, a4, c3), pawn checks (e6+, h4+, f5+, b4+, f3+), or pawn captures giving check (dxc4+, fxg4+). The feature fires on only 0.1% of all positions, targeting this specific pattern of overlooking a rook check for a tempting but inferior pawn move.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they either give check with a low-value pawn (gaining no material) or make a quiet pawn advance, while the rook check would exploit the exposed enemy king to win a full piece via fork, skewer, or deflection. The pawn moves often additionally leave material en prise (50% hung a pawn), while the rook check would have both won material and maintained piece safety. The average cp_loss of 254 shows these missed checks often convert winning positions into draws.

analysis.label: Player missed a capture (usually with the Queen) that simultaneously delivers check, winning material for free.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 95% of best moves win material (median value 3.0), 95% of best moves are checks, and 78% are captures — meaning the best move is overwhelmingly a capturing check. In 10 of 12 top-activating boards, the missed move is specifically a Queen capture with check (Qxa1+, Qxc3+, Qxd4+, Qxe4+, Qxf2#, Qxf4+, Qxe5+), with 2 being Bishop captures with check (Bxc3+, Bxf5+). The player instead played quiet developing moves (Ne5, Nc6, Nd8, O-O, d6) or irrelevant captures (cxd6, Nxc6, Qxa7) only 28% of the time. Only 29% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging, confirming this is predominantly a 'missed winning tactic' rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that an enemy piece (often centrally placed or on a weak square) can be captured WITH check, making the material gain essentially free since the opponent must respond to the check rather than recapture. By playing a quiet move instead, the player forfeits winning material worth a median of 3.0 pawns (often a full piece or more), and in one case even misses checkmate (Qxf2#).

analysis.label: Player ignores an infiltrating enemy bishop that can be trapped by a rook move, instead playing something else that often leaves their own rook hanging.
analysis.description: In 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 7% of the time and never a check (0%). This indicates the material is won through positional trapping rather than direct capture. The geometry is highly consistent: an enemy bishop has infiltrated deep into the player's camp (e.g., b2, g2, g7, h7) and is attacking a rook. The correct response is a rook repositioning move (Rb1, Rh2, Rg8, Rg1, etc.) that simultaneously saves the rook AND traps the invading bishop. Instead, 59% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 'major' pieces—overwhelmingly rooks—being the most common class at 93 instances). The player's move was only a capture 22% of the time, suggesting most errors are quiet moves that simply ignore the tactical situation.
analysis.why_bad: By playing a quiet or irrelevant move instead of the rook reposition, the player (1) misses winning the trapped enemy bishop (worth ~3 points) and (2) leaves their own rook en prise to that same bishop. The net swing is enormous—often 5+ points—because the correct move both saves material and wins material simultaneously. The player appears to overlook that the infiltrating bishop, while threatening their rook, has actually overextended and can be entombed by the very piece it attacks.

analysis.label: In the opening, a minor piece is moved aggressively (often with check or as a capture) to a square where it is left en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 85% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 2.0), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 37 out of 39 cases. Only 50% of positions had a best move that wins material, meaning the positions were often roughly equal before the blunder. The played move was a capture 44% of the time, indicating many of these are hasty recaptures or exchanges that leave the piece undefended. The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase (10/12 top boards). The typical pattern is a bishop sortie with check (Bb5+, Bxf7+, Bxb5+, Bb4+) or an aggressive knight jump (Nb4, Nd5) that lands the minor piece on a square controlled by the opponent's pawns or undefended by friendly pieces, immediately losing material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are attracted by superficially aggressive ideas—giving check, making captures, or placing a piece on an 'active' square—but ignore that the destination square is attacked by enemy pawns or pieces with no adequate support. After the opponent simply captures the hanging minor piece (often with a pawn), the player has lost a full piece for nothing or for insufficient compensation, resulting in an average cp_loss of 347.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting check with a minor piece (knight or bishop) but the move leaves their own major piece (queen or rook) hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates that 97% of activating positions involve the player's move leaving their OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to queens and rooks), with the hung-piece class distribution showing 185 major pieces and 114 minor pieces. All 12 top-activating moves are checks delivered by knights or bishops (Nxf6+, Nf3+, Nc3+, Bxf7+, Bxc6+, etc.), and in every case the checking move removes a defender or vacates a square that was protecting a more valuable piece—most commonly the queen (hung value 6 or 9) or a rook (value 5). Meanwhile, 58% of best moves win material, suggesting the player often had a legitimate material-winning continuation available that didn't require giving a reckless check.
analysis.why_bad: The checking move relocates a minor piece to deliver check, but in doing so it either abandons defense of a major piece (queen/rook) or moves away from a square that was critical for protecting that piece. The opponent simply takes the hanging major piece after dealing with the check, resulting in a massive net material loss (avg 257cp). The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check without calculating whether their back-rank or mid-board pieces remain safe.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing move instead of making the mandatory central pawn capture (exd5, exd4, cxd5), leaving their own pawn or piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 99% of activating positions, yet the player's move is a capture only 6% of the time — they almost always play a quiet move instead. The player's move leaves their own piece hanging 46% of the time (median value 1.0; distribution: 21 pawns, 18 minors, 1 major), typically because failing to resolve central tension allows the opponent to capture favorably, exposing an undefended central pawn or a bishop on an open diagonal (e.g., Bc4 left en prise after ...dxe4). The best move wins outright material 29% of the time (median 1 pawn), while in the remaining 71% the capture is an equal exchange that is nonetheless essential to prevent the opponent from exploiting the unresolved tension.
analysis.why_bad: When central pawns are in direct tension (e4 vs d5, d4 vs e5, c4 vs d5), failing to capture allows the opponent to resolve the tension on their own terms. This typically leaves the player's central pawn undefended (e.g., e5 falls to dxe5) or exposes a piece behind the pawn (e.g., a bishop on c4 becomes hanging after ...dxe4 removes its pawn shield). The quiet developing moves (Bg2, Nf3, d3, Be2, Bb4, c6) lose a tempo in positions where the tactical obligation to capture is absolute.

analysis.label: The player misses a simple capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, instead playing a quiet or irrelevant move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 8.0 (consistent with capturing a queen), and the best move is a capture 64% of the time. Meanwhile, the player's move was itself a capture only 16% of the time, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves while an enemy queen sat en prise. The 60% own-hang rate (median 3.0) is a secondary consequence: by failing to take the free queen, the player's quiet move often leaves their own pieces exposed in the ensuing tactics. Across 11 of the 12 top-activating positions, the opponent's queen is directly capturable—often by a pawn (exf6 appears in 5 positions) or by a piece simply taking an undefended queen (Qxc7, Rxd4, Rxd5, Nxd4, Bxc3). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, reflecting how rare yet catastrophic this oversight is.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore that the enemy queen—the most valuable piece on the board—is undefended and can be captured immediately for free. Instead of taking 8-9 points of material, the player makes a purposeless quiet move (a king shuffle, a rook retreat, a pawn push) that squanders a decisive advantage or turns a winning position into a losing one.

analysis.label: Player gives check (often via pawn promotion) with a major piece that is immediately captured by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 94% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 9.0, i.e., a queen), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly 'major' (33 out of 34 cases). The played moves are captures only 67% of the time, while 11 of the top 12 examples are checks—predominantly pawn promotions to queen with check (c8=Q+, d1=Q+, d8=Q+, b8=Q+) or rook/queen moves giving check (Rg5+, Rxb3+, Qxf2+, Qd4+). The best moves are checks only 28% of the time and captures only 8%, indicating the correct plays are typically quiet preparatory moves (Kd7, Kf6, a4, h4) that maintain the winning advantage without sacrificing material. The feature fires on endgame positions where a flashy checking move with a major piece lands it on a square where it is immediately recaptured.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the checking piece (usually a newly promoted queen or an active rook) lands on a square controlled by the opponent's king or piece, resulting in immediate recapture and loss of the major piece. The player is seduced by the immediate tempo of a check or the instinct to promote, but the opponent simply captures the piece. Quiet preparatory moves (king approaches, pawn advances, underpromotions) would maintain the winning advantage by properly supporting the piece before committing it.

analysis.label: Player makes a move while their own queen on g4/g5 is left en prise on an open bishop diagonal in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., the queen), with the piece class distribution confirming 'major' pieces. The best moves win no material in most cases (only 65% win material, median 2.0, likely from minor recaptures), indicating the priority was simply saving the queen. Only 17% of best moves are captures, and 12% are checks — the overwhelming best response is a quiet queen retreat. The player instead plays captures (52%) or developing moves, completely ignoring that their aggressively posted queen on g4 (White) or g5 (Black) sits undefended on an open diagonal (c8-g4 or c1-g5) where an enemy bishop can take it for free.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes material gain (exd5, Nxd5, Bxd4, Qxb5, cxd4) or routine development (Nf3, O-O) while their queen is immediately capturable by a bishop along an unobstructed diagonal. The queen on g4/g5 was posted aggressively in the opening but became a tactical liability once the diagonal opened (typically after ...d5 or similar pawn moves). Ignoring this threat costs approximately 9 points of material — the queen itself.

analysis.label: Player misses a queen capture with check (typically Qxe6+ or Qxe3+) that wins material, instead playing another move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 87% of positions have a best move winning material (median value 3.0), with 74% being checks and 73% being captures — meaning the overwhelming pattern is a queen capturing with check that wins material. The played move was only a capture 20% of the time, and in 36% of cases left the player's own piece hanging. Across the top 12 boards, the missed best move is nearly always Qxe6+ or Qxe3+ (with one Qxa1+), exploiting an undefended or underdefended pawn/piece on the e-file that the queen can take while simultaneously checking the king. Instead, players made alternative queen moves (Qf6, Qa5, Qf3, Qh5+, Qg4, Qb6, Qxb2) or developing moves (Bf4, Be3, d4) that ignore the tactical shot.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they pass up an immediate tactical combination — a queen capture with check — that wins material with tempo. By playing a non-capturing queen move or quiet developing move, the player allows the opponent to defend the vulnerable piece (usually the e6 or e3 pawn) or reposition, eliminating the tactical opportunity entirely. The check ensures the opponent cannot counterattack, making the material gain essentially free.

analysis.label: Player makes a catastrophic king move (or quiet move) in a clearly won endgame, throwing away the win through improper technique.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows this feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player's move is overwhelmingly quiet (only 4% captures) and 30% of the time leaves an own pawn hanging (median value 1.0, all pawns). The best move wins material only 15% of the time, and is rarely a check (4%) or capture (7%), indicating the optimal continuation is also typically a quiet positional move. The enormous average cp_loss of 3397 confirms these are positions where massive winning advantages (including forced mates) are squandered. The pattern is a player making the wrong king move in a won endgame — misplacing the king such that it loses opposition, allows stalemate, abandons pawn protection, or misses a forced mating sequence.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in minimalist endgames, king placement is everything. Moving the king to the wrong square (e.g., Kf6 instead of Kf7, Kf4 instead of capturing, g6+ instead of Kf7) either creates stalemate (position 7), loses the opposition needed to escort a pawn (positions 5, 9, 11), abandons protection of a critical pawn (the 30% own-hang pattern), or misses a forced checkmate by failing to restrict the enemy king (positions 1, 3, 6, 12). The king goes to a natural-looking but fatally incorrect square.

analysis.label: Player missed a king move that attacks or traps the opponent's rook, winning decisive material.
analysis.description: In 98% of activating positions, the best move wins material worth a median of 5 (a rook), yet the best move is a capture only 7% of the time and never a check. All 12 top-activating positions share the same geometry: the best move is a king move (Kf7, Ke7, Kf2, Kg7, Kb5, etc.) that attacks or traps an enemy rook that has overextended or infiltrated. The player instead makes a different move—quiet (88%) or capture (12%)—sometimes hanging their own piece in the process (47%, mostly pawns). The feature fires on only 0.5% of positions, isolating this specific tactical motif where king activity is the key to winning material.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore the opponent's rook being in a vulnerable position where a king approach wins it. Players often focus on pawn pushes, rook moves, or captures that feel natural but miss that their king can directly threaten or trap the enemy rook, which is stuck on a file/rank with limited escape squares.

analysis.label: Player makes a routine capture instead of inserting an intermediate check (zwischenzug) that would save or win a piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a natural-looking capture (71% of played moves are captures) but misses a critical intermediate check (best move is a check 61% of the time, a capture 72% of the time). The result is that the player's own piece is left hanging in 65% of positions (median value 3.0 = minor piece, with minor pieces comprising 41/64 of hung pieces). The correct move is typically a bishop or knight capture/move with check that must be inserted BEFORE the routine recapture, either winning material outright or preventing the opponent from capturing the player's loose piece on the next turn. Over 500 positions, only 33% show the best move directly winning material (median 97cp), suggesting many zwischenzugs simply equalize or maintain material rather than creating a net gain — the key point is avoiding the loss that the premature capture causes.
analysis.why_bad: By playing the 'obvious' capture (usually a pawn recapture like dxc6, dxe5, cxd5, bxa3), the player skips the critical intermediate check (Bxd2+, Bxc3+, Bxd7+, Nd3+, Rxe8+, Nxc8+). This zwischenzug forces the opponent to respond to check first, after which the player can THEN make the intended capture while their previously-loose piece (typically a bishop) is no longer en prise. Without the intermezzo, the opponent simply captures the hanging piece next move.

analysis.label: Player develops a piece instead of resolving tension on their attacked central knight (d4/e5), leaving it hanging to capture by ...Nxd4 or ...Nxe5.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 68% of activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece class overwhelmingly being minor pieces (49 of 61). The best move is a capture in 98% of cases but wins material only 7% of the time—indicating an equal exchange (Nxc6) that resolves tension. The pattern is remarkably specific: the player has a centralized knight on d4 or e5 attacked by an enemy knight on c6, and instead of trading with Nxc6 (the near-universal best move across all 12 top boards), the player develops another piece (Bd3, Bd2, Bg5, Bd5, f3, Qf3, etc.), leaving their knight completely undefended and capturable for free.
analysis.why_bad: The centralized knight on d4/e5 is attacked by the enemy Nc6 and typically defended only indirectly (e.g., by the queen on d1). By ignoring this tactical tension and playing a development move, the player allows the opponent to simply capture the knight (…Nxd4 or …Nxe5), winning a full piece (~3 pawns of material) since the knight has no adequate defender after the developing move blocks or abandons the defense.

analysis.label: The player moves an exposed king to the wrong square (or ignores the king's need to move) when a specific king move is critical for safety or activity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the king is exposed and a precise king move is required—either to escape threats, maintain activity, or enable tactical wins. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 56% of the time (median value 3.0), indicating the correct king square often enables winning enemy pieces or supporting promotion threats. Meanwhile, 48% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns: 137 of 211 cases), suggesting the wrong king placement or non-king move exposes the player's pieces. The played move is rarely a capture (16%), and the best move is only a check 9% of the time—these are quiet king-navigation decisions, not flashy tactical shots. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, targeting specifically those critical moments when the king is exposed and the exact square matters enormously.
analysis.why_bad: With the king exposed (nearly every top position shows 'king exposed' or 'weak pawn shield'), there is typically only ONE correct king square that avoids checks, maintains piece coordination, or enables winning threats (like supporting a passed pawn). Moving the king to the wrong square (or playing a different move entirely) allows the opponent to gain tempo with checks, win material through newly-exposed lines, or neutralize the player's winning advantage. The enormous average centipawn loss (1768) confirms these are catastrophic navigational errors—often converting forced mates or decisive advantages into drawn or lost positions.

analysis.label: Player moves their exposed king to flee instead of capturing the opponent's queen (or high-value piece) that is actually en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has an exposed, seemingly endangered king and reflexively plays a king move (or other defensive/irrelevant move) rather than capturing a high-value enemy piece — almost always the opponent's queen. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 99% of the time, winning material in 87% of positions with a median value of 9 (queen). The played move is rarely a capture itself (only 13%), and in 79% of cases the king flight also leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3, distributed across majors 42, pawns 37, minors 34). In 10 of the top 12 positions, the best move captures a queen-value piece (Bxe6, axb5, Bxf3, gxf6, cxd6, Bxf5, Bxe4, Bxe7, Bxb2, Rxd6), and in 9 of 12 the played move is a king move. The positions share the common geometry of an exposed king with an enemy queen aggressively placed nearby — but actually capturable.
analysis.why_bad: The king move fails because it ignores the fact that the attacking enemy queen (or major piece) is actually vulnerable to capture. By fleeing instead of taking the attacker, the player allows the opponent to maintain or increase the attack, often resulting in immediate checkmate (average cp_loss of 5475, many positions going from already-lost to forced mate). The flight also frequently leaves the player's own pieces undefended, compounding the disaster.

analysis.label: King retreats passively toward the edge or corner in an endgame instead of staying active and centralized.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions (all endgames), the feature fires when the player moves their king toward the board's edge rather than centralizing or maintaining activity. The SEE aggregate shows that 22% of the time the passive king move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns: 36 pawns, 3 minor, 1 major out of 40 instances), because the retreating king abandons defense of its own pawns. Only 15% of the time does the best move win material outright (median 1.0), and only 3% of played moves are captures—confirming the player consistently chooses quiet, retreating king moves. The best move is a check only 1% and a capture only 9% of the time, indicating the correct alternatives are usually quiet centralizing king moves (e.g., Kb5, Ke6, Kf5, Kd6) rather than tactics. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, targeting specifically those endgame moments where king activity is critical.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, the king must be an active piece. Retreating toward the edge or corner cedes control of key central squares, abandons the defense of passed or advanced pawns (explaining the 22% own-hang rate on pawns), and allows the opponent's king to dominate. This transforms drawn or slowly-losing positions into immediately lost ones (average cp_loss of 1594), as the opponent's king freely escorts passed pawns or captures undefended material.

analysis.label: In won King+Pawn vs King endgames, the player moves the king (or underpromotes) instead of making the critical pawn advance, allowing a draw.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player has a theoretically won pawn endgame but throws it away with an incorrect king move (or underpromotion). The SEE aggregate shows low rates across all tactical indicators—only 14% best-move-wins-material, 5% best-move-is-capture, 5% best-move-is-check—because the correct move in these positions is almost always a quiet pawn push (e.g., b2, e7, c7, f2, g7) rather than a tactical blow. The 10% own-piece-hung rate is incidental. The enormous average cp_loss of 7559 reflects positions going from forced mate or +500cp evaluations to dead draws (eval 0). All 12 top positions are pure endgames with passed pawns one or two squares from promotion, where the textbook winning technique requires pushing the pawn at a precise moment.
analysis.why_bad: In King+Pawn vs King endings, the critical moment often requires advancing the pawn (especially to the 7th rank) while the king is optimally placed. Moving the king instead wastes a crucial tempo, allowing the defending king to reach the drawing square or creating a stalemate resource. For example, with King on d6 and pawn on c6 vs King on c8, c7 wins but Kc5 retreats the king and allows Black's king to reach the opposition. These king moves turn textbook wins into immediate draws.

analysis.label: Black captures a knight on c6 with bxc6 (defended by the Bb5) instead of counterattacking the undefended bishop with a queen move that wins material cleanly.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player greedily captures a piece that is defended by another piece, allowing recapture and positional damage, when a counterattacking move (usually a queen move) would win the defender itself. The SEE aggregate shows that in 88% of cases the best move wins material (median value 3, i.e., a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 19% of the time—meaning the winning move is typically a queen threat, not a direct capture. The player's move was a capture 73% of the time (bxc6 capturing the knight), and 73% of the time it left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, typically the newly-placed pawn on c6 which the bishop recaptures). The pattern is overwhelmingly a Ruy Lopez or Scotch setup where White has Nc6+Bb5, the knight attacks Black's queen, and Black reflexively takes bxc6 instead of moving the queen to attack the now-undefended bishop.
analysis.why_bad: After bxc6, the bishop recaptures Bxc6, restoring material equality while gaining devastating threats (forking the rook on a8, controlling the diagonal toward the king). The player wins nothing net. The correct queen move (Qd7, Qb6, Qg5) simultaneously escapes the knight's attack AND targets the undefended bishop on b5, winning a clean piece since the knight on c6 then also falls without its defender.

analysis.label: A central pawn capture (d- or e-pawn exchange) that leaves the player's own piece or pawn undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 87% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed as 151 pawns, 78 minor pieces, 41 major pieces), while 71% of the played moves were captures and the best move was almost never a capture (only 6%). The best moves were typically quiet developing or consolidating moves (O-O, Nc3, Bd3, Bg4, etc.). The feature fires overwhelmingly in the opening phase (8/12 top boards) on central pawn exchanges—dxe5, exd4, dxc5, exd5, dxc6, exf4—where the moving pawn had been shielding or protecting another friendly piece. After the greedy pawn trade, the player's formerly-protected piece (usually a pawn on an adjacent file, sometimes a knight or bishop) is left en prise.
analysis.why_bad: The central pawn capture opens lines and removes a key defender from the player's own structure. The pawn that moved was serving a protective role for another piece or pawn, so after the exchange the opponent can simply pick off the now-undefended piece. Meanwhile, the best alternative moves (castling, developing pieces, consolidating) would have maintained the protective pawn chain while improving the position, avoiding the net material loss.

analysis.label: A bishop (or minor piece) makes a tempting capture on a back-rank or first-rank square but leaves its own piece undefended or abandons a critical defensive duty.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a greedy capture—95% of activating moves are captures, almost exclusively by bishops (Bxf8, Bxe8, Bxa8, Bxd1, Bxe1, Bxf1). In 99% of cases the capture leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece being predominantly a minor piece (163/247 = 66%) but also frequently a major piece (74 cases, typically the queen at value 6 when the bishop abandoned its defense). Meanwhile, 82% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0), meaning a superior alternative existed. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, isolating this specific tactical error pattern of a bishop diving into enemy territory to grab material while ignoring recapture or leaving a bigger piece unprotected.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a piece (usually a rook on f8/e8/a8 or a piece on d1/e1/f1), but either lands on a square where it is immediately recapturable with no compensation, or by moving it removes the defense of a more valuable piece (queen or rook). The net result is a material loss despite the capture appearing to win material, because the player failed to account for the recapture or the defensive role the bishop was performing. A better move—often a check, a central pawn push, or a different capture—would have maintained or gained material advantage.

analysis.label: Player missed a strong non-capturing queen move that would win material through tactical threats, instead playing a passive or careless move.
analysis.description: In 74% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), yet only 11% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks—indicating the winning move creates threats (forks, attacks on loose pieces) rather than immediately capturing. Across the top 12 boards, 9 of 12 best moves are queen relocations to aggressive squares (Qh5, Qg4, Qf5, Qc6, Qh3, Qxh4, Qh5, Qf3, Qa4) that generate winning tactical pressure. The player's actual moves are overwhelmingly quiet or mistimed (only 25% are captures), and 51% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0; distribution: 135 pawns, 73 minors, 45 majors), indicating tactical blindness. The feature fires on 2.3% of positions, targeting moments where a powerful queen redeployment was available but overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore an available queen repositioning that would create decisive threats—double attacks, pressure on undefended pieces, or forcing sequences that win material. Instead, the player makes routine quiet moves (rook lifts, pawn pushes, king moves) that miss the tactical moment entirely, and frequently leave their own pieces unprotected as a further sign of tactical inattention.

analysis.label: Player misses a simple capture of an opponent's major piece (usually a rook or queen) in an already overwhelming position, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 85% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with the best move being a capture 51% of the time and a check 43% of the time. Despite this, the player's move was only a capture 31% of the time, meaning ~69% played quiet moves instead. The feature fires on positions where the player already holds a crushing advantage (often two queens vs a rook, or massive material surplus) and the opponent's last active piece is en prise or capturable—frequently by the king itself (Kxd1, Kxb1, Kxg3) or by a simple pawn/piece capture (fxe3, fxe6, Rxd1, Qxc8). The own-hang rate of 39% with median value 1.0 (pawns) is secondary noise rather than the defining pattern. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions with an average cp_loss of 4118, reflecting catastrophic missed wins and mates.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a trivially available capture of the opponent's only remaining active piece (typically a rook worth 5 pawns or a queen worth 9). By playing a quiet king retreat, pawn push, or wrong capture instead, the player either throws away a forced mate, allows perpetual check, or needlessly prolongs the game. The opponent's active piece—often generating annoying checks—can be simply eliminated, but the player seems fixated on evading rather than capturing.

analysis.label: The player misses a non-capturing check that wins decisive material or delivers checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check in 100% of activating positions and is never itself a capture (0%), yet it wins material 100% of the time with a median value of 95 (approximately queen-value). This means the check forces a position where the opponent loses massive material on the follow-up (e.g., the king moves and a piece is won, or it's outright checkmate). The played move was only a capture 22% of the time and left the player's own piece hanging 67% of the time (median value 5). The positions consistently feature an exposed or uncastled enemy king (often on e1) where a rook check on the e-file, a bishop check, or a queen check either delivers mate or wins the queen/major pieces through a forced sequence.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a check that either delivers immediate checkmate (e.g., Qd2#) or forces the opponent's king to move into a position where major material is lost. By playing quiet moves or captures on other squares, the player gives the opponent time to consolidate, escape the mating net, or bring defensive resources to bear. The missed checks exploit the king's vulnerability with tempo, and any delay allows the opponent to survive.

analysis.label: Player avoided a decisive queen exchange that would have converted a winning advantage into a trivially won endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 92% of the time, yet it 'wins material' only 20% (because the captures are mostly equal queen exchanges, SEE = 0). The player's move was itself a capture only 10% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly played quiet moves instead of the winning trade. In 31% of cases the quiet move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0). Across the top 12 boards, 11 of 12 best moves are queen exchanges (Qxe3, Qxg4, Qxf4, Qxf6, Qxe4, Qxf5, Qxg5) all evaluating as equal material swaps that convert massive positional/structural advantages into trivially won pawn endgames. The average cp_loss of 1108 confirms these missed trades represent catastrophic conversion failures.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (king walks like Kc4/Ka5/Kg8, quiet queen moves like Qg2/Qd5+/Qc7, or non-converting captures like Nxg6) all avoid the simplifying queen trade. By keeping queens on the board, the player allows the opponent counterplay through perpetual check threats, active queen maneuvers, or tactical complications. The queen trade would have eliminated all defensive resources, converting into a won pawn/piece endgame where structural advantages (passed pawns, extra pawns, superior king activity) are decisive.

analysis.label: The player missed a pawn advance that wins material by attacking or trapping an enemy piece (usually a knight).
analysis.description: In 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 2.0 pawns), yet the best move is a capture only 1% of the time and a check 0% of the time. Examining the top 12 boards reveals that every single best move is a pawn advance (g4, a3, c4, a6, g4, e5, f4, h6, b4, a5, g5, a6) that attacks or traps an enemy piece—typically a knight stationed on a seemingly strong central or advanced square. Instead, the player chose a quiet developing or flank move 88% of the time (only 12% played captures). In 35% of cases the move played also left the player's own piece hanging (mostly pawns at median value 1.0), compounding the error. The feature fires on 4.8% of all positions, indicating this is a common class of oversight.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete pawn advance that attacks an enemy piece with no safe retreat square. The enemy piece (often a knight on squares like d5, f5, e5, b5, or f6) appears actively placed but is actually vulnerable to a simple pawn push that wins it or forces a materially losing exchange. By playing a slow positional or flank move instead, the player squanders a tactical opportunity worth approximately a full minor piece.

analysis.label: Playing routine quiet development or castling moves when the position demands immediate concrete action, especially resolving central pawn tension.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'normal-looking' quiet move (castling, bishop development, pawn push) while ignoring a critical concrete demand in the position. The SEE aggregate shows that 30% of the time the best move is a capture and 35% of the time it wins material (median 1 pawn), yet the player's move was a capture only 9% of the time. Only 13% of played moves left own pieces hanging, confirming this isn't primarily a 'hung piece' pattern. Instead, the dominant pattern (firing on just 0.4% of positions) is that players make autopilot developing moves—O-O, Bf4, Nf3, Bd3, e6, c6, c5—when the position urgently requires resolving central tension (exd5, dxe4, Nxe4), repositioning a tactically vulnerable piece, or seizing a concrete opportunity. The average cp_loss of 291 confirms these are catastrophic misjudgments of priority, not slight inaccuracies.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the specific concrete demands of the position. In many cases, central pawn tension (e4 vs d5) creates tactical obligations—failing to capture allows the opponent to seize the initiative, win space, or execute combinations. In other cases, a piece is placed on a square where it becomes a target or blocks critical plans (e.g., Bd6 blocking the d-pawn, castling into a position where a bishop is tactically vulnerable). The player treats the position as 'still developing' when it has actually reached a critical moment requiring precise calculation rather than general principles.

analysis.label: In Rook vs minor piece endgames, the player captures the enemy minor piece with their Rook but leaves the Rook hanging to the opponent's King, throwing away the exchange advantage.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 60% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0 = Rook), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being major pieces (19 of 32 classified). Meanwhile 47% of the played moves were captures, indicating the player is taking something while leaving their own piece exposed. The median value hung is 5 (Rook) and the typical captures target minor pieces or pawns worth 3. Across the top boards, positions 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 12 all show a Rook capturing an enemy knight or bishop (on squares like d3, d5, c4, f4) only for the Rook to be immediately recaptured, typically by the opponent's King. The best moves (Kd4, Ra3, Kd6, etc.) are quiet moves that maintain the Rook vs minor piece imbalance rather than cashing it in.
analysis.why_bad: By capturing the minor piece with the Rook in a position where the Rook is recapturable (usually by the nearby King), the player trades a Rook (5 points) for a minor piece (3 points), converting a winning Rook-vs-minor-piece endgame into a drawn or lost pawn endgame. The correct approach is to maintain the exchange advantage by keeping the Rook active and using its long-range superiority to dominate the minor piece positionally.

analysis.label: Player misses a decisive check (often a rook penetration on an open file) and instead plays a slow quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 56% of best moves are checks and 72% win material (median value 100cp), while only 14% of played moves are captures and just 16% of best moves are captures themselves. This means the winning tactic is predominantly a forcing check that opens up material gain or checkmate, not a simple capture. The player's move left their own piece hanging only 32% of the time, so the primary error is failing to exploit the opponent's vulnerability rather than self-inflicted damage. The top boards confirm a pattern where open-file rooks (or other pieces) have access to devastating checks—often back-rank intrusions like Rd8+, Rf1+, or Rd1#—but the player instead repositions quietly (Bd3, Bc5, g4, Rae1, Rh6) or even plays a check in the wrong direction (Ne4+, R8c3+), missing the killing blow.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves squander overwhelming tactical opportunities. The positions feature exposed enemy kings and open files where a forcing check either wins material immediately (via follow-up threats or forks after the king moves) or delivers checkmate. By playing slow repositioning moves instead, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, defend the back rank, or escape the tactical net entirely—turning winning positions into equal or lost ones (average cp_loss: 1028).

analysis.label: Player makes a routine-looking opening move (fianchetto prep, pawn push, quiet development) that ignores an existing tactical threat, leaving their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 71% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value: 1.0, i.e. pawn-sized), with the piece class distribution heavily weighted toward pawns (161) and minor pieces (110), plus 28 major pieces. Only 5% of played moves are captures, and the best move wins material only 24% of the time—meaning the mistake is primarily about failing to defend rather than missing an attack. The feature fires on positions where the player ignores an immediate tactical threat (e.g., a queen attacking f7/e5, a bishop targeting a fianchettoed piece, an open diagonal to a rook) and instead plays a 'natural' but slow opening move like g6, g3, c4, d6, f3, or Bc5 that would be reasonable in a threat-free position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize long-term plans (fianchetto setup, pawn structure, generic development) while a concrete tactical threat already exists on the board. The played move either fails to block/address the threat or actively worsens the situation (e.g., g6 weakening f7 when a queen already targets it, or d6 blocking a needed retreat square), allowing the opponent to win material immediately. In the opening with both kings in the center, concrete threats must be addressed before positional plans.

analysis.label: Player ignores an advanced pawn's ability to simply capture an undefended enemy knight, playing a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 2.0, consistent with a pawn capturing a knight netting +2). The best move is always a capture (100%) and never a check (0%). The player's actual move was a capture only 21% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly chose quiet moves (development, pawn advances) instead. The recurring geometry across all 12 top boards is an advanced pawn (on d-file or e-file) directly attacking an enemy knight (on c3, c6, f3, or f6) with no adequate defense, and the player simply ignoring this free capture. All positions are in the opening phase, where players appear focused on development or positional plans and overlook the elementary tactical pawn capture.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (f5, f4, d4, Nc3, Nf6, e4, c5, Nc6, d5, Nf3) fail because they forfeit a free minor piece worth ~3 points. The player's advanced pawn already attacks an undefended or inadequately protected enemy knight, and simply taking it (exf6, dxc3, dxc6, exf3) would win material immediately with no compensation for the opponent. By playing a developing or positional move instead, the player gives the opponent time to move the knight to safety, squandering a decisive material advantage.

analysis.label: Player plays a slow quiet move when an immediate game-winning tactic (often a check or checkmate) is available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 80% of activating positions the best move wins material with a median value of 5.0 (queen-level), and 42% of the time the best move is a check—yet the player's actual move was a capture only 16% of the time. The average cp_loss is a catastrophic 2625. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet, positional, or preparatory (rook lifts, king moves, piece repositioning), while the position demands immediate decisive action. The secondary 58% own-hang rate (median 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that by playing slowly, the player sometimes also leaves minor material loose, but the primary mistake is failing to deliver the knockout. Boards show missed mate-in-1 (Rh1#, Ra6#), missed mate-in-2 (Rg4+), and missed winning checks (Qc8+) in favor of moves like doubling rooks or centralizing the king.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves squander an immediately winning position—often a forced checkmate or a check that wins decisive material—allowing the opponent to survive, consolidate, or counterattack. Instead of delivering the final blow, the player 'improves' a piece that doesn't need improving, turning a won game into a drawn or even lost one.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture but leaves their own queen or rook en prise to the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a capture (83% of played moves are captures) but catastrophically leaves their own major piece hanging (97% of positions leave an own piece en prise, median value 5.0, with 142 of the hung pieces being major pieces—queens or rooks). The best move often wins material itself (70%, median 3.0) but through a quieter or more precise continuation (only 20% of best moves are captures, 7% are checks), meaning the player chose the wrong way to gain material. The feature activates on only 0.1% of positions, reflecting how specific this blunder pattern is: a greedy but tactically unsound capture that overlooks the vulnerability of one's own highest-value piece.
analysis.why_bad: The captures fail because they either move a piece that was defending the player's queen/rook, ignore that the queen/rook is under attack on its current square, or place the queen on an undefended square (e.g., Qxd8 where the queen becomes trapped). The player focuses on the immediate material gain from capturing an enemy piece but overlooks that the opponent can simply recapture the now-undefended major piece, resulting in a net material loss far exceeding what was captured.

analysis.label: Player ignores a trivially capturable enemy piece in the endgame and plays an irrelevant quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 77% of activating positions (median value 3.0), with 81% of best moves being simple captures. Yet the player's move was a capture only 1% of the time — an almost total failure to take free material. In 44% of cases the move played also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, predominantly major pieces: 31 of 45 hangs). The feature fires exclusively in endgames where an enemy piece (typically a rook on an open file or rank) is undefended and directly capturable, often by a king, rook, bishop, or knight. Instead of the obvious take, the player plays a quiet pawn push, king retreat, or check that not only misses the winning capture but frequently exposes their own rook to recapture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore immediately available material, converting winning or decisive positions into draws or losses. A free rook capture (worth ~5 pawns) is the most consequential single move available, and by declining it the player both forfeits that material gain and often hangs their own piece in the process, causing catastrophic evaluation swings (avg cp_loss: 4553).

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing check (usually queen or rook to a king-adjacent square) that would have delivered mate, created perpetual, or prolonged survival, and instead played a passive move allowing immediate checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a check in 96% of the top 500 activating positions — an extraordinary concentration on a single move type. The best move is also a capture 60% of the time (capturing with check, e.g., Qxg2+, Qxh7+, Qxf6+), though SEE material gain is often 0 (meaning the piece is defended but the check itself is critical). Only 42% show material won (median 95cp ≈ a pawn), confirming the check's value lies in forcing sequences rather than material gain. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 18% captures), and 51% leave their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), reflecting moves that simply ignore the opponent's mating threats. The feature fires on 0.0% of all positions, indicating a rare and specific pattern of desperation.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in positions where checkmate is imminent (avg cp_loss ~6092, with most being mate-in-N blunders), the only defense or counterplay is a forcing check that disrupts the opponent's mating attack — creating perpetual check, winning back material with tempo, or delivering mate first. By playing quiet or aimless moves (Qc4, Qb2, Qd1, h3, Qe4, etc.), the player surrenders the initiative entirely and allows the opponent's mating net to close immediately, typically resulting in mate within 5-18 moves.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available winning capture to play an active-looking quiet move that often also hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 71% of the time the best move was a simple capture (median value won: 6.0, i.e., queen-level), yet the played move was a capture only 11% of the time. Instead, 64% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value: 3.0). The moves played are characteristically 'active-looking' quiet moves — knight jumps (Ne5, Nd3, Ng5, Nc7+, Nd2), queen centralization (Qd5, Qg2+), king moves (Ke7, Kb1), and rook redeployments (Rb8, Rd7, Ra7) — that aim for activity or even deliver check, when a straightforward capture was available and often mandatory. The combination of missing the winning capture AND hanging one's own material yields enormous evaluation losses (avg cp_loss: 1204).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize apparent activity (checks, centralization, piece deployment) over concrete material gains. A simple capture — often a queen recapture or a piece winning an undefended enemy piece — was available. The 'flashy' alternative not only forfeits that material gain but frequently places the moved piece (or another piece) on an undefended square, compounding the loss by hanging additional material to the opponent's reply.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move that hangs their own piece, ignoring a necessary queen capture or trade.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 81% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors/minors/pawns), while 93% of the time the best move was a simple capture — overwhelmingly a queen capture (Qxd5, Qxe5, Qxd4, Qxb5, Qxb6, etc.). The best move 'wins 0' by SEE in most cases, indicating these are queen trades or recaptures rather than free material, yet they are essential tactical obligations. Instead, the player plays a quiet piece move (Nd7, Bc4, Bf6, Bd3, Be7, Nf6, Rd1, a6, etc.) that ignores this obligation and consequently leaves their own material undefended. Only 21% of played moves were captures themselves, confirming players chose quiet moves over the required tactical response.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the mandatory queen capture or trade, the player leaves their position tactically unresolved. The quiet developing move fails to address the immediate threat, and the piece that was previously protected (or the square that was covered by the queen's presence in a trade) becomes undefended, allowing the opponent to win material on the next move. The player prioritizes development or repositioning over the concrete tactical requirement of the position.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning rook (or major piece) infiltration along an open file, instead playing a passive or irrelevant move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 96% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e. a whole piece). Yet the played move is a capture only 9% of the time, and the best move is a capture only 23% of the time — meaning the typical winning move is a quiet rook penetration that attacks or traps enemy material. The positions consistently feature open files (d, c, e) with rooks already placed on them, and the best moves are infiltrations to the 7th/2nd rank or deep squares (Rd8, Re7, Rd7, Rc2, Rc5, Qc2). Players instead make aimless quiet moves (king shuffles, pawn pushes, retreats) that squander the open-file advantage. Only 31% of played moves hang the player's own material, confirming the primary error is one of omission — failing to exploit an available penetration — rather than a self-inflicted blunder.
analysis.why_bad: These passive moves fail because they waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate action. The rook (or queen) has a clear path to infiltrate along an open file to a dominant square where it attacks undefended pieces, creates back-rank threats, or forks multiple targets. By playing something irrelevant (a3, b5, f5, Ke3, Ra2), the player allows the opponent to consolidate, defend the weak point, or seize the initiative themselves, turning a winning position into an equal or lost one.

analysis.label: Player ignores a central pawn advance that attacks an enemy piece and wins material, instead playing a quiet developing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 2.0), yet the best move is a capture only 8% of the time and never a check (0%). This means the winning move is overwhelmingly a non-capturing pawn advance that attacks an enemy piece. Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: the best moves are almost exclusively central pawn pushes (e4, e5, d4, d5, g4, dxe4) that attack or trap enemy pieces—typically knights on f3/f6/c3/c6. The player's move was a capture only 11% of the time, and 63% of the time the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, distribution heavily skewed to pawns at 72/110). All 12 top-activating positions occur in the opening phase with closed or tense centers and uncastled kings, representing the classic scenario where a decisive central pawn thrust is available but overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes quiet development (Bf5, Ne2, Qf6) or passive pawn moves (f5, f4, c6) over a concrete central pawn advance that immediately attacks an enemy piece with tempo. The pawn push typically hits an undefended or poorly-supported knight, winning at least a pawn's worth of material through the threatened piece displacement. By ignoring this tactic, the player not only forfeits a material advantage but often simultaneously weakens their own pawn structure or leaves their own pieces undefended.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture the opponent's undefended or insufficiently defended queen, which is directly capturable by a piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 91% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 6.0, consistent with capturing a queen minus the exchange of the capturing piece), and 99% of best moves are captures. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 25% captures), meaning the player simply ignores the free queen. The median won value of 6.0 corresponds to queen captures where the capturing piece (typically a minor piece worth 3) may be recaptured. In cases where the capturing piece is safe (e.g., knight takes undefended queen), the value reaches 9. The 48% own-hang rate reflects that players sometimes compound the blunder by leaving their own piece loose, but the primary and universal mistake is missing the enemy queen capture. Positions are heavily opening-phase (8/12), suggesting the queen was prematurely placed or left on a vulnerable square early in the game.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that the opponent's queen is directly capturable—often by a knight or bishop with a clear path to the queen's square (typically the d-file: d2, d4, d5, d7, d8). Instead of winning approximately 6-9 pawns of material instantly, the player makes a developing or positional move that squanders a decisive advantage, often equalizing or even losing the game.

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop capture of an undefended enemy piece (often on its starting square), leaving their own piece hanging instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of best moves are captures and nearly all are bishop captures (Bxg8, Bxc8, Bxf1, Bxg1, Bxb1, Bxc1) targeting undeveloped or undefended enemy pieces on starting squares. These captures show SEE value of 0, indicating equal trades (bishop for bishop/knight). Meanwhile, 55% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, overwhelmingly minor pieces — 29 out of 36 cases). Only 12% of played moves are captures themselves, and only 12% of best moves technically 'win' material outright. The pattern is clear: the player has an active or exposed bishop that should trade itself for an opponent's undefended piece, resolving a tactical tension, but instead plays a developing or positional move that leaves the bishop (or another minor piece) en prise.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an urgent tactical obligation: their bishop has access to capture an undefended enemy piece (typically sitting on a home square like g8, c8, b1, c1, f1, g1), but by playing something else, they leave their own piece hanging. The opponent then captures the exposed piece for free on the next move, resulting in a net material loss of approximately a minor piece (≈3 pawns), explaining the average 370cp loss across these positions.

analysis.label: Player plays a passive quiet move when the position demands an urgent capture (trade, recapture, or simplification) to survive.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 90% of the time the best move is a capture, yet only 9% of the played moves were captures—an enormous disconnect. The best captures win material only 19% of the time (median 5.0, i.e., queen-level), meaning the vast majority are equal exchanges or recaptures that are nonetheless critical for survival. 26% of best moves are checks (often captures with check). The player's quiet moves leave their own pieces hanging 49% of the time (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns: 167 pawn, 50 major, 30 minor), a secondary consequence of ignoring the forced line. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2455 confirms these are existential misses—often the difference between holding a position and immediate checkmate.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because the position requires a forced capture—often a queen trade (Qxe5, Qxe4, Qxf6+, Qxe6, Qxd5), a rook exchange (Rxd2+, Rxf3+, Rxc6, Rxf7+), or a key recapture—to neutralize an overwhelming threat (usually checkmate or decisive material gain). By playing passively, the player allows the opponent's existing tactical threats to execute unchallenged, often resulting in immediate mate or terminal material loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (often with check) that leaves their own major piece undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a capture (79% of moves are captures) that leaves their own piece hanging (93% of the time, median value 5.0 — typically a queen or rook). The own-hang piece distribution skews heavily toward major pieces (36 major vs 13 minor vs 3 pawn). Meanwhile, the best move wins material 84% of the time (median 3.0), indicating that a safer path to gain material existed. The player is lured by an immediate capture — often flashy, sometimes with check (Qxh7+, Qxe1+, Rxe7+, Rxf8+, Qxc1+) — but by moving their attacking piece to that square or vacating a defensive post, they leave a higher-value piece completely unprotected. The average cp_loss of 1120 confirms these are catastrophic blunders, typically losing a queen (value 9) or rook (value 5).
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because the player prioritizes grabbing an immediate target over board safety. By moving the capturing piece (or by removing a defender), a more valuable piece is left en prise. The opponent simply recaptures or takes the hanging piece, netting significant material. The better moves (Bxc6, Rf2, Qxd6, Rxg2, etc.) either win material cleanly without exposure or address the defensive needs first, preserving piece coordination.

analysis.label: The player missed a bishop move that wins the opponent's queen (or equivalent major material), typically via a tactical diagonal attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 83% of top-activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 6.0 — strongly consistent with winning a queen for a bishop (9-3=6). Remarkably, in 11 out of 12 top boards the best move is a bishop move (Bb6, Bg5, Bxe2, Bh6, Bg5, Bh4, Bxe2, Bxa2, Bb4, Bf4, Bh6). Only 31% of these best moves are captures, meaning the majority are quiet bishop moves that attack or trap the queen along a diagonal. The player's own move was rarely a capture (14%) and only 21% hung their own piece, confirming this is a missed-opportunity feature rather than a hung-piece feature. The positions frequently feature exposed kings or queens on vulnerable diagonals that the bishop can exploit.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Kh7, Ne5, a6, e5, Bf6, Qb8, etc.) are quiet or irrelevant moves that completely overlook a decisive bishop intervention. By ignoring the bishop's tactical potential on a key diagonal — often attacking an exposed queen or exploiting a pin — the player throws away winning material (typically a net gain of a full queen) and converts winning or equal positions into lost or equal ones.

analysis.label: The player missed an immediate or near-immediate back-rank checkmate delivered by a rook.
analysis.description: In 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material valued at 100 (checkmate), and in 99% of cases the best move is a check — yet only 6% are captures, confirming these are rook-to-back-rank mating moves rather than piece wins. The player's actual move was a capture only 24% of the time, and 41% of the time it incidentally left an own piece (usually a pawn, median value 1.0) hanging — but the decisive error is completely ignoring the lethal back-rank geometry. All 12 top-activating boards show an enemy king entombed on the first/eighth rank by its own pawns or pieces, with the player's rook having a clear path (via an open file) to deliver mate in 1 or 2, yet the player instead made an irrelevant capture, pawn push, or quiet move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they squander an immediate forced checkmate. The opponent's king is trapped on the back rank with no flight squares, and the player's rook has a clear line to deliver check on that rank — producing mate in 1 or at most 2 moves. By playing something else (a greedy capture, a pawn advance, a king move), the player throws away the win and often allows the opponent to escape or even turn the tables entirely, as reflected in the catastrophic average centipawn loss of ~9800.

analysis.label: In opening positions, the player makes an aggressive-looking move (pawn push, capture, or check) that leaves their own piece undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows this feature fires on moves that hang the player's own piece: 94% of played moves leave an own piece en prise (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece). The hung pieces are distributed across types (major 37%, pawn 34%, minor 29%). Only 48% of positions have a best move that wins material, confirming the mistake is not about missing enemy hanging pieces but rather creating new vulnerabilities in one's own position. The feature fires almost exclusively in opening positions (11/12 top boards) where both kings typically remain in the center, and the player makes a move that appears active—an e5/d6 pawn push, a dxe6/exd3 capture, a Qf7+ check, or a greedy Qxb1—without noticing it removes protection from or exposes their own piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize aggression, greed, or initiative (pawn advances, tempting captures, showy checks) while overlooking that the move removes a defender from one's own piece or places a piece on an unprotected square. For example, e5 pushes remove a pawn that was defending a bishop; exd3 captures leave queens exposed to discovered attacks; Qxb1 grabs material but places the queen in a trapped/capturable position; Qf7+ gives a pointless check while leaving the queen en prise.

analysis.label: Player ignores a critical knight capture (Nx...) that eliminates a dangerous or exposed enemy piece, instead playing a passive quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 98% of activating positions, and across all top-12 boards this capture is specifically a knight taking an enemy piece (Nxh4, Nxe4, Nxd4, Nxb5, Nxa3). These captures are SEE-neutral (wins 0), meaning they're equal exchanges, yet missing them costs ~261cp on average because the captured piece is either aggressively placed (e.g., a knight on h4/e4 dominating the position) or the exchange unlocks decisive tactical follow-ups. Meanwhile, the player's quiet alternative leaves their own piece hanging 49% of the time (median value 3.0, spread across minor/pawn/major). Only 17% of positions show outright material advantage in the best move; the remaining 83% are strategically vital equal exchanges the player fails to recognize.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the available knight exchange, the player allows the opponent's aggressively-placed piece to remain dominant (creating threats, controlling key squares), while their own quiet move often creates new vulnerabilities. The equal-material exchange removes a key attacking/defensive piece whose positional value far exceeds its material worth.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move instead of resolving pawn tension with a critical capture, often leaving their own pawn en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 58% of cases the best move is a capture (overwhelmingly pawn-takes-pawn), yet the player's move was a capture only 7% of the time. Meanwhile, 53% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being a pawn in 83 out of 88 cases. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames where mutual pawn tension exists (pawns attacking each other), and the correct move is to capture first. Instead, the player plays a quiet move — usually a king move or a pawn push elsewhere — ignoring the tension. This move-order error allows the opponent to capture the player's pawn on favorable terms, effectively losing material for nothing.
analysis.why_bad: By not resolving pawn tension when it is critical (capturing first), the player loses the initiative in the pawn race. The opponent can now capture the abandoned pawn at a moment that suits them, gaining a material or positional advantage. In king-and-pawn endgames, even a single pawn loss is often decisive, and the move-order of when to capture in pawn tensions is the key calculation that determines passed pawn creation and king activity.

analysis.label: In a critical endgame position (usually already losing), the player makes a quiet, passive move with the wrong piece, catastrophically worsening the position by hanging material or missing the only defensive resource.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows a dual signal: 49% of best moves win material (median 2.0 pawns) and 47% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median 2.0, distributed as pawn:37, major:28, minor:17). Only 11% of played moves were captures, confirming the moves are overwhelmingly passive/quiet. The feature fires on 0.1% of positions, concentrated in endgames (10/12 top boards). The hung-major-piece count (28) aligns with Queen-vs-Rook endgames where the rook gets exposed to the queen's attack lines. The pattern shows players either moving the rook when the king should retreat to safety (positions 2,3,6,8: Rf6/Rd6 instead of Kh7/Kf7/Kg6), or moving the king passively when a piece needed to take tactical action (positions 1,4,7,9: Ke5/Kf7/Ke7/Kb8 instead of Rd6+/Re4/Ne4/c8=Q).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in critical endgame defensive positions, piece coordination is razor-thin. Moving the rook exposes it to the opponent's queen along diagonals or files (hanging a major piece), while passive king moves abandon the only defensive resource (a tactical shot or precise king placement), typically converting a difficult-but-holdable loss into immediate forced mate or decisive material hemorrhage.

analysis.label: A rook check (or rook move/capture) in an endgame that leaves the rook itself en prise and undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows an overwhelming 97% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the hung-piece class distribution being almost entirely major pieces (30 major vs 2 minor). The played moves are captures only 39% of the time, indicating many are quiet checks that simply leave the rook unprotected. The best move is a check only 6% of the time, confirming the engine recommends quieter, safer alternatives rather than the desperate rook checks the player chose. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames featuring a rook giving check (or moving to an attacked square) where the opponent can simply capture it on the next move.
analysis.why_bad: The rook checks are typically desperation moves in losing positions. After the check, the opponent's king simply captures or sidesteps and wins the rook for free, converting a difficult (but still contested) endgame into an immediately won position. The player trades a slow loss for an instant one by throwing away their last major piece with a hollow check that accomplishes nothing strategically.

analysis.label: Player moves a knight to an aggressive or central square, leaving it or another piece unprotected and hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly shows this is a 'hung own piece' pattern: 72% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece). The own-hang distribution (pawn:39, minor:38, major:24) confirms knights/bishops are frequently the hung piece. Only 32% of the moves are captures, meaning most are quiet knight relocations. The best move wins material in 50% of cases (median 3.0), often because the correct move would have captured the opponent's piece instead or simply castled to safety. Across the top 12 boards, 9 of 12 played moves are knight moves (Ne4, Ne5, Nc4, Nb4, Nfxe4, etc.) to active-looking squares, and in most cases the knight itself ends up en prise on that square.
analysis.why_bad: The knight moves to a central or aggressive square (e4, e5, c4, b4) that appears active but is insufficiently defended. The opponent can simply capture the knight (or the piece it previously protected) for free. The player prioritizes piece activity or an attractive-looking jump over basic piece safety, ignoring that the destination square is controlled by the opponent or that moving the knight uncovers an attack on another piece.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet move (usually a king move) instead of capturing an available enemy piece that was the critical best move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 84% of the time and wins material in 60% of positions (median value 1.0), yet the player's move was itself a capture only 7% of the time. The player's move left their own piece hanging just 25% of the time, so the dominant error is not hanging a piece but rather MISSING an available capture. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and in 10 of 12 the played move is a king move or quiet piece move when the best move was a straightforward capture (Kxb6, Kxf8, Nxh5, Rxe2+, Bxb6, hxg5, Rxd3, Nxb6, Bxb2, Rxb8). Many of these captures represent critical drawing resources (eliminating the last piece to reach insufficient material) or winning an undefended high-value piece.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available capture that either wins material outright, eliminates a dangerous enemy piece, or achieves a theoretically drawn position. By playing a passive king move instead, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, promote pawns, or escape with their hanging piece, often turning a drawn or winning position into a decisive loss.

analysis.label: Black (or occasionally White) ignores critical central pawn tension and plays a non-essential move, leaving their own center pawn or piece en prise to the opponent's d-pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 70% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 1.0, with pawn=51 and minor=42 in the distribution), while the best move is a capture 79% of the time. Nearly all top-activating positions are Italian Game / Scotch Gambit openings where White has played d4 creating direct tension against Black's e5 pawn. Instead of resolving the tension with the critical exd4 capture (which wins 0 net material but removes the threat), Black plays irrelevant moves (Na5, h6, a6, f6, Bc5, Ne5) that ignore the attacked e5-pawn or place a piece directly in the path of the advancing d-pawn. The best move being a capture in 79% of positions confirms the pattern: the correct response is to take the d-pawn, but the player doesn't.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to capture exd4 (or address the central tension), Black leaves the e5 pawn undefended against dxe5 (or places a piece like a bishop on c5/knight on e5 where it is immediately captured by the d-pawn). White wins material for free—typically a pawn but sometimes a minor piece—while simultaneously gaining a commanding center and development advantage in the opening.

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the player makes a passive king move instead of executing a critical pawn breakthrough.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material 66% of the time (median value: 1.0 pawn), yet the player's move is almost never a capture (9%), and the best move itself is rarely a capture (6%) or check (6%). This indicates the winning resource is a pawn advance/breakthrough that gains material indirectly. In 20% of cases the king move even leaves the player's own pawn hanging (all 16 cases are pawns). Across the top 12 boards (all endgames, avg cp_loss 437), 11 of 12 played moves are king moves while the best moves are consistently pawn breaks (e5, f5, b5, c5, g5, c6) — tactical pawn advances that create decisive passed pawns or win material through breakthrough combinations.
analysis.why_bad: The king moves are passive and squander the critical timing window for a pawn breakthrough. In these endgame positions, the pawn break is urgent — it creates an unstoppable passed pawn or wins material through a forcing sequence. By playing a king move instead, the player allows the opponent to reposition defensively, close the breakthrough opportunity, or seize the initiative. The window for the pawn break is often a single-tempo opportunity that, once missed, turns a won/drawn position into a lost one.

analysis.label: The player grabs a peripheral pawn (typically with the queen on the a/b-file) instead of pressing a winning attack against the exposed enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 66% of positions the best move wins significant material (median value 5.0, i.e. queen/rook-level wins or checkmates), yet the player's move was a capture only 31% of the time—almost always a low-value pawn grab on the a- or b-file. The best moves are overwhelmingly queen moves toward the enemy king (Qf6, Qf4, Qf5, Qf7, Qf4+, Qd4+, Qxh6#, Qxe6). Meanwhile, 54% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, dominated by 102 pawns), because redirecting the queen to a remote file abandons defensive duties. The opponent's king is consistently noted as exposed (g7, h7, h2, h3), making the attacking queen move decisive. The average cp_loss of 2004 reflects that these pawn grabs forfeit mating attacks or large material wins.
analysis.why_bad: By sending the queen to a wing pawn (Qxa7, Qxa2, Qxb2, Qxa5), the player wins a pawn worth ~1 point but misses a crushing attack against the exposed enemy king—often checkmate in few moves or winning a queen/rook. The queen ends up offside and unable to participate in the attack, while the opponent's king that was on the verge of collapse gets time to consolidate or even launch a counter-attack.

analysis.label: Player misses a rook move along a file that would win the opponent's queen, instead playing a quiet or irrelevant move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 74% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (a queen), while the player's actual move was only a capture 17% of the time — overwhelmingly quiet king moves or pawn pushes (Kg2, g3, Ke2, Kc3, g4). The best moves are almost exclusively rook moves to open files (Re1, Rg1, Rf1, Rb1, Rc8) that attack or trap the opponent's queen which has ventured onto that file. The 66% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental — the catastrophic error is ignoring the rook move that wins the queen. The enormous average cp_loss of 5357 confirms these are game-deciding blunders where a single rook placement would have won decisive material.
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's queen has infiltrated onto an open file (e.g., Qe2, Qg2, Qe4) where it appears active but is actually vulnerable. A simple rook move to that file traps or wins the queen outright. Instead, the player makes a passive king move or pawn push that completely ignores this tactical opportunity, turning a won or salvageable position into an immediate loss or forced mate.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning check (often checkmate or queen-winning) by playing a tempting capture or quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 87% of the time the best move is a check, and 93% of the time it wins material (median value 91, corresponding to queen-level gains or mate). Despite the availability of these devastating checks, the player's actual move was a capture 60% of the time—grabbing lesser material rather than delivering the killing blow.
