The feature fires on only 0.0% of all positions, indicating these are rare but catastrophic missed tactical opportunities where an exposed enemy king (typically stuck in the center) allows a forcing check that wins immediately. The 57% own-hang rate on the played move is a secondary consequence: by missing the decisive check, the player sometimes also leaves their own pieces vulnerable in the ensuing inferior position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing check that either delivers immediate checkmate or wins the opponent's queen/major material via a discovered attack or fork. By playing a capture or quiet move instead, the player allows the opponent's king to escape to safety or the opponent to consolidate, turning a completely won position (often forced mate) into merely a large or even negligible advantage. The checks are decisive precisely because the enemy king is exposed with no shelter, and one tempo (the check) is all that's needed to exploit this.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player makes a natural-looking advancing move that leaves their own piece (usually a pawn) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows a dominant pattern of the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (67% of positions, median value 1.0), with the hung piece distribution strongly favoring pawns (20 pawn, 10 minor, 5 major). The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (11/12 boards). Only 6% of played moves are captures, and 35% of best moves win material (median 1.0), indicating that by hanging their own piece the player often also misses recapturing or winning the opponent's material. The best move is a check only 8% of the time and a capture 27%, showing the correct alternative is often a quiet repositioning or defensive move rather than a flashy tactic.
analysis.why_bad: The player fixates on an advancing plan (pushing a passed pawn, repositioning a king, or relocating a piece toward a promotion square) while neglecting that the move removes defense from one of their own pieces. In positions 4 and 7, moving a pawn or bishop leaves the bishop directly capturable by the opponent's king. In positions 2 and 6, advancing or moving a piece abandons defense of a pawn. In extreme cases (positions 5, 8, 10, 11), the tunnel-vision pawn push throws away a forced mate, sometimes even allowing the opponent to mate instead.

analysis.label: Player captures or makes a materialistic move while ignoring the opponent's forced checkmate threat, leaving their own piece hanging in the process.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 82% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed across pawns:243, minors:107, majors:62), while 44% of the moves were themselves captures. The best moves win material only 59% of the time and are rarely captures (16%) or checks (7%), indicating the correct responses were typically defensive/prophylactic. The astronomical average cp_loss of 9154 confirms that nearly every activation involves transitioning from a playable position into a forced mate for the opponent. The player greedily captures an enemy piece (often on e5, f3, c6, or e1) but the capturing piece lands en prise, and more critically, the move either removes a key defender, opens a fatal line, or simply ignores an existing mating threat.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes material gain over king safety. By capturing (e.g., Nxe5, Bxe5, Bxf3, Bxe1), they either remove a piece that was blocking a mating diagonal/file, ignore an immediate checkmate threat (like Qxh7# or Qg7#), or waste a critical tempo needed for defense. The captured material is irrelevant because the opponent delivers forced checkmate before it matters. The best moves typically address the mating threat directly through blocking, defensive retreats, or prophylactic pawn moves (h6, g6, f4, d5).

analysis.label: Player gives a flashy check (almost always a knight check) that leaves the checking piece unprotected and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 90% of positions show the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the piece class distribution heavily favoring minor pieces (86 minor vs 43 major vs 18 pawn). The played moves are checks in all 12 top-activating boards (Ne5+, Nd3+, Nxf7+, Nc5+, Nc4+, Ng6+, Bf5+, Nf6+, Nd5+, Ne6+), yet only 12% of best moves are checks and only 20% of played moves are captures. This means the player is seduced by an available check — overwhelmingly a knight fork/check pattern — that jumps the piece into an undefended square where it is simply captured. Meanwhile, the best move (a capture 43% of the time, winning median 3.0 pawns of material 65% of the time) is a non-checking move that maintains or wins material without sacrificing a piece.
analysis.why_bad: The checks look forcing and aggressive but accomplish nothing: the opponent simply captures the undefended checking piece (usually a knight) after moving their king or interposing. The player trades a minor piece for no compensation when a stronger non-checking alternative existed — often a quiet capture or consolidating move that would have maintained or increased the advantage.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture a critically advanced passed pawn (often one square from promotion), playing a flashy or quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 83% of best moves are captures and 36% are checks, yet only 8% of actually-played moves are captures. The best move consistently wins 0-1 in SEE (pawn value), confirming the target is a pawn, not a piece. Across all 12 top-activating positions, the opponent has an extremely advanced passed pawn (typically on the 2nd/7th rank, one step from queening) that demands immediate capture. The best move eliminates this existential threat—often via Rxa2, Nxc2, Bxa2, etc.—yet the player ignores it in favor of a check, a quiet king move, or some other seemingly active but strategically irrelevant move. The 24% own-hang rate and moderate 30% material-winning rate reflect that in some variants the neglected pawn promotes, costing the equivalent of material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because an advanced passed pawn one square from promotion is the highest-priority threat in the position. Playing a check or quiet move that doesn't address it gives the opponent time to promote (or force promotion threats), converting a drawn or winning position into a lost one. The captures are often 'boring' (taking an undefended pawn, SEE=0) but are absolutely forced—one tempo of delay is fatal in a promotion race.

analysis.label: Player makes a routine developing move instead of an urgent prophylactic pawn advance or bishop retreat in a closed-center opening position.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, only 38% of best moves win material (median just 1 pawn), and only 22% are captures, indicating the missed opportunity is primarily positional rather than tactical. The played moves are rarely captures (11%) and only 15% leave own pieces hanging. The feature fires on closed-center openings (all 12 top positions are opening phase with closed centers) where the best move is a prophylactic flank pawn advance (h5, h4, a4, a5) or a piece retreat (Bc8, Be7, Be2, Bb3) to prevent an enemy pawn storm from trapping or attacking a vulnerable piece—typically a bishop. Instead, the player makes a normal-looking but ill-timed developing move (e6, Nf6, Nc6, Nd7, d5, d3, b3) that ignores the positional urgency, resulting in an average 290cp loss as the opponent executes the threatened pawn advance.
analysis.why_bad: In closed positions, timing prophylactic pawn advances or piece retreats is critical. The routine moves fail because they allow the opponent to execute a pawn advance (g4, b5, a5, etc.) that attacks or traps a piece—usually a bishop on an exposed diagonal. The 'normal' developing move wastes the one tempo needed to prevent this threat, converting a balanced or slight-edge position into a strategically lost one.

analysis.label: Player makes a developing or positional move that leaves one of their own pawns undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player is hanging their own material: 88% of played moves left the player's own piece en prise (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn). The hung-piece class distribution is dominated by pawns (132 pawns vs. 36 minors vs. 7 majors out of ~175 cases). Meanwhile, 48% of the time a better move existed that would win material, suggesting the player had active alternatives but chose a passive or misdirected move instead. Only 24% of the played moves were captures, confirming these are typically quiet positional or developing moves that inadvertently leave a pawn unguarded. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting a specific blunder pattern in the opening or early middlegame where a 'normal-looking' move ignores an immediate tactical threat to one's own pawn.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes development, repositioning, or a positional idea while ignoring a concrete tactical vulnerability to one of their own pawns. Whether it's playing h6 when e6 was needed, playing Nf6 when fxe6 was critical, or playing Nd2 when h3 was required to defend, the result is the same: an opponent captures a free pawn, gaining material and often momentum. The player essentially 'forgets' about a pawn's need for protection.

analysis.label: In pawn endgames, the player moved the king in the wrong direction (or pushed a pawn) instead of approaching a winnable enemy pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 83% of the time the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), yet only 13% of best moves are captures — meaning the material is won by king proximity threats, not immediate captures. The played move was a capture only 9% of the time, and only 17% of played moves hung own material. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames (mostly pure king-and-pawn), and the best moves are overwhelmingly king moves toward a specific vulnerable enemy pawn (Kb3→b4, Ka4→a5, Kg5→h5, Kh5→h6, Kg6→h6, Ka6→a5, etc.). The player instead moved the king the wrong way or made a pawn push, failing to approach the attackable pawn.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, every tempo is critical. Moving the king away from a vulnerable enemy pawn (or pushing a pawn instead of activating the king) allows the opponent to consolidate or advance their own pawns. The winning idea — approaching and capturing an enemy pawn — becomes impossible once the king is misdirected, often converting a drawable or winning position into a loss.

analysis.label: The player missed a bishop capture that wins the exchange (bishop takes an enemy rook) with a consistent SEE gain of 2.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 92% of positions feature a best move winning material with a median value of 2.0 (the exchange), and 99% of best moves are captures while only 19% of played moves were captures. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is always a bishop capture (Bxf1, Bxd1, Bxf8, Bxb8, Bxd8, Bxa1) with SEE value exactly 2, corresponding precisely to the exchange value (rook minus bishop ≈ 2 pawns). The player instead chose quiet positional moves—castling, pawn pushes, bishop retreats—completely ignoring the tactical opportunity. The 49% own-hang rate (median 3.0, heavily minor pieces at 86 instances) is a secondary effect where some of these quiet moves also left pieces loose, but the primary and universal pattern is the missed exchange-winning bishop capture.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves squander an immediate tactical opportunity where the player's bishop has a clear capture of an enemy rook, winning the exchange (~2 pawns of material). By ignoring the capture, the player allows the opponent to move the rook to safety or interpose, neutralizing the advantage completely—as shown by the average cp_loss of 173 centipawns.

analysis.label: In the opening, the player makes a passive developing move or greedy capture while missing a much stronger tactical blow and often leaving a pawn hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' but suboptimal move—typically a quiet piece development (Bb3, Bd2, Nf6, Na6, Be6, Bd3) or a greedy/wrong-direction capture (dxc4, exd3, gxf4, gxh4)—while a concrete tactical opportunity exists. The SEE aggregate shows that 60% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 66% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung pieces overwhelmingly being pawns (58 of 82 cases). Best moves are checks 14% of the time and captures 23% of the time—often forks, discovered attacks, or forcing central pawn pushes. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, highlighting a specific failure mode: prioritizing routine positional moves over concrete forcing options in tactically rich opening positions.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they prioritize 'normal' opening principles (develop a piece, grab material on an obvious square) over concrete calculation. In each case, a forcing move—a check, a pawn push attacking a piece, a capture of a hanging pawn, or a knight fork—would win significant material or create a decisive advantage. Instead, the routine move not only misses this opportunity but frequently leaves a pawn undefended (66% of cases), giving the opponent counterplay and squandering the position's tactical potential.

analysis.label: Player captures a piece with Queen (giving check) but leaves the Queen hanging afterward, missing a stronger continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a Queen (or major piece) capture that delivers check, but the piece is left en prise once the check is resolved. The SEE aggregate shows 99% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a Queen), with 86% being captures and the hung-piece distribution overwhelmingly 'major' (425/500). Meanwhile, 82% of the time a better move existed that wins material (median value won: 3.0), with 43% of best moves being checks themselves (often devastating discovered checks, fork checks, or even checkmate like Rg1# in Position 2). The player is seduced by the immediate 'capture with check' pattern but fails to see the superior continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The Queen capture with check appears attractive because it wins material while forcing the opponent to respond. However, after the opponent deals with the check (typically by recapturing or interposing), the Queen is undefended and gets captured, resulting in a net loss of a Queen. Meanwhile, the player missed a stronger move—often a different check, a quiet winning move, or even checkmate—that would have preserved or increased their advantage without sacrificing the Queen.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture that leaves their own piece (often the captured square's occupant or an undefended piece) tactically vulnerable, when a non-capture move would have cleanly won material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a capture (95% of activations) that leaves their own piece hanging (92%, median value 3.0 — minor pieces most common at 116/234, then majors 66, pawns 52). Crucially, the best move also wins material in 87% of cases (median value 3.0) but is almost never a capture itself (only 11% are captures). The dominant pattern in the top activations is Black playing bxc6 to capture a White knight, opening the diagonal for White's Bb5 to recapture with devastating effect (Bxc6+ forking king and rook). The best moves in these positions were quiet queen retreats (Qd7, Qb6, Qg5) that both escape the knight's attack and maintain material advantage without opening any dangerous lines.
analysis.why_bad: The capture is reflexive — it removes an annoying piece but opens a critical line (usually a bishop diagonal) that the opponent immediately exploits. In the dominant bxc6 pattern, taking the knight with the b-pawn opens the a4-e8 diagonal for White's bishop on b5 to recapture Bxc6+, forking the king and rook on a8. The player wins a knight (3 points) but loses the exchange or more in return. A non-capture move (queen retreat) would have maintained material while keeping the position closed and safe.

analysis.label: Player missed a pawn advance that wins material (typically attacking a trapped or insufficiently defended enemy minor piece), instead playing a quiet non-critical move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of the time the best move wins material with a remarkably consistent median value of 2.0, yet only 12% of best moves are captures — meaning the winning resource is almost always a pawn advance that creates an irrefutable material threat. All 12 top-activating positions confirm this: the best move is invariably a pawn push (e4, e5, d5, b4, b5, g5) that attacks an enemy piece for a net gain of ~2 (a minor piece won minus the potential pawn cost). The player's move was a capture only 7% of the time, and own-piece hanging (25%, mostly pawns) is an occasional side-effect of the passive alternative chosen. Positions commonly feature closed or semi-closed centers where the key pawn break was the critical moment to seize the advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (piece repositioning, prophylactic pawn pushes, developing moves) waste a critical tempo in positions where a pawn advance immediately wins material by attacking an enemy piece that cannot adequately escape or be defended. The closed center masked the tactical urgency of the breakthrough, and the player chose positional maneuvering over the concrete pawn strike that would have netted approximately a minor piece.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet bishop (or minor piece) repositioning move instead of capturing hanging enemy material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 58% of positions have a best move that wins material (median 2.0 pawns), and 60% of best moves are captures, yet only 11% of played moves are captures. The player's own piece hanging rate is only 25%, confirming the dominant mistake is MISSING a winning capture rather than hanging their own piece. Examining the top 12 boards, 7 of 12 played moves are quiet bishop moves (Bf3, Bd3, Bg6, Be5, Bc1, Bf6) and the remainder are quiet knight/pawn moves—all natural-looking 'developing' or 'repositioning' moves that ignore concrete tactical opportunities to win material via capture (Nxe5, Qxc6, Qxd5, Bh6, etc.).
analysis.why_bad: These quiet bishop and minor piece moves prioritize abstract positional improvement (development, controlling diagonals, retreating to safety) while overlooking that an enemy piece is hanging or can be won by a simple capture. The player is 'playing chess' positionally when a concrete tactical shot wins material immediately.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture (or move) that leaves one of their own pieces undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (92% of top 500 positions, median value 3.0 = minor piece). The played move is itself a capture 65% of the time, suggesting the player grabs material greedily without noticing they expose their own piece. The hung piece class distribution (minor: 236, major: 129, pawn: 50) shows bishops and knights are most commonly left hanging, followed by rooks. While the best move does win material in 61% of cases (median 3.0), the critical signature is the own-piece hanging rate of 92%. The feature fires predominantly in openings (9/12 top boards) where development is incomplete and pieces lack mutual protection.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player focuses on the immediate gain (often capturing an advanced pawn like d6, or a seemingly free piece) without checking whether their own pieces remain protected after the move. The capturing piece itself often lands on a square where it lacks support (e.g., Bxd6 leaving the bishop en prise, Nxd4 leaving the knight undefended, Rxh2 leaving the rook trapped), or the move vacates a square that was defending another piece (e.g., bxc4 exposing a bishop, Ne7 abandoning rook defense). The result is a net material loss despite the apparent gain.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an undefended or inadequately defended enemy queen, instead making a less consequential move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'missed winning capture' pattern: 84% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 9.0 = queen), and 91% of best moves are captures. Only 27% of played moves were captures, showing the player chose something other than the winning capture. The enemy queen is typically hanging on squares like f5, f4, e5, or c7, capturable by the player's own queen or rook. The secondary stat of 57% own-piece-hanging (median value 2.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the inferior moves played sometimes additionally leave the player's own material loose, compounding the blunder. In 27% of cases the best capture also delivers check (e.g., Qxf5+), making the miss even more egregious.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a freely capturable enemy queen (worth ~9 points of material) in favor of lesser goals—grabbing a b2 pawn, making a pointless check, developing a piece, or making a quiet positional move. Missing a hanging queen typically converts a winning or already-won position into an equal or losing one, which is reflected in the enormous average centipawn loss of 3390.

analysis.label: In sparse endgame positions, the player makes a quiet move (often a king move or piece repositioning) that leaves their own piece undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates this feature detects positions where the player's move hangs their own piece: 76% of activating positions leave an own piece en prise (median value 3.0), with the hung piece being a minor piece (46 cases), major piece (34 cases), or pawn (15 cases). Additionally, 49% of positions have a best move that wins material (median 3.0), reflecting cases where the player also misses capturing a free enemy piece. Only 14% of played moves are captures, confirming the player consistently chooses quiet moves. The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (all 12 top boards) with exposed kings and minimal material, where piece coordination is paramount but the player breaks it with a careless move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in sparse endgame positions with few pieces, every piece's protection depends on precise coordination. By moving the king away from a defended piece (e.g., Ke6 abandoning a bishop, Ke2 abandoning a rook), moving a piece that was guarding another (Nb3 leaving a bishop), or placing a piece on an undefended square (Bd6+, Rh2), the player creates a free capture for the opponent. The better moves either maintain piece coordination, retreat the endangered piece itself, or simply capture the opponent's undefended material first.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting check (or flashy capture) that leaves their own piece undefended elsewhere on the board.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes an aggressive-looking move — overwhelmingly a check or capture — that leaves one of their own pieces hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 86% of played moves left the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 79% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 3.0). The best move is a check in 36% of cases and a capture in 29%, meaning superior forcing moves existed, but the player chose the wrong forcing move. The own-hang distribution (minor: 6, pawn: 4, major: 2) shows that minor pieces (bishops/knights) are most commonly left undefended. In the top-12 boards, 9 of 12 moves played are checks and the average cp_loss is 978, indicating catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The player is seduced by giving check or making a flashy capture ('patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check') without verifying that the move leaves another piece undefended. The check typically achieves nothing — the opponent's king simply moves to safety — and then the opponent collects the hanging piece. A better move (often a quiet consolidation, a different check, or a material-winning capture) was available that either protects the vulnerable piece or wins more than it costs.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive-looking queen or piece move to the h-file (Qh3/Qh4/Qh5/Qh6/xh3) while missing a stronger tactical continuation that wins decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 76% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0 pawns—often a queen or rook), yet the played move was only a capture 21% of the time, meaning players chose quiet aggressive-looking moves instead. The best move is a check 35% of the time and a capture 37%, indicating decisive tactical blows were available. Meanwhile, the played move left the player's own piece hanging 68% of the time (median value 2.0), with the hung pieces distributed across pawns (48), minors (36), and majors (30). The player becomes fixated on kingside/h-file aggression—nearly all top activating moves are queen or piece moves to h3/h4/h5/h6 or captures on h3—while missing winning checks, captures, or forks elsewhere on the board.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a visually aggressive h-file attacking continuation over objectively superior tactics. The 'attacking' queen placement or h-file capture typically doesn't create a genuine mating threat, while the ignored best move (often a discovered check, deflection, or simple capture of an undefended piece) wins decisive material immediately. Worse, the played move frequently leaves the player's own pieces unprotected (68% hung rate), meaning the opponent can counter-attack and turn the position around.

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the player moves the king in the wrong direction—retreating or drifting passively—instead of advancing toward critical squares.
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on king-and-pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king away from the optimal active square. The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material 47% of the time (median 1 pawn), indicating the correct king advance would attack or win an enemy pawn. Meanwhile, 28% of played moves leave the player's own pawn hanging (median value 1.0, with 16 pawns in the class distribution), because retreating the king abandons defense of the player's own pawns. Only 12% of played moves are captures and only 14% of best moves are captures, confirming the pattern is about king maneuvering rather than tactical exchanges. The consistently low cp_loss (avg 95) reflects the subtlety of king opposition and triangulation errors in pawn endgames.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king activity is paramount. By retreating or drifting sideways (e.g., Kc3 instead of Ke5, Ke2 instead of Ke4, Kd7 instead of Kd5), the player loses critical tempi needed to reach key squares, attack enemy pawns, or maintain opposition. This allows the opponent to advance passed pawns, win the king-activity race, or capture undefended pawns that the retreating king can no longer protect.

analysis.label: The player missed a checking move that wins the opponent's queen (or equivalent major material).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: in 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 98% of positions the best move wins material with a median value of 100 (queen-level). Only 15% of best moves are captures, meaning the check itself isn't capturing the queen but rather sets up a fork, skewer, or discovered attack that wins the queen on the subsequent move. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (77% non-captures) — the player simply failed to notice the tactical check. The 49% own-hang rate (median value 1, mostly pawns) is incidental, not the core mistake. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, consistent with a specific tactical motif requiring a checking piece to simultaneously threaten the king and queen.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a forcing check (rook, knight, or bishop) that would either fork the king and queen, create a skewer, or set up an unavoidable discovered attack on the queen. By playing a quiet or non-forcing move instead, the player forfeits winning the opponent's queen — typically a game-decisive material gain (median ~9 pawns worth). Many of these missed opportunities turn winning or equal positions into losses.

analysis.label: Player makes a move (often a panicked king retreat or misguided queen move) that leaves their own queen or rook en prise in a tactically critical position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 72% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to queen/rook material), with the hung piece class distribution dominated by major pieces (98 major vs 29 minor, 43 pawn). Only 24% of the played moves were captures, meaning most blunders were quiet moves. The best move won material in 59% of cases (median 3.0), often because the correct defense involved a tactical counter or exchange that the player missed. The feature fires on positions where the player's king is typically exposed or under attack, and instead of finding the precise defensive resource, the player makes a reflexive king move (Kc6, Ke6, Kh1, Kg3, Kd7, Kh8) or an ill-considered queen move (Qa8+, Qxd3, Qxe3, Qd6, Qg5, Qc7) that fatally leaves their own major piece undefended—often resulting in immediate mate or decisive material loss (avg cp_loss: 7161).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in tactically critical positions with an exposed king, the player ignores the opponent's concrete threats. King moves often remove a defender from the queen or allow discovered attacks/forks, while queen moves to unsafe squares leave the queen capturable. The correct move typically involved a precise tactical defense (recapture, exchange, or interposition) that addressed the immediate danger while keeping major pieces defended.

analysis.label: Player misses a forced checkmate or overwhelming material win in a dominant position, instead playing an inferior move that often hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a devastating best move is available — 79% of the time winning material with a median value of 9.0 (queen-level or checkmate), and 48% of best moves being checks (frequently delivering immediate mate). Instead, the player plays a weaker move that 57% of the time leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns, minors, and majors). Only 25% of played moves are captures, indicating the player typically ignores the tactical opportunity entirely. The average cp_loss of 3344 confirms these are catastrophic blunders — winning positions converted to losses or draws. The feature fires on just 1.2% of positions, consistent with the rarity of having an overwhelming tactic available yet completely missing it.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a forced checkmate or game-deciding material gain (often a simple one-move mate like Ra1#, Qh1#, Rdf7#, or a queen capture) and instead plays a casual or thematic-looking move (doubling rooks, making a non-mating check, capturing an irrelevant pawn, or developing a piece). The played moves frequently compound the error by leaving the player's own pieces unprotected, turning a completely won position into an equal or lost one.

analysis.label: Player captures material with check (usually with the queen), but the checking piece is trapped and lost after the opponent responds.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., the queen), while 68% of moves are captures. The own-hang piece class is overwhelmingly 'major' (60 out of 80 cases). In the top 12 boards, 10 of 12 moves are captures with check (Qxe1+, Qxf7+, Qxh2+, Nxf3+, Nxc2+, etc.), revealing a consistent pattern: the player grabs material while delivering check, believing the tempo advantage protects them, but the capturing piece—almost always the queen—is subsequently trapped or recaptured. The median cp_loss of 477 reflects the catastrophic cost of losing the queen for a rook or pawn. Many positions arise in the opening (8/12) with kings still in center, and several involve classic Scholar's Mate-style Qxf7+ attempts where the queen is lost after the king escapes.
analysis.why_bad: The check creates an illusion of safety—the player assumes they gain a free tempo to escape. But after the opponent blocks or moves their king, the capturing piece (usually the queen) has no safe retreat square and is captured. The player trades their queen for a rook, pawn, or minor piece, resulting in massive material loss despite the initial appearance of winning material with tempo.

analysis.label: Player gives an aimless rook check in a winning endgame instead of making the decisive quiet move (king advance or pawn push).
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, every played move is a rook check in an endgame, yet the best move is a check only 3% of the time—revealing these checks accomplish nothing. The best move wins material 45% of the time (median 1.0, typically winning a pawn via promotion threats or captures enabled by quiet moves), while the player's check was itself a capture only 6% of the time. Furthermore, 43% of the time the rook check leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0; distribution: 50 pawns, 7 major, 4 minor), because relocating the rook to deliver a meaningless check abandons defense of key pawns. The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet—king marches (Kf6, Kb6, Kd4, Ke1, Kf4, Kg6), pawn pushes (g6, e3, d3, b5), or piece repositioning (Bf5)—that make concrete progress toward promotion or material gain.
analysis.why_bad: These rook checks are the classic 'patzer check'—they force the opponent's king to a square it often wanted to go anyway, waste a critical tempo in a position where quiet progress (advancing passed pawns, centralizing the king) was decisive, and frequently displace the rook to a worse square while leaving pawns undefended. The opponent simply sidesteps the check and the attacker's winning advantage evaporates or is significantly reduced (average cp_loss: 2451).

analysis.label: In critical rook endgames, the player chooses a passive or retreating move instead of maintaining maximum rook activity (distant checks, open files, or behind passed pawns).
analysis.description: This feature fires on rook endgame positions where the player makes a catastrophic passive move (avg cp_loss 4295). The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material in 33% of cases (median value 5.0, often reflecting promotion threats), while only 21% of played moves hang own material—indicating the core mistake isn't about hanging pieces but about choosing passivity in positions demanding active play. Only 11% of played moves are captures and best moves are checks only 13% of the time, confirming this is about positional rook placement rather than tactical oversights. Across all 12 top-activating positions (100% endgame), the best move almost always places the rook on a maximally active square (Ra1, Ra8, Rh2+, Ra3+) to maintain checking distance, control open files, or stay behind passed pawns, while the blunder is typically a king retreat or a rook move to a passive square.
analysis.why_bad: In rook endgames, rook activity is often the decisive factor between winning/drawing and losing. These passive moves (king retreats like Kg1/Ka8/Kh5, or rook placements to blocked files) surrender initiative, allow opponent's passed pawns to advance unopposed, permit the enemy king to infiltrate, or forfeit stalemate/perpetual check resources. The resulting positions collapse immediately because the defender no longer has the checking distance or file control needed to hold.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free enemy piece that can be captured in one move, instead playing a quiet or irrelevant move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 93% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a minor piece or rook), and 95% of the time that best move is a simple capture. Yet the player's move was a capture only 19% of the time — overwhelmingly they played quiet, non-capturing moves while a major enemy piece sat en prise. The top boards confirm this: Bxe7, Kxf1, Bxd2, Qxe7, Rxd2, Nxd7, etc. are all one-move captures of undefended enemy pieces that the player completely overlooks. The secondary 66% own-hang stat (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the quiet moves played sometimes leave the player's own pawns loose, compounding the error, but the primary mistake is failing to take the free enemy piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are terrible because the player passes up a free piece worth approximately a rook or minor piece (median 5.0 pawns of material). Instead of a trivially winning capture, they play a quiet developing or regrouping move that accomplishes nothing comparable to gaining a full piece of material, often turning a won position into an equal or lost one (average cp_loss: 370).

analysis.label: Player fails to promote a pawn to a queen, either underpromotion to a knight or neglecting promotion entirely in a won endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 83% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 91, i.e., queen-level), yet the best move is NEVER a capture (0%) and is a check 50% of the time — a signature consistent with queen promotions giving check. The player's move was a capture only 17% of the time and left own material hanging only 17% of the time, confirming the mistake direction is missed winning material rather than hanging one's own piece. All 6 top positions are endgames (avg cp_loss 3547), and the top three strongest activations explicitly show the player underpromoting to a knight (c8=N, g1=N) or moving the king (Kb8) instead of promoting to a queen. The remaining positions involve failing to execute the correct winning technique to achieve or capitalize on promotion.
analysis.why_bad: Promoting to a knight instead of a queen squanders overwhelming material advantage (a queen is worth ~9 pawns vs. 3 for a knight). In positions 1-3, the queen promotion either delivers immediate checkmate sequences or creates an easily winning Q vs. lone-king endgame, while the knight promotion or king move throws away the entire win, turning decisive advantages into draws or even losses.

analysis.label: Player makes a piece move (knight, bishop, queen, or king) instead of a critical pawn advance or pawn break that was required by the position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material only 25% of the time (median 1.0) and is a capture only 8% of the time, confirming the best move is typically a quiet pawn advance rather than a tactical capture. The player's move left their own piece hanging 40% of the time (median value 1.0, distribution: 64 pawns, 50 minors, 17 majors), indicating that the misplaced piece frequently ends up en prise. In 11 of the top 12 boards, the best move is a pawn push (f4, e5, a4, d6, gxf5, e4, h5, c5, h4, d5, d5, c5) while the played move is invariably a piece relocation (Na6, Qd2, Be7, Ne4, Ba6, Ne5, Nb5, Kb8, Ba8). These occur predominantly in the opening (8/12), where the player prioritizes piece repositioning over the structurally critical pawn advance.
analysis.why_bad: The piece moves ignore a time-sensitive pawn break that would seize space, open lines, or create threats. Instead of exploiting the concrete pawn advance, the player repositions a piece to a square that is often suboptimal or tactically vulnerable—knights go to the rim (Na6, Nb5), bishops drift passively (Be7, Ba8, Ba6), and the misplaced pieces frequently become hanging targets because the opponent can exploit the tempo gained from attacking them.

analysis.label: The player missed an immediately available pawn promotion (usually to a queen), playing a different move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 59% of cases with a median value of 91 (consistent with gaining a queen via promotion). The best move is a check 36% of the time, matching promotions with check. The player's move was only a capture 23% of the time, meaning they typically played quiet or irrelevant moves instead of promoting. Across the top 12 boards, 10 out of 12 positions feature a pawn on the 7th (or 2nd) rank with an immediately available promotion (c1=Q+, g8=Q, a8=Q, c8=Q+, b1=Q, e8=Q+), yet the player chose king moves, piece moves, or captures elsewhere. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12), the phase where promotion races are most critical. The average cp_loss of 3918 reflects the catastrophic nature of missing a promotion that often delivers forced mate.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because promoting a pawn to a queen is almost always the most urgent priority when available—it creates an overwhelming material advantage or delivers checkmate. By playing any other move (king shuffles, captures of lesser pieces, positional moves), the player allows the opponent time to blockade, capture the pawn, or counter-promote, squandering a won position that was often a forced mate.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive King move when an active Queen move (often a check or winning threat) is available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 32% of best moves are checks and 32% win material (median value: 100cp/pawn), while the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet King moves (10% captures, 10% hang own piece — both low). The best moves across the top 12 positions are almost exclusively Queen moves (Qh2, Qg5, Qe7, Qg2, Qg7, Qd7, Qc6+, Qh5+, Qh7, etc.), yet the player consistently chooses King moves (Kf3, Kf7, Kc6, Ke3, Ke6, Kf6, Kf4, Kd8, Ke8). The feature fires on only 0.0% of all positions, indicating a specific pattern of Queen-available positions where the player defaults to King shuffling.
analysis.why_bad: Moving the King passively when the Queen can deliver checks, create mating threats, or win material squanders the Queen's dominant power. The King moves achieve nothing active while the Queen moves (32% of which are checks) generate immediate threats or win pawns/pieces.

analysis.label: Player fails to make a critical pawn capture (exf6, dxc6, exd6, etc.) when the opponent challenges their pawn chain, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 98% of cases, yet these captures win 0 material (even pawn exchanges). The played moves are quiet (only 12% captures), and 41% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0; 76 pawns, 30 minors, 1 major). All 12 top-activating positions share the same structure: the best move is a pawn-takes-pawn capture (exf6 in 7/12, dxc6 in 2/12, exf3 in 2/12, dxe6 in 1/12) resolving tension created when the opponent challenges an advanced or central pawn. Instead of capturing, the player plays a passive developing or repositioning move, typically in closed-center positions (French Defense, King's Indian, Pirc structures).
analysis.why_bad: By declining the critical pawn capture, the player allows the opponent to either win the challenged pawn outright (explaining the 41% own-pawn-hanging rate) or favorably resolve the tension themselves on the next move. The exf6/dxc6-type captures are often tactically forced because the advanced pawn is only defended by the capture itself — ignoring the challenge cedes material or structural advantage, resulting in an average 216 cp loss.

analysis.label: Player fails to take a mandatory rook capture on a contested open file, leaving their own rook hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture in 98% of cases (almost always a rook capture on an open file like Rxe8, Rxf8, Rxd8, Rxh1, etc.), while only 13% of played moves were captures. In 54% of positions the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the piece class heavily skewed toward majors (43 of 73 hung pieces). The position features consistently show opposing rooks on the same open file (e-file, d-file, f-file, g-file, or h-file). Instead of taking the exchange or trading rooks, the player makes a quiet rook move (or other piece move) elsewhere, which leaves their own rook undefended and capturable.
analysis.why_bad: When opposing rooks face each other on an open file, the capture is often forced or mandatory — declining it means your opponent simply takes your rook for free on the next move. By moving a rook elsewhere (Rb5, Rd4, Rf7, Rc5, etc.) or playing an unrelated piece (Nc7, Ng3, a5), the player abandons the critical file and leaves their rook en prise with no compensation, typically losing a full exchange or rook (~5 points).

analysis.label: In rook endgames with passed pawns, the player makes a passive king move or pawn push instead of finding a critical tactical rook move that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 84% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), yet the player's move was a capture only 6% of the time, indicating they consistently chose quiet, non-forcing moves. The best move is a check 27% of the time and a capture 13% of the time — both hallmarks of active rook tactics. Only 27% of played moves left own material hanging (median just 1.0), confirming the mistake direction is overwhelmingly about MISSING winning opportunities rather than blundering material. Across all 12 top-activating positions, the pattern is strikingly uniform: rook endgames with advanced passed pawns where the best move is always a rook maneuver (Rg8+, Rc1+, Rg1+, Ra1, Re8, Rh1, etc.) that exploits geometry — checks, deflections, or attacks on key pawns — while the player instead makes a slow king move (Kh7, Kd3, Kf8, Kd4, Kg6, Kg3, Kc8) or a quiet pawn push (h4, d2, b2, f4).
analysis.why_bad: The passive king moves and pawn pushes fail because they surrender the initiative in positions where tempo is critical. The rook moves exploit tactical geometry — often checking the enemy king to deflect it from defending key squares, or attacking undefended pawns/pieces — creating immediate material gains or decisive promotion threats. By playing slowly, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, coordinate defenses, or advance their own passed pawns in what are essentially pawn-race positions where one active rook move decides the game.

analysis.label: Player plays a tempting check or active-looking move that leaves their own piece (usually a minor piece) hanging and undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 86% of positions show the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece distribution heavily skewed toward minors (53 minor, 22 major, 20 pawn out of 95 cases). While 59% of positions had material available to win via the best move (median 3.0), the critical signature is the self-inflicted hanging. Only 29% of played moves were captures, meaning most were quiet moves or checks that simply left the active piece unprotected. The top boards reveal the typical geometry: the player gives check with a bishop or knight (Be5+, Bf3+, Be4+, Ne7+, Bxf7+) or makes a greedy capture (Bxg7, Bxf6, Rxf2, Qxb1+), but the piece lands on a square where it has no defender and the opponent can simply capture it next move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is seduced by the immediate 'activity' of giving check or capturing material, without verifying that their piece will be safe after the opponent's forced reply. The check forces nothing meaningful—the opponent simply moves their king to safety and then captures the undefended checking piece, netting a free minor piece (or worse). The player trades a tactical illusion for a real material deficit, often converting a playable or even winning position into a lost one (average cp_loss: 980).

analysis.label: Player ignores a necessary equal trade (usually between major pieces facing each other on an open file) and instead makes a quiet king move, leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture 100% of the time but wins 0 material in 91% of cases (meaning it's an equal exchange). Meanwhile, the player's move left their own piece hanging 66% of the time with a median value of 5.0 (major pieces: 26 out of 44 hung pieces). Only 19% of played moves were captures. The pattern is unmistakable: two major pieces (typically queens or rooks) face each other on an open file in mutual attack. The correct move is to take the trade (Qxd6, Qxf4, Rxd4, etc.), but the player instead makes a quiet king move (10 of 12 top boards show king moves), ignoring the immediate threat to their own piece and leaving it en prise. The 21% check rate for best moves reflects cases where the exchange also delivers check.
analysis.why_bad: When two equal pieces mutually attack each other, declining the exchange without relocating your own piece leaves it hanging. The opponent simply captures for free on the next move, gaining a full major piece (often a queen worth 9 points). The king moves provide no compensation—they neither escape threats nor create counterplay—and result in catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss of 3354).

analysis.label: The player had a decisively won position (often forced mate) and played a passive or aimless move that dissipated the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player holds a forced mate or overwhelming advantage but plays the wrong quiet move, throwing the win away. The SEE aggregate shows 48% of played moves left own material hanging (mostly pawns, median value 1.0), which is a symptom rather than the cause — when you abandon a mating attack, pieces left en prise for tactical reasons become genuine liabilities. Best moves win material only 43% of the time (median 1.0) and are checks only 3%, indicating the correct continuations are typically quiet positional squeezes (king marches, rook lifts, pawn advances) that maintain an inescapable net. The enormous average cp_loss of 5706 confirms these aren't small inaccuracies but catastrophic failures to convert won positions.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves look plausible but fail because they release pressure on the opponent's king or allow defensive resources. Instead of playing the one precise move that maintains the mating net or decisive zugzwang (e.g., Kc3/Kd3 centralizing, f6/g6 cutting off escape squares, Rf3/Rg5 delivering the killing blow), the player makes a natural-looking but non-critical move that gives the opponent time to escape or consolidate.

analysis.label: Player missed a check (queen or rook) that skewers the opponent's king and queen, winning decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 91% of best moves are checks and 96% win material with a median value of 100 (queen-equivalent), yet only 11% of best moves are captures — meaning the material is won not by direct capture but through a forcing check that creates a skewer or fork on the next move. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames with exposed kings on both sides, where a well-placed check along a rank, file, or diagonal simultaneously attacks the king and lines up a skewer against the opponent's queen. Players instead chose various alternatives (43% captures, often grabbing a pawn like Qxh4 or Qxh2, or quiet moves like Kf3, g4, Kb1) that squandered the tactical opportunity. The 48% own-hang rate (median value 1, mostly pawns) reflects that many of the suboptimal captures or pawn pushes inadvertently left a pawn loose, compounding the mistake.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing check that geometrically skewers the opponent's king and queen. By playing a pawn capture, a quiet king move, or a non-forcing queen move instead, the player gives up the chance to win the opponent's queen (or equivalent major material) through a simple two-move tactical sequence: check, then capture the now-undefended queen.

analysis.label: The player makes a quiet non-queen move (or misplaces the queen) when the queen had a powerful centralizing, capturing, or defensive move available.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a strong Queen deployment but the player moves a different piece instead. The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material in 52% of cases (median 1.0 pawn), best move is a capture 26% of the time, and the played move was only a capture 20% of the time. The player's move left their own piece hanging 40% of the time (median value 1.0, distributed across pawns 116, majors 42, minors 42), indicating that by ignoring the Queen's potential, the position deteriorates. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is invariably a Queen move (Qc4, Qe5, Qg5, Qxd4, Qxe5, Qe6, Qe7, Qc5, Qxf5, Qd5), while the played moves are quiet moves with other pieces—often Knights to the very same square the Queen should have gone (Ne6 instead of Qe6, Ne7 instead of Qe7, Nge6 instead of Qe6), or passive King/pawn/Rook moves.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the Queen's unique power to simultaneously attack, defend, and centralize with maximum force. By moving a lesser piece (or the Queen to the wrong square), the player forfeits winning material, misses tactical opportunities, or allows their position to collapse—as evidenced by the average cp_loss of 1067. In several cases (positions 7, 8, 10), the knight occupies the same square the Queen should have, gaining far less impact while the Queen's absence leaves critical tasks unaddressed.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet move (often a king move) instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of best moves win material (median value 5.0 — typically a rook or higher), yet only 19% of the played moves were captures. The best move is a direct capture 62% of the time, confirming the player consistently overlooked freely takeable pieces. Only 25% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging, ruling out 'hung own piece' as the primary pattern. The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (12/12 boards) where simplified material makes the hanging piece conspicuous — kings that can step onto an undefended bishop or knight, knights that can take an unprotected rook or queen, bishops that can capture an unguarded rook — yet the player chose a non-capturing king maneuver or passive piece retreat instead.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a free piece sitting en prise. Instead of a trivial one-move capture worth 3–9 points of material, they play a quiet positional move (king walk, pawn push, or retreat), immediately losing the game by forfeiting decisive material advantage or allowing forced mate that the capture would have prevented.

analysis.label: Player jumps a knight aggressively to a central/forward outpost (e5, f5, d4) when the move is tactically flawed or misses a stronger continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes an aggressive-looking knight leap—almost exclusively to the squares e5, f5, or d4—that is actually a mistake. The SEE aggregate shows that in 47% of the top 500 positions the best move wins material (median value 2.0), meaning the knight jump ignores a superior tactical opportunity. In 37% of cases the played move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being a minor (the knight itself) in 114 of 187 hang instances. Only 9% of the played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet knight jumps rather than recaptures. The best move is a check only 5% of the time, and the feature fires on just 1.5% of positions, indicating a specific pattern of overaggressive knight centralization.
analysis.why_bad: The knight jump to an 'outpost' square looks active and tempting but is tactically unsound—the knight is often capturable at its destination (hanging a minor piece for nothing), or the move wastes tempo when a concrete winning move (a capture worth ~2 pawns or a positionally superior regrouping move) was available. The player is seduced by the visual appeal of the knight on e5/f5/d4 rather than calculating whether the square is truly safe or whether the position demands something else entirely.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture the opponent's undefended queen, instead playing a quiet or irrelevant move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player missed winning the enemy queen: 99% of positions have a best move that wins material with a median value of 9.0 (queen value), and 99% of best moves are captures. Yet only 18% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves (often king moves like Kc3, Kg1, Kc2, Kb1, Kd8) instead of taking a free queen. The boards confirm this: Bxb4 captures a queen on b4, Nxe7 captures a queen on e7, Qxa5 captures a queen on a5, Qxh4 captures an undefended queen on h4, Qxe2 captures a queen on e2, etc. The 58% own-hung rate (median value 5.0) is a secondary effect — some of the quiet moves also blundered pieces — but the primary and consistent mistake is ignoring the opponent's completely undefended queen.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a trivially available queen capture (worth ~9 points of material) and instead plays a purposeless quiet move. This squanders a winning or decisive advantage, as shown by the average cp_loss of 2166 and multiple missed forced mates. The opponent's queen was left en prise — undefended and directly capturable — yet the player moved elsewhere, sometimes even losing the game as a result.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning knight capture on a central square (e4/e5/d4/d5) in the opening, instead playing a quiet developing move.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a knight capture on a central square (Nxe5, Nxd4, Nxe4, or Nxd5) that the player ignores in favor of a routine developing move. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 95% of the time and wins material in 40% of positions (median value 3.0, a minor piece). The player's move is almost never a capture (only 14%), and instead consists of quiet moves like Be2, O-O, or h3. In 35% of cases the quiet move additionally leaves the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0, predominantly minors at 39/64). Many positions involve a Bg4 pin on Nf3, making the knight appear immobile—but the Nxe5 capture actually works tactically despite the apparent pin, winning material through discovered attacks or favorable exchanges. The feature occurs almost exclusively in the opening (11/12 top positions).
analysis.why_bad: The player treats the position as a normal development situation and plays routine moves (especially Be2 to break a pin passively, or h3/O-O), failing to calculate that a concrete knight capture on a central square wins material immediately. In pin situations (Bg4 pinning Nf3), the player assumes the knight cannot move, but the capture actually refutes the opponent's setup—often because taking the knight leads to a discovered attack on the pinning bishop, or the recapture sequence nets material. By playing a quiet move, the player squanders a ~400-600 centipawn advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy minor piece (bishop or knight) that can be simply captured, instead playing a quiet non-capturing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 90% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, exactly a minor piece), and 98% of the time the best move is a capture. Yet the player's move was a capture only 15% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly played quiet moves while a free bishop or knight sat en prise. Across the top 12 boards, the best move is consistently a straightforward capture of an undefended minor piece — often by a pawn (exd5, dxc6, exf5, gxh6, dxc3, bxc3, axb5, fxe5) but sometimes by a queen or other piece. The 54% own-hang-after rate is a secondary consequence: by playing a quiet move instead of the winning capture, the player sometimes also leaves their own material vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player completely overlooks a free minor piece (worth ~3 pawns) sitting undefended on the board. Instead of the trivial winning capture, they play a developmental or positional move that ignores the immediate tactical gift, resulting in an average cp_loss of 408. The opponent's piece was genuinely hanging with no compensation or trick — the player simply didn't see it.

analysis.label: Player ignores a forcing rook exchange (often with back-rank check) and instead makes a non-forcing move that frequently hangs material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a strikingly consistent pattern: the best move is a capture 99% of the time and a check 66% of the time, yet it 'wins 0' material (only 2% win material via SEE), indicating the best move is an equal rook-for-rook exchange — typically on the back rank with check (Rxf8+, Rxe8+, Rxd8+, Rxd1+, Rxe1+, Rxg8+, etc.). Instead of playing this forcing simplification, the player makes a quiet or irrelevant move, and 54% of the time leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 pawns; piece distribution: 135 major, 84 pawn, 51 minor). All 12 top-activating positions feature opposing rooks on the same open file with the best move being a rook exchange. The player's moves (Bg5, Re4, Qd2, e4, Ba3, Qg4, Bg4, e6, etc.) are overwhelmingly non-forcing and ignore the critical file tension.
analysis.why_bad: The forcing rook exchange with check seizes the initiative, simplifies favorably (gaining tempo or exploiting back-rank geometry), and denies the opponent counterplay. By ignoring this exchange, the player loses the forcing sequence, often leaves their own pieces unprotected on the now-contested file or elsewhere, and allows the opponent to exploit the remaining rook's activity. The resulting position swings dramatically (avg 133cp loss) because the opponent retains threats the exchange would have neutralized.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move instead of capturing a free central pawn via favorable pawn tension resolution.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 65% of the time (median value: 1 pawn), the best move is a capture in 84% of cases, yet the player's move is a capture only 7% of the time. The player's move also leaves their own piece hanging 49% of the time (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 125/168). All top-12 positions feature a concrete central pawn capture (fxe5, cxd5, dxe5, or dxe4) that nets a pawn because the opponent cannot recapture effectively, but the player instead makes a routine quiet developing move (Nf3, Nc3, Be2, a3, h3, Bf4, etc.). The 49% self-hang rate occurs because by declining the capture, the player's own advanced pawn (f4, c4, d4) — the very pawn that should have captured — often becomes a target itself.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet developing moves fail because the position demands concrete action: a central pawn is genuinely free to capture (the opponent's structure or piece placement prevents proper recapture, often due to fork tricks like e4 hitting Bf5/Nc6 after cxd5). By playing a routine development move, the player loses a full pawn of advantage (~270cp average loss) and often leaves their own capturing pawn vulnerable, giving the opponent time to resolve the tension favorably.

analysis.label: Player captures a pawn/piece with check using a rook or queen, but the capturing piece is left hanging after the king moves away.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the played moves are captures and 85% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook). The hung-piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (36 out of 45). All 12 top-activating boards show the same geometry: a rook or queen captures material with check (Rxb3+, Rxc3+, Rxg7+, Qxa7+, etc.), but after the opponent's king escapes the check, the capturing piece sits undefended on its new square. The best moves (only 9% are captures, 19% are checks) are typically quiet advancing or repositioning moves that maintain the player's winning advantage without sacrificing a major piece. The average cp_loss of 1653 confirms these are often catastrophic—players throw away forced mates or decisive advantages by grabbing a pawn with check instead of playing a clean winning continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The capture-with-check feels forcing and 'free,' but the king simply sidesteps, and now the opponent can recapture the undefended rook/queen on its new square. The player trades a dominant major piece for a worthless pawn, converting a won position into a draw or loss. The check creates an illusion of gaining tempo, but it actually loses tempo because the piece sacrifice gives the opponent material back with interest.

analysis.label: Player ignores or actively opens a diagonal where an enemy bishop attacks their queen, leaving the queen en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 6.0 = queen, piece class 'major': 70), while the best move wins material 85% of the time (median value 3.0 = bishop). In every top-activating position, an enemy bishop sits on a diagonal aimed at the player's queen (Bg5 targeting Qd8 via g5-f6-e7-d8, or Bg4 targeting Qd1 via g4-f3-e2-d1). The player either ignores this direct threat by making an unrelated developing move (Nc6, d5, Nd2, c3) or actively opens the critical diagonal by moving a blocking pawn (e6 moving the e7-pawn off the diagonal, e5 clearing the path). The best move would block the diagonal (Be7, Be2, f3, f6), capture the attacking bishop (Qxg5), or kick it (h6) — all saving or winning roughly a minor piece's worth of material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the queen completely undefended on a diagonal where an enemy bishop has a clear line of attack. By ignoring the threat or removing the only blocking piece, the player allows the opponent to simply capture the queen (worth ~9 points) for a bishop (worth ~3 points), resulting in catastrophic material loss of approximately 6 points — matching the median hung value in the aggregate.

analysis.label: Player moves a minor piece to an attractive-looking square (or captures a peripheral target) instead of the concrete best move, often leaving major pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a tempting minor piece relocation or capture that is tactically unsound. The SEE aggregate shows 61% of positions had winning material available (median 2.0 pawns) via the best move, while the played move left the player's own piece hanging 45% of the time (median value 3.0, with majors comprising the plurality at 52 instances). Only 27% of played moves were captures, meaning most were quiet piece moves to 'active' squares. The piece class hung is overwhelmingly major pieces (rooks/queens), suggesting the relocated minor piece was defending something critical. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions with catastrophic average cp_loss of 986.
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece either abandons a defensive duty (leaving a rook or queen en prise) or grabs a low-value peripheral target while a much stronger tactical shot exists. The player prioritizes piece aesthetics—outposts, active diagonals, edge captures—over concrete calculation, resulting in material disaster.

analysis.label: Player declines a strategically critical bishop exchange (Bx-something), playing a quiet move instead and losing the window for the favorable trade.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals the pattern with extreme clarity: the best move is a capture in 100% of cases, yet the best move wins material only 2% of the time (SEE = 0 in nearly every case, indicating an equal exchange). The player's move is a capture only 4% of the time, meaning they almost always play a quiet move instead. In 37% of positions, the quiet move actually leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, mostly minor pieces: 102 minor, 55 pawns, 29 major). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is invariably a bishop trade — Bxc3, Bxd5, Bxd3, Bxf3, Bxg6, Bxb3, Bxc5 — where the bishop has a time-sensitive exchange that resolves strategic tension favorably (e.g., doubling pawns in the Nimzo-Indian, eliminating a strong piece, or resolving diagonal pressure). The player instead retreats, repositions, or develops, missing the narrow window.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the bishop exchange was tactically or strategically time-sensitive. By declining the trade, the player either: (1) loses the opportunity entirely as the opponent repositions to avoid the exchange, (2) leaves pieces misplaced or hanging on inferior squares (37% hang own piece), or (3) allows the opponent to consolidate a structural or positional advantage that the exchange would have prevented. The average cp_loss of 273 reflects how costly missing these windows is.

analysis.label: Player develops or leaves a bishop on a square directly attacked by an enemy pawn, ignoring central pawn tension that should be resolved first.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = bishop), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 82/86 classified cases. The best move is a capture 84% of the time (typically resolving central pawn tension), winning material in 57% of cases (median 1.0 = one pawn). The played move is almost never a capture itself (only 4%). Across the top 12 positions—all in the opening phase—the player either places a bishop on a square directly controlled by an enemy pawn (e.g., Bc4 into a d5 pawn, Bf4 into an e5 pawn, Bf5 where Nh4 or exd5 exploits it), or ignores that their bishop is already attacked by an advancing enemy pawn, choosing passive development instead of addressing the threat.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the bishop is placed on (or left on) a square where an enemy pawn can simply capture it for free, resulting in the immediate loss of a minor piece (~3 pawns of material). The correct move was almost always to resolve the central pawn tension by capturing (exd5, dxe5, dxe4, Nxe5, Bxe5, etc.), which either eliminates the attacking pawn or wins material outright. By developing while ignoring the pawn's attack, the player loses a piece for nothing.

analysis.label: Player grabs material with a capture or quiet move instead of delivering a forced checkmate or decisive check-based attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 79% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, often representing mate or queen-winning), and 39% of best moves are checks — typically initiating a forced mating sequence. Yet the player's actual move is a capture 41% of the time (grabbing a lesser piece or pawn) while only 15% of played moves leave own material hanging. The enormous average cp_loss of 2356 confirms these are positions where forced checkmate (SEE value 100) or queen-winning tactics existed, but the player opted for materialistic grabs (Qxc6, Qxa4, Qxc2, Qxe5, hxg4, Qxh5) instead of the knockout blow. Positions consistently feature exposed enemy kings and open lines that enable forcing continuations.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize winning a pawn or minor piece over delivering forced checkmate or winning far more material through a tactical sequence (usually starting with a check). The greedy capture allows the opponent's king to escape the mating net, converting a forced mate into merely a large advantage — or sometimes squandering the win entirely.

analysis.label: Player missed capturing an undefended or en prise enemy queen (or equivalent major piece), often distracted by a lesser capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material in 100% of the top 500 positions with a median value of 6.0 (queen/major-piece level), and the best move is a capture 71% of the time (with 24% being checks that win material). Despite this massive winning opportunity, the player's move was itself a capture only 59% of the time—meaning they often took a lesser piece or made a quiet move instead of claiming the big prize. In 88% of cases the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), compounding the blunder. The average cp_loss of 2702 reflects that these missed captures are catastrophic, frequently turning winning or equal positions into immediate losses or mates.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is capturing a lesser target (e.g., a pawn on a4, a rook on h1, a pawn on e6) or making a positional move while ignoring that an enemy queen or major piece is directly capturable. The played move wastes the decisive tactical opportunity and often exposes the player's own pieces, turning a winning position into a losing one.

analysis.label: The player captures a pawn or piece with a rook (or occasionally bishop), but the capturing piece lands on an undefended square where it is immediately en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of the played moves are captures and 82% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the hung piece class being 'major' in 53 of 67 cases. Only 15% of best moves are captures themselves, meaning the correct approach was typically a quiet retreating or repositioning move rather than grabbing material. The best move wins material in 52% of cases (median 3.0), indicating the player often missed a superior way to win material without self-harm. The feature fires overwhelmingly in endgames (10/12 top boards) where a rook greedily takes a pawn or minor piece but is left unprotected on the landing square.
analysis.why_bad: The rook captures low-value material (a pawn or minor piece) but lands on a square where it has no defender and can be immediately recaptured or trapped by the opponent. This results in a catastrophic net material loss—typically trading a rook (5 points) for a pawn (1 point) or minor piece (3 points)—often converting a close or even drawn position into a hopeless loss, as shown by the average cp_loss of 2417.

analysis.label: The player captures a pawn or piece with their rook (or knight), but the capturing piece lands on an undefended square where it is immediately en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a tempting capture that leaves their own piece hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 100% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (137 major vs. 46 minor). The player's move was itself a capture 66% of the time, confirming the pattern of a greedy capture that backfires. Only 10% of best moves are captures, indicating the correct continuation typically involves non-capturing alternatives (repositioning, prophylaxis, or king moves). The feature fires in 0.1% of positions, mostly in endgames (11/12 top boards), where rooks are highly active but vulnerable on open files and ranks without adequate support.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece (almost always a rook) lands on a square where it has no defender and can be recaptured or won by the opponent's pieces. The player wins a pawn or minor piece (median SEE of best move: 1.0) but loses a rook (value 5), resulting in catastrophic net material loss. The player is lured by the immediate material gain of the capture while failing to check whether their piece survives on the destination square. The average cp_loss of 1787 reflects that many of these also miss checkmates or decisive advantages.

analysis.label: Player moves a rook onto a file (or square) already controlled by the opponent's heavy pieces, leaving the rook en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 86% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (148 major vs 28 minor vs 28 pawn). The played move is rarely a capture itself (only 21%), confirming these are quiet rook repositioning moves. In nearly every top-activating position, the player moves a rook onto an open or semi-open file where the opponent already has a queen-and-rook battery or superior heavy-piece presence (e.g., Rc8 into a White-controlled c-file, Rd8 into a White Queen+Rook d-file, Rfe1 into a Black Queen+Rook e-file). The best move wins material only 51% of the time, meaning the alternative was often simply a safe move that avoids the catastrophic hang.
analysis.why_bad: These rook moves place the rook on a square where it lacks sufficient defensive support while the opponent's heavy pieces (typically a queen + rook already aligned on that file) can immediately capture it. The player misjudges file control—contesting an enemy-dominated file without adequate backup results in an outright loss of the rook (or worse, allows a devastating tactical sequence exploiting the undefended piece).

analysis.label: Player captures with a minor piece (usually a bishop) that is left hanging and undefended on the destination square, squandering a superior alternative.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 99% of activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging after the move (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 88% of the played moves are captures. The hung-piece class distribution is overwhelmingly minor pieces (449/496 ≈ 90%). Meanwhile, 60% of the time the best move wins material (median 2.0), often through checks (10%) or positional threats rather than the greedy capture chosen. The player sees a tempting target to take with their bishop or knight, executes the capture, but the piece lands on an undefended square where it can be immediately recaptured or attacked, negating or reversing the material gain. The better moves are frequently non-captures (76%) like pawn advances (d6, e5, e4), castling, or queen checks that exploit the opponent's structural weaknesses far more effectively.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing minor piece (almost always a bishop) lands on a square where it has no defenders, making it immediately recoverable by the opponent.
