This trades a well-placed, active piece for typically less valuable material or simply loses it back, while simultaneously forfeiting a much stronger continuation that would have exploited positional advantages like an exposed enemy king, development lead, or pawn breakthrough.

analysis.label: A minor piece (usually a knight) greedily captures the f2 or f7 pawn but is left hanging without adequate support or follow-up.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates that the player's own move hangs a piece (84% of positions, median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 72% of cases. The played move is a capture 51% of the time, and 55% of the time the best move would have won material instead. The top 12 boards show a strikingly consistent pattern: 10 of 12 moves involve a knight or bishop taking on f2 (or f7), typically from g4, in Italian Game-style or similar structures where the f-pawn appears vulnerable. The knight captures the tempting f-pawn but ends up unprotected and easily recaptured, squandering a better position where quiet or alternative tactical moves were available.
analysis.why_bad: The f2/f7 capture looks aggressive—winning a pawn and often giving check—but the attacking piece (almost always a knight) lands on a square where it lacks support and is immediately recaptured. The player prioritizes a superficially attractive tactical shot over maintaining piece safety, often missing that the position required development, king safety, or a different tactical idea (like Qh4, Rb8, or a positional move) that would have preserved or increased their advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available material-winning capture and instead plays a quiet move that frequently hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 96% of positions the best move is a capture winning material (82% of the time, median value 3.0 — typically a minor piece or equivalent), yet the player's actual move is a capture only 7% of the time. Instead, the player makes a passive quiet move (king retreats, piece repositions, etc.) that in 72% of cases leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors: 148, pawns: 132, minors: 79). This creates a compound blunder: not only is free enemy material left on the table, but the played move also exposes the player's own material to capture. The enormous average cp_loss (~4101) reflects this double cost.
analysis.why_bad: The player overlooks a straightforward capture that would win material (often a simple pawn-takes-piece or piece-takes-undefended-piece), and instead plays an aimless quiet move that ignores the tactical opportunity. Worse, the quiet move frequently leaves the player's own pieces undefended or in the line of fire, compounding a missed gain with an actual loss. The result is a swing of roughly two pieces' worth of material.

analysis.label: The player misses an immediate checkmate (almost always delivered by a rook) and plays an irrelevant move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 positions, with a median material value won of 100 (representing checkmate). Only 16% of best moves are captures, meaning the mating piece usually moves to an empty square. The player's actual move was a capture only 29% of the time and left their own piece hanging 39% of the time (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), indicating completely aimless play when a forced mate exists. The feature fires on 0.5% of all positions—those rare moments where a mating move is available but overlooked. Across the top 12 boards, 10 show explicit checkmate-in-one (Rf2#, Rf4#, Rxc4#, Rxe5#, Rf6#, Rb2#, Rh7#, b3#), predominantly rook mates against exposed kings in endgame positions.
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores a forced checkmate in one move. Instead of delivering the decisive blow with a rook (or pawn) to a mating square, they play positional moves, random captures, or even leave their own pieces hanging—all completely irrelevant when the game could be ended immediately.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple capture of a hanging or inadequately defended enemy piece, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 96% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, roughly a rook), and 97% of best moves are straightforward captures. Yet the player's move was a capture only 18% of the time — overwhelmingly they played quiet moves (king retreats, pawn pushes, piece repositioning). In 54% of cases the played move additionally left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/98, majors/85, minors/80), compounding the error. The feature fires on only 0.3% of positions, indicating these are rare but catastrophic oversights with an average centipawn loss of ~1306.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player completely overlooks a freely capturable enemy piece (often a queen worth 9 or a rook/minor piece worth 3-5) sitting undefended or inadequately protected. Instead of taking the free material, the player makes an irrelevant quiet move — frequently a king move (Ke7, Kh1, Kd1, Ke6, Kd2) or piece repositioning — that ignores the tactical gift and often simultaneously exposes their own pieces to capture, turning a winning or dominant position into a lost one.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive quiet move that both misses a concrete tactical win and often leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player plays a quiet, repositioning move (never a capture — only 10% are captures) while ignoring sharp tactical demands. The SEE aggregate shows that 69% of the time a best move wins material (median value 3.0, often a simple capture at 36% or a check at 11%), yet the player instead makes a passive move like a knight retreat, king shuffle, or piece repositioning. Simultaneously, 60% of the time the played quiet move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), predominantly minor pieces (82 of 165 hangs). The combination of both indicators being high (69% missed win + 60% hung own piece) indicates the player is completely blind to the tactical state of the position, making routine-looking moves while both offensive and defensive tactics scream for attention.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because the position demands concrete tactical action — there is typically a hanging enemy piece to capture or a forcing sequence (check/capture) that wins material. Instead of seizing this opportunity, the passive move wastes a tempo and, worse, often moves a piece away from a defensive duty, leaving the player's own minor piece or rook en prise. The result is a double-whammy: missing a winning tactic while simultaneously creating a new vulnerability.

analysis.label: Player moves a knight (often capturing) instead of using the queen to win material on the same or a nearby square.
analysis.description: In the top 500 activating positions, 79% feature a best move that wins material (median value 3.0), and the best move is overwhelmingly a queen move (Qxd7, Qxc7, Qxf2, Qa6, Qc4, Qg4, etc.). Instead, the player frequently plays a knight move (Nxd7, Nxc7, Nxf2, Nf3, Nd7) — often capturing on the same square with the wrong piece. The player's move was a capture only 28% of the time (vs. 40% for the best move), and 40% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), which happens because a knight landing on the target square is often unprotected and en prise, whereas the queen could safely collect the material.
analysis.why_bad: Capturing with the knight (or making a knight developing move) instead of the queen typically fails because: (1) the knight becomes exposed and hangs after landing on the capture square, costing material back; (2) the queen capture wins cleanly since the piece is undefended or the queen can retreat safely; (3) playing a quiet knight move entirely misses a tactical queen shot that exploits hanging or undefended enemy pieces, squandering a decisive advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy knight/bishop forking on f7 (or f2) that should simply be captured by the king, leaving their own major piece hanging to the fork.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 90% of activating positions the best move wins an enemy piece (median value 3.0, i.e., a knight or bishop), and in 86% of cases the played move leaves the player's OWN major piece hanging (median value 5.0, with the hung piece class distribution being 22 major vs 3 minor). The best move is a capture 86% of the time and never a check (0%). Examining the top boards reveals a nearly uniform pattern: an enemy knight (or occasionally bishop) has landed on f7 (or f2) delivering a fork against the player's queen and rook. The correct response is the simple king capture (Kxf7/Kxf2), winning the invading piece worth 3. Instead, the player makes a quiet developing move or irrelevant capture, allowing the forking piece to remain and collect a queen (value 6) or rook (value 5).
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the forking piece on f7/f2, the player leaves their own queen or rook en prise to the fork. The king capture is safe and wins a full piece, but by playing a quiet move instead, the opponent simply takes the hanging major piece on the next move, resulting in catastrophic material loss (median cp_loss ~490).

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive queen check (often on the h-file) that wins material or delivers checkmate against an exposed king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 87% of best moves win material (median value 91, i.e., queen-level), and 72% of best moves are checks, while only 17% are captures. The player's actual move was a capture only 27% of the time and hung their own piece 43% of the time (median value just 1 pawn). Across the top 12 positions, the best move is almost always a queen delivering check—specifically Qh5+, Qh4+, Qh3+, Qxh6+, Qb3+, or Qa4#—targeting an exposed enemy king (frequently on h3 or h6 in endgame positions). Instead, players chose quiet queen moves (Qb3, Qf6, Qf7), greedy captures (Qxc7, Bxa8, Qxb5), or inferior checks (Qb3+, g4+, Qf1+) that fail to exploit the king's vulnerability. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions and averages 2610 centipawn loss, indicating rare but catastrophic oversights.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the exposed enemy king in favor of materialistic or aimless alternatives. The missed queen checks either deliver immediate checkmate or force the king into positions where decisive material is lost. By playing quiet moves, capturing unimportant pieces, or giving inferior checks, the player squanders a winning tactical blow and often allows the opponent to consolidate or escape.

analysis.label: The player gives a Queen check (often capturing a pawn) that leaves the Queen en prise or trapped, losing it.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a tempting Queen check that fatally hangs the Queen. The SEE aggregate shows 82% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0), with 'major' pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (218 of 282 identified cases — mostly Queens valued at 9). Meanwhile, 48% of played moves are captures (grabbing pawns on g7, f2, g2, h7, b7, etc.) and 100% of the top-12 boards show Queen checks. The best move wins material 73% of the time (median 3.0), indicating strong alternatives existed. The best moves are checks only 29% of the time and captures 42%, showing the engine prefers quieter or differently-directed moves over the flashy Queen check.
analysis.why_bad: These Queen checks look attractive — they give check and often win a pawn — but the Queen lands on a square from which it cannot escape. After the opponent's king moves (or interposes), the Queen is captured on the next move, resulting in catastrophic material loss (avg cp_loss ~1170, approximately a full Queen). The player is seduced by the forcing nature of check and the immediate material grab, failing to verify the Queen's safety after the check is dealt with.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a simple pawn capture that wins a minor piece, opting for a quiet developing or positional move instead.
analysis.description: In 97% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 2, consistent with a pawn capturing an undefended or insufficiently defended minor piece). The best move is a capture in 100% of cases, and critically, every single top example shows a pawn capture (exf6, exd5, exd6, dxc6, cxd4, bxc3, axb3, exf3). The player's actual move was a capture only 20% of the time—the vast majority played quiet moves (O-O, Bd2, Be7, Qf3, Bd3, Ba6, f5, b5, h4). The feature fires predominantly in opening positions (6/12), where players appear focused on development or king safety and overlook that an enemy piece is hanging to a straightforward pawn capture. Only 1% of best moves are checks, confirming the pattern is about simple material capture rather than tactical sequences.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available pawn capture that wins a minor piece (~2+ points of material) for free. By playing developing moves like castling, bishop retreats, or pawn pushes instead of the winning pawn capture, the player squanders a decisive material advantage—often turning a winning position into an equal or losing one (average cp_loss: 210).

analysis.label: The player fails to find a king move that wins enemy material, instead playing a different or wrong king move that often hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: In 95% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins enemy material (median value 3, i.e., a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 21% of the time and a check 0% of the time—indicating the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet king move that attacks or approaches an enemy piece. Examining the top 12 boards confirms this: 10 of 12 best moves are king moves (Kd7, Kd6, Kf3, Ke3, Kf7, Kf7, Kxe6, Kf2, Kg4, Kd2). Meanwhile, 47% of the time the player's chosen move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 2, distributed across pawns, minors, and majors), compounding the error. The player either moves the king to the wrong square, castles inappropriately, or ignores the king entirely in favor of a piece move or pawn push.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that their king can actively win material—typically a minor piece—by moving to the correct adjacent square (attacking an undefended enemy piece, escaping a dangerous file, or centralizing to collect material). Instead, the played move either walks into mate (positions 3, 4, 10, 12 with cp_loss ~9200), leaves own pieces undefended (47% hang rate), or simply squanders the opportunity to gain decisive material through king activity.

analysis.label: The player moves their Queen (usually capturing a piece) to a square where the Queen itself is immediately lost or trapped.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 9.0 = Queen), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (409/427). In 52% of cases the played move was itself a capture, and 11 of 12 top-activating moves are Queen moves (mostly Qx captures on various squares). While the best move wins material 62% of the time (median 3.0), the player instead chose a greedy Queen capture or Queen placement that walked the Queen into a trap or onto a defended/attackable square, resulting in an average cp_loss of ~1010. The feature fires on only 0.3% of positions, identifying a specific blunder pattern of Queen self-destruction.
analysis.why_bad: The Queen captures an enemy piece (typically a pawn or minor piece worth 1-3 points) but lands on a square where it is immediately captured back or trapped, losing 9 points of material. The net result is catastrophic — the player trades their Queen for a pawn/piece, often deciding the game. A non-greedy move (retreating, developing, or capturing elsewhere) would have preserved the Queen.

analysis.label: A knight prematurely captures the f-pawn (f7 or f2) in the opening, leaving itself hanging with no sufficient compensation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the played move is a capture, and 96% of the time it leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece — 23/27 are minors). The best move wins material in 68% of cases (median value 1.0), indicating simple positional or tactical alternatives existed. Only 18% of best moves are checks and 25% are captures, meaning the correct continuations were typically quiet developing or consolidating moves (e.g., c3, Bc4, Nc5, d6) rather than aggressive tactics. The feature fires exclusively on opening positions where a knight lunges at the f-pawn, lured by its apparent vulnerability (defended only by the king), but the sacrifice is unsound.
analysis.why_bad: Capturing on f7/f2 with a knight wins only a pawn (worth 1) but leaves the knight en prise to recapture by the king or other pieces (losing a piece worth 3), resulting in a net loss of approximately 2 points of material. The attack typically lacks sufficient follow-up — the opposing king steps aside and the sacrificing side has no forced continuation to justify the material investment. Better moves would maintain or increase the advantage through development, central control, or positionally sound threats.

analysis.label: Player ignores a queen (or major piece) exchange with check when pieces face each other on an open file, leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture 100% of the time and a check 93% of the time, yet wins 0 material (an equal trade). The player's move left their own piece hanging 50% of the time with a median hung value of 9 (queen), with the piece class distribution heavily weighted toward major pieces (6 major, 1 pawn). The pattern across all 12 boards is nearly identical: both queens (or rooks in one case) oppose each other on an open file (usually the e-file), and the correct move is to initiate the trade with check (Qxe2+, Qxe7+, Qxd1+, Rxd1+). Instead, the player develops a piece or plays a random move, ignoring the forced exchange opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: When major pieces face each other on an open file and one side can capture with check, failing to do so effectively donates the piece. The opponent will simply capture the player's undefended queen/rook on their next turn, since the player wasted tempo on an irrelevant move instead of resolving the critical file tension. The check component means the trade is essentially forced and free—ignoring it is catastrophic.

analysis.label: Player missed placing a rook on an open file to win an undefended or trapped enemy piece.
analysis.description: In 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). Crucially, the best move is a capture only 8% of the time and a check only 8%, meaning the winning move is almost always a quiet rook placement on an open file that creates an unavoidable threat to win material. The positions overwhelmingly feature open central files (d, e, c) with exposed or poorly-coordinated enemy pieces. Instead of the decisive rook invasion, the player chose quiet pawn pushes, irrelevant captures, or non-critical moves (only 26% played captures). In 49% of cases the played move additionally left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most critical feature of the position: an open file that a rook can exploit immediately to attack an undefended or trapped enemy piece (typically a minor piece worth ~3 pawns). By playing irrelevant moves—pawn pushes (a2, b6, g6, f5, h4, d4), wrong captures (fxe4, Bxd2+, Nxd6), or misdirected rook moves (Rc2+)—the player squanders a decisive tactical opportunity and often allows the opponent to consolidate or equalize.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive king or piece move in the endgame instead of advancing a critical passed pawn at the decisive moment.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material only 19% of the time (median 1.0) and is a capture only 10% of the time, indicating this is primarily a positional/tempo mistake rather than a tactical oversight. The player's move hung their own piece 36% of the time (median value 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns: 46 pawns vs 6 minors and 2 majors), which likely reflects pawns becoming vulnerable after the king walks away instead of pushing them forward. The played moves are almost exclusively quiet king moves (Kf5, Kc5, Kg6, Kh4, Kc2, Kf2) or piece repositionings, while the best moves in 10+ of 12 positions are pawn advances (e6, d3, f3, d6, e3, h6, c6, b5, d6, h3, d4). The feature fires on endgame positions (11/12) at just 0.1% of all positions, capturing the specific scenario where a passed or critical pawn must be advanced immediately but the player instead temporizes.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames with passed pawns, timing is critical. Each tempo spent on a king move or piece reposition rather than advancing the pawn allows the opponent to establish a blockade, activate their pieces defensively, or create counterplay. The pawn advance creates immediate threats (promotion, space gain, deflection) that the opponent must address, while king moves are passive and squander the initiative. In many cases, the king move also physically abandons the pawn, leaving it hanging (36% of positions).

analysis.label: Player misses a queen check that delivers immediate or near-immediate checkmate in an endgame with exposed enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of best moves are checks and 99% win material (median value 91-100, indicating checkmate-level wins), while the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 12% captures). The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (12/12 boards) where the player has a queen and the opponent's king is exposed. The best move is almost always a queen delivering check — frequently mate in 1 (Qh2#, Qh8#, Qh1#) or a forcing check sequence leading to mate in 3-14 moves. Instead, players make passive king moves (Kg6, Kd7, Kd2, Kc3) or reposition their queen to suboptimal squares (Qd4, Qf6, Qf7, Qf4+). The low own-hang rate (31%, median value 1.0 = pawn) confirms the mistake is not about leaving pieces en prise but about failing to spot the mating pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they squander an immediate or near-immediate forced checkmate. By playing quiet moves instead of the decisive queen check, the player allows the opponent's king to escape the mating net, lets dangerous passed pawns advance toward promotion, or converts a won position into a draw or even a loss. The average centipawn loss of 7353 reflects that missing checkmate is the most catastrophic type of error possible.

analysis.chip: Ignored Pawn Threat to Minor Piece
analysis.label: Player makes a quiet/developing move while their own minor piece is directly attacked by an enemy pawn, leaving it hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 100% of positions have the player's move leaving their OWN piece hanging (median value: 2.0), with the overwhelmingly dominant piece class being minor pieces (109 minor vs 4 major out of the top 500). Only 10% of played moves are captures, meaning 90% are quiet moves that simply ignore the threat. The best moves win material only 19% of the time (and only at median value 1.0), indicating the best move is usually just saving the threatened piece rather than winning anything. All 12 top boards are opening positions where an enemy pawn directly attacks a bishop or knight (e.g., e5 pawn hitting Nf6, e4 pawn hitting Bf5, b4 pawn hitting Bc5, d4 pawn hitting Nc3), and the player plays an unrelated developing move instead of addressing the attacked piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore an immediate pawn-takes-piece threat. A pawn attacking a minor piece is one of the most forcing threats in chess since the material exchange (pawn for knight/bishop) is catastrophically losing. By playing an unrelated move—whether it's developing another piece, pushing a pawn, or making a rook move—the player allows the opponent to simply capture the minor piece on the next move for just a pawn, resulting in approximately 300-450 centipawns of evaluation loss.

analysis.label: The player avoids a necessary queen exchange (often with check) and instead plays a move that leaves their position collapsing.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a capture 98% of the time and a check 58% of the time, yet every visible example specifically shows a queen-takes-queen exchange (Qxe4+, Qxe6+, Qxc5+, Qxe5, Qxf3+, etc.) as the correct play. The SEE consistently reports 0 material won by the best move, confirming these are equal queen trades rather than material-winning captures. After the played (non-trade) move, the player's own piece is left hanging 58% of the time (median value 4.0, with major pieces dominating the hung-class distribution at 14 out of 25 instances). The average cp_loss of 4017 — with many positions transitioning to forced mate — confirms these missed trades are catastrophic. Only 12% of played moves were captures, showing a strong tendency to avoid the exchange entirely.
analysis.why_bad: By refusing the queen trade, the player keeps queens on the board in positions where their opponent's queen is far more dangerous (attacking the exposed king, controlling open files). The queen trade would simplify into a survivable endgame or defuse an attack, but instead the played move leaves the player's own queen or major pieces en prise, or allows the opponent's queen to deliver forced checkmate sequences against the exposed king.

analysis.label: Player pushes a central pawn (e5/d5/e6) forward prematurely, leaving a pawn en prise or tactically indefensible.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 51% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the overwhelmingly dominant class being pawns (207 of 257 hung pieces). The best move wins material only 22% of the time, confirming this is a 'hung own piece' pattern rather than a 'missed capture' pattern. The best moves are almost never captures (10%) or checks (2%), indicating the correct alternatives are quiet consolidating/developing moves. Across the top 12 positions, the played move is always a central pawn advance (e5 in 8 cases, d5 in 3, d4 and e6 in 1 each), executed during the opening or early middlegame when the player has not yet completed development or secured the king.
analysis.why_bad: The central pawn advance overextends beyond its support chain—typically pushed before the player has castled, developed minor pieces, or reinforced the center with c3/f4. The advanced pawn becomes a target that cannot be adequately defended, or the advance vacates a square that leaves a neighboring pawn unprotected. The correct moves (Nc3, O-O-O, c3, h3, Be3, Rc1, a3) all consolidate the existing structure, complete development, or address immediate tactical issues before committing to an aggressive pawn push.

analysis.label: Player's king is adjacent to a capturable enemy piece but makes a different move, missing a critical king capture in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 64% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 3.0, typically a rook), with 68% of best moves being captures, yet the player's move is almost never a capture (only 2%). Examining the top 12 boards reveals the specific geometry: in 11 of 12 cases, the best move is a King capture (Kxg7, Kxb3, Kxg5, Kxf2, Kxb5, Kxb3, Kxa4, Kxd4, Kxd7, Kxf6, Kxd8) where an enemy piece sits directly adjacent to the player's king. Instead, the player makes a quiet move—often a different king move or an irrelevant pawn push. These are overwhelmingly endgames (11/12) with enormous cp_loss (avg 7047). The 45% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary consequence of making a losing alternative move rather than capturing.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail catastrophically because the player ignores a free or nearly free capture by their own king of a major/minor piece sitting on an adjacent square. In desperate endgame positions, capturing this piece is often the only way to avoid immediate forced mate or reduce a decisive material deficit. Instead, the played moves accomplish nothing meaningful and allow the opponent's overwhelming advantage to deliver mate or promote.

analysis.label: The player misses a winning bishop-takes-bishop capture where the opponent's bishop on d6 or d3 is undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly indicates a 'missed winning capture' pattern: 85% of the top 500 positions have a best move that wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), 97% of best moves are captures, yet only 6% of actually-played moves were captures. Only 15% of played moves hung the player's own piece. Across all top boards, the specific geometry is a bishop-versus-bishop tension along a diagonal (typically Bg3 targeting Bd6, or Bf5 targeting Bd3) where one side's bishop is undefended or insufficiently protected, allowing a clean Bxd6 or Bxd3 that wins a full piece. Instead, the player consistently plays quiet developing moves (Nf3, Nbd2, Qc2, Ne7, e6, etc.), completely overlooking the free capture.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available material-winning capture. The opponent's bishop sits unprotected on d6 or d3, and the player's own bishop can simply take it for free. By playing a positional or developmental move instead, the player gives the opponent time to move the bishop to safety or add a defender, permanently squandering a full piece (≈3 pawns) of material advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive capture or check that leaves their own piece hanging and undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a flashy tactical move—typically a capture (48%) or check—that leaves one of their own pieces en prise. The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of played moves hang the player's own piece (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece), with the distribution being minor pieces (38), major pieces (21), and pawns (20). Meanwhile, 84% of the time the best move actually wins material (median 1.0 pawn), meaning the player chose a losing aggressive shot over a quieter move that would have gained material. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically these unsound sacrificial attempts.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is attracted to aggressive-looking tactics (captures on f7, checks, exchanges) without verifying that the resulting position leaves their own pieces adequately defended. The capturing/checking piece (or another piece left behind) becomes en prise after the opponent recaptures or simply takes the hanging piece, resulting in net material loss. A calmer move would have maintained or even improved the material balance.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet, non-forcing minor piece move that ignores the position's urgent tactical demands, leaving material undefended or missing winning tactics.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive piece maneuver (typically a knight or bishop reposition) instead of addressing the position's concrete tactical requirements. The SEE aggregate shows that 47% of the time the best move wins material (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 46% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 134/228, then minors at 81/228). Only 18% of moves played are captures, confirming the player is choosing quiet repositioning over concrete action. The best move is a check only 8% and a capture only 22% of the time, meaning the correct action is often a quiet but purposeful move (like a prophylactic defense or positional consolidation) rather than these aimless piece shuffles. The feature fires on 2.3% of all positions with an average centipawn loss of 1019.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the position's tactical realities. By repositioning a minor piece to a passive or irrelevant square (Nh4 to the rim, Nb7 retreating, Ba6 offside, Nd2 passively), the player leaves pawns or pieces undefended, misses winning captures or forks, and squanders decisive advantages. The moves address no threat and create no threat, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected tactical vulnerabilities.

analysis.label: In endgames with locked/semi-locked pawn structures, the player makes a passive move (usually a king move) instead of executing the critical pawn break or pawn capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/12 boards) where the player fails to execute a timely pawn break or pawn capture. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 51% of the time (median value 2.0), and 25% of best moves are captures — yet the player's move was a capture only 5% of the time, indicating they consistently miss the critical pawn action. Only 17% of played moves hang own material, confirming this is a 'missed winning action' pattern rather than a self-hanging pattern. The played moves are overwhelmingly passive king moves (10/12 boards) in positions where a pawn advance or pawn capture would break through the locked structure decisively.
analysis.why_bad: These passive king moves fail because in locked pawn endgames, the timing of the pawn break is everything. Once the opponent's king repositions or the window closes, the breakthrough is no longer available. Moves like Kg7 instead of e5, Kf6 instead of fxg4, Ke6 instead of d4, and Kc6 instead of dxe4 all surrender the one dynamic lever (the pawn break) that gives the position its winning or drawing potential. The resulting positions become lost or drawn when they should have been won or held.

analysis.label: A minor piece (usually a knight) captures or moves to a rim/corner square to grab a pawn, missing a far stronger central or active move.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player moves a minor piece (overwhelmingly a knight) to the edge of the board—typically capturing a pawn on a2, b2, b7, a7, or g2—while missing a much stronger alternative. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 64% of cases (median value 1 pawn), yet the player's move, while itself a capture 58% of the time, gains only a rim pawn at the cost of piece activity or positional collapse. In 35% of cases the played move even leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, mostly pawns). The played moves cluster on squares like b2, a7, b7, a2, c2, g2—classic rim/corner pawn-grab squares—while the best moves (Ne4, Nxe5, Nd4, Nf5, Nc5, Ne5, Nc6) are centralized, active alternatives. The average cp_loss of 982 reflects how severely the piece gets misplaced or trapped.
analysis.why_bad: Grabbing a rim pawn with a knight sends the piece to a passive, often trapped square far from the center of action. The knight takes multiple tempi to return to useful squares, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with central play, open file pressure, or direct attacks on the exposed king. Meanwhile, the much stronger central moves would have maintained piece dominance, won equal or greater material in active positions, or exploited tactical motifs like forks and outposts.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy major piece (rook or queen) that can be freely captured, instead making a quiet king move in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a capture that wins material (median value 5.0, corresponding to rook/queen-level pieces). The player's move was a capture in 0% of cases, and 0% of positions involve hanging one's own piece. The best move is always a capture (100%) and never a check (0%). This means the feature fires precisely when a player overlooks a free take of a high-value undefended enemy piece. Across the top boards, the targets include undefended rooks on open files (Positions 1, 5) and queens attacked by knights (Positions 3, 4), all in sparse endgame positions where the player instead retreats or repositions their king.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves (or the knight check in Position 3) are catastrophic because they forfeit the opportunity to capture a completely undefended enemy piece worth 3-9 points of material. In several cases (Positions 3, 4), this transforms a drawn position into a lost one, and in others (Positions 1, 5), it squanders a trivially winning endgame. The player appears distracted by king activity or checking sequences while ignoring the simple tactical reality that an enemy piece is en prise.

analysis.label: Player makes a rook move that leaves the rook (or another major piece) en prise or tactically undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's chosen move is always a rook move that constitutes a significant blunder. The SEE aggregate shows that 57% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being major pieces (160 of 284 instances, i.e. rooks/queens). Meanwhile, 61% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0), indicating the player also misses winning opportunities. The played move is a capture only 29% of the time, meaning most blunders are quiet rook repositioning moves to vulnerable squares. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, targeting a specific failure mode: moving a rook to an undefended or tactically exposed square.
analysis.why_bad: The rook is moved to a square where it can be captured by the opponent (often entering an enemy-controlled file or rank without adequate support), or the rook makes a capture that loses material because it lands on an undefended square. In cases where the rook isn't directly hanging, the passive rook move ignores urgent tactical threats or misses winning continuations, resulting in massive evaluation losses (average ~1012 cp).

analysis.label: The player makes an enticing capture (or active move) that leaves one of their own pieces undefended and en prise elsewhere on the board.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly shows the 'hung own piece' pattern: 89% of activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The own-hang distribution is dominated by minor pieces (292), with major pieces (119) and pawns (34) trailing. 50% of the played moves are captures, indicating the player is typically grabbing enemy material while overlooking that their move removes a defender or exposes another piece. Only 15% of best moves are captures, showing the player is often drawn to take material when a quiet defensive or repositioning move was superior. The feature fires on just 0.5% of positions, targeting this specific failure mode of distraction-by-capture.
analysis.why_bad: By capturing material (or making a flashy active move like a check or aggressive placement), the player either removes a key defender from another piece, moves a piece away from protection duties, or places the capturing piece itself on a square where it cannot be supported. The opponent then simply recaptures or wins the hanging piece, resulting in a net material loss that far exceeds whatever was gained from the initial capture. The average cp_loss of 259 reflects losing roughly a minor piece net.

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king moves to the wrong square—abandoning critical opposition, pawn protection, or missing a decisive pawn advance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes an incorrect king move (or occasionally a passive pawn push) that goes in the wrong direction. The SEE aggregate shows 31% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the overwhelmingly dominant class being pawns (112 of 153 hung pieces). This is because the king walks away from defending its own pawns or from the critical squares needed to win. Only 17% of best moves win material outright—the real issue is positional: the king must reach the right square for opposition, penetration, or pawn support. The best moves are often quiet king moves to the correct adjacent square (e.g., Kd4 instead of Kf4/Kc3) or critical pawn pushes (e.g., e7, c6, b5, d3) that the player neglects in favor of an aimless king wander.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves fail because in pawn endgames, king placement is everything—a single square in the wrong direction loses opposition, allows the opponent's king to penetrate, abandons protection of critical pawns, or misses the window for a decisive pawn advance. The king's wrong step often immediately converts a won position into a draw or a drawn position into a loss (average cp_loss of 367).

analysis.label: The player missed a decisive queen exchange (usually with check) that transitions into a winning endgame, instead playing an inferior queen move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 97% of best moves are captures and 87% are checks, yet only 5% 'win material' (median value 9.0 when they do) — because the best move is almost always a queen-for-queen trade (SEE = 0) that liquidates into a won pawn endgame. The played moves are all queen moves (often pointless checks or greedy captures), with 55% leaving the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, split among majors/pawns/minors). The pattern is consistent across all 12 top boards: the best move is Qx[enemy queen]+ forcing recapture, yielding a winning simplified position (typically due to passed pawns or king activity), but the player chose a flashy or greedy alternative.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they keep queens on the board in positions where the decisive advantage can only be converted through simplification. By avoiding the queen trade, the player either allows perpetual check counterplay, lets the opponent's queen stay active defensively, or (in 55% of cases) actually hangs material. The winning queen exchange leverages a structural advantage (passed pawns, king proximity) that only manifests after queens leave the board — an average cp_loss of 1092 shows these are catastrophic strategic misses.

analysis.label: The player moves a rook or queen (or exposes one) to a square where it is left en prise and can be captured by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate makes the direction unambiguous: 82% of the top 500 activating positions show the player's own piece left hanging after the move, with a median hung value of 5.0 (major piece range). The piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (355 of 409 non-pawn hangs, i.e. rooks and queens). In only 27% of cases was the played move itself a capture, meaning most of the time the player simply placed their major piece on an unsafe square or moved another piece exposing it. While 52% of positions also had a best move winning material, the dominant and consistent signal is the self-inflicted hanging of a rook or queen. The feature fires on just 0.4% of all positions and produces an average cp_loss of 881, reflecting the catastrophic nature of losing a major piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player places their rook or queen on (or leaves it on) a square where it lacks adequate defense and can be captured by an opponent's piece. In many cases (e.g., Ra3, Qb4, Qf5, Rh6, Rfe6), the piece is moved to an open square attacked by an enemy piece. In other cases (Kg3, Kb8), the player moves the king or another piece, breaking the defensive connection to their major piece and leaving it unprotected. The result is a free or near-free capture of a rook (~5 points) or queen (~9 points).

analysis.label: In Italian Game / Two Knights Defense positions with Bc4 and Ng5/Ne5 both targeting f7, the player captures with the knight (Nxf7) instead of the far superior bishop check (Bxf7+).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 95% of activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 95% it wins material (median value ~1 pawn). The best move is a capture only 50% of the time (Bxf7+ vs. Bf7+/Bf7#), confirming the key element is the CHECK, not merely the material gain. The played move was a capture 48% of the time (Nxf7 vs. Nf7), and left own pieces hanging in 36% of cases (median value: 1 pawn). All 12 top-activating positions show the identical geometry: a bishop on c4 and a knight (g5 or e5) both attacking f7 in an opening with Black's king on e8. The player invariably plays Nxf7 or Nf7, missing that Bxf7+ delivers check—or in two cases, checkmate (Bxf7#). The feature fires on essentially 0% of all positions, confirming this is a narrow, specific tactical pattern.
analysis.why_bad: Nxf7 captures a pawn but does NOT give check, allowing Black a free tempo to consolidate, counter-attack (e.g., Qg5 threats, Nd4 activity), or simply recapture. Bxf7+ forces the king to move (often to f7 or f8), disrupting castling rights, exposing the king to further tactical blows, and sometimes delivering immediate checkmate. By choosing the knight, White squanders a decisive attacking tempo and often ends up worse because the knight on f7 can become trapped or Black's counterplay (already present on the board) proceeds unimpeded.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player makes a quiet advancing move (pawn push or king march in the wrong direction) instead of a simple material-winning capture or forcing check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 67% of best moves win material (median value 3.0), with 50% being captures and 25% being checks. Yet the played move was only a capture 17% of the time, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves over available winning captures. Only 17% of played moves hung the player's own piece, confirming this is primarily a 'missed winning material' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and the played moves (Kf3, Ke8, f4, h5, c4, a4, Kg6, a5, Kf6) are consistently quiet king maneuvers or pawn pushes that ignore an immediately available capture—often a king taking an undefended pawn/piece (Kxh4, Kxf6, Kxa2, Kxh5, Kxc4) or a knight capture with check (Nxh4+, Ne5+, Nd7+).
analysis.why_bad: These quiet advancing moves fail because they forfeit immediate material gains (often a full piece or critical pawn) in favor of slow plans. In endgames, material advantage is decisive—ignoring a free capture to push a pawn or wander with the king allows the opponent to equalize or consolidate. The missed captures are often with tempo (check) or remove a critical defender/passed pawn, making the resulting position trivially won. Instead, the quiet moves allow the opponent to save the hanging piece or advance their own counterplay.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning rook check (usually delivering immediate checkmate or forced mate) in a rook endgame, instead playing a quiet non-forcing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 91% of best moves win material (median value 100, indicating mate-level wins), and critically 84% of best moves are checks while only 3% are captures. This means the winning tactic is almost always a checking move rather than a simple capture. The average cp_loss of 5193 confirms these are predominantly missed checkmates. The player's move left their own piece hanging only 12% of the time, and only 12% of played moves were captures — confirming the mistake is not about hanging pieces but about failing to deliver a forcing check. All 12 top-activating positions are rook endgames where an exposed enemy king can be mated or decisively skewered via a rook check along an open rank or file, but the player instead makes a quiet king move or passive rook repositioning.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (king walks, passive rook shuffles) waste a critical tempo and allow the opponent's king to escape the mating net. The winning checks exploit the opponent's king being trapped on a back rank or file edge with no escape squares, and delaying even one move often lets the king flee or allows counterplay that draws or reverses the position entirely.

analysis.label: Player makes a premature aggressive move in the opening (capture, check, or greedy development) that leaves their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly confirms this is a 'hung own piece' pattern: 100% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The piece class distribution (minor: 14, major: 5, pawn: 5) shows knights and bishops are most frequently hung, though queens are also lost in spectacular cases. Only 12% of best moves win material and only 4% are captures, indicating the correct alternatives are typically quiet developing moves. All 12 top-activating positions are in the opening phase, and the average cp_loss is 466, reflecting severe blunders. The player's move is itself a capture in 29% of cases — often a greedy pawn-grab (Qxa5, Qxh5, Bxe3, Nxd5) — while the remainder are premature checks (Nc7+) or developing moves that ignore existing threats to their own pieces (Be2 ignoring attacked knight, Be7 ignoring e5 hitting Nf6).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes immediate aggression or material gain over piece safety. Queen captures grab pawns but land on squares where the queen is trapped or captured. Knight checks (Nc7+) fork nothing useful and leave the knight en prise after the king moves. Quiet moves like Be2 or Be7 ignore an existing pawn threat to a knight, effectively donating a piece. In all cases, the player neglects basic piece safety — the opponent simply captures the hanging piece on the next move.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting direct move (promotion or capture) that leaves their own major piece immediately en prise, missing a stronger intermediate move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 67% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 5, all majors — rooks and newly-promoted queens). In 50% of positions the best move is a check (often a zwischenzug), and in 50% the best move wins material (median 95 centipawns). The best move is never itself a capture (0%), indicating the correct play was a quiet intermezzo or check before committing to the 'obvious' action. The player's move was a capture only 33% of the time; the rest are predominantly under-promotions to queen that are immediately recaptured. The feature fires on 0.0% of all positions, isolating a rare but catastrophic endgame blunder pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player grabs material or promotes 'one tempo too early.' In positions 3 and 5, promoting to queen allows immediate recapture by a rook already controlling the promotion square. In positions 1 and 6, capturing a piece leaves the rook en prise when a zwischenzug check (Qe5+, Rg7+) would have won decisively. The player prioritizes the direct/greedy move over an intermediate forcing move that would have kept the major piece safe while achieving a stronger result.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture but leaves their own Queen en prise, losing it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of activating positions involve the player making a capture, and 100% of the time this capture leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 9 = Queen, with the 'major' piece class confirmed). Only 33% of the time does the best move win material, and critically the best move is never a capture (0%), indicating the correct approach was a non-capturing move (a positional retreat, check, or quiet prophylactic move) rather than grabbing material. The player consistently prioritizes taking an enemy piece or pawn over addressing the safety of their Queen.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they ignore a critical threat to the player's Queen. In positions 1-2, the Queen captures an advanced pawn with check but ends up trapped or lost to promotion. In position 3, the player captures a knight with a bishop while ignoring that their Queen is under attack by an advancing pawn with no safe retreat. In all cases, the correct move was to prioritize Queen safety (via repositioning or delivering a precise check) rather than greedily grabbing material.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy piece (usually a rook) that has deeply infiltrated their position, instead making a different move that often leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 98% of the time (usually recapturing or exchanging off a dangerous infiltrator, with median value won 5.0 when material is won but only 36% of best moves actually win material outright). The player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging 68% of the time (median value 3.0, with major pieces comprising 35/75 of the hung pieces). The pattern across 500 positions is consistent: an enemy piece—most often a rook—has penetrated deep into the player's territory (back rank or second rank), and the correct response is to capture or exchange it off immediately. Instead, the player makes an unrelated move (greedy capture elsewhere, passive king move, or promotion), fatally ignoring the infiltrator and frequently leaving their own queen or rook en prise as a result.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to neutralize the infiltrating enemy piece (typically a rook on the back rank like c1, b1, or f1), the player allows devastating tactical consequences—back-rank mates, discovered attacks, or simply lets the opponent exploit the uncontested infiltrator while the player's own pieces become undefended. The infiltrator gains tempo or creates unstoppable threats because it was never challenged.

analysis.label: The player missed a check that wins decisive material or forces mate, instead playing a non-checking move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate unambiguously identifies this pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, and that check wins material 91% of the time with a median value of 97 (approximately queen-value or mate-equivalent). The played move was a quiet non-capture 77% of the time, and left the player's own piece hanging 66% of the time (mostly pawns, median value 1.0—a minor secondary consequence). The average centipawn loss of 6168 reflects that these missed checks typically lead to forced mate (many positions show eval swings to #±N). The checking moves include back-rank checks (Rc8+, Rd8+, Re8+), knight forks (Ne7+, Nf2+), queen checks (Qe1+, Qe7+, Qc6+), and bishop checks (Bd4+)—all of which are immediately decisive.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a check that either forces immediate checkmate or wins overwhelming material through the check's forcing nature (the opponent must respond to check, allowing the attacker to execute a winning sequence). Instead, the player makes a passive or irrelevant move, often allowing the opponent to consolidate or deliver mate themselves.

analysis.label: Player makes a non-urgent or developing move that leaves their own piece undefended, ignoring an available tactical solution (often a capture).
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player chooses a quiet, developing, or plan-oriented move while neglecting immediate tactical obligations. The SEE aggregate shows that in 61% of cases (median value 3.0), the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging—distributed broadly across pawns (113), minors (110), and majors (81). Simultaneously, in 67% of cases the best move wins material (median 3.0), and 48% of best moves are captures, indicating the correct response was typically a concrete tactical strike. Only 21% of played moves are captures, confirming the player consistently chose passive or positional moves over required tactical action. The feature fires on just 0.5% of positions, marking these as distinctive blunders where ambition or routine development overrides piece safety.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize non-urgent goals (castling, development, pawn pushes, speculative knight jumps) while leaving pieces undefended or ignoring available captures. The resulting positions immediately lose material—often a minor piece or more—because the opponent can exploit the newly hanging piece. The correct move was typically a capture or exchange that both secured material advantage and resolved the tactical tension.

analysis.label: Player develops their bishop to g4 or g5 (typically a pin move) when it hangs the bishop itself or ignores a critical tactical priority.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 49% of the top 500 activating positions, the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 79 of 128 classified cases — strongly indicating the bishop just developed to g4/g5 is itself the piece that becomes en prise. Additionally, 41% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 2.0), and only 12% of played moves were captures, showing these players chose a routine developing move over urgent tactical actions. The best moves across the top boards include capturing strong centralized pieces (Nxd5, Nxd4, Nxe4, Nxe5), resolving critical pawn tension (fxe4, cxd4), or castling to safety — all ignored in favor of the superficially attractive pin move.
analysis.why_bad: Bg4/Bg5 is a stereotyped 'pin the knight' developing move that players play on autopilot. In these positions, the bishop lands on an exposed square where it is tactically vulnerable (e.g., to h3/h6 kicks, queen attacks, or simply being captured because it's undefended), while simultaneously ignoring far more pressing needs like eliminating a dominant centralized knight, winning material through captures, or castling to escape a dangerous center. The routine development squanders concrete tactical opportunities and often creates a new weakness.

analysis.label: Player makes a greedy capture (typically with a bishop) while ignoring a decisive mating attack against their own king.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player makes a material-grabbing capture that fatally exposes their king to checkmate. The SEE aggregate shows 86% of played moves are captures and 95% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces at 129/227). The enormous average cp_loss (~8224) and evaluations jumping to forced mate (#+1, #+2, etc.) confirm these aren't simple piece losses but game-ending blunders. While 65% of positions had best moves that won material (median 2.0), the critical factor is that best moves were rarely captures themselves (only 29%), indicating the correct approach was typically a defensive/developing move (like Bh5, Rc8, Qd7, d5, Nbd7) rather than snatching material. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, reflecting these catastrophic tactical oversights.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece (usually a bishop) either removes itself from a critical defensive role, ignores the opponent's existing mating threats, or moves to a square where it hangs with check/tempo, enabling the opponent to execute an immediate forced checkmate. The player prioritizes winning material over king safety in positions where mating attacks are already in progress.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player plays a quiet king move (or other non-capturing move) instead of simply capturing an undefended enemy piece worth roughly a rook.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a missed-capture pattern: 83% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), 89% of best moves are captures, yet only 7% of played moves are captures. The own-hang rate of 27% (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is secondary noise. Across 500 positions, the player consistently overlooks a free or lightly-defended enemy piece and instead plays a quiet move. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and 10 of 12 played moves are king moves (Kh5, Ke6, Kd6, Kd7, Kf1, Kc3, Ka3, Kf2), suggesting the player is focused on king activity or centralization while an enemy rook, bishop, or queen sits undefended and capturable by a simple one-move take (Rxc5, Bxb5, Qxh3, Rxf7, Bxg7, etc.).
analysis.why_bad: These quiet king moves (or other non-captures) fail because they completely ignore a free piece. The opponent's piece is hanging—undefended and directly capturable—meaning the player could gain decisive material (typically a whole rook or equivalent) in one move. By playing a king walk instead, the opponent gets a chance to move the hanging piece to safety, erasing a winning advantage or converting a won position into a draw/loss.

analysis.label: Player hangs their own major piece (usually a rook) in a winning endgame, often through a greedy capture that throws away a decisive advantage.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 74% of the played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 4.0, with 13 major pieces, 6 minor, 6 pawns in the distribution), while 50% of the moves were captures. Only 38% of best moves won material, confirming the mistake is not about missing an enemy hanging piece but rather about the player's own piece becoming en prise. All 12 top positions are endgames with an average cp_loss of 2813 centipawns, with many evaluations collapsing from winning to 0 (drawn). The dominant pattern is a player with a winning material advantage (typically rook or queen vs a lone king or passed pawn) who impulsively captures a pawn, gives a check, or makes a flashy move that leaves their decisive piece hanging—destroying their winning position. Minor cases include underpromotions (c8=N, a1=B) that also discard winning advantages.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an immediate tactical impulse (capturing a pawn, giving check, or choosing an aesthetically unusual promotion) over maintaining the safety of their key winning piece. In most cases, after the rook or queen is left en prise, the opponent can capture it, reducing the position to insufficient material or a drawn endgame. The correct approach is to preserve the dominant piece and use proper endgame technique to convert the advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores a critical pawn action (capture winning material or passed pawn advance) in favor of a flashy or distracting alternative.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material 38% of the time (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn capture), the played move is itself a capture only 15% of the time, and the played move leaves own pieces hanging 37% (median 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 130/184). The best move is a capture just 17% and a check only 6%, meaning the correct move is usually a quiet pawn advance or pawn capture. Across the top 12 boards, the best move is almost always a pawn move — a4 (positions 2,3,6,7), b3 (position 4), e3 (position 11), dxc3 (positions 5,10), cxb4 (position 12), axb4 (position 8), gxf5 (position 1) — that either captures hanging material or decisively advances a passed pawn. The played moves are invariably piece maneuvers (Nd6, Nf5, Bc5, Bb3), checks (Bd4+), king moves (Kd2, Kd7, Kxd8), or wrong-side pawn pushes (h4, h3, f3, a7).
analysis.why_bad: The player gets distracted by seemingly active piece moves, flashy checks, or wrong-sector pawn pushes while ignoring the concrete, decisive pawn action available. The missed pawn moves either capture undefended material (often winning a full piece via pawn recapture) or advance a passed pawn to a point where it becomes unstoppable. The average cp_loss of 1141 reflects that these quiet pawn moves are the key to the position, and missing them squanders winning advantages or turns forced wins into draws.

analysis.label: A bishop captures a piece but lands on a square where it is undefended and immediately hangable, when a better non-capturing move was available.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where a player captures with their bishop (97% of moves are captures, and all 12 top-activating moves are Bx... captures) but leaves that bishop completely unprotected on its landing square. The SEE aggregate shows 100% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece being a minor piece (bishop) in 452 out of 500 cases (90.4%). The best moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (only 16% are captures) and non-checks (only 5%), indicating the correct action was typically a quiet developing or consolidating move (castling, central breaks, retreats) rather than the greedy bishop capture. The feature fires on 6.7% of all positions, and the best move would have won material 45% of the time (median 2.0), suggesting the premature bishop trade often forfeits tactical opportunities.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a piece but lands on an undefended square where it can be immediately recaptured, resulting in a net material or positional loss. In most cases, the player prioritized an immediate exchange over a superior quiet move (castling, a central pawn break, or development) that would have maintained the bishop's activity while addressing more critical positional needs like king safety or piece coordination. The trade-off is particularly costly because the bishop is often the more valuable minor piece in the position.

analysis.label: The player ignores a critical queen move (for defense, exchange, or material gain) and instead plays a weaker alternative that often hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 53% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns, minors, and majors), and 47% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0). Only 20% of played moves were captures. Across the top 12 boards, the best move is a queen move in 10 out of 12 cases (Qb6 appearing 4 times, plus Qxe5, Qe7, Qc6, Qxb2, Qe5, Qc4), yet the player consistently plays a non-queen piece move (Bf5, e6, Be6, Bxh6, Ng6, Ra5, h3) or moves the queen to the wrong square (Qb5, Qd7, Qd8, Qa5+). The correct queen move typically neutralizes pressure, enables a queen trade, centralizes defensively, or captures hanging material—but the player overlooks it in favor of a 'developing' or routine-looking move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the queen's unique ability to solve the position's critical demand—whether that's trading queens to neutralize an attack (Qb6 vs Qb3), defending a vulnerable piece, or capturing unprotected material. By playing minor piece moves or wrong queen squares, the player either leaves their own pieces unprotected (53% hang rate) or forfeits freely available material (47% missed wins), resulting in an average 207cp loss.

analysis.label: Player missed a queen delivery to the back rank (typically Qc8# or Qc1#) giving check or immediate checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of best moves are checks and 98% win material with a median value of 91 (roughly queen-value or mate-equivalent). The best move is a capture only 34% of the time, meaning the queen is usually invading an empty square on the back rank. Across the top 12 boards, the missed best move is overwhelmingly Qc8# (or Qc8+) for White when Black's king remains on e8, or Qc1# for Black when White's king is vulnerable on the first rank. The played moves are diverse (captures, development, castling) with only 27% being captures, indicating players are simply oblivious to the back-rank mating possibility. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, consistent with this requiring a specific geometric alignment where the queen has access to c8/c1 with no adequate defense.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate mate-in-one (or forcing check winning decisive material). The player makes routine moves—developing pieces, capturing pawns, or castling—while a lethal queen invasion on the c-file back rank (c8 or c1) delivers instant checkmate or wins the equivalent of a queen. The opportunity is irreversibly lost as the opponent can subsequently defend.

analysis.label: The player makes a passive or misdirected move in an endgame when a decisive king activation, infiltration, or redirection was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/12 confirmed endgame) where the player fails to find the most active/decisive continuation, typically involving king placement. The SEE aggregate shows 55% of best moves win material (median 1 pawn—usually a king capturing or reaching a winning square), while only 14% of played moves are captures, indicating the player chose slow moves over immediately decisive ones. The best move is a king move in 8/12 top positions (Kf4, Kd4, Kf5, Kb5, Kd6, Kd7, Kf2, Kxa4), yet players frequently pushed pawns (g5, a3, d6, d4, c5) or moved the king in the wrong direction (Kh5 instead of Kf5, Ke7 instead of Kd6, Kd4 instead of Kb5). The 25% own-hang rate (median value 1 pawn) is incidental to the main pattern of choosing passive moves over decisive ones. Average cp_loss is ~1100, reflecting that these tempo errors are catastrophic in endgames.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, king activity and tempo are paramount. These moves fail because they waste critical tempo—either pushing a pawn when the king should infiltrate to win material, or directing the king away from the decisive sector. The resulting delay allows the opponent to establish a drawn position, activate their own king, or promote their own pawns first, converting a winning advantage into equality or a loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move in the opening that places or leaves their own piece (usually a knight) en prise to an enemy pawn, when they should have resolved central pawn tension by capturing.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that 92% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece), while the best move was a capture only 37% of the time and the played move was almost never a capture (1%). The hung-piece class distribution (67 minor pieces, 55 pawns, 5 major pieces) confirms the dominant pattern: players develop a knight to a square controlled by an enemy central pawn (e.g., Nc3 into a d4 pawn, Nf6 into an e5 pawn, Nc6 into a d5 pawn), or make an unrelated quiet move while their knight already sits on such a square. In all 12 top-activating positions—all in the opening phase—there exists unresolved central pawn tension where a simple pawn capture (dxe5, exd4, exd5, dxe4, etc.) would maintain equality or win material, but instead the player ignores it.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the pawn tension and developing a piece to (or leaving it on) a square attacked by an enemy pawn, the player gifts the opponent a free piece or pawn. The enemy simply captures with their pawn, winning material cleanly. The correct approach was to resolve the central tension first—typically by recapturing the pawn—before continuing development.

analysis.label: The player missed a check (or checkmate) that wins decisive material or ends the game immediately.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, and that check wins material 99% of the time (median value won: 97.0, indicating often a full piece or more). Only 29% of these best checks are captures—meaning most are non-capturing checks that set up unstoppable follow-ups or deliver mate. The player's actual move was a quiet non-capture 80% of the time, and only 22% of played moves hung the player's own piece. The enormous average centipawn loss (5503) confirms many of these are missed forced mates (positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 all show mate-in-N evaluations). The feature fires on positions where a devastating check exists—sometimes a capture-check (Qxd7+, Qxh5+, Qxc8+, Rxh3#), sometimes a quiet check that wins through the resulting tactic (Qd5+, Ra4+, Rd3+, Rb8+, Ra1#)—and the player completely overlooked it.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore the opponent's exposed king and fail to deliver a check that either mates outright or wins massive material through a forcing sequence. By playing quiet, non-checking moves, the player squanders a decisive tactical blow and allows the opponent to survive or consolidate.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy pawn directly attacking their own knight, making a quiet developing move instead of saving it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 95% of activating positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value: 2, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly being 'minor' (100 out of 106 instances). Only 12% of played moves are captures, confirming the player chose a quiet/developing move instead. The best move wins material only 34% of the time (median 1.0), indicating the best move is usually simply saving the threatened knight rather than winning material. All 12 top boards show the identical geometry: an enemy pawn has advanced to directly attack a knight (e.g., e5 attacking Nf6, or e4 attacking Nf3, or d5 attacking Nc6), and the player makes a quiet developing move (e6, Nc6, Bg2, Be2, O-O, d3, d4, etc.) that completely ignores the pawn threat, leaving the knight en prise.
analysis.why_bad: The pawn directly attacks the knight and can simply capture it next move. By playing a quiet developing move instead of relocating the knight, the player loses a full minor piece (≈3 pawns of material) for nothing. The 'developing' move provides no compensation because the opponent just takes the free knight on the next turn.

analysis.label: The player fails to reposition an exposed or misplaced queen, either moving it to a worse square or ignoring its vulnerability entirely.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a queen is on an aggressive but unstable square (e.g., g4, h5, a5, d5) and the player fails to retreat or reposition it correctly. The SEE aggregate shows that 45% of the time the best move wins material (median 1 pawn), indicating the correct queen reposition maintains tactical threats, while the played move (only 16% captures) is typically a quiet developing move or a queen move to a worse square. In 22% of cases the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 41/62). The best move is rarely a check (4%) or capture (19%), confirming the pattern is about positional queen placement rather than direct tactics. Across the top boards, the best moves are almost always queen moves to safer, more functional squares (Qf3, Qe5, Qb6, Qc2, Qa3), while the played moves are either knight developments (Nf3, Nge2) that ignore the queen's predicament or queen moves to inferior squares (Qg5, Qh3, Qb5).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the exposed queen demands immediate attention—it is either tactically vulnerable, blocking development, or about to be driven away with tempo. By playing a developing move instead (often Nf3, which actually blocks the queen's best retreat square) or moving the queen to an even more exposed square, the player allows the opponent to gain tempo, win material through tactical motifs exploiting the queen's misplacement, or seize the initiative. The resulting positions average 341cp loss.

analysis.label: Player misses a forced checkmate (usually starting with a simple capture) and instead plays an inferior move that often leaves their own queen hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a forced mate exists but the player catastrophically misses it. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 91% of cases (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-equivalent or higher), with 65% being captures and 31% being checks—typical of mating combinations initiated by material-winning captures. The played move was only a capture 18% of the time, meaning players chose quiet moves instead of the decisive blow. Critically, 59% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0), with 30 out of 40 hung pieces being major pieces (queens/rooks). This reflects the pattern of a queen being moved to a wrong square (missing the winning capture) and becoming en prise. The average centipawn loss of 7260 confirms these are catastrophic blunders, typically converting forced mates (#+3, #-2, #+5, etc.) into merely advantageous or even losing positions.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a simple winning capture (usually taking an enemy queen or rook) that initiates or completes a forced mating sequence. Instead, they play a quiet king move or a flashy-looking but inferior queen move that not only throws away the forced mate but frequently leaves their own queen undefended and capturable by the opponent, converting a trivial win into a complex or even lost position.

analysis.label: In endgame positions with exposed kings, the player misses a check (fork, skewer, or forcing sequence) that would win significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 73% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91, indicating a piece or exchange), and 42% of the best moves are checks — an extraordinarily high rate. Only 13% of played moves are captures, and only 15% leave own material hanging, confirming this is overwhelmingly a 'missed winning tactic' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgame positions (11/12 boards) where both kings are exposed and centralized. The tactical resource is typically a rook check creating a skewer/fork (Rf4+, Rd4+, Rf5+, Rf2+), a knight fork check (Nf6+), or a pawn advance with check (d5+) that wins a hanging piece. Instead, players choose quiet positional moves (king walks, pawn pushes, piece repositions) that ignore the forcing tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves played fail because they surrender a concrete tactical win. In endgames with exposed kings, checks are extraordinarily powerful since there are few pieces to interpose or shelter behind. The missed checks typically exploit the geometry of exposed enemy kings relative to undefended pieces — after the forced king move, the checking piece captures hanging material. By playing slowly, the opponent gets time to reposition and eliminate the tactical vulnerability.

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece or pawn but leaves their own capturing piece (usually a rook) undefended and en prise on the destination square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 74% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with major pieces (rooks/queens) being the most frequently hung class (23 of 45 sampled).
