The played move was itself a capture 41% of the time, confirming a pattern of greedy captures that leave the capturing piece en prise. The best move wins material 43% of the time (median 3.0) and is a capture 59% of the time—indicating that a superior capture or tactical sequence existed that wouldn't leave material hanging. The piece class distribution (major: 23, minor: 13, pawn: 9) and the boards (Rxg5, Rxa5, Rxe2, Rxd4, Rxa5+, Nxc3, Bxg7 all leaving the piece hanging) confirm rooks are the most common offenders, greedily capturing on squares defended by the opponent.
analysis.why_bad: These captures win a piece or pawn but place the capturing piece on a square defended by the opponent (or unprotected from attack), resulting in a net material loss when the opponent recaptures. The player prioritized immediate material gain without verifying the safety of the capturing piece on its new square. The best moves typically involved a different capture on a safe square, a check-then-capture sequence, or a quiet move maintaining existing material advantage.

analysis.label: Player gives a check (usually with the Queen) that leaves the checking piece en prise after the opponent escapes, instead of playing a stronger non-checking move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 92% of these positions the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, indicating the Queen), with the hung-piece distribution dominated by major pieces (148 major vs. 36 minor). Meanwhile, 69% of the time the best move would have won enemy material (median 3.0 pawns), and 49% of best moves were simple captures. All 12 top-activating moves are checks—every single one. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check but fails to notice that after the opponent sidesteps, the checking piece is left undefended and capturable. The best moves were overwhelmingly quiet captures or positional moves that won material without needing to give check (only 14% of best moves were checks).
analysis.why_bad: A check forces the opponent to respond, but if the checking piece lands on an undefended square with no follow-up, the opponent simply escapes the check and captures the hanging piece (usually the Queen worth 9 points). The player trades a winning or stable position for catastrophic material loss, often resulting in immediate resignation or forced mate against them. The 'give check at all costs' instinct overrides calculating whether the piece remains safe afterward.

analysis.label: Player grabs material with a capture instead of playing a stronger check (often checkmate) that wins decisively.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 68% of best moves are checks and 82% win material (median value 100cp), yet only 18% of best moves are captures. Meanwhile, 75% of the played moves are captures. This signature clearly shows players choosing greedy captures over forcing checks. The pattern is consistent across 500 positions: a winning check (frequently checkmate, as seen in positions 3, 6, 7, and 9) or a check that leads to decisive material gain is available, but the player is distracted by an immediate capture opportunity. The 43% own-hang rate on the played move (median value 5 = a rook) further indicates that some of these greedy captures even leave the capturing piece itself vulnerable, compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they ignore a more forcing continuation. Checks must be answered immediately, often allowing the attacker to win material through follow-up tactics, deliver checkmate, or gain a tempo that makes the position trivially winning. By capturing instead, the player either misses outright checkmate (positions 3, 6, 7, 9), allows the opponent's king to escape to safety, or even leaves their own capturing piece en prise. The capture wins 'something' but the check wins everything.

analysis.label: Player ignores a forced checkmate threat along the diagonal to h7 or h2, failing to play the essential g6 or g3 defensive pawn move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows massive cp_loss (avg ~9105) with the best move being a non-capture (only 14% captures) and rarely a check (2%). The best moves are overwhelmingly g6 (for Black) or g3 (for White) — defensive pawn pushes to block a lethal queen/bishop battery aimed at h7 or h2. The 53% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, heavily pawns at 145/218) likely reflects the g-pawn becoming tactically loose after the ignored move. The 46% 'best wins material' (median 3.0) arises because the defensive g-pawn move sometimes also attacks an enemy piece on h5/h3. Instead of addressing the immediate mating diagonal, players make irrelevant moves (captures at 28%, queenside operations, or positional moves) and allow mate-in-1.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore an immediate checkmate threat. The opponent has a queen (often supported by a bishop on a diagonal like b1-h7 or b8-h2) ready to deliver Qxh7# or Qxh2#. The only defense is the pawn push g6/g3 to block the diagonal, but the player instead pursues an unrelated plan (capturing material, advancing queenside pawns, developing pieces) and is mated on the next move.

analysis.label: Player had a winning check (often leading to forced checkmate) but played a quiet, non-forcing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 78% of best moves are checks and 71% win material (median value 91, i.e. a queen-equivalent), while the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 24% captures). Only 22% of played moves hang the player's own piece (median value just 1 pawn), confirming this is NOT about self-hanging but about missed tactical blows. The feature fires on positions where the player has a completely winning forcing sequence beginning with a check—typically a mating attack—but instead plays a passive or developing move, squandering a forced mate (average cp_loss 6230). The best moves include Qh7+, Qxg3+, Qd1+, Rd1+, Nxg3+, Nh3+, and Rxg3+, all checks initiating unstoppable mating nets or decisive material wins against exposed enemy kings.
analysis.why_bad: By playing quiet non-forcing moves (Nf3, Rde8, Ra2, Rd2, Kf6, etc.) instead of the available winning check, the player allows the opponent to escape the mating net, consolidate defenses, or activate counterplay. A forced mate or decisive material gain via check is irreversibly lost, often converting a #+N position into merely a large but non-decisive advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a greedy or flashy move in the opening that leaves their own minor piece (knight or bishop) en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 85% of positions show the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the piece class distribution being overwhelmingly minor pieces (21 minor vs 2 pawns). The player's move was a capture 56% of the time, indicating greedy material-grabbing that ignores the vulnerability of their own pieces. While 48% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 2.0), the primary signal is the self-inflicted hanging. All 12 top positions occur in the opening phase with an average cp_loss of 281, showing these are costly early-game tactical oversights.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a superficially attractive action—a flashy check (Bxf2+), a greedy capture (Nxe4, Nxe5), or an ambitious development (Bb4)—while overlooking that their own minor piece is left undefended or becomes trapped. In the Bxf2+ cases, the bishop sacrifices itself for a check with no follow-up, when simply capturing the free enemy knight (Nxe5) would win clean material. In other cases, the player moves a piece that was defending another, or places a piece where it has no support, allowing the opponent to win a full minor piece.

analysis.label: The player's move leaves their own rook or queen en prise to immediate capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows an overwhelming 98% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to rook/queen weight). The hung-piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (29 major vs 13 minor vs 8 pawn). Only 26% of the moves were captures themselves, meaning the majority were quiet moves that inadvertently placed a piece on an undefended square. The best move wins material in 47% of cases (median 3.0), suggesting many positions had tactical opportunities the player ignored while blundering their own piece. The average cp_loss of 4072 reflects the catastrophic nature of losing a queen or rook outright.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player places or leaves their own major piece (rook or queen) on a square where it can be captured for free by the opponent. Whether the move is a tempting capture (Qxc5, Rxd6, Qxg4), an active-looking placement (Re6, Rf8, Rb1), or a quiet developing move (Bg6, f6), the player overlooks that the opponent can simply take the undefended piece on the next move, resulting in catastrophic material loss.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a forcing check (often a bishop check like Bb5+ or Bb4+) that wins major material, instead playing a passive move that frequently hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a check in 75% of activating positions, winning material 60% of the time with a median gain of ~95 (queen-level). Meanwhile, the played move is usually quiet (only 26% captures) and leaves the player's own piece hanging 66% of the time (median value 3, distributed evenly across pawns, minors, and majors). The dominant concrete pattern visible in the top boards is a bishop check to b5 or b4 (Bb5+/Bb4+) exploiting an enemy king stuck in the center, forking or pinning to win the queen. Other cases involve tactical checks (Qxd1+, Nxf6+, Qxf8+) that are either defensive saves or equally forcing. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a rare but devastating oversight.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the available check, the player forfeits a winning tactical blow (often capturing or trapping the opponent's queen). The quiet moves played instead are strategically aimless in positions demanding immediate tactical action, and frequently leave the player's own pieces undefended—compounding the error by both missing a win and creating new vulnerabilities.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player ignores a simple winning capture (often an exchange leading to a won simplified position) and instead plays an 'active' but inferior move, frequently a check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in a remarkable 96% of activating positions, yet the player's move was itself a capture only 4% of the time—a near-total avoidance of the winning take. The best move wins material outright in 29% of cases (median value 5.0, i.e., a full rook), while hanging one's own piece accounts for only 11% (median value 1.0, just a pawn). The best move is a check in only 14% of cases, yet the played moves are frequently checks (Rg3+, Rc2+, Raf2+, Rf3+, Nc5+—about half the top examples). The feature fires exclusively in endgames (11/12 confirmed), where the correct move is typically a clean capture—often exchanging rooks/queens to enter a trivially won king-and-pawn endgame (e.g., Rxb4, Rxe2, Rxb2, Qxf6, Nxd2) or simply taking a hanging piece (Kxf4, Rxa1+, cxd2).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize 'activity'—checks, rook placements on open files, or flashy maneuvers—over the concrete winning capture. In endgames, simplification into a won position is typically strongest, and a check that doesn't achieve anything concrete just gives the opponent time to consolidate. The average cp_loss of 306 shows these moves squander decisive advantages, often turning wins into draws.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an enemy piece that has invaded deep into their position, often hanging their own material instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 83% of best moves are simple captures, and 59% of positions have material to be won (median 2.0). Critically, 75% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors: 93, minors: 53, pawns: 53). The top boards reveal a consistent geometric pattern: an enemy piece has penetrated deep into the player's camp (Rook on f7/f6/d8, Bishop on e7, Knight on h4/g3), and the simple best move is to capture it (Qxf7, Qxf6, Qxd8, Qxe7, Qxf5, hxg3, Nxh4). Instead, the player makes an unrelated move—often repositioning their queen or king—that ignores the intruder and simultaneously leaves their own piece en prise.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring a capturable invading enemy piece, the player allows it to continue wreaking havoc (controlling key squares, pinning, threatening mate), while their own move typically worsens their position by hanging material. The combination of missing a free/cheap capture and simultaneously creating a new vulnerability causes devastating centipawn losses (avg 2595 cp_loss), frequently leading to immediate checkmate or decisive material deficit.

analysis.label: Early aggressive Queen move in the opening that neglects development and hangs own pieces.
analysis.description: The feature fires on positions where the player makes a premature Queen sortie (Qh5, Qf6, Qg5, Qd5, etc.) in the opening with both kings still in the center. The SEE aggregate shows that 53% of the time (median value 2.0) the Queen move leaves the player's own piece hanging—typically a pawn (113), minor piece (92), or major piece (59). Only 12% of played moves are captures, confirming the Queen is moving to an empty aggressive square rather than winning material. Meanwhile, in 28% of positions the best move wins material (median 2.0), indicating the player misses tactical opportunities involving their existing developed pieces. The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet developing moves (O-O, Nf3, Be2, Nc3, d6, c5) rather than checks (2%) or captures (19%), underscoring that solid development was needed instead of the Queen adventure.
analysis.why_bad: These early Queen moves violate opening principles by deploying the Queen before minor pieces are developed and the king is castled. The Queen sortie fails because: (1) it leaves other pieces undefended—especially knights and bishops that were protecting each other—since the Queen has abandoned its defensive duties; (2) the Queen becomes a target for tempo-gaining attacks by enemy minor pieces (Nc3 hitting Qd5, Nf3 hitting Qh5); and (3) it does not address the actual tactical needs of the position (capturing hanging material, completing development, or castling to safety).

analysis.label: Player ignores a mutual bishop confrontation (bishops attacking each other) and plays a quiet developing move, leaving their own undefended bishop en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 59% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution overwhelmingly being minor pieces (66 out of 74 cases). The best move is a capture 94% of the time yet wins material only 10% of the time—meaning the correct capture is almost always an equal exchange (SEE = 0). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the pattern is identical: two bishops are directly attacking each other (e.g., Bd3 vs Bf5, Be3 vs Bc5, Bc4 vs Be6), the player's bishop is undefended, and instead of resolving the tension by capturing first (Bxd3, Bxe3, Bxe6, Bxd6), the player plays an unrelated quiet move (O-O, d4, Nf6, f6, Re8, etc.), leaving their bishop to be captured for free on the next move.
analysis.why_bad: When two bishops directly confront each other and yours is undefended, you must either exchange first or defend it. Playing a quiet move ignores the immediate threat, gifting the opponent a free minor piece (~3 pawns of material) since they simply capture your undefended bishop next turn.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (often a capture) that leaves their own knight or bishop undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player's move leaves their own minor piece hanging. The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of activating positions result in the player's own piece being left en prise (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the overwhelming majority being minor pieces (474/500 knights or bishops, vs only 21 major pieces and 4 pawns). Notably, 64% of the played moves are themselves captures, suggesting the common pattern is capturing with one piece while inadvertently removing the defense of (or ignoring a threat to) another minor piece. Meanwhile, the best move wins material in 65% of cases (median 3.0), indicating the player often had a way to win material instead of blundering it. The best move is rarely a check (9%) or capture (20%), suggesting the correct alternative was typically a quiet defensive or repositioning move that maintained piece safety.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave a knight or bishop undefended and capturable. Common mechanisms include: (1) capturing with a piece that was defending a minor piece elsewhere (e.g., Nxd2 abandoning a key square), (2) moving a piece that was indirectly protecting a knight/bishop (e.g., Be7 removing indirect defense of a centralized knight), or (3) ignoring an existing threat to a minor piece (e.g., playing g6 while a knight is attacked by a queen). The opponent simply captures the undefended minor piece, gaining material worth ~3 pawns.

analysis.label: Player missed a check (often a fork or back-rank tactic) that wins the queen or forces checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 87% of the best moves are checks, and 82% win material with a median value of 97 (approximately a queen). Only 28% of best moves are captures, meaning the material is typically won indirectly through forks, discovered attacks, or forced sequences after the check. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (78% non-captures), indicating the player completely overlooked the checking resource. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, and the average centipawn loss of 3272 (with many positions showing missed forced mates at 9400+ cp_loss) confirms these are catastrophic oversights.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a decisive tactical check. In the top boards, we see missed knight forks (Nc2+, Nxe6+, Nf6+), back-rank exploits (Qxc1+, Re1+, Qe8+), and discovered/direct checks that trap or win the opponent's queen (Bg2+, Rxh5+). By playing quiet developing moves, pawn pushes, or inferior captures instead, the player throws away a forced win—often converting a winning or mating position into a roughly equal or merely advantageous one.

analysis.label: In critical king-and-pawn endgames, the player pushes a pawn or moves the king in the wrong direction instead of finding the precise king placement needed to draw or maintain advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (12/12 endgame) that are overwhelmingly king-and-pawn endings requiring precise technique. The SEE aggregate confirms this is NOT a tactical/material pattern: only 9% of best moves win material, 0% of played moves are captures, and only 4% leave own pieces hanging (just a pawn). The near-zero rates across all tactical categories indicate the feature detects positional/technical endgame failures rather than tactical oversights. The median cp_loss of 256 reflects positions where the theoretical result (draw vs. loss, or win vs. draw) swings dramatically due to a single imprecise move.
analysis.why_bad: In K+P endgames, the player's king must reach specific critical squares to maintain opposition, blockade passed pawns, or enable stalemate defenses. The played moves fail because they either waste tempo on pawn pushes (b6, h6, a5) when immediate king repositioning was essential, give pointless checks (Bc4+) instead of activating the king, or move the king in the wrong direction (Kb4, Ke4) away from the one square that holds the position. Each error turns a drawable or won position into a loss by allowing the opponent's king to seize key squares or escort a pawn to promotion.

analysis.label: Player makes a queen move (often a greedy capture or repositioning) while missing a stronger tactical opportunity with another piece.
analysis.description: In 59% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0 pawns), yet the player opts for a queen move instead. Only 18% of played moves are captures, meaning most are quiet queen repositionings to seemingly active squares. In 40% of cases (median value 1.0, dominated by pawns at 135/200 hangings), the queen move also leaves the player's own material exposed. The best moves are typically non-queen tactical shots (Rc1, h4, Bf6, Rxh7+, Bd7, Kf4, cxd4, Bxd6) — concrete actions with other pieces that exploit vulnerabilities. Nine of the top 12 played moves are queen moves (Qg4, Qxf4, Qxc4, Qf6, Qxc3, Qc7, Qd7, Qg4), showing a clear fixation on the queen at the expense of board-wide tactical awareness.
analysis.why_bad: The player over-invests in queen activity — making captures or repositionings that look aggressive but lack tactical justification — while missing stronger moves with other pieces that win material or deliver decisive attacks. The queen moves often fail to address the most critical feature of the position (hanging enemy pieces, mating threats, or passed-pawn advances), and sometimes create new vulnerabilities by leaving pawns or minor pieces undefended.

analysis.label: Player makes a suboptimal promotion choice (underpromotion or wrong promotion square) or similarly misses winning captures in won endgames.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a suboptimal quiet move — most characteristically an underpromotion or promotion on the wrong square — instead of the winning tactical move. The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material in 43% of cases (median value 3.0, consistent with capturing while promoting), best move gives check in 29% of cases (promotion with check), and the played move is never a capture (0%). In 29% of cases the played move even hangs the player's own piece (median value 9.0, i.e., hanging a queen). Five of the top seven activating positions involve pawn promotion where the player chose a knight, bishop, or rook instead of a queen, or promoted on the wrong square missing a capture-promotion. The remaining positions show analogous mistakes where a piece moves to a passive square instead of capturing a hanging enemy piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves throw away winning advantages because underpromotion to a minor piece or rook yields far less material/mating force than a queen, and promoting on the wrong square misses capturing an enemy piece in the process. Similarly, moving a piece to a quiet square when it could capture a hanging enemy piece squanders decisive material. In all cases, the player had a clearly superior tactical option that would maintain or increase a winning advantage.

analysis.label: The player misses that their queen can capture an undefended enemy rook (typically in a corner square), instead playing a different 'active' move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the best move wins material in 96% of cases with a median value of 5.0 (a rook), while the best move is a capture 80% of the time. The player's actual move was a capture only 27% of the time, meaning they typically played quiet moves ignoring the free rook. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is specifically the queen capturing an undefended rook on a corner square (Qxa8, Qxa1, Qxh8) or back-rank piece (Qxd8). The 48% check rate reflects that some of these queen captures also deliver check. Instead of taking the free rook, players chose aggressive-looking alternatives—queen repositioning moves (Qg5, Qf4, Qf5, Qd5+), knight moves (Nf4, Ne5, Ne7, Ne4), or inferior captures (fxe4, Qxd2+, Qxc7+)—losing an average of 1111 centipawns.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a freely capturable rook (worth ~5 points). Players are distracted by seemingly aggressive ideas—checks, attacks, or piece development—while overlooking that their queen already has an unobstructed path to an undefended enemy rook sitting on a corner square (a1, a8, h8). The 'active' alternatives gain nothing comparable to winning a whole rook for free.

analysis.label: Player misses a quiet developing move (Bc4/Ng5/Ng4) that builds a winning attack on f7/f2, often instead rushing with a premature knight sacrifice.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 80% of positions (median value: 1 pawn), yet the best move is a capture only 18% of the time—indicating the winning line is typically a quiet piece deployment that THREATENS f7/f2 rather than immediately capturing. The player's move was a capture only 25% of the time, and critically, 38% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3, i.e., a knight), consistent with premature Nxf7 sacrifices where the knight is lost without compensation. The own-hang distribution (97 minors, 65 pawns, 28 majors) confirms it is predominantly knights being sacrificed prematurely. The feature fires exclusively in openings (100%) on 0.4% of positions, targeting the classic pattern where both kings remain in the center and f7/f2 is inadequately defended.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they either (1) sacrifice a knight on f7 prematurely without a second attacker in place (Bc4 hasn't been played yet), leaving the knight en prise for ~3 points of material loss, or (2) play routine developing/castling moves that ignore the tactical window to deploy Bc4/Ng5/Ng4, which would add a second attacker to the f7 square and force material gain. The correct quiet moves (Bc4 aiming at f7, Ng5 attacking f7, Ng4 attacking f2) create unstoppable dual threats that win at least a pawn, but the player either rushes the tactic or misses it entirely.

analysis.label: Player ignores a powerful knight move (fork, capture, or tactical breakthrough) and instead plays a passive or blundering move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 61% of the time (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-level gains) and is a capture 48% of the time, while the player's move leaves their own piece hanging 49% of the time (median value 3.0). Examining the top 12 boards reveals that in 11 of 12 cases, the best move is a knight move — Nxg6 (5 positions), Nb3/Nxb3 (3 positions), Nxc3, Nxf7, Ng6, Ng1. These knight moves create forks, win exchanges, or initiate tactical breakthroughs (e.g., Nxg6 opening lines to win a rook on h8). Instead, players make quiet developing moves (Bc4, Be2, Bd3, a3, Kb1) or wrong captures (dxc4, Rxe5, dxe5), often hanging their own queen or rook in the process.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore an immediate knight tactic that either forks material, wins an exchange, or initiates a decisive tactical combination. By playing a passive or irrelevant move, the player not only forfeits the winning opportunity but frequently leaves their own pieces undefended on squares now vulnerable to the opponent's tactics.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning rook placement on the open d-file that would exploit a pin or tactical threat against the opponent's king or queen.
analysis.description: In 94% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 4.0, i.e., roughly a whole piece or exchange). The best move is a capture only 13% of the time and a check only 2%, meaning the winning move is typically a quiet rook lift to the d-file (Rd1 or Rad8/Rd8) that creates an irresistible tactical threat—usually a pin against an exposed king or undefended queen sitting on the open d-file. The played moves are overwhelmingly non-capturing quiet moves (73%) that ignore this critical file, and 45% of the time the played move even leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minors, pawns, and majors). The feature fires on only 0.2% of all positions, isolating this specific geometric pattern of an open d-file with a vulnerable target.
analysis.why_bad: By playing quiet developing moves, pawn pushes, or irrelevant captures instead of the rook move to the d-file, the player forfeits a winning tactical blow (typically exploiting a pin against the enemy king stuck in the center or an undefended queen on the d-file). The opponent then escapes the tactical vulnerability, consolidates, and often the player's own position deteriorates since the ignored d-file pressure was the key to the position.

analysis.label: Player misses a forcing check (often a capture-with-check by a different piece) that wins decisive material or forces mate, instead playing a less forcing move that often leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 69% of best moves win material (median value 3.0) and a striking 42% of best moves are checks, while only 38% are captures. Meanwhile, 47% of the played moves are captures and 62% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across 160 minor pieces, 82 pawns, 67 major pieces). This combination indicates players routinely capture or play active-looking moves while missing that a different piece could deliver check—often on the very same target square. The top 12 positions confirm this: in 9 of 12, the best move is a check (Bxg2+, Rxf5+, Rf8+, Nxh6+, Bxf2+, Nf5+, Rxf8+, Rxc5+, Bxf7+), while the played move captures the same target without check or ignores the tactic entirely. The massive average cp_loss of 2653 reflects that many missed checks lead to forced mate or win of heavy material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they forfeit the decisive tempo that check provides. A check forces the opponent to address king safety before anything else, enabling discovered attacks, piece-winning follow-ups, or forced mate. By capturing with the wrong piece (no check) or playing a quiet move, the player gives the opponent a free response—allowing them to defend, counterattack, or exploit the now-hanging piece that was committed without forcing continuation.

analysis.label: The player moves their queen elsewhere instead of capturing an enemy rook on an open file (often with check).
analysis.description: In 71% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 76% of best moves are captures while 59% are checks. The player's move was a capture only 21% of the time, indicating they consistently missed the winning queen capture. The geometry is strikingly consistent across all 12 top boards: the player's queen shares an open file (e-file, d-file, c-file, or a-file) with an enemy rook, and the best move is a queen capture of that rook (Qxe1, Qxe8, Qxd1, Qxc8, Qxa8, Qxd8) — frequently with check. Instead, the player makes a quiet queen retreat or repositioning move (Qg3, Qd7, Qb6, Qa7, etc.). In 52% of cases the played move additionally leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0, mostly majors), compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: By moving the queen to a non-capturing square, the player forfeits a free or near-free rook capture (often with check that forces a losing reply). The opponent's rook is undefended or insufficiently defended on the open file, and the queen can simply take it. Instead, the quiet queen move both misses winning material and often exposes the player's own rook or queen to tactical threats.

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king greedily captures a pawn/piece instead of attending to a more critical positional duty like stopping or racing a passed pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame in the top 12) where the player's king captures a seemingly free pawn or piece, but this diverts the king from a critical task. The SEE aggregate shows the played move was a capture 48% of the time (almost always Kx__ captures), while the best move wins material 49% of the time (median value 1.0 pawn) — indicating the correct plan often involves advancing one's own pawn toward promotion rather than grabbing the opponent's material. Only 8% of best moves are themselves captures, confirming the best plan is usually positional (pawn advances, key-square occupation) rather than material. The 26% own-hang rate is incidental to the king moving to a vulnerable square. The average cp_loss of 1145 centipawns shows these are catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king position and pawn-racing tempo are paramount. Capturing a pawn with the king often moves it one or more tempi away from the critical sector — whether that's blockading an enemy passed pawn, supporting one's own passer, or reaching a key square. The captured pawn is effectively 'bait' that costs the game by diverting the king from its essential duty, often turning a drawn or winning position into a loss.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own queen en prise, allowing the opponent to capture it.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player's move leaves their queen hanging and capturable. The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 100% of the top 500 activating positions result in the player's own piece being left en prise, with a median hung-piece value of 9.0 (queen value), and the piece class distribution is overwhelmingly 'major' (498/500). The moves are often greedy queen captures (41% are captures—e.g., Qxd4, Qxd5, Qxb4, Qxc4) or careless queen repositionings (Qg4, Qa6, Qb5, Qf4, Qe4) that place the queen on a square where it can be taken. In a few cases (Nd2, Bxc4), moving another piece uncovers an attack on the queen or removes its defender. The best move wins material 52% of the time (median 3.0), indicating that a better alternative often existed that maintained the queen while winning something.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they place or leave the queen on a square where the opponent can capture it, typically losing 9 points of material (the queen). Many are greedy captures where the queen takes an unprotected pawn or piece but lands on a square attacked by the opponent's minor pieces, rooks, or pawns. Others are quiet queen repositionings to tactically vulnerable squares. The result is almost always a decisive material loss (~562 centipawns average).

analysis.label: The player makes a slow, non-forcing move (often a flank pawn push) while missing a concrete tactical opportunity to win material worth roughly a minor piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 76% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the player's move was a capture only 11% of the time—meaning they consistently chose quiet, non-tactical moves instead of striking. The best move is a capture 48% of the time and a check 15% of the time, confirming concrete tactical shots are available. Additionally, 44% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), suggesting that the quiet move not only misses winning material but often creates fresh vulnerabilities. Across the top boards, the played moves are overwhelmingly slow pawn pushes (b6, g6, g3, b5) or passive piece repositionings (Rd4, Nf5, Kc8, Qh6) in positions that demanded immediate tactical action—typically a capture or forcing check that nets a piece.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves waste a critical tempo in tactically sharp positions. The opponent's pieces are already vulnerable (hanging, trapped, or exposed to forks/captures), and a slow pawn push or repositioning allows the opponent to consolidate, defend the weakness, or even counterattack. Worse, in 44% of cases the passive move itself leaves the player's own material en prise, compounding the error by turning a winning position into an equal or lost one.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning check (often immediate checkmate) and played an inferior move instead, typically a capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 100% of best moves are checks and 95% win material with a median value of 97 (essentially game-deciding). Only 28% of these best-move checks are captures, meaning most are quiet or non-capturing checks that the player overlooked. The played moves were captures 37% of the time—players got distracted by material grabs or positional moves instead of finding the decisive check. The average centipawn loss of 5458 confirms these are catastrophic misses, frequently immediate checkmates (Rd8#, Rxd1#, Bf6#, Ra8#, Qxf8#) or short forced mating sequences. The 43% own-piece-hanging rate on the played move (median value 2) is a secondary symptom: by missing the check, the player sometimes made an inferior move that also left material loose.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooked a check—often a simple one-move checkmate or a short forced mating sequence—and instead played a capture, king move, or other non-checking move. The resulting position goes from a forced win (mate in 1-3) to merely a large advantage or even an unclear position, squandering thousands of centipawns of evaluation.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available central pawn capture and instead develops a piece (typically a bishop) onto the square attacked by that uncaptured pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where central pawn tension exists (e.g., e4 vs d5 or d4 vs e5) and the player fails to make the obvious pawn capture. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 100% of the time, while the player's move was a capture only 3% of the time. In 63% of cases (median value 2.0, with 18 minor pieces and 17 pawns in the distribution), the player's own piece is left hanging—almost always because a bishop is developed directly onto the square attacked by the very pawn that should have been captured (e.g., Bc4 into a d5-pawn, or Bc5 into a d4-pawn). The feature fires exclusively in the opening phase across all 12 top examples, with an average centipawn loss of 355.
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they simultaneously miss a free or advantageous pawn capture in the center AND place a piece (usually a bishop) on a square directly controlled by the uncaptured enemy pawn. The bishop is immediately en prise to a pawn (losing ~3 points for a piece vs ~1 point pawn), resulting in catastrophic material loss. Even when the piece isn't directly hung (Ke2, Bd3 cases), the player forfeits the central capture and worsens their position structurally.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move (usually a king retreat) in an endgame instead of capturing a hanging enemy piece or promoting a pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 60% of best moves win material (median value 3.0), while the player's move was a capture 0% of the time — a stark mismatch indicating the player consistently overlooked available captures. Best moves are captures 43% of the time, and only 17% of played moves hung the player's own material. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames (avg cp_loss 4345), and in each case an enemy piece or pawn sits en prise (queens, rooks, knights, pawns, or promotion squares) yet the player chose a purposeless quiet move — overwhelmingly a king move to an adjacent square — instead of taking the free material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore immediately available material gains (often capturing an undefended queen or rook, or promoting a pawn) and instead make aimless king moves that allow the opponent to consolidate, escape, or deliver checkmate. In several cases the position flips from drawn/winning to lost because the hanging piece moves away or the opponent promotes first.

analysis.label: The queen grabs a wing pawn in the opening and gets trapped or misses winning a more valuable piece elsewhere.
analysis.description: This feature detects the classic opening mistake of grabbing a wing pawn with the queen. The SEE aggregate shows 74% of played moves are captures (all queen takes on b2, g2, h7, a2, or b7), while 61% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 'major' pieces—mostly the queen itself at value 9—dominating the hung-piece distribution at 70 instances). Meanwhile, 68% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 3.0, typically a free minor piece). The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase (11/12 top boards), with both kings still in the center, representing the archetypal 'queen trapped by pawn-grab' scenario.
analysis.why_bad: These queen pawn-grabs fail because the queen ventures to the edge of the board (a2, b2, b7, g2, h7) where it can be trapped by developing moves (Nc3, Ra1, Rg1, etc.), losing the entire queen for a single pawn. In other cases, the player fixates on grabbing a low-value wing pawn while a free enemy piece (knight or bishop worth 3) sits undefended elsewhere on the board. The development time lost chasing pawns with the queen compounds the material or positional damage.

analysis.label: Player ignores a beneficial minor-piece exchange (SEE=0 capture), playing a quiet move that often leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a capture, yet only 27% of those captures win outright material (most are SEE=0 exchanges). Despite the engine strongly favoring these captures (avg cp_loss 255), the player opts for quiet moves—only 15% of played moves are captures. Critically, 51% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to minor pieces which dominate the hung-piece distribution at 91 minors out of 187 total). The best moves are overwhelmingly minor-piece exchanges (Bxf3, Nxd2, Nxf6+, Bxd7+, Bxe2, Bxg2, Nxc6), with 24% coming with check. The pattern is a tension between minor pieces where resolving it via capture is strongly indicated—often to remove a defender, gain tempo via check, or eliminate a key piece—but the player plays a passive move instead, frequently leaving that same minor piece (or another) en prise.
analysis.why_bad: By not resolving the piece tension with the indicated exchange, the player loses material in two ways: (1) the opponent can now capture favorably since the exchange opportunity is gone, and (2) the quiet move often leaves the player's own minor piece undefended (51% of cases), resulting in a net loss of a full piece. The 'equal' exchanges (SEE=0) were actually forced or highly favorable due to accompanying checks, removal of defenders, or positional dominance gained afterward.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player moves their King away from an undefended enemy piece that their King could approach or capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 76% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a Rook), yet the best move is only a capture 7% of the time—meaning the winning move is typically a King approach that threatens to capture an undefended piece next. The player's own move was a capture only 10% of the time, and only 17% hung their own piece (median value 1.0, minor cases). All 12 top positions are endgames, and 11 of 12 played moves are King moves going in the wrong direction. The positions consistently feature an exposed, undefended enemy piece (usually a Rook) that the player's King could walk toward to win, but instead the King retreats or wanders away from the prize.
analysis.why_bad: By moving the King in the wrong direction, the player misses that a high-value enemy piece (typically a Rook) is undefended and within reach of the King. In positions like Rook+King vs lone King or similar stripped-down endgames, the enemy Rook is often left unprotected, and a simple King approach wins it outright. Walking away loses this unique window, often converting a drawable or losing position into a forced mate against them (avg cp_loss: 3958).

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an enemy queen that is en prise, instead making an irrelevant move.
analysis.description: In 95% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 9.0 (a queen), and 96% of the time the best move is a simple capture. The player's move was itself a capture only 22% of the time, meaning the vast majority of played moves were quiet or misdirected. Additionally, 63% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns, minors, and majors), compounding the blunder. Across all 12 top boards, the pattern is strikingly consistent: an enemy queen sits en prise to a rook, knight, or bishop, and the player ignores this free queen capture in favor of passive retreats (Bf1, Nf1, Nh2), pawn pushes (f5, a5, h3), or inferior captures (Nxd6, Bxg2). The average centipawn loss is 901, consistent with failing to win a queen.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a freely capturable enemy queen — the highest-value piece on the board. Instead of winning ~9 points of material with a trivial one-move capture, the player makes a quiet or irrelevant move that often also weakens their own position by leaving pieces undefended. The resulting position swings from winning to losing as the opponent subsequently moves their queen to safety.

analysis.label: In endgame positions with advanced passed pawns, the player makes a quiet/strategic move instead of capturing an available enemy piece or executing an immediate tactic.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions (0.1% of all positions, overwhelmingly endgames) where the player is distracted by pawn promotion races and plays quiet moves while ignoring concrete tactical opportunities. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 64% of the time (median value 3.0 — typically a minor piece or rook), yet the player's move was a capture only 20% of the time. The best move is a capture in 47% of cases. Critically, in 52% of positions the player's quiet move also leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minor pieces 25, major pieces 24, and pawns 22). This dual pattern — missing available captures AND exposing own material — reflects a tactical blindness driven by focusing on strategic goals like king activity or pawn advancement rather than calculating immediate exchanges.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore immediately available captures (Nxh1, Rxf8, Kxe3, Rxd2, Kxe8, etc.) that would either win material outright or resolve the position favorably. By prioritizing king repositioning (Kf1, Kd7, Kd5, Ke3) or passive piece moves (Rh8, Rc6, Rc1, h4) in promotion race scenarios, the player both misses winning material and often leaves their own pieces undefended, turning winning or equal positions into losses or immediate checkmates.

analysis.label: In critical endgame positions, the player makes a quiet retreating or aimless move instead of an available forcing tactical blow (check, capture, or fork) that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 50% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. a whole rook), and 33% of best moves are checks. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 17% were captures), and 40% of them additionally left the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0, split between minor pieces and pawns). The feature fires exclusively in endgames on quiet moves—primarily knight retreats to passive squares (Ng2, Nb2, Nc1, Nb3) and aimless king moves (Kg6, Kf5, Ke4, Kf2, Kd3)—when the position demands an urgent tactical response such as a capture with check, a fork, or a critical king capture of an undefended piece.
analysis.why_bad: These passive moves fail because they ignore the one forcing continuation that either wins decisive material (e.g. Kxf8 capturing an undefended rook, Nc6+ forking king and pawn, Nxc5+ winning with check) or saves a lost position (e.g. Rxc2+ eliminating a promotion threat). By retreating instead of engaging tactically, the player allows the opponent's threats to become unstoppable—often leading to immediate mate or promotion—while simultaneously sometimes leaving their own pieces undefended.

analysis.label: Player captures the opponent's queen on d1/d8, trading queens unnecessarily, when a superior queen move would have won material or delivered a decisive attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where both queens face each other on the open d-file and the player reflexively trades queens (Qxd8 or Qxd1) instead of finding a stronger queen move. The SEE aggregate shows 100% of played moves left the player's own queen hanging (median value 9.0 = queen), meaning the opponent simply recaptures. Meanwhile, 77% of the time the best move would have won material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The played move was a capture 78% of the time (the queen exchange itself), and the best alternative was a check 25% of the time or a different capture 39% of the time. The piece class distribution (121 major, 9 minor) confirms it is overwhelmingly the queen being 'hung' via the voluntary trade. All 12 top-activating moves are Qxd8 or Qxd1 in positions with an open d-file.
analysis.why_bad: By trading queens on the d-file, the player eliminates their most active piece and enters a roughly equal or worse endgame/middlegame. The better moves (Qc2, Qg4, Qa4+, Qc4+, Qxh4, etc.) exploit tactical features the queen uniquely enables—winning undefended pieces, delivering forks, or launching attacks against the exposed king—netting at least a minor piece worth of material. The queen trade neutralizes all these advantages.

analysis.label: The player advances a pawn (or plays a quiet move) instead of making a critical pawn exchange that the position demands.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 93% of best moves are captures, yet only 7% of played moves are captures — nearly every activation represents a missed pawn exchange. The best captures are SEE=0 (equal exchanges, not material wins — only 10% win material), indicating these are structurally or tactically critical pawn trades rather than simple material grabs. After the quiet move is played, 34% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with 37 pawns, 10 majors, 4 minors in the distribution), showing that failing to exchange often leaves the advanced or exposed pawn itself vulnerable. The top boards confirm: best moves are pxp captures (hxg4, hxg5, cxb4, cxb5, axb5, gxf5, bxc4) and the played moves are frequently advances of the very same pawn past the capture square (h4 instead of hxg4, h5 instead of hxg5, c5 instead of cxb5, a5 instead of axb5).
analysis.why_bad: By pushing the pawn past its capture opportunity (or ignoring the exchange entirely), the player loses the option to favorably resolve pawn tension. This often leaves the advanced pawn overextended and undefended, creates structural weaknesses, or allows the opponent to dictate the pawn structure. The resulting positions collapse quickly — average cp_loss is 875 — because the missed exchange was often the only move holding the position together, and the alternative leaves pieces (especially the pushed pawn) tactically vulnerable.

analysis.label: Player neglects a forced bishop trade, leaving their own bishop hanging and lost on the next move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 71% of the time the played move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung piece overwhelmingly being a minor piece (122 of 139 cases). The best move is a capture in 96% of positions (29% with check), yet these captures win 0 material — indicating they are equal exchanges. In every top-activating position, a bishop is in mutual tension with an enemy piece (e.g., Bg5 vs Be7, Bb5 vs Bd7, Bg4 vs Be2), and the correct move is to execute the bishop exchange immediately (Bxe7, Bxd7+, Bxe2, Bxd2+). Instead, the player ignores this tension and plays a developing or other move, after which the opponent simply captures the now-undefended bishop for free.
analysis.why_bad: When two bishops (or a bishop and another piece) are in mutual tension and one side's bishop is undefended or will become undefended, the exchange must be resolved immediately. By playing something else, the player loses the right to trade equally — the opponent captures the hanging bishop on the next move, winning a full minor piece (~3 pawns) for nothing.

analysis.label: Player moves a knight to an aggressive or capturing square where it is left undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player hangs their own piece: 87% of played moves leave an own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece class distribution dominated by minor pieces (153 of 204 cases). All 12 top-activating moves are knight moves (Nd5, Nxd5, Nf5, Nxe5, Nxd3, Nxc6, etc.), and in nearly every case the knight itself is the piece left hanging after the move (value 2-3). Meanwhile, 60% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 2.0), meaning the player not only hangs their knight but also misses a stronger alternative. Only 40% of the played moves are captures, showing the pattern includes both knight captures and quiet knight jumps that land on undefended squares.
analysis.why_bad: The knight move — whether a tempting capture or an aggressive-looking centralization — places the knight on a square where it lacks sufficient defense. The opponent can simply recapture or pick off the unprotected knight, resulting in a net material loss (typically a full minor piece). The player is lured by the knight's activity or a seemingly attractive exchange but fails to verify the knight's safety on its destination square.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of making a capture (SEE=0) that leads to a strategically or tactically winning position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of best moves are captures, yet these captures register as SEE=0 (materially even exchanges). Only 9% technically 'win material' per static exchange, meaning the overwhelming pattern is captures that appear equal in immediate material but produce enormous positional or tactical gains (average cp_loss of 292). The played moves are quiet (only 9% are captures themselves), and 26% leave own pieces hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 81 of 132 hung pieces). The player consistently retreats, repositions, or makes prophylactic moves when an apparently equal exchange would have been devastating — removing key defenders, opening critical lines, or creating unstoppable follow-up threats.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they surrender a concrete tactical opportunity. The captures (Rxb5, Qxd4, Rxc4, Qxd5, Qxc5, Qxe4, Rdxd3, Qxf5, Rxe4, Rxd3, Rxd5) all appear to be even exchanges by SEE, but they actually remove critical defenders, open decisive lines, or trigger winning tactical sequences. By playing passively instead, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, reposition the threatened piece, or equalize what was a dominant position.

analysis.label: Player ignores a straightforward winning capture and instead plays an ambitious move that leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a simple material-winning capture available (best move is a capture 91% of the time, winning material 52% with median value ~1 pawn/piece) but instead plays a different move—often an aggressive or 'fancy' alternative—that simultaneously leaves their own piece en prise (67% of played moves hang own material, median value 2.0, distributed across minor pieces 29, pawns 28, and major pieces 13). The feature activates on only 0.1% of positions, targeting a specific pattern where tactical greed or overambition causes the player to bypass a concrete win. The played move is itself a capture only 19% of the time, meaning players usually ignore the winning capture entirely rather than choosing the wrong capturer.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a 'fancier' plan (queen attacks, castling, pawn pushes, developing moves) over a concrete tactical capture that immediately wins material. By not taking the available capture—often a knight or pawn recapture that resolves central tension or collects a loose piece—the player not only forfeits the material advantage but also creates a new tactical vulnerability where their own piece (frequently a knight, bishop, or even queen) is left undefended and can be taken on the next move. The classic examples are playing Bxd5 instead of exd5 (wrong capturer exposing the bishop), or playing Qf3/Qh4/O-O instead of Nxc6/Nxd4/Nxc3 (ignoring a winning knight capture to pursue a speculative plan).

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy piece sitting en prise and plays a quiet developing move instead of the obvious winning capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 94% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0), and 98% of the time the best move is a simple capture. Yet only 11% of the actually-played moves were captures — the player overwhelmingly chose quiet moves. In the top boards, the pattern is consistent: an enemy piece (frequently a queen, sometimes a bishop) has moved to a square directly capturable by a pawn or piece (e.g., gxh5, Rxh7, exf4, dxc4, Bxb6, exf6), and the player completely ignores this free material to play a routine developing move. The 46% own-piece-hanging rate reflects that some of the quiet moves played also leave pieces loose, compounding the blunder, but the core mistake is the failure to capture the opponent's undefended piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they forfeit massive free material — often an entire queen — by ignoring an enemy piece sitting undefended on a square directly attacked by the player's pawn or piece. Instead of collecting the free capture (typically worth 3–9 points), the player makes a quiet positional or developmental move, handing the opponent time to move the hanging piece to safety and sometimes even leaving their own pieces exposed in the process.

analysis.label: Queen captures a pawn/piece but walks into a losing queen exchange in a queen endgame.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player greedily captures material with their Queen, but the capture square allows the opponent to recapture the Queen (forcing an unfavorable queen trade). The SEE aggregate confirms this: 97% of played moves are captures, and 96% leave the player's own piece hanging with a median value of 9 (a Queen), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (63/64). The best move wins material 67% of the time (median 3.0 = a piece/pawn), often through checks (40%) that maintain queen activity rather than trading. The pattern occurs in queen endgames and middlegames where keeping queens on the board—exploiting perpetual check chances, exposed kings, or dynamic piece activity—is far superior to capturing material that forces a queen exchange into a lost pawn endgame.
analysis.why_bad: The Queen captures a pawn or piece on a square where the opponent's Queen can immediately recapture, forcing a queen trade. In these positions, the resulting pawn endgame is losing (or much worse) because the opponent has a structural advantage, passed pawns, or king activity. The better approach is to maintain queen activity through checks, threats, or repositioning moves that exploit the opponent's king weaknesses without surrendering the queen.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player overlooks a simple king capture of an adjacent undefended enemy piece, instead playing a tempting but inferior move that often hangs their own material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (11/12 boards) where the player commits a catastrophic tactical oversight. The SEE aggregate shows that 63% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0), yet players choose wrong moves—50% of which are captures themselves (often the WRONG capture) and 50% of which leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distribution: 36 pawns, 20 majors, 13 minors). Only 27% of best moves are captures in the SEE sense, because many winning moves are king steps onto an undefended piece. The pattern repeatedly shows a king adjacent to an unprotected enemy rook or knight (positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 12) where the player inexplicably plays a different move—a flashy check (Nxd4+, e4+), a greedy but wrong capture (Kxf5 instead of Kxe6), or a passive quiet move (c3, Rh3, Kd3)—throwing away a completely won position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores the simplest and most decisive option—capturing a free enemy piece with the king—and instead plays a superficially attractive move (check, different capture, pawn advance) that either misses the winning material entirely or actively hangs their own piece. In endgames where material advantage is decisive, overlooking a free rook or knight is immediately fatal.

analysis.label: Player blunders their queen en prise in a completely won position (often with forced mate available) instead of finding the decisive check or capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 80% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 8.0, corresponding to a queen), with the piece class distribution confirming major pieces (55 out of 60 instances). Simultaneously, 79% of best moves win material (median 6.0), and critically 52% of best moves are checks and 44% are captures—indicating precise finishing moves were available. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (10/12) where the player already has a decisive advantage or forced checkmate, yet instead of delivering the killing blow, they make a queen move (or a move that leaves their queen undefended) that allows the opponent to capture it, converting a won game into a draw or losing position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the player's queen (worth ~9 points) completely undefended or on an attacked square. In most cases, the player had a forced checkmate but chose a 'fancy' or imprecise move—a check on the wrong square (Qa4+ instead of Qb1+), a greedy capture (Qxa7+ instead of Qb5+), a premature promotion (f1=Q+ where the queen is immediately capturable), or a random non-queen move (Be4, Kf7, Kf4) that abandons defense of the queen. The opponent then simply captures the hanging queen, erasing a material or mating advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a seemingly natural Queen or Rook repositioning move that misses concrete tactics or leaves own material undefended.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player chooses a 'positionally motivated' but tactically poor Queen or Rook move—typically placing the piece on a central or open-file square—when the position demands concrete action. The SEE aggregate shows that in 48% of cases, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, suggesting a minor piece or equivalent), and in 46% of cases the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0; distribution: 44 pawns, 41 majors, 6 minors). Only 12% of played moves are captures, confirming the passive nature of the chosen moves. The best moves include checks (19%) and captures (27%), with many others being pawn pushes or king moves—all concrete actions the player bypassed in favor of piece shuffling. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a specific failure pattern rather than general weak play.
analysis.why_bad: These Queen/Rook repositioning moves fail because they prioritize vague piece activity over concrete positional or tactical demands. By moving a major piece to a 'nice-looking' square, the player often removes the piece from a defensive duty (hanging a pawn or another major piece in 46% of cases) or overlooks a forcing sequence—a check, capture, or pawn advance—that wins material or delivers decisive threats. The result is an average centipawn loss of 1130, reflecting catastrophic missed opportunities in favor of aimless piece shuffling.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy knight on a kingside square (g4/g5/h5) that can be freely captured by the queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e. a knight), and 98% of the time the best move is a capture, yet the player's move was a capture only 10% of the time. The median value won of exactly 3.0 corresponds precisely to what the boards confirm: in every single top-activating position, an enemy knight has aggressively lunged to a kingside square (g5, g4, or h5) and sits completely undefended, while the queen has a clean capture available (Qxg5, Qxg4, or Qxh5). The pattern overwhelmingly arises in Italian Game / Two Knights-style openings where White plays Ng5 targeting f7, but the knight is unprotected. Only 28% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median 1.0, mostly pawns), confirming the primary error is missed winning rather than self-hanging.
analysis.why_bad: Instead of taking the free knight (worth ~3 pawns), the player makes a developing or positional move (Nf6, Nh6, a6, Nc6, etc.) that ignores the immediate tactic. This squanders a full piece of material and often converts a winning position into an equal or even slightly worse one, typically losing 300-500 centipawns of evaluation.

analysis.label: Player missed a simple capture of an undefended enemy piece (usually a rook) sitting directly on the same open file or line.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 92% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 95% of the time the best move is a capture, yet only 10% of the played moves were captures. This overwhelmingly indicates the player missed taking a hanging enemy piece. The 45% own-hung-after rate is a secondary consequence: when two pieces face each other on the same file and you fail to capture first, your own piece becomes the one that gets taken. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 boards) where rooks confront each other on open files, with one rook undefended and freely capturable — often with check (36% of best moves are checks). Instead of the winning capture, players chose quiet king moves or passive pawn pushes.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (typically a rook worth ~5 pawns). In many cases the opponent's piece is directly attacked with no defender, and delaying the capture either allows the opponent to move their piece to safety or — worse — allows the opponent to capture YOUR undefended piece first, turning a winning position into a lost one. The average cp_loss of 3278 centipawns reflects full-piece swings.

analysis.label: The player retreats their king (or makes a passive move) in a critical pawn endgame instead of maintaining opposition, blockade, or active positioning, turning drawn or won positions into losses.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player makes a catastrophic passive king move (avg cp_loss: 3535). The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material in 29% of positions with a median value of 9.0 (reflecting eventual queen promotions secured by correct technique), while the played move is almost never a capture (2%) and rarely hangs material (12%, median 1.0). The critical pattern is a king retreating toward the back rank or corner instead of maintaining opposition or blockade on a critical square. Positions 1, 3, 10, 12 show drawn positions collapsing into losses; positions 11, 7, 6 show advantages being thrown away—all because the king moved backward when it needed to hold ground or advance.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king must maintain opposition (staying directly facing the enemy king with one square between), blockade passed pawns by standing in front of them, or centralize actively. Retreating the king surrenders these critical geometric relationships—allowing the opponent's king to outflank, the opponent's pawn to advance past the blockade square, or losing the opposition that held the draw. Once the king retreats one square, the position transitions from theoretical draw to theoretical loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting pawn/piece capture that leaves their own more valuable piece hanging, when a better move would have safely won material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a greedy capture (97% of played moves are captures) that leaves their own piece en prise (88% of moves hang an own piece, median value 3.0 — distributed evenly across pawns, minors, and majors including queens). Crucially, the best move also wins material in 84% of cases (median 3.0), meaning the player could have profited without the self-inflicted tactical damage. The pattern is overwhelmingly an opening-phase impulsive recapture (often a pawn take like dxe7, dxc6, dxc3) that ignores a back-rank or open-file/diagonal vulnerability, most commonly leaving a queen or minor piece undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because the player is distracted by an immediate material grab (taking a piece or pawn) while ignoring that the capture removes a defender, opens a line, or simply leaves a higher-value piece (often the queen on an open d-file, or a bishop/knight) unprotected. The opponent then wins back more material than was captured, resulting in massive centipawn losses (avg ~1274cp). A calmer move — often a retreat, development move, or king move — would have consolidated the advantage and still won material.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing or routine move, missing a concrete tactical opportunity to win significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly shows a 'missed winning' pattern: 75% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while the player's move is almost never a capture (6%) and rarely hangs their own piece (10%). The best moves are checks 22% of the time and captures 20% of the time, indicating concrete tactical strikes. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet developmental moves—Qe2 (appears 3 times), Nc3, Nf3, Be3, Bc1, O-O, O-O-O, d6—standard positional or developmental continuations chosen instead of tactical shots. Most positions (7/12) are in the opening phase, where players appear to be on autopilot with routine development while overlooking forcing sequences (forks, checks winning material, pawn advances winning pieces) that exploit concrete vulnerabilities in the opponent's position.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they waste a critical tactical moment. The opponent has a concrete vulnerability (undefended piece, exposed king, alignment for a fork) that can be exploited immediately. By playing routine development instead, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, defend the weakness, or untangle—permanently losing the window to win material. The average cp_loss of 142 reflects squandering winning advantages by treating a sharp tactical position as a calm positional one.

analysis.label: Player makes an active or greedy move (often a capture) that leaves their own major piece undefended, missing a better tactical continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a severe tactical error by making a superficially attractive move that leaves their own piece en prise. The SEE aggregate shows 59% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with major pieces—rooks and queens—comprising 47 of 98 classified hung-piece instances). Simultaneously, 58% of positions had a best move that wins material (median value 3.0), indicating the player not only hung their own piece but also missed a winning opportunity. The played move was itself a capture 45% of the time, suggesting players are lured by material gain on one square while overlooking that their piece is unprotected on its destination or that a critical tactical shot existed elsewhere. The extremely high average centipawn loss (3556) reflects that many of these errors are game-ending, sometimes allowing immediate checkmate.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a tempting capture or active placement without verifying that the moved piece (usually a rook or queen) is safe on its new square, or without checking for more forcing alternatives (checks, winning captures, defensive necessities). The result is either the immediate loss of the moved major piece to a recapture/tactic, or the squandering of a decisive tactical opportunity such as a winning check or fork.

analysis.label: The player makes a greedy capture or routine move instead of creating a king escape square (luft) with a kingside pawn push, allowing immediate forced mate on the back rank.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is trapped behind its own pawns (typically f2/g2/h2 or f7/g7/h7) with an enemy rook poised on an open file to deliver back-rank mate. The best move in these positions is nearly always a kingside pawn push (h3, h4, g3, g4, f4) that creates luft while often simultaneously winning material—the aggregate shows best move wins material 50% of the time (median value 2.0) despite only 12% being captures and 7% checks, confirming these are quiet pawn moves that save the king while also gaining. The player instead plays a capture 39% of the time (grabbing pawns or pieces elsewhere on the board), completely ignoring the mating threat. The 34% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 76/142) likely reflects that the greedy captures leave the position open for the opponent's mating combination. The average cp_loss of ~9685 confirms these moves convert survivable positions into immediate forced mates.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most urgent threat in the position—back-rank mate. While the player grabs material (Rxb4, Rxc4, Rxa7, Rxe6, etc.) or makes positional moves, the opponent's rook(s) crash through on the open d/e-file to deliver checkmate on the enclosed back rank. A simple one-square pawn push would have created an escape square, often even winning material in the process since the opponent's pieces are committed to the now-refuted mating attack.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move instead of exploiting the opponent's vulnerable f7 square (or exposed king in center) with a forcing tactical blow.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the time the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), yet the player's move was a capture only 5% of the time — a classic 'missed winning tactic' signature. Best moves are checks 19% and captures 33%, indicating forcing tactical strikes. Only 14% of played moves hang the player's own piece, confirming the mistake direction is failing to exploit rather than blundering material. The boards overwhelmingly feature Italian Game-type structures where Black's king remains on e8, the f7 pawn is under-protected (often only by the king, with Nd7 blocking support), and White's Bc4 directly targets f7. The missed best moves are almost always tactical blows at f7 (Bxf7+, Ng5, Qd5 threatening f7, Ne5) or exploiting the uncastled king (d5+).
analysis.why_bad: The quiet developing moves (O-O, Nc3, Be3, Bb3, Kh1) are bad because they surrender a decisive tactical advantage. By castling or developing another piece, White gives Black time to complete development, castle, and neutralize the f7 weakness. The position demands immediate action — the tactical window to exploit the opponent's undeveloped state and vulnerable f7 square is temporary, and once Black consolidates, White's advantage evaporates (average cp_loss of 379).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet/passive move (usually a king move) in a critical position with an advanced passed pawn, missing the urgent tactical response needed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a pawn is typically one square from promotion, creating extreme tactical urgency. The SEE aggregate shows 60% of best moves win material (median value 3.0), 58% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns: 110, minors: 94, majors: 86), and only 23% of played moves are captures. The best moves are often forcing (42% captures, 8% checks), but the player instead chooses a quiet move—most commonly a passive king retreat. The feature fires on 0.6% of all positions, nearly all in endgames (9/12 top boards), with an extraordinarily high average cp_loss of 1662.
analysis.why_bad: In positions with advanced passed pawns about to promote, only concrete tactical responses (checks, forks, captures, counter-promotions) can save or win the game. A passive king move or quiet piece retreat ignores the immediate crisis—the promotion will occur next move, often winning decisive material or the game outright. The quiet move both misses the critical counter-tactic and frequently leaves the player's own pieces vulnerable to the newly promoted queen or the opponent's tactical follow-ups.

analysis.label: Player misses a decisive rook check (often mate or winning major material) and instead plays a quiet king or pawn move in a rook endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of the time the best move is a check and 98% of the time it wins material (median value 100, indicating checkmate or decisive gain), while only 8% of best moves are captures — meaning the winning resource is almost always a non-capturing rook check. The played moves were captures only 18% of the time, and in 25% of cases the player's own piece was left hanging. The feature fires exclusively in endgames (all 12 top positions) where both kings are exposed and a rook check would deliver immediate checkmate or force a winning sequence. Instead, the player chose quiet king moves (Ke2, Kh4, Kf4, Kb3, Kd1) or passive pawn pushes (e4, g3, g2, h3, b4, c7), completely overlooking the rook's checking power along open files and ranks.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available rook check that either delivers checkmate outright (Rh1#, positions 6 and 10) or initiates a forced sequence winning decisive material or mating. By playing a king move or pawn push, the player allows the opponent to escape the mating net, equalize, or even win, squandering positions that were objectively won in one or a few moves.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive move (capture or check) that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows an overwhelming 86% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), with 57% of the played moves being captures. The hung pieces span pawns (3), minors (2), and majors (1). Only 29% of best moves win material, and critically 0% of best moves are captures — meaning the correct response was usually a quiet consolidating move rather than a tactical one.
