The feature fires almost exclusively in the opening (5/7 top boards), suggesting players are lured by forcing/aggressive continuations before securing their own material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize tactical initiative (checks, captures, threats) over piece safety. The player grabs a pawn, delivers a check, or plays an active developing move without noticing that the piece they moved — or a piece they left behind — is now undefended and can be captured by the opponent. The resulting material loss (typically a pawn or minor piece) outweighs any temporary initiative gained.

analysis.label: The player promotes a pawn to a Queen on a square controlled by an enemy piece, immediately hanging the newly-created Queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 89% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being 'major' pieces (15 of 16 classified instances — here Queens and Rooks). Examining the top 12 boards, 8 of 12 moves are pawn promotions to Queen (e8=Q, c8=Q, g8=Q, b8=Q+, g1=Q, g1=Q, f8=Q, c1=Q), where the promotion square is guarded by an enemy rook, bishop, or knight that immediately captures the new Queen. The best move wins material 61% of the time (median 91 centipawns) and is a check 33% of the time but never a capture (0%), indicating the correct play is typically a patient king retreat, underpromotion, or a deflecting check — not the greedy promotion.
analysis.why_bad: The promoted Queen lands on a square already controlled by an enemy piece (rook, bishop, or knight), so it is immediately captured. The player invests the irreplaceable passed pawn for a Queen that survives zero moves, often converting a salvageable endgame into a lost one. Patient alternatives (king moves, underpromotions, or intermediate checks) would preserve the pawn's potential or win material through better move order.

analysis.label: Player continues aggressive/greedy play in a sharp opening instead of castling, leaving their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 84% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece), with the distribution showing minors (16), pawns (13), and majors (9). The best move wins material 64% of the time (median 2.0), largely because castling would have consolidated the position and saved the threatened piece. Only 36% of the played moves were captures and only 16% of best moves were captures, confirming the pattern: the correct response was typically a quiet defensive/consolidating move (O-O), not a tactical strike. The feature fires almost exclusively in opening positions (11/12) where the king remains in the center, and the player extends an aggressive attack (often in Fried Liver / Italian Game structures) rather than castling to safety.
analysis.why_bad: By continuing the attack with captures (Nxe5, Nxh8, Bxb4, Nxe4, Rxe5) or aggressive developing moves (Qh5, Bg4, Bb3, Nf3, g3) instead of castling, the player leaves a piece undefended — typically the bishop on the attacking diagonal or the knight that has ventured forward. The opponent can then exploit the uncastled king and capture the hanging piece, converting their counterplay into decisive material advantage. Castling would simultaneously protect the vulnerable piece (often via rook connection) and remove the king from the dangerous center.

analysis.label: Player ignores a decisive check (often a back-rank or king-hunt tactic) that wins major material or forces mate, opting instead for a greedy capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: the best move is a check in 97% of the top 500 activating positions, and in 65% of those the check wins material with a median SEE value of 95 (Queen-equivalent). Instead of delivering the crushing check, the played move was a capture only 28% of the time (often a greedy queen capture on an unrelated square) and a quiet move the rest. The 'own hung' rate of 64% with a median value of just 1 (mostly pawns) is a secondary artifact—playing the wrong move sometimes leaves a pawn loose—not the primary error. The true pattern is a player who overlooks a check that either mates or wins a Rook/Queen via tactics (back-rank, king exposure, or discovered attack) in favor of an inferior alternative.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they squander a forced tactical sequence. The available check either delivers immediate checkmate (avg cp_loss ~3456) or wins decisive material through a forcing line that the opponent cannot parry. By playing a quiet move or greedy capture elsewhere, the player gives the opponent time to consolidate, defend the back rank, or even counter-attack—often turning a won game into a loss or draw.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free capture of an undefended enemy knight (typically on e5/d4) in the opening, often seduced by a flashy Bxf2+ check that leaves their own bishop en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 68% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = minor piece) and 80% of best moves are captures, indicating a consistently available free piece. Meanwhile, 57% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0, distribution heavily minor pieces at 19/25). Only 27% of played moves are captures. The pattern is clear: in the opening, an enemy knight sits undefended on a central square (e5, e4, or d4), and the player's knight can simply take it for free. Instead, the player is seduced by an alternative—most often Bxf2+ (a check that looks forcing but leaves the bishop hanging after the king moves) or a quiet developing move that ignores the tactical gift entirely.
analysis.why_bad: Bxf2+ gives check but after Kxf2 or the king sidesteps, Black has traded a bishop for a pawn while the free enemy knight on e5/d4 remains alive—a net loss of ~2 pawns worth of material. Similarly, quiet developing moves simply ignore a hanging piece worth 3 points. The simple Nxe5/Nxd4/Nxe4 wins a full minor piece with no compensation for the opponent, but players are distracted by the allure of giving check or 'improving' their position.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple capture of an undefended enemy rook (or equivalent major piece), instead playing a check or quiet king move in an endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 84% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 91% of best moves are captures, yet only 9% of the actually-played moves were captures. Only 28% of played moves hung the player's own piece, confirming this is overwhelmingly a 'missed winning capture' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. Across all 12 top-activating positions (100% endgame, avg cp_loss 723), the best move is a trivially available capture of an undefended enemy rook — via Rxh6, Rxc6, Kxf6, Kxb3, Kxc5, Rxf3, Rxa4, Kxh2, Rxd2, Rxa8, Kxb5 — but the player instead plays a tempting check (Rc2+, Rb2+, Qb4+, Rb1+) or a purposeless king/rook move (Ke2, Ke8, Kb3, Kf5, Rg8, Kd7, Kc6).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available free capture of a major piece (almost always a rook worth ~5 points). The players get distracted by giving checks, advancing their king, or pursuing phantom plans, while a completely undefended enemy rook sits en prise. The resulting positions collapse from decisive advantages (or winning positions) into draws or losses, with a median loss of ~700+ centipawns.

analysis.label: Player misses a forcing check that delivers checkmate or wins decisive material, playing a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 95% of the best moves are checks and 90% win material with a median value of 95 (essentially game-ending). The average cp_loss is 6425, consistent with missing forced mates. Only 25% of played moves were captures, and the vast majority of played moves were quiet non-forcing moves. The 58% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental — the real catastrophe is ignoring the winning check. Across the top boards, positions consistently show forced mate-in-2 to mate-in-5 via a check (Ra7+, Rxf7+, Rf8+, Qe6+, Re6+, Ra2+, Qe1+, c8=Q+) that the player completely overlooks in favor of an aimless quiet move like a pawn push or passive piece shuffle.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they squander a forced checkmate or near-instant win. The opponent's king is fatally exposed (back rank, weak pawn shield, or cornered), and a single check initiates an unstoppable mating net — often mate-in-2 with doubled rooks on the 7th rank or a queen/rook delivering discovered/corridor mate. By playing a quiet move, the player gives the opponent time to escape, defend, or generate counterplay, converting a trivial forced win into a long grind or even a draw.

analysis.label: The player missed a tactical check (often a sacrifice or fork) that wins material or initiates a decisive combination.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: the best move is a check in 88% of the top 500 activating positions, while the player instead chose a quiet move (only 25% captures played). The best move wins material 64% of the time with a median value of 97 (approximately a minor piece), indicating knight/bishop forks or sacrificial checks that win back more. The 43% best-move-is-capture rate combined with the 88% check rate shows many are sacrifice-checks (Bxh2+, Bxf2+) that appear to win nothing on SEE but unlock devastating follow-ups like winning the queen. The 48% own-hang rate (median value 3, i.e. a pawn) is a secondary consequence—by playing a passive move instead of the forcing check, the player sometimes also left material loose.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore a forcing check that either forks the king and a major piece (Nf6+, Nf3+, Nxe7+, Bb5+), or sacrifices a piece with check to deflect the king away from defending a more valuable piece (Bxh2+, Bxf2+ winning the queen). By playing a non-forcing move, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, eliminating the tactical opportunity and often resulting in 500-900 centipawn losses.

analysis.label: In a winning endgame, the player fails to make a simplifying capture (usually with check) that would immediately convert the advantage, instead playing an aimless quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 91% of the time and a check 60% of the time, yet the player's move was itself a capture only 6% of the time—they almost always played a quiet move instead. The captures have SEE value of 0, meaning they are equal exchanges (e.g., rook takes rook), but they are tactically decisive because they simplify into trivially won positions or come with check preventing recapture. The 'best_wins_material' figure is only 26% because the exchanges are materially neutral (rook for rook, queen for queen), yet the strategic gain is overwhelming. In 37% of cases (median value 5.0, mostly major pieces), the quiet move even left the player's own piece hanging, compounding the error. All 12 top positions are endgames with an average cp_loss of 1123.
analysis.why_bad: The played quiet moves (king retreats, passive rook moves, wrong promotions) fail because they allow the opponent to maintain their last defensive piece or even create counterplay. The correct captures—almost always with check—remove the opponent's only active piece, convert to a trivially won simplified position, or force immediate mate. By declining the exchange, the player either throws away the entire winning advantage or hangs their own piece on the next move.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive queen retreat (often to a1/a8) instead of initiating a forcing check sequence that draws or wins in endgames with advanced passed pawns.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 63% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, i.e. queen-equivalent), 32% of best moves are checks, while only 10% of played moves are captures and most are quiet retreats. The 25% own-hang rate (median 1.0, mostly pawns) is secondary noise. The dominant pattern across 500 positions is the player missing a critical checking sequence: in queen endgames (11/12 top boards) featuring dangerous passed pawns near promotion, the player retreats their queen to a passive corner square (Qa1 or Qa8 appear in 7/12 top positions) to blockade or monitor the pawn, completely missing that an immediate check initiates a perpetual or decisive forcing sequence. The enormous average cp_loss of 2620 reflects that these passive moves typically convert a drawable position into a loss, or a won position into a draw/loss.
analysis.why_bad: By playing passively (Qa1/Qa8/king moves), the player allows the opponent's passed pawn to promote or the opponent to consolidate. The missed checking sequence (Qf5+, Qd1+, Qh1+, Qa7+, Qb7+, Re8+) either forces perpetual check for a draw in otherwise lost positions, or creates a decisive attack/mate. Once the quiet move is played, the opponent's advanced pawn promotes and the forcing geometry is gone forever.

analysis.label: Player makes a flashy aggressive piece move (typically Bxf7+ or a knight lunge) instead of a strong positional pawn break that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 68% of the time (median 1 pawn), yet the best move is NEVER a capture (0%) and NEVER a check (0%) — indicating the material is won through positional pawn breaks that create unavoidable threats. Meanwhile, the player's move left their OWN piece hanging 46% of the time (median value 2.0, predominantly minors at 126/230). Only 19% of played moves were captures. The pattern is unmistakable: in opening positions where a simple pawn advance (d4, c6, d5, f6, c3, etc.) would win material through positional pressure, the player instead launches a premature tactical strike — most characteristically Bxf7+ bishop sacrifices or aggressive knight moves — that leaves their piece en prise without adequate compensation.
analysis.why_bad: The premature sacrifices (especially Bxf7+) don't have sufficient tactical justification — after the king recaptures, the sacrificed bishop is simply lost without a winning follow-up. Similarly, aggressive knight moves to exposed squares get trapped or captured. Meanwhile, the ignored pawn breaks (d4, c6, f6, d5) would have exploited concrete positional weaknesses — undermining pawn chains, opening lines, or attacking inadequately defended central pawns — gaining material through positional logic rather than speculative tactics.

analysis.label: Player makes an obvious capture but misses a far stronger intermediate check (zwischenzug) that wins material or avoids leaving their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player executes a straightforward capture (80% of played moves are captures) but overlooks a powerful zwischenzug — an intermediate check available as the best move in 92% of activating positions. The best move wins material in 73% of cases (median value ~queen). By skipping the intermediate check, the player's capture often leaves their own piece hanging (67% of the time, median value 3 centipawns ≈ minor piece; distribution: 31 major, 21 minor, 11 pawn). The player sees an 'obvious' recapture or material grab but fails to insert the check first, which would either net additional material, reposition a piece to safety, or create a decisive tactical follow-up. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating a specific tactical geometry where a check intersects with a capture opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: By capturing immediately instead of inserting the intermediate check, the player gives the opponent a tempo to respond — typically recapturing or counterattacking the player's now-hanging piece. The zwischenzug check would force the opponent's king to move first, allowing the player to then complete the capture sequence with extra material or without losing their own piece. The average cp_loss of 1208 reflects that these missed zwischenzugs often convert winning positions into losing ones.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free enemy minor piece (bishop or knight) that can be captured in one move, instead playing a routine developing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 90% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = minor piece), and 95% of the time the best move is a simple capture. Yet the player's move was itself a capture only 15% of the time, confirming the player consistently missed taking a free enemy piece. Only 32% of positions involved hanging one's own piece, so the dominant pattern is the missed capture, not a self-hang. The feature fires exclusively on opening positions (11/12 boards) where an enemy bishop or knight sits undefended on a square already attacked, and the player continues normal development (Be2, Nc6, O-O, d5, c3, etc.) rather than collecting the free material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical reality—an undefended enemy minor piece worth ~3 points that can be taken immediately. By playing routine developing or positional moves, the player throws away a full piece of material (average cp_loss ~428), turning a winning position into an equal or losing one. In chess, material gains trump abstract development when the capture is safe and free.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a quiet king move instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece worth a rook or more.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the player missed winning material: 88% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 91% of best moves are captures, yet only 5% of played moves were captures. Own-piece hanging is low at 16% (median 1.0), confirming this is a 'missed capture' pattern, not a 'hung own piece' pattern. Across the top 12 boards—all endgames—10 of 12 moves played are king moves (Kh3, Ke7, Kf5, Kg7, Ke7, Kd6, Kh2, Kg6, etc.), while the best move is a trivial one-move capture of a completely undefended enemy rook or queen by a bishop, knight, pawn, or rook. The player reflexively centralizes or repositions their king while a free major piece sits en prise.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves fail because they ignore a free capture worth 5+ pawns of material. The enemy piece (usually a rook or queen) is completely undefended and directly capturable in one move. By playing a quiet king move instead, the player throws away a decisive material advantage—often converting a winning position into a draw or even a loss, with average centipawn loss of 2844.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning check that simultaneously captures a pawn near the enemy king, often delivering immediate checkmate or a decisive attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a check (93% of cases) that is also a capture (85%), typically taking a pawn on the g- or h-file adjacent to the enemy king (median material won: 1.0 pawn). In many cases this delivers outright checkmate (positions 3, 6, 12: Qxh7#, Qxg7#, Qxg2#). The player instead played a quiet or inferior move, and in 52% of cases also left their own piece hanging (median value 2.0). The average cp_loss of 5124 reflects that these missed opportunities are catastrophic—often missed mates. The feature fires on only 0.2% of positions, representing rare but obvious tactical finishes on a weakened king pawn cover.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore an immediately decisive blow—a capture with check on the enemy king's pawn shield (g2/g4/g7/h6/h7) that either mates outright or wins overwhelming material. Instead, the player makes a quiet developing move, a wrong check, or an inferior capture, squandering a position where the enemy king's exposed pawns create an instant tactical finish.

analysis.label: Player overlooks that their bishop can capture an undefended enemy piece (usually a rook) in an endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 72% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 66% of best moves are captures, yet the player's move was a capture only 9% of the time. In 10 of the top 12 positions, the best move is specifically a bishop capture (Bxh8, Bxa1, Bxe3, Bxd8, Bxc3, Bxd4) taking a hanging or undefended major piece. The player instead plays quiet king moves (Kf5, Kc2, Kf4, Kb2, Kf6, Kh5) or pawn pushes (g5, f5, g4), completely ignoring the bishop's attacking diagonal. The 38% own-hang rate is a secondary effect in some cases, but the dominant and consistent pattern is failing to use the bishop to capture free material.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (mostly king walks or pawn advances) ignore a free tactical capture by the bishop. The hanging enemy piece—almost always a rook worth ~5 points—sits undefended on the bishop's diagonal. By not taking it, the player throws away a decisive material advantage, often converting a near-equal or losing position into a hopeless deficit (average cp_loss ~1086).

analysis.label: Player makes a queen move (often a greedy capture) instead of delivering a devastating check with a non-queen piece against an exposed king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 95% of the time the best move is a check and 95% of the time the best move wins material (median value ~97, i.e., winning a queen or forcing mate), yet only 14% of best moves are captures — meaning the winning checks are positional piece intrusions, not recaptures. The played moves are exclusively queen moves (often greedy captures of wing pawns like h2, h6, h7, b2 at 27% capture rate). The feature fires when a non-queen piece (rook, knight, bishop, or even pawn) can deliver a crushing check against an exposed enemy king, but the player instead uses their queen for an inferior purpose. Own-hang rate is only 23% (mostly pawns), confirming the mistake is missed opportunity rather than blundering material.
analysis.why_bad: The queen moves fail because they waste tempo on captures or repositioning while ignoring a check from another piece (Re2+, Rc2+, Ne2+, Bf2+, Nd5+, e5+, etc.) that exploits the exposed enemy king. These checks typically force mate or win decisive material through discovered attacks, forks, or forcing the king into a mating net. The queen captures gain at most a pawn while missing forced mates or queen-value gains.

analysis.label: Player makes a move that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise, often while missing a concrete tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move leaves their own piece hanging: 62% of the top 500 positions show the played move left an own piece en prise (median value 3.0, corresponding to minor/major pieces; distribution: 141 minors, 90 majors, 79 pawns). Meanwhile, the best move was a capture 53% of the time and won material 49% of the time (median value 1.0). The player frequently chose an 'active-looking' move — a check (Ng2+, Bxg2+, Rxg2+), a capture (Bxf7), a piece relocation (Bf4, Bh3, Qc1, Re2) — that neglected the safety of an existing piece. The feature fires on 0.4% of positions with an average cp_loss of 1883, indicating catastrophic tactical oversights in complex middlegame positions.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the immediate tactical requirements of the position. By playing an 'attractive' or seemingly purposeful move, the player overlooks that their existing piece coordination has been disrupted, leaving a minor piece, major piece, or pawn undefended and capturable. Simultaneously, the correct move was typically a concrete tactical shot (a capture winning material or maintaining coordination), making the mistake doubly costly — they both miss winning material and lose their own.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy queen (or major piece) that can be captured for free, instead playing an unrelated quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the best move wins material 90% of the time (median value 9, i.e. a queen), and 94% of best moves are captures, while only 8% of played moves were captures. This means the player consistently ignored a freely capturable enemy piece. The median value of 9 confirms the hanging piece is almost always a queen. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top positions) where the opponent's queen sits undefended on an open file or diagonal, and the player's own piece can simply take it. Additionally, 63% of the time the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5, mostly majors), compounding the error.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves are quiet moves (king walks, queen repositions) that completely ignore an enemy queen sitting en prise. Instead of winning ~9 points of material with a trivial one-move capture, the player throws away a winning position—often swinging from a decisive advantage (or forced mate) to an equal or lost position. In many cases, the quiet move also leaves the player's own major piece undefended, turning a won game into a loss.

analysis.label: The player makes an unrelated move while their own bishop (or minor piece) is under attack, leaving it hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that 93% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward minors (110 minor vs 35 major vs 2 pawn). Across the top boards, the pattern is strikingly consistent: the player has a bishop currently under threat (attacked by an advancing pawn like a5 hitting b6, g4 hitting h5, or g5 hitting f4) and instead of addressing that threat—by retreating the bishop (Bg6, Be5, Bb6), capturing the attacker, or making a tactical counter (Bxf2+, Bxc5)—the player makes an unrelated developing or positional move (O-O, Qd2, b6, g6, Ne4, Bg4). The best move wins material only 42% of the time (median 3.0), confirming this is primarily about saving one's own piece rather than missing an enemy hanging piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore an immediate tactical threat to the player's own minor piece. The opponent simply captures the undefended bishop on the next move, gaining a free piece (worth ~3 pawns). The played moves may have positional logic in a vacuum but are tactically refuted by the elementary capture of the abandoned piece.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning pawn advance (often d5, g6, f6, or c3) that wins major material, and instead plays a distracting move that frequently hangs their own pieces.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 78% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 4.0, indicating a full piece or more), while 57% of the time the actually-played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 16 majors, 10 minors, 8 pawns affected). The best moves are predominantly pawn advances (d5 appears 3 times, g6 twice, c3/f6 also present in the top 12) that create devastating tactical breakthroughs. Only 35% of best moves are captures and 12% are checks, confirming that the winning idea is usually a quiet pawn push rather than an obvious recapture. The played moves are a mix of peripheral captures (32% capture rate — bxa5, Nxa8, Bxf2+, Bxc5) and passive quiet moves (Nh7, Rf8, Nfd2, Kh2) that ignore the critical breakthrough opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a powerful pawn advance or central tactical shot that wins substantial material (often a full piece or exchange). Instead they play a move motivated by greed (grabbing peripheral material), defense, or repositioning that not only misses the win but frequently places their own pieces on unprotected squares where they become tactically vulnerable. The average cp_loss of 1118 reflects this double catastrophe of missing a major win while simultaneously creating new weaknesses.

analysis.label: In pawn endgames, the player moves the king in the wrong direction (or makes an irrelevant move) instead of heading toward a winnable enemy pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 76% of the time the best move would win material (median value: 1 pawn), yet the best move is a direct capture only 10% of the time — meaning the pawn is won through king maneuvering and penetration rather than immediate tactical capture. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, overwhelmingly pure king-and-pawn positions. The player's move was a capture only 24% of the time, and left their own piece hanging just 32% of the time (mostly pawns). The dominant pattern is the player choosing the wrong king direction or pushing a pawn when king infiltration was required: e.g., Kd4 instead of Kxb3 (Pos 7), Ke4 instead of Kc3 (Pos 8), Kf6 instead of Kxh5 (Pos 6), d4 instead of Kf2 (Pos 5), h4 instead of Kd4 (Pos 9). The material is there to be won by correct king routing, but the player misjudges the king race or target.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king tempo and direction are decisive. Moving the king away from the critical target pawn (or pushing a pawn when king penetration is needed) wastes vital tempi, allowing the opponent to achieve a drawn position through counter-infiltration or pawn races. The player fails to identify the correct pawn target and optimal king path, squandering a winning advantage.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting queen capture (often with check) that leaves the queen itself hanging on the capture square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 80% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 9.0 (queen), and the piece class distribution confirms 6 major pieces (queens/rooks) among the top hung cases. Meanwhile, 50% of the played moves are captures and many involve checks (Qxe4+, Qxf5+, Qxe6+, Qxg6+). The best move wins material 70% of the time (median 2.0), often through quieter or more positional alternatives. The feature consistently identifies positions where the player is lured by an aggressive queen capture—frequently with check—but fails to see that the queen will be recaptured or trapped on its destination square, resulting in catastrophic material loss (avg cp_loss: 181).
analysis.why_bad: These queen captures look attractive because they win material and/or deliver check, creating the illusion of a forcing sequence. However, after the opponent responds to the check (moving the king or interposing), the queen sits undefended on the capture square and is simply taken, losing approximately 9 points of material. The safer best moves (like Qe2, Qc4+, Bb5+, Rg1) either win material without exposing the queen, or address more urgent positional needs.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting move (often a capture or pawn advance) that leaves their own piece—usually a minor piece—undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 71% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece en prise (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece), with the piece class distribution dominated by minors (7) over majors (3) and pawns (2). While 59% of positions also feature a best move that wins material, and 41% of played moves are captures, the dominant error is that the player's own move creates the vulnerability. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (9/12 top boards), where players get drawn into greedy captures (Kxb2, Bxa4, Rxa3+, Bxf6+) or tempting pawn advances (b2, e7, h7) while overlooking that a piece they relied on is left unprotected.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an immediate tactical idea—capturing material, pushing a pawn toward promotion, or giving check—while overlooking that their move removes defense from (or moves away from) one of their own pieces. The opponent simply captures the hanging piece, often a knight or bishop worth 3 points, negating or reversing whatever the player hoped to achieve with their 'active' move.

analysis.label: Player fails to promote a pawn on the 7th/2nd rank, instead playing an inferior quiet move (often a rook check or pawn push).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 79% of the time with a median value of 9.0 (queen), and best move is a check 41% of the time — both perfectly consistent with missed pawn promotions (some with check). The played move is only a capture 26% of the time, meaning players overwhelmingly choose quiet alternative moves instead of promoting. All 12 top-activating positions feature a pawn on the 7th/2nd rank ready to queen, yet the player opts for a rook check, king move, or irrelevant pawn push. The 45% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the alternative moves sometimes leave pawns tactically vulnerable. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, consistent with the specific endgame scenario of having an immediately promotable pawn.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because promoting the pawn immediately creates a queen (worth ~9 points of material), which is almost always decisive in the endgame. By playing rook checks, king moves, or other pawn pushes instead, the player gives the opponent time to blockade the promotion square, capture the pawn, or generate counterplay. In many cases (positions 1, 3, 5, 9, 11), the delay converts a forced mate into a merely winning or even drawn position, squandering massive advantages.

analysis.label: Player makes an active-looking move (capture, check, or repositioning) that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 94% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-level material). The hung pieces are distributed across major pieces (30) and minor pieces (20), with queens and rooks being the most frequently exposed. Meanwhile, 74% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0), meaning the player both misses a winning continuation AND creates a tactical vulnerability. The played move is itself a capture 56% of the time, indicating the player is often lured into a tempting but flawed capture (e.g., Qxf3, Rxe5, Qxd6) that lands the piece on an attacked square or removes a key defender. The average cp_loss of 1974 confirms these are catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player either (1) moves a piece to an attacked square where it can be captured for free (e.g., Rd7+ where the rook is en prise, Qxd6 where the queen is capturable), or (2) moves a piece that was defending another piece, leaving the latter unguarded (e.g., Kg1 abandoning queen defense, Be4 leaving the queen capturable). In both cases, the opponent simply captures the hanging piece, winning decisive material.

analysis.label: Playing a purposeless a- or h-pawn push (a3/a6/h3/h6) in the opening while ignoring urgent tactical obligations.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player makes a quiet rook-pawn advance (exclusively a3, a6, h3, or h6) during the opening instead of addressing pressing tactical demands. The SEE aggregate shows that 52% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 40 and minors at 23), and 48% of the time the best move wins material for the player (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). Only 2% of moves played are captures, confirming the passive nature of the chosen moves. The best move is a capture 32% of the time and a check 12%, underscoring the tactically rich positions being ignored. Many positions feature an enemy knight on g5/g4 where h6/h3 is the instinctive 'kick' move, but the timing is catastrophically wrong because a more urgent action (winning material, exchanging queens, or defending a hanging piece) takes priority.
analysis.why_bad: These rook-pawn moves waste a critical tempo in tactically sharp opening positions. They either fail to address an immediate threat (leaving a bishop or pawn en prise), or they miss a forcing move (capture, check, or central strike) that would win material. The a/h pawn push gains nothing strategically in these positions while the opponent's tactical threats or the player's own winning opportunities demand immediate attention.

analysis.label: Player missed a queen check that wins decisive material or delivers checkmate against an exposed king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 91% of positions the best move wins material (median value 91, i.e., queen-level), and 79% of the time the best move is a check — while only 36% are captures, meaning the checks win material indirectly by forking or mating. The player's actual move was a capture only 33% of the time and left their own piece hanging 33% of the time (mostly pawns). All 12 top-activating positions feature a queen check as the best move (Qa5+, Qg5+, Qh5+, Qh6+, Qh3+, Qxf2+, Qxe5+, Qd5+, Qd7#) targeting exposed kings on squares like g7 or f7. The players instead chose routine captures, quiet developing moves, or even castling, completely missing the decisive tactical blow.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a queen check that exploits the opponent's exposed king. The check either delivers immediate checkmate (e.g., Qd7#) or forks the king with another high-value piece (typically winning the enemy queen). By playing a routine move instead, the player squanders a decisive tactical opportunity and often converts a winning position into an equal or losing one.

analysis.label: The player develops or pushes pawns instead of castling when the king is critically exposed on an open or semi-open e-file.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, 49% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces at 22/42), while 47% of the best moves win material (median value 1.0). The best move is O-O (castling) in 11 of the top 12 positions. Only 14% of played moves are captures and only 1% of best moves are checks, confirming these are quiet developing/pawn moves played when castling was urgently required. The feature fires in the opening phase (10/12 boards) when the king remains on e1/e8 with an open e-file and an enemy queen bearing down it. By failing to castle, the player's centralized king creates tactical vulnerabilities (pins, discovered attacks) that leave their own pieces hanging.
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the critical king safety problem. With the e-file open and an enemy queen aimed at the uncastled king, developing moves or pawn pushes (Bf4, f3, f4, Bg5, Nf3, etc.) leave the king exposed to immediate tactical exploitation—pins along the e-file, discovered attacks, and fork opportunities that cause pieces to hang or positional advantages to evaporate. Castling would simultaneously resolve king safety AND often defend or connect pieces.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move (usually a queen repositioning) while a winning capture—often with check—is available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 89% of the top 500 positions (with 34% also giving check), winning material 49% of the time at a median value of 5.0 (rook/queen level). Yet the player's actual move is a capture only 10% of the time—overwhelmingly they play quiet, repositioning moves instead. The secondary 45% own-hung rate (median value 1.0, heavily pawns) reflects that by ignoring the forcing capture, the player sometimes also inadvertently leaves material loose. The average cp_loss of ~1100 confirms these are catastrophic oversights. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is a clear capture (Rxc8, Qxe7+, Qxf2, Qxb8, Rxd1+, Nxc4, Rxf1+, Qxg8+, Rxg6, Qxd3, Rxc2+, Nxd5) while the player instead makes a passive quiet move—most often shuffling their queen to a non-forcing square.
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores an immediately winning or strongly forcing capture (often with check) and instead plays a non-forcing quiet move that allows the opponent to consolidate, escape, or counterattack. This squanders decisive material or a mating attack, typically swinging the evaluation by hundreds of centipawns or more.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free capture of an undefended or insufficiently defended enemy piece, playing an irrelevant quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'missed winning capture' pattern: 85% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a full rook), and 98% of best moves are simple captures — yet the player's move was a capture only 11% of the time. Instead, players chose quiet moves (king walks, rook repositions, queen relocations) while enemy queens, rooks, and minor pieces sat en prise. The 58% own-hang rate (median 3.0) is a secondary effect: playing an aimless quiet move while ignoring tactics often inadvertently leaves one's own material loose too. Across the top boards, we see undefended queens (Qxa5, Qxd8, gxf6, Qxg4 winning 8-9 points), hanging rooks (Rxc8, Bxa1, Rxf4), and exposed pieces simply available for taking — all ignored in favor of purposeless moves.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail catastrophically because a free capture of significant material (median ~5 points) exists on the board and the player completely overlooks it. By playing an irrelevant quiet move, the player forfeits a decisive material advantage — often a whole queen or rook — and frequently the opponent then consolidates or the hanging piece moves to safety, turning a winning position into a losing one. The average cp_loss of 2298 reflects the severity of missing these elementary captures.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (often a greedy capture or an irrelevant quiet move) that leaves their own queen en prise, losing it immediately.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player's move catastrophically hangs their own queen. The SEE aggregate shows 99% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., a queen), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly 'major' (278 out of 281 cases). Despite having strong positions (76% of best moves win material, median 5.0), the player instead blunders their queen — either by making a greedy queen capture onto a square where it is immediately recaptured or trapped (25% of played moves are captures, e.g., Qxa2, Qxf1, Qxa7, Qxf3), or by playing an irrelevant quiet move (e.g., a6, b6, h4, Be6) while the queen is already under direct attack. The best moves frequently involved checks (36%) or captures (26%) that would have maintained the queen's safety while pressing the advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the immediate safety of the player's queen. In capture cases, the queen grabs material on a square where it is easily recaptured or trapped by lower-value enemy pieces. In quiet-move cases, the player ignores an existing threat to their queen (e.g., a rook attacking it on an open file), allowing the opponent to simply take it next move. The result is an average 1852cp loss — essentially the full value of the queen.

analysis.label: Player ignores a straightforward material-winning capture, opting instead for an active-looking but inferior move (often a check or piece redeployment).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 92% of activating positions, the best move wins enemy material (median value 5.0 pawns), yet the player's move is only a capture 20% of the time. The best move is a direct capture 53% of the time, indicating a simple take was available. The player frequently plays checks (Rh8+, Rh7+, Bd5+), aggressive repositioning (Re3, Re1, Kg5), or inferior captures (exd6, axb4) instead. As a secondary consequence, 51% of the played moves also leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed across pawns (29), major pieces (25), and minor pieces (21). The average centipawn loss of 1118 confirms these are catastrophic errors—the player prioritizes superficial activity over concrete material gains.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they sacrifice a clear material win (often a rook or queen capture worth 3-5 pawns) in favor of moves that look active but accomplish far less. Checks and piece maneuvers may appear forcing or aggressive, but they allow the opponent to retain or protect the hanging piece. Worse, in half the cases the played move also creates a new vulnerability in the player's own position, compounding the missed opportunity into an outright blunder.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an undefended enemy piece (often a major piece) in the endgame, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 4.0, i.e. roughly a rook), and the best move is a capture in 100% of cases. Meanwhile, the player's actual move is a capture in 0% of cases, and only 14% of moves leave the player's own piece hanging (just pawns). This strongly indicates the player is missing a free capture of a hanging enemy piece rather than hanging their own material. The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions where a major enemy piece (queen or rook) is directly capturable but the player instead plays a passive quiet move, typically a king retreat or rook repositioning.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are catastrophic (avg cp_loss 4247, with many resulting in forced mate) because the player ignores a freely capturable enemy piece—often a queen or rook that is completely undefended. In many cases (e.g., Positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9), capturing the hanging piece would have drawn or kept the position competitive, but the quiet move allows the opponent to consolidate a winning or mating advantage.

analysis.label: The player captures material (or moves a piece) that lands on an unprotected square where it is immediately recapturable, hanging their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 98% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), with the piece class distribution dominated by minors (81) and majors (47). Critically, 62% of the played moves are themselves captures—the player grabs a pawn or piece but the capturing piece (typically a knight or bishop) lands on a square where it is en prise and can be recaptured at a net loss. Meanwhile, 65% of the time a better move existed that wins material (median 5.0), meaning the player chose a self-destructive capture over a stronger tactical continuation. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, isolating this specific greedy-capture blunder pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece lands on a square insufficiently supported, allowing the opponent to recapture and win net material. The player is lured by an apparent material gain (taking a pawn or piece) but fails to notice the capture square is defended. A superior move—often a fork, check, or positional consolidation—was available that would have won cleanly without leaving anything hanging.

analysis.label: Developing a bishop to g4 or g5 in the opening where it is immediately capturable by the opponent's queen along an open diagonal.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value: 3.0, corresponding to a bishop), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being minor pieces (65 minor vs 1 major out of 66 cases). Only 8% of the played moves were captures and only 28% of the best moves won material, confirming this is a 'hung own piece' pattern rather than a missed capture. Across all top 12 activating positions, the move is exclusively Bg4 (by Black) or Bg5 (by White) in the opening phase, where the bishop lands on a square directly accessible to the opponent's queen along an unobstructed diagonal (d1-g4 or d8-g5). Because these are very early opening positions with minimal development, the diagonal from the queen to g4/g5 is completely clear, allowing an immediate queen capture of the undefended bishop.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop moves to g4 or g5 with no protection, and the opponent's queen on its starting square (d1 or d8) has a completely open diagonal (through e2-f3 or e7-f6) to capture it immediately for free. In these early opening positions with few pieces developed, there is nothing blocking the queen's path, so the bishop is simply left en prise — a full piece lost for nothing.

analysis.label: The player's move exposes their own queen on an open or semi-open file to an enemy rook, leaving it en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with 498/500 classified as 'major' pieces—specifically queens (marked as Q in all 12 top boards). 41% of the triggering moves are captures (often pawn captures that open a file), while 68% of best moves win material (median 3.0), indicating the opponent can exploit the exposed queen. The consistent geometric pattern is a queen sitting on the same file as an enemy rook, where the player either (a) moved a pawn/piece off the file that was shielding their queen from the rook (positions 1,2,3,5,10: dxc5, dxc3, cxb4, Bxg5, Bxd4), or (b) moved their queen directly onto a file controlled by an enemy rook (positions 7,9,12: Qc2, Qxf7, Qd6). The feature fires on only 0.4% of positions, targeting this specific tactical motif.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they remove the piece (pawn or bishop) that was blocking the line between the player's queen and an enemy rook on the same file, or they place the queen directly into the rook's line of fire. The opponent then wins the queen outright or wins decisive material (median cp_loss 387) through the newly opened file attack, since the queen has no safe square that doesn't cost further material.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture the opponent's queen (an even trade) as the only defensive resource, instead making a passive move that leaves their own queen hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 99% of cases, yet the capture 'wins 0' material (an even queen trade). The player's move left their own piece hanging in 68% of cases with a median value of 9 (queen), and the hung piece class is overwhelmingly 'major' (35 of 56 non-pawn instances). All 12 top-activating positions show the best move is Qx-something — always capturing the opponent's queen. Instead of executing this forced queen trade, the player makes a quiet move (often a king retreat like Kh2, Kh1, Kf8, Kg3, or an aimless queen move), leaving their own queen en prise to the opponent's still-alive queen. The positions are typically desperate (avg cp_loss: 6348) where trading queens is the only way to avoid immediate checkmate or massive material loss.
analysis.why_bad: By refusing the queen trade, the player leaves their own queen attacked and undefended while the opponent's queen remains on the board coordinating lethal mating threats. The opponent simply captures the hanging queen next move (or delivers forced checkmate), converting what could have been a survivable (though worse) endgame into an instant loss.

analysis.label: The player promotes a pawn to a queen that is immediately capturable, instead of playing a stronger preparatory or intermediate move first.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 84% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 9 = queen), and the own-hang piece class is overwhelmingly 'major' (newly created queens). Meanwhile, 63% of positions had a best move that wins material, and best moves are checks 37% of the time and captures 21%—indicating powerful intermediate moves were available. All 12 top-activating boards show pawn promotions (g1=Q+, e1=Q+, c8=Q+, d8=Q+, etc.) in endgames where the newly promoted queen is immediately captured or the promotion leads to stalemate/drawing resources for the opponent. The correct moves were consistently preparatory king moves (Kh2, Kd7, Kf6, Kd8), intermediate rook checks (Rd1+, Re1+, Rd8+, Rf2+), or simple captures (hxg4), all of which maintained the winning advantage before promoting.
analysis.why_bad: The immediate promotion places a new queen on a square where the opponent can capture it (the enemy king is adjacent to the promotion square, or an enemy rook/piece controls it), or it creates stalemate. By promoting prematurely without first repositioning the king to guard the promotion square, delivering an intermediate check to deflect the enemy king, or using an existing piece to clear the path, the player throws away a won position—typically losing a full queen (9 points) and converting a decisive advantage into a draw or loss.

analysis.label: Player captures a piece with check (usually with the Queen) but leaves the capturing piece en prise, throwing away a winning position.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player makes a greedy capture—92% of fired moves are captures, and 96% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 9 = Queen; piece class distribution heavily 'major' at 23/25). The played move is almost always a Queen capturing a pawn or piece with check (Qxg6+, Qxd4+, Qxb7+, etc.), but after the opponent's forced reply the Queen is left en prise. Meanwhile, the best move is a check 58% of the time but a capture 0% of the time—meaning the correct continuation was typically a precise non-capturing check or quiet move that maintained the winning advantage without sacrificing the queen. The median material won by the best move is 97 (≈ queen value), confirming that the correct line preserves the queen while the played line loses it.
analysis.why_bad: These captures with check are seductive because they grab material AND give check, creating an illusion of dominance. But the Queen lands on a square where it is unprotected and immediately recapturable. The player squanders a completely winning position (avg cp_loss: 2546) by trading their queen for a pawn or minor piece, often missing a forced mate (positions 4, 8, 10) or a superior check that keeps the queen safe while maintaining decisive pressure.

analysis.label: Player promotes a pawn to a queen on a square controlled by the opponent, immediately hanging the new queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 95% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., a queen), with the hung piece class being overwhelmingly 'major' (91 of 93 instances). Every single top-activating move is a pawn promotion to queen (f1=Q, c8=Q, a1=Q, etc.), where the promotion square is attacked by an enemy piece, meaning the newly-created queen is immediately capturable. The best moves (29% checks, 28% captures) are typically intermediate tactics—rook checks, captures, or positional moves—that should have been played instead of the premature promotion. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, consistent with this being a specific endgame blunder pattern involving advanced passed pawns.
analysis.why_bad: The promoted queen lands on a square defended by an enemy piece (rook, knight, or bishop) and is immediately captured, turning what should be a winning advantage into equality or a loss. The player fixates on the tempting promotion rather than recognizing an intermediate move (often a devastating rook check or capture) that would have been far stronger, or that the promotion square simply isn't safe yet.

analysis.label: Player gives an impulsive or premature check instead of a stronger quiet move or capture that wins material or maintains a forced mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move wins material 62% of the time (median value 1.0) and is a capture 35% of the time, yet only 4% of best moves are checks themselves. Meanwhile, the player's move is a check in all top-12 activating positions and a capture only 8% of the time. The 36% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns, majors, and minors) indicates that some of these impulsive checks also leave the player's own material en prise. The feature fires on 0.6% of all positions, specifically targeting moments where a player succumbs to the classic 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' tendency, choosing a flashy but inefficient or outright losing check over a decisive quiet move or material-winning capture.
analysis.why_bad: These checks fail because they drive the opponent's king to safety, release mating pressure, or squander forced wins. In many top-activating positions, forced checkmates (#+6, #+8, #-7, #-12) are thrown away in favor of checks that merely harass without constructing a mating net. The checks often allow the opponent to consolidate, escaping from a losing position into one that is merely bad, with average centipawn loss of 2288 across the top boards.

analysis.label: Player ignores a clearly available capture of an enemy piece and instead plays a quiet move that often leaves their own material hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 96% of the top-500 activating positions, the best move is a capture (median value won: 5.0, i.e., a rook), yet the player's actual move was a capture only 9% of the time. In 54% of positions, the best move wins material outright from an enemy piece that is en prise or inadequately defended. The player instead plays a quiet repositioning move (typically a king walk or piece shuffle), and in 70% of cases this quiet move additionally leaves one of their own pieces hanging (median value 5.0, predominantly major pieces at 201/348). The average centipawn loss of 4378 reflects the catastrophic nature of ignoring a free or winning capture while simultaneously exposing one's own material.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available capture that would win material (taking an undefended queen, rook, or piece) or make a defensively essential trade. By playing a passive king move or piece relocation instead, the player not only forfeits the winning capture but often places their own pieces on squares where they become undefended, giving the opponent a counter-capture or forcing mate. The positions show enemy pieces literally en prise on the same rank, file, or diagonal as the player's pieces, yet the player moves away.

analysis.label: Unsound bishop sacrifice on f7 or f2 with check in Italian Game openings, leaving the bishop hanging without compensation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player plays Bxf7+ or Bxf2+ in the opening (93% leave their own piece hanging, with median value 3.0 corresponding to a minor piece; the hung piece class is 'minor' in 77/82 cases). The move is itself a capture 89% of the time, and the best move wins material only 47% of the time (often simple development like O-O, d3, or Nc3 is preferred). The positions are overwhelmingly Italian Game / Giuoco Piano / Two Knights Defense setups where the bishop on c4 (or c5) impulsively captures the f7 (or f2) pawn with check, but the resulting position offers no adequate follow-up, leaving the bishop en prise.
analysis.why_bad: After Bxf7+ (or Bxf2+), the king simply captures or sidesteps, and the bishop is left hanging on f7/f2 with no second attacker or tactical continuation to justify the sacrifice. The player gains a check and a pawn but loses a full minor piece (net loss of ~2 points), while the opponent's king displacement is insufficient compensation since the position remains closed and the attacker lacks developed pieces to exploit the exposed king.

analysis.label: In a decisively won endgame, the player makes a slow or aimless move instead of executing the immediately winning action (capturing an undefended piece or pushing a passed pawn to promotion).
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/12 boards) where the player has a decisive advantage but fails to land the killing blow. The SEE aggregate shows 39% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, indicating undefended rooks/bishops available for capture), while the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 12% captures). The 34% own-hung rate (median 1.0, 55 pawns) reflects that the aimless moves sometimes also create minor weaknesses. The average cp_loss of 3457 centipawns — often converting forced mates into merely large advantages — confirms these are catastrophic misses of simple decisive moves. The best moves are captures only 21% of the time because the other winning blows are pawn advances to the 7th/8th rank, equally simple but non-capture in nature.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available decisive action — capturing an undefended rook/bishop (positions 1, 2, 5, 9) or pushing a passed pawn to promotion (positions 6, 8, 11, 12). Instead, the player makes a purposeless king move, develops a piece to a square that doesn't address the critical threat, or pushes the wrong pawn. The delay allows the opponent to reorganize, defend the hanging piece, or set up counterplay, converting what should be an instant win into a prolonged fight or even a draw.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move that leaves their own piece (rook, bishop, or queen) en prise, ignoring the immediate need to save or exchange the threatened piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 94% of activating positions show the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 3.0). The hung piece class distribution (major: 243, minor: 169, pawn: 58) shows rooks and bishops are most commonly left en prise. Only 14% of played moves were captures, meaning players chose quiet, irrelevant moves while their piece was under attack. In 54% of cases the best move also won enemy material (median 3.0), often because the correct response was to exchange the threatened piece (best move is a capture in 34% of cases). The average cp_loss of 6379 reflects how catastrophic ignoring a hanging piece typically is.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediate tactical necessity—their own piece is attacked and will be captured for free on the opponent's next turn. Instead of saving the piece (by moving it, capturing the attacker, or making a profitable exchange), the player makes an unrelated quiet move like a king walk (Kb5, Kb3, Kg1), a pawn push (f5, a5), or repositions a different piece, effectively gifting material to the opponent.

analysis.label: Player missed a check (usually a knight fork) that wins the enemy queen.
analysis.description: In 94% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 96% of cases it wins material with a median value of 97 centipawns (queen value). The player's move was itself a capture only 16% of the time, meaning the player typically played a quiet or irrelevant move instead of delivering the decisive check. The dominant motif is a knight check forking king and queen (Nf5+, Nc4+, Nd3+, Ng3+, Nf6+, Nd6+ appear across the top boards), though pawn advances with discovered check (g5+, h7+) and rook checks (Ra2+) also appear. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically those where a tactical check wins the queen but was overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a forcing check—typically a knight fork or discovered attack—that would win the opponent's queen outright. By playing a quiet developing move, a random capture, or a non-forcing continuation, the player squanders a decisive tactical blow (average cp_loss ~1656), often converting a winning position into an equal or lost one as the opponent can then move their queen to safety.

analysis.label: The king moves away from an enemy bishop on f7/f2 instead of capturing it, missing a free piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 84% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 88% of best moves are captures, yet the played move was a capture only 6% of the time. Nearly every top-activating position features an enemy bishop aggressively placed on f7 (against Black) or f2 (against White) — typically from Italian Game / Fried Liver-style sacrifices — where the king can simply capture it. Instead, the player moves the king sideways (Kf8, Kd7, Kf1, Kd2, Ke7, Ke1), declining the free piece. The 50% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary consequence: by retreating the king to a suboptimal square, the player often exposes their own pawns or pieces.
analysis.why_bad: By declining Kxf7 or Kxf2, the player leaves a full bishop (3 points) on the board for the opponent for free. The bishop on f7/f2 is typically undefended after a speculative sacrifice, so capturing it is both safe and materially winning. Moving the king elsewhere not only forfeits this material but often places the king on a worse square, worsening coordination and sometimes exposing other pieces.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move (king move, pawn push, or piece reposition) while ignoring a critical available capture that was essential to the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a capture (92% of the time across 500 positions) but the player instead plays a quiet, non-tactical move (only 10% of played moves are captures). The best captures have a median material gain of just 1.0 (often SEE-equal exchanges), meaning many are not 'free pieces' but are positionally or tactically forced. The quiet moves played are so poor that 40% of the time they leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors 28, pawns 26, minors 18). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating rare, high-cost blunders with an average centipawn loss of 1966. The endgame-heavy activation (8/12 top positions) suggests players focus on king activity or pawn advancement while missing concrete captures.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical obligation — a capture that resolves a critical tension, wins material, saves a trapped piece, or prevents the opponent's threats. By playing king moves (Ke4, Kg2), pawn pushes (e5, g6, g4, h6), or piece repositions (Ne2, Nd4, Rg1) instead of taking available captures, the player loses material, hangs their own pieces (40%), or allows the opponent to consolidate or promote. The captures were 'forced' in the sense that any other move catastrophically worsens the position.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but unproductive check that leaves their own piece (or another piece) hanging after the opponent escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 68% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minors: 175, majors: 105, pawns: 59), while the best move wins material 69% of the time (median 3.0). Critically, every single one of the top 12 played moves is a check (+), yet only 18% of best moves are checks. This reveals the pattern: the player is seduced by giving check — often a flashy knight, rook, or queen check — but the check is unproductive (doesn't lead to mate or a decisive continuation). After the opponent simply moves their king or interposes, the checking piece or another piece left undefended is captured, resulting in significant material loss. The 44% capture rate among played moves shows that many of these are also capture-checks (e.g., Nxf7+, Rxg7+), making them even more superficially attractive.
analysis.why_bad: These checks accomplish nothing — the opponent escapes easily, and the checking move either displaces the player's own piece to an undefended square or removes a defender from a critical piece. The player prioritizes the psychological lure of check over board reality. A calm non-checking move (capturing a hanging piece, defending, or delivering a more precise blow like an actual mate) would maintain or increase the advantage rather than blundering material back.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting knight check that leaves the knight (or another piece) hanging after the king moves, instead of playing a stronger move that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 81% of activating positions, the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 150 minor pieces out of 253 total—overwhelmingly knights). Simultaneously, 70% of the time the best move would have won material (median value 4.0), and the best move is a capture 40% of the time or a check only 24% of the time. All 12 top-activating moves are knight checks (Nf6+, Ne2+, Nf3+, Nd4+, Nc7+, Ng3+, Ne6+, Nf2+, Nc4+), yet the knight is left en prise once the king simply sidesteps. The player is seduced by a flashy check that accomplishes nothing structurally, while the genuinely strong continuation—often a simple capture or positional move—would have consolidated or increased a significant advantage.
analysis.why_bad: The knight check forces the king to move but the knight lands on a square where it has no support and is easily captured. After the king steps away, the player has lost a full piece (≈3 pawns) for nothing—no fork, no discovered attack, no follow-up. Meanwhile, the position's real tactical opportunity (a winning capture, a better check, or a consolidating move) is squandered, typically costing 400-700 centipawns.

analysis.label: The player makes a seemingly active but purposeless queen move that neglects concrete tactical demands of the position.
analysis.description: In the top 500 activating positions, 55% feature a best move that wins material (median value 2.0), yet the played move is a quiet queen relocation only 17% of the time involving a capture. Additionally, 48% of the time the queen move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed across pawns 116, minors 68, majors 56). The top 12 boards show 11/12 played moves are queen moves (Qe3, Qd7, Qg6, Qe5, Qf4, Qf5, Qd2, Qe7) to active-looking squares, while the best moves are typically non-queen moves: pawn captures (exd4), rook placements (Rd1, Rf8, Rb8), exchanges (Qxe2+, Bxf3), or king safety moves (Kg2). The average cp_loss of 333 confirms these are serious blunders disguised as purposeful play.
analysis.why_bad: The queen moves to an ostensibly active square but ignores the position's concrete requirements — winning available material, defending hanging pieces, or executing forced tactical sequences. The player is 'doing something' with the queen rather than solving the position's actual problem, resulting in missed wins and/or hanging their own material due to neglected defensive duties.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet move (often a pawn push) that leaves their own piece tactically undefended, primarily in opening positions.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 64% of positions have the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, typically a pawn). The hung-piece distribution is pawns (65), minors (44), and majors (27). Only 10% of the played moves are captures, and the best move is a check only 1% of the time — indicating these are not complex tactical positions but rather cases where the player overlooks a simple threat to their own material. While 25% of best moves win material, the dominant and consistent signal across 500 positions is that the player's chosen move creates a vulnerability in their own camp. The feature fires mostly in the opening phase (7/12 top boards) on moves that appear strategically motivated but are tactically careless.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a slow strategic idea (pawn push like a6, h6, g5, c5, or a piece repositioning like Bf6, Be4) while ignoring that the move either removes defense from an existing piece or places a piece on a square where it can be captured. The best moves (Nf6, O-O, Be3, Bb3, etc.) are typically simple developing moves or safety moves that maintain piece coordination and don't create tactical liabilities.

analysis.label: Player ignored a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (typically a minor piece) and played a quiet positional or developing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that the best move wins material in 99% of cases (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and the best move is a capture in 99% of positions. Meanwhile, the player's actual move was a capture only 6% of the time, and the player's move left their own piece hanging only 16% of the time (median 1.0, mostly pawns). This confirms the pattern is NOT about hanging one's own piece, but about failing to capture an undefended enemy piece. Across the top 12 boards, the best moves are simple captures (Qxd3, Qxc6, Qxd6, Rxe7, Qxh4, Qxc3, Qxe7, etc.) on unprotected enemy pieces, while the played moves are quiet non-tactical moves like O-O, a4, Bd6, Ne5, or Bb3.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because there is an enemy piece (usually a minor piece worth ~3 pawns) sitting undefended that can be captured immediately. By playing a positional or developmental move instead, the player forfeits free material—typically a full minor piece—causing average centipawn losses of ~178 and individual losses often exceeding 400cp. The opponent then has time to defend or move the hanging piece.

analysis.label: A rook (or queen) greedily captures a peripheral pawn when a superior move exists, often leaving own material hanging or missing a better win.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows a dual-nature mistake: 48% of the time the best move wins material (median 1.0), while 46% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed across majors 25, pawns 24, minors 10). The played move is a capture 40% of the time — almost always a rook grabbing a pawn on the b-file or h-file (Rxh6, Rxh2, Rxb7, Rxb4, Qxh7, etc.). The best moves are diverse (quiet moves, different captures, king moves), indicating the error is not positional but a consistent tactical misjudgment: the player sees a 'free' pawn and snatches it without verifying the consequences. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific greedy-capture pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These rook pawn grabs fail because the captured pawn is either poisoned (the rook lands on a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable or overloaded) or the tempo spent grabbing a peripheral pawn allows the opponent to execute a stronger tactical idea. In many cases (46%), the rook or another piece is left en prise after the capture. In others, the best move would have won equal or greater material through a more central or forcing continuation. The greed for a wing pawn blinds the player to the position's real tactical demands.

analysis.label: The player's Queen captures a defended piece (usually a Rook), leaving the Queen itself hanging and losing massive material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player impulsively captures a piece with their Queen, only to lose the Queen immediately afterward. The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of activating positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 9.0 = Queen), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (55 of 58 instances). The player's move was itself a capture 84% of the time. While the best move wins material in 68% of cases (median 3.0), the player instead opts for an attractive-looking but ultimately losing Queen capture. All 12 top-activating boards show Queen captures (Qxe8+, Qxg8+, Qxf1+, Qxe1+, Qxc1) targeting Rooks on open files, where the Queen is subsequently recaptured. The average centipawn loss of 2535 confirms these are catastrophic blunders, with several leading to forced checkmate.
analysis.why_bad: The Queen (worth 9) captures a defended Rook or minor piece (worth 5 or less), but the Queen is immediately recaptured on that square by a defending piece. The net result is trading a Queen for a Rook — a devastating material loss. Often the Queen capture gives check, making it look forcing and attractive, but the recapture still wins the Queen. Meanwhile, better moves (castling, developing, or winning material elsewhere) were available that maintained or improved the position without sacrificing the most valuable piece.

analysis.label: Player ignores a favorable central pawn capture (usually dxe5/dxe4) in the opening, instead making a developing or flanking move that often leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 79% of the time (winning material in 64% of cases, median value 1.0 pawn), while the played move is almost never a capture (only 9%). Critically, the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging 51% of the time (median value 2.0, with minors dominating at 15 out of 27 hung pieces). The pattern across all 12 boards is remarkably consistent: there is unresolved central pawn tension (d4 vs e5, e4 vs d5, d4 vs c5), the best move resolves it favorably with a pawn capture (dxe5, dxe4, dxc5, or e5), but instead the player develops a piece to an aggressive-looking square (Bg4, Ng5, Bf4, Qh5, Bxf7+) or pushes a flank/center pawn (f4, g5, d5). These moves ignore the tactical obligation in the center and frequently place the developed piece on an undefended square.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the central pawn capture, the player both forfeits material gain (the free center pawn or favorable exchange) and often places a piece on a square where it has no support, since the central pawn structure that should provide cover remains unresolved. The opponent can then resolve the tension themselves while simultaneously attacking the newly-placed undefended piece, resulting in large material and positional losses (average 337cp).

analysis.label: Player missed a check that wins significant material, instead playing a quiet non-forcing move in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the best move wins material in 98% of positions (median value 95), and crucially, the best move is a check in 78% of cases while being a capture only 15% of the time. The played moves were captures only 15% of the time, and only 15% hung the player's own piece (median value just 1.0, i.e., a pawn). This establishes the pattern as consistently missing a winning check rather than hanging material. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames where both kings are exposed, and the best move is a rook, pawn, or bishop check that wins material through forced sequences—forks after check, back-rank tactics winning a defender, or discovered attacks. The feature fires on only 0.0% of all positions, indicating a rare but high-impact tactical pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (c5, Rd7, Rf3, Kc4, h4, etc.) fail because they ignore an immediately available check that exploits the opponent's exposed king to win material by force. After the check, the opponent is compelled to move their king, which either leaves a piece undefended, allows a fork, or permits a decisive follow-up.
