By playing a non-forcing move instead, the player gives the opponent time to protect the vulnerable piece, reposition their king, or create counterplay, squandering advantages averaging ~1935 centipawns.

analysis.label: The player makes a passive or aimless rook move that leaves their own piece or pawn undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, often retreating rook move that neglects the safety of their own material. The SEE aggregate shows that 58% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across minors: 115, pawns: 113, majors: 63), while in 52% of positions the best move could have won enemy material (median 2.0). Only 13% of played moves are captures, confirming the passive nature of the chosen moves. The best moves are typically active alternatives—checks (10%), captures (29%), or rook penetrations to the 7th rank—that either win material or maintain tension. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, targeting the specific pattern of a quiet rook repositioning (often to the back rank like Rc1, Re1, Rd1) that simultaneously misses tactical opportunities and leaves other pieces unprotected.
analysis.why_bad: These passive rook moves fail because they prioritize abstract rook placement (often retreating to the first rank or a neutral square) over concrete tactical requirements. By moving the rook away, the player removes a defender from other pieces or pawns, leaving them en prise. Simultaneously, the player misses more forcing alternatives (checks, captures, 7th-rank penetrations) that would have maintained or increased their advantage. The rook move gives the opponent a free tempo to exploit the newly undefended material.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (often a tempting capture) that leaves their own rook undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 93% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with the piece class distribution showing 242 out of 280 are major pieces (rooks/queens). The player's move was itself a capture 47% of the time, indicating the player is frequently lured into grabbing material while neglecting rook safety. The best move wins material 68% of the time (median 2.0), often by simply moving the threatened rook to safety or using it actively (Rc8, Re8, Rf8, Rd8, Rxd6, Ra8+ appear as best moves). Only 15% of best moves are captures and 5% are checks, meaning the correction is usually a quiet rook repositioning move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an immediate objective (a queen capture, a knight development, a pawn grab) while overlooking that their rook is left undefended on an open file or diagonal where the opponent can immediately win it. The tempting capture or active-looking move is net-negative because losing a rook (5 points) vastly outweighs whatever was gained.

analysis.label: Player ignored a strategically essential equal exchange that would neutralize a dominant or dangerous enemy piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 99% of activating positions, yet these captures show SEE = 0 (materially equal exchanges) with only 8% winning outright material. This means the correct move is almost always trading a piece for an equally-valued enemy piece—not winning free material. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 10% captures), and 42% of them leave the player's own piece hanging afterward (median value 2.0, with 102 minor pieces, 79 pawns, 28 major pieces). The top 12 boards consistently show the best move is a knight or bishop capturing on a central square (Nxd4 appears 5 times, plus Nxe4, Nxd5, Nxf4, Bxf5, Bxa6, Bxe4)—all equal exchanges targeting powerfully placed enemy pieces on dominant central or attacking squares.
analysis.why_bad: By playing quiet developing or prophylactic moves instead of the critical exchange, the player allows the opponent's dominant piece to persist unchallenged. That piece (typically a centralized knight or bishop on d4, d5, f4, f5, or e4) exerts enormous tactical and positional pressure, creating threats that quickly become overwhelming. The average cp_loss of 209 centipawns demonstrates that these 'optional' even exchanges are in fact tactically mandatory—not capturing allows the opponent's piece to participate in decisive combinations or maintain crushing positional dominance.

analysis.label: Player misses Qe7 pinning and winning an enemy knight on the open e-file in Petroff Defense positions.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 88% of top-activating positions have a best move winning material (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), yet only 6% of those best moves are captures and 0% are checks — indicating the material is won through a positional mechanism (pin) rather than direct capture. The player's move was a capture only 24% of the time, and 29% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0, all minor pieces). The boards overwhelmingly show Petroff Defense positions (4.Qe2 line) where both kings are in the center, a knight sits on e5, and the correct Qe7 pins that knight against the king on the open e-file, winning it. Instead, players make natural-looking but losing knight moves.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Nf6, Ng5, Nxd2, Nxf2, etc.) move the player's own knight away from e4 — either retreating it or making tempting captures — without first exploiting the open e-file geometry. By failing to play Qe7, the player misses a devastating pin on the enemy's centralized knight on e5 that would win a full piece. Worse, moving the blocking knight often exposes the player's own king to discovered attacks on that same e-file, compounding the error.

analysis.label: Player moves a piece that was blocking the enemy queen's attack along an open file (usually the e-file), exposing their own king to a devastating discovered or direct attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 49% of best moves win material (median value 2.0, consistent with winning an enemy minor piece) and 46% of played moves leave an own piece hanging (median 1.0, with 131 pawns among the hung pieces). Only 18% of played moves are captures—nearly all are quiet developing moves. The dominant pattern across the top 12 boards involves a Petroff Defense configuration where a knight on e4 blocks the enemy queen on e2 from attacking along the open e-file toward the exposed king on e8. The player moves this blocking knight (Nf6, Ng5) instead of counter-blocking with Qe7 (or the mirror: Qe2). In secondary cases (positions 7, 8, 9, 10, 11), the player makes a developing move instead of addressing king exposure on an open file via a king retreat (Kh1, Kf8, Ka8, Ke8). The best move is a check only 3% of the time and a capture only 26%, confirming the correct response is usually a defensive blocking or evacuating move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves remove a critical blocker from the open file, allowing the opponent's queen (or rook) to deliver a discovered attack, pin, or direct threat along the file against the uncastled/exposed king. In the Petroff cases, moving the e4 knight allows White's Qe2 to strike along the e-file, winning the e5 knight with check (value ~3). In back-rank cases, making a developing move instead of evacuating the king allows lethal tactics exploiting the file geometry.

analysis.label: Playing a premature bishop check (Bb5+/Bb4+/Bg5+) in the opening that wastes tempo and leaves own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a pointless bishop check in the opening (every top-12 activation is Bb5+, Bb4+, or Bg5+) instead of addressing urgent tactical or developmental needs. The SEE aggregate reveals that 52% of the time the played check leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece predominantly being a minor piece (28 minor vs 20 pawn vs 15 major). Simultaneously, 65% of the time the best move would have won material (median value 3.0), indicating a strong tactical opportunity was missed. Only 2% of played moves were captures, confirming these are quiet spite-checks rather than productive tactical moves. The best move is itself a check only 22% of the time, showing the player chose an inferior check over better alternatives.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop check is easily parried (king steps aside or a piece blocks) and accomplishes nothing strategically. Critically, by moving the bishop away from its current post, the player often leaves a knight or other piece that was previously defended now hanging en prise. The wasted tempo compounds the problem — the opponent gains time to consolidate while the checker falls behind in development. In many cases the best move was a simple capture, retreat of an attacked piece, or natural developing move that maintained material equality or won material outright.

analysis.label: In a won endgame, the player makes a move that leaves their own Queen (or major piece) undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of activating positions involve the player's move leaving their own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 9 (Queen). The piece class distribution confirms all top examples involve major pieces. Only 40% of best moves win material (median 3.0), indicating the primary mistake is not missing an opponent's hanging piece but rather carelessly exposing one's own. The player's move is a capture only 20% of the time, and the best move is a check only 20% of the time, showing these are typically quiet moves (King repositions, pawn pushes, or misguided checks) that overlook a basic threat to the player's own Queen or Rook. All 10 top positions are endgames where the player holds a decisive material advantage but throws it away in a single move.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore the immediate tactical vulnerability of the player's own major piece. In many cases, the player moves their King away from defending their Queen (e.g., Kd4 abandoning the Queen to a knight, Kd6 leaving a Rook capturable by the enemy King), gives a flashy check that places the Queen on a capturable square (Qd4+, Qf5+), or makes a non-urgent move while their Queen sits en prise to a pawn or minor piece (a4 with Queen hanging to cxb5, Be4 with Queen hanging to bxc5). The result is typically a swing from a won/mating position to drawn or lost.

analysis.label: The player gives a tempting Rook check that leaves the Rook undefended and capturable after the opponent escapes check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 87% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a Rook), with the hung-piece class distribution overwhelmingly 'major' (97 out of 116). All 12 top-activating moves are Rook checks (Rd7+, Rd6+, Re2+, Rxe4+, Re3+, etc.) where the Rook lands on a square it cannot be defended. Meanwhile, only 2% of best moves are checks and only 29% are captures — the correct moves are typically quiet consolidating or material-winning moves (g4, Bg5, Rcc1, Rf8, c4, etc.) that maintain the Rook's safety. The player's move was a capture only 35% of the time, confirming these are mostly quiet Rook moves that simply deliver check while hanging the piece.
analysis.why_bad: The Rook check is superficially forcing but tactically unsound: after the opponent's king moves, blocks, or captures on the checking square, the Rook is left en prise with no defender. The opponent simply takes the Rook, netting approximately 5 pawns of material. The player is seduced by the 'free' check rather than playing the objectively stronger quiet or capturing moves that preserve material.

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing check (often with a rook or queen) that would win major material, instead playing a quiet rook reposition.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 71% of best moves are checks, 85% win material with a median value of ~95 (approximately a queen), and only 12% of played moves were captures while 18% hung their own piece. The overwhelming pattern is that the opponent's king is exposed or awkwardly placed, and a check (typically Rx?+, Qx?+, or a rook/queen deflection check) initiates a tactical sequence winning the enemy queen or decisive material. Instead of finding this forcing check, the player makes a quiet, developmental-looking rook move (Rbb8, Rb8, Rc7, Rbd7, Rc8, Rg4, Rg8, Rab8 appear in the top boards) that completely ignores the tactical opportunity. The average cp_loss of 1227 confirms these are catastrophic misses.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet rook moves fail because they surrender a winning tactical blow. The exposed enemy king allowed a check that would fork, skewer, or deflect a defender of the queen, netting roughly a queen's worth of material. By playing a passive rook move instead, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, often turning a completely won position into equality or even a loss.

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing check (usually with the queen) that wins decisive material or leads to mate, instead playing a non-forcing or inferior move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 86% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0), and critically, 71% of the time the best move is a check while 60% are captures. The player's actual moves were captures only 32% of the time and were predominantly quiet or inferior forcing moves. In 42% of cases the played move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0). The top boards confirm that the missed best move is overwhelmingly a queen check (Qxe4+, Qe5+, Qxh3+, Qxg3+, Qd6+, Qg4+, Qxg4+, Qh4+, Nxe6+) — a forcing move exploiting an exposed enemy king that either wins material via the attack or delivers mate (several positions show SEE value 91 indicating mate). The player instead chose non-checking alternatives like quiet queen retreats, minor piece moves, or materially inferior captures.
analysis.why_bad: By not delivering the available check, the player surrenders the initiative and misses a concrete tactical blow. Checks force the opponent's reply, and in these positions the check directly wins material (via fork, discovered attack, or mating net) or forces immediate mate. Playing a non-forcing move instead allows the opponent to consolidate, defend, or counterattack, squandering a decisive advantage — average cp_loss is 948 centipawns.

analysis.label: The player missed a check that wins material, instead playing a quiet or less forcing move.
analysis.description: In the SEE aggregate over 500 positions, 52% of the best moves are checks and 65% win material (median value 100 centipawns, i.e., a pawn). Only 10% of played moves hang the player's own piece, confirming the mistake direction is missed-winning rather than hung-own. The player's move was a capture only 21% of the time, meaning the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet or non-forcing. The best moves in the top boards (Qh5+, Re1+, h7+, Rh5+, Ra1+, Rf5+) consistently show checks that exploit the opponent's exposed king to win material, while the player instead chose mundane king moves, pawn pushes, or non-optimal captures.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing check that would win material. Checks are the most forcing moves in chess—they demand immediate response—and when a check also attacks or wins a piece, skipping it surrenders a concrete material advantage. The player's quiet alternatives allow the opponent to consolidate or escape the tactical vulnerability.

analysis.label: In critical endgame races, the player makes a slow or misdirected move instead of the decisive tempo-winning action (often a promotion push or key capture).
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (12/12 boards) where the player fails to execute the single critical tempo move in a time-sensitive position. The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material 53% of the time (median value 3.0, consistent with promotion-related gains), yet the played move is a capture only 8% of the time—players choose passive quiet moves instead. The best move is a check 22% of the time and a capture 18%, reflecting the tactical urgency missed. After the wrong move, 38% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 94/117 cases), suggesting the slow move also creates new vulnerabilities. The enormous average centipawn loss (1159) reflects that in endgame races, one wrong tempo often flips the evaluation completely.
analysis.why_bad: In endgame races (especially pawn promotion races), a single tempo decides the outcome. The played moves—pushing the wrong pawn (e5 instead of f7, a5 instead of axb5, e3 instead of exd3), moving the king the wrong direction (Ka5 instead of a2, Kf7 blocking own g-pawn, Kg6 instead of Ke4), or making aimless piece moves (Rd5 instead of a7, Rf7 instead of Rc7)—all waste the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to promote first, establish a winning blockade, or convert their own passed pawns.

analysis.label: Player moves their King instead of using their major piece (Rook/Queen) to capture, leaving that major piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 87% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0), with the hung piece class being overwhelmingly major pieces (33 of 34 tracked). Meanwhile, 77% of the best moves are captures and 54% win material outright (median value won: 5.0). Only 8% of the played moves were captures themselves. The pattern is unmistakable: in every case, the player makes a quiet King move (all 12 top activations are King moves like Kg2, Kg7, Kf5, etc.) while their Rook or Queen is attacked or becomes undefended. The correct move was almost always to use that very major piece to capture an enemy piece (Rxf1, Rxf6, Qxg5+, Rxd1, etc.), simultaneously solving the tactical problem and saving the piece.
analysis.why_bad: By moving the King instead of the threatened/undefended major piece, the player abandons their Rook or Queen to capture. The correct move uses that piece actively (capturing an enemy piece or making a forced exchange), which both saves the piece and resolves the tactical tension. The King move addresses no threat and fatally neglects the piece left behind.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet (non-capturing) move that leaves their own piece en prise, often when a tactical capture was available to address the threat.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively shows that 83% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors 41%, minors 37%, pawns 18%). Meanwhile, in 57% of positions the best move wins material (median 3.0) and 59% of best moves are captures. The played move is almost never a capture itself (only 11%). This indicates the player consistently makes a quiet repositioning move while ignoring that one of their own pieces is attacked or left undefended. The best move was frequently a capture that would simultaneously win material and/or eliminate the threat to the player's own piece (e.g., Qxf3 removing an attacking bishop, bxc3 capturing a piece attacking a rook, Rxa3 eliminating a passed pawn).
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical threat to the player's own piece. Instead of capturing the threatening piece or addressing the attack (which would often win material), the player makes a move with a different purpose — developing, repositioning, or pushing a pawn — while leaving a major or minor piece completely undefended or under unresolved attack. The opponent then simply captures the hanging piece.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning Queen capture (Qx___) that would have won significant material, instead making an inferior move with the Queen or another piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 94% of the top-500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 3.0 = a minor piece), and in 86% of cases that best move is a capture. Crucially, all 12 top-activating boards share the same geometry: the best move is specifically a Queen capture (Qxd2, Qxh3, Qxe7, Qxc3, Qxd3, Qxb6, Qxe6, Qxe4, Qxf2+, Qxf7). The player's move was only a capture 14% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly played quiet moves or moved the Queen to the wrong square instead of taking the hanging piece. The 54% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the inferior alternative sometimes also worsened the player's position tactically, but the defining error is failing to execute the available Queen capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that their Queen can immediately capture an undefended or insufficiently defended enemy piece (often worth 3-5 points of material). Instead they play developing moves (Bd3), reposition the Queen to a less effective square (Qg5, Qf6, Qc7, Qd6), or even give a check (Qh1+, Qxb1+) that gains tempo but nets far less material than the clean Queen capture available.

analysis.label: Player makes a move that leaves their own major or minor piece undefended, ignoring an available tactical capture or check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the defining signal: 72% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-equivalent). The hung pieces are predominantly major pieces (28 major vs 14 minor out of 43 instances). Meanwhile, the best move was a capture in 77% of cases and a check in 37% of cases, often winning material (47%, median 3.0). The player's actual move was rarely a capture itself (only 13%), meaning they chose a quiet or irrelevant move instead of the critical tactical continuation. The pattern across the top boards confirms this: the player ignores an immediate tactical obligation—such as resolving mutual piece tension, capturing an undefended enemy piece, or delivering a forcing check—and instead plays a passive or misguided move that leaves their own piece completely unprotected.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the available capture or check, the player fails to resolve tactical tension in their favor. Their move leaves a piece (often a queen, rook, or knight) en prise with no compensation, allowing the opponent to simply win major material on the next move. In many cases the best move would have won material while simultaneously defending, making the played move doubly catastrophic.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet, often piece-hanging move while a strong tactical capture was available on the board.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 78% of these positions the best move was a capture (median value won: 3.0 when material is winnable at 29%), yet the player chose a quiet move instead. Critically, 60% of the time the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns 35, minors 33, and majors 14). Only 23% of played moves were captures themselves. This dual error—missing a forcing capture while simultaneously leaving one's own material en prise—produces the large average centipawn loss of 317. The best moves across the top boards (Rxe7, Rxb3, Rxb2, Bxe2, Nxd6+, Nxe4, Nxe7+, Nxd4, bxa1=Q) are all concrete tactical shots, often involving checks (16%) that amplify the advantage.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Rb2, Qa5, Qb4, e5, c5, Na5, Qa3, Kd7, Ne4, Ba6, e6) pursue slow strategic ideas or reposition pieces without addressing the immediate tactical reality. By ignoring an available forcing capture, the player forfeits material or a decisive tactical advantage. Worse, the quiet moves often leave their own pieces undefended, compounding the error by allowing the opponent counter-tactics on the next move.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture that leaves their own major piece (rook or queen) en prise to the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 88% of activating positions show the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook). The piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (34 major vs 10 minor vs 5 pawn). Crucially, 80% of the played moves are themselves captures — the player grabs enemy material but in doing so exposes their own capturing piece (or another major piece) to recapture or trapping. While 61% of positions also had a best move winning material (median 2.0), the best moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (only 21% are captures, 0% are checks), indicating the correct approach was typically a quiet defensive or positional move rather than the greedy tactical grab.
analysis.why_bad: The captures are tempting because they win immediate material (a pawn, a knight on d6, a piece on e7, etc.), but they leave the capturing piece — usually a queen or rook — undefended, trapped, or subject to a discovered attack or back-rank/promotion tactic. The correct alternatives (Kf7, Ke7, Bb7, Ke3, Kg1, Ree1, etc.) are typically quiet moves that address the real positional threat (passed pawn promotion, king safety, piece coordination) rather than grabbing material while ignoring defensive obligations.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting but flawed move (often a capture) that hangs their own piece, while missing a stronger tactical continuation that would have won material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a dual error: missing a winning tactical move while simultaneously leaving their own material vulnerable. The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0), yet the best move is a capture only 10% of the time—indicating the winning continuation is typically a quiet attacking move (frequently a queen redeployment to an aggressive square like Qb3, Qg4, Qf4, Qe5). Instead, the player's move is a capture 53% of the time (a greedy-looking take) and leaves their own piece hanging 58% of the time (median value 3.0, evenly distributed across minors, pawns, and majors). The average cp_loss of 956 reflects the compounding of these two errors: failing to win material AND giving up material in one move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is drawn to a superficially attractive action—usually capturing an enemy piece or making a natural developing move—without checking whether a stronger tactical shot exists (often a queen move to a multi-purpose attacking square). The played move frequently leaves the moved piece or another piece undefended on its new square, compounding the error by both missing the win and creating a new vulnerability. The player is essentially playing routine chess in a position that demands precise tactical calculation.

analysis.label: The player played a quiet move (typically a pawn push) instead of delivering a check that wins decisive material or forces checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of best moves are checks and 90% win material (median value won: 95.0, indicating queen-level captures or forced mates). The played moves were overwhelmingly quiet (only 21% captures), usually innocuous pawn pushes (g3, g6, f5, h3, g5, c5, f3). The 60% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns) is incidental — the real mistake is ignoring a devastating check. The enormous average cp_loss of 5074 confirms these are catastrophic oversights where the player had a forcing check leading to mate or winning the opponent's queen/major pieces, but instead made a non-urgent positional move.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet pawn pushes ignore an immediately winning tactical blow. The check forces the opponent's king to move or interpose, after which decisive material is captured or checkmate follows. By playing a passive move instead, the player gives the opponent time to consolidate, escape the mating net, or even launch a counterattack — often turning a completely won position into a draw or loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (or flashy check) instead of a stronger forcing move that wins decisive material or delivers mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 74% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., roughly a rook), while the player's move is itself a capture 59% of the time—indicating the player grabs an immediately available piece rather than finding the stronger blow. The best move is a check 41% of the time, revealing that many of the missed tactics involve forcing checks leading to mate or winning major material. Additionally, 53% of the player's moves leave their own piece hanging (median value 3.0), meaning the greedy capture often comes with a tactical liability that a stronger continuation would have avoided entirely. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2592 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but massive blunders where a decisive win (often mate-in-few) is squandered for a superficially attractive but tactically shallow capture.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they prioritize immediately visible material gain (capturing a piece) or a flashy check over a more forcing continuation that wins decisively—often a check leading to mate (Positions 3, 4), a fork winning a queen (Positions 7, 8), a promotion with check (Position 1), or a penetrating move that wins the whole game (Position 5). The captures frequently leave pieces en prise or allow the opponent to escape, converting a won position into a draw or loss.

analysis.label: Player missed an available checkmate (or forcing check leading to immediate mate) and instead played a capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of best moves win material valued at 100 (representing checkmate/king), and 97% of best moves are checks, while only 13% are captures. The played moves were captures 37% of the time, indicating players often grabbed material instead of delivering mate. Only 5% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is a checkmate (Qg8#, Qe5#, Qg3#, Qc3#, Qg4#, Qfe2#, Qd7#, Qf5#, Ra1#, Qa5#) or a check leading to forced mate (Qh5+, Qb3+), yet the player chose a different move—typically a queen capture on an unrelated square or a quiet developing move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they pass up an immediate checkmate. No matter how much material is won (e.g., Qxg6 winning a pawn or piece), it is strictly inferior to delivering checkmate on the spot. The player prioritized material gain or positional play over the ultimate tactical blow.

analysis.label: Player blunders their own Queen by playing an impulsive move (often a check or capture) in a winning position, when a simple winning continuation was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a catastrophic blunder by simultaneously missing a winning move (77% of positions had a best move winning material, median value 9.0 = Queen-level) AND leaving their own piece hanging (62% of played moves hung their own piece, median value 9.0 = Queen, piece class distribution: 7 major, 1 minor). The best move is frequently a check (38%) or capture (38%) that either delivers forced mate or wins decisive material. Instead, the player plays an impulsive alternative—often a flashy but incorrect check (Qe8+, Qxe7+, Qe3+, f3+), a tempting capture (Qxd8+, Rxf8), or a quiet move that abandons the Queen's protection (Be4, Kg7, Qc2, d1=Q)—resulting in a catastrophic average cp_loss of ~5000. The feature activates on only 0.0% of all positions, reflecting how rare yet devastating this specific blunder pattern is.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they abandon the defense of the player's own Queen (or major piece) while a clearly superior forcing move existed. The player is drawn to a 'natural-looking' move—often a check or recapture—without noticing that it leaves their most valuable piece en prise. The correct move typically exploits the same tactical themes (checks, captures, forks) but in the right order, maintaining piece safety while delivering the decisive blow.

analysis.label: Player gives a check with a major piece (rook or queen) that is left hanging and lost after the opponent deals with the check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 100% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly 'major' (429/500 rooks+queens). Every single top-12 activation is a check move (all ending in '+'), yet the best move is a check only 22% of the time, showing the check was unnecessary. The player's move was a capture 63% of the time (capture-checks like Qxg7+ or Rxf7+), but the checking piece ends up en prise on its destination square with no escape or sufficient compensation. The best moves were typically quiet or positional (b3, c3, h4, Kh2, b4) that preserved material.
analysis.why_bad: These checks are futile — the opponent simply captures or moves the king while winning the undefended checking piece. The check gains one tempo but loses an entire major piece (worth 5-9 points). The player gets lured by the forcing nature of a check without calculating that after the king moves or interposes, their piece is lost. Often the position was already bad, and the spite check converts a losing position into an immediately terminal one.

analysis.label: Player reflexively captures on g4/g5 with the h-pawn, fatally opening the h-file against their own castled king instead of winning material with a quieter move.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player plays hxg4 or hxg5, recapturing a piece that has been placed on the g-file. The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, a minor piece), the played move is a capture 62% of the time, and critically the played move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging 76% of the time (median value 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 135/231). The best move is rarely a capture itself (29%) and rarely a check (11%), indicating the correct approach is typically a quiet developing or strategic move that exploits the opponent's overextension on the g-file rather than reflexively recapturing. The feature fires in only 0.2% of positions, specifically targeting this hxg pawn-grab trap.
analysis.why_bad: Capturing hxg4/hxg5 opens the h-file directly against the player's own castled (or soon-to-castle) king. The opponent typically has pieces (especially a rook on h1/h8 or a queen) pre-aligned to exploit the newly opened h-file, turning what looks like a free piece capture into a devastating kingside attack. The piece on g4/g5 was placed there precisely as bait to provoke this weakening pawn move. Instead, ignoring it and playing a strategic move (d5, Nc6, Re1, etc.) would win material since the opponent's g4/g5 piece is often already trapped or overextended.

analysis.label: Player ignores a decisive pawn capture (often with check) in favor of a passive quiet move, losing significant positional or material advantage.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 95% of top activating positions the best move is a capture, and 40% of the time it delivers check, yet the played move was a capture only 7% of the time — meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead. The best captures have a SEE value of 0 (median), indicating they are even exchanges in pure material terms (pawn takes pawn, rook takes rook), but they are strategically decisive — creating passed pawns, breaking through pawn chains, or exploiting king exposure via check. Only 12% of best moves 'win material' outright. In 21% of cases the quiet move actually hung the player's own pawn (median hung value: 1.0). The positions are typically simplified middlegames or endgames with pawn tension (dxc4+, axb4+, gxf6+, exf5+, fxg4+, gxf5) where resolving the tension is critical.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves (mostly king walks or piece repositioning) ignore the critical pawn tension on the board. In these positions, the pawn capture — even though materially 'even' by SEE — transforms the position decisively by creating a passed pawn, breaching the opponent's pawn structure, giving check to gain tempo, or securing a winning king position. By not capturing, the player loses the window for the breakthrough, often allowing the opponent to consolidate or advance their own plans. The average centipawn loss of 991 reflects that these missed captures often decide the game.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting but inferior capture (or plausible move) while missing a much stronger tactical shot that wins decisive material.
analysis.description: In 89% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins significant material (median value 6.0, often a queen at value 9), yet the player's actual move was a capture only 57% of the time—typically taking a lesser piece or making an exchange rather than finding the winning blow. In 54% of cases the played move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), compounding the error. The best move is a check 27% of the time and a capture only 25%, indicating the winning tactic is often a non-obvious forcing move (fork, discovered attack, back-rank threat) rather than a simple recapture. The average cp_loss of 4388 reflects that these are game-deciding oversights.
analysis.why_bad: The player is drawn to a superficially attractive capture (recapturing an exchanged piece, grabbing a free pawn, or completing a trade) but completely overlooks a much stronger tactical resource—typically a knight fork winning a queen (Nf5/Nf6 pattern seen repeatedly), a check leading to massive material gain, or a move that simultaneously attacks while defending against a back-rank threat. The 'greedy' or routine capture blinds the player to the position's true tactical potential.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture that leaves their own capturing piece (typically a minor piece) en prise, when a quiet positional move was superior.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move hangs their own piece: 67% of played moves left an own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 67% of played moves were captures. Meanwhile, best moves are captures only 17% of the time and checks 0% of the time—meaning the correct alternatives are overwhelmingly quiet moves. The own-hang piece distribution (3 minor, 1 major) confirms that typically a knight or bishop is lost after an ill-advised capture. The player grabs material (usually a pawn) but places their piece on a square where it is immediately recapturable without adequate compensation.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because the captured material (usually a pawn worth 1) is far less valuable than the piece left hanging (worth 3-5). The player is seduced by an immediate material gain but overlooks that the capturing piece lands on an undefended square where it can be recaptured. The better moves (quiet retreats, pawn advances, or positional improvements) maintain the piece and preserve a larger advantage—often converting a winning position rather than squandering it for a pawn.

analysis.label: The player makes an aggressive capture or check that leaves their own queen (or major piece) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is overwhelmingly clear: 91% of moves in this feature left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0), with the piece class distribution dominated by major pieces (49 major vs 24 minor vs 11 pawn). The played moves are 51% captures and many are also checks, indicating tempting tactical moves. Meanwhile, best_wins_material is only 47%, confirming the error is not about missing enemy material but about exposing one's own. In the top 12 boards, 9 out of 12 positions involve hanging the queen specifically (values 6-9), typically by playing a flashy capture (Qxh7, Qxe6, Qxd5, Qxf5) or a minor-piece check (Bb5+, Ng4+, Nh4+, Ne5+) that abandons the queen's protection.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is lured by immediate tactical rewards—winning a pawn, giving check, or capturing a piece—while overlooking that their most valuable piece (usually the queen) is left undefended on its square. The opponent simply captures or attacks the exposed queen on the next move, resulting in a catastrophic net material loss that far exceeds whatever the aggressive move gained. The average cp_loss of 307 reflects losing roughly a queen's worth of compensation.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a strong Queen capture (Qx__) and instead plays a quiet move, often also leaving own material hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's Queen has an available capture that is clearly the best move, but the player plays a quiet/passive move instead. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 86% of the time, with every single top-12 position featuring a Queen capture (Qxd4, Qxe4, Qxf4, Qxc1, Qxd5, Qxd2, Qxf2, Qxh5) as the best move. Only 13% of played moves were captures, confirming the player consistently chose non-captures over the Queen's available take. Additionally, 44% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns/58, majors/42, minors/40), compounding the error. The best move wins material outright in 23% of cases (median value 5.0), while in the remaining cases the Queen capture leads to decisive strategic/tactical gains despite an SEE of 0 (suggesting even exchanges that are nonetheless critical to play).
analysis.why_bad: By not using the Queen to capture (either winning material, recapturing, or making a critical exchange), the player allows the opponent to retain or activate dangerous pieces, often while simultaneously leaving their own pieces undefended. The average centipawn loss of 344 reflects that these missed Queen captures frequently turn winning or equal positions into losing ones.

analysis.label: The player makes a quiet move while an enemy piece (typically a rook) is freely capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player missed winning free material: 93% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 96% of best moves are captures. Yet the player's move was a capture only 13% of the time, meaning the player almost always played a quiet move instead. The positions are predominantly endgames (9/12) where an enemy major piece — usually a rook on an open file or the 7th rank — is en prise to a bishop, knight, pawn, or king capture. The 40% own-hang rate is a secondary consequence (the quiet move sometimes leaves the player's own material loose), not the primary error. The massive average cp_loss of 4698 reflects that missing free major-piece captures typically converts winning positions into draws or losses.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a simple, free capture of an enemy piece (typically worth 5+ points of material). Instead, the player makes positional king walks, pawn pushes, or piece repositioning moves that accomplish far less than simply removing the opponent's hanging rook or queen from the board. The oversight often turns a forced mate or decisive advantage into a merely better position.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of trading an undefended, aggressively-posted knight, leaving it hanging for the opponent to capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of best moves are captures with a median SEE of 0 (equal exchanges), while 62% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece). The hung-piece distribution is overwhelmingly minor pieces (71 out of 100). This indicates a consistent pattern: the player has an active but undefended knight (typically on e5 or e4) that must be exchanged immediately via NxD7/NxD2/NxE7/NxC6 before the opponent captures it. Instead, the player plays routine quiet moves (O-O, Bf4, Nc3, Bb5, Be2, Qa5) ignoring the tactical obligation to resolve the tension, leaving the knight en prise. The feature fires in openings (10/12 positions) where aggressive knight outposts are common but easily punished if unsupported.
analysis.why_bad: The knight is posted aggressively but has no defenders. The opponent's piece (usually a bishop on d7 or d2) can capture it. The best move is to trade now (equal exchange, SEE=0) to avoid losing the knight entirely. By playing a quiet developing move instead, the player gifts the opponent a free minor piece capture, resulting in average losses of ~410 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move in an endgame while an undefended enemy piece sits freely capturable, often by the king itself.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a missed-capture pattern: 87% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook-class piece), and 89% of the time the best move is a capture, yet the player's move was a capture only 11% of the time. The own-hang rate of 36% (median value just 1.0, typically a pawn) is a secondary side-effect, not the primary mistake. Nearly all positions (11/12) are endgames where an enemy piece—often a rook, sometimes a bishop, knight, or queen—is completely undefended and trivially capturable. In many cases the best move is simply a king capture of an adjacent unprotected piece (Kxg5, Kxe4, Kxa4, Kxf4, Kxd3). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating these are rare, extreme oversights.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (king walks, pawn pushes, piece maneuvers) pursue some long-term plan while ignoring that a high-value enemy piece has no defenders and can be taken immediately. By missing the free capture, the player forfeits material worth a rook or more (median 5.0), converting winning or equal positions into losses (average cp_loss: 2154).

analysis.label: Player gives a check with a minor piece (knight or bishop) that is left hanging after the opponent deals with the check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution being overwhelmingly minor pieces (40 out of 48 cases). Crucially, only 2% of best moves are checks, yet every single top-12 activated move IS a check (Ng5+, Nd1+, Nxe5+, Nxc6+, Bb8+, Nb2+, Nxf3+, Nf8+, Nb3+, Nf7+, Bg1+, Nxf2+). The player plays a flashy-looking check with a knight or bishop that lands on, or ends up on, a square where it is undefended and capturable once the opponent simply moves the king or interposes. The best moves (only 14% are captures, mostly quiet improving moves) indicate the correct strategy was consolidation or winning material another way, not a speculative check.
analysis.why_bad: The check accomplishes nothing strategically — the opponent simply moves the king (or captures) and then wins the undefended minor piece on the next move. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check without verifying whether the piece survives afterward. This typically costs a full minor piece (≈3 pawns) for no compensation, converting winning or equal positions into lost ones (avg cp_loss: 2436).

analysis.label: Player makes a bishop capture/exchange that leaves their own piece (typically a minor piece) en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 83% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 72% of the played moves are captures. The hung-piece class distribution is dominated by minors (36 out of 72 classified). The best move is a capture only 44% of the time and never a check, indicating the correct response was often a different tactical operation (like Nxe4, Nd4, or a quiet defensive move). The feature fires on positions where the player makes a tempting-looking bishop exchange (Bxf6, Bxe5, Bxc6, Bxd6) or pawn recapture that fails to address a critical threat to another of their own pieces, which remains or becomes undefended after the capture.
analysis.why_bad: These bishop captures/exchanges are superficially natural (trading pieces, winning material on one square) but ignore a more urgent tactical problem: another piece — usually a bishop or knight elsewhere on the board — is attacked or left undefended. The correct move typically either eliminates the attacking piece (e.g., Nxe4 removing a forking pawn), retreats the threatened piece, or defends it. By executing the tempting capture instead, the player loses material net because the opponent recaptures the hanging piece with no compensation.

analysis.label: Player gives a check instead of simply capturing an undefended enemy piece, often leaving their own piece hanging in the process.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a remarkably consistent pattern: in 84% of these positions the best move wins material (median 5.0 pawns) and 85% of best moves are captures of hanging enemy pieces. Yet the played moves are overwhelmingly checks (11 of 12 top-activating moves are checks), with only 22% being captures themselves. Critically, 70% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, predominantly major pieces at 34/57). The player is irresistibly drawn to a check—often a rook or queen delivering check on an open file or rank—while a free enemy piece (usually a rook or queen) sits undefended elsewhere on the board. This is the classic 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' syndrome.
analysis.why_bad: The checks are typically aimless—they force the king to move but achieve nothing concrete, while the player's checking piece lands on an undefended square (hanging it 70% of the time). Meanwhile, a simple capture of the opponent's undefended piece would win decisive material cleanly. The net result is often swinging from a winning position to losing, with an average centipawn loss of 1712.

analysis.label: The player chose a quiet developing or positional move instead of capturing an undefended or under-defended enemy piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates missed winning captures: 62% of best moves win material (median value 4.0, roughly a minor piece), and 70% of best moves are captures, yet the player's actual move was a capture only 23% of the time. The played moves are typically quiet developing moves (Nf6, Nbc3, Rfd1, Re8, Kg2, g3, h3, c5) — routine positional improvements — while an enemy piece sits undefended or tactically vulnerable. The 30% own-hang rate is a secondary byproduct (sometimes the quiet move also leaves something loose), but the dominant signal is the missed capture opportunity. Positions span all phases (opening through endgame) with an average cp_loss of 268, reflecting the substantial material cost of ignoring a free piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a concrete tactical opportunity — a free or cheaply available enemy piece — in favor of a 'natural-looking' but strategically irrelevant improvement. In chess, material advantage is decisive; playing Nf6 when Qxg5 wins a free knight, or Nbc3 when Nxd6 wins a queen, squanders a winning position by prioritizing abstract development over immediate material gain.

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing check (usually exploiting back-rank or king entombment) that leads to immediate checkmate or decisive material gain.
analysis.description: In the SEE aggregate, 96% of best moves are checks and 97% win material with a median value of 97 (queen/mate-level). Only 18% of best moves are captures, confirming the winning tactic is almost always a non-capturing check that forces mate. The played moves were overwhelmingly quiet (only 33% were captures), meaning players completely overlooked the tactical shot. The 53% own-hang rate (median value just 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental—the real catastrophe is missing forced mate, reflected in the enormous average cp_loss of 7712. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move exploits a trapped or back-rank king via Qe8+, Qa8+, Qe1#, Qb8+, Qg8+, d2+, Rd8+, Qe6+, Qc1+, Rc8+—consistently a single check delivering mate or winning the opponent's queen.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (h4, a5, Nf3, Kh7, b5, Rd1, Qe4, etc.) ignore the opponent's fatally weak back rank or enclosed king. By playing a slow positional or irrelevant move, the player throws away a forced checkmate (often mate-in-1 to mate-in-3), converting a completely won position into a loss or draw.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy piece attacking their queen, failing to simply capture it and leaving the queen en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires when an enemy piece (typically a bishop) has aggressively infiltrated to directly attack the player's queen, yet that enemy piece is itself undefended and freely capturable. The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of the time the best move is a capture (winning median 3.0 — a minor piece), while 89% of the time the player's actual move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 6.0, i.e., a queen). The 93% 'best wins material' and 89% 'own hung' figures are not contradictory — they describe the same geometric situation from both sides: the undefended attacker can be captured (winning material) and by not doing so, the queen remains attacked/hanging. The own-hang class is exclusively 'major' pieces (queens/rooks), with queens dominating at value 6.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player develops a piece or makes a pawn move while completely ignoring an undefended enemy piece that is directly attacking their queen. By not capturing the free attacker (e.g., Qxc7, Bxe7, Qxg5, Bxf4), the player simultaneously misses winning a free piece AND leaves their queen en prise, resulting in catastrophic material loss (~900+ centipawns average).

analysis.label: Player makes a move that leaves their own minor piece (usually a bishop) undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move leaves their own minor piece hanging. The SEE aggregate shows an overwhelming 88% of moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward minor pieces (150 minor vs 13 pawn vs 10 major out of ~173). In 58% of cases, the best move was a capture — often using the very piece that ends up hanging — and 48% of best moves win material outright. The pattern is clear across the top boards: players make quiet developing moves (Nc6, Be7, O-O, Rhg1, Nc3) or misdirected captures (Bxc4, Bxf4) while their own bishop or knight remains or becomes undefended. The correct move typically involves that threatened piece capturing an enemy piece (Bxd2+, Bxe2, Bxf6, Bxe7, Bxc3) to save itself productively.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores that their own minor piece (overwhelmingly a bishop) is attacked or undefended. By playing a different move — whether developing, castling, or capturing on the wrong square — they gift the opponent a free minor piece worth ~3 pawns, turning winning or equal positions into losing ones (avg cp_loss: 297).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move (often castling or a queen maneuver) while leaving their own minor piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly indicates the player hung their own piece: 69% of positions show the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece class distribution heavily favoring minors (31) over pawns (21) and majors (9). Only 27% of played moves were captures, and most were quiet moves like castling (O-O appears 4 times in top 12) or queen relocations (Qg5, Qf3, Qg7, Qb3). While the best move wins material 47% of the time (median 3.0), this is typically because the best move was to capture/defend the piece that the player instead left hanging. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting a specific class of blunder where players prioritize a strategic goal over an immediate tactical obligation.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability—their own knight or bishop is undefended or attacked—in favor of a 'desirable' positional move like castling for king safety or repositioning the queen. The opponent can simply capture the hanging piece on the next move, gaining material worth approximately a minor piece (≈3 pawns). The strategic benefit of the played move (e.g., king safety from castling) does not compensate for the material loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting move (often a capture) that leaves their own piece hanging, while missing a stronger forcing continuation that wins far more material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move hangs their own piece (75% of cases, median value 3.0 — typically minor pieces at 32/62, with major pieces at 16/62 and pawns at 14/62) while simultaneously missing a best move that wins significant material (70% of cases, median value 6.0). The best move is a check 30% of the time, indicating missed forcing sequences. The played moves are captures 42% of the time, suggesting the player is drawn to 'grabbing' material without seeing the refutation. The combination of high own-hang rate AND high best-wins-material rate indicates positions where the player makes a greedy or aggressive-looking move that backfires tactically, while a stronger forcing move (often a devastating check) was available.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an attractive-looking capture or aggressive move without verifying that their active piece remains safe afterward. The piece that moves (or another piece left undefended) becomes hanging, typically losing 3+ points of material. Meanwhile, a forcing move — often a check that leads to winning a queen or delivering decisive threats — goes unseen. The player's tactical vision is drawn to the immediate material gain rather than the geometrically superior forcing line.

analysis.label: Player promotes a pawn to queen instead of playing an urgent check or capture that wins the position.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check 50% of the time and a capture 42% of the time, with 61% of best moves winning material (median value ~97cp, i.e., roughly a queen). The player's move was almost never a capture (6%), confirming they chose the non-forcing promotion instead. In 50% of cases the promotion even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 4). All 12 top-activating boards show pawn promotions to queen (a8=Q, c1=Q, c8=Q, h8=Q, etc.) in endgames where an immediate check or tactical blow was critical. The average centipawn loss is a staggering 4365, indicating these promotions often lead directly to getting mated or throwing away a forced win.
analysis.why_bad: Promoting a pawn to a queen is psychologically irresistible but tactically irrelevant when the position demands an immediate forcing move. In these positions, the opponent has lethal threats (often back-rank mates or king hunts) or the player has a winning check/capture sequence available. The new queen arrives too slowly—it doesn't give check, doesn't capture a critical piece, and doesn't address the immediate tactical crisis. The opponent either mates immediately or neutralizes the advantage on the very next move.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move (often a bishop move) instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece, frequently hanging their own material in the process.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where an enemy piece is freely capturable but the player ignores it. The SEE aggregate shows that in 85% of top-500 positions the best move wins material (median value: 3.0 pawns), and 83% of the time the best move is a simple capture. Yet only 22% of the actually-played moves are captures — players overwhelmingly choose quiet developing moves instead. In 61% of cases the played move also leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value: 3.0), with the hung-piece distribution being minor pieces (36), major pieces (27), and pawns (17). The feature fires predominantly in the opening phase, where players appear focused on development patterns rather than board scanning for tactical opportunities.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore an immediately available material win — typically an undefended enemy bishop, knight, queen, or rook that could be captured for free. Instead, the player makes a routine-looking developing move (Bb7, Bf6, Be6, Bd6, Bd5, Nh6, O-O, etc.) that doesn't address the tactical reality. Worse, 61% of the time these moves also leave the player's own piece undefended, compounding a missed gain with an additional loss.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning knight move (fork or tactical jump) that wins significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value: 6.0), yet the player's move was only a capture 23% of the time—meaning the tactic was frequently overlooked entirely. Crucially, every single best move across all 12 top-activating positions is a knight move (Nf2, Nxc6, Nd3, Nc6, Nc7, Nd3, Ng3, Nf2, Ne3, Nxf7, Nxf7, Nxc3). Only 27% of these best moves are captures and only 23% are checks, indicating the typical pattern is a quiet knight jump to a square that creates a devastating fork of multiple enemy pieces (rooks, queen, king). The 36% own-hang rate on the played move (median 3.0, dominated by minor pieces) is incidental—the core error is failing to spot the knight's tactical potential.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a powerful knight tactic—typically a fork of two or more high-value enemy pieces. Instead of exploiting the knight's unique L-shaped geometry to land on a square attacking multiple targets simultaneously, the player makes routine developing moves, wrong captures, or positional moves that squander a concrete tactical opportunity worth significant material (often an exchange or more).

analysis.label: Player develops a piece (usually their own bishop) instead of recapturing or capturing a hanging enemy bishop worth ~3 pawns.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material in 85% of the top 500 positions (median value 3.0 = minor piece), and the best move is a capture 85% of the time. The player's move left their own piece hanging 78% of the time (median 3.0). All 12 top-activating positions feature an enemy bishop sitting en prise—either having just captured a piece (demanding recapture on f3, f6, or c3) or having infiltrated deep into the opponent's position undefended. The player ignores this free bishop and instead plays a quiet developing move—overwhelmingly a bishop development move (Be2, Be7, Bd3, Bd2 appear in 8/12 cases). All positions are in the opening phase with both kings still in the center.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to recapture or capture the free enemy bishop, the player loses approximately a full minor piece (3 pawns of material). The quiet developing move they play instead is irrelevant compared to the immediate tactical obligation to take a hanging piece. In many cases, the developing move also leaves their own material en prise, compounding the loss.

analysis.label: The player missed a knight or bishop move to an aggressive square that wins material (typically the exchange or a minor piece).
analysis.description: In 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 2.0 pawns. Strikingly, every single top-12 best move is a minor piece relocation (knights: Ng4, Nf5, Ng5, Ne5, Nf4; bishops: Bg4, Bb7, Be7, Bf4, Bg5, Bxa6, Ba3) — a knight or bishop jumping to a tactically potent square that attacks an insufficiently defended enemy piece. Only 20% of these best moves are captures and 0% are checks, meaning 80% are quiet minor-piece moves that create decisive threats (forks, attacks on rooks/queens, piece traps). The player instead plays a slow positional move (only 17% of played moves are captures), and in 45% of cases the played move additionally leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces). The feature fires on 2.1% of positions — those where a minor piece tactic is available but overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves are slow, positional, or prophylactic (Nd4, b6, Kf8, Rab1, f4, c3, c4, a5, etc.) that ignore an immediate tactical opportunity. By failing to jump a knight or bishop to an aggressive square that attacks a vulnerable enemy piece, the player forfeits winning material (median ~2 pawns, i.e., the exchange or a full minor piece) and often converts a winning or equal position into a losing one.

analysis.label: In pure king-and-pawn endgames, the player makes an aimless or misdirected king move instead of the critical winning continuation (often a decisive pawn advance or correctly-routed king march).
analysis.description: This feature fires on suboptimal king moves in pawn endgames. All 12 top-activating positions are pure pawn endgames, and every single played move is a king move (Kf3, Ke6, Kf5, Kb3, Kd3, Ke3, Kg5, Ke5, etc.). The SEE aggregate shows that 40% of the time the best move wins material (median value 100cp, i.e., a pawn—likely via decisive pawn advances toward promotion), and 28% of best moves are checks (pawn checks like g7+ or d2+ that force promotion). Meanwhile, 31% of the played king moves leave the player's own pawn hanging (median value 1.0, with 23 of 28 instances being pawns), because the king stepped away from defending a pawn. Only 10% of played moves were captures. The feature consistently identifies positions where the player chose a king move in the wrong direction or at the wrong time, missing critical pawn pushes (b2, c4, c6, g7+, d2+) or better-directed king routes.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves fail because they waste tempo, move the king away from the critical sector, or abandon support for a decisive pawn advance. In pawn endgames, precision and timing are everything—a single lost tempo or misdirected king step can turn a forced mate (positions 4 and 10 lost mate-in-6 and mate-in-9) into a grinding advantage, or can allow the opponent's king to reach a key defensive square. The correct moves are often pawn pushes that force immediate promotion or king routes that support the passed pawn while cutting off the opponent.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player moves their king (or plays another irrelevant move) instead of advancing a critical passed pawn, leaving that pawn undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 64% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being a pawn in 35 out of 41 cases. Only 12% of played moves were captures and just 2% of best moves were checks, confirming the mistake is not about missing tactics but about neglecting pawn advancement. The best moves win material in 30% of cases (often because the correct pawn push wins a tempo or promotes). Across all 12 positions—exclusively endgames—the player's king wanders off or makes a tempting but irrelevant move (a capture, a check, or repositioning) instead of pushing a decisive passed pawn (g7, d7, d2, g5, gxh4, etc.), abandoning protection of their own pawn which then becomes en prise.
analysis.why_bad: By moving the king away from (or failing to advance) a critical passed pawn, the player allows the opponent to capture the undefended pawn. Meanwhile, the correct move—pushing the pawn toward promotion—would have created an unstoppable queening threat or immediately won the game. The king move wastes a crucial tempo in positions where the pawn race is razor-thin.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (usually with a rook) in the endgame that leaves the capturing piece itself undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 82% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with the 'major' piece class dominating at 39 out of 53 hung instances. The player's move was itself a capture 57% of the time, confirming the pattern of greedily taking material only to leave the capturing piece unprotected. The best moves win material only 49% of the time—often the correct move is a quiet repositioning (Re1, Rh1, Rd5, Kh4) or an active check (Rf7+, Re8+) that maintains piece safety. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames with an average cp_loss of 1796, indicating catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The captures look attractive because they win immediate material (a pawn or piece), but the capturing piece—almost always a rook—lands on a square where it has no defender and can be taken by the opponent's king, rook, or other piece. In the endgame with few pieces, there is no backup to protect the rook on its new square, so the player loses more material than they gained, often losing the entire game immediately.

analysis.label: Player ignores a tactically critical bishop capture (Bx__) that resolves a key tension or exploits an opponent's weakness, instead playing a quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 97% of best moves are captures—and every single top-12 best move is a bishop capture (Bxh6, Bxa6, Bxe3, Bxh7, Bxe6, Bxc7, Bxa3). These captures register as SEE=0 (equal exchanges, median value won 2.0 in the 14% that do win outright), yet they carry enormous positional or tactical weight (avg cp_loss 186). Only 9% of the played moves were captures themselves, confirming the player consistently chose quiet moves over the available bishop trade. In 35% of cases (median value 3.0, dominated by minor pieces at 86 instances), the quiet move actually left the player's OWN piece hanging—often the very bishop or piece that should have initiated the exchange. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, pinpointing a narrow pattern where an obvious-looking bishop capture resolving a critical tension is overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the bishop capture, the player fails to resolve tactical tension at the optimal moment—missing chances to remove key defenders (Bxh6 exploiting an exposed knight), win strategically dominant trades (Bxa6 capturing an undefended bishop), or open attacking lines against an uncastled king. The quiet alternative often leaves their own pieces in limbo and, in 35% of cases, actually hangs a piece (typically the minor piece that could have been actively traded away).

analysis.label: The player makes a greedy or active move (often a capture) that leaves their own rook undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 94% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the hung piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (263 major out of 434 total). While 37% of the played moves are captures themselves (often rook captures like Rxe7, Rxe6, Rxc7, Rxg2, Rxe8), the critical error is that these moves place or leave the player's rook on an undefended square where the opponent can win it. The best moves are frequently quiet defensive resources (king moves like Kf7, Kd7, Kf2, Ke2, or retreats like Ree1) that would preserve the rook. Only 54% of best moves win material, meaning nearly half the time the correct play is simply to not hang the rook rather than to seek gains.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an immediate tactical action (capturing an enemy piece, centralizing, or making an 'active' move) while ignoring that their own rook is left undefended on its current or new square. The opponent then simply captures the hanging rook, resulting in a net material loss far exceeding whatever the played move gained. The correct approach is usually a quiet defensive move that maintains the rook's safety.

analysis.label: Player makes an inconsequential pawn move (push or low-priority pawn capture) that leaves their own material hanging while missing a stronger tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 80% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distribution heavily pawn-dominated at 274 pawns, with 70 minor and 57 major pieces also hung). Simultaneously, 58% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). Every single top-12 move is a pawn move — flank pushes like h3, g6, b6, b3, e6 or low-priority pawn captures like fxg3, fxg6, bxa3. These pawn moves are tactically irrelevant to the critical demands of the position, ignoring threats against the player's own pieces or missing devastating tactical shots (e.g., Qb5+ winning 91, Rf6 winning 9, Be4 winning 6). The average cp_loss of 1821 reflects the catastrophic cost of these slow, non-urgent pawn moves.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn moves fail because they address a non-critical part of the position (often a flank or recapture of marginal importance) while ignoring urgent tactical needs. The player's existing pieces are left undefended or their coordination collapses, allowing the opponent to exploit the hanging material. Meanwhile, a much stronger move — often a piece move delivering check, winning material, or addressing the key tactical tension — goes unplayed.

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing check that wins decisive material or forces mate against an exposed king in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the best move wins material (median value 97, i.e., essentially winning a queen or forcing mate), and 75% of the time the best move is a check. The played moves were overwhelmingly quiet (only 15% captures), and only 18% left the player's own piece hanging. This clearly indicates a 'missed winning' pattern rather than 'hung own piece.' Across all top-activating positions, both kings are exposed with weak pawn shields in endgames, and a tactical check exists that either wins outright material or initiates a forced mating sequence. The player instead played a passive repositioning move, missing the critical forcing blow.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves fail because they surrender an immediately winning tactical opportunity — a check that exploits the enemy king's exposure to win material, force a trade that stops a promotion, or deliver a mating attack. By playing a non-forcing move, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, promote a pawn, or escape the dangerous king position, often converting a won game into a draw or loss (average cp_loss of 4075).

analysis.label: Player fails to play a critical bishop move (usually blocking a diagonal threat) and instead hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a bishop deployment—typically an interposition or development to block a diagonal attack—but the player plays something else entirely. The SEE aggregate shows 55% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 112 minor pieces, 99 pawns, and 62 major pieces affected), while 45% of best moves win material (median 3.0). Strikingly, in 11 of the top 12 activating positions the best move is a bishop move (Be7, Bf5, Bf4, Bf3, Be2, Bd2, Bd4, Bd6). The best move is a check 0% and a capture only 11% of the time, confirming these are quiet defensive bishop moves that the player overlooks.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the required bishop move (often needed to block an enemy bishop's diagonal attacking their queen), the player leaves high-value pieces en prise. In the strongest activations, queens are left hanging to diagonal attacks (positions 1, 3, 6, 11 all show value-6 pieces hung). The player typically develops or moves a different piece, completely missing the urgent diagonal geometry.

analysis.label: The player gives a tempting check (or aggressive lunge) that leaves their own piece undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 71% of positions have the player's move leaving their own piece en prise (median value 2.0, corresponding to minor pieces). The hung-piece class distribution is heavily minor (47) and pawn (37), with few majors (9). Meanwhile, the best move is a check only 2% of the time, yet the vast majority of the top-activating moves played ARE checks (f6+, Rd7+, Nxe5+, bxc4+, Qh5+, Nc7+, Bf6+). The player is seduced by delivering check rather than playing the objectively superior move (which wins material in 41% of cases, often a simple capture at 30%). The checks land the piece on an unprotected square where it is lost once the king sidesteps.
analysis.why_bad: Checks are psychologically alluring because they force the opponent to respond, but here the checking piece (typically a knight or bishop) lands on an undefended square. After the king simply moves, the piece is captured for free. The player trades a sound position (or material gain) for a meaningless check that costs a whole piece.

analysis.label: The player missed a winning knight move (fork or tactical strike to a central square) that wins significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 87% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 6.0 (a rook or equivalent). Strikingly, every single best move across all 12 top boards is a knight maneuver (Nd4, Nd5, Ne4, Ne5, Nf5, Nxe5, Nxd4, Nxd5) — always jumping to an aggressive central square that forks or tactically wins heavy material. The player's move was a capture only 20% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly played passive quiet moves (Be7, Kh8, a6, O-O-O, Nb1, etc.) instead of the decisive knight strike. The 47% own-hung rate (median value 2.0, mostly pawns/minors) is a secondary symptom of the passive, non-forcing nature of the chosen moves. Best move is a capture only 30% and a check only 3%, indicating these knight tactics win material primarily through forks or attacks on undefended pieces rather than checks.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves are passive or developmental (bishop retreats, king safety moves, pawn pushes, retreating knights) that completely overlook a tactical knight jump to a central square that forks or attacks multiple enemy pieces simultaneously, winning a rook or queen's worth of material. The player fails to recognize the knight's unique geometry and the vulnerability of the opponent's piece placement.

analysis.label: Player misses capturing an undefended central e-pawn with a knight (Nxe4 or Nxe5) in the opening, playing a quiet developing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 92% of best moves win material (median value: 1 pawn) and 95% of best moves are captures, yet only 3% of played moves are captures—the player consistently plays quiet moves instead. All 12 top-activating positions are in the opening phase with the identical tactical motif: the opponent's e-pawn (e4 or e5) is undefended, and a knight can simply take it for free.
