The best move is always Nxe4 or Nxe5. The 24% own-hang rate is incidental to some played moves creating new weaknesses, but the primary pattern is clearly a missed free pawn capture. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, reflecting the specificity of this opening central-pawn-hanging geometry.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet developing moves (Bd3, b3, Nbd7, Bd7, b6, Qe7, h6, etc.) ignore a concrete tactical opportunity to win a free central pawn. By failing to capture the undefended e-pawn with the knight, the player gives the opponent time to consolidate their center, often turning a clear advantage into equality or worse. The average cp_loss of 263 centipawns reflects not just the material missed but the positional consequences of allowing the opponent to stabilize.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own piece hanging and undefended, typically while ignoring a critical threat such as an impending mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 90% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value: 1.0), with the hung-piece distribution being pawns (53), minor pieces (30), and major pieces (22). Additionally, 66% of best moves win material (median 3.0), meaning the player also misses winning opportunities. Only 34% of moves are captures and only 15% of best moves are captures, showing the pattern isn't about trade miscalculations. The extraordinarily high average cp_loss of 4808 and the prevalence of mate-in-N outcomes across the top boards indicate these self-hangs occur in positions with urgent tactical threats—the player makes a seemingly purposeful move (a capture, a rook relocation, a pawn push) that both leaves material en prise and fatally ignores the opponent's attacking resources.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail on two levels: they leave the player's own pieces undefended and capturable (90% of cases), and they ignore critical tactical demands of the position—most commonly an impending mating attack. The player appears to pursue a local goal (capturing a pawn, repositioning a piece) while missing that their move creates a new vulnerability and fails to address the most urgent threat, resulting in catastrophic material or positional loss.

analysis.label: Player fails to promote a pawn (usually to Queen) that is one square from queening, instead playing checks, quiet moves, or underpromotions.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material 55% of the time with a median value of 5.0 (consistent with the net gain of promoting a pawn to a Queen), while the played moves are rarely captures (10%) and occasionally leave own material hanging (30%). Across all top 12 boards, the best move is invariably a pawn promotion to Queen (a8=Q, h1=Q, h8=Q, b8=Q, d1=Q, c8=Q, etc.) with the pawn sitting one square from the back rank. Instead, players choose rook checks (Rb5+, Rb6+, Re1+, Rg2+, Re3+, Rxg7+), quiet king/rook moves (Kf2, Ra6, Kb8), or suboptimal underpromotions (a1=B, b8=R). The feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (11/12) where an immediate Queen promotion was available but not played.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they delay or forfeit the decisive material advantage of creating a new Queen. Giving checks with the rook or playing quiet moves allows the opponent to reorganize defensively or approach the promotion square, turning won positions into draws or even losses. Underpromotions (to Bishop or Rook) forfeit the Queen's superior power. In several cases (cp_loss of 558-9434), the missed promotion turns a winning/mating position into a draw or loss.

analysis.label: A bishop captures on f7 (or f2) with check in the opening without sufficient tactical follow-up, leaving the bishop en prise to the king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and the piece class distribution confirms 132 minor pieces out of 145 cases. The played move is a capture 84% of the time, yet the best move wins material only 23% of the time and is never a check (0%). This indicates the player is initiating a premature sacrifice rather than missing an opponent's hanging piece. All 12 top-activating positions show Bxf7+ or Bxf2+ in Italian Game / Two Knights / Philidor-type openings where the bishop on c4 (or c5) lunges at f7 (or f2) with check, but the king simply captures the bishop and there is no adequate continuation to recover the material.
analysis.why_bad: After Bxf7+ Kxf7, the bishop is lost for only a pawn. The king displacement to f7 provides no tangible advantage because the attacker lacks the coordinated pieces (typically a knight on g5 or queen access) needed to generate a real mating attack or win back material. The correct moves are quiet developing moves (d3, Nc3, Nf3, c3, d4) that build toward a real position rather than sacrificing a piece prematurely. The sacrifice nets -3 material (bishop for pawn) with no compensation, resulting in average 342cp loss.

analysis.label: The player makes a passive, unnecessary king move instead of executing a decisive winning action (promotion, queen maneuver, or capture).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player blunders by making an aimless king move (10/12 top activations are king moves) when a far stronger action is available. The SEE aggregate shows that 25% of best moves win material (median 3.0 pawns), 19% of best moves are captures, and 0% of played moves are captures—the player consistently chooses passive king shuffles over decisive actions. The best moves across positions include pawn promotions (f1=Q, b8=Q), powerful queen maneuvers (Qe7, Qg5, Qh2, Qd7, Qg7, Qg2), and winning captures (hxg5, Nxd2). The 12% own-hang rate is low, confirming the mistake is not about self-hanging but rather about missing winning continuations. The average cp_loss of 2330 centipawns reflects these are catastrophic missed wins.
analysis.why_bad: The king moves are passive and purposeless, wasting tempo in positions where immediate decisive action (promotion, queen activity, or capturing undefended pieces) would win quickly or deliver checkmate. By moving the king instead of promoting, deploying the queen, or capturing material, the player throws away completely winning positions, often converting forced mates into merely large advantages or even draws.

analysis.label: The player missed a knight fork that delivers check while simultaneously attacking (and winning) a major piece, typically the queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: 98% of best moves are checks and 77% win material with a median value of 97 (queen-equivalent). Every single top-12 position features a knight delivering a discovered or direct check that simultaneously forks the king and a high-value piece (Nf6+, Nc1+, Nh6+, Ne3+, Ng4+, Nxe7+, Nxf3+). The best move is only a capture 31% of the time, meaning the knight usually lands on a clean square giving check while threatening the queen or rook. The played moves are diverse (24% captures, various quiet moves), and 52% leave own pieces hanging — indicating the player was distracted by other plans and completely overlooked the devastating knight geometry.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a knight fork that gives check — an essentially forced sequence where the opponent must address the check, after which the knight captures the undefended major piece. By playing greedy captures (Qxb7, Rxb2), routine developing moves (Ng5, Re5), or defensive moves (Kf8, Kd2), the player throws away a decisive tactical blow worth roughly a queen.

analysis.label: The player moves a bishop (or exposes it) to a square where it is left en prise and can be captured for free.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The piece class distribution is dominated by minor pieces (100 minor vs 60 major vs 17 pawn). Examining the top 12 boards, 9 out of 12 specifically involve hanging a bishop — moves like Bc7, Bg6+, Bxf3, Bb4, Bxg4, Bc3, Bg4, and Ba4 all place a bishop on an undefended square where it can be captured. Only 17% of positions had the best move winning material, confirming this is not a 'missed capture' pattern but overwhelmingly a 'hung own piece' pattern. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific minor-piece-hanging blunder.
analysis.why_bad: These moves place the player's bishop on a square with no adequate defense, allowing the opponent to simply capture it for free (or win it in a one-move exchange), resulting in a net loss of approximately 3 pawns' worth of material. The players typically misjudge the safety of the destination square, either overlooking an opponent's attack on that square or failing to realize that after a capture exchange the bishop remains unprotected.

analysis.label: Player misses a decisive queen check in a queen endgame with exposed kings, playing a passive quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies positions where the best move is a check (92%) that wins material (98%, median value 100). The played moves were captures only 2% of the time, confirming that players chose passive alternatives. Only 24% of played moves left own pieces hanging (median value just 1 pawn), so this is not a 'hung own piece' pattern—it is a 'missed winning check' pattern. All top-12 positions are queen endgames featuring dangerously exposed enemy kings (often near the board edge or with passed pawns restricting escape) where a forcing queen check—sometimes a capture-check on an enemy pawn—would either deliver forced mate or win decisive material. Instead, players consistently chose quiet king retreats (Kd7, Kd2, Ke3, Kc3, Kd3, Kh4) or passive queen repositioning (Qh2, Qf7, Qh1, Qa1, Qe5, Qg2).
analysis.why_bad: These passive moves squander winning positions (average 4108 cp loss) by ignoring forcing checks that exploit the exposed enemy king. In many cases the missed check leads directly to forced mate (multiple positions show #+3 to #+15 converted to draws or near-equality), while the quiet alternative either allows the opponent to promote dangerous passed pawns, reach a fortress, or escape to safety. The fundamental error is choosing a non-forcing move when a forcing queen check immediately decides the game.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a simple capture of an undefended enemy piece (usually a rook) in the endgame, instead playing an irrelevant quiet move or check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 75% of the top 500 activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. a rook), and 88% of the time the best move is a capture—yet only 6% of the actually-played moves were captures. The player's move left their own piece hanging in just 38% of cases, confirming the dominant direction is not 'hung own piece' but rather 'failed to take a free enemy piece.' Across the top 12 boards, the missed capture is overwhelmingly a rook (Rxb6, Rxf3, Kxc5, Rxg5, Rxe8, Bxd6, Rxh3, Rxa8, Bxf8) that is completely undefended. Instead, the player chose a king retreat, a purposeless check, or a passive positional move, turning winning positions into losses with an average centipawn loss of 1610.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available free capture worth approximately a full rook (5 points of material). The played moves—often king moves or flashy checks—accomplish nothing concrete while the opponent's undefended piece remains on the board, and in many cases the opponent then consolidates or gains a decisive advantage themselves.

analysis.label: Player ignores a central pawn's attack on their own bishop (c4 or c5), leaving it en prise while making another move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 56% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being minor pieces (18 of 20 classified). The best move is a capture in 69% of cases and wins material 50% of the time (median 1.0 pawn). Across the top 12 boards, the recurring pattern involves a bishop on c4 (White) or c5 (Black) that is attacked by the opponent's d-pawn (d5 or d4 respectively). The correct response is to retreat the bishop to safety (Bd3 or Bd6), but instead the player makes a developing or aggressive move with another piece—typically a knight—completely ignoring the pawn threat to the bishop. All 12 positions are in the opening phase with an average cp_loss of 258.
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they leave an undefended bishop on c4/c5 directly attacked by the opponent's central d-pawn. After the opponent captures the bishop with the pawn (dxc4 or dxc5), the player loses a full minor piece (3 points) for nothing. The aggressive-looking knight moves or development choices cannot compensate for the outright material loss of the bishop, which the opponent simply takes on the next move with a pawn.

analysis.label: The player missed capturing an undefended g-pawn (or b-pawn) with the queen in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), and 80% of the time the best move is a queen capture. Examining the top 12 boards reveals an overwhelmingly specific pattern: 9 of 12 positions feature Qxg2 or Qxg7 as the best move, and 2 more feature Qxb7—all capturing an undefended pawn with the queen. The positions are predominantly in the opening (10/12) with kings still in the center, where the g-pawn (or b-pawn) is left unprotected due to underdevelopment or awkward piece placement. The player's move was only a capture 19% of the time, confirming they consistently chose quiet or positional moves over the available pawn grab. The 41% own-hang rate is secondary collateral from the suboptimal moves chosen.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (c6, f6, Ng4, Qe4+, Qe5, h3, O-O, etc.) ignore a concrete tactical opportunity—a free pawn capture with the queen—in favor of slow positional or developing moves. By not grabbing the undefended g-pawn (or b-pawn), the player surrenders a clean material advantage (median 1 pawn, avg 336cp loss) and often allows the opponent to consolidate their king or seize the initiative.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available winning capture and instead makes a move that leaves their own piece en prise, compounding the error.
analysis.description: In 88% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn, with 75% of best moves being captures), yet the player makes a different move that 75% of the time leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value hung: 2, distributed as 7 minor pieces, 4 major pieces, 1 pawn among the top cases). Only 19% of played moves are captures themselves, meaning the player typically opts for a quiet/developing move. The compounding mistake is clear: an enemy pawn or piece is both capturable AND threatening one of the player's pieces, but the player ignores the tactical capture—often choosing development or the wrong recapture—leaving their piece still under attack and therefore hung.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical reality: an enemy piece or pawn is simultaneously winnable and dangerous. By not capturing it (e.g., Nxe4 in Caro-Kann positions, gxf6 against an advanced pawn, Bxf6/Bxd4 against an exposed piece), the player leaves their own piece attacked by the very unit they could have removed. The result is typically a swing of 2+ pawns: missing ~1 pawn of material gain while also losing ~2 pawns worth of their own piece, for a net loss far exceeding either mistake alone.

analysis.label: Player misses a quiet pawn advance (or occasional piece reposition) that would win material, often distracted by a tempting capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of the time the best move wins material (median value: 2.0, roughly a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 5% of the time and a check 0% of the time — meaning the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet threat (pawn advance or piece repositioning). The player's move is itself a capture 24% of the time, suggesting frequent distraction by available captures rather than finding the stronger quiet tactical thrust. In 39% of cases the played move also hangs the player's own piece (median value 1.0; distribution: 108 pawns, 59 minors, 27 majors), compounding the error. Across the top 12 boards, the missed best moves are predominantly pawn advances (e5, d5, c6, f5, c5, e4) that create forks, traps, or decisive threats against enemy pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they pursue superficially appealing goals (grabbing available material via captures, making natural developing moves) while missing a quiet pawn advance or piece move that creates an unstoppable tactical threat — typically forking, trapping, or attacking an enemy minor piece. The tempting capture or quiet alternative doesn't address the critical tactical opportunity, surrendering roughly 2 pawns' worth of material advantage (average 274cp loss).

analysis.label: The player captures an enemy piece with check using a rook or queen, but the capturing piece is left undefended on its destination square and will be recaptured.
analysis.description: In 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and 80% of the played moves are captures. All top-12 examples are captures with check (Rxe8+, Qxd1+, Rxe1+, etc.) using major pieces. The own-hang piece class distribution is heavily major pieces (69 major vs 22 minor). Meanwhile, 79% of positions had a best move winning material (median 3.0), with only 6% of best moves being checks—showing the player was seduced by the forcing 'capture-with-check' rather than the stronger quiet or non-check continuation. The average cp_loss of 1853 confirms these are catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The capture-check appears forcing and attractive, but once the opponent deals with the check (typically by moving the king or interposing), the capturing rook or queen sits undefended on the back rank or open file and is simply recaptured. The player trades a major piece for a piece of lesser or equal value when a better move (often a quiet threat, a different capture, or a positional squeeze) would have preserved the full material or mating advantage.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive tactical shot (often a check) that would win the opponent's queen or deliver a game-ending blow.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 81% of activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 9.0 pawns—queen-equivalent. Crucially, the best move is a check 36% of the time but a direct capture only 20%, indicating the winning pattern is typically a fork, skewer, or discovered attack initiated via check that wins the queen indirectly. The player's move was a capture only 30% of the time, and while 37% of played moves left an own piece hanging, the median hung value is just 1.0 (mostly pawns), confirming this is secondary. The overwhelming signal is missed winning: the player overlooks a forcing tactic—often check-based—that would net the opponent's queen. The average cp_loss of 2644 confirms these as catastrophic oversights.
analysis.why_bad: The player overlooks a forcing move (frequently a check producing a royal fork, skewer on the queen, or unstoppable mating threat) that would win the opponent's queen or equivalent decisive material. Instead, they play a quiet or irrelevant move, allowing the opponent to consolidate or even counter-attack, squandering a winning position entirely.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet developing move while leaving their undefended bishop on g5 en prise to the opponent's queen (typically via Qa5 along the 5th rank).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 72% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = bishop), with the hung piece being a minor piece in 71% of cases (45/63). The best move wins material 67% of the time (median 6.0), typically because retreating the bishop (Bd2) would prevent the loss. In the top 12 boards, the overwhelming pattern is an opening position where White has developed a bishop to g5 which becomes undefended and tactically vulnerable to Black's queen on a5 exploiting the open 5th rank. Instead of playing Bd2 to retreat the bishop to safety, the player makes an unrelated developing move (Bd3, f3, Bg2, a3, Qb3, Nbd2, etc.), leaving the bishop hanging. The analogous Black-side cases involve leaving a bishop on f5 unprotected when Bd7 was needed.
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore an immediate tactical threat: the opponent's queen has a clear path (usually along the 5th rank from a5 to g5) to capture an undefended bishop. By making a quiet developing move instead of retreating the bishop with Bd2 (or protecting it), the player loses a full minor piece for nothing, turning an equal or slightly better position into a losing one (~400+ centipawn loss).

analysis.label: Player ignores a straightforward bishop capture (winning or correctly recapturing) and instead plays a different move that typically hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture 79% of the time (median value won 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the player's actual move was a capture only 26% of the time — meaning the player overwhelmingly ignores the correct capture. Furthermore, 55% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces: 32 minor, 13 major, 12 pawn). Examining the top boards reveals the best move is almost always a bishop capture (Bxe5, Bxg7, Bxd5, Bxe4, Bxb7, Bxc6) or a queen capture of an undefended piece. Instead, the player typically makes a knight move (Nxe5 wrong recapture, Nd4, Nb5, Ne7, Ng6) or a quiet bishop development move (Bb7, Bf5, Bf6), which leaves their own piece undefended on its new square.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because (1) when the player captures with the knight instead of the bishop (Nxe5 vs Bxe5), the knight lands on a square where it is undefended and immediately attacked, losing material; (2) when the player plays a quiet developing move, they ignore a free or winning capture (often of a bishop that has over-extended into their territory), simultaneously leaving their own piece tactically vulnerable due to the skipped defensive priority of the capture.

analysis.label: Player recaptures an enemy piece immediately instead of first inserting a devastating intermediate check (zwischenzug) that wins far more material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of the time the best move wins material (median value 9, i.e. queen-level), and 74% of best moves are checks, while the played move is a capture 91% of the time that leaves the player's own piece hanging 74% (median value 3, predominantly minor pieces at 31/42). This signature reveals positions where an enemy piece (usually a queen) has infiltrated and appears capturable, but before recapturing, the player should insert an intermediate check—typically with the very knight or bishop that will be left hanging after the routine recapture. The zwischenzug wins enormously more material (often the enemy queen plus additional pieces) compared to the straightforward recapture that nets far less and leaves one's own piece en prise.
analysis.why_bad: By immediately recapturing the infiltrating piece (e.g., Raxd1 taking a queen on d1), the player forfeits the chance to play an intermediate check (e.g., Nxe7+, Nc7+, Nf3+) with the very piece that becomes undefended after the recapture. The zwischenzug exploits the tempo of check to win vastly more material—often a full queen's worth—before then collecting the original piece. The routine capture not only misses this windfall but often leaves the unchecking piece hanging for free.

analysis.label: The player missed an available checkmate (almost always mate-in-one) and played an irrelevant move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of activating positions, and it wins material 99% of the time with a median value of 100 (representing mate). Only 32% of the best moves are captures — the rest are pure piece-delivery checks that are themselves checkmate. The played moves show no coherent theme (36% are captures, 26% leave own material hanging with median value 1.0), confirming the player simply failed to notice the mating opportunity. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting the rare scenario where a forced mate exists but is completely overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail catastrophically because the player overlooks an immediate or near-immediate checkmate — most commonly a back-rank mate (Re1#, Rd1#, Qf8#, Qxe8#) exploiting the opponent's king being trapped behind its own pawns. Instead of delivering the decisive blow, the player makes a routine developing move, captures on the wrong square, or pursues an irrelevant plan, converting a won game (mate-in-1 or mate-in-2) into a position where the advantage may be drastically reduced or even lost.

analysis.label: Player missed a queen check (typically to the back rank) that wins the opponent's queen or equivalent material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: 99% of best moves are checks, 99% win material with a median value of 100 (a queen), yet only 23% are captures—meaning the queen check initiates a forcing sequence (fork, skewer, or back-rank exploitation) rather than directly taking material. The player's actual moves were captures only 16% of the time and were mostly quiet repositioning or greedy captures. In 46% of cases, the played move even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, predominantly pawns). The top 12 boards confirm the geometry: best moves are universally queen checks to the 1st/8th rank (Qb1+, Qf8+, Qd8+, Qf1+, Qa1+, Qe1+, Qc1+, Qd1+), exploiting exposed kings to win the opponent's queen.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a forcing queen check that wins the opponent's queen through a tactical sequence. Instead of delivering check and exploiting the opponent's vulnerable king position to win decisive material, players chose greedy captures (Qxa2, Qxc4, Qxc6), passive repositioning (Qa5, Qf3, Qg4), or positional moves (c5, f4, Ke2)—none of which are forcing and all of which forfeit a game-winning tactical opportunity worth approximately a full queen.

analysis.label: Player ignores the critical move that would trap an enemy piece that has ventured deep into their territory or to the board's edge.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best_wins_material at only 24% (median 2.0) because trapping moves restrict rather than immediately capture—SEE undervalues them. The played move left own pieces hanging 35% of the time (median value 2.0, split across minor:22, pawn:21, major:7), likely a secondary consequence of leaving the dangerous enemy piece active. Only 9% of best moves are captures and 3% are checks, confirming the best move is typically a quiet restricting pawn push or piece placement. Across all 12 top-activating positions, the best move wins 0 material immediately but creates an inescapable cage: b3 traps a bishop on a2 (positions 1,2,4), b6 traps a bishop on a7 (position 7), c6 restricts a knight on a7 (position 5), Kg4 traps a knight on g2 (position 9), Bd3 traps a knight on d2 (position 10), g3 traps a knight on e2 (position 12), g6 entombs a bishop on h7/h8 (positions 3,6), and b4 traps a bishop on a3 (position 11).
analysis.why_bad: The played moves pursue general plans (kingside attacks, piece development, centralization) while completely overlooking that an enemy piece is overextended and can be permanently trapped by a simple restricting move—typically a pawn advance that cuts off all retreat squares. The missed trap would win roughly a full piece worth of material over the next few moves, explaining the average 270cp loss.

analysis.label: Player captures with a bishop or knight that is left en prise on the destination square in an endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward minors (135 minor vs 18 major vs 2 pawn). The played move is a capture 85% of the time, and all top-12 positions show a bishop or knight capturing an enemy piece (Bxc4, Bxg5, Nxd5, Nxe6, etc.) only to be left undefended on the new square. Meanwhile, the best move wins material only 54% of the time (often via quiet repositioning like Bb1, Be4, Kf5, Ne2), indicating the correct play was usually to preserve the minor piece rather than grab material. The feature fires exclusively in endgames where the minor piece is a critical strategic asset.
analysis.why_bad: In these endgame positions, the minor piece (bishop or knight) is essential for defense, blockading passed pawns, or controlling key squares. By capturing an enemy piece, the minor piece lands on an undefended square where it can be immediately recaptured or won, effectively trading away a strategically indispensable piece for insufficient material compensation. The better alternatives preserve the minor piece's activity and defensive function.

analysis.label: The player made a quiet move while an enemy bishop (or minor piece worth 3 points) was left completely undefended and freely capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates missed captures of unprotected enemy minor pieces: 92% of best moves win material with a median value of exactly 3.0 (bishop/knight), and 98% of best moves are captures. Meanwhile, only 16% of played moves were captures — the player almost always chose a quiet move instead. Across the top 12 positions, every single best move captures an undefended enemy bishop (Rxd4, Rxd5, fxe6, Rxg5, bxc4, Nxf4, Rxg5, Nxd3+, Rxc2, Rxd3, Nxg3, Rxe6). The 50% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary effect — some played moves additionally weakened the player's own position — but the primary and consistent error is ignoring the free enemy piece.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (king walks, rook repositions, pawn pushes) fail because they ignore a trivially available capture of an undefended enemy bishop sitting en prise. The player gives up approximately 3 pawns' worth of free material and often squanders a winning or dominant position, typically losing 250-500 centipawns of evaluation by choosing to do something else while a free piece is sitting there.

analysis.label: Player gives an aimless check (usually with the queen) instead of finding the decisive winning move, often leaving the checking piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 74% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), yet the played move was a capture only 31% of the time—indicating the player chose a non-winning action. Critically, 46% of the time the played move left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, heavily skewed toward major pieces: 15 major, 7 minor, 6 pawn), while the best move is a check only 33% of the time. Examining the top 12 boards, at least 8 of 12 moves played are checks (Qe6+, Qc6+, Qe3+, Be5+, Qf7+, Qf3+, a6+, Qxb6+), yet the best moves are often quiet material-winners (Qxe2, Qxc3, Nf3, Bxe7, Qxc7) or even immediate checkmate (Qe3#). The player reflexively gives check—especially with the queen—rather than calculating the truly winning continuation. The enormous average cp_loss of 3971 confirms these are catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These checks are pointless because after the opponent moves their king, the checking piece (usually the queen) is left en prise or displaced to an inferior square, squandering a winning position. The player misses immediate checkmates, material wins, or forced mating nets because they reflexively chose the most forcing-looking move (a check) without verifying it actually accomplishes anything. The opponent simply sidesteps the check and the advantage evaporates.

analysis.label: The player missed a forcing check (often a capture-check or fork) that decisively wins material, instead playing a plausible but losing non-forcing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 64% of best moves are checks and 62% are captures (with heavy overlap indicating capture-checks and fork-checks), while 69% of best moves win material with a median gain of 3.0 (a minor piece). The player's actual move was a capture only 31% of the time, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet or less forcing alternatives. Only 33% of played moves hung own material, confirming the dominant mistake direction is failing to WIN material rather than giving it away. The feature fires on endgame-heavy positions (7/12) with exposed kings on both sides, where tactical geometry (forks, captures-with-check, discovered attacks) creates decisive forcing opportunities that the player overlooks in favor of greedy pawn captures, instinctive recaptures, or king moves in the wrong direction.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they surrender the initiative and throw away a decisive tactical advantage. Instead of a forcing check that either captures material directly (Nxe7+, Bxd3+, Bxc6+) or sets up an unavoidable fork (Nd2+ winning a rook), the players chose non-forcing moves like grabbing a pawn (Kxh7, cxb5), recapturing a traded piece (Qxd2), moving the king the wrong direction (Kb6, Ke4), or making a slow plan (f5, Re7). The resulting position swings from winning to losing (avg 711cp loss) because the opponent stabilizes and the tactical opportunity vanishes.

analysis.label: The player makes a greedy capture or careless move that ignores an immediate mating threat, allowing the opponent to deliver checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move—often a greedy queen capture on the periphery—walks into a devastating mating attack or massive tactical blow. The SEE aggregate shows 61% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, heavily pawn-weighted: 170 pawns, 46 minors, 43 majors), indicating the move typically abandons defensive duties. Meanwhile, 56% of the time the best move would have won material (median 2.0), suggesting the correct response often involved addressing the opponent's threat while simultaneously winning material. The average cp_loss of 6011 and numerous mate-in-1 evaluations confirm these are catastrophic blunders. Only 21% of played moves are captures, but the top activations are dominated by greedy queen captures (Qxc2, Qxh3, Qxc7, Qxa2, Rxf7) that snatch material far from the player's king while a lethal mating pattern exists.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize irrelevant material gain (or make aimless king moves) while the opponent has an immediate mating combination available. The queen or rook leaves its defensive post to grab a pawn or minor piece, and the opponent delivers checkmate—typically exploiting back-rank weakness, exposed kings, or undefended mating squares. The player focuses on the wrong part of the board at the critical moment.

analysis.label: Player misses an immediate or near-immediate queen check (often checkmate) in favor of a greedy capture or inferior move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91, indicating checkmate-level gains), and 92% of the time the best move is a CHECK, while only 37% are captures. The player's actual move was a capture 38% of the time (typically grabbing a rook on a8 or other loose piece). The enormous average cp_loss of 7137 confirms these are predominantly missed checkmates. The pattern across all 12 boards is consistent: an exposed enemy king is vulnerable to a decisive queen check—often immediate checkmate (Qb3#, Qxc5#, Qd7#, Qg3#)—but the player instead plays a materialistic queen capture or a non-optimal check/quiet move, completely missing the killing blow.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize capturing material (often a rook on a8) or deliver a check that doesn't lead to mate, when an immediate queen check delivers checkmate or forces a winning sequence exploiting the exposed enemy king. The player's greedy instinct or pattern-matching to 'check then take' causes them to overlook the geometrically available mating square for their queen.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy queen that is directly capturable (usually by a pawn) and instead plays a quiet, aimless move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (queen-level), and 81% of best moves are captures, while the player's move was a capture only 12% of the time. The top boards overwhelmingly show positions where the enemy queen has wandered onto a square directly attacked by a pawn or minor piece (dxc5, fxe6, exf6, axb3, Nxd7, Bxd4, Bxe4), yet the player plays a quiet king move or pawn push instead. The 44% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental and secondary to the catastrophic failure to capture the enemy queen. The enormous average cp_loss of 4040 confirms the player is routinely forfeiting the equivalent of a queen.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (mostly king shuffles like Kh3, Kh2, Ka1, Kh8, or passive pawn pushes like f3, g3, b6) completely ignore the tactical reality that the opponent's queen is en prise to a simple pawn or piece capture. By failing to take the queen, the player throws away a massive material gain that would either win the game or dramatically improve a lost position.

analysis.label: The queen greedily captures the b2 or b7 pawn ('poisoned pawn') instead of developing or pursuing a superior alternative.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the queen captures the b-pawn (Qxb2 for Black, Qxb7 for White) in a classic 'poisoned pawn' scenario. The SEE aggregate shows that 78% of played moves were captures (the Qxb2/Qxb7 grabs), while 75% of positions had a better move that won material (median value 1.0 pawn), yet only 12% of best moves were themselves captures — indicating the correct approach was usually a quiet developing move. The 40% own-piece-hanging rate reflects positions where the queen becomes vulnerable or trapped after entering enemy territory. The feature fires on just 0.2% of all positions, targeting this specific and well-known opening trap pattern where both kings are typically still in the center and development is incomplete.
analysis.why_bad: The queen ventures deep into enemy territory to grab a single pawn, but gets driven back or trapped by the opponent's developing moves (e.g., Rb1, Na4, Nc3 attacking the queen on b2; or Rb8, Nc6 trapping it on b7). The opponent gains multiple tempi developing with threats against the exposed queen, creating an overwhelming positional and developmental advantage that far outweighs the captured pawn. The correct moves were almost always quiet developing or consolidating moves (O-O, Nf6, c6, d3, Bd2, etc.) that maintained coordination.

analysis.label: Player captures with check using a major piece but leaves it en prise after the opponent responds to the check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 96% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0), with the hung piece being a major piece (rook or queen) in 382/500 cases. The played move is a capture 71% of the time, and all top-12 activating moves are captures with check (Rxg8+, Rxc3+, Qxf8+, etc.). The player is seduced by a seemingly forcing capture-plus-check combination, but after the opponent deals with the check (typically by moving the king), the attacking piece sits undefended on its new square and is simply recaptured. Meanwhile, the best move wins material 70% of the time (median 3.0 pawns), usually via a quieter move that preserves the existing advantage rather than a flashy but self-destructive check.
analysis.why_bad: The capture-with-check feels like a 'free' tempo gain, but the piece lands on a square where it has no support. Once the opponent escapes the check (king moves or interposes), they simply capture the hanging rook or queen, netting material. The player trades a winning or balanced position for a significant material deficit by choosing a superficially attractive forcing move over a calm best move.

analysis.label: Player makes an active-looking move (often a check or capture) that leaves their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move leaves their own material hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 49% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), with the hung piece class distribution skewing toward major pieces (23) and pawns (22), with fewer minor pieces (8). Meanwhile, 52% of the time the best move would win material (median 1.0), suggesting the player both misses a positional/material opportunity AND creates a new vulnerability. Only 19% of played moves are captures and 6% of best moves are checks, indicating these are mostly quiet or pseudo-aggressive moves that inadvertently expose the player's own pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The player is attracted to forcing-looking moves—checks (Rd1+, Rhc8+, Nxf3+, Rxb2+), captures (Qxb5), or aggressive piece activations (Rh6)—without verifying that the moved piece remains safe. After the opponent responds to the check/threat, the player's piece is simply captured, typically losing a rook or more. The correct move is usually a quieter consolidating move that either defends or wins material by positional means.

analysis.label: Player gives an aimless check (usually with the queen) in a winning endgame instead of playing the correct quiet or material-winning move.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player delivers a purposeless check—almost always a queen check—rather than executing the correct winning plan. The SEE aggregate shows that in 33% of positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, often a queen-value capture), yet the player's move was a capture only 10% of the time, and only 5% of best moves are themselves checks. The played moves are overwhelmingly checks (11/12 top boards), revealing the 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' syndrome. The 38% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that these aimless checks sometimes leave material undefended as a secondary consequence. The average cp_loss of 2387 is enormous because many positions had forced mates (positions 1, 2, 10 show mates in 6-9 thrown away).
analysis.why_bad: These checks accomplish nothing—they merely drive the opponent's king to a safe square while squandering a forced mate or decisive advantage. The correct moves are typically quiet king advances (Kd2, Kd3), pawn breaks (h4, f4, g4), or targeted captures (Rxf1, Qxb3, Rc6) that tighten the mating net or win material. The checks give the opponent's king activity or allow defensive resources, converting a won position into a drawn or lost one.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet repositioning move that leaves their own piece en prise, ignoring urgent tactical demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player plays a non-tactical quiet move (only 18% captures) that leaves their own piece hanging (71% of positions, median value 3.0 — distributed across minors: 28, majors: 22, pawns: 18). Simultaneously, the best move wins material in 70% of cases (median 2.0), indicating the position demanded tactical action. The best move is a capture 38% of the time and a check 12%, confirming that the correct response was concrete and forcing, not quiet. The feature activates on just 0.1% of positions with an average cp_loss of 1129, marking catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores the tactical reality of the position — either a piece that needs defending or an opportunity to win material — and instead plays a quiet developing or repositioning move (e.g., Ng3, Qe7, Na6, Bd2). This leaves their own piece undefended and attackable, often resulting in immediate material loss. The best moves (d5, Nxb5, Nd5, Qxd4+, Rxg7) were forcing moves that either won material or addressed the tactical emergency first.

analysis.label: Player prematurely advances an already-advanced passed pawn (typically to the 7th/2nd rank) instead of first improving king position to support promotion.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 45% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with pawns dominating at 18/29 cases), consistent with pushing a pawn to a square where it becomes capturable or stuck. The 38% 'best wins material' (median 3.0) reflects cases where the correct king move would also win enemy material. Only 9% of played moves were captures, confirming the pattern of quiet pawn pushes. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (10/12 top boards) where the player has a dangerous passed pawn one or two squares from promotion but pushes it prematurely—g3→g2, b3→b2, h3→h2, d3→d2, f6→f7, c6→c7, f3→f2—instead of the correct king activation (Kg4, Kb4, Kc7, Kd4, Kf5, Kd5, Kh3). The best moves are overwhelmingly king moves that escort the pawn properly or win material en route.
analysis.why_bad: Pushing the pawn too early (to the penultimate rank) without king support allows the opponent's king or piece to blockade or capture it. The pawn becomes stuck or lost, squandering a winning advantage. The correct technique is to first centralize/activate the king to control critical squares around the promotion path, then advance the pawn with unstoppable support.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player makes a tempting but inferior move (capture, check, or misplacement) instead of the correct quiet move addressing a dangerous passed pawn or critical positional threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/12 boards) where the best move wins material 93% of the time (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn) yet is rarely a capture (14%) or check (6%)—indicating the correct move is typically a quiet piece repositioning. The player's move leaves their own piece hanging 49% of the time (median value 3.0, heavily weighted toward major pieces at 29/62 cases), suggesting the impulsive move neglects piece safety. The played moves are often greedy captures (31%), pointless checks, or misplaced pieces—moves like Kxa6, Nxg7, g5+, Bf4+, Qe1+—while the correct moves are invariably precise rook/piece placements (Rc5, Rc8, Rc1, Ra8, Rf4, Re5) that blockade or address an opponent's advanced passed pawn. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1144 reflects that ignoring a pawn one or two squares from promotion leads to immediate collapse.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize short-term tactics (captures, checks, material grabs) while ignoring the most urgent positional need—typically stopping an opponent's passed pawn from promoting. By playing Rb5 instead of Rc5, Ra8 instead of Rc8, or Nxg7 instead of Rc1, the player allows unstoppable promotion. Additionally, the impulsive moves frequently leave the player's own major pieces undefended (49% hang rate), compounding the disaster as the opponent gains both a new queen and wins hanging material.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a necessary minor piece exchange (Bishop or Knight capture) and instead plays a move that leaves their own material hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 91% of the time the best move is a capture—overwhelmingly a minor piece exchange (Bx_ or Nx_ with SEE value of 0, i.e., even trade). Yet the player's move left their OWN piece hanging 68% of the time (median value 2.0, distributed across minors: 30, pawns: 29, majors: 19). All 12 top-activating positions confirm the best move is a straightforward piece capture (Nxa7, Nxd5, Bxh6, Bxc5, Bxe7, Nxd4, Bxb7, Nxf4, Nxe7, Nxc5, Bxd7, Qxd2), nearly always a simple exchange. Only 36% of best moves actually net material in SEE terms (most are equal trades), suggesting the exchange was necessary to maintain material balance. The player ignores this available trade and plays a different—often ambitious or irrelevant—move that leaves pieces undefended.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to make the available exchange (typically an even minor piece trade that resolves tension), the player leaves their own piece undefended on the next move. The opponent then captures the hanging piece for free, resulting in a net material loss that could have been avoided by simply completing the straightforward trade. The average cp_loss of 1913 reflects that these oversights often lose a full piece or more.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but aimless check that leaves their own piece (or another piece) hanging after the king escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 87% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0), with the hung piece distributed across minor pieces (74), major pieces (59), and pawns (37). All top 12 activating moves are checks (Be4+, Bh6+, b4+, Nd3+, Rxf2+, Ra3+, Rxd7+, Rf4+, Rb6+, Rd5+, Qxa2+, Bg4+), yet the best move is a check only 27% of the time—meaning the engine preferred a quiet move in 73% of cases. The best move wins material 58% of the time (median 2.0), showing strong alternatives existed. The average cp_loss of 1003 confirms these are catastrophic blunders driven by the impulse to give check rather than play the objectively strongest continuation.
analysis.why_bad: After the king simply sidesteps the check, the checking piece (or a piece left undefended because it moved to deliver check) is captured for free. The check accomplishes nothing—it doesn't lead to mate, doesn't fork, and doesn't win tempo—while costing a minor or major piece. The player prioritized the psychological appeal of 'giving check' over board evaluation.

analysis.label: The player gives check (often a capture-check) with a rook or queen that is left en prise after the opponent addresses the check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e. a rook), with the piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (452/500 rooks/queens). 74% of the played moves are captures, and examining the top boards reveals nearly all are checks (Qxg4+, Rxh4+, Rxa4+, Rxe6+, Re7+, Qxb2+, Rxd3+, Qxc7+, Rxb3+, Rg6+, Qxg5+). The best move wins material 69% of the time (median value 9.0), and 39% of best moves are themselves checks — indicating the correct continuation often involves a different, more accurate check or quiet move that doesn't leave the piece hanging. The player is seduced by giving check with a major piece (typically capturing a pawn or minor piece en route) but the checking piece lands on or remains on a square where it is undefended and capturable once the opponent moves out of check.
analysis.why_bad: After the opponent steps out of check (or interposes), they simply capture the undefended rook or queen. The player trades a forced mate or decisive advantage for a single pawn/piece capture, losing their major piece and often converting a won game into a draw or loss. The check creates an illusion of aggression but has no follow-up support.

analysis.label: The player prematurely exchanges their bishop for a knight (typically Bxf3/Bxf6/Bxc3), surrendering the bishop pair and relieving positional tension.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player voluntarily trades their active bishop for a knight in the opening/early middlegame, leaving the capturing bishop en prise for immediate recapture. The SEE aggregate confirms: 93% of played moves are captures, and 99% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = the bishop just moved), with the hung piece distribution overwhelmingly minor pieces (254 of 279). The best moves (only 21% captures, only 32% winning material) are typically quiet developing moves (Nc6, Bb4, e6, Nd5, g5) that maintain tension rather than resolve it. The pattern is dominated by Bg4xNf3 captures (10 of 12 top boards) where Black had an actively-placed bishop pinning or pressuring White's knight, but traded it off prematurely instead of building further pressure.
analysis.why_bad: These exchanges surrender the bishop pair, relieve the opponent's structural/tactical tension (removing the pin on the knight), develop the opponent's position (the recapturing piece gains activity, e.g., Qxf3 centralizes the queen or gxf3 opens the g-file), and waste tempo that should be spent on development or king safety. The bishop was exerting lasting pressure from g4/similar squares, and trading it converts dynamic advantage into a worse static position.

analysis.label: Player makes a move (often an aggressive bishop move or capture) that leaves their own minor piece hanging and undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move leaves their own material en prise: 68% of the time the played move hangs the player's own piece (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece-class distribution showing minors (62) as the most common hung piece, followed by pawns (53) and majors (30). Meanwhile, 52% of the time the best move wins enemy material (median 1.0), and only 30% of played moves are captures. The top-12 boards are dominated by bishop moves (Bb6, Bb5, Bxf3, Bxh2+, Be7, Bh3, Bxh7) — 7 of 12 are bishop moves — and in positions 4, 6, 9, and 12 the specific piece hung is a bishop (value 3). The pattern is players making impulsive or aggressive-looking moves, particularly with bishops, that leave their own minor piece unprotected.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that their move removes a defender or places a piece on a square where it cannot be supported, leaving a minor piece (typically a bishop) en prise. Examples include unsound Greek-gift sacrifices (Bxh2+, Bxh7), exchanges that lose material (Bxf3 leaving a piece hanging), captures that uncover attacks on other pieces (Nxe5 leaving a bishop loose), and passive retreats that allow opponents to win material tactically (Be7 allowing a fork). The player pursues an aggressive or aesthetic idea while ignoring immediate tactical consequences.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning central pawn advance (d4/e4/e5/d5) that forks or attacks enemy pieces, winning material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 8% of the time and a check only 7% — meaning the winning tactic is a pawn thrust, not a direct capture. All 12 top boards confirm the pattern: the best move is always a central pawn advance (d4, e4, e5, or d5) that attacks or forks enemy pieces (typically a bishop and knight aligned on adjacent squares). The played moves are natural quiet developing moves (O-O, Be7, Qd7, etc.) with only 24% being captures. The 33% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a minor secondary effect of the passive moves chosen, not the core pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet developing moves (castling, piece repositioning, prophylactic pawn pushes) ignore a concrete tactical opportunity: a central pawn advance that simultaneously attacks two or more enemy pieces, typically forking a bishop and knight on adjacent squares. By playing routine moves instead, the player squanders a winning advantage (avg cp_loss 323), allowing the opponent to reposition their pieces out of the fork's reach or complete their own development.

analysis.label: Player makes an irrelevant move in a rook endgame instead of using the rook to address a dangerously advanced enemy passed pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate over 500 positions shows 28% of best moves win material (median 1.0, consistent with stopping promotion being worth material), while 29% of played moves leave own pieces hanging (median 1.0, mostly pawns at 28/41). Only 9% of played moves are captures and only 8% of best moves are captures, indicating the critical action is positional rook placement rather than tactical exchanges. All 12 top-activating positions are rook endgames featuring an advanced passed pawn 1-2 squares from promotion, where the best move is almost always a rook redeployment to blockade or attack the passer (Rc2, Rc4, Rd7, Ra5, Rb5, Ra2, etc.), while the played moves are irrelevant pawn pushes (f5, g5, h4), aimless king moves (Ke2, Kg3), pointless checks (Rc7+), or greedy captures (Rxh7) that ignore the existential promotion threat.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in rook endgames, an advanced passed pawn 1-2 squares from promotion is the highest-priority threat. By playing irrelevant pawn pushes, king moves, or greedy captures, the player allows the passed pawn to queen (or forces desperate material sacrifice to prevent it). The rook is the only piece that can efficiently stop a distant passed pawn from behind or from the side, and misplacing it for one tempo in these critical positions is catastrophic — explaining the enormous average cp_loss of 1151.

analysis.label: The player moves their queen to an inactive or greedy square instead of delivering a winning queen check that forces mate or decisive material gain.
analysis.description: In 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a queen check, and in 96% of cases this check wins material (median value 100, i.e., equivalent to winning the opposing queen or forcing checkmate). Only 27% of these best moves are captures—most are non-capturing checks that exploit an exposed enemy king. The played moves are overwhelmingly non-checking queen moves (only 17% are captures), often to squares adjacent to the correct checking square (e.g., Qd5 instead of Qd6+, Qc5 instead of Qf5+), or greedy captures of peripheral material (Qxa7, Qxb2, Qxe6) while the opponent's king is fatally exposed. The average centipawn loss of 4015 reflects that these missed checks typically convert forced checkmates into merely winning positions.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they surrender a forced checkmate or decisive tactical sequence initiated by a queen check. The queen check either creates an unstoppable mating net against the exposed enemy king, or forks the king with a subsequent material-winning follow-up. By choosing a non-checking alternative—whether a quiet repositioning move or a material-grabbing capture elsewhere—the player allows the opponent's king to escape the mating zone, converting a won game into a merely advantageous one or even an unclear position.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive or misguided quiet move that overlooks a concrete tactical opportunity or disrupts piece coordination.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a non-forcing, 'positional-looking' quiet move (87% non-captures) when the position demands concrete tactical action. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 52% of cases (median value 2.0, i.e. a minor piece), yet only 22% of best moves are captures and only 6% are checks — meaning the correct moves are often quiet but purposeful moves that set up material gains or maintain critical coordination. The player's move left their own piece hanging only 23% of the time (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), indicating the primary error is not self-hanging but rather missing offensive opportunities. The feature fires on 1.1% of positions with an average cp_loss of 300, reflecting serious blunders disguised as reasonable moves.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize vague positional objectives (piece relocation, pawn pushes, passive development) over concrete tactical demands. In positions 1 and 8, the player puts the queen on the exact square the bishop should occupy (Qd6 vs Bd6, Qd3 vs Bd3). In position 4, a crucially-placed defensive bishop is moved away. In positions 3, 5, and 12, winning tactical shots (Bh6 wins 5, Qf7 wins 9, Ne3 wins 6) are ignored for aimless flank moves or piece shuffles. The result is either missed material gains or positional collapse from miscoordination.

analysis.label: Player reflexively moves the king when the correct move is a critical queen relocation that wins or saves approximately a queen's worth of material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 88% of the time with a median value of 9 (queen-value), yet the best move is almost never a capture (5%) or a check (3%)—it is overwhelmingly a queen repositioning move. The played move is always a quiet king move. After the king move, the player's own piece hangs 55% of the time (median value 1, distributed across pawns/125, majors/46, minors/41), indicating the king move neglects defensive duties the queen was performing. The pattern across all 12 top-activating boards confirms: every played move is a King move (Kf7, Kg8, Kd2, etc.) while every best move is a Queen move (Qf8, Qg7, Qb1, Qe7, etc.). The 'wins 9' SEE on the best move reflects that the queen move either saves the player's own queen from being captured or creates a decisive threat worth a queen.
analysis.why_bad: By moving the king instead of the queen, the player either leaves their own queen (or other pieces) en prise, abandons a critical defensive/attacking function the queen was performing, or misses a queen move that would decisively win material or force mate. The king move is typically a passive retreat that fails to address the position's tactical demands, often turning a winning or holdable position into an immediate loss.

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop capture of an undefended pawn on a long diagonal (typically g7, g2, b7, or b2), playing a quiet developing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value: 1.0, i.e., a pawn), and 69% of the time the best move is a capture. The player's move was only a capture 21% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the missed best move is uniformly a bishop capturing an undefended pawn on a long diagonal (Bxg7 in 7 cases, Bxg2 in 2, Bxb7 in 2, Bxb2 in 1). These positions predominantly occur in the opening (9/12) where both kings are often still in the center and the opponent's fianchetto square or rook-pawn is left unguarded. The feature fires on only 0.3% of positions, indicating a specific geometric pattern: a bishop with an unobstructed diagonal to a pawn defended by nothing or only by a trapped rook.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet developing moves (Nc3, Nf3, Be2, O-O, etc.) waste a concrete tactical opportunity to win a free pawn. In many cases, the bishop capture also traps the rook behind the captured pawn (e.g., Bxg7 trapping Rh8), meaning the missed gain often exceeds a single pawn in practice. By developing instead, the player allows the opponent to eventually defend the weakness or castle away from it, permanently losing the tactical window.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning queen-for-queen capture with check, instead making a move that often leaves their own queen en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a distinctive pattern: the best move is a check 100% of the time AND a capture 100% of the time, yet wins 0 material (median value won: 0), indicating the best move is always a queen trade (equal exchange) delivered with check. The player's move is never a capture (0%), and in 50% of cases it leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 9.0 = queen). All four top-activating positions are queen endgames where one side can capture the opponent's queen with check (Qxc1+, Qxa8+, Qxh7+, Qxg6+), leading to a won simplified endgame, but the player instead makes an inferior move that squanders the position entirely (avg cp_loss: 3020).
analysis.why_bad: By failing to trade queens with check, the player misses the critical simplification into a won endgame. The queen trade with check is tactically forced (opponent must deal with check before recapturing), guaranteeing the favorable trade. Instead, the played moves either leave the player's own queen hanging to the opponent's still-active queen, or lose all winning chances by allowing the opponent to equalize in a position where the queen trade would have been decisive.

analysis.label: A knight captures an enemy piece on a square where it is immediately recapturable, trading itself off when a much stronger tactical continuation was available.
analysis.description: In 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with 171 of 176 hung pieces being minors (knights/bishops). The played move was a capture 96% of the time — almost exclusively knight captures (Nxd7, Nxe7, Nxf8, etc.). Meanwhile, 63% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0), and 20% of best moves were checks. This indicates the player greedily took a piece with their knight, but the knight landed on a recapturable square — resulting in a simple even trade — when a far superior move (often a fork, discovered attack, or devastating check like Qh4+ or Nd5) would have won significantly more material or delivered a decisive blow.
analysis.why_bad: The knight capture results in an immediate recapture (even trade at best) because the knight lands en prise. The player is seduced by the obvious capture but misses that maintaining the knight's position — or redirecting it to a superior square — would exploit tactical motifs (forks, king attacks, checks) worth far more than the simple exchange. The knight's active placement before the capture was often its greatest asset.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple winning capture (typically of a rook or equivalent) and plays an aimless quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 85% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0 pawns, i.e., a rook), and 89% of best moves are captures. Yet the player's move is a capture only 26% of the time—most played moves are quiet king moves or piece retreats (e.g., Ke6, Kb7, Kf2, Ka4, Kh1, Be5, Bc4). Additionally, 62% of these played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), compounding the mistake. The pattern across all 12 top-activating boards is consistent: an enemy piece (usually a rook or queen on d8, e8, h1, etc.) is freely capturable, but the player makes an irrelevant quiet move—often a king walk—missing the decisive material gain and frequently exposing their own material in the process.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available capture that wins a full rook or more (median 5 pawns). Instead of cashing in the material, the player makes a purposeless quiet move that not only forgoes the winning capture but often leaves their own pieces undefended (62% of cases), turning a winning or tenable position into a losing or immediately lost one (avg cp_loss: 2621).

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the player moves the king in the wrong direction (or pushes a pawn instead), losing a critical race against an enemy passed pawn or failing to reach the decisive sector of the board.
analysis.description: This feature fires on pure pawn endgame positions where the player fatally misjudges king direction in a race scenario. The SEE aggregate shows modest material-winning opportunities for the best move (31%, median 1.0 pawn) and own pieces left hanging after the played move (28%, median 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 30/41), reflecting how one wrong king step abandons defensive coverage of one's own pawns while forfeiting the chance to reach the opponent's. Only 13% of played moves are captures, and the best move is rarely a check (4%) or capture (16%), confirming that the correct idea is typically a quiet king retreat or redirection rather than a tactical blow. The feature activates on just 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically those critical moments where a single directional king error transforms a winning or holdable position into a loss.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, tempi are razor-thin. These moves fail because the king heads toward the wrong flank, captures a non-critical pawn, or the player pushes a pawn when the king itself must race to blockade or capture an enemy passed pawn. By moving away from the critical sector, the king arrives one or more tempi too late to stop promotion or to maintain control of key squares, often turning decisive advantages into draws or losses (average cp_loss: 517).

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames involving pawn races, the player moves their king instead of pushing a critical pawn, wasting decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on pure king-and-pawn endgames where the player makes a king move when a pawn push is urgent. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 29% of the time (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), consistent with the idea that pushing a pawn secures a promotion advantage or wins a tempo in the race. The played move is almost never a capture (8%), and 18% of the time the king move leaves a pawn hanging (own-hang class distribution: all pawns), because the king abandons its defensive duty. The best move is a capture only 2% of the time and never a check (0%), confirming the pattern is about pawn advances rather than tactical strikes. Across the top 12 boards, every single played move is a king move (Kf5, Ke6, Kd5, Kd2, etc.), while the best moves are overwhelmingly pawn pushes (h5, g5, c5, b4, g4, c4) — the hallmark of a lost tempo in a critical pawn race.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn-race endgames, a single tempo often decides whether a pawn promotes or gets stopped. Moving the king when a pawn push is available wastes that critical tempo, allowing the opponent's passed pawn to queen first, or letting the opponent's king reach a key intercepting square. The king move neither advances the player's own pawn threat nor blocks the opponent's, turning winning or drawn positions into losses.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player captures a pawn or piece with their rook that is defended by the adjacent enemy king, allowing the king to simply recapture the rook.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 93% of activating positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), and 85% of the played moves are captures. The hung piece class is overwhelmingly 'major' (89 of 114 instances). Across all 12 top-activating boards, a rook captures a pawn or piece on a square directly adjacent to the enemy king (e.g., Rxc2+ with Black king on d2, Rxg7+ with White king on f7, Rxd7+ with king on e7, Rxh2 with king on g3). The enemy king simply recaptures, netting a rook for a pawn. The best moves (only 7% are captures themselves) instead preserve the rook via repositioning (Rc1, Rf1, Ra8), king moves (Ke4, Kf7, Kd6), or checks (Rg8+, Rb1+) that maintain strategic pressure without sacrificing the rook.
analysis.why_bad: These moves trade a rook (worth ~5 points) for a pawn or occasionally a minor piece (worth 1-3 points), because the captured target sits on a square defended by the enemy king. In endgames, losing the rook is typically catastrophic—it eliminates the player's ability to check, blockade passed pawns, or create counterplay. The greedy capture accelerates the opponent's winning plan (usually pawn promotion) by removing the one piece that could provide resistance.

analysis.label: A knight (or piece) grabs material greedily but lands on or exposes a square where it is left en prise, losing more than it gained.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the player's move left their OWN piece hanging in 94% of cases (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece). The piece class distribution is dominated by minor pieces (102 out of 119 instances), and the played move was a capture 58% of the time. In 63% of positions, the best move could have won material (median 3.0) safely, but the player instead chose a greedy capture—almost always with a knight—that landed the knight on an undefended square where it could be recaptured. The best move was rarely a capture itself (12%) or a check (10%), indicating that superior alternatives involved quiet repositioning or indirect tactical ideas rather than the impulsive material grab.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures a pawn or piece on a square where it has no support, so the opponent simply recaptures the knight. The net exchange is often losing (e.g., winning a pawn but losing a knight), or at best equal when a better alternative existed that won material cleanly or maintained a positional advantage. The player is seduced by an immediate material grab without checking whether the landing square is safe.

analysis.label: Player plays a flashy check or attack (often Bxf7+/Ng5+) instead of simply recapturing an enemy piece, leaving their own major piece hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a simple capture wins material (98% of best moves are captures winning median 3.0 pawns worth), but the player instead plays a speculative attacking move — typically a check like Bxf7+ or Ng5+ — that leaves their own piece en prise (90% of played moves hang own material, median value 3.0, with 48 major pieces and 41 minor pieces in the distribution). The classic scenario, seen in 8+ of the top 12 boards, involves a Black knight intruding on c3 that can be captured with bxc3, but White ignores it to play a flashy Bxf7+ 'sacrifice' or Ng5+ check that accomplishes nothing tactically and leaves the queen hanging. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific pattern of prioritizing a showy but unsound attack over a trivially winning recapture.
analysis.why_bad: The checks and attacks are unsound because the opponent's king simply escapes (e.g., Kxf7 after Bxf7+), leaving the attacker down material with no compensation. Meanwhile, the ignored enemy piece (usually knight on c3) remains active and the player's queen is now hanging because it lost its defender or got exposed during the speculative attack. A simple bxc3 would have won a full piece for free.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player makes a tempting king capture of nearby material instead of the strategically critical move (blockading, promoting, or capturing a higher-value target).
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player greedily captures a piece—usually with the king—instead of finding the objectively best move. The SEE aggregate shows that 57% of played moves are captures, yet 64% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 3.0 (a minor piece), meaning the player often takes the wrong target or captures when a non-capture (like blockading a passed pawn or promoting) is far stronger. The 51% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the greedy king move often exposes the player's own pawns. The best move is a check 23% of the time and a capture 45%, suggesting the optimal line frequently involves a different tactical sequence entirely. The enormous average cp_loss of 1682 confirms these are catastrophic decisions despite looking natural.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they prioritize immediately visible material over critical positional requirements of the endgame—such as blockading a passed pawn (positions 4, 8), maintaining a drawing fortress (position 1), capturing a more valuable piece elsewhere (positions 3, 7, 11), or advancing one's own passed pawn (positions 9, 10, 12). The king walks to the wrong square, losing control of the strategically decisive area of the board.

analysis.label: Retreating an exposed king backward toward the back rank, abandoning defense of pieces that then hang.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player with an exposed king (typically on f7/f3/h2) reflexively retreats it toward the back rank (Ke8, Kf8, Ke1, Kg1) instead of finding a more active solution. The SEE aggregate shows that 66% of the time the played move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, evenly distributed across minors/pawns/majors), while in 52% of cases the best move wins material (median 3.0). The best move is almost never a check (0%) and only 19% are captures, indicating the correct solution is usually a counterintuitive king advance (e.g., Kg6) or a piece move that maintains defensive coordination. The player's move is rarely a capture itself (13%), confirming these are passive retreats rather than active decisions.
analysis.why_bad: The backward king retreat abandons the king's role as a defender of nearby pieces. When the king was on f7/f3/h2, it was often covering key squares or shielding pieces. By retreating (Ke8, Kf8, Ke1, Kg1), the player leaves formerly-protected pieces en prise. The counterintuitive forward king move (like Kg6) often finds safety by escaping attack lanes while maintaining piece coordination, whereas the passive retreat walks into discovered attacks or removes critical defense.

analysis.label: Player makes a materialistic or impulsive move (usually a capture) that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 97% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), and 75% of the played moves are captures. The hung pieces span all classes (pawns: 89, majors: 77, minors: 52). While the best move often wins material (60%, median 1.0) or delivers checkmate (20% checks), the player instead grabs a pawn or piece greedily, leaving their capturing piece (or a piece it was protecting) en prise. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating these are particularly egregious blunders with an average cp_loss of 5558.
analysis.why_bad: The player focuses on taking enemy material or executing a natural-looking plan while completely overlooking that their own piece (often the very piece that moved) lands on or is left on an undefended square. In many cases (positions 4-8, 10, 12), a forced mate or decisive breakthrough existed, but the player's tunnel vision on a greedy capture or routine move caused them to blunder their own piece instead of delivering the knockout blow.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet or ambitious move in an endgame, overlooking a simple capture that wins material while often leaving their own piece undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player ignores a straightforward tactical capture in favor of a quiet or 'strategic' move. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 54% of the time and wins material in 57% of positions (median 1 pawn), yet the player's actual move is a capture only 7% of the time. Additionally, 53% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, distributed across pawns: 24, majors: 16, minors: 15).
