The typical scenario involves an endgame (9/12 top boards) where the player makes a king move, rook repositioning, or even a promotion instead of taking a free or favorable capture—compounding the error by also leaving their own material unprotected. Examples include playing Kg3 instead of exd4, playing a1=Q instead of hxg4, and playing Re1 instead of Nxe7+.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore concrete tactical obligations—available captures that either win material or are necessary to maintain the safety of one's own pieces. By playing quiet moves (king walks, rook shuffles, unnecessary promotions or checks), the player both forfeits winnable material and frequently exposes their own pieces to capture, turning advantageous or holdable positions into losing ones.

analysis.label: Player passively moves/retreats a knight attacked by e5 instead of playing the d5 pawn counter-strike that wins material (usually a bishop on c4).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 66% of positions (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece), with the best move being a capture 62% of the time — overwhelmingly the d5 pawn break hitting an undefended bishop on c4. The player's move was a capture only 24% of the time (confirming they chose a passive alternative), and in 52% of cases their knight move left their own piece hanging (median 3.0, predominantly minors at 126/261). The top 12 boards uniformly show Italian Game / Two Knights Defense structures where White's e5 pawn attacks Black's Nf6, and Black reflexively retreats or relocates the knight (Ne4, Ng8, Ne8, Ng4, Nh5, Nd5, Nfd7) rather than striking back with d5, which exploits the exposed Bc4 to win material. This is a classic opening pattern where the instinct to save the attacked knight overrides the tactical opportunity of a central counter-blow.
analysis.why_bad: Moving the knight is passive and concedes White's space advantage while missing that d5 (or similar pawn captures like bxc3/b4) attacks a loosely-placed White bishop on c4, winning at least a pawn and often a full piece through the fork/discovered attack. Additionally, many of the knight moves (Ne4, Ng4, Nh5) place the knight on an insecure square where it becomes a target itself, compounding the error.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player fails to capture a freely available undefended enemy piece (typically a minor piece), instead playing an unrelated quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates a 'missed capture' pattern: 75% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 77% of best moves are captures, yet only 20% of played moves were captures. Only 25% of played moves hung the player's own piece, confirming the primary mistake is failing to take free material rather than blundering one's own. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames where an undefended enemy piece (bishop, knight, or rook) sits en prise—often directly adjacent to the player's king or within reach of a pawn/piece capture—but the player plays a quiet king move, pawn push, or other non-capturing move instead.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are catastrophic because they forfeit a free piece worth approximately 3 pawns (or more), turning winning or comfortable endgames into drawn or lost ones. The missed captures are trivially available (Kxa3, Kxe6, Rxf7, dxc5, Kxd8, Kxa2, etc.) and require no calculation beyond seeing the enemy piece is undefended. By playing a quiet alternative, the player allows the opponent to move the hanging piece to safety, erasing a decisive material advantage.

analysis.label: Player ignores a critical queen exchange (Qx_), instead playing a quiet move that leaves material hanging to the opponent's dominant queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly identifies this pattern: 98% of best moves are captures, and nearly all are queen takes queen (SEE value 0, indicating equal exchange). Meanwhile, 70% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 31 major pieces and 28 pawns among the hung pieces). The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 13% are captures), confirming the player avoids the trade. All 12 top-activating boards show the same geometry: the opponent has a powerfully placed or threatening queen (on d6, e2, e7, e8, d8, c3, f4, e4, d7), and the correct response is to immediately trade queens. Instead the player makes an unrelated move (king move, knight move, quiet queen sidestep), leaving material undefended against the very queen that should have been exchanged.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the queen trade, the player leaves the opponent's dominant queen active on the board, where it immediately captures undefended material. The queen that should have been neutralized instead exploits hanging pieces or delivers devastating threats (including several mate-in-1 situations, as seen in the enormous average cp_loss of 1825). The defensive necessity of simplification is ignored in favor of moves that address neither the queen threat nor the hanging material.

analysis.label: The player captures a piece with their rook, but the rook lands on an undefended square where it is immediately won back at a material loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a rook capture that leaves the rook itself hanging. The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 100% of activating positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the hung piece class being overwhelmingly major pieces (363/384 ≈ 95%). The player's move is a capture 70% of the time, and 11 of the top 12 moves are explicit rook captures (Rx__). While the best move sometimes wins material (57%, median value 2.0), the best moves are rarely captures themselves (only 15%), suggesting quiet or positional alternatives were available. The feature fires on only 0.2% of positions, isolating this specific tactical blunder pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The rook captures a piece (often a minor piece worth 3 points or a defended pawn) but lands on a square where it is insufficiently protected and can be recaptured by the opponent. The net result is a losing exchange: the player wins a minor piece or pawn but loses a rook (worth 5), resulting in typical cp_losses of 185-515. The greedy capture overlooks that the rook has no safe retreat and no adequate defender on the target square.

analysis.label: The player gives a tempting but futile check that leaves the checking piece itself en prise and lost.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 90% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece overwhelmingly being a minor piece (28 minor vs 8 major vs 2 pawn). All 12 top-activating moves are checks (Nc7+, Bc6+, Nf4+, Bc3+, Bb5+, etc.), and in every case the checking piece lands on a square where it can simply be captured after the king moves or interposes. The best moves (64% win material, median 3.0) are typically quiet developing moves (Nc3, d4, e3) or straightforward captures of hanging enemy pieces (Rfxd1, Qxg4, Bxb2), meaning the player ignores concretely superior options to play a flashy but self-destructive check. The opening phase dominance (9/12 positions) reflects premature knight/bishop sorties early in the game.
analysis.why_bad: The check accomplishes nothing lasting — the opponent's king simply sidesteps or the checking piece is captured — and the player loses a whole minor piece (or worse) for free. Meanwhile, far stronger moves existed that would maintain or increase the advantage through development, material gain, or positional improvement.

analysis.label: Player misses a devastating queen check (Qh5+ or Qh4+) exploiting a king exposed along the diagonal after the f-pawn has moved.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions the best move wins material (median value 91), and in 98% of cases the best move is a check (only 2% are captures). This means the consistent mistake is failing to play a queen check that exploits a structurally weakened king. The played moves are instead quiet developing moves or minor captures (only 24% are captures). The 39% own-hang rate is incidental — it reflects poor alternatives chosen rather than the core error. All 12 top boards show opening positions where the opponent's f-pawn has moved (Latvian Gambit, Petrov with f4, etc.), leaving the h5-e8 or h4-e1 diagonal fatally open. The best move is always Qh5+ (for White) or Qh4+ (for Black), initiating a tactical sequence that wins significant material through the exposed king.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Nc3, d3, Bc4, f4, Nf3, Bc5, etc.) are 'normal' developing moves that ignore the opponent's critical structural weakness. By not delivering the immediate queen check, the player allows the opponent to castle, block the diagonal, or consolidate, squandering a one-move tactical window. The check typically leads to winning material (e.g., Qh5+ g6 Nxg6 winning a rook) or delivering a devastating attack that the opponent cannot survive.

analysis.label: The player makes an active or greedy move that leaves their own piece undefended and capturable, typically while ignoring a critical defensive need.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 92% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 2.0), with the distribution spanning pawns (123), minor pieces (102), and major pieces (72). Only 26% of the played moves are captures themselves, meaning most are quiet moves that simply neglect defense. The best moves win material only 44% of the time (often the best move is purely defensive—king moves like Kb1, Kd1, Kh4, or pawn shields like g6, c6, h3, g3, g5). The enormous average cp_loss of 3223 and multiple transitions to forced mate confirm that these are catastrophic oversights where the player ignores urgent threats to their own position while simultaneously leaving material hanging.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an existing threat (often to the king or to an undefended piece) in favor of an active-looking or material-grabbing continuation. The resulting position both concedes the hanging piece AND allows the opponent's threat to execute—frequently a mating attack. The player needed to play a defensive move first (king retreat, pawn shield, piece interposition) rather than leave material en prise.

analysis.label: Player misses a queen capture on d4, d5, or d6 that wins an undefended central pawn or piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 86% of cases (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece equivalent), and the best move is a capture 66% of the time. The player's own move was rarely a capture (23%), indicating they ignored the tactical opportunity. Only 37% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, usually a pawn), confirming the primary mistake is MISSING winnable material rather than hanging one's own piece. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the best move is exclusively a queen capture on the d-file (Qxd4, Qxd5, or Qxd6), targeting an undefended or under-defended central pawn or piece. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (7/12), where central pawns on d4/d5 become tactically vulnerable after piece development shifts defenders away.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (quiet developing moves like Nd7, Nc6, e6, Bb3, or misguided captures like dxc5) ignore the immediate tactical fact that the opponent's central d-pawn or d-file piece is en prise to the queen. By not capturing, the player forfeits free material (typically a pawn, sometimes a minor piece worth 3 points) and allows the opponent to consolidate or defend the weakness, turning a winning position into an equal or losing one.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture or aggressive move that leaves their own piece (typically a minor piece) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's move hangs their own piece (88% of the time, median value 3.0 — a minor piece). The own-hang piece distribution is heavily weighted toward minor pieces (44 minor, 27 pawn, 14 major over 85 instances). The played move is frequently a capture itself (46%), suggesting the player is lured by winning material on one square while overlooking that the move leaves another piece undefended. Meanwhile, 72% of the time a superior move existed that would win material (median 4.0), meaning the player both missed a better opportunity AND blundered their own piece — a double error. The best move is a check 13% of the time and a capture 21%, indicating the correct play was often tactical but less flashy than the greedy capture chosen.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is attracted to an immediate material gain (capturing a pawn or piece) or an aggressive-looking move, but overlooks that the move removes a piece from a defensive role or places the capturing piece on an unprotected square. The result is typically a net loss of a minor piece (knight or bishop), turning a winning or equal position into a losing one. Many positions also had a stronger tactical continuation (check or winning capture) that the player missed entirely.

analysis.label: Player fails to execute a critical rook trade (Rx__ with SEE=0) and instead plays a quiet move that often leaves their own pieces hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the best move is a rook exchange or rook capture (98% of best moves are captures, all top-12 are 'Rx__' moves with SEE=0 indicating an even trade). The player instead makes a quiet move (84% non-captures), and in doing so leaves their own piece hanging 63% of the time (median value 3.0, distributed across major pieces 81, pawns 69, minor pieces 41). Only 20% of positions involve actually winning material—the vast majority require an even rook trade that is positionally or tactically mandatory. The feature fires on just 0.2% of all positions, indicating a specific scenario: opposing rooks on the same open file or a rook aimed at an exchangeable target, where avoiding the trade is a significant error (avg cp_loss 176).
analysis.why_bad: By declining the mandatory rook exchange, the player leaves the position tactically unstable. The opponent's rook remains active and often creates threats that exploit the player's now-vulnerable pieces. The quiet moves played (a3, b3, g4, Nd2, etc.) ignore the critical tactical tension on the file, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, win material, or exploit the hanging pieces that result from the unresolved rook confrontation.

analysis.label: Player missed a materially-equal but positionally crushing exchange (capture), playing a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of best moves are captures, yet these captures win 0 material by SEE in nearly all top-activating positions (only 8% show material gain). This means the missed captures are EQUAL exchanges that yield enormous positional or tactical advantages—removing key defenders, exposing the king, or creating irresistible follow-ups. The player instead plays quiet moves (only 10% played a capture), and 35% of the time their quiet move even leaves their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed across pawns: 87, minors: 61, majors: 28). The best move is a check 27% of the time, indicating many of these exchanges come with tempo-gaining forcing sequences. The feature fires on 0.3% of positions with an average cp_loss of 174.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves fail because they ignore a forcing exchange (often Bx or Rx with check) that, while materially equal, shatters the opponent's coordination—removing a key defender, exposing the king, or creating a tactical cascade. By playing passively, the player not only forfeits a massive positional gain but frequently leaves their own pieces tactically vulnerable in the resulting position.

analysis.label: Player avoids a rook exchange (often with check) that would liquidate into a winning pawn endgame, instead playing a quiet rook move that squanders the advantage.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of best moves are captures and 44% include check, yet SEE material won is 0 in almost all cases — indicating equal-material rook exchanges, not piece wins. The feature fires overwhelmingly in endgames (10/12 boards) where the correct move is Rx__ (trading rooks) to enter a winning king-and-pawn endgame. The player's move is a capture only 10% of the time, meaning they consistently avoid the exchange. The 35% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 5.0, 74 majors) from the broader 500 positions suggests that in some cases the quiet rook alternative even leaves the player's own rook en prise. All 12 top-activating positions confirm the identical pattern: a rook endgame where one side is winning, the engine's top move trades rooks (Rxe7+, Rxg7+, Rxc4+, Rxc2+, Rxf2+, Rxf6+, Rxd5, Rxc7+, Rxe3+, Rxb4), and the player instead retreats or repositions the rook passively.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet rook moves fail because the player's advantage is rooted in superior pawn structure or king activity that only manifests after simplification. By keeping rooks on, the player allows the opponent counterplay, drawing chances via perpetual activity, or time to reorganize. The rook trade forces the opponent into a hopeless king-and-pawn endgame where the structural or material edge is decisive — average cp_loss of 290 confirms these moves throw away roughly 3 pawns of advantage.

analysis.label: A bishop captures the h-pawn in front of the castled king but is left hanging with no sufficient attacking compensation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 96% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 447/500 being minor pieces — i.e., the bishop itself). The player's move is a capture 85% of the time, and the best move wins material only 31% of the time (meaning the correct plan was usually quiet, not tactical). The best move is a check only 3% and a capture only 12%, confirming that positional continuations were called for. All top-12 activating positions show the identical move pattern: Bxh3 (Black) or Bxh6 (White), a bishop capturing the h-pawn guarding the opponent's castled king. After recapture (gxh3/gxh6), the bishop is simply lost for a pawn — a net material loss of ~2 pawns. Positions feature closed centers and same-side kingside castling, where the attacker mistakenly judges the h-file opening will yield a decisive attack.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop sacrifice on h3/h6 is unsound because after the opponent recaptures with the g-pawn, the attacking side lacks sufficient follow-up pieces or tactical motifs (no aligned queen/rook on the h-file, no supporting knight on g5/g4) to generate a real mating attack. The result is simply losing a minor piece for one pawn, with the opponent's king remaining adequately sheltered behind remaining pawns or easily escaping to safety.

analysis.label: Player makes a reflexive pawn capture that leaves the capturing pawn recapturable, releasing critical tension when a stronger move was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a pawn capture (84% of played moves are captures) that leaves their own pawn immediately en prise (98% of positions, median hanging value 1.0, with 264 of the hung pieces being pawns). The player initiates or accepts a pawn exchange that resolves tension prematurely. In 59% of cases, the best move would have won material (median 2.0 pawns worth), while only 16% of best moves are themselves captures—indicating the correct approach usually involves piece moves, advances, or maintaining the tension. The feature fires on just 0.2% of all positions, specifically targeting moments where a greedy or reflexive exchange squanders a large advantage (average 234cp loss). Across all 12 example boards, every played move is a pawn-takes-pawn exchange (exd4, exf6, dxc3, cxd4, etc.) where the resulting pawn sits undefended on its new square.
analysis.why_bad: These captures release pawn tension at exactly the wrong moment. The player often has a powerful advanced pawn (e.g., a cramping e4 or d4 pawn) doing strategic work, and the reflexive capture trades it for an equal pawn exchange—giving up a strong structural asset for nothing. Meanwhile, the position demanded either maintaining tension, advancing to gain space (e.g., c5, e5, b4), or exploiting a tactical opportunity such as winning a piece. The exchange removes dynamic potential and often activates the opponent's position in the process.

analysis.label: Player captures attacking b-pawn with a knight (Nxb5/Nxb4) instead of retreating the threatened bishop, leaving the knight hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 2.0, overwhelmingly minor pieces: 118 of 119), and 85% of moves were captures. The best move wins no material in 81% of cases (just a quiet bishop retreat). The pattern is extremely specific: the player has a bishop on the a-file (a4 or a5) attacked by an enemy b-pawn. Rather than safely retreating the bishop (Bb3 or Bb6, the best move in nearly every case), the player greedily captures the b-pawn with a knight (Nxb5/Nxb4). The knight then sits unprotected on b4/b5 and is simply recaptured by a pawn (cxb5, axb4, etc.), resulting in a net loss of knight-for-pawn (~2 pawns of material). This fires on only 0.1% of positions, reflecting its narrow geometric specificity.
analysis.why_bad: After Nxb5 or Nxb4, the knight is undefended on the b-file square and immediately gets recaptured by a neighboring pawn (typically ...cxb5, ...axb5, axb4, or cxb4). The player trades a knight (worth ~3) for a pawn (worth 1), losing approximately 2 pawns of material. Meanwhile, the simple bishop retreat (Bb3/Bb6) saves the bishop with no material loss and maintains a sound position.

analysis.label: Player captures material instead of delivering a winning check or checkmate.
analysis.description: In 87% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins decisive material (median value 91, near queen-value or mate). Critically, 69% of best moves are checks (often immediate checkmate), yet the player's actual move is a capture 80% of the time — grabbing a lesser piece while missing the killing blow. The player's greedy capture also leaves their own piece hanging 67% of the time (median value 5, mostly major pieces at 186/335), since by failing to end the game with the check, the opponent gets a chance to counterattack. The feature fires on only 0.4% of positions, isolating those rare moments where a decisive check/mate coexists with an attractive but inferior capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because capturing material is irrelevant when a forced checkmate or game-deciding check exists. By grabbing a piece (e.g., Nxc2 instead of Qxg2#, Rxb6 instead of Nxf2#, Qxb6 instead of Qxe7#), the player squanders a won position — often converting a mate-in-1 into a merely advantageous game or even allowing counterplay against their now-exposed capturing piece.

analysis.label: Player gives check (or makes a capture) with a major piece that is left hanging after the opponent responds.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the player's move left their OWN piece hanging in 93% of cases, with a median hung value of 5.0 (rook-equivalent). The hung piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (260 major vs. 31 minor vs. 8 pawn out of ~299 cases). Across the top 12 boards, 10 of 12 moves are checks and nearly all involve rooks (hung value 5) or queens (hung value 9) being left en prise. While 62% of positions had material to be won by the best move (median 3.0), the player's chosen move—typically an impulsive check or capture—hangs their own far more valuable major piece, converting an often winning or equal position into a losing one (avg cp_loss: 410).
analysis.why_bad: The player is seduced by the forcing appearance of a check or capture, playing a rook or queen to an aggressive square without verifying that the piece is safe after the opponent simply moves out of check. The opponent sidesteps the check and captures the undefended major piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss that far outweighs any tactical threat the check posed.

analysis.label: Player missed a best move that is always a check—often delivering immediate checkmate or winning decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 positions, wins material in 79% of cases (median value 9.0, i.e., queen-level gains), and is also a capture in 63% of cases. Meanwhile, the played move was only a capture 25% of the time, indicating the player chose quiet, non-forcing moves. The 44% own-hang rate (median 2.0) is a secondary byproduct of playing aimless moves in sharp positions. The avg cp_loss of 5654 confirms these are catastrophic misses. The top boards confirm the pattern: multiple missed Qb8# checkmates, missed Qxd8+ queen captures, missed Nxc2+ forks, and missed Qxf7+ forced mating attacks—all checks the player simply overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Bb6, Ng4, Rg1, c5, Bd3, h4, etc.) are quiet non-forcing moves that completely ignore an available check delivering either immediate checkmate or winning the opponent's queen/major piece. By failing to check, the player squanders a decisive tactical blow and allows the opponent to escape, consolidate, or even turn the tables.

analysis.label: Player moved their king (or other piece) instead of promoting an advanced passed pawn that was one square from queening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 83% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 91 (queen value = pawn promotion). 67% of best moves deliver check (promotions with check), while only 4% of played moves were captures — the players chose quiet moves instead. The played moves are overwhelmingly king moves (10 of 12 top boards), and across nearly all positions a pawn sits on the 7th/2nd rank ready to promote. The median SEE value of 91 precisely corresponds to gaining a queen via promotion. The 29% own-hang rate is incidental — some king moves accidentally exposed pieces, but the core pattern is the failure to promote.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves fail because they waste a critical tempo in positions where immediate pawn promotion (often with check) either wins decisive material, forces mate, or saves a lost position. By not promoting, the player allows the opponent to reposition defensively, blockade the pawn, or deliver their own mating attack. The promotion was the single most forcing move available, and any delay is catastrophic in these razor-sharp endgame positions.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting-looking aggressive move (often a queen capture or check) that leaves their own major piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 69% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., rook-level or higher), with the own-hang class distribution skewed toward major pieces (25 major vs 11 minor vs 8 pawn). Meanwhile, 38% of the played moves are captures and 64% of positions have a best move that wins material (median 3.0), meaning the player often had a genuinely good tactical option but chose the wrong aggressive continuation. The top boards overwhelmingly show queens grabbing edge pawns (Qxf7+, Qxf2+, Qxh2, Qxf5) or making flashy but unsound checks/promotions (e8=Q+, Rd5+) that leave the active piece trapped or undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These moves look attractive because they win material, deliver check, or appear active, but they place the moving piece (usually the queen) on a square where it has no safe retreat or is insufficiently defended. The opponent can then win back far more material than was gained—typically netting a queen (value 9) or rook (value 5) in the resulting exchanges or traps.

analysis.label: The player missed a critical check (99% of best moves are checks) that wins the game, forces mate, or secures a draw via perpetual, often choosing a greedy capture or passive move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that the best move is a check in 99% of the top 500 activating positions, with 98% winning material (median value 97, indicating queen-level or game-winning gains). Only 25% of these best checks are also captures, meaning most are pure non-capturing checks that exploit an exposed enemy king. Meanwhile, the player's actual move was a capture only 30% of the time, and 62% of the time left their own piece hanging (median value 1, mostly pawns). The average cp_loss of 5923 confirms these are catastrophic blunders—missed forced mates, missed perpetual checks to save draws, or missed checks that win decisive material.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because the player prioritizes material greed (Qxa2, Qxa1, Qxa8, Qxh4, Qxh2 grabbing loose pieces/pawns) or passive development (Kh7, Re8, e2) while ignoring that the opponent's king is fatally exposed. The available check either forces immediate mate, wins the queen/game through a forcing sequence, or delivers perpetual check to save an otherwise lost or equal position. By not checking, the player either throws away a winning attack or allows the opponent's threats (passed pawns, counterplay) to become decisive.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet, irrelevant piece move (typically a bishop repositioning) while facing an immediate checkmate threat, allowing mate in one.
analysis.description: The feature fires on positions where the player ignores a lethal checkmate threat to make an irrelevant quiet move — overwhelmingly bishop moves (Bf4, Bg5, Bf3, Bf6, Bc4, Bg7, Bd1 dominate the top activations). The SEE aggregate shows 75% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, heavily pawn-weighted with 114 pawns, 45 minors, 39 majors), which is a side-effect of the actual catastrophe: the move allows immediate mate. The best move wins material 57% of the time (median 3.0) because the correct defensive resource often incidentally captures attacking material (e.g., gxh3 winning a piece while parrying mate). Only 28% of played moves are captures and only 5% of best moves are checks, confirming that the pattern is a quiet, aimless piece move versus a necessary defensive intervention. The astronomical average cp_loss of 8295 confirms nearly every position results in immediate checkmate.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore an immediate checkmate threat (typically a queen + supporting piece mating battery aimed at the king). Instead of addressing the mate with the only defensive resource (blocking, interposing, capturing the attacker, or fleeing), the player makes a developmentally irrelevant bishop/piece repositioning move, allowing the opponent to deliver checkmate on the very next move.

analysis.label: Player moves their king to the wrong square in a pawn endgame, losing a winning/drawn position by failing to find the correct maneuvering path.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king-and-pawn endgames where the player sends their king in the wrong direction, catastrophically mishandling opposition, outflanking, or penetration. The SEE aggregate shows this is NOT primarily a material-hanging or material-winning pattern: only 20% of best moves win material (median just 1 pawn), only 11% of played moves hang own material, and only 5% are captures. The vast majority (~80%) are quiet positional king-maneuvering errors with zero material change on the move itself, yet the average cp_loss is 461—showing these directional errors turn wins into draws or draws into losses. The feature fires on 0.1% of positions, exclusively in endgames, with 11/12 top activations being king moves to the wrong square.
analysis.why_bad: In locked or minimal-pawn endgames, the king's path is the sole determinant of the outcome. Moving the king one square in the wrong direction (e.g., Kg2 instead of Ke2, Kc5 instead of Ke4, Ke4 instead of Kg6) loses opposition, abandons the critical penetration route, or allows the opponent's king to outflank. Because no pawn breaks are available, a single misplaced king move is irreversible and immediately decisive.

analysis.label: Player makes an aimless or non-addressing move that both misses a winning capture and leaves their own material en prise.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player commits a severe tactical blunder by making a quiet, non-forcing move (king retreat, wrong castling, purposeless queen move, or frivolous check) while ignoring the position's critical tactical demands. The SEE aggregate shows 66% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns:81, minors:74, majors:44), while simultaneously 62% of positions have a best move that wins enemy material (median 3.0). Only 18% of played moves are captures, versus 51% of best moves being captures. This dual signal—hanging own piece AND missing enemy material—indicates the player is tactically blind to the most forcing elements. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions with an enormous average centipawn loss of 2563, consistent with catastrophic oversights.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most critical tactical issue on the board—typically an available capture that would win significant material or a threat that must be addressed. Instead, the player makes a 'routine' move (king tuck, castling, aimless queen relocation, or pointless check) that neither captures hanging enemy material nor defends their own vulnerable pieces, often resulting in immediate decisive loss.

analysis.label: Player advances or captures with the f-pawn in a King's Gambit-type opening instead of developing a knight (Nf3/Nf6) that simultaneously attacks the opponent's undefended central pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a premature f-pawn push or capture (f5, fxe5, f4, fxe4) instead of developing a knight. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 71% of the time (median value 1.0 = a pawn), which corresponds to developing Nf3/Nf6 attacking an enemy central pawn under tension. The best move is rarely itself a capture (10%) or check (5%), confirming it's a quiet developing move that indirectly wins material. The played move leaves the player's own piece hanging 48% of the time (median 1.0, distributed as 6 pawns, 3 minors, 1 major), reflecting the newly advanced/captured f-pawn becoming vulnerable or the opened diagonal exposing material. All 12 top positions are in the opening phase with an average cp_loss of 382.
analysis.why_bad: The f-pawn advance or capture opens the e1-h4 diagonal (or equivalent for Black), fatally exposing the uncastled king to queen checks (typically Qh4+). By not developing the knight to f3/f6, the player misses both blocking that diagonal AND attacking the opponent's central pawn. The result is an immediate tactical catastrophe where the opponent exploits the open diagonal for a devastating attack, often winning material or delivering a winning attack against the exposed king.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing move instead of capturing a free or favorable central pawn (dxc4, exf4, or dxc5) that resolves pawn tension.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 93% of the time with 42% winning material (median 1 pawn), yet the player's move is virtually never a capture (1%). All 12 top-activating positions are opening-phase positions with unresolved central pawn tension (f4 vs e5, c4 vs d5, or d4 vs c5), and in every case the best move is a simple pawn capture resolving that tension (exf4, dxc4, or dxc5). Instead, the player makes quiet developing moves (Nf6, Bf5, Be6, Bd7, Qf6, Nbc6, Bg5, etc.) or ill-timed pawn pushes (e4, b5, c4), ignoring the free or favorable pawn grab. The 31% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects a secondary consequence: by failing to resolve tension at the right moment, the played move sometimes leaves the player's own pawns or pieces tactically vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves ignore a concrete tactical opportunity to win or favorably capture a pawn in the center. By not resolving the tension, the opponent retains the pawn, often consolidates, and gains a structural or developmental advantage. The 'developing' moves aren't truly useful because the center remains unstable—the opponent can then capture or advance on their terms, gaining tempo and initiative. Average cp_loss is 242, showing these are significant missed opportunities.

analysis.label: Player misses the opportunity to double rooks on the 7th (or 2nd) rank, typically winning a pawn, and instead plays a passive or misdirected move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 69% of cases with a median value of 1.0 (a pawn), consistent with doubled rooks on the 7th/2nd rank harvesting a weak pawn (g7, b7, etc.). Only 24% of best moves are captures and just 4% are checks, indicating the winning move is usually a quiet rook lift (e.g., Rdd7, Rgg7, Ree7, Rcc7, Ree2, Rff2). The played moves are captures (25%) or quiet moves that often leave the player's own piece hanging (50%, median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 68 and majors at 49). The player either grabs an inferior target, plays a prophylactic move like h3/h5, or repositions a piece aimlessly, completely missing the devastating rook-doubling motif on the penultimate rank.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the strongest positional/tactical resource available—doubling rooks on the 7th or 2nd rank. Doubled rooks on the penultimate rank create simultaneous threats against multiple pawns and the opponent's king, often winning material by force. Instead, the player wastes a tempo on an irrelevant move (h3, Ra5, Rh1) or captures a less valuable target (Rxd5, Rxb2), surrendering a dominant position and frequently leaving their own pieces uncoordinated or hanging.

analysis.label: The player overlooks that their King can simply capture an undefended enemy Rook sitting adjacent to it, instead playing flashy or active moves with other pieces.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a full Rook), and 100% of best moves are captures (0% are checks). Meanwhile, the player's actual move was never a capture (0%) and never hung their own piece (0%). Across all top boards, the pattern is identical: Black has an undefended Rook parked adjacent to White's King (typically on h2 next to Kg1, or a2 next to Kb1), and the winning move is simply Kxh2 or Kxa2—the King walks over and takes a free Rook. Instead, the player makes an 'active' move with their Rook or Knight (often giving check), completely missing the elementary King capture of the hanging piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a trivially winning capture. By playing checks or repositioning other pieces, the player allows Black to reposition the threatened Rook or advance dangerous passed pawns (often a g2 or b2 pawn one square from promotion). The resulting positions become drawn or even losing, squandering what was a decisive material gain available in a single King move. The player appears psychologically fixated on piece activity and checks rather than the simple, quiet King capture.

analysis.label: Player delivers a tempting but ineffective check (usually with a knight or bishop) that leaves their own Queen undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 94% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0, i.e., the Queen), with 'major' pieces accounting for 74 of 109 classified hung pieces. Every single top-12 move is a check — knight checks (Na6+, Nf3+, Ng6+, Nb5+, Ne6+, Ng4+) or bishop captures with check (Bxe6+, Bxf7+). The best move wins material in 78% of cases (median 3.0 pawns), often via a different check (44%) or capture (40%), indicating a superior tactical continuation existed. The player is seduced by an available check that does not accomplish a constructive goal, while their Queen — typically far from the checking piece — is left undefended and immediately capturable by the opponent after the check is dealt with.
analysis.why_bad: These checks accomplish nothing lasting: the opponent simply moves their king (or interposes), and then captures the player's undefended Queen on the very next move. The checking piece moves away from the Queen's defense, or the check itself doesn't create any follow-up threat that compensates for losing the Queen. The player prioritizes 'giving check' over board safety, resulting in catastrophic material loss (average ~983 centipawns).

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece but in the wrong order, leaving their own piece hanging when a different capture sequence would have maintained or won material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where mutual captures exist and the player selects the wrong one first. The SEE aggregate shows 92% of played moves are captures, yet 60% of those captures leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minors at 160/301). The best move is also a capture 71% of the time and wins material 68% of the time (median 3.0). The pattern is a 'zwischenzug-blind' error: in positions with reciprocal piece attacks (e.g., White's Bg5 attacks Be7 while Black's Bf3 attacks Be2), the player grabs one enemy piece but should have captured the OTHER enemy piece first—specifically the one that was defending or attacking their own vulnerable piece. The correct intermediate capture eliminates the opponent's attacker before it can recapture.
analysis.why_bad: By capturing the wrong piece first, the player's remaining piece becomes undefended and is captured for free on the next move. The correct move order (capturing the piece that defends or threatens your vulnerable piece first) would either maintain material equality or net material, since the opponent can no longer recapture profitably. Essentially, the player loses a tempo in a forced exchange sequence, converting what should be an equal trade or a material gain into a net loss of a minor piece.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player moves their king (or makes the wrong pawn move) instead of a critical pawn advance, leaving an undefended pawn en prise to the opponent's king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 92% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being overwhelmingly a pawn (40 pawns vs 6 minors vs 1 major in the class distribution). The best move wins material only 24% of the time and is a capture only 12%, indicating the correct move is typically a quiet pawn push rather than a tactical strike. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and in 11/12 cases the best move is a pawn advance (h5, h4, a5, c4, c5, f5, a4, g5, etc.) that would secure the pawn structure. Instead, the player plays a king move that walks away from a vulnerable pawn, allowing the opponent's nearby king to capture it.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, precise pawn timing is essential. The critical pawn advance either locks the position to prevent the opponent's king from capturing, creates a passed pawn for counterplay, or maintains a defensive structure. By playing a king move instead, the player wastes the one tempo needed to secure the pawn, and the opponent's king—already positioned adjacent to the hanging pawn—captures it immediately, often converting a draw into a loss or turning a loss into a larger deficit.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an available enemy rook (or major piece) on an open file, typically the c-file, often leaving their own major piece hanging in the process.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates missed winning captures: 89% of best moves are captures, 67% win material with a median value of 5.0 (rook-level), and the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 18% captures). Simultaneously, 59% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, mostly majors: 12 out of 16 classified). The top boards reveal a strikingly consistent geometry: open c-file confrontations where the enemy rook on c8 (or another back-rank square) is capturable by the player's rook or queen. In positions 1-4 and 8, the best move is Rxc8; in positions 7, 9, 10 it's Qxb8+/Qxc8/Rxd8. Players instead make irrelevant quiet moves (king walks, pawn pushes, rook shuffles) that ignore the tactical opportunity and frequently expose their own rook or queen to capture on the same open file.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to take the free enemy rook on the open file, the player squanders a full rook's worth of material (≈5 pawns). Worse, the quiet alternative often leaves the player's own major piece undefended on the same file, since the opponent's remaining pieces can now exploit the same open-file tension. The net swing is catastrophic — typically 500+ centipawns — because the player both misses winning material and frequently donates their own piece.

analysis.label: The player fails to make a necessary bishop capture (usually an equal exchange) to eliminate a dominant or dangerous enemy piece, instead playing a quiet repositioning move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 97% of best moves are captures (overwhelmingly bishop captures like Bxe5, Bxg6, Bxf5, Bxf3, Bxg4, Bxd3, Bxc6, Bxc4—10 of 12 top boards), yet only 25% actually win material (median 2.0 when they do), meaning ~72% are equal exchanges (SEE=0). The player's move was a capture only 11% of the time, meaning they almost always play a quiet move instead. After the played move, 49% leave their own piece hanging (median value 1.0; mostly pawns at 107, then minors at 59, majors at 30). The pattern is clear: a bishop should capture an enemy piece to neutralize a positional threat (centralized knight, attacking bishop), but the player moves the bishop elsewhere or plays an unrelated quiet move, often creating new vulnerabilities.
analysis.why_bad: The equal exchange is positionally mandatory—it removes a dominant enemy piece (e.g., a centralized knight on e5, an attacking bishop targeting the king). By avoiding the trade, the player allows the opponent's strong piece to persist, often compounds the error by misplacing their own bishop or hanging material, and the opponent's positional advantage snowballs into a large evaluation swing (avg 276cp loss).

analysis.label: Player makes a developing or quiet move (typically a bishop move) instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece, often simultaneously hanging their own material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player ignores a free capture to play a developing move. The SEE aggregate shows that in 94% of cases the best move is a capture (winning material 72% of the time with a median gain of 3.0 pawns—typically a minor piece). Meanwhile, only 19% of played moves are captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet/developing moves. Compounding the error, 69% of the played moves additionally leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed across major pieces (58), minor pieces (50), and pawns (37). The most common pattern involves a centralized enemy knight on e4/e5 that should be captured (Nxe5, Nxe4 appear repeatedly as best moves) while the player instead develops a bishop (Bf4, Bb5, Bd6, Bc4, Bd3) or repositions their queen, ignoring the free material and creating fresh tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize positional development or flashy ideas (like Bxf2+ checks) over a simple, clean material win. By leaving the enemy piece alive on its strong central square, the player allows the opponent to maintain tactical threats (often against f7 or the king), while the developing move itself frequently leaves the moved piece or another piece undefended, compounding a missed opportunity into an outright material loss.

analysis.label: Developing a bishop to g4 or g5 as a routine move while ignoring urgent tactical obligations, typically a powerful centralized enemy knight that should be captured.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' bishop development to g4 (Black) or g5 (White) when the position demands an urgent tactical response. The SEE aggregate shows that 58% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed across pawns: 144, minors: 119, majors: 28), and 41% of the time the best move wins material (median value 2.0). Only 3% of played moves are captures, confirming the player chose a quiet developing move over critical captures. The best move is a capture 30% of the time—frequently Nxd5, Nxd4, or Nxe5—eliminating a dominant centralized enemy knight. The feature fires on 5.7% of all positions, indicating this is a common amateur mistake pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop moves to g4/g5 ignore urgent positional and tactical demands: typically a powerful enemy knight sits unchallenged on d4/d5 (or similar tactical threats exist). By developing the bishop 'routinely,' the player either exposes it to attack (making it or pawns hanging), misses capturing a strong centralized piece that dominates the position, or walks into known tactical patterns where the opponent's Bc4+Qf3 setup exploits the bishop's vulnerability on g4. The resulting positions often swing 200-600 cp against the player.

analysis.label: In completely won endgame positions, the player misses a simple decisive capture in favor of an imprecise king move or flashy check, often squandering a forced mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly indicates the 'missed winning' direction: 69% of best moves win material (median value 3.0), best moves are captures 42% of the time, yet the player's move was a capture only 18% of the time. The feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (100%) with an astronomical average cp_loss of 6336, indicating most involve missed forced mates. Only 36% of played moves hang own material (median 1.0, mostly pawns), confirming the primary error is not self-harm but failure to take what's available. The 26% best-move-is-check rate shows some winning moves are checks that lead to captures or mates, yet the player often plays different, non-winning checks instead.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they allow the opponent to survive in positions where a simple capture (bxa6, Nxe5, Kxd1, Rxd1, Qxd5, Kxe6, Rxg5) would end the game immediately via overwhelming material or forced mate. The imprecise alternatives—king moves to wrong squares (Kf6, Kh3, Kf2, Kxg6, Ke5), purposeless checks (Qe6+, Nf4+, Qh3+), or passive rook moves (Rb5)—reduce winning margins from forced mates to mere advantages, giving opponents survival chances.

analysis.label: The player's move leaves their own queen en prise, often via a futile check that traps or exposes the queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 100% of the top 500 positions feature the player's move leaving their own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 9.0 (queen). The piece class distribution is 499 major / 1 minor, confirming the queen is the piece being hung in virtually every case. Many of the blunders (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 7) involve giving check with the queen that accomplishes nothing—the opponent simply deals with the check and captures the now-exposed queen. Other instances (positions 5, 8, 10, 12) involve moving another piece or the queen itself to a square where it becomes capturable. The best move wins material only 56% of the time, confirming the primary error is not missing a win but rather self-inflicting a catastrophic loss of material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because after execution, the queen is left on a square where it can be captured (or trapped) by the opponent, losing approximately 9 points of material. In the check cases, the check is meaningless—the opponent blocks or moves the king while simultaneously attacking the queen, which has no safe retreat. In non-check cases, the player overlooks that the queen's defender was removed or that the queen's new/current square is attacked.

analysis.label: Player jumps a knight aggressively to the rim (Nb5, Nb4, Ng5) in the opening instead of making a sound central/developing move, often leaving the knight itself vulnerable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a premature aggressive knight jump to squares like b5, b4, or g5 instead of solid central moves (e3, e6, d4, c3). The SEE aggregate over 500 positions shows that 52% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece — the knight itself — with 124 out of 233 hangs being minor pieces). Additionally, 46% of the time the best move wins material (median 2.0), indicating the player misses tactical opportunities while chasing an aggressive but unsound knight maneuver. Only 13% of the played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet knight repositioning moves rather than tactical attempts. The feature fires in just 0.3% of all positions, isolating a specific opening error pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These knight jumps violate opening principles: the knight lands on an aggressive-looking but unstable square where it can be easily attacked, chased, or captured (especially by pawns like ...a6 or ...h6). Meanwhile, the player neglects critical central pawn moves (e3, e6, d4) that would solidify the position and prepare natural development. The knight sortie wastes tempo and often leaves the knight itself en prise, resulting in material loss averaging ~267 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player makes a developing or active-looking opening move that leaves one of their own pieces (usually a minor piece) en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 95% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward minors (13 minor, 4 pawn, 3 major). Only 10% of the moves are captures, meaning these are quiet 'developing' moves that ignore piece safety. The best move wins material in 48% of cases (median 1.0), often because the correct move would save or reposition the threatened piece. All 12 top positions are in the opening phase, with both kings still in the center.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes making a 'developing' or active-looking move (Ba6, Bg4, Bg5, Ne5, Qg5, Bg2, etc.) while either placing the moved piece on an undefended square where it can be immediately captured (often by a pawn), or ignoring an existing threat to another one of their pieces. For example, Bg2 ignores that e4 attacks Nf3, d6 ignores that d5 attacks Nc6, Ba6 places the bishop where it has no defenders, and Ne5 puts the knight on a square attacked by the d4 pawn. The result is a free piece for the opponent.

analysis.label: Player ignores a decisive forcing move (check or capture) and instead plays a move that hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 61% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns, majors, and minors). Meanwhile, the best move was a capture 77% of the time and a check 35% of the time, indicating a strong forcing continuation was available. The best move wins material only 30% of the time (median 3.0), meaning many of these forcing moves initiate winning sequences (mates or decisive combinations) rather than simply picking up a loose piece. The average cp_loss of 1785 confirms these are catastrophic blunders—the player overlooks a tactical blow (often a back-rank check, a winning recapture, or a mating attack) and instead plays a quiet or misdirected move that leaves their own material en prise.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a forcing continuation (check/capture) that either wins immediately or enters a decisive sequence. By playing a non-forcing move instead, the player not only misses the win but often places a piece on an undefended square or moves a defender away, leaving their own material hanging to the opponent's next move. The combination of missing the tactic AND creating a new vulnerability makes the position collapse immediately.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own rook (or occasionally minor piece) undefended and capturable by the opponent, typically in endgame positions.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming 92% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e. a rook), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward major pieces (325 major out of 462 total hanging instances). The feature fires in endgame positions (9/12 top boards) where the player either moves their rook to an unsafe square (e.g. Rh1 into a bishop's diagonal, Rd3/Ra3/Rc1 into capture range of a minor piece) or makes an unrelated quiet move (a5, f3, fxg4) while their rook is already under attack. The best move wins material in 55% of cases (median 3.0 pawns), often by capturing the attacking piece (Kxd5) or repositioning to safety, but the player ignores the threat entirely.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the player's rook (worth 5 points) completely undefended against capture by an enemy minor piece or other attacker. Whether the rook is actively moved to an unsafe square or simply left hanging while the player makes an irrelevant move, the opponent can win a full rook on the next move, resulting in the massive average cp_loss of 708.

analysis.label: Player fails to execute a necessary bishop exchange (Bx...), leaving their own minor piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 100% of cases, yet it only wins material 2% of the time (median value won: 2.0), meaning the correct move is almost always an equal exchange. In 56% of positions the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being minors (208 out of 277). Across all top 12 boards, the best move is always a bishop capture (Bxf6, Bxf3, Bxe6, Bxd6, Bxe2) with SEE = 0, indicating an equal trade. The player instead plays a quiet developing or repositioning move, ignoring the obligation to resolve the tension their bishop has created against an enemy piece.
analysis.why_bad: The player's bishop is aggressively placed attacking an enemy piece (typically a knight on f6/f3 or a piece on an open diagonal). The position demands resolving this tension by exchanging. By playing a different move, the player allows the opponent to exploit the exposed bishop's position — often by attacking it with tempo or trapping it — resulting in the bishop (or the piece it was supposed to protect) becoming en prise. The ~200cp average loss reflects the cost of losing a minor piece or falling into a much worse structural/tactical position.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet or non-urgent move (often a pawn push) that leaves their own piece—typically a minor piece—hanging and undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move left their own piece en prise: 74% of the time the played move hung an own piece (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the distribution skewing toward minors (42) and pawns (33) over majors (8). Simultaneously, 70% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0), suggesting that the correct continuation would have either safeguarded the vulnerable piece or exploited a tactical opportunity instead. Only 20% of the played moves were captures, confirming that players typically chose passive/quiet moves (pawn pushes like f6, f5, d4, g5, b6, a3 or piece retreats like Qd8) rather than addressing the tactical needs of the position. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a specific and costly error pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the immediate tactical vulnerability of the player's own pieces. By pushing pawns or repositioning pieces without addressing defensive obligations, the player allows the opponent to capture an undefended minor piece or pawn on the next move. The best moves (Nb4, dxc3, Bxe6, exf7+, etc.) either secure the threatened piece, win material through a tactic, or address the real priority of the position rather than playing an irrelevant quiet move.

analysis.label: Player missed a check that wins decisive material through a fork, skewer, or forcing sequence against an exposed king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: 96% of best moves are checks, and 95% win material (median value 100, indicating winning a major piece or more). Only 12% of best moves are captures, meaning the check itself creates a tactical threat (fork/skewer) rather than directly capturing. The player's actual moves were quiet 82% of the time, completely ignoring the exposed enemy king. The 40% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental — the real blunder is missing the decisive check. Across all 12 top-activating positions, every best move is a check (Bxf4+, Bd4+, Qh4+, Bxe4+, Ng5+, Qb5+, Qf6+, Be3+, Be5+, Qf5+, Rf3+, Nc5+), typically exploiting an exposed king to fork or skewer a high-value piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a check that simultaneously attacks the king and a major/minor piece (fork geometry) or initiates a forcing sequence that wins material. By playing a quiet move instead, the player squanders a decisive tactical opportunity, often turning a winning position into an equal or lost one (average cp_loss: 2046).

analysis.label: In simplified endgames, the player makes a 'strategic' or impulsive move that simultaneously misses winning an enemy piece and leaves their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a striking dual-error signature: 71% of best moves win enemy material (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece) while simultaneously 71% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value also 3.0). The hung pieces span minors (5), majors (4), and pawns (1). The best move is a capture 64% of the time, yet the player's move was a capture only 7% of the time. The feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (12/12) with massive average cp_loss of 2096. This indicates positions where a concrete tactical capture exists but the player instead makes a 'natural' endgame move—a king walk, a check, a piece redeployment, or a promotion—that both ignores the winning capture AND exposes their own piece to recapture or attack.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in simplified endgames the player prioritizes apparent strategic goals (checking, centralizing, promoting, advancing pawns) over concrete board reality. By ignoring an available capture (often of a piece worth 3+ material), they forfeit winning material; simultaneously, by moving their piece away from a safe square or abandoning a defensive duty, they leave their own piece (knight, rook, or queen) unprotected for the opponent to take. The net swing is catastrophic—often 6+ pawns of value when both the missed gain and the self-inflicted loss are combined.

analysis.label: In closed-center openings, the player makes a slow/routine move instead of the critical flank pawn advance (a4/a5/h4/h5) that seizes space or launches an attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows this is primarily a strategic/planning error rather than a tactical blunder: only 21% of best moves win material (median just 1.0 pawn), only 2% are captures, only 2% are checks, and only 5% of played moves hang a piece. The player's move was a capture just 7% of the time. The feature fires on 0.0% of all positions, indicating a very specific scenario. Across the top 12 boards (all opening phase, avg cp_loss 259), the positions share a closed center and the best move is overwhelmingly a flank pawn advance: a4 (4 times), a5 (twice), h4 (twice), h5 (twice). Instead, players chose passive developing or reorganizing moves (Bb6, d5, h3, Bb3, Nc6, d3, O-O, b3, Bg5, c3, Bd6, e6) that ignore the urgency of wing expansion.
analysis.why_bad: In closed-center positions, piece maneuvering alone is insufficient—flank pawn advances are the primary method of creating breakthroughs, seizing space, and generating threats. By playing slow, routine moves instead, the player allows the opponent to stabilize or launch their own flank attack first, squandering a tempo-sensitive window where the pawn push (often a4/h4 on attack, or a5/h5 to restrain) is the only way to maintain or create an advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move (often castling) that leaves their own bishop undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 89% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece-class distribution dominated by minor pieces (209 out of 247 instances). Examining the top 12 boards confirms that in 11 of 12 cases, the hung piece is specifically a bishop ('B'). The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 22% captures), with castling (O-O) appearing in 5 of the top 12 positions. The best move wins material only 41% of the time (often just 0), meaning the correct move was typically a defensive relocation or prophylactic move to save the bishop rather than a tactical strike. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, indicating a specific tactical blindspot rather than a general blunder pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes a 'routine' or 'natural' developing move (castling, pushing a pawn, developing another piece) while ignoring that one of their own bishops is undefended or will become tactically exposed after the move. In many cases, the bishop sits on an open file facing an enemy battery (queen + rook), or stands undefended on an open diagonal/rank where the opponent's queen can capture it. The correct move would be to relocate the threatened bishop or add a defender before proceeding with development.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive Queen check that wins massive material or forces mate, instead playing an inferior move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of the time the best move is a check, and 91% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91, indicating near-decisive gains such as forced mate or queen wins). Only 26% of best moves are captures, meaning most winning checks are non-capturing Queen moves to open squares that exploit an exposed enemy king. The played moves were captures only 31% of the time, and 61% of them left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3, with majors and pawns most common). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions—specifically those where a powerful Queen check exists but was overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a crushing Queen check against an exposed enemy king. Instead of delivering a forcing check that leads to immediate mate or wins decisive material through follow-up threats, the player makes a routine move (capturing a less important piece, developing a rook, etc.) that surrenders the initiative and often leaves their own pieces undefended. In many cases (avg cp_loss ~4295), the missed check led to forced mate, turning a winning position into a loss or draw.

analysis.label: In endgames with far-advanced passed pawns, the player makes an ineffective move instead of first eliminating or neutralizing the piece/pawn blocking promotion.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 48% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, consistent with capturing blocking minor pieces or rooks), while the played move is almost never a capture (only 6%). The best move is a capture 27% of the time, reflecting positions where the correct approach is to remove the obstacle to promotion. The 39% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the premature pawn pushes or misguided king moves sometimes leave the advanced pawn itself vulnerable. Across the top 500 positions, the pattern is endgame positions with advanced passed pawns where the critical move is a precise piece maneuver, capture, or reposition that eliminates the blocker—but instead the player pushes the pawn prematurely (e7, g6, b2), makes a wrong capture (gxf5 instead of fxg5), or moves the king aimlessly (Kb3, Kb2, Kc3, Kc6) rather than executing the tactical solution.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the primary obstacle to promotion. Pushing the pawn into a blockade (e7 into f7, g6 instead of gxf6) or making king moves (Kb3, Kc6 instead of Na4 or Kxb5) allows the opponent to maintain their defensive setup. The correct moves either capture the blocking piece directly (fxg5, exf7, gxf6, Kxb5, bxa2), reposition a piece to neutralize the defense (Na4, Nd7), or sacrifice to clear the promotion path (Bb4). The played moves squander decisive advantages because they don't address WHY the pawn can't promote.

analysis.label: Player makes a slow move (king move or wrong-flank pawn push) instead of executing a decisive pawn breakthrough in king-and-pawn endgames.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 88% of best moves win material (median value: 1.0, i.e., one pawn), yet only 7% of best moves are captures and only 10% are checks. This indicates the material is won indirectly—through pawn breakthrough combinations (e.g., g4, h5, b4, a5) that force the opponent to concede a passed pawn or lose a pawn in the resulting exchanges. The player's move was a capture only 10% of the time and left own pieces hanging only 18% of the time, confirming the error is one of omission: failing to execute the breakthrough. The feature fires overwhelmingly in endgame positions (11/12 top boards) that are pure or near-pure king-and-pawn positions.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because pawn endgame breakthroughs are extremely time-sensitive. By playing a king move (Kc5, Ke2, Kg4, Kg3, Kd6) or a pawn advance on the wrong flank (g3, c4, d4, h4), the player gives the opponent time to reposition their king to cover the breakthrough square, converting a won position into a draw or even a loss. The breakthrough works NOW because the opponent's king is too far away or the pawn structure allows a forced sequence; one tempo later, the window closes.

analysis.label: The player makes a quiet move instead of penetrating with a rook along an open file to exploit back-rank weakness, winning major material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 70% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. a rook's worth or more), and only 16% of played moves are captures—meaning players choose passive quiet moves instead. The best move is a check 24% of the time (back-rank checks like Re1+ or Re8+) and a capture 25% of the time. Across the top 12 positions, the best moves are nearly all rook invasions along open d- or e-files (Re1+, Re1, Rd1, Rc8, Rb8, Re8+, Rc1, Rxc1) that exploit critically weak back ranks. The 48% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary effect of the passive move allowing counterplay, not the primary error. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions—specifically those where open central files and back-rank fragility create a decisive rook penetration opportunity that the player overlooks.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Qc6, a5, f6, Bg5, g4, Bd6, Qd4, Bc3) waste a critical tempo where a rook could invade along an open file to the opponent's back rank, winning material (often a queen via SEE=95, or a full rook via SEE=5) through mating threats or forced trades. By playing passively, the player squanders a concrete tactical advantage that the position's open-file geometry and back-rank vulnerability provide.

analysis.label: The player missed a pawn advance or capture that delivers a devastating discovered check, winning massive material or delivering checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a check in 82% of the top 500 activating positions, and wins material 60% of the time with a median value of 95 (approximately a queen). The best move is a capture in 49% of cases, reflecting pawn captures that simultaneously open lines. The pattern is overwhelmingly one of missed discovered checks: a pawn move (advance or capture) unveils a powerful piece (queen, bishop, or rook) that delivers check to an exposed king, winning enormous material or forcing mate. The 57% own-hang rate (median value 2, mostly pawns) reflects that the quiet moves played instead are strategically aimless and leave minor weaknesses, but the real disaster is the missed tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing pawn move that opens a critical line (d-file, diagonal, e-file) delivering discovered check. The exposed enemy king—often uncastled on d1, d7, e8, or weakened on b7/g7—is fatally aligned with a powerful piece behind the movable pawn. By playing quiet developing or repositioning moves instead, the player squanders a winning tactic that typically nets a queen or delivers checkmate, often turning a decisive advantage into an equal or lost position.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive, purposeless move (often a king move) that both misses winning available enemy material and frequently leaves their own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, aimless move in a tactically rich position. The SEE aggregate shows that in 81% of cases (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), the best move wins enemy material, yet the player's move is a capture only 20% of the time—they overwhelmingly play quiet, non-tactical moves instead. Compounding this, 67% of the played moves also leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), predominantly pawns (197) but also minors (71) and majors (66). The best move is rarely a check (4%) or even a capture (13%), suggesting the winning tactic is often a positional threat or fork-setup rather than an obvious recapture. The average centipawn loss of 1568 confirms these are catastrophic blunders. The top boards show king wandering moves (Kg4, Kh3, Kd1, Ke8), aimless rook relocations (Rg1, Re2, Rd3), and wrong captures (Rxh1 instead of Rxd7)—all ignoring the critical tactical demands of the position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore immediate tactical opportunities (winning enemy pieces worth ~3 pawns on average) while simultaneously creating new vulnerabilities by leaving own pieces undefended. The player appears completely disconnected from the tactical requirements, making purposeless moves that worsen their position in two ways at once: missing material gains and creating material losses.

analysis.label: Player missed a knight capture (usually with check) that wins material or tempo, instead playing an inferior move.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a knight capture—almost always with check (71% of best moves are checks, 89% are captures). All 12 top-activating positions show the best move is a knight taking a piece (Nxf3+, Nxe3+, Nxg3+, Nxf6+, Nxc6), typically forking the king and another piece or winning material through the tempo gained. The best move wins material outright 40% of the time (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). Meanwhile, the played move is often a quiet or misdirected capture (only 22% are captures), and 48% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, mostly pawns). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, highlighting rare but severe oversights of available knight tactics.
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores a knight capture with check that either wins material directly via a fork (king + another piece) or gains decisive tempo. Instead they play passive moves or premature captures elsewhere, often compounding the error by leaving their own material en prise. The check aspect means the opponent would have no choice but to address the king attack, making the knight tactic essentially free.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (often a tempting capture or passive king move) that leaves their own rook undefended and en prise on an open file.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with major pieces accounting for 109 of 148 hung-piece instances. The best move wins material 69% of the time (median 4.0), but this is often because simply defending or exchanging the threatened rook would preserve the material balance. Only 44% of played moves were captures, indicating that both greedy captures and passive/irrelevant quiet moves trigger the pattern. The feature fires on positions where the player ignores that their rook is under attack—typically on an open or semi-open file contested by the opponent's doubled rooks or heavy pieces—and plays an unrelated move that allows the opponent to win the rook for free.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player either grabs material elsewhere (e.g., Rdxc6, Qxd7, dxe5) or plays a passive king/pawn move (Kf7, Kf6, Ke5, g5) while their rook sits undefended on a contested file. The opponent simply captures the hanging rook, netting a full exchange or more and converting a roughly equal or losing position into a decisive advantage.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an undefended enemy queen that is directly attacked by their own minor piece (bishop or knight).
analysis.description: This feature fires when the opponent's queen is freely capturable — typically by a bishop along a clear diagonal or a knight fork — and the player ignores it. The SEE aggregate shows 91% of best moves win material with a median value of 6.0 (queen), and 99% of best moves are captures. Only 28% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet moves instead of taking the queen. The positions are predominantly in the opening (9/12 boards), where the enemy queen remains on its starting square (d8/d1) or has moved to an exposed square (g3, g6, c6, d2) while a minor piece has a completely unobstructed line of attack. Additionally, 57% of played moves also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, mostly minors at 79 instances), compounding the blunder by not only missing a queen capture but also creating fresh tactical weaknesses.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that their bishop or knight has a direct, unobstructed path to an undefended enemy queen.
