Instead of collecting massive material (a free queen), they play routine developing moves (castling, pawn pushes, knight maneuvers) or even leave their own pieces en prise. The result is swinging from a winning position (~+500cp) to equality or worse, throwing away a full queen's worth of material advantage.

analysis.label: Player promotes a pawn to a queen on a square controlled by an enemy piece, immediately hanging the newly created queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 64% of positions show the player's move leaving their own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with the piece class distribution heavily weighted toward major pieces (14 major, 11 pawn, 2 minor). In 10 of the top 12 boards, the player promotes a pawn to a queen on a square directly controlled by an enemy rook or queen (e.g., promoting on f8 when a rook covers f8, promoting on c1/e1/f1 when a rook sits on that file). The best move is almost never a capture (only 7%) or a check (0%), but rather a preparatory move—typically a king retreat or piece maneuver—that either removes the enemy piece's control of the promotion square or waits for a safer moment. The 55% 'best wins material' stat reflects that the correct sequence often wins material eventually through a safe promotion or other tactic, but NOT by rushing the promotion.
analysis.why_bad: The newly promoted queen lands on a square already attacked by an enemy piece (usually a rook on the same file or rank), so it is immediately captured. Instead of gaining a queen (~9 points), the player loses both the promoting pawn and the queen in one move, often converting a defensible or winning position into an immediate loss. The correct approach is an intermediate move (king repositioning, interposing, or deflecting the enemy piece) before promoting safely.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an enemy queen that is freely capturable, usually by a pawn or simple piece move, playing a quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 78% of the time with a median value of 9.0 (queen), and 78% of best moves are captures — yet the player's move was a capture only 19% of the time, confirming they overwhelmingly play quiet moves instead of taking the hanging piece. In 9 of the top 12 boards, an enemy queen sits en prise to a pawn capture (exf6, cxb5, axb4, axb5) or a simple piece capture (Rxc2, Rxa3, Bxf3, Rxe1, Rxc7). The 72% own-hang rate (median value 5.0, mostly rooks) reflects that the desperate quiet moves played — often checks or pointless piece shuffles — leave the player's own material undefended, compounding the catastrophic oversight.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a trivially capturable enemy queen (often attacked by a pawn or lined up on an open file with an opposing rook/bishop). Instead, the player makes purposeless quiet moves like king moves (Kc2), pawn pushes (h3, g3, f3), or speculative checks (Re6+, Rb1+) that fail to address the tactical reality and simultaneously leave their own pieces undefended, resulting in forced mate or decisive material loss.

analysis.label: In a dominant/winning position, the player overlooks a simple forcing capture (often with check) and instead plays a quiet non-capturing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates that the best move is a capture 88% of the time, yet the player's move was a capture only 10% of the time—showing a systematic failure to take available material or deliver decisive forcing blows. The best move is a check 31% of the time, and wins material outright 38% of the time (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The positions are typically already crushing (avg cp_loss 1564, inflated by cases where forced mates are missed), yet instead of the clean capture, the player makes a quiet move (king retreats, piece repositioning). The own-hung rate of 29% at median value 1.0 (pawns) is secondary noise—the primary signature is the overwhelming capture-vs-quiet discrepancy between best and played moves.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they allow the opponent to survive or regroup in positions where a simple capture (often with check) would immediately win material, force checkmate, or conclusively simplify. By not taking the hanging/vulnerable piece or delivering the forcing check-capture, the player converts a quick decisive win into a prolonged struggle, and in the worst cases (positions 1 and 2) squanders forced mates entirely.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own queen or rook completely undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of the 500 activating positions involve the player's move leaving their own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 9.0 (queen). The piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (496/500 major, 4/500 minor), confirming the pattern involves queens and rooks. Only 36% of the played moves are captures and 15% of best moves are checks, indicating the blunder is not always a greedy grab but often a quiet move or misguided relocation that neglects the safety of an already-placed major piece. The feature fires on 14% of all positions, consistent with a broad class of tactical oversights involving undefended major pieces.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore that a major piece (usually the queen, sometimes a rook) is left on a square where it can be captured for free. Whether the player makes a tempting capture (Rxe3+, Qxd4, Rxf5), a seemingly active move (Qc5, Qe5, Re4, Re1), or even a king move that abandons defense of a rook (Kf6), the result is the same: the opponent simply takes the undefended major piece, winning decisive material (median loss of 9 points). The average centipawn loss of 2093 reflects the catastrophic nature of losing a queen or rook outright.

analysis.label: Player throws away a winning King+Pawn endgame by pushing the pawn prematurely or misplacing the king, allowing a draw.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the side to move has a theoretically winning King+Pawn endgame but plays a move that throws the win away (avg cp_loss: 392, typically from ~±550 to 0). The SEE aggregate confirms this is NOT about capturing or hanging pieces: only 23% of best moves win material, only 4% of played moves are captures, and only 10% hang own material (median value just 1.0 — a pawn). The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet king repositioning moves (only 7% captures, 11% checks). The feature specifically identifies the classic K+P endgame error where the player violates the 'king must lead the pawn' principle — either advancing the pawn ahead of the king (positions 1, 2, 5, 8, 11) or moving the king to a square that loses opposition/critical geometry (positions 3, 7, 9).
analysis.why_bad: In King+Pawn vs King endgames, the winning technique requires the king to stay ahead of or beside the pawn to control key squares on the promotion path. Pushing the pawn prematurely (or retreating/misplacing the king) allows the defending king to reach opposition or the critical drawing zone (e.g., the corner for wrong-bishop-color endings), converting a theoretical win into a book draw by stalemate or blockade.

analysis.label: Player ignores an immediate mating threat and plays a quiet move that allows forced checkmate in 1-3 moves.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that allows forced checkmate (avg cp_loss: 9501, corresponding to eval swings from playable/winning positions to #±1 through #±3). The SEE aggregate shows 55% of best moves win material (median 3.0), reflecting that many correct defensive moves also happen to capture or neutralize attacking pieces. Only 22% of played moves were captures, indicating players chose passive quiet moves instead. The 37% own-piece-hanging rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns at 108/186) is a secondary artifact — when you're about to be mated, incidentally exposed pieces barely matter. The feature fires on just 0.5% of positions, consistent with the rarity of allowing immediate forced mate from previously reasonable positions.
analysis.why_bad: In every top-activating position, the player had a winning or playable position but played a 'normal' quiet move (Ne2, Rh2, Kg1, d6, g5, a6, Nb2, Rc4, Kg8, Rg3) while completely ignoring the opponent's mating threats. The correct moves (Kf8, f3, Ke1, Rxg3, g6, Kh6, etc.) would have escaped the mating net or neutralized the attack, but instead the player walked directly into checkmate by failing to address king safety.

analysis.label: In endgames with exposed kings, the player makes a passive king move or greedy capture that leaves their own major piece (Queen or Rook) undefended and capturable, when a forcing move was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player's move leaves their own piece hanging 60% of the time (median value 5.0, predominantly major pieces: 43 major vs. 24 pawn vs. 4 minor). The best move wins material 67% of the time (median value 5.0) and is a check 37% of the time, indicating active forcing continuations were available. The player's move was a capture 49% of the time, suggesting greedy pawn-grabbing (often with the king: Kxh4, Kxg2, Kxb7) rather than the precise forcing move. The dominant pattern is a king wandering aimlessly or greedily capturing a pawn while abandoning protection of a Queen or Rook, in positions where a check or active piece move would have won decisively.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an irrelevant king maneuver or low-value capture over maintaining piece coordination. By moving the king (or making a suboptimal capture), the player removes defense of their own major piece—typically a Queen or Rook—allowing the opponent to simply capture it. The best move was usually a forcing check or active piece move that would maintain the winning advantage by exploiting the opponent's exposed king, not a passive king stroll that abandons piece safety.

analysis.label: Player fails to trap the opponent's overextended queen (typically on b2 or b7) by moving a rook to the b-file.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (a queen). Critically, the best move is a capture only 3% of the time and a check 0% of the time—meaning the winning move is almost always a quiet rook lift to the b-file that traps or wins the enemy queen. The opponent's queen has typically infiltrated deeply to b2 (against White) or b7 (against White's queen invading Black), and the player misses the simple Rb1/Rb8 resource that boxes it in. The 62% own-hang rate (median value 1, mostly pawns) reflects that the alternative moves played often leave minor weaknesses, but the core mistake is ignoring the queen-trapping opportunity worth ~9 points of material.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (developing pieces, castling, pushing pawns, or repositioning knights) ignore the concrete tactical reality that the opponent's queen is overextended on b2/b7 with limited escape squares. A simple rook move to the b-file (Rb1 or Rb8) would either trap the queen outright or force it into a losing exchange of material. By playing positional or routine moves instead, the player allows the enemy queen to escape or consolidate its invasive position, squandering a decisive material gain.

analysis.label: Player gives a pointless or harmful check instead of simply capturing a hanging enemy piece worth major material.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player plays a check (100% of top activating moves are checks) instead of capturing a hanging or winnable enemy piece. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 95% of the time (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook or queen-level gain) and is a capture 85% of the time but almost never a check (only 2%). Meanwhile the played check leaves the player's own piece hanging 79% of the time (median value 3.0, distributed across majors 40%, pawns 31%, minors 25%). The player is seduced by the 'flashy' check but it accomplishes nothing decisive — the opponent simply moves their king and the position has worsened because the player missed winning material and often exposed their own pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The checks are ineffective because they don't lead to checkmate or a winning attack — the opponent's king simply escapes. Meanwhile, the player forfeits a free capture of a major enemy piece (queen, rook, or minor piece) and frequently leaves their own piece en prise after the check, resulting in a net material swing of roughly 5-8 points compared to the best move. Classic 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' syndrome.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture but leaves their own queen (or major piece) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player grabs material via a capture but catastrophically leaves their own major piece hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 100% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0), with the piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (103 out of 109 cases). Meanwhile, 67% of played moves were themselves captures, showing the player was grabbing material. The best moves (which win material 75% of the time, median 5.0) are often simple king retreats to safety (Ke7, Kg8, Kd6) or powerful checks (Qg1+, Qe5+, Qe4+) — 28% are checks — that maintain the queen's safety while exploiting the position. The average cp_loss of 456 reflects the enormous cost of losing a queen for a minor gain.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is lured by a capture (often a pawn or minor piece) but overlooks that their move either relocates the queen to an unsafe square, moves the king away from defending the queen, or moves a piece that was shielding the queen. After the greedy capture, the opponent simply takes the undefended queen, resulting in a massive net material loss despite the initial capture.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece worth significant material in an endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player missed winning free material: 88% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), 92% of the time the best move is a simple capture, yet only 12% of the time did the player actually play a capture. The own-hung rate of 30% is low and incidental (mostly pawns, median value 1.0), confirming this is not a 'hung own piece' pattern. Across the top boards, the missed captures are straightforward takes of undefended pieces—rooks on e2/f2/c4/e4, bishops on e4/c5, knights on e5/d6—often capturable by the king or a simple piece/pawn capture. The positions are almost exclusively endgames (11/12) where reduced piece counts make the hanging piece starkly obvious, yet the player instead plays a quiet pawn push or king move.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (pawn pushes like b6, c6, b5, a6, or king moves like Ke4) completely ignore free material worth 3-5 points sitting undefended on the board. By not capturing, the player allows the opponent to save or reposition the hanging piece, squandering a decisive material advantage and often converting a forced win or mate into a much smaller edge or even a loss.

analysis.label: Player plays an active-looking move (often a rook check) instead of simply capturing a hanging enemy piece, simultaneously leaving their own major piece en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a double blunder: they miss capturing an undefended enemy piece (81% of positions have a best move winning material, median value 5.0, with 70% of best moves being captures) while simultaneously leaving their own piece hanging (81% of played moves leave an own piece en prise, median value 5.0). The hung pieces are overwhelmingly majors (41 major vs 8 minor vs 7 pawn in the distribution). The played moves are typically 'active' rook moves—often giving check (Rg1+, Re1+, Rh1+, Rxg2+) or repositioning (Rf1, Rg1)—that look purposeful but completely miss a free enemy queen or other high-value piece sitting undefended. Only 25% of played moves are captures, meaning players chose non-capturing moves despite a free piece being available.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes apparent activity (especially giving check with a rook) over a simple winning capture. The check or aggressive move doesn't accomplish anything meaningful—the opponent simply moves their king—while the player has thrown away a game-winning opportunity to take a free queen/rook. Worse, the 'active' move often displaces the rook from a defended square, leaving it or another piece completely unprotected, turning a winning position into a lost one.

analysis.label: Player plays a passive, non-tactical quiet move when a winning capture or forcing move is available, often simultaneously leaving their own piece undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 75% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), and 63% of best moves are captures, yet the player's move was a capture only 12% of the time — meaning the player consistently chose a quiet, non-forcing move over an available winning capture. Compounding the error, 59% of the played moves also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns (133), majors (85), and minors (78)). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3360 reflects both the missed material gain and the simultaneous self-inflicted material loss. Best moves are checks 24% of the time, indicating forcing continuations were also overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore the critical tactical demands of the position. Instead of capturing a hanging or inadequately defended enemy piece (winning material), or executing a forcing check that wins material, the player makes an irrelevant positional or developmental move. This not only forfeits the opportunity to win material but frequently leaves the player's own pieces undefended — effectively turning a winning or equal position into a lost one by ignoring both the attacking opportunity and the defensive obligation simultaneously.

analysis.label: The player plays a flashy check or aggressive-looking move that leaves their own piece hanging or fatally removes a critical defender.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 66% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns: 11, minors: 7, majors: 7), while the best move was a check only 3% of the time — yet 7 of the top 12 activating positions feature the player giving check (Ne7+, Ne2+, Qg4+, Qe6+, Rf3+). The player's move was itself a capture only 5% of the time, confirming these are mostly quiet or check moves that backfire. The best move wins material 47% of the time (median value 3.0), indicating that a simple capture was often available instead of the flashy forcing move. The enormous average cp_loss of 4211 reflects how many of these checks/aggressive moves allow immediate mate or catastrophic material loss.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is drawn to giving check ('patzer sees a check, gives a check') or playing an aggressive-looking move without calculating the opponent's response. The check or active move displaces a piece from a critical defensive post (e.g., Ne7+ removing the knight guarding g3), or moves a piece to a square where it has no support (e.g., Rf3+ leaving the rook capturable, Qg4+ leaving the queen en prise). The opponent simply captures the undefended piece or exploits the removed defender to deliver mate.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a slow positional move instead of the concrete move that wins an undefended pawn (or forces mate).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 89% of the time the best move wins material (median value: 1.0, i.e., a pawn), yet only 14% of played moves were captures, indicating the player consistently chose quiet 'improving' moves over concrete material-winning ones. The best move is a check 30% of the time and a direct capture only 14%, meaning the winning tactic is typically an indirect attack on an undefended pawn (e.g., a rook swing to the a-file or h-file) rather than an immediate recapture. The feature fires overwhelmingly in endgames (10/12 top positions) where undefended pawns are available to be won by piece activity, but the player instead plays king walks, pawn pushes, or suboptimal rook placements.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize vague king activity or positional 'improvement' over the concrete winning of a pawn. In endgames, a single extra pawn is often decisive, and the missed material gain (Ra5 winning a4, Rh3 winning a h-pawn, Nd7+ forcing mate) represents either the conversion of a winning advantage or the difference between winning and drawing. The 'slow' moves allow the opponent to defend the hanging pawn or equalize.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (or other move) that leaves their own more valuable piece undefended, missing a stronger move that wins material.
analysis.description: In the SEE aggregate over 500 positions, 94% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minors, majors, and pawns), while 62% of the played moves were captures themselves. Meanwhile, 62% of the best moves would have won material with a median value of 5.0 (rook-level). This creates a distinctive pattern: the player grabs a lesser piece or makes a secondary move while leaving a higher-value piece (often a rook or queen) en prise. The best move typically captures the bigger prize or delivers a forcing check that wins even more. The feature fires on positions where the player prioritizes a local gain while ignoring a larger vulnerability in their own camp.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player captures a lower-value target (or plays a non-critical move) while their own more valuable piece is left undefended or becomes unprotected as a consequence. The opponent then recaptures or takes the hanging piece, resulting in a net material loss far exceeding whatever the player gained. The correct move would typically win more material outright (e.g., capturing an undefended rook, delivering a winning check, or taking the bigger hanging piece first).

analysis.label: In endgames, the player pushes a pawn when king activation or piece repositioning is the critical priority.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, 39% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the overwhelmingly dominant class being pawns (187 of 195 hung pieces). Only 3% of played moves were captures, and just 29% of best moves win material. The top 12 boards reveal the concrete pattern: every single played move is a quiet pawn push (c4, g4, b4, h5, f5, g5, h4, f4), while in 8 of 12 cases the best move is a king relocation (Ke3, Kb8, Ka4, Kf6, Kf8, Kf8, Kh5, Ke4), and the remaining best moves are active piece moves (Rb8, Rc7+, Rg5). The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (10 of 12). The 39% own-pawn-hanging rate reflects that these premature pushes frequently leave the advanced pawn itself unprotected or structurally weak.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, king activity is typically more important than pawn advances. These pawn pushes waste critical tempo, commit pawn structure irreversibly, often weaken the pushed pawn (making it a target), and neglect the king's role as an active fighting piece. The resulting positions lose coordination — the king stays passive while the opponent exploits the weakened pawn structure or gains decisive piece activity.

analysis.label: A knight move that leaves the player's own piece undefended and hanging to capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 90% of positions show the player's own piece left hanging after the move (median value: 3.0), distributed across minor pieces (85), major pieces (77), and pawns (21). Critically, every single one of the top 12 activating moves is a knight move (Nxe6, Nc6, Ng5, Ne3, Nd6, Nh4, Nd4, Na5, Nf6, Nxf3). The knight was serving a defensive role—protecting a queen, rook, or other piece—and by moving it, the player exposes that defended piece to immediate capture. Only 31% of the played moves are captures themselves, meaning most are quiet knight repositioning moves that overlook the defensive duty the knight was fulfilling. The best move wins material in 51% of cases (median 3.0), suggesting alternative tactical opportunities are also being missed.
analysis.why_bad: The knight was a key defender of another piece (often a queen or rook on a contested file). By moving the knight—whether to attack, capture a pawn, or reposition—the player removes the only protection from their own higher-value piece, allowing the opponent to win material immediately. The knight's offensive ambition blinds the player to its critical defensive role.

analysis.label: Player makes a greedy capture that leaves their own piece (usually a rook) hanging, missing a superior intermediate check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 87% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 5 = rook, with 10 major pieces in the distribution), while 80% of the played moves were captures. Crucially, the best move was a check 67% of the time, and in 60% of cases it won material (median 100cp). This signature indicates the player consistently chose a materialistic capture—grabbing an enemy piece—without first inserting an intermediate check that would have either gained a critical tempo or avoided leaving the capturing piece en prise. The positions overwhelmingly involve endgames with passed pawns or exposed kings, where the opponent can exploit the tempo lost by the capture (e.g., via promotion threats or counterattacks against the now-hanging piece).
analysis.why_bad: By capturing immediately instead of checking first, the player's piece (typically a rook) lands on a square where it is undefended and vulnerable to the opponent's next threat—usually a pawn promotion, a counter-check, or a simple recapture. The intermediate check would have either deflected the opponent's king, gained a tempo to reposition, or directly won back enough material to compensate. The greedy capture forfeits this tempo advantage and often converts a winning or holdable position into a lost one.

analysis.label: Playing g6/g3 to shoo away an enemy queen on h5/h4 instead of addressing the real threat via king move or queen capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player reflexively pushes g6 (or g3) to chase an aggressive enemy queen posted on h5 (or h4) in the opening, rather than solving the underlying king-safety problem. The SEE aggregate shows 74% of these moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 128/188), because the g-pawn advance weakens the king shield and opens new lines for the attacker. Meanwhile, 55% of the time the best move actually wins material (median 3.0), ranging from winning exposed pawns via king escapes to outright capturing the enemy queen (Nxh4/Nxh5 winning 9 in several cases). The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet king retreats (Kf8, Kd7, Kd8, Ke7, Kd2) or piece captures — never the g-pawn push. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific opening geometry.
analysis.why_bad: The g6/g3 push looks natural ('kick the queen') but fatally weakens the kingside pawn shield, opens the h-file or diagonal for the attacker, and fails to solve the real problem: an uncastled king stuck in the center. The queen often stays dangerous after the push (retreating to a still-active square), while the newly weakened pawns become targets. In some cases, the queen is actually hanging and can simply be captured — making the pawn push a catastrophic miss of free material.

analysis.label: King retreats passively in pawn endgame instead of advancing toward critical squares or pawns.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 40% of best moves win material (median 1.0, i.e., a pawn), while the played move is never a capture (0%) and only 12% of played moves leave own pieces hanging. All 12 top-activating positions are king-and-pawn endgames where the player moves the king backward or sideways (often toward the back rank) instead of advancing it toward enemy pawns, critical opposition squares, or the center. The best moves consistently involve the king stepping forward (Ke3, Kd3, Kf5, Kf6, Kc4, Ka6, etc.) to capture pawns, block promotion paths, or maintain active opposition, but the played moves (Kf1, Ke1, Kd1, Kc1, Kc2, Kc8, Kf7, Ke8) all retreat or drift away from the action zone.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king must be active and centralized. Retreating the king surrenders critical tempos and abandons the ability to capture enemy pawns, contest key squares, or maintain opposition. This typically converts a drawn or slowly losing position into an immediate forced mate, as the opponent's passed pawns promote unopposed (average cp_loss of 5532 centipawns reflects many positions collapsing to forced checkmate).

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture (often with a Queen or Rook) that leaves the capturing piece or another own piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 74% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a Rook-value piece), with the hung piece class heavily skewed toward majors (22 major vs 15 pawn vs 1 minor). Notably, 45% of the played moves are themselves captures, indicating the player greedily takes material but lands the capturing piece on a vulnerable square. Only 12% of best moves are captures, showing the engine preferred quiet defensive or repositioning moves over the tempting material grab. The median value of the best move's material gain (5.0 when applicable) confirms that the opponent's recapture wins back equivalent or greater material, making the greedy capture a net loss.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece (typically a Queen or Rook) lands on a square where it is undefended and can be immediately recaptured or trapped by the opponent. The player wins a pawn or minor piece but loses a major piece in return, resulting in catastrophic material loss. In some cases (positions 4, 8, 10), this directly allows forced checkmate. The player prioritizes short-term material gain over piece safety, failing to notice that the destination square is controlled by the opponent.

analysis.label: The player either underpromototes (choosing bishop/knight/rook instead of queen) or fails to promote a passed pawn when possible.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates missed material gain via pawn promotion: best move wins material in 56% of positions with a median value of 100 (queen-equivalent), best move is NEVER a capture (0%) confirming the material is gained through promotion rather than taking pieces, and best move gives check 44% of the time (consistent with promotion-with-check patterns like Q+ on the back rank). The player's own piece is never left hanging (0%), and only 22% of played moves are captures. The top 3 activating positions are all explicit underpromotions (a1=B, c8=N, b8=R instead of queening), while positions 6 and 8 show failure to advance/promote a passed pawn (playing Rc7 instead of d8=Q+ and Nf4 instead of d7). The remaining positions involve missing decisive king-safety tactics in endgames with passed pawns.
analysis.why_bad: Underpromotion to a bishop, knight, or rook throws away the massive material advantage that a queen provides. In positions 1-3, the player gains a minor piece or rook instead of the most powerful piece on the board. In positions 6 and 8, failing to promote or advance the passed pawn allows the opponent to regroup defensively, squandering a decisive advantage that was immediately convertible through promotion.

analysis.label: Player ignores a critical rook capture (usually with check) of a dangerous passed pawn about to promote, instead playing a passive quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 90% of activating positions the best move is a capture and in 80% it is a check, yet the best move 'wins' only 0 material by SEE in most cases (only 10% show material gain, median 97). This paradox is explained by the rook capturing a defended pawn (SEE ≈ 0) that is one square from promotion—the capture is strategically decisive but not materially winning per static exchange. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (only 10% captures), and only 20% leave own pieces hanging. The cp_loss averages 2160, reflecting catastrophic consequences of allowing promotion. All top boards are endgames featuring a rook needing to eliminate an advanced passed pawn (a2, b7, d2, e2, f7, g7, h7) often with check due to the enemy king's proximity on the promotion file.
analysis.why_bad: By playing passive quiet moves (king retreats, pawn pushes, irrelevant rook moves) instead of capturing the critically advanced passed pawn, the player allows immediate or near-immediate promotion to a queen, converting a defensible (or even winning) position into a hopeless loss. The tempo spent on an irrelevant move gives the opponent an unstoppable queening threat.

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing knight capture with check (Nx__+) that, while materially equal in isolation, initiates a winning combination through defender removal or follow-up tactics.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a check in 97% of cases and a capture in 100% of cases, yet only 'wins' material 6% of the time (SEE=0 in nearly all top boards). This means the knight captures a defended piece of equal value with check — an apparently even exchange — but the forced recapture removes a critical defender or creates a follow-up tactic that wins decisively. Instead, players chose quiet moves (only 19% played a capture), and 54% of the time the played move actually left their OWN minor piece hanging (median value 3.0, 81 of which were minor pieces). The pattern is remarkably consistent across all 12 top-activating boards: Nxe7+, Nxf6+, Nxf3+, or Nxe2+ — always a knight capturing a same-value piece with check, always missed in favor of a passive developing or prophylactic move.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves fail because they forfeit a forcing tactical sequence. The knight exchange with check compels the opponent to recapture (removing a key defender from its post), after which a second tactical blow (e.g., Bxf6 winning an unprotected piece, or exploiting a newly unguarded square) wins material or creates a crushing advantage. By playing passively, the player not only misses this combination but often leaves their own pieces undefended, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.

analysis.label: Player misses a pawn advance (g6/g3) that traps an aggressively-posted enemy queen on h5/h4, instead making a panicked king move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 99% of activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (a queen), yet the best move is a capture only 6% of the time and a check only 1% — meaning the winning resource is a quiet pawn push that traps the enemy queen. The played move was a capture just 12% of the time, and 57% of the time the played move left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, mostly pawns/minors). Across virtually all top-12 boards, the opponent's queen sits aggressively on h5 (or h4 from Black's side) in an early opening attack, and the simple pawn advance ...g6 (or g3) would trap and win it outright. Instead, players panic and play king retreat moves (Ke7, Kd1, Kd2, Kd7) or irrelevant captures (gxh5), failing to recognize that the 'scary' queen is actually overextended and trapped.
analysis.why_bad: The king moves (Ke7, Kd1, Kd2) do nothing to address the tactical reality: the enemy queen on h5/h4 has no escape squares after a pawn advance. By panicking and moving the king, the player throws away a won queen (9 points of material) and instead often walks into a worse position or even immediate checkmate, as evidenced by the enormous average cp_loss of 3755. The aggressive queen placement that looks threatening is actually a blunder by the opponent that must be punished immediately.

analysis.label: The player grabs an enemy piece with a tempting capture but leaves their own major piece (rook or queen) hanging, resulting in a net material or positional catastrophe.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a clear pattern: 94% of the played moves are captures, yet 85% of those moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging with a median value of 5.0 (rook/queen level). The hung-piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (313 out of 426 hangs). Meanwhile, 73% of the time a better move existed that would win material (median 3.0 pawns' worth), typically through a quieter or more precise continuation. Only 10% of best moves are captures themselves, meaning the correct approach was usually non-greedy (a retreat, a check, an intermezzo, or a positional move). The feature fires on just 0.4% of positions, isolating these specifically catastrophic 'grab-and-hang' blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The player is lured by an immediately available capture—taking a pawn, knight, or undefended piece—but fails to account for the tactical consequence: their capturing piece (or a piece it was protecting) is left en prise to a recapture, discovered attack, or back-rank tactic. The average cp_loss of 4815 (with many positions going from winning to checkmate-in-N against them) shows these are game-ending oversights where greed overrides safety.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive-looking move (often a knight jump to a central square) that leaves one of their own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move hung their own piece: 79% of positions show the player leaving their own piece en prise (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The hung-piece distribution is split between majors (53) and minors (48), with pawns less common (22). The player's move was a capture only 43% of the time, meaning many of these are quiet 'active' moves. The best move wins material in 49% of cases (often the recapture of the soon-to-be-won piece), and 24% of best moves are checks (often winning the hanging piece with tempo). The feature fires overwhelmingly in opening positions where the player makes an enticing tactical or developmental move—frequently a knight jump to d5/e5/c4/d4 or an aggressive bishop placement—without noticing that the moved piece was defending something else.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player's piece was serving a defensive role (protecting a bishop, knight, or queen). By moving it to an active-looking square or making a tempting capture, the player inadvertently removes the defender of their own piece, allowing the opponent to win material immediately. The resulting loss typically exceeds any positional or material gain from the aggressive move itself.

analysis.label: Player develops a piece instead of playing a winning d-pawn advance (d4 or d5) that exploits unresolved central pawn tension to win a pawn.
analysis.description: In 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), yet the best move is a capture only 18% of the time — indicating the winning resource is almost always a pawn advance rather than a direct take. Across the top 12 boards, the best move is consistently d4 (for White) or d5 (for Black), a central pawn thrust that exploits unresolved e4/f4 vs e5 or e4 vs f5 tension in King's Gambit / Vienna Game structures. Instead, the player makes a developing move (most commonly Bc5 or Bc4). Because the central break is missed, the player's move often leaves their own pawn hanging (55%, median value 1.0, distributed as 7 pawns and 5 minors), since the opponent can now favorably resolve the tension themselves.
analysis.why_bad: By developing a piece (typically a bishop) instead of striking with d4/d5, the player forfeits a concrete central pawn win. The d-pawn advance exploits the opponent's overextended or under-defended central pawns, and delaying it allows the opponent to consolidate or counter-strike, often netting a free pawn from the unresolved tension. The 'developing' move is strategically passive and tactically inferior because it ignores the one-move tactical window to exploit the center.

analysis.label: Player captures with their bishop on a square where it is immediately recapturable, making an unnecessary or disadvantageous trade instead of maintaining the bishop's pressure.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 100% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily dominated by minor pieces (353/500). The player's move is a capture 76% of the time, and almost exclusively a bishop capture (Bxc3, Bxd6, Bxf3, Bxf6, etc.). In 66% of cases the best move actually wins material (median 3.0), meaning the player not only makes a bad trade but also misses a superior tactical option. The best moves are frequently bishop retreats that maintain tension (Bh5, Bh4, Be6, Bd3, Bh7) or entirely different tactics (Nbd5, Nb5, Bxf7). The feature fires on only 0.3% of positions, isolating this specific pattern of impulsive bishop captures.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a defended piece and is immediately recaptured, resulting in an equal or losing trade. The player squanders the bishop's positional pressure, activity, or pin for a pointless exchange, often missing a much stronger continuation that exploits the very tension the bishop was creating. The average cp_loss of 348 reflects both the strategic loss of the bishop's influence and the missed tactical opportunities.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of taking a mandatory equal exchange, leaving their own major piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of best moves are captures (mostly equal exchanges with SEE=0, median material won only 2.0), while 62% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0). The hung pieces are overwhelmingly major pieces (70 major vs 12 minor vs 19 pawn). The played moves are almost never captures themselves (only 9%). This indicates a consistent pattern: mutual piece tension exists (typically on open files between rooks or queens), the correct response is to take the equal exchange, but the player plays an irrelevant quiet move (frequently a king move like Kg7, Kc7, Kf8, Kf7, Kg1) or a pawn push, leaving their own undefended major piece to be captured for free on the next move.
analysis.why_bad: When two pieces attack each other (e.g., rooks on the same open file, queens in mutual contact), the exchange is effectively forced—if you don't take, your opponent takes your piece for free. By playing a quiet move that ignores this tension, the player converts what would have been an equal trade into a catastrophic material loss, typically losing a whole rook (5 points) or queen (9 points) for nothing.

analysis.label: Player moves the queen when the king urgently needs to move for safety or activity, leaving own material hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 52% of the top 500 positions the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 82 cases, with 52 major and 24 minor pieces), while 51% of positions had a best move that wins material (median 1.0). The best move is a king move in every single top-12 example (Kf7, Kd6, Ke2, Kg7, Kg1, Kf2, Kb1, Kg1, Kb3, Kf1, Kh6, Kh6), yet the player consistently plays a queen move instead. Only 6% of played moves were captures, confirming the queen moves are quiet repositioning errors. The feature fires primarily in endgames (7 of 12) where king activity is paramount, and the average centipawn loss is 280, reflecting the severity of neglecting king placement.
analysis.why_bad: In endgame and late middlegame positions with exposed kings, the king must move either to escape threats (perpetual checks, back-rank issues) or to centralize for activity. By moving the queen instead, the player leaves pawns and other pieces undefended (since the king's position was the root problem), allows drawing perpetuals in winning positions, or misses that the king move itself enables winning tactics. The queen move addresses the wrong piece's needs.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (usually with Queen or Bishop) in the opening that leaves the capturing piece itself en prise or trapped.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a greedy capture that directly exposes their own piece. The SEE aggregate shows 94% of played moves are captures, and 92% of those moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0). The own-hang piece distribution (minor: 95, major: 90, pawn: 11) reflects that both Queens (hung at value 9) and Bishops (hung at value 3) are the typical pieces left en prise. Meanwhile, 67% of positions had a best move that would win material (median 3.0), meaning the player often had a safe way to win material but chose a reckless capture instead. Nearly all positions (11/12) occur in the opening phase, consistent with classic 'poisoned pawn' or bait-style traps.
analysis.why_bad: The captures look superficially attractive—winning a pawn or piece—but the capturing piece (usually the Queen or a Bishop) lands on a square where it is immediately captured back or trapped by the opponent's minor pieces, discovered attacks, or pins. The net result is a catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss 363), often losing the Queen for a pawn or minor piece. The correct approach is typically quiet development or a different tactical sequence that wins material safely.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing/regrouping move while ignoring critical pawn tension, leaving their own pawn hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 60% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 149/175 of hung pieces), while 56% of the time the best move wins material (median 1.0). Only 12% of played moves were captures, confirming the player chose a quiet move. The best move is a capture 49% of the time. This indicates a consistent pattern where the player ignores an existing pawn tension (typically a pawn being attacked) and instead plays a quiet piece move or unrelated pawn push, after which their pawn is simply taken. The best move either advances the threatened pawn to safety (e.g., b4 pushing past the attacker), captures the opponent's attacking/loose pawn, or otherwise resolves the tension favorably.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Bd7, Nd7, g6, Qc2, Ng3, Ba2, Kb7, etc.) ignore an immediate tactical demand—a pawn under attack or a pawn tension requiring resolution. By developing a piece or making a prophylactic move that doesn't address the threatened pawn, the player allows the opponent to simply capture it on the next move, losing material (typically a pawn, sometimes more when the pawn chain collapses). The best move resolves the tension first, after which the quiet improvement can be made at leisure.

analysis.label: Player makes an active-looking move (capture, check, or development) that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player blunders by leaving their own piece hanging. The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 2.0), with the hung pieces distributed across pawns (101), minor pieces (85), and major pieces (31). Meanwhile, 68% of the time a better move existed that would win material (median 3.0), and the best move is a capture 51% of the time. The played moves are often captures themselves (38%) but the WRONG capture — e.g., playing bxc3 instead of axb4, exd4 instead of axb4, fxe4 instead of axb5 — or seemingly active moves like Nf3+ (a flashy check that loses the knight), Nd6 (developing to a hanging square), or Bc3 (placing a bishop where it's undefended). The feature fires on only 0.2% of positions with an average centipawn loss of 266.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes activity, checks, or the wrong capture over piece safety. By playing a different capture or an aggressive-looking move, they leave one of their own pieces undefended on the board. The opponent can simply take the hanging piece for free, resulting in net material loss — often compounded by also missing a simple winning capture that was available.

analysis.label: The player moves their king to the wrong square in a critical endgame position, often walking away from the zone where precise king placement is required to hold a draw or convert a win.
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a catastrophic king move in the wrong direction (average cp_loss: 2017). The SEE aggregate shows this is NOT primarily a material-hanging or material-winning pattern: only 25% of best moves win material, only 4% of played moves are captures, and only 17% leave own pieces hanging (median value just 1.0, mostly pawns). Instead, the best moves are overwhelmingly quiet positional moves (only 3% are captures, 13% are checks), indicating the correct play requires precise endgame technique—opposition, pawn proximity, stalemate defense, or mating net closure—rather than tactical exploitation. The player consistently moves the king to a plausible-looking but fatally wrong square, violating specific endgame principles.
analysis.why_bad: In critical endgame positions, king placement is everything—one tempo or one wrong direction can convert a draw into a loss or throw away a win. These moves fail because they move the king away from its duty: away from supporting/blocking passed pawns (Positions 1,5,6), away from stalemate defenses (Position 2), away from opposition or key squares (Positions 3,4,10), or away from enabling tactical resources like perpetual checks or promotions (Positions 8,9,11). The king goes to a square that looks natural but violates the specific geometric or tempo requirements of the endgame.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available pawn capture (usually resolving central tension) and instead plays a quiet move, often losing material or positional advantage.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture in 94% of activating positions, with 44% directly winning material (median value 1 pawn). The player's move is almost never a capture itself (only 7%), and 41% of the time the quiet move played actually leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2, distributed across minors: 99, pawns: 94, majors: 11). Across the top 12 boards, every single best move is a pawn capture resolving tension (dxe5, dxe4, exf4, cxd5, exd5, axb5, cxd4), while the played move is invariably a quiet developing or advancing move (b6, d4, e4, d5, f3, Bf4, d3, Re1, Nd5, c4, O-O). The feature fires overwhelmingly in opening positions (9/12) with closed or tense pawn centers.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the available pawn capture, the player forfeits material (a free or favorably-exchanged pawn) and leaves central tension unresolved. This often allows the opponent to dictate the pawn structure, and in 41% of cases the quiet move played actually creates new tactical vulnerabilities by leaving the player's own pieces undefended — pieces that were previously protected by the tension now become hanging once the opponent captures first with initiative.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive Queen move (often a greedy capture or check) that leaves the Queen itself en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 74% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0, with 'major' pieces dominating at 27/38 instances), while the best move wins material 82% of the time (median value 3.0). The best move is a capture 65% of the time and a check 28%, indicating safer winning continuations existed. The player's move is a capture only 37% of the time, yet the hung value of ~9 (Queen) recurs in nearly every top position. The pattern is unmistakable: the player moves their Queen—often capturing a lesser piece or delivering a seemingly forcing check—into a square where it is immediately capturable, throwing away massive advantages including forced mates.
analysis.why_bad: The Queen moves to an undefended square where it can be captured by an enemy piece. Whether the Queen grabs material (Qxd3+, Qxf3+, Qxc2, Qxe6+, Qxb2, Qxd7) or repositions aggressively (Qg4, Qc3, Qa8+), the critical blind spot is the same: the player fails to verify that the Queen's destination square is safe. Meanwhile, the objectively best move often wins material cleanly or delivers checkmate without risking the Queen at all.

analysis.label: Player captures a central pawn with the queen (d4/d5/c3) instead of playing a stronger move that wins significantly more material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of positions have a best move winning material (median value 3.0, i.e., a full minor piece), while 54% of the played moves are captures — predominantly queen takes on d4, d5, or c3. Critically, only 16% of best moves are captures themselves, meaning the truly winning continuations are usually quiet tactical or developing moves (Bd7, g6, Nc6, e4, Rxe1+, Qh4, etc.) that exploit deeper tactical vulnerabilities. Only 24% of played moves hang the player's own piece, confirming this is primarily a 'missed winning' pattern rather than a 'hung piece' pattern. The player is seduced by grabbing an obvious central pawn with the queen while overlooking a much stronger non-obvious continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The queen pawn capture wins only ~1 pawn of material, but the position offered ~3 points of material through a more subtle tactical idea. By grabbing the pawn, the player often misplaces their queen in the center (exposing it to tempo-gaining attacks), wastes a critical tempo, or allows the opponent to consolidate. The correct moves — often quiet developing moves or retreats — set up forks, discovered attacks, or exploit the opponent's uncastled king more effectively.

analysis.label: The player missed an immediate queen checkmate (or queen check winning decisive material), playing an inferior move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 positions, with 99% winning material (median value 3.0). The best move is a capture 58% of the time—corresponding to the queen capturing a shielding pawn or piece to deliver mate. The average cp_loss of 7246 confirms these are catastrophic misses (mate-in-one blunders). The played move was a capture only 33% of the time, and 48% of the time it left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), indicating the alternative moves were often tactically careless. Across all 12 top boards, the missed best move is a queen delivering immediate checkmate (Qxg4#, Qxb7#, Qxc7#, Qxh7#, Qxb2#, Qxc2#, Qxg2#, Qe8#, Qxg7#, Qxe7#), typically capturing a pawn that served as the enemy king's last shield.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore an immediately available queen checkmate. Players are distracted by alternative checks (Qd3+, Qf5+, Nf4+, Qd4+), greedy captures (Rxd2, Qxh1+, Qxh4, Qxb6, Qxa7), or quiet moves (Ka2, Rg3, f3)—none of which end the game on the spot. By missing mate in one, they allow the opponent to survive and potentially counterattack, converting a won game into a much less decisive position.

analysis.label: A pawn capture that gives check but leaves the capturing pawn en prise, sacrificing positional or material advantage for a meaningless check.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a pawn capture with check (85% captures, 100% leaving own piece hanging with median value 1.0, piece class overwhelmingly pawn at 99/123) that squanders a better alternative. The best moves win material 48% of the time (median 2.0 value) and are rarely captures themselves (only 14%), indicating the correct plans were quiet positional moves (king maneuvers, piece improvements, passed pawn advances) rather than the flashy checking capture. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check but the resulting pawn is immediately recapturable, effectively trading a structurally important pawn or wasting tempo in a way that ruins the position.
analysis.why_bad: The pawn capture gives check but the capturing pawn lands on an undefended square. After the opponent's king simply sidesteps, they recapture the hanging pawn, and the player has exchanged pawns on unfavorable terms—destroying their own pawn structure, opening lines for the opponent, or forfeiting critical tempi needed for king activity, piece maneuvers, or passed pawn promotion. The check gains nothing because the opponent's king often reaches a better square after moving.

analysis.label: The player captures material (often with check) using a queen or rook, but the capturing piece lands on a square where it is immediately en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 100% of positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging after the move (median value 5.0), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being major pieces (197 major vs 33 minor). The player's move is itself a capture 77% of the time, and the best move wins material in 63% of cases (median 3.0), indicating there was often a safe way to gain material instead. The feature fires on tempting but fatal captures where a queen (value 9) or rook (value 5) grabs a piece or pawn but ends up undefended on its landing square, allowing the opponent to recapture and win the major piece. The best move is a check only 16% of the time and a capture only 33%, suggesting the correct play was often a quieter developing or retreating move rather than the flashy capture chosen.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing major piece (queen or rook) lands on a square that is insufficiently defended, allowing the opponent to recapture or attack it, resulting in a net material loss far exceeding what was captured. The player is lured by the immediate material gain or check but fails to evaluate whether their piece survives on the destination square.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture that leaves their own major piece (queen or rook) en prise, missing a stronger tactical alternative.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 67% of the time the player's move was itself a capture, and 67% of the time that move left the player's OWN piece hanging (median hung value: 9, i.e. a queen; piece class distribution: major pieces). Meanwhile, the best move wins material 33% of the time (median value 91 = mating sequences) and is a check 33% or a capture elsewhere 67%. This indicates the player is drawn to an obvious-looking capture — often one that even gives check — but that capture leaves the attacking piece unprotected, while a superior move (a different check or capture on another square) would have won the game outright or preserved a decisive advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These captures are superficially attractive (they win material or deliver check) but after the opponent responds, the capturing piece is left en prise with no way to save it. In Position 1, Qxe7+ grabs a piece but the queen is lost afterward, missing Qb8+ which forces mate in 7. In Position 3, Rxf3+ captures with check but the rook is subsequently taken, missing Rxa7 which stops a lethal promotion. The players prioritize immediate tactical flash over calculating the follow-up, losing their major piece in the process.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture or check instead of taking a free enemy piece, simultaneously leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: In 87% of the top 500 activating positions (median value 3.0 = minor piece), the best move wins an undefended enemy piece via a simple capture (79% of best moves are captures). Instead, the player chooses a different capture (75% of played moves are captures) — often a flashy check, a sacrifice, or a grab on a different square — and in 93% of cases this move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, split roughly evenly between majors and minors: 75 major, 71 minor, 9 pawn). The pattern is consistently: an enemy piece is free to take, but the player prioritizes a different tactical operation (Bxf7+, Rxd8+, Nxc2+, Bxh7+, etc.) which both misses the free material and exposes their own pieces.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player selects an inferior tactical motif (a check, a different capture, or an apparently active move) over a clean material win. The alternative move typically moves a piece away from a critical defensive role or places it on a square where it becomes en prise, resulting in a net material loss. The simple recapture or free capture was worth more than the flashy line the player chose.

analysis.label: In positions where the opponent has multiple queens (from promotion), the player fails to capture one of the available enemy queens.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates a missed-winning-capture pattern: 65% of best moves win material with a median value of 9 (queen), 80% of best moves are captures, yet only 20% of actually played moves are captures. Every top-activating board features an opponent with TWO queens (from pawn promotion), and the critical best move is to capture one of those queens (Qxh8, Qxc8, Rxc1, Qxc2, Qxg6, Raxc1, Bxh1, Rxd8, etc.). The 50% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns) is a secondary effect of the weak quiet moves chosen, not the primary mistake. The astronomical average cp_loss of 6297 reflects that ignoring a capturable queen in a multi-queen position almost always allows immediate checkmate.
analysis.why_bad: When the opponent has two queens, their coordinated checking power creates unavoidable mating nets. Capturing one queen—whether it wins material outright (rook takes undefended queen) or simply exchanges—is virtually always the top priority because it halves the opponent's mating potential. By playing quiet moves instead, the player allows the dual-queen coordination to deliver forced checkmate within just a few moves.

analysis.label: Knight captures a seemingly free central pawn (usually e4) in the opening, but this greedy capture is tactically refuted while quiet development was superior.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a knight captures a central pawn (89% of played moves are captures, almost exclusively Nxe4/Nxe5/Nxd5) in the opening, but this material grab is premature or poisoned. The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material in 82% of cases (median value: 1 pawn), yet only 7% of best moves are captures — meaning the correct approach was a quiet developing move (Be7, O-O, Nc6, g6, etc.) that would maintain or eventually win material through superior coordination. The knight capture leaves the player's own pieces hanging 43% of the time (predominantly pawns at 80/123 cases). The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, targeting a specific opening trap pattern where the central pawn appears undefended but capturing it leads to tactical punishment due to underdevelopment or exposed king position.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures a central pawn that appears free but is actually a tactical trap or 'poisoned pawn.' After Nxe4/e5, the knight is exposed in the center and the opponent gains tempo attacking it, often exploiting the fact that the capturing side's king remains uncastled (Black's king on e8 in most examples). The correct moves (O-O, Be7, Nc6, etc.) complete development first, maintaining or improving the position, while the premature capture squanders coordination for a pawn that cannot be safely held.

analysis.label: Player gives a rook check that leaves the rook hanging and undefended, losing it for nothing.
analysis.description: In 98% of the top 500 activating positions, the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the hung piece class being overwhelmingly 'major' (110 of 112 cases). All 12 top-activating moves are rook moves delivering check (Rb8+, Re8+, Rd8+, Rxd8+, Rc1+, Rd1+, Rxe1+). The best moves are almost never checks themselves (only 5%), instead being quiet improvements like Rad1, c3, Rd7, Rc6, Rd2, or captures/tactics elsewhere. The player is drawn to a superficially aggressive rook check, but the rook lands on a square where it is en prise after the king moves, resulting in a full rook loss. The median cp_loss of 285 centipawns matches losing an uncompensated exchange or full rook.
analysis.why_bad: These rook checks are tactically hollow — the king simply sidesteps or a piece captures the rook on the checking square. The check gains no tempo, wins no material, and creates no mating threats. After the king moves, the rook is undefended and captured, losing approximately 5 points of material. The player is seduced by the principle of 'always check, it might be mate' but fails to verify that the rook survives after delivering the check.

analysis.label: Player makes a greedy capture with a non-queen piece while their own queen is under attack, leaving the queen en prise.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player's queen is attacked and the correct response is to use the queen (often to capture an enemy piece worth ~3 points, median), but instead the player makes a different capture with another piece, leaving their own queen hanging. The SEE aggregate shows: 90% of played moves are captures, yet 98% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 6.0, i.e., a queen). The hung-piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (46 major vs 4 minor). Meanwhile, 94% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0), and 69% of best moves are captures—frequently Queen captures (Qxf6, Qxf3, Qxe2, Qxb6, Qxe7, etc.) that simultaneously save the queen and win material.
analysis.why_bad: The player captures a piece with a bishop, knight, pawn, or rook, but ignores the fact that their own queen is under attack. The opponent simply takes the hanging queen on the next move, netting approximately 6-9 points of material. The correct move was almost always to use the queen itself to capture an enemy piece, which both saves the queen from the threat and wins material.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet, aimless move (often a king move) that leaves their own piece undefended while ignoring tactical opportunities.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 65% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed as 50 pawns, 20 minors, 18 majors), while 51% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0). Only 15% of played moves are captures, and best moves are captures 39% of the time. This combination indicates the player ignores both offensive opportunities and defensive obligations by making passive, purposeless quiet moves. King moves are disproportionately represented (5 of 12 top boards: Kf3, Kg1, Ke6, Kf5, Kh2), and the average centipawn loss is an enormous 907, confirming catastrophic blunders rather than subtle inaccuracies.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address neither the tactical demands of the position (available captures winning material) nor the safety of the player's own pieces. By playing a quiet, often retreating move—especially aimless king moves—the player simultaneously misses winning enemy material and exposes their own pieces to capture, resulting in massive material or positional losses.

analysis.label: Player missed a check (usually checkmate or a check winning massive material) and instead played a different move, often a capture elsewhere.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 95% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 95% of cases that check wins material (median value won: 91, indicating checkmate in the majority of positions). The player's actual move was a capture only 42% of the time and a quiet move otherwise, meaning the player was frequently distracted by material grabs or positional moves while a lethal check—often an immediate mate—was available. Only 32% of positions involved the player hanging their own piece, confirming this is fundamentally about missing an offensive tactical blow rather than a defensive blunder. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating these are rare, dramatic oversights in positions with concrete forced wins via check.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a forcing check that either delivers immediate checkmate or wins decisive material through a tactical sequence. By playing a capture or quiet move instead, the player allows the opponent to survive (often escaping a mating net) and squanders a completely winning position. The checks work because they exploit exposed kings, back-rank weaknesses, or undefended squares adjacent to the king, forcing the game to end immediately.

analysis.label: The player makes a bad king move, missing winning tactics and/or leaving their own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on king moves that are serious mistakes. The SEE aggregate shows that 66% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0), indicating the player missed strong tactical continuations (captures, checks, or mating sequences) by moving their king instead. Additionally, 57% of the played king moves left the player's own pieces hanging (median value 1.0), with the distribution heavily weighted toward pawns (189), followed by minor pieces (54) and major pieces (44). The best move is a check 10% of the time and a capture 14% of the time. All 12 top-activating positions involve king moves (Kxf2, Kxe5, Kc3, Kg5, Kd6, etc.), predominantly in middlegame positions (9/12) where the king walks to exposed squares rather than remaining safe while executing available tactics. The average cp_loss of 3398 reflects many missed checkmates.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves fail because they waste a critical tempo on an unnecessary or counterproductive king relocation—often walking the king to a more exposed square—while ignoring forcing moves (captures winning material, checks leading to mate, or defensive moves protecting hanging pieces). The king move frequently exposes pawns and pieces that were previously shielded by the king's position, compounding the error.

analysis.label: Player gives a futile check (usually with a rook) that leaves their own major piece hanging instead of playing a constructive quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 60% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 4.0, corresponding to a rook), with the hung-piece distribution dominated by major pieces (161/300). Meanwhile, the best move is a check only 3% of the time, confirming that the checks played are unjustified. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames where the player delivered a check — every single played move ends in '+' — yet the best moves (Re1, Rh2, Ra5, Kd3, Bc6, Kf3, Rxg3, a5, Rf3, Ke5) are quiet constructive moves. The player's move was a capture only 7% of the time, meaning these checks are not tactical sequences but aimless forcing moves. The average cp_loss of 2459 reflects how catastrophic these checks are.
analysis.why_bad: The checks accomplish nothing — they typically drive the enemy king to a safer or equally good square while leaving the checking piece (usually a rook) undefended and capturable on the next move. Instead of addressing the position's real needs (defense, blockade, pawn restraint, king centralization), the player reflexively gives check, squandering their most valuable remaining piece for no compensation.

analysis.label: Player plays an active-looking move that leaves their own major piece hanging, when a simple winning capture (often with check) was available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly indicates this is a 'hung own piece' pattern: 84% of the time the player's move left their own piece en prise (median value 5.0, i.e. rook-class), with the piece distribution skewing heavily toward major pieces (61 major, 18 minor, 20 pawn). Meanwhile, the best move was a capture 84% of the time (often winning material with median value 9.0, i.e. queen-level) and was a check 56% of the time. Only 25% of the played moves were captures—most were quiet or aggressive-looking moves (king moves, pawn pushes, checks with the wrong piece) that failed to address the most forcing continuation. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a specific scenario where a decisive capture exists but the player instead plays a move that catastrophically exposes their own material.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because instead of playing the strongest forcing move (typically a winning capture with or without check that eliminates threats and wins material), the player chooses an inferior continuation—often an aggressive-looking check, attack, or repositioning move—that leaves a major piece (queen or rook) completely undefended. The opponent then simply captures the hanging piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss ~3536).

analysis.label: The player delivers a tempting Queen check that leaves the Queen itself hanging and capturable after the opponent escapes check.
analysis.description: In 92% of the top 500 activating positions, the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., the Queen), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly 'major' (162 of 177 classified instances). Every top-12 move is a Queen check (Qb1+, Qd8+, Qe4+, etc.), and in each case the Queen lands on a square where it is en prise once the opponent steps out of check or blocks. The best move wins material 82% of the time (median value 9.0), and is itself a check only 41% of the time—meaning the correct continuation was often a non-check move that preserved the Queen while maintaining the advantage. The player's move was a capture only 25% of the time, confirming most of these are quiet checks to bad squares rather than sensible exchanges.
analysis.why_bad: These Queen checks are superficially attractive ('patzer sees a check, gives a check') but place the Queen on a square with no safe retreat once the opponent sidesteps the check. The opponent simply moves their king or interposes a piece, then captures the undefended Queen on the next move. In many cases the player had a winning position—sometimes even a forced mate—but the impulsive check squanders the entire advantage by losing the Queen for nothing.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture that leaves their own major piece hanging, missing a stronger forcing move (often a check or intermediate tactic) that would have won material cleanly.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player grabs material with a capture (98% of played moves are captures) but in doing so leaves their own piece en prise (93% of the time, median value 5.0 = rook, with major pieces accounting for 300/464 hung pieces). The best move was available to win material (87%, median value 6.0) and was frequently a check (39%) or other forcing intermediate move (only 13% were captures themselves). The average cp_loss of ~5050 reflects that these greedy captures often result in immediate tactical refutations—back-rank mates, forks, or discovered attacks—that far outweigh the captured material. The own-hang distribution (300 major, 147 minor, 17 pawn) confirms that it is typically a rook or queen left exposed after the ill-advised capture.
analysis.why_bad: The captures fail because they ignore the opponent's tactical resources. By taking material without first inserting a forcing move (check, intermediate threat, or deflection), the player leaves their own major piece undefended or walks into a devastating counter-tactic. In many cases (positions 7, 10, 2), the capture walks into back-rank mate; in others (positions 6, 9, 11, 12), a powerful intermediate check would have won far more material. The player is drawn to the immediate material gain but misses that their capture creates a worse vulnerability than the piece it wins.

analysis.label: The player plays a quiet developing or prophylactic move, missing a devastating knight fork that wins the queen or equivalent major material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 98% of positions have a best move winning material with a median value of 6.0 pawns—perfectly matching a knight fork winning a queen (value 9) where the knight can be recaptured (net 9-3=6). Only 9% of played moves are captures and only 21% of best moves are captures, confirming these are knight jumps to fork squares rather than simple recaptures. The best move is a check in 0% of cases, meaning these are pure positional/tactical forks rather than discovered checks. In 11 of 12 top-activating positions, the best move is a knight leap (Nd4, Nd5, Ne4, Ne5, Na5, Nxh5) exploiting an exposed queen alongside another undefended piece—typically White's misplaced queen on f3 alongside a loose bishop. The played moves (h6, e6, d6, Bc5, Bg7) are routine quiet moves that completely overlook the tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (h6, d6, e6, Bc5, Bg7) waste a critical tempo where a knight fork would win the queen or a full piece. Instead of exploiting the opponent's geometric vulnerability—an exposed queen and a second undefended piece on the same knight-jump pattern—the player makes a routine move that allows the opponent to reposition and eliminate the tactical opportunity, squandering a decisive advantage (average 251cp loss).

analysis.label: Player gives a pointless queen check that leaves their own pieces (especially the queen) hanging after the king escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 72% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with major pieces being the most frequent casualty (74 of 148 total hung pieces). Every single top-12 activating move is a queen check, yet only 5% of best moves are checks—showing the check is almost never the right idea. The best move wins material 56% of the time (median 3.0), meaning the player consistently passes up genuine winning opportunities for a flashy but hollow check. The player's move is a capture only 13% of the time, confirming these are mostly quiet queen repositions that happen to give check but land the queen on a tactically vulnerable square.
analysis.why_bad: A queen check gives the opponent a forced reply (move the king or interpose), but once the king steps away, the queen is often stranded on an exposed square with no follow-up threat, leaving it or other now-undefended pieces en prise.
