The check creates an illusion of initiative while actually wasting a tempo and misplacing the queen, allowing the opponent to consolidate or win material on the next move.

analysis.label: Aggressive knight lunges (Nh5/Nh4) or queen sorties (Qa5/Qa4) in the opening that leave the player's own minor piece—usually a bishop—undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 78% of positions have the player's own piece left hanging after the move (median value 3.0), with the hung piece class distribution overwhelmingly being minor pieces (85 out of 102 cases). Only 28% of the played moves are captures, and the feature fires on premature aggressive moves rather than missed winning opportunities. The best moves are typically quiet bishop developments (Be6, Be3) or safe retreats (Na6, Na3) that maintain coordination. The pattern is concentrated in the opening phase (8/12 boards), where players sacrifice positional safety for flashy knight edge-maneuvers or early queen activity, inadvertently leaving a bishop en prise to simple tactics.
analysis.why_bad: Moving the knight to h5/h4 (or deploying the queen to a5/a4) breaks the coordination that was protecting a bishop elsewhere on the board. The knight that moved may have been shielding the bishop from attack, or the tempo spent on the aggressive move allows the opponent to exploit the undefended bishop with a simple capture or fork. The resulting material loss (~3 pawns, i.e., a full minor piece) far outweighs any speculative attacking chances from the rim knight or offside queen.

analysis.label: A knight greedily captures a central or advanced pawn but lands on a square where it is left undefended and hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a knight captures a tempting pawn (84% of moves are captures) but the knight ends up en prise on the landing square (87% of played moves leave own piece hanging, median value 3.0 = minor piece, with 31 of 33 hung pieces being minors). The best moves are typically quiet pawn levers or retreats (only 16% are captures, only 3% are checks) that win a pawn's worth of material more safely (71% best-move-wins-material, median 1.0). The feature activates exclusively in openings where an advanced/undefended pawn appears free but the knight becomes stranded after taking it.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures a pawn worth 1 point but becomes undefended on its new square, allowing the opponent to win back the knight (worth 3 points) with a simple recapture or fork, resulting in a net loss of approximately 2 points of material. A quiet pawn move (like ...c6, ...e6, ...f6, or ...d5) would undermine the opponent's structure or win the pawn without exposing the knight to danger.

analysis.label: Player missed a devastating capture that simultaneously gives check, allowing free material gain because the opponent must address the check before recapturing.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 90% of best moves are checks and 92% are captures, meaning the overwhelming pattern (~90%) is a capturing check. The SEE values for the best move consistently show 'wins 0' because the captured piece is nominally defended — but static exchange evaluation ignores that check forces the opponent to address king safety before recapturing, making the material gain effectively free. Only 11% register as 'winning material' in SEE terms precisely because SEE doesn't account for check tempo. The player's move left their own piece hanging 61% of the time (median value 3.0, distributed across major/pawn/minor pieces), a secondary consequence of playing an aimless move instead of the decisive tactic. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, reflecting how specific this tactical motif is.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Rd3, Re3, Re1, Rab1, Qd8, Rad1, etc.) are quiet developing or repositioning moves that completely miss that an enemy piece can be captured with check. Because check forces the opponent to move their king or block, they cannot recapture the taken piece on the next move, making what SEE evaluates as an 'even exchange' actually a free piece. The average cp_loss of 1716 confirms these are game-deciding blunders.

analysis.label: Player makes a panicked king move or greedy capture that leaves their own piece en prise, missing a move that wins enemy material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 70% of the top 500 activating positions the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns:105, majors:99, minors:80), while simultaneously 70% of positions had a best move that won enemy material (median 3.0). The player's move was a capture only 36% of the time, meaning the majority of blunders are quiet moves—particularly king moves (Ke1, Kh7, Ke8, Ka5, Ke3, Kf2 appear in the top 12)—that inadvertently expose a piece. The best move is a capture 36% of the time and a check 16%, indicating the correct response often involved taking enemy material or delivering check rather than making the passive/panicked move chosen. The average centipawn loss of 4927 confirms these are catastrophic blunders, many converting winning or equal positions into forced mates.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player either panics with a king move that walks away from defending a critical piece, or greedily captures the wrong target while leaving a higher-value piece unprotected. In positions with exposed kings and tactical tension, the player ignores the concrete tactical requirement (capturing an enemy piece, delivering check, or maintaining piece coordination) and instead makes a move that drops material or walks into a mating net.

analysis.label: Player missed a winning bishop check that would have won significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check in 98% of activating positions and wins material in 97% (median SEE value won: 97 centipawns). Examining the top 12 boards reveals that 11 of 12 feature a bishop delivering the critical check (Bc4+, Bc5+, Bb7+, Bf4+, Bh6+, Bh3+). Players instead chose quiet or irrelevant moves (only 29% captures), with 54% of played moves leaving their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The best move is a capture in only 22% of cases, confirming the bishop check is typically a non-capturing move that exploits an open diagonal to the king, winning material indirectly through the forced king displacement. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions, indicating a precise tactical motif.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a forcing bishop check along an open diagonal that would attack the king while simultaneously threatening or winning other pieces (often via fork, discovered attack, or trapping a piece after the king is forced to move). By playing non-forcing moves, the player squanders a decisive tactical blow and often leaves their own material vulnerable.

analysis.label: In pawn endgames, the king captures an enemy pawn but abandons defense of its own pawns, leaving them hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 60% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being overwhelmingly pawns (51 of 57 instances). Meanwhile, 28% of the played moves were themselves captures and only 45% of best moves won material (median 1.0), confirming the pattern is not about missing a winning capture but about making a greedy capture that costs more than it gains. All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and 9 of 12 moves are king captures of enemy pawns (Kxh6, Kxe4, Kxe6, Kxh7, Kxg2, Kxh4, Kxa2). The correct moves are typically positional king maneuvers (Kh5, Kf4, Kf6, Kc4, Kg6) or strategic advances (b4, Na1, Kd6) that maintain the king's defensive duties.
analysis.why_bad: By moving the king to capture a seemingly free enemy pawn, the player repositions the king away from defending their own pawns. In pawn endgames where king proximity is everything, this leaves the player's own pawns en prise or allows the opponent's king to invade decisively. The material gain of one pawn is offset by losing a pawn in return (or worse, losing critical tempo/position), often converting a draw into a loss or a win into a draw.

analysis.label: The player missed a classical bishop sacrifice on f7 (or f2) with check, exploiting the opponent's uncastled king in the opening.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the best move is a bishop sacrifice on the f-pawn with check (Bxf7+ or Bxf2+), but the player instead makes a quiet developing or prophylactic move. The SEE aggregate is definitive: the best move is a check in 100% of positions and a capture in 73%, yet the played move was a capture only 16% of the time. The sacrifice registers as SEE = 0 (materially neutral statically since the bishop is recaptured), but yields massive dynamic advantages against the exposed king. By missing the tactic, the player's quiet move often leaves their own piece hanging (50% of cases, median value 2.0, distributed across pawns: 117, minors: 77, majors: 58), as the lost tempo allows the opponent to seize the initiative. The feature fires on only 0.4% of positions, reflecting the specificity of this classical tactical motif.
analysis.why_bad: Moves like h3, O-O, Be2, Nc3, and Bd7 squander the critical moment to exploit f7/f2 with a checking sacrifice. The Bxf7+ (or Bxf2+) forces the king off its square, destroys castling rights, and typically leads to a winning attack or material recovery with interest. The quiet alternatives lose the window as the opponent consolidates, castles, or gains counterplay—turning a decisive advantage (avg cp_loss: 270) into an equal or lost position.

analysis.label: Player missed a checking move (usually a queen fork) that would have won the opponent's queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an unmistakable pattern: the best move is a check in 100% of cases, and it wins material 98% of the time with a median value of 91 (queen-scale). Only 23% of these best moves are captures, meaning 77% are non-capturing checks that win material through a fork or discovered attack geometry. The player instead chose quiet moves (79% non-captures) with an average cp_loss of 240. The best moves are predominantly queen checks (Qb6+, Qd4+, Qg5+, Qb3+, Qc5+) or bishop checks (Bc4+) that simultaneously attack the opponent's queen—a classic fork pattern. The 46% own-hang rate on played moves (median value 3) is secondary collateral from the suboptimal move chosen, not the core mistake pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an available check that forks the king and the opponent's queen. By playing a quiet developing or positional move instead, the player forfeits winning roughly a queen's worth of material (median ~9 pawns). The opponent escapes the tactical vulnerability, and the resulting position swings dramatically (avg 240cp loss), often turning winning or equal positions into losing ones.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive knight centralization instead of executing a critical bishop-takes-knight exchange, leaving pieces vulnerable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture 98% of the time (almost always BxN for an equal exchange, winning 0 material per SEE), while the played move is quiet (only 18% are captures). After the played move, 48% of cases leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 74 minors, 29 pawns, 14 majors). The top boards show a strikingly consistent pattern: in every case the best move is a bishop capturing a knight (Bxf6, Bxf3, Bxc6, or Bxc3), and the player instead makes a knight jump (Nd5, Nd4, Ne4, Ng6) or other quiet developing move. The positions arise predominantly in the opening (8/12) with active bishops already placed on attacking diagonals pinning or pressuring enemy knights.
analysis.why_bad: The knight centralization ignores a critical positional/tactical obligation to resolve bishop-knight tension. By not executing the BxN exchange (which, while materially equal, is positionally necessary), the player's knight move often leaves their own bishop or other minor piece undefended, or creates tactical vulnerabilities the opponent exploits. The opponent can then win material or gain a decisive positional advantage because the unresolved pin/tension works against the player who failed to capture.

analysis.label: King moves to the wrong square in a pawn endgame, losing opposition, key squares, or leaving pawns undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows this feature fires in endgame positions where the player's king (or pawn) move is suboptimal. The 'own piece hanging' rate is 30% (median value 1.0, with 63 pawns, 8 minors, 6 majors), indicating that the king frequently walks away from pawn defense. The 'best wins material' rate of 20% (median 1.0) suggests the correct king placement would sometimes win an enemy pawn. Only 6% of played moves are captures and only 8% of best moves are captures, confirming these are quiet positional/king-maneuver decisions rather than tactical exchanges. All 12 top-activating positions are pure pawn endgames where the king chooses the wrong destination square—losing opposition, failing to blockade a passed pawn, or abandoning its own pawns.
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, precise king placement determines the outcome. These moves send the king to the wrong square—losing the opposition (critical tempo relationship between kings), abandoning key defensive squares that blockade enemy passed pawns, or moving away from own pawns that then become indefensible. Examples include Kb5 instead of Kb3 (losing a drawn position by 681cp), Kg4 instead of Kg6 (turning a draw into a loss at 692cp), and Kc2 instead of Kb4 (allowing immediate promotion, cp_loss 8917).

analysis.label: Player fails to use the King to capture a hanging enemy piece in the endgame, choosing a passive or diversionary piece move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 76% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 3.0), yet only 17% of the played moves are captures—indicating the player consistently misses a winning capture. The best move is a capture in 34% of cases and a check in 22%, with the feature firing exclusively on endgames. The dominant pattern across the top boards shows an enemy rook (or piece) left hanging, capturable by the King (Kxh2, Kxg6), often in positions where a nearby enemy pawn threatens promotion. The player incorrectly fears the promotion threat and plays a rook maneuver or other quiet move instead of simply taking the hanging piece with the King, after which any promotion is immediately recaptured.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Rf3, Ra1+, Rg8, Rg3+, Re6, etc.) fail because they ignore the immediately winning King capture of an undefended piece. The player overestimates the danger of a nearby pawn promotion or doesn't realize the King itself is the right piece to solve the tactical problem. After Kxh2 (or Kxg6), any resulting pawn promotion is harmless because the King recaptures, leaving the player up decisive material (typically a full rook). The alternative moves either draw or even lose the game.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy queen attacking their undefended rook, leaving the rook hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the hung piece being a major piece in 61/84 cases. The best move wins material 82% of the time with median value 9.0 (queen-level), consistent with best moves that either trade queens or deflect the enemy queen's attack on the rook. In virtually every top-activating position, an enemy queen has deeply infiltrated (typically to g2 threatening h1, g7 threatening h8, or b2 threatening a1) and the player makes a developing or other non-urgent move that completely ignores this concrete threat to their corner rook. The best moves (Qf3, Qf6, Qc3, Bf3, Bf6) all directly confront or block the invading queen.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical threat: the enemy queen is one move away from capturing an undefended rook worth 5 points of material. By playing quiet developing moves (d4, Nge2, f4, Bc4, Ke7, etc.) instead of addressing the queen's attack on the rook—via queen trade, interposition, or deflection—the player simply donates a rook, turning what might be a manageable disadvantage into a lost position.

analysis.label: Player ignores a strong tactical move (often a knight/piece deployment) that would win significant material, instead playing a passive move that also leaves own material undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 79% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 5.0 (a full piece or more), yet the played move was a capture only 16% of the time—indicating overwhelmingly quiet, passive choices over decisive tactical blows. Additionally, 48% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0), distributed across pawns (25), minors (24), and majors (6). The best moves across the top boards feature knight and bishop deployments to powerful squares (Nf6, Ne5, Nc3, Ne4, Bc4, Nxd5) and central breaks (d4, dxe5), showing that strong piece activity creating multiple threats was consistently available. The 10% check rate and 33% capture rate for best moves confirm that winning tactics often come via positional piece placements rather than simple captures.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves are quiet pawn pushes or minor repositioning (g4, c6, c5, c4, a4, f6) that ignore available tactical resources winning a full piece or more. By choosing passive play over the critical tactical blow, the player forfeits massive material (median 5 pawns of advantage) and frequently also leaves their own pawns or minor pieces undefended, compounding a game-losing error (avg cp_loss 919).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet/passive move (often a King move) that leaves their own piece undefended, missing a strong tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 78% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, spread across minor pieces 18, pawns 16, and major pieces 12), while only 14% of played moves were captures. Meanwhile, 59% of the time the best move won material (median 3.0), with 54% being captures and 29% being checks. This indicates the player consistently chose passive, non-tactical moves—frequently King moves (Kh1, Kg2, Kg3, Kg6, Ke2 appear in the top 12)—that simultaneously abandoned the defense of their own pieces while ignoring forcing tactical shots. The enormous average cp_loss of 2070 reflects this double error: failing to play the winning tactic AND leaving material en prise.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player moves a piece (often the King) away from its defensive duties, leaving another piece unprotected and capturable. Simultaneously, the player misses a strong tactical resource—a check, capture, or promotion—that would have won material or forced a decisive advantage. The passive move thus converts a winning or equal position into a lost one by gifting the opponent free material.

analysis.label: Player ignores h3 or h6 pawn push that would win an enemy piece aggressively placed on g4/g5.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 98% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 2), yet only 2% of those best moves are captures and 0% are checks—indicating the winning move is a quiet pawn push that traps or kicks a piece. Examining the top boards reveals the best move is overwhelmingly h3 (attacking a piece on g4) or h6 (attacking a piece on g5): positions 1, 4, 9, 10, 11 feature h3 against Bg4 or Ng4, and positions 3, 7, 12 feature h6 against Ng5 or Bg5. The player's move left their own piece hanging 53% of the time (median value 1, predominantly pawns at 83 occurrences), suggesting they chose committal or aggressive-looking moves that also created new weaknesses rather than first addressing the tactical opportunity. The played moves are mostly quiet (only 22% captures), confirming the player simply overlooked the pawn kick.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the simple h-pawn push, the player allows the opponent's aggressively-placed minor piece (typically a bishop on g4 or knight on g5) to remain active and unchallenged. The h3/h6 pawn kick would either trap the piece outright (e.g., h3 followed by g4 caging a bishop) or force it into a disadvantageous retreat, netting roughly a minor piece. Instead, the player pursues other plans, often creating weaknesses of their own and surrendering a large evaluation swing.

analysis.label: Player captures material with a major piece (often giving check) but leaves that piece hanging on the destination square, typically squandering a winning advantage.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of the time the played move is a capture, and 96% of the time the player's move leaves their OWN piece hanging (median value 5, i.e., a rook). The hung piece class is overwhelmingly major pieces (24 major vs 2 minor out of 26 cases). Meanwhile, only 7% of the best moves are captures, and 22% are checks—indicating the best move was usually a quiet move or a non-capturing check rather than the greedy material grab. The feature fires in endgames where the player already holds a significant advantage but throws it away by capturing a pawn, minor piece, or opponent's rook with their own Queen or Rook, landing on a square where the major piece is immediately en prise.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing major piece lands on a square where it is undefended and can be immediately recaptured or won by the opponent. In most cases the player was already winning decisively, and the tempting capture-with-check offers only marginal or no material gain while allowing the opponent to win back the major piece, collapsing the position to equality or even turning a won game into a draw. The quiet alternatives (retreats, pawn pushes, positional checks) maintain the full advantage without exposing the valuable piece.

analysis.label: The player fails to capture an undefended enemy queen (or equivalent high-value piece) that is freely available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 98% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 8.0 (queen-level), and 99% of best moves are captures, yet only 12% of played moves are captures. This means in the overwhelming majority of cases, the player ignores a freely capturable enemy piece—almost always the queen—and plays a quiet developing or repositioning move instead. The 56% own-hung rate (median 3.0) is a secondary consequence: by failing to simplify via the free capture, the player's quiet move often leaves their own piece en prise as well. Across the top 12 boards, 10 out of 12 feature an enemy queen sitting completely undefended (on squares like g5, d8, h6, b3, d7, h6, a6) that can be taken with a straightforward one-move capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a simple one-move capture of an undefended enemy queen (or major piece), instead making quiet moves like king walks, pawn pushes, or rook repositions that accomplish little while forfeiting enormous material. The enemy's highest-value piece is left unmolested, squandering a decisive advantage or converting a winning position into a losing one.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing move instead of making a critical pawn capture to resolve central tension.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 96% of cases, yet these captures only win material 15% of the time (median 1.0 pawn), indicating the correct moves are mostly equal pawn exchanges (SEE = 0) — resolving tension rather than winning pieces. The played move is almost never a capture (only 8%), confirming the player consistently ignores the pawn tension. By failing to capture, the player leaves their own pieces hanging 42% of the time (median value 1.0), with the distribution heavily weighted toward pawns (121) and minor pieces (76). All 12 top-activating boards show the same structure: the best move is a pawn capture (dxe4, hxg5, dxe5, cxd4, exd5, exf4, dxc4, etc.) while the played move is a quiet piece maneuver or development move (g5, Nc5, Qe2, c3, O-O, Bb3, Bb2, Qg4, Bc8).
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the critical pawn capture, the player allows the opponent to maintain or strengthen central tension, which either directly hangs a piece/pawn (now unprotected because the pawn structure shifted), or gives the opponent a free tempo to exploit the unresolved tension tactically. The quiet move wastes a critical moment where the concrete pawn exchange was necessary to maintain structural integrity and piece safety.

analysis.label: Player overlooks a strong checking move (often winning material) and instead plays a move that leaves their own piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, spread across minor/major/pawn pieces), while the best move was a check 47% of the time and a capture 70% of the time. In the top 12 positions, 10 out of 12 feature a missed check as the best move (Rb1+, Bxc2+, Nf4+, Qxc3+, Rxc2+, Rg8+, etc.), many of which win decisive material or force promotion. Instead of playing these forcing tactical blows, the player chose passive, greedy, or misdirected moves (quiet retreats, wrong captures, pawn pushes) that left their own pieces undefended. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, indicating a specific tactical pattern where a powerful check is available but overlooked in favor of a self-damaging alternative.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing check that would either win material outright, deflect a defender, or create an unstoppable threat (like promotion). By playing a non-forcing move instead, the player gives the opponent tempo to exploit the newly-hanging piece, often swinging the evaluation by hundreds of centipawns (avg cp_loss 407). The check would have seized the initiative; the played move surrenders it while also leaving material en prise.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (often a capture) that leaves their own piece undefended and en prise, while a superior tactical continuation was available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the 'hung own piece' pattern: 71% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minor pieces 17, major pieces 15, and pawns 3). Simultaneously, 71% of best moves won material (median 3.0), showing a clean tactical alternative existed. The played move was itself a capture 55% of the time, suggesting players frequently grab material greedily while overlooking that their own piece becomes undefended. The best move was a check only 14% and a capture only 26% of the time, indicating the superior alternatives were often quiet consolidating or repositioning moves rather than obvious tactical strikes. The feature fires on 0.0% of positions, isolating these rare but catastrophic blunders (avg cp_loss: 3228).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player focuses on an immediate gain (capturing a piece, giving check, or repositioning) without noticing that the moved piece—or another piece it was protecting—is left completely undefended. The opponent simply captures the hanging piece on the next move, often leading to decisive material loss or immediate checkmate. The correct alternatives would either win material cleanly without leaving anything en prise, or consolidate existing advantages safely.

analysis.label: Player misses a check (often winning a queen or forcing mate) in endgame positions with exposed kings, instead playing an inferior quiet move, wrong check, or suboptimal capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 71% of best moves are checks and 71% win material (median value 91, corresponding to queen-value gains), confirming the core pattern is a missed check that wins decisive material or forces mate. Only 21% of best moves are captures, showing the winning mechanism is predominantly a check leading to material gain rather than a direct recapture. The played moves were captures only 21% of the time, and only 29% left own pieces hanging (median value just 1, i.e., a pawn)—meaning the mistake is overwhelmingly about failing to find the winning check rather than hanging material. Positions are mostly endgames (8/12) with exposed kings on both sides, creating geometric opportunities for decisive checks that go unexploited. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 5050 reflects missed forced mates and missed queen wins.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because a check exists that would win a queen-value piece or force checkmate due to the exposed enemy king geometry. Players instead play aimless or wrong checks (Qb4+, Qd5+, Qb7+) that allow the opponent to escape, make greedy captures (Qxf2+, Qxb6, Kxf8) that squander the decisive tactical blow, or play passive quiet moves (Qf6, g3, Nf3, Qd6) that let the opponent consolidate. The key missed resource is typically a queen or minor piece check exploiting the opponent's king exposure on an open file, diagonal, or rank.

analysis.label: Player gives a flashy but counterproductive check instead of simply capturing hanging enemy material, leaving their own piece undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a tempting check (11/12 top moves are checks) rather than a straightforward material-winning capture. The SEE aggregate shows the best move was a capture 71% of the time (winning material 73%, median value 3.0 pawns), but the played move left the player's own piece hanging 80% of the time (median value 4.0 pawns, distributed across majors 38, minors 19, pawns 15). Only 14% of played moves were captures themselves. The player plays an aggressive-looking check that either displaces their piece to a vulnerable square or removes a defender, allowing the opponent to recapture or win a now-unprotected piece. The enormous average cp_loss of 3338 reflects that these checks often squander forced mates or decisive advantages.
analysis.why_bad: The checks are tactically shallow — they force the opponent's king to move but create no lasting threat, while the checking piece (or another piece left behind) becomes en prise. Meanwhile, the simple capture the player ignored would have won material cleanly or delivered a faster mate. The check gains one tempo but costs a whole piece.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive Rook check (often exploiting back-rank weakness) that wins major material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the best move wins material in 98% of positions (median value 100), and critically, 99% of best moves are checks while only 14% are captures — indicating non-capturing Rook checks that force the king to move and then win material on the follow-up. The player's actual move was a capture only 20% of the time and was mostly a quiet, non-tactical move. While 50% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value just 1 pawn), this is a secondary effect — the primary mistake is failing to deliver the winning Rook check. All 12 top-activating positions feature the same geometry: an available Rook check (Ra1+, Rb8+, Re1+, Rc8+, Rd8+) exploiting an exposed or back-rank king, where the check either directly wins material or initiates a forced sequence winning decisive material. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, reflecting these specific tactical configurations.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Qf7, Qe2, Rxd5, Rb8, Rc6, Re1, Ra7, Re2, Re5, Rb1, Qe6, f4) are all non-checking moves that completely miss the most forcing continuation. By failing to deliver the Rook check, the player allows the opponent's king to remain safe, squandering a winning tactical blow — often a back-rank invasion — that would have won a full piece or more through the forced sequence following the check. The eval swings (200-564 cp loss) confirm these are game-changing misses.

analysis.label: Player captures (usually with check) forcing an equal trade of major pieces when a non-trading move would win significantly more material.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a capture (89% of cases) that leaves their own piece hanging to recapture (100%, median value 5.0 — typically a rook or queen). The piece class distribution confirms major pieces dominate (7/9). Meanwhile, 78% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0 pawns). The player opts for a flashy but equal exchange — often a back-rank capture with check — squandering a position where they could win material outright by maintaining piece activity.
analysis.why_bad: By trading major pieces (typically rooks on e1/e8 or queens), the player simplifies into a worse or merely equal endgame, forfeiting a position where a non-trading move (like repositioning the rook, advancing a passed pawn, or finding a fork) would have won material or maintained a decisive advantage. The check or capture is psychologically tempting but strategically wasteful.

analysis.label: Player missed a devastating central knight fork (Nd4/Nd5/Ne5) winning major material, typically a queen, and played a quiet developing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of positions have a best move winning material with a median value of 6 (consistent with winning a queen for a knight). Only 17% of best moves are captures and just 3% are checks, indicating the winning move is typically a quiet knight jump that creates a fork threat. The played moves were captures only 12% of the time — players chose routine quiet moves (castling, bishop development, pawn pushes) instead. All 12 top-activating positions feature a knight jump to a powerful central square (Nd4, Nd5, or Ne5) that simultaneously attacks two undefended or poorly defended high-value pieces — most commonly an exposed queen on f3/f6 and a loose bishop on b4/b5. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (11/12), where one side has prematurely developed the queen to an exposed square alongside an undefended bishop, creating a geometric vulnerability to a central knight fork.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Bc5, a6, O-O, h6, Rc1, Qc2, Bg7, etc.) are routine developing or prophylactic moves that completely ignore the concrete tactical opportunity. By missing the knight fork, the player forfeits approximately 6 pawns worth of material (typically winning the opponent's queen for the knight) and instead allows the opponent to reposition or defend, neutralizing the tactical advantage that existed in the position.

analysis.label: The player ignores a straightforward capturing move that wins material (or a necessary exchange) and instead plays a passive quiet move, often also leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 85% of positions the best move is a capture, and in 72% of cases that capture wins material outright (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). Yet the player's actual move is a capture only 18% of the time—overwhelmingly they play a quiet, non-tactical move instead. Compounding the error, in 50% of positions the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed across minors (99), pawns (95), and majors (56). The enormous average cp_loss of 1896 reflects how these blunders combine missing a free capture with simultaneously worsening one's own position. Many top-activating positions feature mutual queen attacks or exposed enemy pieces where the simple recapture or exchange is mandatory, but the player instead makes a developing or repositioning move that ignores the tactical reality.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore an immediately available capture that either nets free material or is a forced exchange necessary to prevent the opponent from capturing first. By playing a passive move, the player both forfeits the winning capture AND often leaves their own piece (frequently a queen or minor piece) undefended, resulting in a catastrophic swing—the position goes from winning or equal to losing.

analysis.label: Player captures with a rook (often with check) on a square where the rook is immediately recaptured, losing the exchange for inadequate compensation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), with the hung piece class overwhelmingly being major pieces (25/27). The played move is a capture 96% of the time, confirming a pattern of rook captures that are immediately recaptured. Only 11% of best moves are captures, meaning the correct continuation was usually a non-capturing move (quiet advance, repositioning, or a different check). The best move wins material 56% of the time (median 91, suggesting a whole rook win was available via a better line), and the best move is a check 33% of the time — indicating the correct approach often involved a different checking sequence. All 12 top positions are endgames (avg cp_loss 1112), where impulsive captures are especially costly since piece activity and pawn promotion matter more than raw captures.
analysis.why_bad: The rook captures a piece (often a pawn or minor piece defended by the opponent's king) and gives check, but the king or another piece simply recaptures the rook. The player nets only the value of the captured target (often 1-3 points) while losing a 5-point rook, resulting in a catastrophic material deficit. The better move typically maintains the rook's activity, pursues a promotion, or finds a more effective check sequence that doesn't allow immediate recapture.

analysis.label: The player moves their queen to an aggressive-looking square instead of making the correct queen capture (exchange or winning take).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture 93% of the time, yet the player's move was a capture only 13% of the time—a massive divergence. The best captures are overwhelmingly queen captures (Qxd5, Qxd3, Qxg6, Qxc4, Qxf5, Qxh6, Qxf3, Qxg5+, Qxe3) that are typically equal exchanges (SEE wins 0 in all top 12 boards, with only 18% winning material overall). Instead of taking, the player repositions the queen to aggressive-looking kingside squares (Qg4, Qh3, Qf5, Qg6, Qf6). This speculative queen placement leaves own material hanging 60% of the time (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 34/65 cases, with 17 major and 14 minor pieces also hung). The player sacrifices concrete tactical gains for illusory attacking chances.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the available queen capture (often a clean queen exchange or favorable tactical simplification), the player loses the concrete advantage the position offered. The aggressive queen relocation to squares like g4/h3/g6 typically creates no real threats while leaving pawns or pieces undefended, resulting in a net material loss. The correct captures often led to favorable simplifications or won material after forced sequences.

analysis.label: A tempting knight move (to an aggressive square, often with capture or check) that leaves the player's own piece undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes an active-looking knight move that hangs one of their own pieces. The SEE aggregate shows 66% of the played moves left the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0, distribution: 123 minor, 94 pawns, 58 major pieces), while 70% of the time a better move existed that would win material (median 3.0). Every single top-12 move is a knight move (Nf7, Nd7, Nb6, Nxf2, Nc2, Nc2+, Ne3, Nxf7, Nc3, etc.), many to squares that look aggressive or tactically appealing. Only 41% are captures, meaning most are quiet knight jumps to seemingly active squares. The knight's departure often uncovers an attack on the player's bishop or rook, or the knight itself lands on a square where it becomes trapped or undefended.
analysis.why_bad: The knight move looks active (landing on f7, c2, f2 — squares near the enemy king or with fork potential, sometimes with check) but fails because it either removes protection from another piece, moves the knight to a square where it is itself lost, or ignores a more profitable continuation. The opponent simply captures the hanging piece, netting material that far outweighs whatever the knight achieved.

analysis.label: The player makes a non-urgent move instead of castling, leaving their king dangerously exposed in the center.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, the best move is castling (O-O or O-O-O) in virtually every case, yet the player chooses a quiet flank push, capture, or developing move instead. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 24% of the time (median 1.0 — typically a pawn gained through tactics enabled by a safe king), while the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging 37% of the time (median value 1.0), distributed as pawns (99), minors (63), and majors (22). This indicates that failing to castle exposes pieces to tactical exploitation along open central files and diagonals. Notably, the best move is almost never a check (0%) or a capture (1%) — it is simply castling, a quiet king-safety move that the player neglects.
analysis.why_bad: By delaying castling when the center is open or semi-open and the opponent has pieces trained on the e-file or d-file, the player's king becomes a tactical target. This creates pins, discovered attacks, and threats that cause material loss. The uncastled king also prevents rook coordination, and the resulting vulnerability turns otherwise playable positions into losing ones (average cp_loss of 293).

analysis.label: A pawn capture (typically on an adjacent file) leaves the player's own piece undefended by removing its pawn defender or opening a line of attack.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (98%, median value 1.0), with the played move being a capture 84% of the time. The hung piece distribution is heavily skewed toward pawns (273 pawn, 61 minor, 21 major), indicating the capturing pawn was typically defending a neighboring pawn or the capture opened a file/diagonal exposing the player's material. Only 35% of best moves win material outright, confirming this is primarily a 'hung own piece' pattern rather than a missed-winning pattern. All 12 top-activating moves are pawn captures (exf4, fxe4, cxd5, etc.) where moving the pawn off its original file/diagonal removes protection from the player's own pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The pawn capture is greedy—it wins enemy material on the target square but the capturing pawn was serving a critical defensive role (shielding another pawn or blocking a line). After the capture, the opponent can exploit the newly undefended piece or the opened file/diagonal to win back more than what was captured, resulting in a net material loss (avg ~101cp loss).

analysis.label: In the opening, the bishop greedily captures a defended pawn and is left hanging with no retreat, losing a minor piece for a pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 93% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the own-hang distribution overwhelmingly minor pieces (33 of 39). The played move is a capture 62% of the time, and only 24% of best moves win material—meaning the position before the blunder was roughly equal. All 12 top-activating boards are opening positions where a bishop (on f4, b2, or g7) lunges to capture a pawn on c7, g7, b7, or d4 that is adequately defended (typically by the opponent's queen or dark-squared bishop). The bishop ends up stranded on the capture square with no escape, immediately recaptured, netting only a pawn for a lost minor piece (~450-550 cp loss).
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a pawn that is defended (usually by the queen on d8 or a bishop on f8/g7), and after recapture the player has traded a 3-point minor piece for a 1-point pawn, losing roughly 2 points of material. In the opening, with no other pieces coordinated to support the bishop's incursion, the bishop has no retreat square and is simply lost. Standard developing moves (e3, Nf3, c4) maintain equality instead.

analysis.label: The player ignores a critical queen exchange or queen capture that was clearly best, instead playing an inferior move that often hangs material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 94% of the time (overwhelmingly queen captures like Qxd2+, Qxc8+, Qxf6+, Qxe7, etc.) with SEE value of 0 (equal exchanges). Despite these queen trades being strategically winning, the player avoids them — their actual move is a capture only 8% of the time. Instead, the player plays flashy queen checks or quiet repositioning moves, and 58% of the time their move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distribution across major pieces, pawns, and minors). The average centipawn loss of 1161 confirms these are catastrophic errors. The best move being a check 23% of the time shows these queen captures sometimes deliver check as well, making the missed opportunity even more egregious.
analysis.why_bad: The queen trade or queen capture leads to a strategically won position (simplified endgame advantage, elimination of opponent's counterplay, or forced material gain), but the player rejects it in favor of moves that look active (checks, threats) yet achieve nothing concrete. By keeping tensions on the board unnecessarily, the player exposes their own pieces to tactical vulnerabilities, frequently hanging queens or major pieces on the very next move.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive check (often a sacrifice) that would win the opponent's queen or major material, instead playing a greedy capture or passive move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 75% of activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 74% of cases it wins material with a median value of 97 (approximately a queen). The player's actual move left their own piece hanging 51% of the time (median value 5, predominantly major pieces at 42/74 cases), indicating they often played greedy queen captures that left the queen en prise. Only 37% of played moves were captures, while many were passive quiet moves. The pattern consistently shows the player overlooking a non-obvious check—typically a rook or bishop sacrifice/deflection (Rc1+, Rg8+, Bg8+, Rh1+, Rxf1+, h2+)—that exploits the opponent's king geometry to win decisive material, usually the opposing queen.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they either greedily capture a less valuable piece while hanging the queen (e.g., Qxf6+ leaves the queen capturable, Qxb3+ ignores a forced deflection), or they play passively (e.g., Qc7, Qe1) allowing the opponent to consolidate their position. In both cases, the player misses that a forcing check—often a surprising piece sacrifice—would deflect a defender or expose the king, netting the opponent's queen or delivering a mating attack.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive knight fork or tactical check winning major material (typically the queen), instead playing a quiet non-tactical move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 92% of best moves win material with a strikingly high median value of 91 (queen-level), and 56% of best moves are checks — yet only 16% are captures. This signature points to missed knight forks with check that win the queen. Among the top activating boards, positions 4 (Ne7+), 5 (Nf3+), 6 (Nc6+), and 11 (Nf6+) all feature textbook knight forks winning 97 (queen). The remaining positions feature other missed tactical shots (double attacks, pawn forks, king-attacks-knight) winning minor pieces or rooks. The player's move was a capture only 33% of the time, confirming they typically chose a quiet positional move instead of the winning tactic. The 32% own-hang rate (median value 3) indicates that some players compounded the error by also leaving their own piece en prise.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a forcing tactical sequence — usually a knight check that forks the king and queen — and instead plays a routine developing or quiet move. By missing the fork, they lose a winning position (median ~queen's worth of material), often turning a decisive advantage into an equal or lost game. The average cp_loss of 486 across the top positions reflects the catastrophic cost of missing these one-move tactical shots.

analysis.label: Player gives an aimless check instead of simply capturing a hanging enemy piece (usually a queen).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 85% of best moves are captures winning material (78% win material, median value 5.0 — typically a queen), yet only 8% of played moves are captures. Instead, players deliver checks that accomplish nothing strategically. In 64% of cases (median value 5.0, mostly major pieces), the checking move also leaves the player's own piece hanging, compounding the blunder. The top 12 boards confirm this: 10 of 12 played moves are checks (Qh6+, Rb5+, Qb5+, Re1+, Qb8+, Qf4+, Qa1+, Rb8+, Rd8+, Ra5+) while the best move is almost always a simple queen capture (Qxf1, Qxf8, Qxb6, Qxc4, Qxd4+, Qxe7, Rxb4, Rxd2). The average cp_loss of 6689 reflects the catastrophic cost of these missed captures.
analysis.why_bad: These checks are seductive but tactically worthless — the opponent simply moves their king and retains or gains material. Meanwhile, the checking piece often lands on an undefended square, leaving it hanging. The player trades a decisive material win (capturing an undefended enemy queen/major piece) for a meaningless tempo that the opponent easily survives, often turning a won position into a loss.

analysis.label: Player captures a pawn with the queen (or makes a routine move like O-O) while ignoring critical king vulnerability on an open central file.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player neglects king safety in favor of material gain or routine play. The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material in 55% of cases (median 1 pawn), the played move is a capture 37% of the time, and 36% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns/79, minors/49, majors/36). The typical scenario involves an open d- or e-file where the player's queen and king share vulnerability. In ~67% of top positions, the player either captures a central pawn with Qxe4/Qxe5 while the king remains uncastled on e1/e8, or castles kingside directly into a prepared Bd6+Bg4 attack. The best moves instead address king safety (O-O-O, Qe2, Nc3 developing) or avoid the exposed file alignment.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize a pawn capture or routine castle over the critical tactical reality: the king sits on (or is about to be exposed on) an open central file. After Qxe4, the queen becomes a target on the open e-file while the uncastled king behind it faces discovered attacks and pins. After O-O into Bd6+Bg4, the h2 pawn becomes indefensible as the pinned Nf3 cannot protect it. In both cases, the opponent exploits the open-file/diagonal geometry to win material or launch a devastating attack against the exposed king.

analysis.label: Player missed a strong knight move to e4 or e5 (usually a capture) that wins material or dominates the center.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material 51% of the time (median value 6.0 pawns) and is a capture 61% of the time. All 12 top-activating boards show the best move is a knight move to e4 or e5 (Nxe4, Nxe5, Ne4, Ne5, or Nd4), making this the defining geometric pattern. Instead of playing the strong central knight move, players chose quiet moves (only 32% played a capture), and 60% of the time their played move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly minors and pawns). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating it captures a very specific tactical oversight involving knight centralization on the e-file.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a powerful knight capture or jump to a central square (e4/e5) that would win material, dominate the position, or create decisive tactical threats. Instead, players make passive or irrelevant moves (castling, pushing flank pawns, retreating queens) that squander the tactical opportunity and often leave their own pieces tactically vulnerable.

analysis.label: Player missed a quiet pawn advance that traps or wins the enemy queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 9, i.e., a queen), yet only 8% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks—indicating the winning move is a quiet pawn push that attacks and traps the enemy queen. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (83% non-captures) and often leave own material hanging (63%, median value 1, mostly pawns). Examining the top boards, the best moves are consistently single-square pawn advances (g3, g6, f5, b4, f3, c4, g5, f4) that attack an aggressively-placed enemy queen which has limited escape squares due to surrounding pieces. The opponent's queen has ventured deep into the position and a simple pawn push seals it off.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore the opponent's overextended queen and pursue other plans (development, quiet repositioning, captures elsewhere), completely missing that a simple pawn advance would trap the enemy queen—winning it outright or netting decisive material. The queen, having infiltrated aggressively, has cut off its own retreat paths, and only the pawn push exploits this.

analysis.label: In critical endgame positions, the player makes a passive quiet move instead of the one active move that wins material or maintains a vital defensive resource.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 68% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), while the player's move was a capture only 12% of the time — a classic 'missed material' signature. Only 30% of played moves hung the player's own piece (median 1.0), making this primarily about failing to seize an available tactical resource rather than blundering one's own material. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top positions) with an extraordinarily high average cp_loss of 3293, indicating these are critical moments where one active move (a capture, a check, or correct king direction) represents the difference between fighting on and immediate collapse. The best moves include Nxg5 capturing a queen, Bc5+ winning with check, Ra2/Rc3 stopping promotion threats, and correct king approaches (Ke6, Ke5, Kd4) that win passed pawns.
analysis.why_bad: These passive moves (wrong-direction king moves, aimless pawn pushes, misplaced pieces) fail because they ignore the one critical tactical resource available. In the featured endgames — often involving dangerous passed pawns or promotion threats — tempo is paramount. Playing passively allows the opponent's threats to become unstoppable (promotions converting to forced mate) or forfeits the chance to capture material that would maintain the balance. The player essentially 'sleepwalks' through a position demanding immediate concrete action.

analysis.label: Player captures or attacks the wrong target, missing a superior material-winning capture available elsewhere on the board.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material 56% of the time (median value 2.0, typically a minor piece) and is a capture 71% of the time, yet the player's move was only a capture 30% of the time. Additionally, 52% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns: 23 of 31 cases). This indicates a pattern where the player is lured to an inferior tactical operation—often capturing the wrong piece, giving a showy check, or making a plausible developing move—while a stronger capture on a different square goes unnoticed. The played moves (Nxd5 instead of Nxc6, Nxf8 instead of Nxc5, bxa5 instead of bxc5, dxe4 instead of Nxf6, Bxe6+ instead of Rxc4) consistently show the player attacking/capturing on the wrong square while the truly winning capture sits elsewhere.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is attracted to an appealing-looking target (a seemingly free piece, a check, a natural recapture) while a superior tactical capture exists on a different square. The chosen move typically wins less material or none at all, and frequently leaves the player's own pieces undefended (52% hang rate), compounding the error by both missing a gain and creating a new vulnerability.

analysis.label: The player moves a pawn off a long diagonal, exposing their own rook in the corner to an enemy fianchettoed bishop or centralized queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player hangs their own piece: 67% of positions leave an own piece hanging (median value 5.0 = rook), with the 'major' piece class dominating at 64 out of 78 cases. Only 11% of played moves are captures and only 7% of best moves are captures, confirming these are quiet positional blunders rather than tactical exchanges. The consistent geometric pattern is: an enemy bishop (on b2, g2) or queen (on d4) controls a long diagonal aimed at a corner rook (h8 or a8), and the player's pawn move (g6, b6, b3) removes the sole blocker from that diagonal, or a rook move (Ra3) places the rook directly on the exposed diagonal. The 27% 'best wins material' cases correspond to positions where the best response simultaneously develops while the rook is already tactically lost.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn pushes (g6, b6, b3) or rook moves (Ra3) remove the only piece/pawn intercepting a long diagonal between an enemy bishop/queen and the player's uncastled rook sitting in the corner. The rook (worth 5 points) becomes immediately capturable with no compensation, typically resulting in 300-550 centipawn losses. The player focuses on a fianchetto or development plan without noticing the diagonal is already controlled by the opponent.

analysis.label: Player ignores an obligatory queen exchange (often with check) and instead plays a developing or repositioning move, leaving their own queen or piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 66% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 'major' pieces dominating at 119/229 instances), while the best move was a capture in 98% of cases and a check in 44%. The best move almost never wins material outright (only 3%), indicating these are queen trades at equal value rather than winning captures. The pattern is overwhelmingly one of open-file or diagonal queen confrontations—typically both queens stare at each other on the e-file—where the correct response is to exchange queens (frequently with check, e.g., Qxe2+, Qxd2+, Qxe3+), but the player instead makes a developing move (Bg4, Nc6, O-O-O) or repositions a piece, completely ignoring that their own queen is attacked and will be captured for free on the next move.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the queen tension and playing a non-urgent developing or quiet move, the player leaves their queen (or another piece) undefended and capturable. Since the opponent's piece is already attacking it, the failure to trade results in losing the queen outright—typically a 9-point loss—when a simple equal exchange (often with the bonus of giving check) was available.

analysis.label: The player missed a Queen relocation (or similar tactical move) that would have won the opponent's queen outright.
analysis.description: In 94% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median SEE value of 9 (queen value). Strikingly, the best move is almost always a Queen maneuver—seen in 11 of 12 top boards (Qe2, Qg6, Qc8, Qa6, Qf3, Qf6, Qh4, etc.)—yet only 23% are captures and 0% are checks, indicating the Queen relocates to a square that decisively threatens or traps the opponent's queen. Only 18% of played moves were captures; most were quiet positional or developing moves. Additionally, 54% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0; distribution: 127 pawns, 79 majors, 62 minors), compounding the error. The feature fires on just 0.7% of positions, capturing a specific tactical blindspot in middlegame positions.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a concrete tactical opportunity where the player's queen can relocate to a square that wins the opponent's queen—via forks, attacking an undefended queen, or creating an inescapable threat. Instead, players make routine development, pawn pushes, or captures on irrelevant squares, missing a ~9-point material swing that would typically be decisive.

analysis.label: Player retreats king from an attacking knight (g5/g4) instead of capturing it with the queen, leaving their own minor piece undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 83% of played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces: 24 minors out of 35 hung pieces), while 95% of best moves are captures. In every top-activating position, an enemy knight sits aggressively on g5 (or g4), pressuring the player's exposed king. The best move is always Qxg5/Qxg4—simply capturing the undefended attacking knight. Instead, the player panics and retreats the king (all 12 top moves are king moves), which removes the king from immediate danger but simultaneously abandons protection of a minor piece (typically a bishop on g4 or similar outpost), leaving it en prise for the opponent to capture next move.
analysis.why_bad: The king moves are bad because they solve the wrong problem: the enemy knight on g5/g4 is actually hanging and can be cleanly captured by the queen for free. By fleeing instead of counter-capturing, the player not only forfeits the chance to win/trade the attacking piece but also leaves their own bishop (or knight) undefended—typically a piece that was tactically active (e.g., Bg4 pressuring the queen) but depended on the king's proximity for protection. The net swing is usually a full minor piece lost.

analysis.label: The player moves their Rook (often greedily capturing a pawn) to an undefended square where it is left en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 98% of positions show the player's move leaving their own piece hanging, with a median hung value of 5 (a Rook), and the piece class is almost exclusively 'major' (476 out of 490). The played move is a capture only 36% of the time, meaning many instances are quiet Rook moves to unsafe squares as well. The best moves rarely involve captures (25%) or checks (13%) — they are typically patient positional moves like pawn advances (h4, g4, h5) or king improvements (Ke7, Ke1). The feature fires in 0.3% of all positions, mostly in endgames (9/12 top boards), where greedy or careless Rook maneuvers are punished.
analysis.why_bad: The Rook moves to a square (often capturing a pawn or minor piece) where it lacks protection and can be immediately captured or trapped by the opponent's pieces. In endgames, the player prioritizes material gain or activity over Rook safety, failing to notice that the opponent can simply take the Rook on its new square. The correct moves are typically quiet improvements (king centralization, pawn advances) that maintain Rook safety while building the position.

analysis.label: Player plays a flashy check, capture, or pawn push instead of using a rook to blockade or capture a critical enemy passed pawn about to promote.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move wins material 63% of the time (median value 1.0 — a pawn, i.e., the passed pawn itself), while the played move was only a capture 24% of the time and left the player's own piece hanging 42% of the time (median value 3.0). The best move is a check only 2% of the time and a capture only 15%, yet the played moves are overwhelmingly checks (Bb3+, Re2+, Bc4+, Rh4+) or irrelevant captures/pushes. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the opponent has a far-advanced passed pawn (nearly always a b7-pawn supported by a rook on the a-file) one step from promotion. The correct move is invariably a rook move to the relevant file (Rb2, Ra2, Rb8, Rb6, Ra5, etc.) to stop or capture the pawn. The average cp_loss of 3588 confirms these are game-losing blunders in endgame positions (9/12 are endgames).
analysis.why_bad: The played moves prioritize superficially attractive tactics — giving check, grabbing unimportant material, or pushing one's own passer — while ignoring the immediate existential threat of the enemy pawn promoting. Once the rook leaves the critical file or the tempo is wasted, the passed pawn queens and the game is lost, often by forced mate.

analysis.label: Playing a passive quiet move that neglects concrete tactical demands, missing material gains while often leaving own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a dual-nature mistake: 61% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the player's move was a capture only 24% of the time. Simultaneously, 52% of the played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung piece spread across all types (pawn: 100, major: 90, minor: 54). The best move is a check only 9% and a capture 27% of the time, indicating the missed tactic is often a quiet tactical blow rather than an obvious recapture. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, targeting moments where concrete tactical action is demanded but the player instead makes a slow, 'improving' move—development (Rd1, Re1, Rhe1), pawn pushes (b3, a4), or queen repositioning (Qe7, Qc7, Qa8, Qe3)—that fails to address the position's tactical urgency.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize general positional goals (development, centralization, prophylaxis) over concrete tactical necessities. The positions demand immediate tactical action—exploiting exposed kings, winning undefended pieces, or executing forcing sequences—but the quiet moves played allow the opponent to consolidate, defend, or even exploit newly unprotected pieces. The result is a large average cp_loss of 214, as both the offensive opportunity is squandered and defensive vulnerabilities are created simultaneously.

analysis.label: Player moves their Queen to a passive or irrelevant square, missing a critical forcing move (often a check or capture) that wins material or saves the game, while frequently leaving own pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a catastrophically passive move—predominantly with the Queen (9/12 top boards)—instead of exploiting a forcing tactical opportunity. The SEE aggregate shows that 80% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0), often via checks (20%) or captures (24%). Meanwhile, 55% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0; distribution: 138 pawns, 92 majors, 43 minors). The enormous average cp_loss of 4862 reflects that these passive Queen placements (Qh2, Qd8, Qa1, Qf8, Qe7, Qh3) simultaneously miss winning tactics against exposed enemy kings AND abandon defense of the player's own material. The feature fires on just 0.5% of positions, indicating these are rare but devastating blunders where the player's Queen retreats to a useless square in a tactically critical moment.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player retreats their most powerful piece to a passive square (often a back rank or corner) precisely when the position demands forcing play. The exposed enemy king or hanging enemy material requires an immediate check, capture, or decisive threat. By moving passively, the player not only misses winning material or achieving perpetual check, but often removes the Queen from defending its own pieces, leading to immediate catastrophic losses—frequently resulting in getting mated or losing decisive material.

analysis.label: The player failed to capture an undefended enemy queen that was freely available for taking.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this feature: 97% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (queen), and 92% of the time the best move is a simple capture. Yet the player's move was a capture only 12% of the time, meaning they almost always played a quiet move instead of taking the free queen. Across the top 12 boards, positions 1-5, 7-9, and 11 all show the best move capturing an enemy queen (Qxc8, Qxc6, Qxe2, Qxd4+, Bxe6, Rxd1, Qxe1, Qxf3, axb5) that was sitting undefended on an open line. The average cp_loss of 5211 is catastrophic and consistent with missing queen-value material. A secondary effect shows 55% of played moves also left the player's own piece hanging (median 3), compounding the blunder.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a freely capturable enemy queen — the most valuable piece on the board — to pursue irrelevant plans like king walks (Kh8, Kh3, Kh2, Ka4), quiet positional moves (c3, Bd2, Nb5), or speculative rook maneuvers (Rh4, Rg5). By not taking the hanging queen, they throw away a decisive material advantage (often converting a forced mate into a drawn or lost position).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet piece repositioning move that leaves own material hanging while ignoring available tactical opportunities.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player chooses a quiet, seemingly developing or repositioning move (only 9% of played moves are captures) that leaves their own material en prise (53% of the time, median value 3.0 — distributed across minors: 52, pawns: 46, majors: 28). Simultaneously, in 65% of cases the best move wins enemy material (median 3.0), with 50% being captures and 16% being checks. The played moves (Bd6, Bf6, Bg5, Nf4, Ne4, Ng4, Bc8, Bd4, Nh6, etc.) are overwhelmingly quiet piece placements to squares that appear active but ignore the tactical demands of the position. The average centipawn loss of 1073 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — the player is both missing winning tactics and creating new vulnerabilities simultaneously.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes piece placement or 'development' over concrete tactical calculation. By moving a piece to a new square without checking whether that piece (or another) becomes undefended, and without scanning for captures/checks first, the player simultaneously gifts material to the opponent while missing their own winning shots. The quiet nature of the move (non-capture, non-check) means it surrenders tempo to the opponent, who can exploit the newly hanging piece immediately.

analysis.label: Player ignores a simple pawn capture of an invading enemy minor piece (typically a knight on g6/g3), leaving their own rook or major piece hanging to the uncaptured attacker.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 76% of the top 500 activating positions the best move is a capture, and in 72% it wins material (median value 2.0, consistent with a pawn netting a minor piece). Meanwhile, 64% of the played moves leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 'major' pieces—mostly rooks—dominating at 29 of 63 identified cases). The top boards reveal a strikingly uniform geometry: an enemy minor piece (usually a knight) has landed on g6 (attacking Black's h8 rook) or g3 (attacking White's h1 rook), and the correct response is a simple h-pawn capture (hxg6 or hxg3) or occasionally bxc3. Instead, the player plays a developing or tactical move elsewhere, leaving their rook en prise to the uncaptured attacker. The feature activates on only 0.1% of positions, isolating this specific tactical oversight.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to capture the invading piece with a pawn, the player leaves a major piece (usually a rook on h1/h8) directly attacked with no defense. The invading piece—often a knight on g6 or g3—simultaneously threatens the rook and supports other tactical motifs (discovered checks, queen coordination). The pawn capture would have eliminated the threat while winning material (net ~2 pawns' worth), but ignoring it typically costs a full exchange or more (rook for nothing), explaining the enormous average centipawn loss of 1857.

analysis.label: Player ignores a necessary rook exchange on a contested open file, often leaving their own pieces hanging as a consequence.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 98% of cases, yet it only wins material 10% of the time (median value 1.0 when it does), meaning the critical capture is overwhelmingly an equal rook-for-rook exchange. All 12 top-activating positions confirm this: the best move is always a rook capture on an open file (Rxc8, Rxd8, Rxa8, Rxc1, Rxb8, Rxe8, Rxa1) with SEE = 0. Instead of taking the exchange, the player makes a quiet move (only 17% captures played). The consequence is severe: 47% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung pieces distributed across pawns (39), majors (39), and minors (20). The average cp_loss of 346 reflects how badly ignoring rook tension on open files punishes the player.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the forced rook exchange on a contested open file, the player leaves the rook confrontation unresolved. The opponent then exploits the tension—often by capturing first with tempo or discovering attacks—resulting in the player losing material (frequently a full piece or rook) because their position collapses once the file-control initiative passes to the opponent.

analysis.label: Playing an early aggressive queen check (Qh5+/Qh4+) in the opening that leaves the queen stranded and hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a premature queen check in the opening (typically Qh5+ or Qh4+, often resembling Scholar's Mate attempts). The SEE aggregate shows that 78% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging with a median value of 8.0 (queen), and the piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (33 major vs 20 minor vs 9 pawn). The best move is rarely a check itself (11%) or a capture (20%), indicating that quiet developing moves were far superior. Only 24% of the played moves were captures, confirming most are quiet queen checks. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, consistent with a specific opening blunder pattern. All 12 top-activating boards are in the opening phase with kings still in the center, and 10 of 12 moves played are Qh5+ or Qh4+.
analysis.why_bad: After delivering the check, the opponent simply blocks or moves the king, and the queen is now marooned on an exposed square (h4 or h5) where it can be attacked by developing moves (e.g., g6, Nf6, Be7) and trapped or won. The check gains no lasting advantage—it merely displaces the king trivially while misplacing the most valuable piece on the board, losing enormous material (typically the whole queen) and squandering any opening advantage.

analysis.label: In endgames with advanced passed pawns near promotion, the king retreats to the wrong square, abandoning critical stalemate resources or promotion support.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) featuring advanced passed pawns—typically Queen-vs-pawn-on-7th-rank or Rook+pawn scenarios—where the player moves their king to the geometrically wrong square. The SEE aggregate shows only 19% of best moves win material (median value 5.0, consistent with enabling pawn promotion to a queen), only 2% of played moves are captures, and just 14% leave own pieces hanging (all pawns, median 1.0). The low capture/hanging rates confirm this is fundamentally a positional/geometric error rather than a tactical oversight involving pieces. The enormous average cp_loss of 2467 reflects that in these knife-edge endgame positions, choosing the wrong king square frequently converts theoretical draws into forced losses (as seen in positions 2, 5, and 8 where eval goes from 0 to forced mate).
analysis.why_bad: In Q-vs-pawn and R+pawn endgames, the defending king must stay on very specific squares (typically the queening square's corner like h1/h2 for f-pawns, or a1/a2 for b-pawns) to maintain stalemate threats that force a draw. Moving to the wrong square (e.g., Kf1 instead of Kh1, Kc1 instead of Ka2, Kb1 instead of Ka1) breaks the stalemate geometry, allowing the superior side's queen to win with checks and force the pawn's capture or deliver mate.

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop move to b4 or b5 that pins or wins the opponent's queen against their king along a diagonal.
analysis.description: In 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 6.0 (consistent with winning a queen for a bishop). The best move is a capture only 11% of the time and a check only 5%, indicating the winning mechanism is overwhelmingly a pin rather than a direct capture. The played move is a capture only 11% of the time, and the own-hang rate is a low 19% (median value 1.0), confirming the mistake is purely a missed tactical opportunity rather than a self-inflicted blunder. All 12 top-activating boards show the same geometry: the best move is Bb4 (for Black, targeting a queen on c3 aligned with the king on e1) or Bb5 (for White, targeting a queen on c6 aligned with the king on e8). The feature fires exclusively in opening positions (11/12) where both kings remain in the center, creating the fatal diagonal alignment.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (quiet developing moves like Be6, Nge7, Nf6, O-O, Bd3, etc.) are natural but miss a crushing tactical blow. By failing to play Bb4 or Bb5, the player passes up winning the opponent's queen via an absolute pin along the a5-e1 or a4-e8 diagonal. The resulting 300+ centipawn losses show these positions collapse from decisive advantages to near-equality.

analysis.label: Player failed to make a critical even exchange, playing a quiet move instead that typically left their own piece hanging in unresolved tactical tension.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a capture (96% of cases) that is materially neutral (SEE=0 in ~86% of cases), representing a necessary exchange to resolve tactical tension. Instead of making this trade, the player plays a quiet move (84% non-captures). In 56% of cases, the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0; distributed as 30 pawns, 29 minors, 12 majors across the top activations). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically those where ignoring an available even trade creates a tactical liability.
analysis.why_bad: When pieces are in mutual tension (e.g., knights confronting each other on e5, rooks facing each other on open files), the exchange is often forced. Ignoring it by playing elsewhere means the opponent can capture your piece for free on the next move, or exploit the unresolved tension.
