The piece that should have taken is left en prise, or the quiet move creates a second weakness that compounds with the existing tension.

analysis.label: Player missed an immediate or near-immediate checkmate (or decisive mating check) delivered by a rook, instead playing a non-forcing move or greedy capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 94% of the best moves are checks and 96% win material with a median value of 100 (representing checkmate/king capture in SEE terms), while only 6% are captures — confirming the best move is almost always a rook delivering check, not taking material. The played moves were captures only 21% of the time (often greedy pawn grabs like Rxh2, Rxh5, Rxg5) and quiet moves the rest, with only 25% leaving own pieces hanging. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the missed best move is a rook check that delivers immediate checkmate (positions 2,3,4,7,8,9,10,12) or a forcing rook check leading to mate in 1-3 moves (positions 1,5,6,11). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions — specifically endgames (10/12) with exposed enemy kings where a single rook move ends the game.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore an immediately available checkmate or forced mating sequence. Instead of delivering the killing blow with a rook check to an exposed king, the player greedily captures a pawn, makes a purposeless rook move, or pushes a pawn — allowing the opponent to survive and potentially escape the mating net, converting a mate-in-one into merely a large advantage.

analysis.label: King moves to the wrong square in a pawn endgame, losing opposition, critical defensive position, or allowing pawn promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player makes a king move in the wrong direction, resulting in catastrophic positional or material loss. The SEE aggregate shows that 24% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn capture the king should approach), while 22% of the time the played king move leaves the player's own pawn hanging (76 out of 84 hung pieces are pawns). Only 7% of played moves are captures and only 5% of best moves are captures, confirming these are quiet king maneuvers gone wrong. The average cp_loss of 926 centipawns reflects that in king-and-pawn endgames, a single wrong king step often converts drawn positions into lost ones or dramatically accelerates defeat.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king placement is everything. These moves fail because the king retreats, moves laterally, or advances toward the wrong flank—losing critical opposition (positions 5, 6), abandoning defense of own pawns (positions 10, 11 where pawns are left hanging), failing to approach enemy pawns for capture (positions 8, 12), or walking into forced mate (position 3). A single tempo or directional error in these simplified positions is decisive because there are no other pieces to compensate.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet or irrelevant move while ignoring an imminent forced checkmate threat, typically a back-rank or rook-dominated mating pattern in endgames.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (11/12 boards) where the player catastrophically ignores a forced checkmate threat, resulting in enormous cp_loss (avg 7868). The SEE aggregate shows best move wins material in 55% of cases (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), indicating the correct move often simultaneously defends against mate AND wins material via counterplay. Only 22% of played moves are captures, meaning players typically make quiet moves that completely ignore the mating net. The 44% own-hung-after rate (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 61/86) is incidental — the real catastrophe is allowing checkmate, not the pawn left en prise. The best moves are overwhelmingly defensive resources (Re8, Rc8, Rg7, Rh1) that address back-rank or king-trapping threats, while only 14% of best moves are captures and 10% are checks.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores that their king is being trapped (usually on the back rank or an edge square) by enemy rooks dominating the 7th rank or key files. Instead of playing the only defensive resource — typically placing a rook on the 8th rank or creating a counter-threat — the player makes an unrelated developing move, captures a peripheral piece, or walks the king into the mating net. The result is an immediate forced checkmate (#+1 to #+3 in most cases).

analysis.label: Player makes a tactically irrelevant move (quiet development, pawn push, or greedy capture) while completely ignoring the opponent's immediate mating or decisive tactical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player is oblivious to a critical tactical threat, typically an imminent checkmate. The SEE aggregate shows that 74% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), indicating a counter-tactical resource was available. Simultaneously, 65% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0; distribution: 76 pawns, 43 minors, 37 majors), meaning the played move also creates fresh vulnerabilities. The player's move was a capture only 22% of the time, and the best move is rarely a check (3%) or capture (10%), suggesting the correct defense is usually a quiet counter-tactical move. The enormous average cp_loss of 4934 and the prevalence of immediate mates (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 all result in forced mate) confirm this fires on catastrophic oversights of the opponent's decisive attack.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player treats the position as if nothing urgent is happening—pushing pawns (g6, c4), developing (Ne2, Nf6, Nc6, Ne7), or grabbing material (Nxg4, Bxd3)—while the opponent has an immediate mating combination or crushing tactical blow ready. The correct move would address the lethal threat, often by counter-attacking to win material or blocking the key diagonal/file. Instead, the played move either weakens the king further (g6 opening lines), blocks escape squares (Ne2), or simply wastes a tempo, allowing the opponent to deliver checkmate.

analysis.label: In a winning endgame, the player makes a quiet king or pawn move instead of simply capturing the opponent's hanging or attacked knight (or minor piece).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates a missed-capture pattern: 84% of the time the best move is a capture, 60% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 34% of best moves deliver check. Only 25% of the played moves were captures and only 32% left own pieces hanging (with a low median of 1.0, suggesting incidental pawn issues rather than the core mistake). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the position is a clearly won endgame (Rook or Bishop vs. Knight) where the best move captures the opponent's knight—often with check (Rxc6+, Rxf6+, Rxf5+, Rxf3+, Rxb5+)—yet the player instead makes an aimless quiet move (typically a king move like Kf5, Kf4, Kh3, Ka4, or a pawn push). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, isolating these specific endgame scenarios where the decisive simplifying capture is available.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet king and pawn moves waste time in a won position by failing to capture the opponent's last remaining minor piece. Taking the knight immediately would simplify to a trivially winning Rook+Pawns vs. King endgame (or equivalent), while the played moves allow the knight to remain active, potentially creating counterplay, blockade, or forking threats, costing significant centipawns (average 146 cp loss).

analysis.label: Player ignores a clearly available winning capture (often of a major enemy piece) and plays an unrelated move that frequently also hangs their own material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly identifies this as a missed-capture pattern: the best move is a capture in 96% of the top 500 positions, winning material 52% of the time with a median value of 4.0 (rook-level). The player's actual move was only a capture 17% of the time, meaning they played quiet or irrelevant moves instead. Compounding the error, 56% of played moves also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, spread across majors, minors, and pawns). The average centipawn loss of 3474 reflects catastrophic blunders. Across the top boards, the missed captures typically target enemy Queens or Rooks that have infiltrated deeply (e.g., enemy Queen on d8 in positions 2-4), yet the player gets distracted by checks (Qh2+, c6+), development (Nc5, Ne3, Nf6), or greedy but inferior captures (Qxb2, Rxd7).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a high-value enemy piece that is available for immediate capture. Instead of collecting decisive material (often a Queen or Rook worth 4-9 points), they play moves pursuing secondary goals—delivering checks, repositioning pieces, or capturing lower-value material on another square. The played moves are doubly catastrophic because they not only forfeit the winning capture but frequently also leave the player's own pieces undefended, converting a winning or equal position into an immediate loss.

analysis.label: The player missed a queen check that simultaneously forks the opponent's king and queen, winning massive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelmingly consistent pattern: 84% of the time the best move is a check, and 85% of the time it wins material with a median value of 91 (a queen). All 12 top-activating boards confirm the best move is a Queen delivering check (Qb5+, Qxd5+, Qa4+, Qe5+, Qe4+, Qxf2+, Qxe7+, Qd5+, Qd4+). Only 37% of best moves are captures, meaning the queen check usually isn't a capture itself but a fork that attacks the exposed king while simultaneously threatening the opponent's queen or other high-value piece. The played moves were mostly quiet (only 22% were captures), and 49% left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, mostly pawns), showing the player made aimless moves instead of exploiting the tactical geometry.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a decisive tactical shot — a queen check that forks the opponent's king and queen. The opponent's king is typically exposed (uncastled, on a weak square, or with a compromised pawn shield), creating a geometric alignment where the queen can deliver check while simultaneously attacking another undefended high-value piece. By playing quiet developing moves or greedy captures instead, the player squanders a winning position and often loses material themselves.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player overlooks that their king is adjacent to an undefended enemy piece and can simply capture it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 84% of best moves are captures, while only 4% of the actually-played moves were captures. The own-hang rate of 28% (median value just 1 pawn) is incidental noise. Across the top 12 boards, 10 of 12 best moves are king captures (Kxg7, Kxf6, Kxh2, Kxb5, Kxf5, Kxc2, Kxg3, Kxb7, Kxc3), targeting undefended bishops, knights, or rooks that sit on squares immediately adjacent to the player's king. The remaining two are pawn captures of adjacent hanging pieces (gxf3, gxf6). All 12 positions are endgames, and the played moves are universally quiet pawn pushes or king moves in the wrong direction.
analysis.why_bad: By playing a quiet pawn push or misdirected king move instead of simply capturing the adjacent hanging piece, the player throws away 3-5 points of material. In an endgame, this material loss is typically decisive—converting a winning position into a draw or loss, often because the enemy piece was the sole blockader of a passed pawn or the only defensive resource.

analysis.label: Player ignores a quiet knight or bishop move that would win significant material, instead playing an aimless positional or developing move.
analysis.description: In 94% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 6.0, typically a full piece or more), yet the best move is a capture only 15% of the time and a check only 9%—meaning the winning shot is almost always a quiet piece redeployment (fork, attack on undefended piece, or threat-creation). The played moves are quiet 84% of the time and often leave the player's own piece slightly exposed (53% hang own material, median value 1.0, mostly pawns). The best moves across the top boards are overwhelmingly knight maneuvers (Na4, Na5, Nc4, Nd2) or bishop repositionings (Be3, Bd7, Bc4, Bd6) that create unavoidable tactical threats.
analysis.why_bad: The player makes a natural-looking quiet move (development, pawn push, or piece repositioning) while completely overlooking that a specific knight or bishop move would create an irrefutable tactical threat—likely a fork, attack on an undefended piece, or creation of dual threats—netting roughly a full piece or more of material. The resulting position is significantly worse because the tactical opportunity is gone and the played move often weakens the player's own structure (53% leave a pawn or minor piece en prise).

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture or aggressive move that leaves their own major piece (usually a rook) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively shows a 'hung own piece' pattern: 70% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging with a median value of 5.0 (a rook). The hung-piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (208 major vs 66 minor vs 75 pawn out of 349 total). Critically, 48% of the played moves are captures themselves, revealing the mechanism: the player grabs material greedily but in doing so exposes a higher-value piece. The best move also wins material 60% of the time (median 3.0), indicating that a more careful sequence—often a quiet repositioning, a different capture order, or a zwischenzug—would still gain material without the catastrophic counter-capture. The feature fires broadly at 8.3% of positions, consistent with a general tactical oversight pattern across endgames (67%) and middlegames.
analysis.why_bad: The player's capture or active move wins a pawn or minor piece but simultaneously leaves a rook or queen undefended—either the capturing piece itself lands on an unprotected square, or the capture removes a defender of another piece. The opponent recaptures the hanging major piece, resulting in a net material loss far exceeding the initial gain (median 5.0 points lost vs. small material won).

analysis.label: The player neglects a simple pawn recapture and instead plays a piece move that leaves their own material hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 56% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distribution: 150 pawns, 62 minors, 61 majors), while the best move was a capture 51% of the time with a median material gain of 1.0 (a pawn). Examining the top 12 boards reveals that nearly all best moves are simple pawn captures or recaptures (hxg6, hxg3, fxg3, axb3, cxb3, fxg3, etc.), suggesting the opponent has just captured a pawn and the player should retake with a pawn. Instead, the player ignores this recapture and plays an unrelated piece move (bishop, knight, queen, or rook relocation), which frequently leaves their own material en prise. The average cp_loss of 2362 indicates these are often catastrophic blunders turning won or equal positions into losses or forced mates.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the simple pawn recapture, the player both loses the material they could recover (typically a pawn) and simultaneously exposes their own pieces to capture. The piece moves played are often tempo-losing or positionally irrelevant compared to the straightforward recapture, and the resulting material deficit (or outright hanging piece) gives the opponent a decisive advantage.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (often with check) that leaves their own major piece hanging and undefended on the destination square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 92% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0), with the piece class distribution overwhelmingly skewed toward major pieces (9 major vs 2 minor vs 1 pawn). Critically, 85% of the played moves were themselves captures, meaning the player is actively capturing enemy material but leaving their capturing piece en prise. The best move wins material only 54% of the time (median 1.0), indicating the correct play was often a quiet consolidating move rather than a capture. The feature fires exclusively in endgames with an average cp_loss of 2756, reflecting catastrophic blunders where queens (value 9) and rooks (value 5) are dropped.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player is seduced by an immediate tactical gain—capturing a piece, often with check—without verifying that their capturing piece will survive on its destination square. In endgames with few defenders, the capturing piece (queen or rook) lands on a square where it is unprotected and can be recaptured or trapped. The check gives a false sense of safety ('I have time because it's check') but after the king moves, the hanging piece is simply taken. The correct moves typically involve patient king maneuvers, quiet consolidation, or winning combinations that don't leave material en prise.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive check (often winning the queen or forcing mate) and played an inferior move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that in 93% of activating positions, the best move is a CHECK, and in 87% of cases it wins material with a median value of 91 (roughly queen-level). The played moves were captures only 44% of the time, and 75% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0). The top boards confirm this: the best moves are checks like Qxc1+, Qd2+, Rf1+, Qxc8+, Qa5+, Qd6+ — powerful checks against exposed kings that either win the opponent's queen, lead to unstoppable mating nets, or gain decisive material through forcing sequences. The opponent's king is typically exposed or poorly shielded, making the check devastating.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore the most forcing continuation — a check that either wins major material or delivers checkmate. Instead, players grab lesser material (like recapturing a piece on f7 or f2), make quiet developing moves, or execute exchanges that are strategically inferior. By not checking first, they allow the opponent to stabilize, neutralize threats, or even turn the tables. The check-first principle ensures maximum forcing power, and missing it often converts a winning position into equality or even a loss.

analysis.label: The player captures material (often with check) using their Queen or Rook, but the capturing piece is left hanging or trapped on the destination square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 90% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 9.0, i.e., a Queen), while 72% of the moves were themselves captures. The own-hang piece class distribution is overwhelmingly major pieces (63 major vs 5 minor). In 60% of cases the best move could win material (median 1.0), indicating the player was often tempted by lesser material gain rather than a quieter continuation. Only 29% of best moves are captures and only 13% are checks, showing that the correct alternative was typically a non-forcing positional move rather than the flashy capture chosen. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, isolating a specific geometry where a Queen (or Rook) enters enemy territory to grab material but cannot escape.
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece (almost always the Queen) lands on a square where the opponent can recapture or trap it, resulting in a net loss of a full Queen or Rook. The check or capture creates an illusion of initiative, but after the opponent responds (moving the king or recapturing), the attacking piece has no safe retreat. The player wins a pawn or minor piece but loses their Queen, a catastrophic net material loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet kingside pawn advance (h3/g3/h4) while missing a decisive tactical opportunity to win material or deliver checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player plays a meaningless kingside pawn push (h3, g3, h4, or g6) while ignoring a critical tactical shot. The SEE aggregate shows that 72% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0 — a full piece), yet only 10% of played moves are captures, confirming the player completely disengages from the tactics. Additionally, 60% of the time the quiet pawn push leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0; distribution: 83 pawns, 55 majors, 33 minors), often because the pawn push fails to address an existing threat. The best moves are frequently checks (19%) or captures (38%) — forcing moves like Qxf7+, Rb7+, Rf6+, Rd1+, Rxb5+ — while the player instead pushes a rook-pawn or knight-pawn one square forward on the kingside, accomplishing nothing.
analysis.why_bad: These h3/g3/h4 moves are completely non-functional — they don't create threats, don't defend attacked pieces, and don't address the critical tactical situation on the board. Meanwhile, the opponent's threats continue unabated (hanging own pieces get captured) and winning tactical blows (captures with check, forks, mating attacks) go unexploited. The player appears to be on autopilot, making a 'safe-looking' pawn move instead of engaging with the position's demands.

analysis.label: In the opening, the player develops or places a piece on a square where it is immediately hanging to an enemy pawn or piece, ignoring an obvious capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 78% of the played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 2.0), with minor pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (35 minors vs 10 pawns vs 4 majors). Meanwhile, 68% of best moves were simple captures (mostly central pawn recaptures like exd4, dxe5, dxe4, cxd5, Bxc4) and 52% won material. The pattern is clear: in the earliest opening phase, the player ignores an available pawn exchange or recapture and instead develops a piece directly to a square controlled by an enemy pawn—Nc3 into a d4 pawn, Nf6 into an e5 pawn, Bg5/Bh6/Ba6 to undefended squares where they are immediately captured.
analysis.why_bad: The developed piece is placed on a square already attacked by an enemy pawn (or left completely undefended), resulting in its immediate capture. Meanwhile, the player forfeits an obvious central pawn capture that would have maintained equality or won material. The net result is losing a minor piece (or pawn) for nothing while also missing out on the natural best continuation.

analysis.label: A challenged bishop retreats to a rim square (a5/a4/h4/h5) instead of making the principled exchange.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a bishop under pressure (typically challenged by a pawn advance like a3, h3, or ...a6) retreats to the edge of the board instead of executing the correct exchange. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture 97% of the time but wins material only 3% (median 2.0), meaning these are equal-value exchanges (bishop for knight/bishop) that should be accepted. The played move is never a capture (0%) and is always a quiet bishop retreat to a rim square. In 29% of cases (median value 2.0, split between minors and pawns), the retreat actually leaves the player's own piece hanging. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, exclusively in the opening phase.
analysis.why_bad: Retreating the bishop to the rim (Ba5, Ba4, Bh4, Bh5) misplaces it on a passive square where it often becomes trapped or tactically vulnerable. The principled exchange (Bxc3+, Bxf6, Bxc6, Bxf3) was available and theoretically sound—accepting doubled pawns for the opponent or resolving tension favorably. The retreat wastes tempo, the bishop frequently needs to be exchanged later under worse circumstances, and in many cases the rim bishop becomes a direct tactical target (29% leave own material hanging). Average cp_loss of 311 confirms these are severe positional/tactical errors.

analysis.label: The player overlooked a forcing check (often a back-rank check) that would deliver checkmate or win massive material, instead playing a quiet or irrelevant move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 48% of best moves are checks and 56% of best moves win material with a remarkably high median value of 9.0 (queen-level or checkmate). Best moves are captures 62% of the time. Only 27% of played moves were captures, meaning players overwhelmingly chose quiet, non-forcing alternatives. The 'own hung' rate of 35% with median value 1.0 is incidental noise — the dominant signal is the missed winning check. Many positions show SEE values of 95-100 (indicating forced mate), consistent with the astronomical average cp_loss of 2513. The pattern fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating these are rare but catastrophic oversights of immediately decisive checks.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a forcing check that either delivers immediate checkmate (back-rank mates in Positions 1, 6, 9, 12) or wins the queen/decisive material through a discovered or direct check. By playing a quiet move instead, the player squanders a completely winning position — often converting a forced mate into a merely advantageous or even losing position. The opponent survives the back-rank weakness or escapes the tactical pattern entirely.

analysis.label: Player develops or repositions a bishop instead of capturing a freely available enemy piece.
analysis.description: In 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 90% of the time the best move is a simple capture. Instead of taking the hanging enemy piece, the player makes a quiet bishop move (Be2, Be7, Bd3, Bd7, Bd2, etc.)—a development or repositioning move that ignores the free material. The played move also leaves the player's own piece hanging 71% of the time (median value 3.0), compounding the error. The feature fires overwhelmingly in the opening (8/12 top boards) where the player instinctively 'develops' a bishop rather than recapturing an enemy piece that just took one of theirs, or collecting an undefended enemy piece sitting en prise.
analysis.why_bad: The player's quiet bishop move forfeits winning a full piece (or more) of free material. In many cases an enemy piece has just captured on an undefended square and demands immediate recapture (e.g., Qxf3, bxc3, Qxf6), but the player instead develops another bishop, losing the exchange opportunity and often simultaneously leaving their own material unprotected, resulting in a swing of ~450-500cp on average.

analysis.label: Player misses a decisive check against an exposed enemy king, opting for a quiet non-forcing move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: 92% of best moves are checks, and 77% win material (median value ~100cp, i.e., a full piece). The played moves were captures only 20% of the time, meaning the vast majority of actual moves were quiet, non-forcing piece maneuvers. All 12 top-activating positions feature an exposed enemy king and a devastating available check (Re6+, Bf3+, Rxh7+, Rd8+, Rh5+, g5+, Rxh2+, Rxb5+, Rxc6+, e3+) that the player completely overlooked in favor of slow rook lifts, piece repositioning, or other quiet moves. The 49% own-hang rate (median value 1, mostly pawns) is a secondary consequence—by playing a slow move, the player sometimes incidentally leaves a pawn loose—but the primary mistake is the missed check. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting the specific geometry of an exposed king plus an available decisive check that was ignored.
analysis.why_bad: By playing quiet, non-forcing moves (rook shuffles, piece repositions) instead of the available check, the player forfeits a winning tactical blow—often a check that wins a piece or forces immediate mate. The opponent then gets a free tempo to consolidate, escape the king, or launch their own counterattack, resulting in an average centipawn loss of 3361.

analysis.label: Player moves their Queen (or Rook) instead of addressing an urgent king-safety crisis, leaving the moved piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of the time the player's move left their OWN piece hanging (median value 5.0, with 317 major pieces among the hung pieces). The best move wins material 65% of the time (median 3.0), typically because it first saves the king and then allows winning something back. Only 21% of moves played were captures and only 8% of best moves are checks, indicating the best response was usually a quiet king retreat. Across the top 500 positions, the player consistently ignores severe threats to their own king and instead plays a Queen or Rook move that leaves that piece en prise to the opponent's already-active attacking forces.
analysis.why_bad: The player's king is under severe attack (often near-mate), and the position demands an immediate king move to escape the mating net or reduce threats. Instead, the player makes a Queen or Rook move—sometimes attempting counterplay or defense from the wrong angle—that completely ignores the opponent's forcing continuation. Because the opponent has such dominant piece coordination aimed at the king, they can simply capture the hanging Queen/Rook (often via an intermediate check or discovered attack), converting their positional advantage into immediate material gain or mate.

analysis.label: Player misses a central pawn thrust (typically ...d5) that wins an undefended bishop on c4 in Italian Game structures.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 92% of positions have a best move winning material with a median value of 3.0 (a minor piece, overwhelmingly the Bc4). The best move is a capture only 24% of the time — meaning it is usually a pawn *advance* (d5) that attacks the hanging bishop rather than a direct capture. The played move is a capture only 16% of the time, confirming players chose quiet developing moves instead. In 45% of cases the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median 2.0, mostly pawns and minors), compounding the error. The feature fires exclusively in the opening (100%) in Italian/Two Knights/King's Gambit positions where White's Bc4 is aggressively placed but tactically vulnerable to ...d5.
analysis.why_bad: Moves like Qe7, Nh5, Ng4, f5, Bd6, and Be6 all fail to challenge White's central structure. They address the e5 threat passively (retreating the knight or blocking) while ignoring that ...d5 simultaneously counter-attacks the undefended Bc4 and neutralizes the e5 pawn. By missing d5, players lose a tempo, forfeit a free minor piece, and often leave their own knight or pawn hanging — turning a winning position into a losing one.

analysis.label: Player makes a greedy capture or poor king move instead of consolidating when their own king is exposed, hanging material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is dangerously exposed and requires careful defensive/consolidating play, but the player instead makes an impulsive move—often a capture (27% of played moves are captures) or a worsening king move. The result is that 52% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 92 instances, with 31 minor and 31 major pieces). Meanwhile, 45% of best moves would win material (median value 3.0), yet only 13% of best moves are captures—indicating the correct continuations are quiet consolidating moves (like Qg2, Be2, O-O-O, h5, Kd7) that address king safety and only win material indirectly through improved coordination.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores the critical vulnerability of their own king. By making greedy captures or moving the king to worse squares, they leave pieces undefended or allow the opponent's active pieces to exploit the exposed king. The correct moves typically consolidate the position—offering trades, castling, or repositioning defensively—which would both protect the king and preserve/win material.

analysis.label: Player gives an ineffective queen check, missing a winning move (often forced mate or decisive material gain).
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player delivers a queen check that accomplishes nothing meaningful while a far superior move exists. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 75% of cases (median value 9.0, i.e., a queen's worth — often indicating missed forced mate), while the best move is a check only 40% of the time and a capture 30%, meaning the optimal continuation is frequently a non-queen, non-check move. The played move is a capture only 20% of the time, and critically, 67% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with 52 major pieces, 42 pawns, 21 minor pieces exposed). This indicates that after the useless check resolves, the queen ends up misplaced and other pieces are left undefended. All 12 top-activating moves are queen checks, predominantly in endgames with exposed kings where mate or decisive wins are available.
analysis.why_bad: These queen checks are impulsive and non-constructive — the opponent's king simply sidesteps, and the checking player has squandered a tempo (or many). Meanwhile, forced mates (positions 1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 all had mates in 1-5), material wins, or decisive quiet moves go unplayed. After the pointless check, the queen is often on an inferior square, leaving the player's own pieces unguarded and allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterattack.

analysis.label: Player makes a prophylactic pawn move (h3/a3/a6/h6) to kick an enemy bishop instead of executing an available tactical blow that wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 51% of cases (median value: 2.0 pawns) and is a capture 41% of the time or a check 11% of the time, yet the player's move is almost never a capture (only 3%). The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet prophylactic pawn pushes (h3, a3, a6, h6) aimed at displacing an enemy bishop that is creating a pin or pressure (typically Bg4 pinning Nf3, Bb5 pinning Nc6, or Bg5 pinning Nf6). Instead of calculating concrete tactics—most commonly Bxf7+ sacrifices deflecting the king, or simple captures of undefended pieces—the player defaults to a routine anti-pin pawn nudge. The own-piece-hanging rate of 25% is secondary noise; the dominant signal is missed tactical opportunities where aggressive play refutes the opponent's bishop sortie far more effectively than passively chasing it.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn moves waste a critical tempo addressing a bishop that is actually tactically vulnerable or irrelevant. In most cases (especially Bxf7+ positions), the opponent's bishop sortie to g4/b4/b5 has left weaknesses elsewhere (f7, hanging pieces, exposed king), and the correct response is to punish the over-extension with a concrete tactical strike rather than giving the opponent time to consolidate. The prophylactic move treats the position as quiet when it demands immediate action.

analysis.label: Player makes a seemingly active or aggressive move (often a check) that leaves their own piece en prise while missing a straightforward material-winning capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses an 'active' non-capturing move that is doubly flawed: 72% of the time the played move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across minors, pawns, and majors), and 63% of the time the best move would have won enemy material via a simple capture (median value 3.0, with best move being a capture 63% of the time). Only 13% of played moves are captures, showing the player systematically avoids material-winning moves in favor of flashy-looking alternatives. The played moves are frequently checks (6 of the top 12 boards feature checks like Nc7+, Qc7+, Qd6+, Rxb4+) that appear tactically active but actually worsen the position catastrophically (avg cp_loss: 2618).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes apparent activity—checks, centralization, threats—over concrete material considerations. The aggressive move typically places a piece where it can be captured (e.g., Nc7+ leaving the knight trapped, Rxb4+ sacrificing the rook for a meaningless check, Ra2 leaving the rook hanging) while simultaneously ignoring a free enemy piece that could have been captured. The result is a net material swing of often 3+ pawns worth against the player.

analysis.label: Player missed a decisive check (usually a rook check) in an endgame that would win material or save the game, instead playing a passive move that often hangs their own rook.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 70% of the best moves are checks and 80% win material with a median value of 100 (i.e., game-deciding). Only 10% of the best moves are direct captures, confirming that the winning tactic is an intermediate check that leads to material gain or a forced sequence, not a simple recapture. Meanwhile, 50% of the played moves left the player's own major piece (rook) hanging (median value 5), showing the player's 'natural' move often walked into a tactic. All positions are endgames—predominantly rook endgames—where a check along a file or rank would exploit the enemy king's exposed position to either win material, force perpetual, or deliver mate.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player makes a seemingly logical move (king retreat, pawn capture, rook repositioning) without noticing that a check-first move order exploits the opponent's exposed king. The check either wins material directly (e.g., forking king and rook), forces a perpetual to save a drawn position, or initiates a mating net. By skipping the check, the player either hangs their own rook to the opponent's piece or squanders a winning/drawing opportunity entirely.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet or irrelevant move that leaves one of their own pieces en prise, ignoring an urgent tactical need to capture or play a forcing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate over 500 positions shows that 86% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, roughly evenly split between major pieces [34], minor pieces [31], and pawns [13]). Simultaneously, 74% of the time the best move would have won enemy material (median value 3.0), with 42% being captures and 21% being checks. Only 30% of the played moves were captures — the vast majority were quiet moves (like a3, h5, b6, Ra7) that ignored an existing or newly-created threat to the player's own piece. The pattern is consistent: rather than addressing the tactical tension by capturing the threatening/vulnerable enemy piece or delivering a forcing check, the player drifts with a passive or irrelevant move, leaving a bishop, rook, knight, or queen undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediate tactical obligation. In nearly every case, an enemy piece is either attacking one of the player's pieces or a simple capture/check would resolve the position favorably. By playing a quiet, non-urgent move instead, the player gifts the opponent a free piece — often a minor piece (bishop/knight worth ~3) or even a major piece (rook/queen). The resulting material deficit is typically decisive.

analysis.label: Player gives a reflexive, non-productive check in an endgame instead of the correct quiet or material-winning move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player delivers a check that accomplishes nothing strategically, while a superior quiet move exists. The SEE aggregate reveals that in 51% of cases the best move wins material (median value 1.0), yet only 4% of played moves are captures—the player chose a check instead of taking hanging material. Critically, only 5% of best moves are checks, yet 100% of the top-12 played moves are checks, confirming the pattern of reflexive, aimless checking. The average cp_loss of 3223 is catastrophic, with multiple positions converting forced mates into draws or large-advantage losses. The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet (Kf4, Kb4, Kg7, Qf5, Qb4, Qh8)—king approaches, captures, or mating-net constructions that make real progress.
analysis.why_bad: The checks drive the opponent's king to safety, allow stalemate defenses (e.g., Position 9: Qb7+ turns mate-in-6 into a draw), waste tempo in critical races against passed pawns, or simply miss capturing undefended material. By checking, the player gives the opponent forced squares that often improve the king's position or enable drawing resources, rather than tightening the net with quiet technique.

analysis.label: Player missed an immediate checkmate-in-one delivered by the Queen capturing a pawn (typically h2, h7, g2, or b2).
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player has a Queen checkmate in one move available but plays something else entirely. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 82% of cases and a check in 70%, with material won of median 1.0 (the captured pawn). The average cp_loss of ~9021 confirms a full mate being missed. All 12 top-activating positions show Qxh2#, Qxh7#, Qxg2#, or Qxb2# available — the Queen captures an undefended or inadequately defended pawn adjacent to the enemy king, delivering immediate checkmate. The 27% own-hang rate is incidental noise from some played moves, not the defining pattern. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, consistent with the rarity of having mate-in-one on the board yet failing to play it.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (quiet developing moves like Nf6, b5, a6, Be6, or mundane captures like dxe5, cxd5) completely ignore the fact that the Queen can immediately end the game by capturing a pawn with checkmate. The players appear to overlook the open diagonal or file leading the Queen to the fatally weak square next to the enemy king, instead pursuing irrelevant positional or tactical ideas.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting but inferior capture while missing a much larger tactical win elsewhere on the board.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of played moves are captures, yet the best move wins material 62% of the time with a median value of 5.0 (rook-level), indicating the player consistently grabs a lesser prize while a bigger one is available. Furthermore, 57% of the played captures leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minor pieces), meaning the inferior capture often comes with an additional cost. The best move is a capture only 38% of the time and a check 14%, showing the superior alternative isn't always an obvious recapture—it may be a quiet move, a promotion, or a checking move that wins much more. The feature fires on a negligible fraction of positions (0.0%), confirming this is a specific tactical error pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The player is lured by an immediately available capture—often a king recapture (Kxg7, Kxf8, Kxe2, Kxf2) or a knight grab (Nxe4, Nxf3+, Nxe5)—but this move either wins less material than the optimal alternative (typically capturing a hanging rook or delivering a winning check) or actively leaves the player's own minor piece undefended. By prioritizing the obvious/nearby capture over the truly best move, the player converts a winning or equal position into a losing one, with average centipawn loss of 232.

analysis.label: Player retreats a knight to a passive square (d2/e2/d7/e7), missing active tactical alternatives and often leaving pawns undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a passive, retreating knight move to a non-active square. The SEE aggregate shows that 42% of the time the best move wins material (median value 2.0, often a minor piece or pawn grab), and 42% of the time the played knight move leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with pawns being the most common victim at 125/202). Only 4% of played moves are captures, confirming the passivity of the chosen knight move. The best move is a capture 27% of the time, showing concrete material is being missed. All top-12 activating moves are knight retreats/repositions to squares like d2, e2, d7, e7 — second-rank or back-rank squares that block development or neglect tactical obligations.
analysis.why_bad: These passive knight retreats waste tempo by repositioning to inactive squares (d2, e2, d7) when the position demands concrete action. The knight often blocks other pieces (e.g., blocking the queen's access to d2) or abandons defense of pawns. Meanwhile, the position contains tactical opportunities — hanging enemy pieces, winning captures, or strong centralizing moves — that go unexploited. The retreat often also leaves pawns undefended because the knight was previously contributing to their protection.

analysis.label: The player moves a piece (predominantly a rook) to an undefended square where it is immediately captured by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate decisively identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 99% of the played moves leave the player's own piece en prise, with a median hung value of 5.0 (rook). The piece class distribution (340 major, 144 minor, 11 pawn) confirms rooks and queens are the primary victims. Only 31% of the played moves are captures, meaning the majority are quiet moves that simply place a piece on an unsafe square. The best moves win material only 46% of the time (often because simply not hanging would suffice), and the best move is rarely a capture (12%) or check (8%) — indicating the correct play is usually a quiet repositioning that keeps the piece defended.
analysis.why_bad: These moves place a piece (usually a rook) on a square that looks active or tempting (capturing a pawn, occupying an open file, centralizing) but is tactically undefended. The opponent can simply capture the hanging piece for free or in an advantageous exchange, resulting in decisive material loss. The player overlooks that their piece has no protection on its destination square and falls into the enemy's attack radius.

analysis.label: Player misses a central pawn advance (d5 or e5) that forks two enemy pieces, typically a knight on c6 and bishop on e6.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 90% of positions have a best move winning material (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 13% of the time and never a check (0%). This indicates the winning move is a pawn advance that attacks multiple pieces simultaneously. The played move is a quiet non-capture (only 8% captures) and rarely hangs own material (22%, median just a pawn). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the missed best move is overwhelmingly d5 (or occasionally e5/e4) — a central pawn thrust that forks two enemy minor pieces clustered on the c6 and e6 squares in the opening. The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting a very specific geometric pattern where Black has developed a knight to c6 and bishop to e6 (or similar alignment) vulnerable to a single pawn advance.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Nf3, g3, O-O, d3, b3, etc.) are routine developing or prophylactic moves that ignore a concrete tactical opportunity. By not playing the central pawn advance immediately, the player allows the opponent to reposition their pieces off the vulnerable squares, dissolving the fork and losing 2-3 pawns' worth of material advantage permanently.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player advances a pawn to a square where it becomes en prise instead of improving the king or choosing the correct pawn advance.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 62% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being overwhelmingly a pawn (31 pawns vs 4 minors). Only 34% of best moves win material, and the best move is rarely a capture (18%) or check (5%). All 12 top-activating positions are endgames, and the played moves are almost exclusively quiet pawn advances (b5, g5, g5, f3, e6, f4, h7, f5+, g4, g3+, e6, h5). The player pushes a pawn forward to a square where the opponent's king or piece can immediately capture it, rather than playing the superior king move (Ka5, Ke2, Kf2, Kg1, Kd6) or a better-timed pawn advance (e3, h4) that maintains pawn integrity.
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance places the pawn on a square controlled by the opponent's king or piece, allowing it to be captured for free. In these endgames, proper king positioning must come first—the king needs to support the pawn advance or the advance must be timed so the pawn is not immediately capturable. By pushing prematurely, the player throws away a pawn (or the game) in positions that were winning or drawn.

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece (usually a queen that infiltrated) but ignores a lethal back-rank mate threat, allowing immediate checkmate.
analysis.description: In the SEE aggregate, 99% of played moves are captures and 88% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 5.0, predominantly major pieces at 53/63). The best move wins material 82% of the time (median 5.0), but critically only 31% of best moves are captures — meaning the correct response was usually a defensive move (like Qe8, Qf8, creating luft, or blocking). The average cp_loss of 9708 confirms these are all mate-in-few blunders. The opponent places a queen deep in the player's territory as a decoy on the back rank; the player greedily captures it (usually Rook takes Queen), but by doing so either removes the only back-rank defender or places the capturing piece on a square where a forced back-rank mate follows immediately.
analysis.why_bad: The captures fail because the opponent's infiltrating piece (usually a queen) is actually bait — a second attacker (typically a rook on an open file) delivers checkmate on the back rank once the defender is lured away. The player's king is boxed in by its own pawns (f/g/h or a/b/c) with no escape squares, making the back-rank mate unstoppable after the greedy capture.

analysis.label: The player fails to promote a pawn on the 7th/2nd rank, playing an inferior alternative move instead.
analysis.description: Across all 12 top-activating positions, the best move is always an immediate pawn promotion (a8=Q, g8=Q, c1=Q, b8=Q, g1=Q, f1=Q+, d1=Q, a1=Q, etc.), yet the player makes a different move—typically a king move (Kh2, Kf1, Ke1, Kb8, Kc7), a capture (Kxg7, gxh4, Rxe7, cxd5+), or a quiet piece move (Rd8, Qe6, Qh1). The SEE aggregate shows best_wins_material at 56% (median value 3.0), reflecting the enormous material gain from queening; best move is a check in 26% of cases (promotion with check); and best move is a capture in only 9% (rarely a capture-promotion). The played moves were captures 35% of the time, indicating players get distracted by tactical captures rather than the decisive promotion. Own-piece-hanging after the played move is 35% (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), suggesting the unprotected promoting pawn sometimes becomes vulnerable when left on the 7th rank instead of being pushed.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to promote immediately, the player squanders a decisive material advantage (gaining a queen). In many cases (avg cp_loss 1931), the delay allows the opponent to counter-promote, set up perpetual checks, activate pieces, or neutralize the passed pawn entirely—turning wins into draws or even losses.

analysis.label: Player moves a minor piece (knight or bishop) to a square controlled by an enemy pawn or piece in the early opening, immediately hanging it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 91% of activating positions result in the player's own piece being left hanging (median value: 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The hung piece class distribution is overwhelmingly minor pieces (36 minor vs 3 pawn vs 2 major out of 41 instances). Only 4% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks, indicating the correct moves were simple developing moves rather than tactics. All 12 top positions are in the opening phase, and the played moves (Nxd5 into a pawn-defended square, Ba6 to an unprotected outpost, Bc4 where d5 attacks it, Nd4/Ne5 into pawn-controlled squares) consistently place a minor piece where it can be immediately won by the opponent.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player places a knight or bishop on a square already controlled by an enemy pawn or piece, allowing the opponent to simply capture the hanging piece for free (or win the exchange after a premature capture of a defended pawn). The moves ignore basic opening principles—the target squares are defended, and the placed pieces have no support, resulting in immediate material loss of approximately 3 pawns worth.

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player makes a move that leaves their own rook undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 100% of the player's moves left their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, corresponding to a rook), with the hung-piece class distribution overwhelmingly 'major' (104 of 108 classified). Only 39% of moves played were captures and just 50% of best moves win material, confirming the error is not about missing an opponent's hanging piece but about carelessly exposing one's own rook. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgame positions (11/12 top boards) involving rook endgames where the king and rook must coordinate carefully.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the player's rook undefended — either the king walks away from protecting the rook (Ke6, Kf6, Kc3, Kb3 abandon the rook's only defender), the rook moves to an unguarded square where it can be captured (Rg6, Rf6, Rh7+), or the rook captures a pawn on a square where it is immediately recaptured at a loss (Rxe4, Rxa7, Rxh7, Rxg5). In each case the opponent wins a full rook (≈5 pawns of material), turning drawn or even winning positions into decisive losses.

analysis.label: Player missed an available checkmate or forced mating attack (usually via a queen check) and instead played a mundane developing move or minor capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 90% of activating positions the best move wins material with a median value of 91 (encoding checkmate), and 75% of the time the best move is a check — while only 26% are captures. The player's actual move was a capture only 41% of the time and left their own piece hanging only 29% of the time. The extremely high average cp_loss of 8546 confirms these are positions where immediate checkmate or short forced mates were available but completely overlooked. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, consistent with the rarity of having mate-in-one or short forced mates available while choosing an entirely unrelated move.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (typically knight developments like Nd2, Nc3, Nf3, Nxe4, or minor captures like Bxh8, Nxb7) completely ignore a lethal king attack. Instead of delivering checkmate or initiating an unstoppable mating sequence with a queen check (Qg6#, Qd3#, Qh5+, Qd2#, Qf6+, Bf7#, etc.), the player makes a positionally plausible but catastrophically suboptimal move that allows the opponent to survive and potentially equalize or fight back.

analysis.label: Player missed a quiet minor-piece move (knight or bishop) that would have won the opponent's queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 9.0 (queen), yet only 7% of best moves are captures and only 1% are checks — indicating quiet piece moves that trap or fork the enemy queen. The best moves across the top boards are overwhelmingly knight moves (Nc3, Nc5, Nf5, Nf1, Nf3, Ne2) and bishop moves (Bd5, Bd4, Bd3, Bc5) that set up unavoidable queen wins. Instead, players make alternative moves that often leave their own pieces hanging (57% of played moves hang material, median value 3.0, distributed across minors, pawns, and majors). The feature fires on only 0.4% of positions, targeting rare situations where an opponent's aggressively-placed queen is actually tactically vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (checks, captures of peripheral material, passive king moves, or misguided piece maneuvers) all miss the critical tactical opportunity to win the opponent's queen via a trap or fork. By ignoring the queen-winning shot, players squander decisive advantages — often turning won positions into draws or losses, with an average cp_loss of 1048.

analysis.label: Player misses a move that attacks or traps the opponent's aggressively-placed, overextended queen.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 100% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 8.0, i.e., approximately a queen). Crucially, only 3% of these best moves are captures and 0% are checks — meaning the winning move is typically a quiet piece deployment that attacks or traps the enemy queen. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (79% non-captures), indicating the player chose a routine developing or repositioning move instead. The 46% own-hang rate (median value just 1.0, mostly pawns) is a secondary consequence of ignoring the threat, not the core mistake. Across all top boards, the opponent's queen is deep in hostile territory (g7, g2, b7, a7, b2, f3) and the best move (Rg8, Rg1, Rb8, Ra8, Rb1, Bg4, g6, f4) directly attacks or boxes in this overextended queen, winning decisive material.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Kd7, Ng1, Bd6, Rf8, O-O, Nb3, etc.) address secondary concerns — development, king safety, or prophylaxis — while completely overlooking that the opponent's queen is tactically vulnerable. By failing to attack the exposed queen with a simple piece or pawn move, the player forfeits a game-deciding material gain (typically winning the queen for little or no compensation).

analysis.label: Player fails to promote (or immediately enable promotion of) a far-advanced passed pawn, typically missing a queening move that often comes with check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 58% of best moves win material with a median value of 91 (queen-equivalent, consistent with pawn promotion), and 31% of best moves deliver check (promotion with check). Only 4% of best moves are captures, confirming the winning move is promotion rather than taking a piece. The played move was a capture only 12% of the time, and positions are exclusively endgames (100%). The player's move left their own piece hanging 36% of the time (median value just 1, i.e., the advanced pawn itself becoming vulnerable after a misguided push or king move). Across all 12 top-activating boards, the player had a pawn on the 7th/2nd rank (or a key preparatory move to enable immediate promotion) but instead played a quiet king move or irrelevant action, squandering a decisive advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available pawn promotion (often with check) that would create a decisive material advantage. By playing a king move or other quiet action instead of queening, the player allows the opponent to reposition defensively, blockade the pawn, capture it, or generate counterplay—turning a forced win (often mate) into a draw or loss.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive quiet move that leaves their own piece en prise, missing a stronger move that would win significant material (often by relocating the very piece that ends up hanging).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 90% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a full piece/rook), while the played move is rarely a capture (only 15%) and leaves the player's own piece hanging 68% of the time (median value 3.0). The hung pieces are predominantly minor pieces (40 instances), followed by pawns (26) and major pieces (18). The best move is a check only 9% of the time and a capture only 15%, meaning it is typically a quiet repositioning move — often moving the very piece that becomes hanging to a winning square. The boards confirm this: Bd7 winning the exchange vs a5 leaving the bishop hanging (Pos 1), Bb3 winning material vs Rdd1 leaving the bishop hanging (Pos 2), Bd6/Bd2/Bd4 as winning bishop relocations vs quiet moves that ignore the bishop's vulnerability (Pos 6, 10, 11, 12), and Ra2 winning a queen vs Qg4 leaving a rook hanging (Pos 7).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores both an opportunity and a threat simultaneously. The correct move typically saves a threatened piece by relocating it to an aggressive square that wins even more material. Instead, the player makes an unrelated quiet move (pawn push, king walk, or piece move to a suboptimal square), which both forfeits the winning opportunity and leaves the vulnerable piece undefended — resulting in a catastrophic net material swing.

analysis.label: Player ignores an available rook recapture (even exchange) and plays a quiet move, often leaving their own material en prise.
analysis.description: Across the top 500 activating positions, 97% of the best moves are captures—and in every one of the top 12 boards, the best move is specifically a rook capture (Rxe5, Rxf3, Rxf6, Rxe3, Rxd5, Rxf5, Rxd4, etc.) with SEE=0, indicating an even exchange or recapture. Only 18% of best moves win net material (median 1.0), confirming most are break-even recaptures rather than winning hanging pieces. Instead of recapturing, the player plays a quiet non-capturing move (only 11% of played moves are captures), and 47% of the time this leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distributed across pawns=93, minors=50, majors=26). The feature fires on just 0.2% of all positions, targeting a specific failure to complete a rook exchange.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to recapture with the rook (an even trade that maintains material balance), the player effectively loses material—either by leaving the original captured piece unrecovered, or by playing a quiet move that additionally leaves their own piece en prise. The resulting position is down material with no compensation, as shown by the average 75cp loss.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but unproductive check instead of simply capturing a hanging enemy piece worth significant material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 78% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0 pawns), and 65% of the time that best move is a capture. Yet the player's move was only a capture 23% of the time. Examining the top 12 boards shows the overwhelming pattern: 9 out of 12 moves played are checks (Rd3+, Rh3+, Rg7+, Bxf2+, Nd3+, Nc4+, Ne5+, Re7+, etc.), while the correct moves are simple captures of undefended or hanging enemy pieces (Bxe2, Rxd1, Bxh2, Bxa1, Nxd1, Nxc2, Nxh1, Nxh8). The 52% own-piece-hanging rate (median value only 1 pawn) is a secondary consequence of moving pieces to tactically exposed squares to deliver the check. This is the classic 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' error.
analysis.why_bad: The checks are unproductive — after the king sidesteps, the checking piece is often misplaced or en prise, and the opportunity to win a major or minor piece (typically worth 5+ pawns of material) has evaporated. The player trades a decisive material advantage for a tempo that leads nowhere.

analysis.label: Playing a pointless check (usually with a bishop) that leaves the moving piece or another piece en prise.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player gives a check—almost always a quiet bishop check (Bc5+, Bh6+, Bc4+, Bb6+)—that accomplishes nothing constructive while leaving material hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 69% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, with minor pieces most common at 29/63), while the best move wins material 59% of the time (median 3.0). Critically, only 6% of best moves are checks, confirming the played checks are not forced or useful. The played moves are captures only 14% of the time, meaning these are quiet checking moves to empty squares where the piece becomes vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: These checks are 'spite checks' or desperate/thoughtless checks that don't improve the position. The checking piece lands on an unprotected square where it can be captured, or the act of moving it leaves another piece undefended. Meanwhile, a better move existed—often winning material (capturing a hanging piece, consolidating, or addressing real threats). The check merely delays the inevitable by one move while making the position worse.

analysis.label: Player moves king elsewhere instead of capturing an adjacent undefended enemy piece (usually a rook) in the endgame.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 88% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook), and in 100% of cases the best move is a capture. The player's move is never a capture (0%), indicating they consistently fail to take a freely available piece. Only 25% of the time does the played move leave an own piece hanging (and only pawns), confirming this is a 'missed winning capture' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. Across the top boards, the geometry is strikingly consistent: the player's king stands directly adjacent to an undefended enemy piece (most often a rook on an adjacent square) in a simplified endgame, yet the player makes a quiet king move in a different direction instead of simply capturing.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to capture the adjacent hanging piece (usually a rook worth 5 points), the player throws away decisive material that would simplify into a winning or drawing endgame. Instead, the quiet king move allows the opponent to move the piece to safety or advance their own plans (pawn promotion, mating attacks), often turning a winning or salvageable position into an immediate loss or forced mate.

analysis.label: Player misses a game-deciding forcing move (winning the queen or forcing mate) and instead plays a greedy capture or passive king move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 71% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 9 (queen-level), and 25% of best moves are checks, while only 36% are captures—indicating many of these decisive blows are forcing check sequences that win the queen or deliver mate. The player's actual moves are captures only 29% of the time (often grabbing lesser material like pawns) while 58% leave their own piece hanging (median value 1, predominantly pawns). The enormous average cp_loss of 4169 confirms these are catastrophic errors: players either grab a pawn/minor piece while missing a queen win (Qxc2, gxh3, Qxd2, exd5, Rxf4) or make passive king moves (Kg8, Kh8, Kg7, Kd7, Kh1) that walk into mate or forfeit a winning attack. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions—specifically those critical tactical junctures where a single forcing move decides the game.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the highest-priority tactical element in the position. By capturing lesser material or making passive moves, the player either allows the opponent to escape a losing position (e.g., Position 4: Qxd2 grabs a piece but misses Qe5+ which forces mate) or walks directly into the opponent's mating net (e.g., Position 6: Kh8 allows immediate mate instead of Nxg6 winning White's queen). The decisive forcing move—typically a check or queen capture—was the only way to realize the position's full potential.

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a purposeless or wrong-direction king move when a concrete action (capturing an undefended piece or pushing a critical passed pawn) is required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame) where the player makes a suboptimal king move instead of executing the position's critical concrete demand. The SEE aggregate shows that in 37% of activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 5.0, typically a king capture of an undefended rook or bishop), yet the player's move is a capture only 3% of the time. In the remaining ~63% of positions, the best move is typically a pawn push in a pawn race or a non-king piece move. The player's move left their own piece hanging 20% of the time (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), often because the king moved away from defending a pawn or blocked its own pawn's path. The best move is a capture in 30% of positions. The average centipawn loss of 421 reflects how catastrophic these errors are in simplified endgames.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, king moves feel natural since king activity is a key principle. But these positions demand specific concrete actions: capturing an undefended piece adjacent to the king (positions 1-4), pushing a passed pawn in a race (positions 5-9, 12), or executing a precise tactical move (positions 10-11). The aimless king move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to promote, escape, or consolidate. The player appears to follow the general heuristic of 'centralize/activate the king' while missing the urgent tactical requirement of the specific position.

analysis.label: Player ignores a freely capturable enemy piece (often a queen) and plays an unrelated quiet move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 89% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material outright (median value: 6.0, i.e., roughly queen-minus-piece or rook-level gains), and 96% of best moves are simple captures. Yet the player's move was only a capture 23% of the time—meaning in the vast majority of cases the player played a quiet move that completely ignored the free enemy piece. The secondary signal that 55% of played moves also left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minor/major/pawn) reflects the compounding error: not only does the player miss the winning capture, but the alternative move chosen is often structurally careless. Examining the top 12 boards confirms the pattern: undefended enemy queens on h8, b5, g5, b3, f5, d6, g5 and rooks on d2 are directly capturable by a single piece, yet the player makes developing moves, checks, or positional shuffles instead.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately available capture of a high-value undefended enemy piece. Instead of collecting free material (typically a queen worth 9 points or a rook worth 5), the player pursues a positional idea, a flashy check, or a developing move that gains far less. The opponent then moves the hanging piece to safety, erasing the winning opportunity permanently. In many cases, the played move additionally leaves the player's own piece undefended, compounding the blunder.

analysis.label: Player makes a purposeless quiet queen move that leaves own pieces undefended or misses winning material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet queen repositioning move that is a serious blunder. The SEE aggregate shows 60% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed across pawns/131, minors/97, majors/72), while 63% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0). Only 12% of played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet queen shuffles. The move is a queen move in 11 of the top 12 activating positions, and the average centipawn loss is an enormous 1001, indicating these are catastrophic mistakes dressed up as normal development or repositioning.
analysis.why_bad: The queen moves to a square that serves no urgent tactical purpose, while either abandoning defense of another piece (rook, knight, or pawn left en prise once the queen departs) or ignoring a concrete tactical opportunity (capture, fork, or combination) that would win material. The queen's relocation fails to address the position's critical demands, resulting in immediate material loss.

analysis.label: Player made a quiet, routine move (often castling or simple development) while missing a decisive tactical blow that wins major material or delivers checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player missed winning material: 82% of best moves win material with a median value of 5.0 (queen-level), while only 13% of played moves were captures and only 22% left own pieces hanging (median just 1.0, mostly pawns). The best moves are checks 30% of the time and captures 29% of the time, indicating sharp tactical opportunities. The played moves are uniformly quiet—castling (O-O appears 4 times), piece development (Be3, Bb4, Ne5, Nd5), or pawn pushes (g3, f3)—all routine moves ignoring the presence of a winning combination. Multiple positions show the best move winning 97 centipawns of SEE material (indicating mate or winning the queen), including Nf3+, Nd6#, and Bd2+.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player defaults to routine opening or middlegame strategy (castling for safety, developing pieces to natural squares) instead of calculating concrete tactics. The position demanded immediate action—a check, capture, or forcing sequence that would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate—but the player chose comfort over calculation, throwing away a winning advantage.

analysis.label: Developing a bishop to g4 or g5 in the opening when it is left undefended and can be captured.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player develops a bishop to g4 or g5 prematurely, leaving it hanging. The SEE aggregate shows 61% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with minor pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (176 of 230 instances). Only 9% of the played moves were captures, confirming these are quiet developing moves that blunder material. In 48% of cases, the best move would have won material (median 3.0), often by addressing the opponent's active knight (frequently on e5) rather than making a bishop move with no support. The pattern overwhelmingly involves opening positions (11 of 12 top boards) with both kings still in the center.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop is developed to g4/g5 expecting to pin a knight on f3/f6 to the queen, but the target knight has often already moved (e.g., to e5), so there is no pin and the bishop sits unprotected on a square where it can be captured by the queen (Qxg4/Qxg5) or another piece. Additionally, the developing move ignores urgent positional needs like addressing a powerful centralized enemy knight or castling, compounding the material loss with a strategic deficit.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy knight that can be captured, usually by a simple pawn take.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e. a knight/minor piece), and 75% of the time the best move is a capture, yet the player's move was a capture only 3% of the time. Across all 12 top-activating positions, an enemy knight sits completely undefended on a central or advanced square (e4, d5, c6, f4, d4) and can be captured—almost always by a pawn (dxe4, cxd5, bxc6, exf4, fxe5). Instead, the player makes a quiet developing or positional move (castling, pawn push, piece development) and forfeits a full piece. All positions occur in the opening phase with an average cp_loss of 470, consistent with ignoring a free minor piece.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks that an enemy knight has moved to a square where it is completely unprotected and directly attacked by a pawn. By playing a quiet move instead of the simple pawn capture, the player gives the opponent time to retreat or defend the knight, permanently losing the opportunity to win a full piece (≈3 pawns of material) for free.

analysis.label: Player gives a tempting but unproductive check that leaves their own piece hanging after the opponent escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 78% of played moves leave the player's own piece en prise (median value 3.0, spread across majors 125, pawns 98, minors 78). Critically, ALL 12 top-activating moves are checks (+), yet the best move is a check only 12% of the time. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check, but after the opponent's king moves or blocks, a piece is left undefended. The best moves (which win material 66% of the time, median 3.0) are typically quiet defensive or positional moves (Qf7, Rb4, Ne8, Qe7, Qg7, f6) that maintain coordination while exploiting the opponent's weaknesses without self-inflicted tactical damage.
analysis.why_bad: A check only delays the opponent by one tempo. Once the king escapes (which it always can in these positions), the checking piece or another piece is left hanging with no compensation. The player squanders a winning or equal position by prioritizing a superficially forcing move over maintaining piece safety and coordination. The massive average cp_loss of 3351 reflects that many of these checks turn decisive advantages into immediate losses or even get mated.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture the opponent's completely undefended queen in the opening, instead playing a quiet developing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 94% of best moves win material with a median value of 9.0 (queen value), and 97% of best moves are captures, while the player's move was a capture only 19% of the time. All 12 top-activating positions occur in the opening phase and feature an opponent's queen sitting en prise on an exposed square (g4, g5, h4, h5, c5, a5, e5) where it can be taken immediately by a piece or pawn. The player instead plays a quiet move (d6, Nf3, Bg2, h3, etc.), completely ignoring the free queen. The 45% own-hang rate (median 3.0) is a secondary effect where some of these quiet moves also leave the player's own pieces tactically exposed, but the primary mistake is failing to capture the undefended enemy queen.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet developing moves forfeit approximately 9 points of material (a full queen) that could be won immediately with a simple capture. The opponent has overextended their queen in the opening to an undefended square, and failing to punish this is the most severe possible positional/tactical oversight — essentially declining a free queen.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own queen en prise, allowing it to be captured.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player hangs their own piece: 90% of positions leave an own piece hanging (median value 4.0), with the piece class distribution dominated by 'major' pieces (260 out of 310 classified instances). Across 11 of the top 12 boards, the specific piece left en prise is the Queen (values of 4-9 in SEE). Only 31% of played moves are captures themselves, meaning most blunders are quiet moves that either ignore an active threat to the queen, move a critical defender of the queen, or misplace the queen onto an unprotected square.
