The best moves (40% captures, 10% checks) often involve simply taking a free piece or sidestepping the danger, yet the player instead makes a move oblivious to the queen's vulnerability.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the player's queen — the most valuable piece on the board — undefended or capturable on the next move. Whether the player moves the king ignoring a queen attack (Ke6, Kf2), moves a knight away from queen defense (Nh5, Ne5, Ng4), places the queen on an unsafe square (Qf4, Qf2, Qe6), or captures with the queen on a trapped/defended square (Qxf7, Qxf6), the result is the immediate or near-immediate loss of the queen, typically costing 4-9 points of material.

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking bishop move to b4/b5/g4/g5 in the opening that appears active but is tactically premature, leaving material undefended or the bishop misplaced.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where a player deploys their bishop aggressively to the 4th or 5th rank (Bb4, Bb5, Bg4, Bg5) — typically creating a pin or attack — when the position demands more urgent moves. The SEE aggregate shows that 26% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0, often a capturable pawn the player ignores), and 26% of the time the played move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 1.0, with 36 pawns and 14 minors in the hung-piece distribution). Only 3% of the played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet bishop development moves. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, targeting a very specific pattern of flashy but unsound bishop sorties in the opening phase (all 12 top positions are opening positions with average cp_loss of 419).
analysis.why_bad: These bishop moves look active (pinning a knight, attacking a piece) but ignore concrete positional or tactical needs: in QGA positions, Bb4 neglects defending the extra c4-pawn (which b5 would secure); Bb5 moves often place the bishop where it has no real target and can be kicked with tempo, wasting development time while the king remains in the center; the sortie frequently leaves pawns undefended or allows the opponent to gain a tempo attacking the misplaced bishop, converting the initiative into a material or positional advantage.

analysis.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, the player moves their king away from (or prematurely promotes) their own critical passed pawn, leaving it undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 62% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distribution: 12 pawns, 3 majors), while the best move wins material only 29% of the time and is never a check or capture (0%/0%). This indicates the mistake is not about missing enemy material but about abandoning one's own assets. Across 500 endgame positions, the player's king walks away from its own passed pawn—often to capture a less important distant enemy pawn (25% captures)—or promotes prematurely into a capturable queen, while the correct move involves quietly supporting or advancing the passed pawn (or repositioning the king to maintain contact with it).
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king proximity to one's own passed pawn is paramount. By moving the king away to capture a distant enemy pawn, or by promoting immediately when the opponent's king sits on the promotion square, the player abandons the pawn that constituted their winning advantage. The opponent's king then captures the undefended pawn (or newly-promoted queen), converting a winning position into a draw or loss. The correct moves—quiet king repositioning or pawn advances—maintain the connection between king and pawn needed for successful promotion.

analysis.label: The player misses a winning check on the e-file (Qe7+, Qe2+, or Re1+) that exploits the opponent's centralized king to win the queen.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a devastating e-file check that wins major material. The SEE aggregate is definitive: the best move is a check in 100% of the top 500 positions, and it wins material 94% of the time with a median value of 91 (queen-level). The best moves are overwhelmingly Qe7+, Qe2+, or Re1+ — all exploiting an uncastled king on e1/e8 along the open e-file. The played moves are mostly quiet (72% non-captures) and leave the player's own piece hanging 60% of the time (median value 3, distributed across minor/pawn/major classes). The feature activates exclusively in the opening phase (10/12 top boards) when both kings remain in the center with weak pawn shields, and the e-file is open or semi-open, creating the tactical precondition for the winning check.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing check on the e-file that either directly wins the opponent's queen (pinned or forked against the king) or forces the king to move, losing castling rights and allowing a decisive material gain. By playing quiet developing moves, captures of lesser pieces, or even castling, the player squanders a one-move tactical shot worth approximately a queen, often turning a winning or equal position into a losing one (average cp_loss: 279).

analysis.label: Player captures with the f-pawn (fxe5/fxe4) in the opening instead of developing a knight to cover the weakened king diagonal.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 84% of the time (median 1.0 pawn) yet is a capture only 6% of the time—meaning the correct move is a developing/defensive move (Nf3, Nf6, d5) that indirectly secures material. The player's move is a capture 27% of the time (mostly fxe5-type pawn takes). The played move leaves the player's own piece hanging 37% of the time (median value 3.0, with minor pieces and pawns most common). The feature fires exclusively in opening positions (100%) where the f-pawn has been advanced in King's Gambit-style structures, weakening the e1-h4 (or e8-h5) diagonal while the king remains uncastled. Instead of developing Nf3/Nf6 to cover the critical h4/h5 square, the player grabs the e-pawn with the f-pawn, catastrophically opening the diagonal.
analysis.why_bad: Capturing fxe5 (or fxe4) removes the f-pawn that was the last barrier on the weakened king diagonal (e1-h4 or e8-h5). With the king uncastled and no knight on f3/f6, the opponent plays Qh4+ (or Qh5+), launching a devastating attack that typically wins at least a pawn and often more, since the king is forced to move and loses castling rights while facing ongoing threats.

analysis.label: Player misses a minor-piece sacrifice capturing a weakened kingside pawn (h6/g6/h3/g4/g3) that opens devastating attacking lines against the enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 91% of best moves are captures, yet only 30% 'win material' by static exchange (median value won just 1.0 pawn). This seeming contradiction is explained by the top 12 boards: in every case the best move is a piece sacrifice on a weakened kingside pawn (Bxh6 x5, Bxg6 x2, Bxh3 x2, Bxg4, Nxg6, Nxg3) where SEE = 0 because the sacrificed piece is recaptured, but the resulting king exposure yields massive dynamic compensation (+200-600 cp). The 42% own-hung rate (median value 2.0, spread across pawns/66, minors/55, majors/27) reflects that the quiet alternative moves often leave the player's own pieces tactically loose, compounding the error. The feature fires on just 0.2% of positions—specifically those where a concrete sacrificial capture on a weakened g/h-file pawn is available but declined in favor of a passive move.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Nh4, Ne5, Be2, Qd3, d4, etc.) waste a critical tactical moment. The weakened kingside pawn (typically h6 or g6 stripped of protection by a knight move or pawn advance) offers a sacrifice that rips open the king's shelter. By playing a slow move, the player allows the opponent to consolidate their kingside, repair the weakness, or generate counterplay, squandering a decisive attacking opportunity worth 200-600 centipawns.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet 'improving' move instead of a forcing check or capture that wins major material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 74% of the time the best move wins material (median value 6.0, i.e., queen-level), with 30% of best moves being checks and 29% being captures. Yet the player's move is a capture only 9% of the time — overwhelmingly they choose quiet, seemingly active moves (queen repositions, piece development) while the winning tactic goes unnoticed. In 54% of cases the played move also leaves an own piece hanging (median value 1.0, mostly pawns), compounding the error. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting specifically those where a decisive forcing blow exists but is missed in favor of a non-tactical alternative.
analysis.why_bad: The player's quiet moves (Qg4, Qc5, Rd1, Bb4, Qe7, etc.) fail because they ignore concrete forcing sequences — checks or captures that immediately win heavy material by exploiting exposed kings, undefended pieces, or tactical alignments. By playing non-forcing moves, the player allows the opponent to escape the tactical crisis, often turning a winning position into an equal or losing one (average cp_loss of 268).

analysis.label: Player captures material with a knight (or piece) but leaves it hanging, missing a far stronger tactical blow—often a check or checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 74% of positions the best move wins significant material (median value 6.0, often queen-level), while 52% of best moves are checks. The player instead makes a capture (53% of played moves), predominantly with a knight, which leaves their own piece hanging in 62% of cases (median hung value 3.0, with 28 of 41 hung pieces being minors—i.e., the capturing knight itself). The pattern is a player seduced by grabbing a piece with Nx__ but missing that the knight lands on a square where it can be recaptured, while a devastating check, checkmate, or queen-winning tactic was available. The enormous average cp_loss of 2532 reflects that the missed best moves often include mate-in-one (Qxg2#, Qg2#) or queen-winning discoveries.
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures win some material (a rook, bishop, or queen on the target square) but leave the knight en prise and unprotected. Meanwhile, the position offered a much stronger move—typically a check or checkmate—that would win the game outright or gain far more material. The player focused on the obvious capture rather than scanning for forcing moves (checks first), resulting in a massive missed opportunity and often a trapped/lost knight.

analysis.label: Player missed an available checkmate (or forced short mate via check) and played a non-mating move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 98% of the best moves are checks and 96% win material with a median value of 97 (the SEE ceiling indicating checkmate). This means nearly every position had an immediate or near-immediate forced mate available. The played moves were captures only 39% of the time, and 45% of played moves even left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0) — showing that the player often made a materially careless move when a decisive mating blow existed. The enormous average cp_loss of ~4886 confirms the catastrophic nature of missing mate. The best moves across the top boards (Ng5#, c3#, Ne4#, Nd4#, Qd6#, Bg5#, Nf3+, Nc3+, Nd5+, Nc7+) are overwhelmingly knight or piece checks delivering mate or forcing it within 1-3 moves.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores an immediate checkmate (or forced short mate) in favor of greedily capturing hanging material (Nxa8, Nxh8, Bxe6, Qxa2+), making routine developing moves (O-O, Nf3, Bb3), or delivering the wrong check (Qa5+). The opponent survives and often consolidates a large material or positional advantage, turning a won game into a loss.

analysis.label: A knight captures the f2 or f7 pawn in the opening but is left hanging and immediately lost, trading a minor piece for a mere pawn.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 99% of activating positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a knight), and 94% of the played moves are captures. The hung piece class is overwhelmingly 'minor' (112 of 113 cases). Only 29% of best moves win material, meaning the correct alternative was usually a quiet developing move (not a tactic). All top 12 positions show a knight lunging to f2 (as Black) or f7 (as White) in the opening, grabbing a pawn worth 1 but leaving the knight (worth 3) completely undefended on that square. The average cp_loss of 268 corresponds almost exactly to the net material deficit of trading a knight for a pawn (~200 cp plus positional damage).
analysis.why_bad: The knight captures a pawn on f2/f7 but has no escape route and no supporting pieces. The opponent simply recaptures with the king (Kxf2/Kxf7), winning a full minor piece for just a pawn. Despite the superficially aggressive appearance (attacking near the enemy king), the move lacks the tactical prerequisites—such as follow-up forks, discovered attacks, or mating threats—needed to justify a genuine sacrifice. The player confuses a sound combinative sacrifice with a simple one-move pawn grab that loses material.

analysis.label: Player makes a slow quiet move (often Qg3) instead of an available forcing capture, frequently with check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 96% of activating positions, the best move is a capture, and in 42% of cases it comes with check. Only 15% of these captures win outright material (median 1.0 pawn when they do), meaning most are equal exchanges that gain tempo or positional advantage via the forcing nature (especially check). The player instead plays a quiet piece move—often Qg3 or similar queen/bishop retreat to the g-file—and in 46% of cases even leaves their own piece (usually a pawn) hanging in the process. The played moves are captures themselves only 31% of the time, confirming the pattern of choosing slow moves over forcing ones.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Qg3, Qh2, Bg3, etc.) ignore a concrete forcing capture—often with check—that disrupts the opponent's coordination, gains tempo, or wins material indirectly. By playing slowly, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, and frequently the quiet move even creates a new weakness (hanging pawn 46% of the time). The average centipawn loss of 148 confirms these are significant missed opportunities where the forcing capture was clearly superior.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting move (often a capture) while their king sits on a vulnerable long diagonal (typically a7-g1 or a8-h1), ignoring the need for a prophylactic king sidestep or queen relocation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material 49% of the time (median 3.0 = minor piece value) yet are only captures 16% of the time, indicating the material is won indirectly through exploiting positional vulnerabilities. The player's move hangs their own piece 33% of the time (mostly pawns at median 1.0, with 121 pawns, 33 minors, 10 majors), suggesting the played moves inadvertently open or fail to shield a critical diagonal. The played moves are captures 25% of the time—greedy captures that ignore the king's diagonal exposure. Across the top boards, recurring analysis explicitly identifies the a7-g1 diagonal (positions 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9) or a8-h1 diagonal (position 6) as the source of vulnerability. The correct moves are frequently prophylactic king moves (Kh1, Kb1) or queen relocations (Qc3, Qd2, Qf3) that break the dangerous king-queen alignment on the diagonal.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize immediate material gain or natural development while leaving the king on a dangerous long diagonal. Opponents can then exploit the diagonal alignment (often queen + bishop batteries) to win material through discovered attacks, pins, or forcing sequences. By not playing Kh1/Kb1 or relocating the queen, the player allows devastating tactical blows along the open diagonal that more than offset any material gained by the greedy capture.

analysis.label: Player missed a rook check that skewers the opponent's king and rook, winning the enemy rook.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a rook check (88% of positions) that wins significant material (91% of positions, median SEE value 95 — corresponding to winning the opponent's rook via skewer). The played move is overwhelmingly a quiet non-forcing move (only 22% captures, 0% checks among played moves), and best moves are rarely direct captures (14%), confirming the material is won indirectly through the geometric skewer after the king is forced to move. The feature fires in only 0.3% of all positions, identifying specifically those endgame configurations where the opponent's king and rook are aligned on a rank or file, vulnerable to a rook check that wins the rook on the second tempo. The 34% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental and secondary to the primary pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Ng7, Rc1, Kg4, Ke4, etc.) fail because they squander a decisive tactical shot. The rook check forces the king to step off the line, leaving the enemy rook undefended and captured for free. By playing a non-forcing move, the player allows the opponent to reposition and break the king-rook alignment, often converting a completely winning position into a draw or drastically reduced advantage (average cp_loss: 254).

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of exchanging off the opponent's powerful centralized knight, often hanging their own piece in the process.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that the best move is a capture 96% of the time, yet wins 0 material (SEE=0) in most cases—indicating an equal knight-for-knight exchange. All 12 top-activating positions have a best move of Nx__ (e.g., Nxd5, Nxe5, Nxd4, Nxe4, Nxd6, Nxc6), targeting an opponent's dominant centralized knight. The player instead plays a quiet move (only 11% captures played), and 51% of the time their move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, predominantly minors at 44 and pawns at 38). The opponent's unchallenged knight then creates tactical threats that exploit the misplaced pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's centralized knight (typically on d4/d5/d6/e4/e5) is a dominant piece creating multiple threats. By playing a quiet move (queen repositioning, bishop development, pawn push) instead of the simple equal exchange Nx__, the player leaves the knight in place to fork, attack, or dominate key squares. The resulting position often means the player's pieces are left undefended because the knight's tactical power wasn't neutralized, leading to material loss averaging ~236cp.

analysis.label: Player misses a rook move delivering check that wins decisive material or forces a winning position.
analysis.description: In 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material, and in 92% of cases that best move is a check. Examining the top 12 boards reveals the best move is always a rook delivering check (Rxd7+, Re7+, Rd7+, Rf7+, Rxf2+, Rxg7+, Rxh7+, Rd6+, Rf2+, Re7+), often penetrating to the 7th rank or capturing a pawn/piece with check. The median value won is 95.0 (SEE units), indicating these are typically decisive blows. The player's actual move was a capture only 9% of the time — instead they play quiet developing or repositioning moves (Rf1, c3, Ne4, Rae1, O-O, Kc2, etc.). The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a rare but highly specific tactical pattern where a rook check wins the game.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves played (repositioning rooks, pushing pawns, castling, knight maneuvers) ignore an immediate rook check that wins massive material or is outright decisive. The check forces the king to move, after which material is lost or the position collapses. By not exploiting the exposed enemy king with the available rook check, the player squanders a winning tactical blow.

analysis.label: Player missed a forcing rook capture with check on an open file, instead making a passive move that often left their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture 94% of the time and a check 78% of the time, yet SEE value is 0 (equal exchange) — indicating a rook-for-rook trade that gives check. All 12 top positions confirm this: the best move is always Rx__+ (rook captures on the back rank with check) on a shared open file. Despite the exchange being materially 'equal,' the check tempo creates decisive advantage (avg cp_loss 2815). Because players ignore this forcing sequence, 56% of the time their own piece ends up hanging (median value 4.0, predominantly major pieces at 94 instances), as the unexchanged rook or other piece becomes tactically vulnerable. The best move wins material only 11% by pure SEE, but the tempo from check converts into overwhelming positional/material gains.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the forcing rook exchange with check, the player loses critical tempo. The opponent then exploits the open file or back-rank weakness to win material or deliver mate. The quiet moves played leave the player's own rooks and major pieces exposed on the very file where the exchange should have occurred, often resulting in immediate back-rank disasters or loss of the unprotected piece.

analysis.label: The player makes a tempting capture (often a peripheral pawn) that hangs their own piece or misses a far superior tactical continuation.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 57% of played moves were captures, while 57% left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, with distribution across pawns, minors, and majors). Simultaneously, 44% of best moves win material with a median value of 5.0, and 20% of best moves are checks—indicating strong tactical alternatives were consistently missed. The combination reveals a pattern where the player is lured by an available capture (frequently a flank pawn on the a, b, g, or h files) but the grab is tactically unsound: either the capturing piece (or another piece) becomes en prise, or a much stronger move (fork, check, or winning combination) was available. The feature fires on only 0.0% of all positions, marking these as specific tactical mistakes rather than generic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they prioritize immediate material gain (often just a pawn) while ignoring the tactical consequences. The capturing piece frequently lands on an undefended square (hanging own piece in 57% of cases), or the player misses a check/fork that would win significantly more material (median 5.0 vs. the small gain from the greedy capture). The net effect is a large centipawn loss (avg 254cp) as the opponent exploits the newly hanging piece or the missed tactic remains unexploited.

analysis.label: The player makes a quiet move that leaves their own Rook (or occasionally Queen) undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player's move left their own piece hanging: 88% of the top 500 positions show an own piece hung after the move, with a median value of 5.0 (Rook value). The piece class distribution is dominated by major pieces (154 major vs 72 minor vs 19 pawn). Only 14% of the played moves were captures, confirming these are quiet moves that inadvertently leave material en prise. In the top 12 boards, 10 out of 12 positions specifically hang a Rook (value 5), either by moving the Rook itself to an undefended square (Rd8, Rf6, Re8, Rf2, Rh8, Rc1, Ra1) or by moving a defending piece away (Kf6, Qc7, Qb3, g5), exposing the Rook to capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores that their Rook is (or will become) undefended after the move. Either the Rook is placed on a square attacked by an opponent's piece without adequate support, or a piece that was shielding/defending the Rook moves away, allowing the opponent to win the Rook for free or via a simple exchange that nets significant material.

analysis.label: Player misses a decisive queen check or checkmate, instead making a greedy capture or routine move that also hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: In 94% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 9.0, i.e., queen-level gains or mate). Critically, 49% of these best moves are queen checks—overwhelmingly leading to forced mate or winning the opponent's queen (positions show Qd4+, Qh4+, Qf5+, Qf6#, Qh8#, Qd5+, Qe6+). Instead, 41% of the played moves are captures (typically greedy bishop takes: Bxh5, Bxg4, Bxd5, Bxb5, Bxd2) and others are quiet moves like O-O or d6. In 81% of cases the played move also leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0; distribution: 64 minor pieces, 62 pawns, 12 major pieces). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions, targeting this specific pattern of a missed devastating queen check in the presence of a distracting capture or routine move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a game-ending queen check or checkmate against an exposed enemy king. The player gets distracted by grabbing material (often a bishop capturing a pawn or minor piece) or making a positional/developmental move (castling, pushing a pawn), while a winning queen check delivers immediate mate or wins overwhelming material. The played move compounds the error by typically leaving the capturing bishop or a knight en prise.

analysis.label: The player missed a knight move that delivers check while simultaneously forking a high-value piece (typically the queen).
analysis.description: In the SEE aggregate over 500 positions, the best move is a check in 100% of cases, and every single best move in the top 12 boards is a knight check (Nf3+, Nf4+, Nxa2+, Nd6+, Nf5+, Na4+, Nxd6+, Nb3+, Ng7+, Ne5+, etc.). The best move wins material in 96% of cases with a median value of 97 (a queen). Only 27% of the played moves were captures, meaning most players chose quiet or irrelevant moves instead. 48% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3, typically a minor piece), compounding the error. The feature fires on just 0.4% of positions, indicating a specific tactical geometry where the knight can leap to a square checking the king while simultaneously attacking an undefended queen or rook.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a decisive tactical shot: a knight fork that checks the king and attacks the queen (or other major piece). Since the opponent must address the check first, the forked piece is captured on the next move, winning roughly a queen's worth of material. Instead, the player makes routine moves—developing, recapturing, or even hanging their own pieces—while the winning knight fork goes unplayed.

analysis.label: An aggressive pawn advance that leaves the player's own minor piece (usually a bishop) undefended or tactically exposed.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 62% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the distribution heavily weighted toward minor pieces (119 minors vs. 88 pawns vs. 36 majors). The played moves are almost exclusively quiet pawn advances (f5, e4, g4, b4, d4, h5, f6) — only 5% were captures. Meanwhile, 47% of positions had a best move winning material (median 3.0) and 38% of best moves were captures, indicating the correct approach was often to address a tactical threat or take material rather than push a pawn. The pattern is consistent: the player makes an ambitious pawn thrust (often a central or flank advance) while ignoring that their own bishop or knight is under attack or becomes tactically vulnerable as a consequence of the push.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn advances prioritize space, attack, or structural changes while neglecting immediate piece safety. The pawn push either removes a key defender from a minor piece, opens a line that exposes a piece to capture, or simply ignores an existing threat against a bishop or knight. The resulting material loss (typically a minor piece) far outweighs any positional gain from the advance.

analysis.label: The player missed a check that wins decisive material against an exposed enemy king, playing a quiet or inferior move instead.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player overlooked a tactical check: 72% of best moves are checks, 90% of best moves win material (median value 95, i.e., roughly a queen-level gain), yet only 21% of played moves were captures and only 18% left own pieces hanging. The opponent's king is consistently exposed (h2, g2, e2, d4, b7, h6, etc.), creating a check that either directly captures material or initiates a forcing sequence winning decisive material. The player instead makes quiet repositioning moves (Ne6, Re8, Bc1, Qc3, Re2, Bf1, Nf4) that completely miss the tactical shot.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most forcing continuation available—a check against an exposed king—that wins major material or delivers a decisive attack. By playing a quiet move, the player gives the opponent time to consolidate their king's safety or re-coordinate their defenses, squandering a winning tactical opportunity that may not recur.

analysis.label: Player ignores a free capture of an undefended major piece (usually a rook) on the back rank.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a simple capture of a loose back-rank piece (76% of best moves are captures, 54% win material with median value 4.0 — consistent with capturing an undefended rook). The player instead makes a quiet move (only 27% played a capture), often redirecting their queen elsewhere. In 47% of cases the played move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), compounding the error. The targets are overwhelmingly rooks or queens sitting undefended on a1, b1, d1, e1, b8, d8, or f8 — classic 'loose piece on the back rank' geometry.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore free material (typically an undefended rook worth ~5 pawns) sitting on a back-rank square. By choosing a quiet positional or attacking move instead of the simple capture, the player throws away a decisive material advantage — often converting a winning position into a loss or missing mate-in-few sequences that begin with the back-rank capture.

analysis.label: Player missed a queen capture of an undefended enemy rook, almost always with check, winning decisive material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of positions have the best move winning material with a median value of 5.0 (a rook), and 90% of the time the best move is a capture while 69% of the time it is also a check. The player's actual move was a capture only 18% of the time, meaning they overwhelmingly played quiet moves instead. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the missed best move is specifically a Queen capturing an undefended Rook (Qxa1+, Qxe1+, Qxf1+, Qxh1+, Qxb1+, Qxc8+, Qxa7), nearly always delivering check simultaneously. The 40% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) is incidental — the defining mistake is failing to capture the free rook.
analysis.why_bad: The quiet moves played (b6, Ng4, Rg8, Rd8, Kh7, Rdb8, Nf6, Rf8, c6, Rf1, h3, e4) ignore a tactically decisive queen capture of an unprotected rook, typically with check. By missing this forcing move, the player throws away a full exchange or more (often the entire game, with average cp_loss of 3084), allowing the opponent to consolidate or even win from a previously lost position.

analysis.label: A bishop makes a capture (usually with check) that leaves itself en prise, missing a stronger move that wins material cleanly.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a bishop capture—90% of played moves are captures, and virtually all are bishop moves to d2, d7, c6, or e2—that delivers check or takes a defended piece, but leaves the bishop hanging to immediate recapture (99% of positions leave own piece hanging, median value 3.0 = bishop; piece class distribution is overwhelmingly minor pieces at 134/149). Meanwhile, 71% of positions had a best move that wins material outright (median value 3.0), typically a queen capture (Qxe4+, Qxd4, Qxe5, Qxd5), a rook capture (Rxe5), or a pawn capture (dxe5, hxg5) that exploits the same tactical tensions without surrendering a piece back. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, targeting this specific pattern of a seductive but self-destructive bishop capture.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures with check (Bxd2+, Bxd7+, Bxc6+) appear forcing and aggressive, but after the opponent sidesteps or recaptures, the bishop is lost for inadequate compensation. The player is seduced by the 'free tempo' of check but fails to see that the bishop ends up undefended on its destination square. The true best move exploits the same positional weaknesses (hanging pawns, exposed kings, undefended pieces) without sacrificing material, resulting in a clean material gain of ~3 centipawns median rather than an even trade or net loss.

analysis.label: Player missed a critical rook/queen check that gains tempo against an advanced passed pawn threatening promotion.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 88% of best moves win material (median value 97, approximately the promoting pawn), and 69% of best moves are checks — while only 9% are captures. This tells us the winning resource is overwhelmingly a check, not a direct capture. The player's moves were quiet (80% non-captures), typically passive king moves or non-checking rook moves. Only 34% of played moves hung own material (median value just 1.0, i.e. a pawn), confirming the mistake is not hanging a piece but rather failing to exploit the geometry. Across all 12 top-activating positions, an advanced passed pawn sits on the 7th rank one square from promotion, and the best move is a rook or queen check that either forces the enemy king onto the promotion square (blocking it), enables capturing the dangerous pawn, or gains a decisive tempo in a promotion race.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames with pawns one step from queening, a single tempo decides the game. By playing quiet moves (Kd2, Kg1, Kf6, Rg8, Rb1, etc.) instead of delivering check, the player loses the critical tempo needed to intercept the promotion. The opponent then promotes unimpeded, converting to a winning queen advantage or forced mate — explaining the enormous average cp_loss of 4826.

analysis.label: In pure king-and-pawn endgames, the player makes a passive quiet move (king walk or pawn push) instead of immediately capturing a vulnerable enemy pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively on endgame positions (12/12 endgame) that are overwhelmingly pure king-and-pawn endings. The SEE aggregate shows that 37% of the time the best move wins material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), yet the player's move was a capture only 4% of the time. Only 3% of played moves hung the player's own piece, confirming this is a 'missed winning capture' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. Best moves are captures 23% of the time and checks 12% of the time (often pawn captures with check like gxf6+). The player consistently chooses quiet king moves or pawn pushes over the critical pawn capture that would decide the endgame.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, a single pawn is often the difference between winning and drawing (or drawing and losing). By making a passive king move or unnecessary pawn push instead of immediately capturing the vulnerable enemy pawn (Kxf3, Kxh5, exd5, gxf6+), the player either gives the opponent time to reposition their king defensively, allows the opponent to capture first, or pushes a pawn to a square where it becomes weak. The average centipawn loss of 174 reflects that these endgame inaccuracies frequently convert a won position into a draw or a draw into a loss.

analysis.label: A bishop makes a tempting capture but leaves itself (or another piece) undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 88% of activating moves are captures and a striking 99% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0). The hung-piece class distribution is overwhelmingly minor pieces (158 out of 180), consistent with the board evidence showing nearly all moves are bishop captures (Bxa3, Bxc5, Bxb5, etc.). In 59% of cases the best move could win material anyway (median 2.0), meaning the player chose a superficially attractive but tactically flawed capture over a genuinely good alternative. Only 20% of best moves are captures themselves, suggesting the correct approach was often a quieter developing, defensive, or positional move rather than grabbing material. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, indicating a very specific tactical pattern where a bishop lunges for material and lands on an unsupported square.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a pawn or piece but lands on a square where it has no protection, allowing the opponent to simply recapture or attack it with tempo. In some cases the bishop's departure uncovers an attack on another piece. The net result is typically losing a full minor piece (≈3 pawns of value), far outweighing whatever was captured.

analysis.label: Player missed a simple pawn advance that would trap or win the opponent's aggressively posted queen.
analysis.description: In 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 8.0 (approximately a queen), yet the best move is a capture only 4% of the time and a check only 1% of the time. This indicates the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet pawn push that traps an exposed enemy queen. The top boards confirm this: the opponent's queen has ventured to an aggressive but vulnerable square (h5, h4, b4, b5, a5, g4), and a simple pawn advance (g6, g3, a5, a6, b4, h5) would win it outright. The played moves instead develop pieces or make other plans, completely ignoring the queen trap. The 54% own-hang rate (median value 1.0, mostly pawns and minors) reflects that the alternative moves chosen are often structurally careless as well, but the defining error is the missed queen win.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a simple one-move pawn advance that would trap or decisively attack the opponent's queen, which has over-extended to an aggressive square with no safe retreat. By playing developing moves or other plans instead, the player forfeits winning approximately a queen's worth of material (~8-9 pawns), turning winning or equal positions into lost or much worse ones (avg cp_loss: 1078).

analysis.label: Developing a bishop (usually to e6) while the king is critically exposed, leaving own pieces hanging to tactical exploitation of the king's vulnerability.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 75% of played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, with minor pieces comprising 51 of the hung-piece instances, pawns 33, and major pieces 21). The best move wins material in 51% of cases (median 3.0), typically because retreating the king would save the position. In the top-activating boards, the overwhelmingly common played move is Be6 (9 of 12 positions), deployed when the king is exposed on f7 (or f2 for White). The best moves are almost always king retreats (Ke8, Kf8, Ke1). Only 23% of played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet developing moves that catastrophically ignore the tactical situation. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions, targeting a very specific blunder pattern.
analysis.why_bad: With the king exposed on f7 (or f2), the opponent's pieces (typically a queen on the a2-g8 diagonal and a knight ready to jump to g5) have immediate tactical threats. Playing Be6 ignores these threats and often places the bishop itself on a tactically vulnerable square where it can be won via discovered attacks, forks, or queen-knight combinations exploiting the undefended king. The correct response is always to retreat the king to safety first (Ke8/Kf8/Ke1), eliminating the tactical motifs before developing.

analysis.label: Player makes a reflexive pawn or king capture while missing a far stronger tactical continuation, often weakening their own position in the process.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a tempting but inferior capture (82% of played moves are captures, often pawn recaptures like fxe3, gxh6, gxf3 or king takes like Kxf2, Kxe3) while missing a much stronger move that wins material (81% of best moves win material, median value 3.0). Crucially, only 28% of best moves are captures themselves—the correct move is usually a quiet retreat, tactical reposition, or check. The greedy capture also weakens the player's own structure, with 70% of played moves leaving an own piece hanging (median value 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 78/145). The average cp_loss of 4810 confirms these are catastrophic—many lead directly to forced mates because the pawn capture opens critical files/diagonals against the player's own king.
analysis.why_bad: These captures are reflexive and materialistic—the player grabs an available piece (usually a pawn) without recognizing that a non-capturing move (king retreat to safety like Kh7/Kh2/Kh4, or a decisive tactical blow like Rxd4/Qg4/Qe6+) was far superior. The capture typically opens lines against the player's own king or squanders a decisive tactical opportunity, often resulting in immediate forced mate or massive material loss.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning check (often winning a queen or delivering mate) and instead plays a move that hangs their own major piece.
analysis.description: In 80% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move is a check, and in 92% of cases that best move wins material (median value ~97 centipawns, i.e., roughly a queen). Instead of playing the winning check, the player makes a different move—a capture 50% of the time—that leaves their own piece hanging 90% of the time (median hung value: 5, i.e., a rook; piece class distribution: 32 major, 12 minor, 10 pawn). The feature fires on positions where a forcing check would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate, but the player chose a tempting but losing alternative.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most forcing option available—a check that wins major material or mates. By playing a non-check move (often a greedy capture or passive move), the player gives the opponent tempo to exploit the newly hanging piece. The check would have forced the opponent to deal with the king threat first, allowing the player to collect material on the next move. Without the check, the opponent instead captures the undefended piece, turning a winning position into an equal or losing one.

analysis.label: Player moves their king instead of capturing a hanging enemy piece worth a minor piece (~3 pawns).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 86% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 98% of best moves are captures, yet the player's move was a capture only 16% of the time. Across the top 12 activating positions, 9 of 12 moves played are king moves (Kh6, Kd7, Ke4, Kg5, Kd7, Kf7, Kf5, Kh5, Kh5), while the best move is invariably a simple capture of an undefended enemy piece—typically a knight or bishop on an exposed square (Rxf6, Bxd4, cxd6, Rxc4, axb5, Rxe6, dxe4, Rxf3, Bxe4). The kings are frequently noted as exposed, suggesting the player prioritizes fleeing or repositioning their king over taking free material. The 43% own-hang rate (median 1.0 = pawn) is a secondary consequence, not the primary mistake.
analysis.why_bad: These king moves forfeit a full minor piece (worth ~3 pawns) that is freely capturable. The player appears distracted by king safety concerns or positional fears, moving their king when no immediate threat justifies ignoring a simple winning capture. The result is a median centipawn loss of ~350+, turning winning or equal positions into losing ones.

analysis.label: Player makes a flashy or aggressive move (often a check) instead of addressing practical concerns like king safety or material, frequently hanging their own pawn in the process.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 56% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 36/61), while 55% of best moves won material (median 1.0). Only 10% of played moves were captures versus 32% of best moves being captures, and only 2% of best moves were checks despite checks being extremely common among the played moves (Rb8+, Rh6+, Rxe5+, Be6+, Rf3+ — 5 of 12 top activations). This reveals a pattern where the player selects an 'active-looking' move—a check, a piece centralization, or an aggressive rook placement—while ignoring the most practical continuation, which is typically a king retreat to safety, a simple capture of hanging material, or a defensive pawn move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize apparent activity (giving check, placing pieces aggressively) over genuine needs of the position. The checks accomplish nothing concrete—the opponent simply moves their king and the attacker's position has deteriorated. Meanwhile, the 'active' move often leaves a pawn or piece undefended, or more critically, walks the king into a mating net. The best moves (Kg1, Kb4, Kc1, Kxg6, Kxh6, exd5) solve real problems: they either secure the king, capture free material, or maintain defensive integrity. The average cp_loss of 3283 (with many blunders into forced mate) shows how catastrophic this 'activity over practicality' mindset is.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting-looking central move (often a knight jump or capture on d4/d5) that both ignores winning tactics and leaves own material hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a catastrophic tactical blunder by making an 'active'-looking central move. The SEE aggregate shows 63% of positions had a best move winning material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 56% of the played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0; distribution: 127 pawns, 86 minors, 51 majors). Only 23% of played moves were captures, confirming players often chose quiet 'aggressive' moves over concrete tactical solutions. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions with an average cp_loss of 2521, indicating extreme blunders—many resulting in immediate mate. The overwhelming geometric signature is movement toward d4/d5 squares.
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize superficial central activity (knight jumps, pawn captures on d4/d5) over concrete calculation. The player is drawn to a tempting-looking square while ignoring that: (1) a better tactical opportunity exists (capturing/winning enemy material), and (2) their own move leaves pieces undefended or exposes the king to mating attacks. The result is a double-whammy blunder—missing a win while creating a new decisive weakness.

analysis.label: The player ignores the urgency of dealing with passed pawns in endgames, choosing captures or irrelevant moves over critical king positioning or pawn blockades.
analysis.description: This feature fires exclusively in endgames where the critical task is addressing passed pawn threats—either blockading enemy passers or rushing the king to stop promotion. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 53% of the time (median value 1.0, typically a pawn gained by correctly addressing the race), yet the player's move was a capture only 20% of the time—often the WRONG capture (e.g., taking a piece while an enemy pawn promotes). The best move is a king repositioning in 8/12 top boards (Kc5, Kd8, Kxf4, Kd4, Kb2, Kc5, Kg6, Kd3), but players instead grab material (Kxb7, Kxg4, Nxe2), push irrelevant pawns (h4, h2, c7), or make aimless piece moves (Nb5). The 29% own-hang rate (mostly pawns, 103/146) reflects cases where the wrong move leaves pawns undefended as the pawn race collapses.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, passed pawn races are often the decisive factor—a single tempo determines who queens first. These moves fail because they prioritize short-term material or non-urgent plans while an enemy passed pawn advances unimpeded, or the player's king drifts away from the critical squares needed to blockade or escort pawns. The massive average cp_loss (1924) reflects that many of these errors turn draws into losses or wins into losses by allowing unstoppable promotion.

analysis.label: Player ignores the forced queen trade with check on the open d-file, playing a developing move or capture that leaves pieces vulnerable.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best move is a check in 81% of cases and a capture in 98%, yet wins material only 6% of the time (because the queen trade is equal material). The player's move leaves their own piece hanging 46% of the time (median value 3.0, predominantly minors at 36 instances). All 12 top-activating positions share identical geometry: an open d-file with both queens facing each other (Qd1 vs Qd8), both kings uncastled in the center, and the best move being Qxd8+ or Qxd1+ — a queen exchange that comes with check, denying the opponent castling rights. Instead, players make normal developing moves (Bg5, Be7, Nc6, Bb3, Nfd2, h3) or greedy captures (Nxe5, Nxe4) that ignore the critical queen confrontation.
analysis.why_bad: By not trading queens with check, the player allows the opponent to seize the queen exchange on THEIR terms (Qxd1+/Qxd8+), displacing the player's king and denying castling. Worse, the player's last move often places a piece (especially a knight on e5 or e4) that becomes hanging once the opponent forces the queen trade with check — the moved piece loses its queen's protection and is simply won. The opponent gets both the positional gain (disrupting castling) and a tactical gain (picking off the undefended piece).

analysis.label: Player ignores a near-mandatory capture and instead makes a quiet move that frequently hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the best move is a capture in 99% of cases, yet the player makes a non-capture (only 12% of played moves are captures). In 54% of activating positions, the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 4.0, corresponding to a rook), with the hung piece distribution skewing heavily toward major pieces (22 major, 8 minor, 13 pawns). The best captures themselves only 'win' material in SEE terms 19% of the time (median 2.0 when they do), suggesting many are necessary recaptures or tactically forced exchanges that appear equal in raw SEE but are essential in the position. The feature fires on just 0.1% of positions with an average cp_loss of 2185, indicating catastrophic blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The player fails to make a forced or critical capture (often a recapture, promotion-capture, or tactically necessary exchange) and instead plays an irrelevant quiet move—a king retreat, queen reposition, or minor piece development—that ignores the tactical demands of the position. By not executing the capture, the player both misses the material/positional gain from the capture itself and frequently leaves their own major piece undefended, resulting in catastrophic material loss on the opponent's next move.

analysis.label: Player pushes a central pawn (d5/e4/e5/f4) prematurely, leaving their own pawn en prise or undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 57% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung pieces overwhelmingly being pawns (277 pawns vs 9 minors). Only 2% of played moves were captures and only 25% of best moves won material, confirming this is primarily about hanging one's own pawn rather than missing an enemy hanging piece. The top boards consistently show ambitious central pawn advances (d5, e5, e4, d4, f4, f5) in positions—often Hedgehog, King's Indian, or Semi-Slav structures—where patient maneuvering (Nd7, O-O, Bb2, Ba3) was required instead. The pawn push either directly lands on a square where it can be captured, or vacates a square that leaves another pawn undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These central pawn breaks are poorly timed: the advancing pawn lacks sufficient support and can be captured cleanly, or the advance exposes another pawn to attack. In cramped but solid positions, the correct approach is quiet regrouping (castling, rerouting knights, repositioning bishops), but the player impatiently lunges forward with a pawn break that simply drops a pawn. The opponent's pieces are well-placed to exploit the premature advance.

analysis.label: Player plays a passive quiet move in a position demanding concrete tactical action, simultaneously missing a winning combination and often leaving own material en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a dual-failure pattern: in 66% of positions the best move wins material (median 3.0 pawns), yet the player's move was a capture only 17% of the time. Simultaneously, 70% of the played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0), distributed broadly across piece types (113 major, 92 minor, 82 pawns). The best moves were checks 30% of the time and captures 45% of the time, indicating sharp tactical positions where concrete forcing moves were required. Instead, the player chose quiet repositioning moves (bishop retreats, pawn pushes, king moves) that ignored both the available tactical shots and the defensive requirements of the position. The average centipawn loss of 4326 confirms these are catastrophic blunders, often turning winning positions into losing ones or missing forced mates.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore the tactical demands of the position on both sides of the board. The player misses winning captures or checks (often involving forks, discovered attacks, or back-rank motifs) while simultaneously moving pieces away from defensive duties, leaving other pieces unprotected. The position required concrete calculation, not positional maneuvering.

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet repositioning move that leaves their own piece undefended and capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's move leaves their own piece hanging: 65% of the top 500 positions show the played move exposes an own piece (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece). The hung pieces are distributed across pawns (82), major pieces (54), and minor pieces (47), indicating a general pattern rather than one specific piece type. Only 9% of played moves are captures, meaning 91% are quiet moves that inadvertently break a defensive connection. The best move wins material only 23% of the time (median 1.0), confirming the primary error is not missing an opponent's hanging piece but rather creating one's own vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 3295 reflects that many of these blunders lead directly to forced mate sequences.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player makes an aimless or repositioning move (king walk, rook shift, queen relocation) while ignoring that a critical piece is left undefended. Examples include Kd4 abandoning a knight to the enemy queen, Rf3 leaving a bishop en prise, Qe2 stranding a knight without protection, and Rc8 leaving a rook capturable. The player focuses on their own plan while missing the immediate tactical threat to their exposed piece.

analysis.label: The player gives an impulsive check (typically with a knight or bishop) that leaves the checking piece itself hanging after the opponent's king escapes.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that the played move leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (91%, median value 3.0 = minor piece), with minor pieces dominating the hung-piece distribution (38 minor vs 12 major vs 11 pawn). Crucially, the best move is almost never a check (only 3%), yet 10 of the top 12 activating moves are checks. This confirms the pattern: the player delivers a superficially 'forcing' check with a knight or bishop that jumps into enemy territory, but after the king sidesteps, the checking piece is left undefended and simply captured. The 36% rate of best-move-wins-material (median 1.0) indicates that in many cases a quiet positional move or simple capture was far superior.
analysis.why_bad: These checks accomplish nothing strategically — the king simply moves to a safe square (often a natural square it was going to anyway), and the checking piece, now deep in enemy territory without support, is captured for free. The player loses a full minor piece (≈3 pawns of material) for a check that neither improves their position nor creates a follow-up threat. The allure of 'giving check' overrides the calculation of what happens AFTER the check.

analysis.label: Player moves or captures with a bishop/knight that ends up undefended and en prise on its destination square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's own move left a piece hanging: 89% of positions show the played move hung the player's own piece (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece). The piece class distribution confirms this with 31 minor pieces (bishops/knights) out of 48 classified cases. Additionally, 56% of the played moves were captures themselves — typically greedy captures on central squares (d4, d5, f3) where the capturing minor piece lands undefended. The best move wins material in 59% of cases (median 2.0), often simply because the opponent can recapture the hanging piece for free or exploit the tactical looseness.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player captures (or relocates) a bishop or knight to a square where it has no defenders, allowing the opponent to simply win the piece. The captures are often tempting — central pawns on d4/d5 or seemingly active squares — but the target is defended while the capturing piece is not supported, resulting in a net material loss of a full minor piece (≈3 pawns). The player prioritizes immediate material grab or 'activity' over basic piece safety.

analysis.label: The player misses a check (usually a capture-check or checkmate) that wins decisive material, instead playing a quiet move that often hangs their own piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 78% of best moves are checks and 67% are captures, with 91% winning material at a median value of 5.0 (rook-equivalent). This means the dominant pattern is a capture-check or checkmate that the player completely overlooks. Instead of executing the winning tactical shot, the player's move was only a capture 26% of the time (mostly quiet), and 70% of the time it left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across majors, minors, and pawns). The top boards confirm this: Rxe1+, Qxc1+, Rxd1+, Qxe1+, Qxb8+, Ne7+, Nxe7+, Qxg7#, Qxf1#, and Qxf8# were all missed in favor of aimless moves like Re2, Nd5, c4, or Qd7. Many exploit back-rank weaknesses or exposed kings where a simple capture with check wins immediately.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player ignores a forcing check (often capturing an undefended or poorly defended piece while giving check) that wins decisive material or delivers checkmate. By playing a non-forcing move instead, the player squanders a winning tactical opportunity and frequently leaves their own pieces unprotected, allowing the opponent to recover or seize the initiative.

analysis.label: Player makes a queen move (or piece move) in a queen endgame when the exposed king urgently needs to relocate to safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions (0.1% of all positions, predominantly endgames at 75%) where the player makes a queen move instead of addressing their own king's vulnerability. The SEE aggregate shows 43% of played moves leave the player's own material hanging (median value 1.0, overwhelmingly pawns at 29/37), and 48% of best moves win material (median 3.0). The best move is frequently a simple king move (6 of top 12 positions: Kg1, Kf2, Kg2, Kg8, Kh8, Kh7), but the player instead moves their queen to an active-looking but inappropriate square. The enormous average cp_loss of 1076 reflects that ignoring the exposed king in these queen-heavy positions leads to catastrophic consequences—forced queen losses, mating nets, or transition into completely lost endgames.
analysis.why_bad: The queen moves fail because the king is the real problem piece—it is exposed (often on a back rank or with weak pawn shield) and the opponent's queen can exploit this with checks, forks, or mating threats. By moving the queen instead of the king, the player either hangs pawns (43% of cases), allows the opponent's queen to gain decisive tempi with checks, or walks into forced sequences where the exposed king gets mated or the queen is lost. The 'active' queen placement is illusory when the king's vulnerability dominates the position.

analysis.label: Player grabs material or plays a non-forcing move instead of a winning check, leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 80% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 5.0, i.e., a Rook), while 56% of the time the best move is a check and 58% a capture. The player's move is itself a capture 47% of the time. The pattern is unmistakable: a strong check (or even checkmate) is available that would win decisively or simplify, but the player gets distracted by capturing a less critical piece or making a non-forcing move, which then leaves their own major piece (predominantly Rooks and Queens, with 'major': 20 in the class distribution) undefended and en prise. The best move's median material won is 4.0 (a minor piece or exchange), but the real cost is the piece hung by the inferior move.
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring a forcing check, the player loses the initiative and exposes their own piece. Checks must be considered first because they force the opponent to respond, often winning material or delivering mate. The greedy captures and quiet moves allow the opponent to counterattack the now-undefended piece, converting what should have been a winning position into a loss of material or even the game (avg cp_loss: 1955).

analysis.label: A bishop makes a capture (Bx__) and is left en prise on the capture square, resulting in material loss or a suboptimal exchange.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a bishop capture that leaves that same bishop hanging. The SEE aggregate confirms: 91% of played moves are captures, 100% leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), and the hung piece class is overwhelmingly 'minor' (204 of 223 classified instances). All 12 top-activating moves are bishop captures (Bxf3, Bxb7, Bxg2, Bxf6, Bxc3, Bxc6), and in every case the bishop ends up en prise on the destination square (own hung after: 3 (B)). The best move wins material only 40% of the time, meaning the primary error is not missing a tactic but rather voluntarily entering a bad exchange or getting the bishop trapped. The feature fires in just 0.1% of positions, consistent with a specific mistake type rather than a general pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a piece or pawn on a square where it is undefended and can be immediately recaptured or trapped. When capturing pawns (e.g., Bxb7 into a rook's domain), the bishop gets trapped, losing a full piece. When capturing equal-value minor pieces (e.g., Bxf3, Bxf6, Bxc3), the player makes an unnecessary exchange that surrenders the bishop pair, releases central tension, or allows the opponent a structurally superior recapture, when stronger non-exchanging moves (development, pawn breaks, or tactics) were available.

analysis.label: Player ignores an enemy bishop left en prise after it just captured a piece, failing to recapture with a simple pawn move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and 94% of the time the best move is a capture — yet the player's move was only a capture 21% of the time. This means the player consistently played quiet or irrelevant moves instead of taking a free piece. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the pattern is remarkably uniform: an enemy bishop has intruded deep into the player's position (c6, c3, a3, g6) — typically after just having captured a knight (as in the Exchange Ruy Lopez Bxc6 or Nimzo-Indian Bxc3) — and sits completely undefended, recapturable by a simple pawn push (dxc6, dxc3, bxa3, hxg6). The player ignores this free bishop and plays a developing or advancing move instead, losing a full piece worth of material.
analysis.why_bad: By failing to recapture the hanging bishop with a pawn, the player forfeits a full minor piece (≈3 pawns) for nothing. The recapture is forced in virtually all these positions because the bishop has no escape — it traded itself for a piece and is now stranded. Playing anything else simply leaves the player down material with no compensation.

analysis.label: The player develops or moves a piece onto a long diagonal already controlled by an enemy bishop or queen, leaving their own piece undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 88% of positions have the player's own piece left hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece), with the hung-piece class distribution heavily weighted toward minors (17) and majors (10). The dominant pattern across the top boards is fianchettoing a bishop (Bg7, Bb7, Bb2) or otherwise placing/exposing a piece on the a1-h8 or a8-h1 long diagonal where the opponent already has an active bishop or queen controlling that line. In rook cases (positions 6-7), the player moves a blocking piece or fails to interpose, leaving the h8 rook exposed to Bb2 along the diagonal. In the queen case (position 8), moving a pinned knight exposes the queen to a bishop. Only 33% of best moves win material, confirming the mistake is primarily about giving material away rather than missing a winning capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves place or expose an undefended piece on a diagonal already dominated by the opponent's long-range piece (bishop or queen). The fianchettoed bishop on g7/b7/b2 has no natural defender on that square in the early opening (no adjacent pawns or pieces protect it), so the opponent simply captures it for free. Similarly, removing a blocking piece from the diagonal exposes a rook or queen to immediate capture.

analysis.label: A bishop (or piece) greedily captures a pawn or piece in the opening but is left completely undefended on the destination square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the player's own move left a piece hanging 96% of the time (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece), with 301 out of 416 hung pieces being minors (bishops/knights). The played move was a capture 68% of the time, and the feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase. In 11 of the top 12 activating positions, a bishop moves or captures into enemy territory (Bxc7, Bxe7, Bxc2, Bxg6, Bxe3, Bxd6, Bf6, Bc2) and lands on a square where it has no defender and is immediately recapturable—typically by a queen, knight, or another piece. The best moves (e3, e6, d5, Qd2, etc.) are quiet developing moves that avoid this trap. The average cp_loss of 447 confirms these are severe blunders.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop captures a tempting pawn or piece but lands on an undefended square deep in enemy territory where it can be immediately recaptured for free. The opponent simply takes the bishop with a piece that was already defending that square (often the queen from d8 recapturing on c7 or e7), netting a full minor piece. The greedy capture ignores basic piece safety in favor of material that cannot actually be held.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive, developing, or greedy move while ignoring an urgent tactical crisis (mating attack or winning combination).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player catastrophically ignores the tactical demands of the position (avg cp_loss: 2537). The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 64% of the time (median value 3.0, often a piece), while the played move leaves own material hanging 49% of the time (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 106/204). Only 20% of played moves are captures, yet many positions involve greedy captures (gxh5, fxg6, Qxc2, Qxe6) or passive/repositioning moves (Be3, Ne3, Qb2, Ra7) while the king faces a decisive attack. The best moves are a mix of defensive resources (Bf8, Ne2, Bd2) and counter-tactical strikes (Nf6+, Rxf3, Rxe4, Qg5), all of which address the critical tactical element the player's move completely ignores.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes routine development, piece repositioning, or greedy material gain while their position faces a decisive tactical threat — often a mating attack on the kingside. By ignoring the urgent tactical demands (e.g., playing Qxe6 for a pawn while Bd2 prevents mate, or playing gxh5 opening the g-file when Bf8 defends), the player allows the opponent's attack to conclude immediately, resulting in mate or catastrophic material loss.

analysis.label: In critical endgame positions, the player makes a quiet move (usually a pawn push) instead of an urgent available capture that wins or neutralizes material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 81% of the time the best move is a capture and 65% of the time it wins material (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), yet the player's move is a capture only 19% of the time. Instead, the player makes quiet moves—predominantly pawn pushes (h4, g3, f4, h6, e6, g4) or passive piece relocations—in positions where an immediate tactical capture is critical. Furthermore, 60% of the time the quiet move also leaves the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0), with the hung pieces distributed across major pieces (10), pawns (7), and minor pieces (5). All 12 top positions are endgames, typically featuring advanced passed pawns or promotion threats where every tempo is critical.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they waste a critical tempo in positions where an immediate capture is necessary—often to eliminate a piece supporting a promotion, take a hanging piece, or neutralize an advanced pawn. By playing an irrelevant pawn push or piece move, the player both misses winning material AND often leaves their own pieces undefended, resulting in catastrophic cp losses (average 1441cp). The positions demand urgent tactical action, not slow positional play.

analysis.label: Player fails to play the critical central pawn advance (d5 or e5) that refutes an overextended enemy minor piece, instead making a passive developing move.
analysis.description: In 92% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0 = a minor piece), yet only 12% of best moves are direct captures — the winning blow is almost always a central pawn thrust (d5 or e5) that attacks or traps an aggressively-posted enemy knight or bishop (Ng5 threatening f7, or Nb5 threatening Nxc7+). Instead, the player makes a quiet developing move (only 13% played captures), and 72% of the time this leaves their own pawn hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 31/44). The positions are overwhelmingly opening-phase (all 12 top boards), typically Two Knights Defense or similar Italian/QP structures where the opponent has overextended a piece into Black's territory.
analysis.why_bad: The passive developing moves (Be7, d6, Bd6, Bf5, Bg4, O-O, etc.) fail because they ignore the opponent's concrete tactical threat. Without the refuting central counter-blow, the overextended piece successfully executes its tactical idea (Nxf7 fork or Nxc7+ fork), winning material. The counter-strike (d5/e5) works because it attacks the supporting piece (e.g., Bc4) or opens lines that trap/win the aggressive piece, turning the opponent's overextension into a liability. By developing passively, the player essentially gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their threat.

analysis.label: Player ignored a simple capture (often a pawn recapture) that wins material, instead playing an aimless quiet move in a winning position.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 80% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value: 1 pawn), and 73% of best moves are captures. Only 12% of played moves were captures—overwhelmingly the player chose quiet moves (king walks, pawn pushes, piece repositions) instead. In 49% of cases the quiet move also left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1, mostly pawns). The best captures are predominantly pawn takes (gxh3, fxg5, cxd3, hxg5, hxg4, bxa5, gxf3, hxg6) capturing hanging enemy material—often a piece worth 3 taken by a pawn. The enormous average cp_loss of 5345 reflects that these are completely won positions (many with forced mates) where the player failed to execute the simplest winning capture.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they pass up immediate material gain—a hanging enemy piece or an undefended pawn that can be trivially captured. By playing aimless king moves, pawn pushes, or piece repositions, the player allows the opponent to rescue the hanging material, create counterplay, or escape what were often forced mating sequences. In some cases the quiet move also leaves the player's own material undefended, compounding the error.

analysis.label: In the Italian Game opening, the player moves their knight aggressively (Ng5 or Nxe5/Nxe4) leaving it hanging on its destination square where it can be won tactically.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player in the Italian Game / Giuoco Piano makes a premature knight lunge that leaves the knight itself undefended. The SEE aggregate shows that 100% of positions result in the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0 = knight), with the piece class distribution confirming 34 out of 37 are minor pieces. The played move is a capture 70% of the time (Nxe5/Nxe4 grabbing center pawns), while the remaining 30% are quiet Ng5 moves targeting f7. Only 3% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks, confirming the correct moves are quiet developing moves (c3, d3, O-O, a3, h3) rather than tactical strikes. The average cp_loss is 352, reflecting how severely the knight is punished.
analysis.why_bad: After Ng5 in the Italian Game, the knight is undefended on g5 and Black plays ...d5!, simultaneously attacking the undefended Bc4 and opening lines against the knight (e.g., ...dxe4 removes its support). After Nxe5, Black recaptures ...Nxe5, and the now-undefended Bc4 is attacked, meaning White effectively loses the knight for a pawn. In both cases, the knight's premature aggressive move breaks the coordination with the bishop on c4, and Black exploits both hanging pieces with tempo.

analysis.label: Player misses a bishop capturing an undefended g-pawn (or b-pawn) along an open long diagonal in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 97% of positions have a best move that wins material (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), and 93% of best moves are captures, while the player's actual move is a capture only 3% of the time. Only 15% of played moves leave own material hanging, confirming this is a 'missed capture' pattern. Across all top-12 boards, the consistent geometry is a fianchettoed bishop (Bb2/Bb7 or centralized on d4) with a completely clear long diagonal (a1-h8 or a8-h1) aimed at an undefended g7, g2, or b7 pawn. The opponent's pawn is left hanging because the dark-squared (or light-squared) bishop has moved away from its defensive post, yet the player opts for a quiet developing move instead of the simple Bxg7/Bxg2/Bxb7 pawn win.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Qe2, f4, Bg2, Be2, O-O, Nf3, d3, etc.) are all quiet developing moves that ignore a free pawn sitting en prise on the long diagonal. By failing to capture, the player forfeits roughly a full pawn of material (median +1.0) and often a much larger positional advantage (avg cp_loss 305), since after Bxg7 the rook on h8 is also frequently compromised.

analysis.label: Player misses a devastating Qh5+ (or Qh4+) check exploiting the open h5-e8/h4-e1 diagonal when the f-pawn is absent in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 89% of the time the best move wins material (median value 91, i.e., a queen), 70% of the time the best move is a check, and only 4% of the time is it a capture — indicating the winning check forces material gain indirectly. Players instead made captures 61% of the time, grabbing lesser material or making routine moves while missing the killer queen check. Only 16% of played moves hung their own pieces, confirming this is a 'missed winning tactic' pattern rather than a self-hanging mistake. The consistent geometry across the top 12 positions is an open h5-e8 (or h4-e1) diagonal created by an early f-pawn exchange in openings like the King's Gambit, From Gambit, or Latvian Gambit, where Qh5+ or Qh4+ wins the opposing queen or forces catastrophic material loss.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (dxe4, fxe5, Bc4, g4, Qf3, etc.) address minor tactical concerns like recapturing a pawn or developing a piece, but completely miss that the opponent's king is fatally exposed on the diagonal vacated by the f-pawn. Qh5+/Qh4+ delivers check with no interposition possible, typically winning the enemy queen or forcing massive material concessions, representing ~250cp average loss by playing the inferior move.

analysis.label: Player misses a queen move that wins an undefended centralized enemy piece (usually a knight) in the opening.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 96% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). Critically, the best move is a capture only 24% of the time and a check only 2%, meaning the winning queen move typically threatens or forks rather than directly captures. All 12 top-activating positions feature a queen move (Qd4, Qd5, Qf6, Qf3, Qh5, Qe7) as the best move that wins approximately a knight's worth of material. The player instead plays quiet developing moves, pawn pushes (f3, f6, g5, b3), or minor captures (fxe4), missing the decisive queen deployment. The 45% own-hang rate is a secondary effect where the played pawn moves (f6, f3, g5) also weaken the player's own structure.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (f-pawn pushes, routine development, or minor captures) ignore that the opponent has an undefended or inadequately supported piece in the center (typically a knight on e4 or e5). A queen move to d4, d5, f6, f3, or similar central squares simultaneously attacks the loose piece and often creates secondary threats (against f7, or controlling key diagonals/files), winning material immediately. By playing routine moves instead, the player squanders a decisive tactical opportunity and often worsens their own king safety.

analysis.label: Player gives a purposeless Queen check instead of the objectively correct move, which typically wins material or consolidates a winning position.
