analysis.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a pointless Queen check (all 12 top-activating moves are Queen checks: Qe1+, Qb1+, Qc1+, etc.) instead of the best move. The SEE aggregate shows that 76% of the time the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece or exchange), and only 4% of best moves are checks — meaning the engine strongly prefers a non-checking move. The player's check was almost never a capture (4%), and 64% of the time the check left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns at 59 instances, with 29 major and 23 minor pieces also left en prise). The feature fires on only 0.1% of positions with an average cp_loss of 990, indicating these are severe blunders where a tempting but useless check squanders a decisive advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These Queen checks achieve nothing constructive — they don't lead to checkmate, don't win material, and don't improve piece coordination. After the opponent sidesteps the check (usually with a simple king move or block), the Queen is often misplaced and the player has wasted a critical tempo. Meanwhile, by moving the Queen away from its defensive duties, the player frequently leaves other pieces (pawns, rooks, minor pieces) unprotected. The best move — typically a quiet capture, attack on a vulnerable piece, or consolidating move — would have won substantial material or maintained a crushing positional advantage.

analysis.label: Player captures with a bishop (or minor piece) onto a square where it is en prise, when a superior material-winning move was available.
analysis.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a capture—76% of fired moves are captures, overwhelmingly with a bishop—that leaves their own piece hanging on its new square (95% of positions, median value 3.0, with 105 of 144 hung pieces being minors). Meanwhile, 74% of the time a better move existed that wins enemy material cleanly (median value 3.0). The player chooses to 'trade' by capturing into a defended square (hanging their own piece for recapture) rather than exploiting a superior tactical opportunity—often capturing an undefended enemy piece elsewhere on the board (e.g., Bxh5 winning a loose bishop, Nxe4 exploiting a pin, Nxd5 winning a centralized piece).
analysis.why_bad: The bishop capture lands on a square where the opponent can simply recapture, resulting in an even trade (or worse), while the player misses a move that wins a full piece outright. The player fixates on one visible capture (often a thematic exchange like Bxf6 or Bxe7) and overlooks that a different target is genuinely undefended or tactically vulnerable, throwing away a 3+ pawn advantage by settling for a trade instead of a clean material win.

analysis.label: Player makes a catastrophic blunder by playing a quiet, non-forcing move in a position demanding immediate tactical action (capture or defense).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 61% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), and the best move is a capture 61% of the time. Yet the player's move was a capture only 21% of the time—meaning ~79% of played moves are quiet. Additionally, 48% of the time the player's quiet move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minors/pawns/majors). The average cp_loss of 5090 across the top 12 boards—with many positions collapsing into immediate mate—confirms these are extreme blunders where the player plays a purposeless quiet move (development, king shuffle, piece repositioning) while completely ignoring both available winning captures and critical defensive requirements of the position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player treats a tactically critical position as though it were calm. They play 'natural-looking' quiet moves (Bf1, Ne5, Kh8, Na5, g5, etc.) while ignoring that: (1) an enemy piece is available for capture winning material (61% of cases), and/or (2) their move leaves their own piece undefended for the opponent to take (48% of cases), and/or (3) the opponent has an immediate mating threat that the quiet move does nothing to address. The result is catastrophic—often immediate mate or loss of substantial material.

analysis.label: The player missed a queen check (or rare rook check) that wins decisive material or delivers checkmate against an exposed enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: the best move is a check 99% of the time, and that check wins material 99% of the time with a median value of 91 (queen-equivalent). Only 18% of the best moves are captures, meaning most are non-capturing checks that force winning the opponent's queen or deliver mate on subsequent moves. The player's actual move was a capture only 33% of the time, and left their own piece hanging 48% of the time (median value just 1, mostly pawns). The enemy kings are consistently exposed or weakly shielded, creating queen-check geometry that the player fails to exploit. The enormous average cp_loss of 5043 reflects many missed forced mates.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because they ignore a forcing queen check that either delivers immediate checkmate or sets up an unavoidable sequence winning the opponent's queen or mating. Instead, players make quiet developing moves, greedy captures, or defensive gestures while the opponent's exposed king offers a decisive tactical blow. By not checking first, the player loses the initiative and often allows the opponent to survive or counterattack.

analysis.label: Player missed a checking move that wins major material through a fork or skewer in an endgame with exposed kings.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals an overwhelming pattern: 97% of best moves are checks, and 95% of those checks win material (median value 100). Only 10% of best moves are captures, meaning the material is won indirectly—through skewers or forks delivered with check. The played moves were almost never captures themselves (14%), and only 31% left own pieces hanging (median value just 1 pawn), confirming the mistake is overwhelmingly a missed offensive tactic rather than hanging one's own piece. The feature fires exclusively in endgame positions (11/12 boards) with exposed kings, where pieces like Rooks and Knights can deliver check while simultaneously attacking an undefended queen or major piece on the same line or fork square.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (quiet king moves, non-checking rook moves, pawn pushes) fail to exploit the exposed enemy king. By not giving the available check, the player forfeits winning the opponent's queen or major piece via skewer (Rook checks lining up king and queen) or fork (Knight checks attacking king and queen simultaneously). This converts winning or drawable positions into losses, with an average cp_loss of 1717.

analysis.label: Player fails to capture or block an enemy pawn one square from promotion, instead playing an irrelevant move like a king move or check.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 66% of best moves are captures (mostly of advanced pawns worth median 1.0) yet only 21% of played moves were captures, indicating players systematically ignored the need to eliminate critical threats. The best move wins material only 38% of the time because many captures of defended pawns don't gain material by SEE standards—but stopping a promotion is worth far more than a pawn. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (10/12 positions) where the opponent has a pawn on the 2nd/7th rank about to promote. The extremely high average cp_loss of 4170 confirms that ignoring these threats is typically game-ending.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the most urgent threat in the position—an enemy pawn one square from queening. Playing a king move, a check, or capturing a different piece allows the opponent to promote next move, transforming a pawn into a queen and typically winning immediately. The flashy or natural-looking alternative (a check, a centralization, a different capture) is irrelevant when promotion decides the game on the next move.

analysis.label: The player makes a move that leaves their own piece en prise, missing a better capturing move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows that 92% of the played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, corresponding to a minor piece). The hung piece class distribution (minor: 6, major: 3, pawn: 2) confirms that bishops and knights are most commonly left en prise, with rooks also vulnerable. Meanwhile, 83% of the best moves were captures and 58% won material outright (median 2.0), indicating the player consistently ignored both an available tactical gain and the defensive necessity of protecting their own piece. Only 25% of the played moves were captures themselves, showing most blunders were quiet moves that either moved a defender away, placed a piece on an undefended square, or simply ignored an existing tactical vulnerability.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the player's own piece undefended and capturable. Whether the move actively undermines a defender (e.g., f3 removing a pawn that protected a bishop, g4 removing a pawn shielding a bishop on h4), places a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (e.g., Bb5 where it's en prise, Bxg5 where it hangs), or simply ignores that a piece is already hanging (e.g., h6 while a rook is undefended), the opponent can immediately capture the hanging piece for free or near-free material, often leading to decisive or mate-level losses (avg cp_loss: 3445).

analysis.label: Player grabs material with a capture instead of delivering a decisive check or checkmate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 95% of the time the best move wins material with a median value of 91 (on a scale where 100 = checkmate), and 71% of best moves are checks — indicating the best move is almost always a forcing check leading to mate or massive gain. Meanwhile, the player's actual move is a capture 71% of the time, revealing a consistent pattern of grabbing available material rather than finding the killing blow. The feature fires on positions where the player is seduced by a tangible capture (a knight, bishop, rook, or queen) while missing a much stronger check or checkmate. The average cp_loss of ~4700 confirms that most of these are missed mates.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they take a lesser material gain (often a piece or pawn) while ignoring a forcing check or checkmate that would immediately end the game or win far more material. In positions 1, 5, 6, and 11, the player misses checkmate in one; in positions 2, 4, 7, and 12, the player misses a forcing check that leads to rapid mate. The greedy capture often also leaves the player's own piece hanging (52% of cases), compounding the error by both missing the win and creating a new vulnerability.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet developing/repositioning move while an enemy piece (typically worth ~5 points) hangs undefended and can be freely captured.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly shows the player missed winning material: 83% of the time the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e., a rook-equivalent), with the best move being a capture in 70% of cases. Yet the player's move was itself a capture only 13% of the time, meaning they almost always played a quiet move instead. While 39% of played moves did leave the player's own piece hanging (median 2.0), this is secondary to the dominant pattern of ignoring free enemy material. The best move involves check 22% of the time, suggesting some of the hanging pieces could be won with tempo via discovered attacks or capture-with-check. The average centipawn loss of 1060 across the top boards reflects the catastrophic cost of ignoring a freely capturable piece.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves (Re1, Be3, Nc6, g5, b6, Nh3, Qe7, Bd2, etc.) fail because they pursue slow positional plans while ignoring an immediate tactical opportunity: an undefended enemy piece (usually a rook on an exposed square like f3, e4, c5, or a piece left en prise) that could be captured for free. The player essentially 'doesn't see' the hanging piece and plays a normal-looking developing move, throwing away a full rook's worth of material.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive or purposeless rook move instead of executing the concrete best action (capture, pawn advance, or king centralization), often abandoning pawn defense.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 55% of positions the best move wins material (median: 1 pawn), yet the player's move is almost never a capture (only 4%). Meanwhile, 30% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value: 1, overwhelmingly pawns at 106/151). The best move is a capture 36% of the time and a check 17% of the time. Across the top 12 boards, 9-10 of the played moves are rook relocations (Rb2, Rd7, Rg6, Ra2, Rh5, Ra7, Ra1, Rc4, Rh8) while the correct moves are concrete actions: winning captures (Rxh3, Rxa5+, Bxf1, Rxb2, Bxa7), pawn advances (g6, a5, a4, c4), or king centralizations (Kf7, Ke4). The feature fires in endgames (7/12) and middlegames (3/12) where concrete play is required.
analysis.why_bad: The rook moves are purposeless redirections that waste tempo in positions demanding concrete action. They frequently abandon defense of pawns (explaining the 30% own-hang rate heavily skewed toward pawns), miss outright material wins (captures of undefended enemy pieces or winning exchanges), and ignore simpler positional improvements like passed pawn advances or king centralization. The aimless rook shuffling allows the opponent to consolidate or create threats.

analysis.label: A knight (or minor piece) is moved to a square where it is left undefended and can be captured for free or with material gain by the opponent.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 96% of positions have the player's own piece left hanging after the move (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the hung-piece distribution heavily skewed toward minors (253 out of 316 non-pawn cases). Only 37% of the moves are captures, meaning many are quiet knight repositioning moves that land on unprotected squares. The best move wins material in 50% of cases (median 2.0), often because the correct alternative avoids hanging the piece while exploiting a tactical opportunity. All 12 top-activating moves except one (Bh6) are knight moves — aggressive jumps or captures (Nxe4, Nxb5, Nxd4, Ng4, Na5, Nf5, etc.) that land the knight on an insufficiently defended square.
analysis.why_bad: The knight moves to a square where it is not adequately protected, allowing the opponent to simply capture it (or win it via a forcing sequence). In capture cases (Nxe4, Nxd4, Nxb5), the knight takes a defended piece and is recaptured at a net loss. In quiet-move cases (Ng5, Na5, Ng4, Nf5, Nd8), the knight lands on a square controlled by the opponent, immediately hanging itself or exposing another piece to attack.

analysis.label: Player makes a routine developing move (fianchetto, castling) while ignoring an enemy bishop that is completely undefended and free to capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 90% of activating positions (median value 3.0 — a bishop), and the best move is a capture 84% of the time. The player's own move was a capture only 5% of the time, meaning they almost always played a quiet move instead. In all 12 top-activating boards, the opponent has overextended a bishop deep into the player's territory (h6, a6, h3, g7, b7, a3) with zero defending pieces, and the player ignores it entirely to play a standard opening move — Bg7, Bb7, O-O, Nc6, d3, or Nd2. The 58% own-hung rate (median value 5.0, mostly majors) is a secondary consequence: by not eliminating the aggressive enemy bishop, the player's subsequent piece placement often leaves their own material vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: These moves are catastrophic because they forfeit a free piece (worth ~3 pawns) that could be captured immediately. The player appears to be on autopilot, executing a memorized opening plan (fianchetto the bishop, castle kingside) without noticing that the opponent's unusual/aggressive bishop sortie has left that bishop completely unprotected. Instead of gaining a decisive material advantage, the player's position collapses from winning to losing.

analysis.label: Player plays a quiet move instead of a devastating rook check that wins material or forces mate.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the best move is a rook delivering check (97% of best moves are checks, all 12 top boards show rook checks like Rf1+, Rg8+, Rd8+, Rxb7+, etc.) that often wins significant material (34% win material, median value 95 ≈ a queen) or forces immediate mate. Instead, the player makes a quiet non-checking move (only 12% are captures), and in 71% of cases this passive move also leaves their own piece hanging (median value 1.0, predominantly pawns: 79 pawns, 41 majors, 14 minors). The best move is also a capture 66% of the time, meaning many are capture-checks with a rook. The average cp_loss of 3086 and numerous mate-in-N missed confirms these are catastrophic oversights.
analysis.why_bad: By playing a quiet developing or repositioning move instead of the rook check, the player misses a forcing sequence that either wins massive material (often a queen via the check) or delivers a quick forced mate. The quiet move gives the opponent time to consolidate, defend, or launch their own attack against the player's now-undefended pieces.

analysis.label: Player advances a pawn to an undefended square where it becomes en prise, predominantly in endgame positions.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate strongly indicates the player's own move left a piece hanging in 88% of activating positions (median value hung: 1.0, i.e., a pawn). The hung-piece class distribution is heavily dominated by pawns (81 pawns vs 29 minors vs 9 majors). Only 27% of best moves win material, confirming the mistake direction is 'hung own piece' rather than 'missed winning enemy material.' The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top boards), where the player pushes a pawn forward (g4, e5, g6, d5, c4, g5, b3, etc.) to a square where it lacks protection and can be freely captured. The best moves are typically quiet king moves or alternative pawn moves that maintain pawn integrity.
analysis.why_bad: Advancing a pawn to an unprotected square in the endgame gives the opponent a free pawn capture. Even though the immediate material loss is 'only' a pawn, in endgames a single pawn can be decisive—enabling a passed pawn, disrupting coordination, or allowing forced mates. The advancing side gains nothing (tempo, space, or threats) that compensates for leaving the pawn en prise.

analysis.label: In endgames with exposed kings, the player moves their king (or makes a move) in the wrong direction, often leaving own pawns undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 38% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, distribution: 31 pawns, 18 minors, 12 majors), while only 10% of best moves win material. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgames (11/12 top boards) where both kings are exposed and the player makes a strategically misdirected move—typically moving the king toward the wrong flank or making an irrelevant pawn push—instead of the correct king centralization or activation move. The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet king repositioning moves (Ke6, Kg1, Kd6, Kf5, Kb4, Kc5, Kd4) heading toward the critical sector. The 38% own-hanging rate arises because the king's departure from the correct zone leaves pawns and pieces undefended.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because in endgames, king activity and direction are paramount. By moving the king away from the critical battle (e.g., toward the kingside when queenside pawns need defense, or making a pawn push instead of centralizing), the player loses tempo on the only piece that matters, often simultaneously abandoning pawn defense. The opponent then exploits the misdirected king by attacking undefended pawns or advancing their own passed pawns unopposed.

analysis.label: The player misses a strong knight jump to b4/b5/d5 that wins material or dominates the position, instead making a passive bishop or other piece move.
analysis.description: Across all 12 top-activating positions, the best move is consistently a knight invasion to b4, b5, or d5 (Nb4 in 6 positions, Nb5 in 4, Nd5 in 1, Ndb4 in 1). The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 69% of the time (median value 1.0 pawn), yet the best move is rarely a direct capture (only 12%) or check (1%), meaning the knight jump itself creates threats (forks, attacks on weak squares like c2/c7) that win material indirectly. The played moves are overwhelmingly bishop moves (Bd6, Bc5, Bd2, Bxe7, Bh6, Bc4) or passive piece shuffles. In 44% of cases (median value 2.0, mostly minors and pawns), the played move also leaves the player's own piece hanging, compounding the error. Positions typically feature kings still in the center during the opening/early middlegame where knight invasions to the 4th/5th rank are especially devastating.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves develop or reposition a bishop (or make a generic move) that ignores the concrete tactical opportunity of a knight invasion. The knight jumps to b4/b5/d5 typically attack multiple weaknesses simultaneously—undefended pawns, exposed kings, or fork squares—winning material. By choosing a slower positional move instead, the player squanders a significant tactical advantage (avg cp_loss ~185).

analysis.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a premature or passive pawn push instead of activating their king, often leaving a pawn hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/12 top boards) where the player chooses a quiet pawn advance instead of the correct move, which is typically a king activation move (Ke6, Kc6, Ke4, Kg5, Kg7 appear repeatedly as best moves). The SEE aggregate shows that 38% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, with pawns dominating at 53/62 cases), indicating the pushed pawn or a previously-defended pawn becomes en prise. Additionally, 32% of the time the best move wins material (median 3.0), suggesting that king activation would also enable capturing enemy material. Only 5% of played moves are captures, confirming the passive nature of the chosen pawn pushes. The feature fires on just 0.1% of all positions, targeting this specific endgame error pattern.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, king activity is paramount—a centralized king both attacks enemy pawns and defends its own. By pushing a pawn instead, the player wastes a tempo on a committal move that often leaves that pawn (or another) undefended, since the king isn't repositioned to support the pawn chain. The pawn push frequently creates a new weakness, squanders the opportunity to centralize the king for attack/defense, and in many cases misses concrete tactical opportunities (winning material, promoting, or gaining opposition).

analysis.label: Player missed a forced checkmate or crushing queen invasion targeting h2/h3/h6 squares against the enemy king.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 73% of best moves win material (median value 3.0, consistent with capturing the h-pawn en route to mate), 40% of best moves are checks (mostly delivering immediate checkmate), and 31% are captures (queen capturing the h-pawn). The average cp_loss of 8162 reflects that nearly all missed moves are forced mates. Across all 12 top-activating positions, the best move is invariably a queen (or piece) landing on the h-file corridor (Qxh2#, Qh2, Qh3, Qh6, Qf6, Rh8, Bh6) to deliver checkmate or an unstoppable mating attack against the castled/exposed king. The 46% own-hung-after statistic (median value 1.0, mostly pawns) reflects that the actually-played moves were often irrelevant captures or quiet moves in the center that sometimes inadvertently exposed pieces, but the core mistake is blindness to the h-file mating pattern.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (cxd5, b5, e5, Bg5, Bxc5, Ba3, Be2, cxd3, Rf8, dxe4, Qb8, Qf5) are all mundane center-focused captures, developments, or quiet moves that completely ignore an immediately available forced mate or crushing queen invasion on the h-file. The player focuses on positional or material concerns (taking pawns, developing pieces) while a lethal diagonal/file to h2 or h6 stands wide open for a decisive queen blow.

analysis.label: Player makes a premature aggressive move (capture or pawn push) in the opening that leaves their own minor piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate clearly identifies this as a 'hung own piece' pattern: 75% of positions leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece). The piece class distribution confirms this with 141 minor pieces (knights/bishops) out of 193 total hangs. Only 8% of best moves win material, and only 6% of best moves are captures, meaning the correct play is almost always a quiet developing move (O-O, Nc3, Be3, etc.). The feature fires on opening positions (8/12 boards) where players make greedy captures (Nxe4, Nxe5, Bxf2+, Bxf7+) or premature central pushes (e4, e5, c4) that leave a knight or bishop undefended. The 36% capture rate in the played moves reflects the pawn-grabbing nature of the mistake.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the attacking piece (typically a knight or bishop) lands on a square where it has no retreat or support, becoming immediately capturable. Moves like Nxe4, Bxf2+, or Bxf7+ win a pawn but lose a full minor piece in return. Pawn pushes like e5 or c4 remove protection from a piece that depended on the pawn's former position. In all cases, the player prioritizes immediate material gain or aggression over completing development (castling, connecting rooks), leaving the position structurally unsound.

analysis.label: The player missed a check (usually a queen check) that would have won decisive material or forced mate.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 97% of activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 91 (essentially a queen/rook-level gain). Crucially, 77% of the best moves are checks, while only 17% are captures — meaning the winning tactic is overwhelmingly a check that subsequently wins material (fork, skewer, or forced sequence) rather than a direct capture. The player's actual move was a capture only 18% of the time and typically a quiet move (king moves, pawn pushes, or queen repositioning) that squanders the tactical opportunity. The exposed enemy kings (seen across all 12 boards) provide the geometric conditions for the check to work, but the player fails to recognize the forcing sequence.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they are non-forcing, allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape. The correct check would force the king to move, after which the checking piece (usually a queen) lands on a square that simultaneously attacks another piece, wins material through a fork/skewer, or drives the king into a mating net. By playing a quiet move instead, the player converts a won/mating position into a merely advantageous or even drawn one (average cp_loss of 2473).

analysis.label: The player ignores an available queen capture/trade, instead playing a different move that often leaves their own queen hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a capture in 100% of cases (always Qx... taking the opponent's queen at SEE value 0, i.e., an even exchange), yet the player's move left their own piece hanging 61% of the time (median value 6.0, with 'major' pieces accounting for 91 of the hung-piece instances—overwhelmingly queens). Only 3% of best moves 'win' material outright because these are equal queen trades. The player instead plays a quiet or unrelated move (only 25% played a capture), failing to execute the mandatory queen exchange and leaving their own queen exposed to capture on the very next move.
analysis.why_bad: By not taking the opponent's queen when it is available for an even trade, the player leaves their own queen undefended or tactically vulnerable. The opponent then simply captures the player's queen, netting a full queen (or large material advantage) because the queen trade that would have neutralized the tension was skipped. In many cases it is a move-order error: the player wanted to accomplish something else first but needed to trade queens immediately before the geometry turned against them.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning Bb4+/Bb5+ bishop check that exploits the opponent's uncastled king in the opening to win material.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a powerful bishop check (Bb4+ or Bb5+) in the opening phase that wins significant material. The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material in 99% of positions (median value: 97), and critically, 90% of the best moves are checks while only 12% are captures — confirming the winning mechanism is a check that then leads to material gain (via pin, fork, or tempo). The player instead makes other moves (only 25% are captures), and in 55% of cases the played move additionally leaves their own piece hanging (median value: 3, predominantly minor pieces). The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, indicating a narrow but high-impact tactical pattern.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore a forcing bishop check from b4/b5 that exploits both kings being uncastled (king on e1 or e8). The check gains a tempo against the exposed king, typically creating an irrecoverable pin on a central piece (e.g., knight on c3/c6 or queen behind it) or winning material through the combination of check + follow-up capture. By playing quiet developing moves, pawn pushes, or greedy captures instead, the player squanders the strongest tactical blow available and often compounds the error by leaving their own minor piece en prise.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting capture (often with check) that leaves one of their own pieces hanging, when a stronger tactical alternative existed.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 73% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), while 46% of the played moves were captures. Meanwhile, the best move wins material 60% of the time (median value 5.0). The own-hang distribution is spread across minors (38), pawns (20), and majors (19). The pattern is a player seduced by an attractive-looking capture—taking a pawn, winning an exchange, or delivering a check—only to leave a more valuable piece (often a rook or the capturing piece itself) undefended. The correct move typically wins more material or achieves a stronger result through a less obvious tactical path (an intermediate move, a different capture, or a quiet but devastating positional stroke like a promotion threat).
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player prioritizes an immediately visible capture or check over the full tactical picture. The capture grabs some material but exposes a piece (often a rook or the piece that just moved) to recapture or counterattack, resulting in a net material loss. The better move either wins material cleanly, exploits an intermediate tactic (zwischenzug, promotion threat, pin), or simply doesn't leave a piece en prise—yielding a far superior position.

analysis.label: Player gives an ineffective check instead of the correct move, often leaving their own piece hanging after the opponent sidesteps the check.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player plays a tempting but counterproductive check (all 12 top activations are checks: Rg8+, Rh3+, Rf3+, Qh5+, etc.) while the best move is almost never a check (only 5%). The SEE aggregate shows that 65% of the time the check leaves the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, with major pieces most commonly hung at 43/98), and in 62% of positions the best move would have won material (median 2.0 pawns). Only 3% of the played checks are captures. The own-hang distribution (major: 43, pawn: 33, minor: 22) shows that queens and rooks are frequently left en prise after delivering the pointless check. The average cp_loss of 3265 confirms these are catastrophic blunders — many squander forced mates (positions 2, 5, 10, 12 all had mates available).
analysis.why_bad: The checks accomplish nothing: after the opponent moves their king to safety, the checking piece (or another piece left unguarded by the checking move) is hanging. Meanwhile, the player misses the correct continuation — often a quiet move, simple capture, or different check that would have won material or delivered mate. The player is seduced by giving check rather than evaluating whether the check actually helps.

analysis.label: Player ignores an undefended enemy bishop that has infiltrated deep into their position, failing to simply capture it.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 90% of top-activating positions have an enemy piece available to win (median value 3.0 = minor piece), with the best move being a capture 92% of the time, yet the player's move was a capture only 9% of the time. Across all 12 boards, the pattern is strikingly consistent: an enemy bishop has aggressively infiltrated deep into the player's territory (Bf6, Bf3, Bc3, Bc6, Be2) and stands completely undefended, yet the player makes a quiet developing or prophylactic move (h6, d3, Be7, O-O, a6, etc.) instead of simply taking the free piece. The 58% own-hang rate (median 2.0) reflects how the quiet move sometimes leaves the player's own pieces tactically vulnerable as a secondary consequence. This fires almost exclusively in the opening (11/12 positions) where bold bishop intrusions demand immediate capture but the player appears distracted by other plans.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a completely free minor piece (worth ~3 pawns) that is undefended and capturable in one move. By playing a quiet move instead, the player gifts the opponent a full piece worth of material and often creates additional vulnerabilities since the intruding bishop continues to wreak havoc on subsequent moves.

analysis.label: Player retreats or sidesteps the king passively in an endgame, missing a winning tactical opportunity or leaving pawns undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 66% of activating positions the best move wins material (median value 5.0, i.e. a rook-level gain), yet only 11% of played moves are captures — indicating the player consistently fails to take available material. Meanwhile, 48% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, dominated by 166 pawns out of 239 hung pieces), showing the king move frequently abandons pawn defense. The best move is a capture 31% of the time and a check 17% of the time. Crucially, 11 of the top 12 played moves are quiet king moves (Kb7, Kg7, Kg2, Ke2, Ke6, Kd6, Kc1, Kb6, Kd3, Kd2, Kg2), predominantly in endgame positions (9/12), where the player aimlessly shuffles or retreats the king rather than centralizing it or executing the winning tactical continuation.
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, king activity and centralization are paramount. These passive king moves retreat from the action or move to irrelevant squares, missing chances to capture undefended major pieces (median 5.0 value), advance decisive passed pawns, or activate rooks. Simultaneously, by moving the king away from its defensive duties, the player leaves pawns unprotected (48% of the time), compounding the error with both a missed opportunity and a positional concession.

analysis.label: The player makes a move (usually a capture) that leaves their own knight or bishop undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is decisive: 99% of the time the player's move leaves their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e. a minor piece), with the hung piece class distribution overwhelmingly being minors (312 out of 342 classified instances). 71% of the played moves are captures—typically the minor piece itself capturing into an undefended square—while the best move wins material in 59% of cases (median 3.0). The best move is rarely a capture (18%) or check (14%), suggesting the correct continuation usually involves a quiet developing/repositioning move or a tactical shot elsewhere rather than the greedy capture the player chose.
analysis.why_bad: The player captures material (often a pawn or similarly valued piece) with a bishop or knight, but the minor piece lands on or remains on a square where it is undefended. The opponent simply recaptures or picks up the hanging minor piece, resulting in a net material loss of roughly a full minor piece (~3 pawns). The player is tunnel-visioned on the immediate capture and fails to notice the piece has no support on its new (or current) square.

analysis.label: An aggressive knight jump to an active-looking square that leaves the player's own pieces or pawns undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on knight moves (100% of the top 12 are knight moves: Nb5, Ne4, Ne5, Nb4, Ng5, Nf4, etc.) that create vulnerabilities in the player's own position. The SEE aggregate shows 56% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, corresponding to minor pieces), with the distribution being 96 minor pieces, 58 pawns, and 22 major pieces across 500 positions. Only 18% of the played moves are captures, and the best move wins material in just 32% of cases (median 1.0), indicating the core mistake is not missing an enemy hanging piece but rather the knight abandoning a defensive role. The best moves are rarely checks (1%) and are quiet positional moves (like g3, Be7, g6, h5, Rae1) that maintain defensive integrity instead of the flashy knight jump.
analysis.why_bad: These knight moves fail because they prioritize placing the knight on an aggressive-looking square (b5, e5, e4, g5, f4) without recognizing that the knight was performing a critical defensive function—guarding another piece, covering a key square, or maintaining piece coordination. Once the knight leaps away, it leaves behind undefended minor pieces, pawns, or even itself on an insufficiently supported outpost, allowing the opponent to win material through simple captures or tactical sequences.

analysis.label: The player misses a quiet move that traps the opponent's overextended queen, instead making an inferior move (often a capture or positional play).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material with a median value of 8.0 (queen-level), yet only 5% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks — indicating the winning resource is a quiet trapping move. The played moves are captures only 25% of the time, and 49% leave the player's own piece hanging (median 3.0). Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: the opponent's queen is infiltrated or overextended on the board's periphery (e.g., Black Qb2 in Position 2, White Qg7 in Position 3, White Qa7 in Position 5, Black Qa5 in Position 8, White Qd6 in Position 9), and the best move deploys a rook or bishop to seal off escape routes (Rhb1, Rag8, Ra8, Bb6, Bf8). Instead of springing the trap, the player grabs material elsewhere or makes a routine developing/positional move.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the opponent's queen being in a precarious, trappable position. By playing a capture on a different part of the board, a pawn push, or a routine move, the player allows the enemy queen to escape and remain active. The missed quiet trapping move would win the queen outright (≈9 points of material) for minimal or no investment, completely deciding the game.

analysis.label: Player misses the precise winning move in a won endgame, often choosing a greedy capture or flashy move over a simple quiet move that addresses the opponent's critical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions (0.1% of all) where a player holds a winning endgame but catastrophically blunders (avg cp_loss: 3763). The SEE aggregate shows 66% of best moves win material (median 1 pawn), yet only 27% of best moves are captures versus 39% of played moves being captures—indicating players are greedily capturing when quiet moves are needed. 29% of played moves leave own material hanging. The best moves are typically simple king moves or pawn pushes that address urgent threats (stopping promotion, avoiding stalemate traps, preventing back-rank mates), while players choose materialistic or flashy alternatives that ignore the one critical tactical issue in the position.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the opponent's most urgent threat—typically a promotion, stalemate resource, or back-rank mate—in favor of materialistic or natural-looking moves. In endgames where one tempo decides the game, capturing an irrelevant pawn (Qxf3 causing stalemate, exf5 allowing Re8#) or promoting (h1=Q while opponent's c-pawn also queens) throws away the entire advantage.

analysis.label: An aggressive pawn advance (usually ...d5 or a flank push like ...g5) in the opening that leaves the advanced pawn or another piece undefended.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 68% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 1.0), with the hung piece being overwhelmingly a pawn (208 out of 245 instances). Only 12% of played moves were captures, and 33% of the time the best move won material (median 2.0), indicating the player also frequently missed better options. The top 12 boards reveal a strikingly consistent pattern: nearly all moves are opening-phase pawn advances (d5 appears 8 times, g5 twice, e5 and b5 once each) in positions with closed centers where the player pushes a pawn into a square where it becomes immediately capturable. The best moves are typically quiet developing moves (Bg7, Be7, Nge7, Nf6) or tactical captures (Nxe4) rather than these premature breaks.
analysis.why_bad: These pawn pushes fail because they advance into squares controlled by the opponent's pieces (bishops on c4 targeting d5/f7, knights covering key squares) without adequate pawn or piece support. The advanced pawn becomes a tactical target that the opponent can capture for free, or the pawn advance creates a gap that exposes other pieces. In the opening, pushing pawns aggressively before completing development violates basic principles, especially when the king remains in the center and the opponent has better piece coordination.

analysis.label: In rook endgames with dangerous passed pawns, the player fails to activate the rook by placing it on the 8th rank (for back-rank pressure, checking distance, or control behind passed pawns), instead making a passive or suboptimal move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows 41% of played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across pawns: 81, majors: 67, minors: 26), while 38% of positions have a best move that wins material (median 1.0). Only 9% of played moves are captures. The best moves are overwhelmingly rook-to-8th-rank placements (Ra8, Rh8, Re8, Rb8 across nearly all top positions), while the played moves are passive rook placements on intermediate ranks (Rb4, Ra3, Ra4, Rc1, Rc6, Rh1) or suboptimal king moves. The feature fires almost exclusively in endgame positions (10/12 boards) with advanced connected passed pawns and exposed kings, where rook activity via the back rank is the critical defensive or offensive resource. The enormous average cp_loss of 3201 confirms these are catastrophic positional errors.
analysis.why_bad: By placing the rook on a passive intermediate square instead of the 8th rank, the player loses critical checking distance against the opponent's exposed king, fails to create back-rank threats that restrain passed pawn advances, and often leaves their own pieces (especially the rook and undefended pawns) vulnerable to being trapped or attacked. The 8th-rank placement would simultaneously threaten promotion interference, enable perpetual check resources, and maintain maximum rook activity—all essential in rook endgames with passed pawns.

analysis.label: Player captures an enemy piece with a minor piece (usually bishop) but leaves the capturing piece itself undefended and en prise on its new square, when a stronger non-capturing move was available.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 99% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), with the piece class distribution heavily skewed toward minors (227/282). Simultaneously, 92% of the played moves were themselves captures, and 64% of the time the best move would have won material (median 3.0). The top boards confirm the pattern: players impulsively capture with a bishop (Bxd2+, Bxe2, Bxf3, Bxf6, Bxd7+, Bxc6+) or knight (Nxd7), grabbing a piece but leaving their capturing minor on an undefended square where it is immediately recapturable. The result is typically an even trade when the position offered a way to win a full piece (e.g., Ne4, Rd8, O-O-O, Ng4) without losing anything back.
analysis.why_bad: The capture appears to win material, but the capturing piece lands on a square where it is undefended and can be recaptured, resulting in only an even exchange. Meanwhile, a superior move (often a centralizing knight move, a developing move, or a rook activation) would have won the same or more material cleanly, or maintained a large positional/tactical advantage without giving back the piece.

analysis.label: Player makes a tempting material-grabbing capture instead of a more forcing move (usually a check) that wins decisively.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals a pattern where the best move wins material or forces mate 62% of the time (median value 100, indicating decisive advantage), with 42% of best moves being checks and 42% being captures. The played moves are captures 58% of the time—greedy grabs at material—but critically, 71% of these played moves leave the player's own pieces hanging (median value 1, mostly pawns). This shows a consistent pattern: the player sees an available capture and takes it, but by choosing the non-forcing recapture or material grab over the correct forcing continuation, they allow devastating counterplay. The average cp_loss of 6637 confirms these are catastrophic errors, often turning won positions into draws or losses.
analysis.why_bad: These captures fail because they prioritize immediate material gain over board control and forcing sequences. By grabbing a piece (Qxa1, Qxe1, Qxd2, gxf5, dxe5) instead of playing the decisive check or zwischenzug (Rc2+, Qg3+, Qe5+, Qc8+, g5+), the player loses tempo, removes a piece from a critical attacking position, and allows the opponent to execute their own threats—counterattacks, perpetual checks, or even forced mates—that the stronger forcing move would have preempted entirely.

analysis.label: Player gives an impulsive check instead of capturing or winning a hanging enemy piece, often leaving their own checking piece en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 77% of positions the best move wins material (median value 3.0), yet only 1% of best moves are checks — while every single top-activating move played IS a check. The player's move was a capture only 34% of the time (check-captures like Qxf8+ or Bxd2+), and critically 66% of the time the checking move left the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed across minor pieces 28, major pieces 22, pawns 11). The best moves are overwhelmingly quiet captures or non-checking material wins (47% captures). This is the classic 'patzer sees a check, gives a check' error: the player reflexively delivers check instead of collecting freely available material.
analysis.why_bad: The check accomplishes nothing strategically — the opponent simply moves their king or interposes, and the checking piece is often now on an unprotected square where it can be captured. Meanwhile, the player missed winning a full piece or exchange (rook on a1, hanging knight, undefended bishop, etc.). The check gives the opponent a forced reply that stabilizes their position, converting what was often a forced mate or decisive material advantage into a much smaller edge or even a loss.

analysis.label: The player captures a piece with their Queen (often a central pawn) in the opening, only to leave the Queen trapped or hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 97% of activating positions leave the player's OWN piece hanging (median value 6.0, i.e., a Queen), with major pieces accounting for 71% of the hung pieces. The player's move is itself a capture 52% of the time, and the feature fires almost exclusively in the opening phase. The top boards show a striking pattern: moves like Qxd4, Qxf7+, Qxe3, Qxf2+, and Qxd7+ where the Queen grabs a tempting pawn or piece but immediately becomes trapped or exposed to overwhelming attack from the opponent's minor pieces and pawns, resulting in catastrophic material loss (median cp_loss ~376).
analysis.why_bad: These Queen captures are tempting because they win immediate material (a pawn or minor piece), but in the opening the opponent has too many undeveloped pieces that can quickly converge on the Queen. After captures like Qxd4, knights on c3/f3, bishops, and pawns can attack the Queen with tempo, leaving it with no safe escape squares. The Queen is lost or traded for far less than its value, turning a small material gain into a decisive material deficit.

analysis.label: The player missed a pawn advance that attacks and wins a misplaced enemy knight with no safe retreat square.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 99% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the best move is a capture only 6% of the time and a check 0% of the time. This indicates the winning move is overwhelmingly a quiet pawn advance. Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: the best moves are pawn thrusts (f4, g4, b4, b5, g5) that attack an enemy knight sitting on an exposed or rim square (e5, h5, a5, h4) where it has no safe retreat. The played moves (22% captures, 39% leaving own pieces hanging) are instead developing or repositioning moves that completely ignore the trapped/attackable knight, squandering the opportunity to win a full piece via a simple pawn push.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves (Bc4, Re1, Qd2, Nb1, c3, Bf3, etc.) are generic developing or regrouping moves that ignore the concrete tactical vulnerability of an enemy knight on an exposed square. By failing to play the pawn advance (f4, g4, b4, g5, etc.), the player allows the opponent to reposition the knight to safety on the next move, permanently losing the chance to win material.

analysis.label: In endgames, the player misses a critical check (often an intermediate check or zwischenzug) that wins material or decisive tempo, instead playing a natural-looking quiet move or capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 62% of best moves are checks and 62% win material (median value 100cp), while the played moves are overwhelmingly quiet moves (76% non-captures). Only 29% of played moves hang the player's own piece (median value just 1cp), so this is clearly a 'missed winning' pattern rather than a 'hung own piece' pattern. The feature fires exclusively in endgames where a forcing check — a pawn promotion check (f5+, f2+), a rook check (Re3+, Rxe7+, Rf8+, Rg3+), or a knight fork-check (Nd5+) — wins material or creates an unstoppable tactical sequence, but the player instead plays a passive king move or a greedy capture that throws away the advantage.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they surrender the initiative at the critical moment. The missed checks either win material directly (forks, discovered attacks), force favorable exchanges (Re3+ leading to Kxe3 Kxg4), or serve as essential zwischenzugs before capturing (Rf8+ before taking on c7). By playing a quiet king move or a routine capture instead, the player allows the opponent to consolidate, escape mating nets, or promote pawns, often converting a drawn or winning position into a catastrophic loss (avg cp_loss: 1830).

analysis.label: In pawn endgames, the player makes a king move when the critical move was a pawn advance or pawn capture.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that 32% of the time the best move wins material (median 1.0, i.e. a pawn capture), 27% of best moves are captures, and 35% of the played moves leave the player's own pawn hanging (median value 1.0, exclusively pawns). The player's move was itself a capture only 5% of the time. Every single top-activating position is a king-and-pawn endgame where the player chose a king move instead of the correct pawn action—either advancing a passed pawn (g5, f5, h5, e3, a4, b4, h6) or capturing an enemy pawn (Kxh4, fxg5, bxa5). The feature consistently detects the endgame technique error of prioritizing king repositioning over concrete pawn action.
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, tempi are critical. These king moves waste time when the position demands immediate pawn action—either capturing a loose enemy pawn to simplify the race, advancing a passed pawn toward promotion, or pushing a pawn to create a breakthrough. The king move often also abandons defense of the player's own pawns (explaining the 35% own-hang rate), allowing the opponent to capture them. The result is losing decisive tempi in pawn races or throwing away material advantages.

analysis.label: Player makes a passive/quiet move instead of taking an available winning capture, often also leaving their own piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that in 66% of top-500 positions, the best move is a capture, and in 57% the best move wins material (median value 2.0 pawns). Yet the player's move is only a capture 12% of the time — overwhelmingly quiet, repositioning moves (king moves like Kc5/Kc6/Kf7, or piece shuffles like Nd7/Ra8/Nh2). Additionally, 49% of the played moves leave the player's own piece hanging (median value 2.0, distributed evenly across pawns, minors, and majors). This suggests the feature detects positions where a clear tactical opportunity exists (a winning capture) but the player instead plays a purposeless quiet move that both misses the win and frequently abandons their own material.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they ignore a critical tactical demand in the position — typically a high-value enemy piece that can be captured immediately. By playing a passive repositioning move instead (often a king retreat or irrelevant piece relocation), the player both forfeits the winning capture and often inadvertently leaves their own pieces undefended, compounding the error. The enormous average cp_loss (2768) reflects that many of these positions go from winning/equal to completely lost or even mate.

analysis.label: The player missed a knight fork delivering check that simultaneously attacks and wins an undefended major or minor piece.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate is unambiguous: 99% of the time the best move wins material (median value 97, roughly a rook), and 97% of the best moves are checks while only 13% are captures — meaning these are almost exclusively knight moves that deliver check to the king while forking another piece. Across all 12 top-activating boards, the missed best move is always a knight check (Ne3+, Ne6+, Nd2+, Nb6+, Nd4+, Nd6+, Ne7+) that simultaneously attacks a rook or queen. The player's actual move was a capture only 22% of the time, showing they were often playing quiet or routine moves rather than noticing the fork geometry. Only 31% of played moves left the player's own piece hanging (median value 1.0, i.e., a pawn), confirming this is not a 'hung own piece' pattern but a missed tactical opportunity.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a knight's unique L-shaped geometry that simultaneously delivers check to the king and attacks an undefended piece (usually a rook). By playing a routine or materialistic move instead, the player forfeits winning approximately a full rook's worth of material, typically converting a winning or equal position into a losing or much worse one (average cp_loss: 442).

analysis.label: Player fails to execute a critical bishop-takes-knight capture at the decisive moment, squandering positional pressure.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 99% of activating positions, yet these captures only win material 12% of the time (median SEE value 0, i.e., equal exchanges). In 41% of cases (median value 2.0, with minor pieces accounting for 77 instances), the player's actual move leaves their own piece hanging. The pattern is remarkably consistent across all 12 top boards: the player has a bishop actively attacking or pinning a knight (Bg4/Bh5 vs Nf3, or Bb4 vs Nc3, or similar), and the critical moment to cash in the exchange (Bxf3, Bxc3, Bxc6, Bxf6) has arrived. Instead of capturing, the player makes a different move, after which the bishop's pressure evaporates and often the bishop itself (or a pawn) becomes vulnerable.
analysis.why_bad: The bishop is at the peak of its tactical influence (pinning or pressuring a knight), and the position demands immediate capture to convert that pressure into a lasting advantage (often shattering the opponent's pawn structure or resolving king safety issues). By playing a different move, the player allows the opponent to break the pin, chase the bishop, or consolidate—turning a winning advantage (often -200 to -350 cp) into an equal or lost position. The played moves frequently also leave the now-misplaced bishop or another piece en prise.

analysis.label: The player pushes a pawn to give check instead of playing a far superior move (often a decisive quiet move or mate).
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows best moves win material in 42% of cases (median value 9.0, indicating mate-level gains), yet the played move is a capture only 4% of the time—meaning the player consistently opts for a non-capturing pawn push that happens to give check. The best move is itself a check 27% of the time (often with a stronger piece delivering mate or decisive threats), showing the player chose the wrong checking move. In 34% of positions the advancing pawn becomes hanging (median value 2.0), confirming the pushed pawn often has no support. All 12 top-activating moves are pawn checks (e2+, g2+, a2+, h2+, d2+, e7+, a7+, c7+) with an average cp_loss of 1928, indicating these are catastrophically bad despite looking 'active.'
analysis.why_bad: A pawn check forces the king to move but rarely creates a lasting threat—the king simply sidesteps and the pawn is often lost or irrelevant. Meanwhile the player misses checkmates (Position 1: Rg1#), decisive material wins (Position 9: Qg3 winning a minor piece, Position 11: Rf8+ winning immediately), or quiet moves that secure a won endgame (Position 12: a6 is mate-in-10). The check gives the illusion of initiative but dissipates the advantage entirely.

analysis.label: Player chooses a quiet developing or repositioning move instead of executing a concrete winning capture or tactical strike.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 47% of positions the best move wins material (median value 1 pawn), and 51% of best moves are captures, yet the player's move is a capture only 4% of the time. The player's move rarely hangs their own piece (5%). This indicates the player consistently selects natural-looking quiet moves (piece development, repositioning, or pawn pushes) while missing concrete tactical captures or strikes that win material. Across the top boards, the played moves are universally quiet (Nf3, Be2, Bd7, Bd3, a4, a5, Rae8, etc.) while the best moves are sharp captures or forcing moves (Bxh7+, dxc3, axb4, Nxg3, Nxb5, axb3). Many missed tactics involve pawn captures (including en passant) or classic sacrificial motifs like the Greek Gift.
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they prioritize 'natural' piece placement or general development over concrete winning tactics. The position demanded immediate material gain through a specific capture or forcing sequence (often a pawn capture, en passant, or a piece sacrifice like Bxh7+), and the quiet alternative allows the opponent to neutralize the tactical opportunity, costing on average ~248 centipawns.

analysis.label: The player advances their already-exposed king forward into a mating net instead of retreating to safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves their exposed king forward (toward the center or toward enemy forces) and walks directly into a checkmate or catastrophic loss, when a retreating king move or other defensive option existed. The SEE aggregate shows 58% of best moves win material (median 3.0 pawns), reflecting how the suicidal king advance allows the opponent to convert decisively. Only 10% of played moves are captures, confirming these are quiet king advances. The 43% own-piece-hanging rate (median 1.0, heavily skewed toward pawns at 117/190) is a secondary consequence of the king abandoning defensive duties as it marches forward. The feature fires on just 0.3% of positions, targeting this specific catastrophic pattern of an exposed king advancing rather than retreating.
analysis.why_bad: In every case the king is already exposed and under pressure. Moving it forward (e.g., Kd5 instead of Kf7, Kf5 instead of Kf3, Kg4 instead of Kf2, Kd3 instead of Ke1) places it on squares controlled by enemy pieces, walking directly into mating patterns. The best moves are almost always king retreats toward the back rank or a sheltered square. The forward king move fatally reduces escape squares and enters the striking range of the opponent's coordinated attacking forces, resulting in immediate or near-immediate checkmate (average cp_loss ~7413, with most positions evaluating to forced mate).

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet, safety-oriented move (castling, king retreat, piece withdrawal) instead of the correct active/tactical move that wins material or addresses the position's critical demands.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 65% of positions, the best move wins material (median value 3.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet the player's move was a capture only 19% of the time — overwhelmingly these are quiet moves. The player's move left their own piece hanging in 31% of cases (median value 1.0, heavily pawns at 91/153). The best moves are captures only 24% of the time and checks only 6%, meaning the winning resource is often a non-obvious counter-tactical move (pawn advance, queen activation, or king capture of an attacker). The feature fires on positions where the player chooses a passive-looking move — castling (O-O, O-O-O), king retreats (Kg8, Kg1), queen retreats (Qa8), or wrong pawn pushes (g5 instead of f5, g3 instead of f3) — while a concrete tactical solution exists. The enormous average cp_loss of 4049 reflects that many of these passive moves allow immediate mates or decisive material loss.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize apparent safety or routine development over the position's concrete tactical demands. In many cases the player is under attack and the only adequate defense is an active counter-blow (capturing an overextended attacker, advancing a pawn to trap/win a piece, or activating the queen). The passive alternatives either leave the existing threats unaddressed (leading to quick mates) or squander a decisive material gain, turning winning or equal positions into lost ones.

analysis.label: Player misses a winning central pawn advance (d4, d5, or e5) that attacks an exposed enemy piece and wins material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that 94% of best moves win material (median value 2.0, i.e., a minor piece), yet only 8% of best moves are captures and 0% are checks — confirming the winning move is a non-capturing pawn advance that creates an unstoppable material-winning threat. The player's move was a capture only 9% of the time; instead, all 12 top-activating positions show quiet developmental or flank moves (b6, a3, Nh5, Bg4, Nbd2, d3, b3, Be7, h6, a6, O-O) played in lieu of the correct central pawn break. In every single top board, the best move is d4, d5, or e5 — a central pawn advance attacking an enemy minor piece (typically a bishop on c5/c4 or knight) that is inadequately defended. The feature fires overwhelmingly in opening positions (9/12) with closed or semi-closed centers where the opponent has placed a piece in the path of the advancing pawn.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves waste tempo on slow development, flank pawn pushes, or prophylaxis while missing the critical moment when a central pawn advance would hit an exposed enemy piece (usually a bishop on c5 or c4) with tempo, winning approximately a minor piece. By playing passively, the player allows the opponent to consolidate and remove the tactical vulnerability, squandering a decisive advantage (average cp_loss of 242).

analysis.label: Player missed a winning queen/rook check (often checkmate) on the opponent's back rank, instead playing a move that typically hangs their own major piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires when the player has a devastating back-rank check or checkmate available but fails to play it. The SEE aggregate shows the best move is a check in 99% of cases (often a capture on the back rank: 59% captures), winning a median of 5.0 material. Instead of exploiting the back-rank weakness, the player makes an unrelated move—sometimes a greedy capture elsewhere (46% captures)—that leaves their own piece hanging 76% of the time (median value 3.0, predominantly major pieces). The top boards consistently show missed Qxc1+, Qxd8+/Qxd8#, Qxe8#, Qxb1+, and Rxd8+ opportunities—all back-rank invasions with check—while the player plays moves like Rxd5, Bxb2, Nxd4, or Qxa5 that ignore the lethal back-rank threat.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore an immediately winning check (or checkmate) on the opponent's back rank. By playing elsewhere—often capturing a less important piece or making a quiet move—the player not only misses a forced win (frequently outright mate in 1-3 moves) but also leaves their own major piece (queen or rook) en prise, turning a won position into an equal or lost one. The cp_loss averaging ~5839 reflects that many positions go from forced mate to merely equal or worse.

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive move (capture, check, or attack) that leaves one of their own pieces undefended and en prise.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate overwhelmingly indicates the player's move left their OWN piece hanging in 93% of the top 500 activating positions, with a median hanging value of 3.0 (a minor piece). The own-hang piece class distribution (minor: 90, pawn: 84, major: 21) shows that knights and bishops are the most commonly abandoned pieces. Meanwhile, 42% of the played moves were themselves captures, and best moves include checks (10%) and captures (40%) — showing the player often had better tactical options. The best move wins material in 58% of cases (median 3.0), suggesting positions where tactical opportunities existed but the player chose a different aggressive-looking move that backfired by leaving something unguarded.
analysis.why_bad: The player makes a tempting-looking move — often a capture (Nxe5, fxe6, Qxc5, Bxg6+), a check (f5+, Nd5+), or an aggressive placement (Ne5, d4) — but in doing so either moves a piece away from defending duty or places a piece on a square where it has no protection. The opponent can then simply capture the hanging piece, gaining material. The player is distracted by the immediate tactical 'threat' they create and overlooks that their move breaks the coordination of their own pieces.

analysis.label: Player ignores a safe queen capture (usually a queen trade on a central square) and instead plays a quiet move that leaves their own major piece hanging.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows that in 94% of cases the best move is a capture (almost always a queen capturing an enemy piece with SEE=0, indicating an equal trade), while the player's move was only a capture 11% of the time. Critically, 74% of the played moves left the player's OWN piece hanging with a median value of 5.0 (queen-level), with the piece class distribution heavily weighted toward major pieces (48 major, 23 pawn, 10 minor out of 81 instances). The top boards consistently show the best move as Qxd4, Qxc6, Qxf5+, Qxe6, or Qxb2 — safe queen captures on central or key squares — while the player instead plays quiet moves like Qf3, Qh4, Be6, Bb3, or Rd1 that fatally expose their own queen or other major pieces.
analysis.why_bad: By declining the available safe queen capture (typically a queen trade on a central/open file), the player leaves their own queen or major piece undefended on its current or new square. The opponent can then simply capture the hanging piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss (average cp_loss of 1923). The quiet moves often look purposeful (checks, attacks, development) but ignore the tactical reality that the opponent's next move wins material.

analysis.label: Player misses a forced checkmate or decisive winning check in a position with an exposed enemy king, instead playing a greedy capture or quiet move.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate shows the best move wins material 74% of the time (often reflecting mating sequences scored as high-value captures), with the best move being a check 33% of the time. The enormous average cp_loss of 3110 confirms these are catastrophic oversights—frequently missed forced mates. The player's move is a capture 49% of the time, indicating distraction by grabbing material elsewhere rather than delivering the killing blow. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (7/12) with exposed kings on both sides, where the opponent's king is vulnerable to a quick mating net via checks or queen/piece coordination. The 38% own-hang rate (median value 1.0) reflects that the greedy alternative moves are also tactically careless.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the player overlooks a forced checkmate or immediately decisive check sequence (e.g., Qxb7#, Bc6+, Qc7+, Qe3+) and instead grabs a pawn or piece elsewhere, or plays a passive move. This converts a won game (often mate-in-1 to mate-in-7) into merely a large advantage or even allows counterplay, squandering the decisive tactical opportunity presented by the opponent's exposed king.

analysis.label: Player ignores a necessary capture (usually a queen trade or recapture) and plays a different move, often hanging their own material.
analysis.description: The SEE aggregate reveals that the best move is a capture in 100% of cases, yet these captures win 0 material by SEE (indicating equal trades/recaptures rather than winning hanging pieces). Only 1% register as 'winning material,' confirming these are forced exchanges, not free takes. The player's actual move was a capture only 12% of the time, meaning they almost always played a quiet alternative. As a consequence, 50% of the time the player's move left their own piece hanging (median value 3.0, distributed evenly across pawns/92, minors/82, majors/77). The feature fires on positions where the only sound continuation is to accept an exchange (overwhelmingly queen captures: Qxd8, Qxe7, Qxe3, Qxd6, Qxf4, Qxe5, Qxb1+, etc.) but the player plays something else entirely, leading to an average centipawn loss of 1063.
analysis.why_bad: When a position demands a forced capture or trade (usually a queen exchange), avoiding it typically leaves the player's position overextended or tactically vulnerable. The alternative moves ignore a concrete threat, allow the opponent to retain a dominant piece, or leave the player's own pieces undefended. The resulting positions collapse because the trade was the only way to neutralize the opponent's initiative or prevent catastrophic material loss.

analysis.label: Player missed a non-capturing quiet move (typically a queen centralization or knight attack) that would have won material through tactical threats.
analysis.description: In 90% of the top 500 activating positions, the best move wins material (median value 1 pawn), yet the best move is a capture only 9% of the time and a check 0% — meaning the winning resource is overwhelmingly a quiet positional/tactical move that creates an unstoppable threat. The played move was a capture 26% of the time (often unsound) and left the player's own piece hanging 48% of the time (median hung value 2, distributed across 64 pawns, 42 minors, and 37 majors). Across the top boards, the best moves are predominantly queen centralizations (Qd3, Qe4, Qd6, Qd4, Qe5, Qc7) or knight attacks to aggressive squares (Ng5, Neg5, Ng4) that create multi-purpose tactical threats the player entirely overlooked.
analysis.why_bad: The played moves fail because players prioritize superficially active moves — unsound sacrifices (Bxh7+), premature captures (Nxd6, dxc4), passive piece shuffles (Rfe1, Rab8), or misplaced attacks (Qb5, Qg4) — over the strongest quiet move that generates decisive threats. The correct move typically places a queen or knight on a dominant central/attacking square creating forks, pins, or unstoppable material-winning threats. Meanwhile, the played move often also hangs the player's own piece, compounding a missed opportunity into an outright blunder.
